I orignially played this game a couple of years ago on a friends Xbox and it was really frustrating because of my awful controller skills. Then I got it a couple of years back and it was just standing in my library. In the last couple of days I realised that I haven't really played a full game in a long time so I installed and started my runner journey. The tutorial was basic stuff and I really liked the mechanics and combos you can do with the walls and jumping on enemies. It felt great, the different routes you could do was quite fun, because the game didn't feel linear. Still it should've been more open, with side quests, different factions, discovering the city, helping other people or something like that, only that was lacking. But again the game was quite fun. Picking up guns was not my style, I only used the guns when there were a lot of enemies. The A.I. was quite good, it actually made me think twice before jumping on more of them, because they kill me fast. Hell, it has better A.I. then most games today. I had problems in some areas because when you jump on the red ledge it does not always work, but maybe it's just me. A couple of times I got stuck in the wall, or got slowed by an invisible bump. The enemies glich and start going bat♥♥♥♥♥♥crazy when I kick them in the ground, but that happened about 3 times in the whole game. It's quite a fast game, if you don't make any mistakes you can finish it in about 4 hours, but if you are like me it takes a bit more. Sometimes I thought I needed to backtrack when I get away from enemies and die, until I realise I just have to go forward. The story was pretty good, but it wasn't all that clear. I felt like it needed more explanation (Yeah, I know I can go on the Wiki and find everything I need to know, but that's not the point). The animations were not that bad, but not that good either. They were a bit messy, if more effort was put into them, the cutscenes would've been so much better.
Do I recommend it? Absolutely, if you like the parkour type games, you will enjoy it a lot.
How would I rate it? 9/10, it's great, but some things are still missing, I pointed it all out.
I've been playing for over a year, I recommend it to everyone.

Finished the game in about 8 hours. There are definitely some pro's a con's with this game.
First, the pro's:
- Beautiful Visuals
- Graphics stand up even today, and that is quite something for a 7 year old game
- The free running is mostly pretty good
- The voice acting is mostly good
- Has a kind of Prince of Persia feel with the figuring out where to go next aspect
Now the con's:
- At times the game mechanics do not click, such as not grabbing an edge or wall running etc. when it should
- Bad checkpoints at times, causing you to replay large portions of levels if you mess up, which can happen quite frequently
- The enemies are far too accurate with the machine guns and assault rifles. When the game is based on running, there are many points that it feels almost impossible to not use weapons yourself
- The FPS aspect when you do pick up weapons is not great, with no amunition counter and no reload feature. I understand that this was probably intentional, but when you get a uzi wiht 20 bullets and then a machine gun with unlimited ammo it is kind of annoying
- The story really wasn't that compelling, and I found a few plot holes and inconsistencies
- Drastic frame rate drops at certain points making it almost unplayable. There was a certain point I had to lower the settings to the absolute lowest they would go, and would still only get 10-12 fps during a heavy combat portion (I have a above average gaming PC and had been playing the rest of the game near the highest settings)
All in all, I would say it's worth a play. However, I would say grab it on sale. It's beautiful to look at and has a great idea behind it, but I feel it was done poorly at points and not optimized very well. I would give it a solid 6/10.

I first played this game when it first cam out on the xbox 360, and immediately fell in love. Now, years later, I've come back to it with slightly more refined tastes, and my affection for it has only increased. The gameplay is fast-paced yet smooth, and the soundtrack is beautiful. Even the much-reviled combat becomes fun once you get used to not attacking head-on, the way you do in most games. The aesthetic of the game - colorful, high-contrast, minimalist environments populated by realisticly-rendered characters - has held up strongly for the past seen years, which is more than can be said for most games. Everthing about this game feels clean and streamlined, but complex enough both pose a challenge and maintain interest in excitement.
The only two noticeable downsides are: the story, which feels as though half of it was chopped out as some point immediately before the game shipped, but doesn't really butt into the gameplay frequently enough to be an issue; and the collision detection issue when grabbing pipes, which is also not too much of an issue due to the high frequency of checkpoints.

Fantastic game. To anyone doubting it, it does take around an hour before it begins to really shine.
Upon starting the game I was reminded of every other RPG I had played and abruptly ended the game. I didn't really like how the game went into turn-based mode during battle... exit exit.
I came back to it because people insisted it was fantastic. So I gave myself an hour to see what the fuss was about. That hour followed another 57 hours over the next few weeks.
The game is beautiful and the mechanics, from the dual-choice conversation paths (as their are 2 main characters in this game, even if you don't co-op) to the rich and varied environmenal interactions during battle give this RPG a refreshing and rewarding experience to any who play it.
The places you visit are large and are overlayed with many questions (and optional quests) and you are subtly guided to complete certain tasks in order due to the difficulty of surrounding mobs. This and the fact that you aren't spoon fed answers to every quest means you must put effort in to be rewarded by the game.
Story isn't ground-breaking but the way in which it's told and how things unfold keep it interesting whilst the game mechanics keep you investigating until the early hours of the morning.

The turn based combat in this game is outstanding if you're into that kind of thing (Xcom, Shadowrun), it is most like Dragon Age if you play DA on nightmare and have to pause a lot to ensure you do the right moves, pretty challenging. There is more depth to the combat in Divinity due to the ability to mix and match different elemental spells to create some interesting combinations.
The game structure could have been your typical obtain quest and follow marker to destination gameplay, but they get rid of that in favor of a more cerebral open ended model where you have to pay attention to the quest dialog and figure out what to do. Honestly, you probably won't be able to do all there is to do in the game without some sort of guide, but to just play and do what you can and miss what you can't figure out is okay and rewarding in my opinion.
You're not locked into doing quests at all if that's not your thing. For example, I've played enough RPGs and MMOs so killing X or fetching Y quests have gotten really stale. I play Divinity like I've got a chip on my shoulder and instead of doing any quest anyone asks me to do I usually just kill them right there, and the game is totally fine with this and it could potentially lead to opportunities and items I wouldn't have had otherwise.
Those are the two strong points of Divinity: combat and openess. The story is probably its weakest point, but it still isn't bad; it just isn't up to the level of some other games of this type. Some people will enjoy it due to it not taking itself that serious, but I prefer more serious stories and dialogue. Keep in mind the game is not fully voiced so you'll have to read quite a bit throughout.
The game has a scenario toolkit so I'm sure we'll be seeing some nice additions in the future, some that are better than the base game even so that's always a plus.
I recommend the game to any RPG gamer that doesn't mind a lot of turn based combat. Over 80% of your time will likely be spent fighting with about 10% inventory/skill management and the other 10% exploring and reading the dialogue.

Nail'd is a fun game, and I really like it. but just for short bursts.
- it's all about dat racing (there are a few challenges and modifiers throughout tournament mode, but nothing that changes your core objective, to be 1st place)

> catch EXTREME AIR
> have a lot of boost/nitro capacity
> you can kinda run other racers off the road so they crash into stuff & that's kinda awesome
So as you can tell, I'm kind of divided on this game. Personally, I wish there was more variety to the game, like with different modes (combat-based, mini-games, et cetera) or perhaps a free-roam mode (what can I say, I loved FUEL). But that said, the core game in Nail'd is still strong and fun for what it is.
If I had to pick: It is a NO for me at regular price. And a CAUTIOUS YES for me IF IT'S ON SALE (for 1 dollar or less). If you enjoy puzzle platformers and prefer exploration vs. being hand-fed what to do through immersion-breaking tutorials, you will love Toki Tori 2+.
The game is remarkably charming and cute, with nice aesthetics and relaxing music.
When you first load the game, you will immediately be dropped into actual gameplay as a baby chick bird - with no tutorials of any sort. There was a part right in the beginning where I had to actually check the control layout, however, I was okay with this because there are very few controls to begin with. After continuing, the title "Toki Tori 2+" rises up as you make your way to the other side of the map. I found that to be a very refreshing intro to a game.
The learning curve for this game is very minimal, as the puzzles do a great job of progressing in difficulty at a reasonable pace - you will always be aware of what mechanic you need to be using by the time you get to the more difficult variations. Trial and error is also convenient because of the very few controls you have at your disposal.
You can't jump in the game, however, you can stomp or sing - and either action usually has an effect on your environment. For example, frogs will orient themselves toward you if you sing, and (if they eat a small animal) they will release a bubble if you stomp. If you are hit by the frog's bubble, it will carry you up and either to the left or right (depending on the frog's orientation) until a short distance has passed or until you stomp. In order to help feed the frog (sometimes its food is not on the same plane), you need to stomp when the prey is near the edge of a ledge, which will cause it to fall to a lower level.
Later, you will unlock special notes that you can sing in order to activate abilities like "rewind" (I was not expecting a mechanic like this and was pleasantly suprised). You can manipulate your singing by changing the timing of your spacebar presses, and using rewind will return you to a previous checkpoint you have activated (gold totem-like objects).
The game map is fairly extensive, with many forks in the road to keep you engaged and challenged. There are also gold puzzle pieces and other things for you to collect.
Highly recommend for puzzle platform enthusiasts.

Toki Tori 2 is the exploration of a metroidvania distilled down into pure joy.  Instead of being a pure puzzler like the first game, #2's challenge lies in learning how things interact, and then using that knowledge to keep moving forward.

I expected a simple timewaster and I got a very solid metroidvania.

Everquest is a game unlike any other that I have played.  I've tried WoW and almost all of its clones.  I have played multiplayer Minecraft, persistent worlds in Neverwinter Nights, Path of Exile, Dungeons & Dragons: Eberron Unleashed, and a cartload of other multiplayer or MMO games, and nothing keeps my interest or brings me back once I've left, the way Everquest does.
Yes, it is 'ugly' compared to new games, but it runs on a game engine built in the early-mid 90's.  Yes, at 17 years old the developers have other games they are putting more effort into, can you blame them?  The code for the base game is so outdated that it's hard to keep adding content without causing one problem or another.  Yes, the playerbase has diminished due to graphics, cost of expansions, and the interactions with many of the more vocal players.
Most of the people I enjoy the game with are not vocal in general chat channels due to the outspoken negative personalities that dominate them.  I appreciate the quiet players that have bothered to learn their class, or are trying a new class and actively seeking feedback on how to play it better.  It can take weeks, sometimes months, to find a really solid group that you truly enjoy spending time with.  Most modern players lack the patience or social graces to "put up with" that time investment, because other MMO's are designed to reward them immediately.  Designed to keep pushing them to new things, new things, higher numbers, more new things, and they don't have to actually grind for their objectives.
I see some people complain about the content difference between current expansions and old expansions, but you do have to realize that the developers don't have to spend any time on this old game and people will still play it.  This isn't their flagship game and will not receive the majority of their attention, so the level of time and detail they do invest in keeping it running is amazing to me.  I do believe they could salvage it completely if they rebuilt Everquest with a few design tweaks in a modern engine, but kept the atmosphere and content mostly identical.

Have played Everquest since Beta testing it 17 years ago and I still come back to every once in a while.  It's worth playing for anyone who is an MMORPG fan, if only just to see where the modern formula truly started.  It probably takes a bit of adjusting for modern MMO players, though you might be surprised how much you enjoy it.  There simply is 17 years of content that you can experience at your own pace.  Open world free-roaming games are becoming popular now and Everquest will appeal to those players somewhat.
WoW and EQ2 (launched the same month) both started the quest grinding pattern in MMOs (one of the few deviations from the EQ formula).  EQ has the original kill grind method.  In a lot of ways I like the kill grinding pattern better, until Old Republic quest grinding was novel for the first handful of hours but it becomes just as tedious as kill grinding.  Kill grinding on the other hand is much more straightforward... you kill things and you get exp.  This frees up quests to be more meaningful than level grinding, they are actually lore centered and/or item/reward centered for the most part (minus daily tasks etc).
This is where it all really started, it's worth playing just to experience a bit of MMORPG history... well and you might find a couple decades later it was worth it too.

Magnetic by Nature is a fun physics based puzzle game that has a good difficulty curve (until the 5th zone) and it’s very easy to pick up for a few minutes at a time to complete a level here and there. I found myself doing the “just one more level” talk more than once! This looks to be a port from a console or mobile platform, hence the short levels.
I find this game similar to “Defy Gravity” in that you can either repel or attract yourself to applicable parts/objects of the level to complete it. There is a very simple story of you waking up your robot friends by completing all the levels within them. Teaching of the game mechanics is done very well. It eases you into new concepts and obstacles. A quick tip may appear but the rest is on the player to discover how it works and improve from there.
The first 4 zones range from easy to intermediate. I never felt like I couldn’t do a level and some required a good amount of thinking for a solution. The fifth zone, which is unlocked after you beat the other 4, is very difficult. I could only beat a handful of levels and ended up calling it quits at that point.
I did glitch more than once and got stuck in a freefall animation while being on the ground. This forced me to restart the level. Luckily the levels are short so there’s not much frustration had.
+Buttery smooth 60fps
+Scaled to 1440p nicely
+Nice colorful visuals
+Great learning curve and teaching of mechanics
+Fun short levels
+I actually wanted to collect the collectables
+Pressing “Y” to retry a level on my Xbox controller didn’t work
+Got stuck in a freefall while on the ground more than once
+Majority of the achievements are speedrun related
+Controls could be tighter and more responsive (personal preference)
While the $9.99 price seems high, it’s definitely a fun puzzle game to pick up if you enjoy the genre. I’d absolutely recommend it in a bundle or when on sale.

Magnetic By Nature isn't a terrible game; on the contrary, it's a somewhat fresh and original platformer! Unfortunately, the pacing and level design, coupled with some bugs and horrible interface made the game boring to me. It was simply not fun, and that's the only reason I'm not recommending.
Again, it's not bad, and you may very well get some enjoyment out of it, if you enjoy platformers! It's rather easy, with most levels being completed in less than 3 restarts, a couple of more difficult ones not passing 15. And I'm not that good at platformers.
I'll just briefly explain each aspect I did (or not) enjoy.
The gameplay revolves around magnets, as the name suggests. You can be attracted or repeled (and attract and repel some objects). It's unique, as far as I know, and it did provide some interesting sections.
The level design, however, lacks a lot of pacing and progression. It seems like just a bunch of random level thrown together. The first two worlds introduced mechanics; that last 3 didn't.
If you look at Super Meat Boy, there's clearly a lot of thought into teaching the player how to overcome certain obstacles that are recurring in later level, in a harder form.
In this game, levels are very, very gimmicky. It's about a quirky feature of the physics system that helps you complete the level, but not really a challenge. And all of the levels are like that, for the most part. There isn't an obstacle that you have to learn, really. It's just... a bunch of levels. And for me, that wasn't fun at all, it just felt like a drag.
The controls are a bit floaty, which I didn't like very much.
Then, there's how levels work: there's a collectible in every level. Some are really easy to get and go well with the level. Others are just completely out of the way. Meh, it can provide a bit more challenge, but I don't feel like it added a whole lot.
The bugs include getting stuck (in mid air, for some reason), leaderboards not seeming to work, levels completed not tracking properly, sometimes, etc.
The getting stuck one was particularly annoying, as it happened several times, for no reason.
The game encourages speedruns, looking at the achievements. That would be really cool! ... If the leaderboards worked. I've never been able to see how other players did in their levels. Which kind of defeats the point. The game wasn't very interesting for me to speedrun it either.
What I mean by horrible interface is how cluttered it is when explaining very simple controls, and how unresponsive and inflexible the menus are.
For example, there's no level selection. What you can do is go to the Hub (always resetting your position to your starting point) lose some seconds (or minute) traversing to the world you want, and then select a level. But, if you're in a level already, you NEED to go abck to the Hub to select another one. And it's a waste of time! When you finish a level, you only have two options: restart, or go to the next level. Nothing else.
There are other problems I could mention, but it's not worth it.
Again, even though my review was very negative, it's not a terrible game. Read other reviews: people seem to like, and that's cool! I'm just writing about my experience with it. Some of the levels were fun, but most were completely forgettable and not challenging.
The other individual aspects are great! The artstyle (although I have some reservations) was pretty good, the soundtrack was very good as well, and used properly, keeping you in the flow of the game.
I just didn't have any fun, by end.

*Note: I played the eLicence version of this game for many hours; the Steam time was just to remind me of the following points*
TEW 2010 is an excellent framework for fantasy booking. It is highly moddable (with a dedicated fanbase which take full advantage of that) and allows a lot of room for imagination. As a game, it's deeply flawed.
The interface is poor, with far too much clicking required to see key information. So much time is wasted finding angles even with the default database, let alone mods which tend to flood the game with them. Want to use the same location for every show? There's no default; you'll have to select it every single time.
Booking is a downright chore. You'll tend to use the same booking notes for most matches, and having to add them match after match, show after show, becomes painfully repetitive. The interface's limitation is exposed all too clearly in this mode - you can't even click and drag to re-order matches, you have to use arrow buttons.
Feedback is limited - you can enable a feature which at least gives some points which affected the rating, but some segments still inexplicably bomb.
Perhaps the biggest structural flaw is the Overness system, which underpins everything in the game. For such a crucial feature, it is woefully simplistic. When a winner has even a little less overness than the loser, that winner will often cannibalise some of their overness.
This has three obvious problems:
1) It ignores everything else. Did the loser get attacked a dozen times by the winner's allies during the match? Did the winner cheat? Was the ref biased? Was it a little show attended by a few hundred people rather than a televised show in the region? It's all ignored.
2) It's easily exploited. Sign a popular wrestler on a short-term deal or, more ridiculously, bring in another promotion's top wrestlers on a talent trade, and just feed them to your up-and-comers for the sort of boost which would take you months of careful booking.
3) It makes playing as a company like TNA (particularly 2006-2012) ridiculous. The likes of Sting and Kurt Angle must have significantly more overness than AJ Styles or Samoa Joe, since it represents their name value. Dare to book them to lose to people like Styles and Joe, and they will argue against it (or outright refuse if they have creative control), and will have their overness cannibalised every match.
It's a nonsensical system, and it underpins the game.
The other flaw is that worker generation and development is broken. The game world simply breaks down over time, as new workers do not develop performance skills - and thus cannot put on good-quality matches.
It is a well-known problem - see the large thread on the official forums
It was never fixed in this game. While the 2013 version finally fixes this, it is not available on Steam and has its own issues - while 2010 has some relatively readily accessible information, such as an exportable roster, a roster overview screen which lets you sort wrestlers by skill and a neat summary of their abilities at the bottom of the profile, 2013 removes all of this for a fog of war system. Even with fog of war turned off, these helpful features are gone.
If you have a lot of imagination and want to write a diary of your experiences, this is a great option for you. There's a lot of potential in the game as an infrastructure for fantasy booking - you can go back into the world of the Monday Night Wars, or the territory days, or even relatively modern times (though modern mods have dried up, given the age of the game).
If you want to play this as a strategic sports management game, though, you may be disappointed. It is too unintuitive, too easily exploited, too clunky to stand alongside others in the genre. Its real advantage here is its lack of competition - if you want a wrestling booking sim, this is pretty much your only option. Still, unless you're dead-set on a wrestling game, the same dev's World of Mixed Martial Arts series is a better option for people more interested in sports management than fantasy booking.

The original Mirrors edge still holds up in its free running parkuor gameplay. At less than $15, It should be a satisfying game to pickup, but i would not recommend it at any higher price.
Despite owning the game for many years(steam sales :P) due to its reputation of being a cult classic. I have only recently put in the time to finish the game. Mostly so that when i play the latest release, i would know how they improved on the original.
Pros
+ When the game finds its rhythm, it can very satisfying running across the urban landscape.
+ The minimalist visuals provide a very clean look to the game, and to an extent even help to hide its age.
+ The Soundtrack is very chill, if your the kind of person who enjoys that sort of music/beat.
Neutral
= The game can be finished in one sitting, I personally like having a complete experience without having to invest a lot of time into a video game, but I acknowledge that personal preferences may vary. For a game like Mirrors edge I personally prefer the shorter game.
= You can get lost in the environment sometimes, but thankfully pressing the Alt key can face you in the general direction of where to go. This is not a perfect solution, but a passable one.
= For the most part, I think they did a decent job with the controls. I had some trouble grappling with them in general but manged to get the hang of it, but this may become a larger issue for some people.
Cons
- The game frequently breaks its own rhythm by either forcing you fight enemies, perform slow vertical climbing sections, respawn at poorly placed checkpoints,or stop and solve navigation puzzles to figure out how to proceed to the next area. While the gameplay for these sections is not bad in their own regard, they mostly only accomplish to distract you form the games core strengths of free running parkour gameplay.
- The combat was unnecessary for the game, while the melee attacks that can be performed have some impact behind them and it can be oddly satisfying performing a quick 1,2 punch to quickly dispatch an enemy directly infront of you, so that you can quickly get past. The gun play should not have been added. Latter enemies who are capable of chasing after you, keep you at a good pace, the other enemies should have served a similar purpose, instead they try to riddle you with bullet holes.
- The story is fairly irrelevant, only serving to string together the levels. I do count it as a negative though considering all the meaningless cut scenes i had to sit though. Thankfully you can skip them.
In summary, I think Mirrors Edge was a somewhat flawed execution of a very cool concept. I can understand why it took so many years for this game to get a sequel. Taken as is the game has a lot of rough edges. Even in my own review it should highlight the fact that I had so much more to say about the games negatives than I did its more positive aspects.
This is because the game offers a very plain appeal, where free running parkour combined with clean visuals, and a chill soundtrack results in a very nice experience. Adding unnecessary elements like a story, gun combat, and slow paced vertical climbing or navigation puzzles only served to detract from that nice experience. As a result the game ended up more tedious and boring than it ever should of been.
All the being said, it still gets a recommendation from me which should go a long way to telling you how fun this game can be during those moments when it manages to get everything just right, with no distractions.

According to Steam, I have 19.2 hours on record for this game and I have to say I'm loving every bit of it.  Crate has done a fantastic job with this game, crafting a truly unique and memorable RPG.
So far, I feel that the main storyline and sidequests are quite engaging, there is plenty of variety of enemies and environments, and a vast array of weapons, equipment, and enhancements.  Character-building is very satisfying with many choices in the skill trees of the six masteries, including the ability to multi-class.  Character progression seems fair and balanced and, while I generally enjoy farming for XP and loot, I've found that there is plenty just by thoroughly exploring the map - I have not had to do any dedicated grinding to find decent items and gain enough experience to continue through the game.  There have been a few challenging battles while not being frustratingly difficult and there are always rewards to match the difficulty of an enemy.  Overall, I feel that Grim Dawn is a fantastic action RPG and well worth the $25 price tag.
I have found a couple of minor negatives though.  Even after 19 hours, I still feel like the movement control is a bit strange, especially in that the character can be a little slow to respond to mouse clicks.  I also have a bit of an issue with money.  Common items are worth almost nothing and even magic items are worth very little meaning you can fill your inventory many times and still not have enough iron to buy anything.  Nearly all of the worthwhile items at vendors are vastly out of range in price and, when you do manage to buy something, the resale value is virtually nothing.  Finally, my biggest complaint about the game is the music.  I generally find the soundtrack to be quite bad - very often slow and somber, even downright depressing.  I would prefer for the music to convey a sense of adventure commernsurate with other aspects of the game.
Music aside, the sound effects are really good.  Graphically, the game is absolutely beautiful.  I don't have a good enough graphics card for high settings yet it still looks fantastic.  The game runs well on my modest machine - I've not had any freezes, crashes, or other glitchy behavior.  Loading seems a bit slow but that's probably dependent on my computer, not an issue of the game itself.  Even though it's technically still in Early Access, the game seems fully polished and I have not noticed any evidence of it not being a complete, ready-for-retail game.
Overall, this is an excellent game and is well worth the asking price.  I highly recommend Grim Dawn to any fan of action RPGs.

This is essentially a much deeper version of the old-school wrestling management sims. You play the role of the 'booker' that needs to construct the flow of the pro wrestling show. This is the core of the game: decide who opens your show, what the storylines are and who to push. You can add notes on who should take bumps, who needs to look strong or which match needs to be scripted beforehand. You can shape your product (WWEntertainment, the modern TNA in its beginning years, traditional old-school family entertainment, hardcore, Puroresu, etc). The financial aspect is very significant as well. The game requires thought at all times. If you book a WWE-style you need to have a plan or you'll get bested by the competition. Talent development is very important, and so is keeping the locker room healthy by managing conflict situations. Besides that, there's more to do such as managing TV and PPV deals, scouting, etc.
The game comes with a surprisingly wellmade fictional universe, but the community mods offer several historic real-world settings. Just the chance to rebook the Invasion angle sold me on this. If anything, get it to understand the position of WWE nowadays. If you are a Cena hater, try playing as E and see if you'd truly discard him. You'll find it's not easy to do. :)
It's true that there's a newer version out there for only 5$ more, but beginners might want to start with this one as the difficulty curve is lessened. There's a demo to help you decide. Most of the 100+ hours spend on this series was with the older TEW07, which is simpler and therefore more fun to start out with.
The game is a dry manager sim so not much action of a graphic nature. You don't get to see the matches, or even get notes on what happened. Feedback is given in the shape of a grade to show how good the match was. There's also no full screen mode. If you don't mind this I'm sure you'll have a lot of fun with the game. Just keep in mind it requires some work to get inducted into the game. This is no game to take lightly.

Did I enjoy my experience with The Banner Saga? My initial response would have been yes, however as I was playing I could only feel that my attitude towards this game shifted from enjoyment to something closer to hatred.
What this game does good, it does really well. The artwork is spectacular, and I don't think anyone would argue with that. The world that was created has a great amount of lore, and an interesting one at that. I felt that playing different point of views throughout the game was quite interesting, even if I would have prefered to have more than three characters to play as (and you only play the first one for a few moments). Also, the music is really good, I don't think anyone can disagree with that. So overall, that made me love the game. At first.
And there comes the main problem, which a lot of other reviews talked about, the combat system. Before addressing the con of the system, I would like to point out that I thought combining strenght and health was a fun thing, it made the system more unique and interesting. Sure, if you get damaged a lot, your character gets almost useless in battle, but then again it's just because you planned your strategy in a wrong way. Managing armor and strenght was not the aspect of the combat that♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off, althought I would understand if some people didn't like the idea. The real problem is the whole turn-based system. Let me explain: You and your ennemy alternate turns, and you do that in a very strict sense, meaning that every time you do an action, your ennemy comes next (except if there is only one of them left, but I won't address that point). Now, this seems okay at first, but you soon realise that it's an insane design decision. If you have five warriors, and your ennemy has only two, he still plays every time after you do. That means that, if he has a very powerful unit, this unit will move more often than if he actually had one more weaker unit. I cannot even understand the reason why this was deemed a good idea, it doesn't add to the strategy at all, it feels more like a major oversight in the game design. I often found myself not killing unit at one hp just so the super powerful guy couldn't move sooner. At first it didn't bother me at all, but as the game progress I soon began to hate this whole turn system, and the game.
Another thing that I find bizarre about the combat is that you choose your turn order before even knowing what you are going to fight. This didn't bother me as much as the other point, but I still think that it would be better to see the board before planning turn order.
I should also point out something about the save system. There isn't one. You cannot save your game, it does so automatically. The game does that so that your choices matter (meaning it prevents you from loading a save game until you get the «good choice»). I didn't mind that, but I think it's worth pointing out since not everyone would be okay with that.
Now, I mentionned choices right above. The choice system is... not that good. I felt more like I played some kind of russian roulette game than making a decision, since really there is no way to know what is the good choice to make. I guess it is made so just so you can make the choices you would in real life, meaning that in real life you don't really know every consequences of your choices, if that's the case then I'd say it's pretty good. Because there is really no way to guess what can be the consequences of your actions, most of the time. I'd also like to point out that the choices during the dialogs didn't seem to matter. I remember two instances in which I happened to have a saved game right before a dialog with multiple choices, just to realise that really, nothing mattered. One of those instances, I had several instances where I had four options of answers, and whatever I chose, one of my characters would just end up dying.
I won't go in details about the whole caravan gameplay (outside of combat), I will just say that nothing really happens. Just manage your supplies and your morale, that's about it. Sometimes events will pop-up, otherwise just sit back and wait.
I will however say that the whole war thing has a system I don't really understand. You are always given several choices when facing a war situation, but I found out that if I choose "Oversee", I would end up dying every time. I don't know if someone actually made it work, but I couldn't every time I tried. Also, you only really need two choices for the whole game: Eitheir Charge or Formations, and I found out that Formations always worked the best. Every time. So, I found out that something was lacking there.
The story in itself it obviously incomplete, since this game is only the first chapter of a series (which  I didn't know until I actually finished the game). The main problem with this in The Banner Saga is that the story gets interesting, but never delivers, because it ends way too prematurely. So, if you want answers, you won't get them here. Nevertheless, I found the setting interesting, enough to make me want to play the next game.
I'd really like to recommend The Banner Saga, but after playing it completely, I cannot. I did have some enjoyment out of it, but the glaring problem in the combat (the switching turns) was enough to almost completely ruin it for me. I know it is a design decision, and some people would argue that "I should make my own game and show I can do better", but really now, I  cannot even fathom how someone can defend such a decision. I don't make game, but I played a lot of them, and I really cannot comprehend how making the ennemy act more as he lose units was even kept in the final game.
That being said, the story, the music and the art were really great. So, if you think you can ignore the problem I mentionned about the battle system, go ahead. But I don't think it's worth $20.

I had heard a lot about the Banner Saga, or rather, heard the title being mentioned a lot by people but I had never gone out of my way to purchase it, as most of my gaming time in recent years has been in the mmo market.  However the Steam Summer Sale offered it at a good price, and so it ended up as a impulse buy and in my library.
The game itself is a story-based game, which are rather rare these days outside of the foreign market as the UK and US game consumers tend to spend more money on action games or mmos than heavy story content. The closest we came to that sort of thing has really been the Bioware games like the Dragon Age and Mass Effect franchises.
The Banner Saga is a mix of Storytelling and strategy turn-based combat and took me around 11-12 hours to complete on normal difficulty.  While this seems short for a game, the Banner Saga actually has a great deal of replayability due to the story-based structure. Since the different story choices you make during the game will affect how the story goes, and thus you are going to get a different playing experience during future play.  There are also a lot of steam achievements to hunt for.  I personally will be playing it again several times.
Game Pacing
In terms of the game pacing, it is fairly slow.  Many times, especially initially when less random events happened, you are just watching them pace across the screen for days, slowly eating up your resources.  This is not a game to play if you are in the mood for lots of action.  It tilts between challenging combat and a lot of watching.
Actually there is less combat in the game than I initially expected.  I expected there to be far more combat in the game, but if I were to guess you spend maybe 1/3 of the game in combat while the 2/3 is storytelling.  This combat time can be decreased a little more with story choices, or increased depending on choices, potentially quite a bit more.  It did surprise me though.
Combat
The combat itself is challenging, and while they give a little bit of a tutorial at the beginning, I actually spent quite a bit of the game working out specifics of it.  I actually don't mind this too much since I plan on replaying the game several times, and perhaps I just didn't pay enough attention to the tutorial or help text.  It is possible.
I have heard that some people have found the combat in The Banner Saga to be really difficult, but I did not find this myself while playing on Normal difficulty.  I think that players used to playing strategy games will not have a difficulty with it, but I expect players that are not coming from playing other strategy games may find the combat more challenging and should play it on a less difficult setting until they learn during their first play-through.  You can change the combat difficulty during the game, so don't feel ashamed to put it down a notch if you are struggling.
User Interface
Overall the user interface is pretty well designed for what it needs to do.  It is simple and pretty straight forward.  It could do with a couple of tweaks though such as having hovering tooltips on the stat choices rather than having to click the help button just to see what each of them mean.
Another thing that I overlooked early in the game was the market sellers full stock.  I was merely looking at them for the character items they hold, but they actually sell supplies to.  Perhaps I was too tired when I started playing, so I didn't notice this till 2/3 into the game and struggling for food.  Those tooltip tutorials would have been super useful to highlight important things like this.
I also found the map a particularly underutilized resource.  There really is no real reason to use it.  It has interesting facts on the different places, but there isn't even a trail to show where your group has been on the saga or where they hope to go to.  Things like that should really have been added, because right now, I found there to be zero reason for me to actually care much about what the text on the map showed or how it related to my own quest.
Three games
One thing players should note is that this is the first of (I believe) three games that make up the entire saga.  While this game has a satisfying ending, many players will be like 'wait, what about 'x' or 'y'.  That was never finished'.  One criticism on this account was that the writers/designers did not make it clear that this was not a full story, but one complete story within three.  While most of the story parts do come to a good conclusion and are satisfying, there are many pieces yet to be told, and players should be aware of this.
Many players may feel that a game of this cost should have a full story arc, rather than having some pieces untold as of yet, but I believe it was generally the lack of clarity on this at the purchase that has garnered the most criticism, rather than the fact that the game is the first part of three.
The cost itself is likely indicative of the time it actually takes of making a choice-based system, as the longer the story gets, the more the writers have to put in for all those characters and choices.
Conclusion
Overall I feel that the game is one that I was happy to purchase and I enjoyed playing it a lot.  It is fairly short and pacing is a bit slow at times, but I will be happy to replay it several times for the story and achievements.  £19 at full price for a replayable game is a fair price, but obviously better if you can get it in a sale.  I am looking forward to the future instalments of the Saga.

Customisation of my vehicle and character came as an afterthought because if you're not actively seeking this feature out, there's not much reason to tinker with it. The performance of the stock vehicle seemed fine for me.

Oh lord, this will get downvoted like crazy but I have to be honest and adress the emperor's new clothes.
Half-Life was a milestone in first person shooters that changed the entire genre for better or worse. Everyone who was around back then can tell you how monumental it felt. It was incredibly well-made, balanced, though linear always gave you the feeling of actually exploring the levels, which in a sense disappeared altogether because the whole game felt unbroken from beginning to end, despite the technical limitations of late-nineties PCs that wouldn't allow entire games streamed without load times. The platforming was a nuisance but everything else aged incredibly well and is still worth checking out. I'm more partial to the jedi knight series and the first Unreal but there's no denying Half-Life's status in the gaming world.
With Half-Life 2 I was just never sure what the fuss was all about. Few games deserve universal acclaim and journalists are quick to jump on the bandwagon. Just try to find a review of Final Fantasy VII from back in the day that doesn't praise every aspect frantically for example. There are games  I don't like but get the appeal of but from day one I found Half-Life 2 to be mediocre and despite several attempts over the years I've yet to complete it. You're on a painfully linear progression from beginning to end. Tunnels connecting stationary shootouts like pearls on a string. There's no fun gunplay in the shootouts and there's no interesting discovery connecting them. Back in an era when gaming quickly moved into character-driven open-world and semi open-world territory (mostly on consoles though with the exception of beyond good & evil) this approach to set-piece focused gamedesign felt really outdated. When gaming embraced deeper characterization and atmosphere, a sense of discovery and adventure you're stuck with a mute protagonist shooting anonymous faceless enemies in a gaming world that feels controlled and lifeless. Physics engines were new back then but there's only so many times you can wow me with a physics puzzle that feels like incredible machine for dummies.
Half-Life 2 isn't horrible, I don't engage in hyperbole, but I find it still as unremarkable now as back then when it was brand-new and I can't for the life of me understand why it gets so much praise. Praise the first one, praise Deus Ex, all of them more worthy. Even Half-Life 2's peer Doom3 aged better and it was mocked mercilessly for its dodgy design decisions. Given the same close scrutiny as other titles Half-Life 2 just falls apart.

If you've had no experience with simulators like Footbal Manager or OOTP Baseball, then be very cautious before purchasing.  You might be dissapointed. The Banner Saga has some beautiful art and scenery. It's fairly reminiscent of early Disney cartoons (think Snow White-styled character animation). As for the game itself, the story is excellent, but rather unforgiving at some points. I found audibly saying things along the lines of "What? No. STOP! NO WHY!" So yes, there are some difficult choices to makes, and even ones that are seemingly easy may wind up coming back up later with serious consequences.
As far as gameplay mechanics, think Oregon Trail while your caravan is travelling, in the sense that you see it traversing a long road with occasional stops with choices to make, supplies to oversee, and morale of your people to consider.
In terms of combat, it is decently straight-forward turn-based grid-style combat. A popular game to compare it to would be Final Fantasy Tactics, if you need an anchor to compare to.
Having said all that -- once you actually get a good pace going, this game ends rather quickly, and it's no fairy tale ending... I won't spoil anything, though.
TL;DR
Pros:
Gorgeous character design and animation
Immersive story and character relationships
You don't get spoon-fed an easy adventure -- you'll lose people, get betrayed, etc.
Combat is easy enough to understand and get the hang of quickly
Cons:
I would've preferred a longer adventure
Left almost a bad taste in my mouth after all was said and done, moreso just because I cared about the characters and the journey, and you'd probably have to see the ending to fully understand
Again, it doesn't spoon-feed you (this is a pro for me, but I can see how it could be a con for others)
Final word:
Personally, if I could do it again, I'd have waited until this game was on sale, purely because I don't like paying full-price for games that end up being shorter than expected, and I weigh my purchases heavily on dollars spent vs. time spend playing. This is an otherwise beautiful and recommended title.

I love tactical fighting games, I was looking forward to The Banner Saga for months, having seen the preliminary art and understanding the scope of Norse myth. Now that I've finished it I'm ready to tell what I think...
So first of all the combat is pretty good. Not to heavy on enemies all scrambling to target one of your characters at once, and your characters don't die in combat if they go to zero health. The turns are a little roughly designed though, as the AI forces each side to alternate active characters, so that when the enemy is down to their last few characters they are getting multiple actions each turn. Some PC's special abilities are practically useless most of the time, and the level cap is 5, so things don't change a whole lot in terms of getting powerful actions or spell effects.
One of the great things is the random events that force you to make decisions. They are 90% text based without combat, and can grant you small bonuses or cause you to loose food or warriors. Some of the events though don't really come back to impact the game as much as they should though.
As for the story, it's pretty good. It's compelling enough to be pulled in for a few hours at a time, but in the end it falls apart fast. That is my biggest complaint actually: This isn't a full game, it's just chapter 1. Sure it could be said that the end was all that was intended, but it certainly didn't feel that it was building toward an end, and more or less, it just sort of happened. Also, since characters don't really die in combat, when they die in cutscenes after combat, it feels a little unfair. Like you easily won the battle but suddenly you find that your character was instead killed by some lurking enemy you couldn't see or fight.
So really, it's a good game, it's worth playing, but in the end it feels a little sore that it wasn't polished a bit more.

According to Steam, I have 19.2 hours on record for this game and I have to say I'm loving every bit of it.  Crate has done a fantastic job with this game, crafting a truly unique and memorable RPG.
So far, I feel that the main storyline and sidequests are quite engaging, there is plenty of variety of enemies and environments, and a vast array of weapons, equipment, and enhancements.  Character-building is very satisfying with many choices in the skill trees of the six masteries, including the ability to multi-class.  Character progression seems fair and balanced and, while I generally enjoy farming for XP and loot, I've found that there is plenty just by thoroughly exploring the map - I have not had to do any dedicated grinding to find decent items and gain enough experience to continue through the game.  There have been a few challenging battles while not being frustratingly difficult and there are always rewards to match the difficulty of an enemy.  Overall, I feel that Grim Dawn is a fantastic action RPG and well worth the $25 price tag.
I have found a couple of minor negatives though.  Even after 19 hours, I still feel like the movement control is a bit strange, especially in that the character can be a little slow to respond to mouse clicks.  I also have a bit of an issue with money.  Common items are worth almost nothing and even magic items are worth very little meaning you can fill your inventory many times and still not have enough iron to buy anything.  Nearly all of the worthwhile items at vendors are vastly out of range in price and, when you do manage to buy something, the resale value is virtually nothing.  Finally, my biggest complaint about the game is the music.  I generally find the soundtrack to be quite bad - very often slow and somber, even downright depressing.  I would prefer for the music to convey a sense of adventure commernsurate with other aspects of the game.
Music aside, the sound effects are really good.  Graphically, the game is absolutely beautiful.  I don't have a good enough graphics card for high settings yet it still looks fantastic.  The game runs well on my modest machine - I've not had any freezes, crashes, or other glitchy behavior.  Loading seems a bit slow but that's probably dependent on my computer, not an issue of the game itself.  Even though it's technically still in Early Access, the game seems fully polished and I have not noticed any evidence of it not being a complete, ready-for-retail game.
Overall, this is an excellent game and is well worth the asking price.  I highly recommend Grim Dawn to any fan of action RPGs.

There are little spinning things to collect, but I didn't find a use for them and there wasn't a counter to tell me how many I had or if I'd gotten all of them from the level I'd finished. X-COM on its own is an intense, tight gaming experience. You can play it as light or as heavy as you want. For example, turning on "ironman" mode means you cannot take back moves. When your soldiers get shot and killed, they're gone. Can you handle that as a player? Many cannot. This game will dig into your soul, if you let it.
But three words spring to mind - Long War Mod. If you buy this game, I highly (!!!) recommend acquiring the Long War Mod. It opens the door to 8 different soldier classes (instead of the conventional 4), larger starting squads (6 instead of 4, up to 8 with the officer school), and a whole ton more for a far more in-depth gaming experience.
It's a hard-slogging, at times very slow and repetitive, ongoing battle against a nasty opposition. Not for the faint of heart. Excellent for veteran players who like to strategize while getting stomped.

The Good: Great production values, graphics look great, uses lesser told stories during the war
The Bad: Typical multiplayer, not very cinematic, objectives are repetitive and boring, highly linear, no gore, nothing new at all
All those World War II shooters we endured for an entire decade felt like a war on its own. Shooter after endless shooter bombarded our systems, and then there were the really bad ones in between the Call of Duty and Medal of Honor yearly releases. Call of Duty 2 was highly anticipated because it was the actual sequel to the award winning original. Does it stand out like the first game did? Is it full of cinematic finesse and finely nuanced mechanics? Not really.
There’s not much of a story here because it’s based off WWII. Black and white footage with a dull narrator telling you about different theaters of the war, then there’s the typical journal entry during the load screen, nothing interesting at all, and even when the game came out I was sick of these WWII shooters. What does Call of Duty 2 build on? Nothing, it’s just more of the same, but at least it has high production values and it does the same stuff right. The game has you following three different soldiers from the Russian, British, and American side. One thing I did like was that you get to play a different side of the Normandy beach storming and that’s the Rangers. They climbed up the cliff side trying to shut down the German pill boxes and various artillery so our troops stopped getting slaughtered on the beachhead. Call of Duty 2 tries to tell the smaller stories in the war which is a nice change of pace.
The same weapons are here that you have shot a million times. Lee Enfield, M1 Garand, Mp40, MP44, Sten, and various others. Of course not ALL WWII weapons are here, but I wanted to see some of the more obscure ones like the Browning or BAR. At this point in time it was just about better graphics and who’s weapon textures looked the most realistic. Call of Duty 2 delivers on the visuals and was a benchmarker much like Crysis is now back in 2005/2006. It was one of the first game to support SLI and really pushed PCs and made you get those $500 graphics cards. It was a must have for PC owners, and was also a GPU seller. With that aside, the textures look great even today and the visuals really pop. The sound is great as well with gunfire chattering in the distance and soldiers yelling all around you. It may seem dated today, but you can really see how much the Call of Duty series hasn’t evolved. There’s striking similarities to the Modern Warfare series because it’s all the same, shoot anything that moves.
The game can be pretty easy at times, I could just rush into a building and blow everyone away with one clip and survive. I still find it painful to know that grenade physics are still really bad and bounce around like rubber balls. There are various things I just really can’t stand about these shooters and that’s the lack of realism. When I shoot enemies blood doesn’t even come out, where’s the gore and violence? Brothers in Arms was the first WWII shooter to use this violence in the genre, but Call of Duty just feels like some sort of censored theme park ride.
CoD2 had a huge multiplayer following, but sadly no one’s online anymore. Even so, it’s just a typical online shooter and isn’t anything special. I was really disappointed to find that CoD2 wasn’t as cinematic as it could have been and just felt the same throughout the whole game. Blow up this door, defend this position, destroy that mortar nest, kill this Flak 88 crew. It’s the same stuff we play in every single WWII shooter and nothing ever changes. Sure it was mindless fun, but I have come to realize why I was so glad everyone moved on.
--Score: 8/10

Yes, I have 20 hours in this game. But first, some background.
Like with Final Fantasy XIII and Remember Me, I avoided this game because people complained about it when it came out despite me being hyped for it. I bought it when it was on sale for a dollar and regret not buying it day-of.
I can see where people can find significant flaws, especially playing now just before the new game comes out, but there's so much good in this game that I think it's okay to overlook. The story's a little undercooked, Merc annoys the hell out of me (the white guy who's talking in your ear for 90% of the game), and for such an important character, you see Faith's sister three times and she does nothing significant. The borderless cartoon animation comic-wannabe cutscenes between levels are tragic and make my heart hurt. The biggest complaint I've seen is also slightly true: yes, some jumps and parkour tricks can be difficult to pull off because of finicky controls and poor item interaction (like not being in the correct centimeter length from a pipe so you fall to your death despite staring right at the bloody thing).
But, honestly, the only parts of the game I got truly and genuinely frustrated at were the fights (particularly one boss fight with a ninja person *spoiler spoiler*). Thank god Catalyst ditched the guns because wow, I didn't get this game to play a shooter.
Despite all of this, which I guess some is enough to ruin this game for people, I cannot recommend this game enough. It is quite possibly one of my favorite games of all time, and I play a lot of games. I spent $200 on Catalyst and got the prequel graphic novel. I own the soundtrack to the first game and will probably get the next. I seriously love this game. So what's good?
It's art, pure and simple. And there's nothing else like it. Maybe some indie stuff popped up in hopes of scratching that virtual parkour itch, but nothing really compares to this full game of jumps and swings. It's like making Assassin's Creed first person and giving you complete control of every wall dash, every jump, every lunge, all those little tricky grabs and spins, and turning travel into the puzzle rather than combat or hacking minigames. Every tiny detail is carefully created and placed to challenge you and force you to think creatively, using the tools you learn in the tutorial on increasingly difficult puzzles. Even the fights can sometimes be enjoyable when you treat it as a marathon instead of an fps shooting gallery.
The game is gorgeous, even for today's standards (though Faith's model is a little choppy). The color contrast and choice in neon vibrance and bright white have been lauded for years now. And it always stands our, no matter how many times you play the game. In a world of greys and browns, this game is quite the visual gem and that can't be understated. Traveling over skyscrapers really shows all these contrasts, then busting into office buildings and cunstruction sites, subways and malls, put those big blues, oranges, and greens right in your face.
I'm a huge cyberpunk fan and there's not a lot of it. People want to think it died in the '80s, but I say ♥♥♥♥ that. Even if we don't have AIs or cyberspace, this is cyberpunk. A small group of rebels try to circumnavigate the system that the ruling totalitatarian government has created in this near-future dystopia. It's guilded, with high-rises and men in swanky suits, but crime and death in the cracks. This point's more about my personal interests, but anything cyberpunk is a win in my book.
The music perfectly frames everything going on. It's fast, it's calm, and it's creepy. People complain about "Still Alive" but I'm one of the nerds who loves that ♥♥♥♥ing song. When i heard the composer for the main soundtrack was coming back, I immediately got the collector's for Catalyst. He's good. It's soft, kinda futuristic (as we'd like to imagine it) and is the perfect audial counterpart to the colorful visuals.
Then there's time trials and doing speedruns of actual levels from the game, which is always fun. There's hackers on the pc, so don't bother trying to be number one on the leaderboards, but it can be very fun to push yourself to beat your own best times. Some of the most fun I had in this game was discovering new and faster ways of completing levels, like trick jumps I missed on my initial run or near-glitches that let you skip whle sections. I suppose these types of things exist in all sorts of games, but it truly feels different in a game with the parkour gameplay like this. I also thought the voice-acting was well done, particularly on faith and Jacknife, even Merc (despite me loathing his voice).
I am a very big fan of this game, now franchise, and will likely love it forever. No, it's not perfect. If it was, would we need a sequel? But it's unique, fun, and stays in your brain. Granted, the folks around here bashing on it aren't likely to think about it again, but how are you to know you won't love it until you try it?
One scene will always stick with me. Faith's sister's first appearance is in a cutscene, and not one with that horrible cartoon animation, but a realtime in-game cutscene in first person. There aren't a lot of these (in fact, off the top of my head, I can only remember two). This one is a good length, the vast city is visible in the background, you don't have control over Faith's actions, and it's emotional. It sets up the plot for the game (which isn't dreadful, they just could've done al ot more with it) and the relationship between Faith and her sister. Faith's personality is on full display here, her drive to run and escape problems rather than face them, and we never see her face. Many fps games don't have cutscenes from first person where the first-person character actually does stuff that the player doesn't do. But it's not awkward, it doesn't feel weird, even when the two sisters embrace and you see Kate's head go over Faith's shoulder. It's fluid and makes me wish there were more of these throughout the game. Even outside of the parkour, the music, and the visuals, this style of cutscene will always stick with me.
TLDR- I love it, you might, there's problems, what game doesn't? You won't know if you're a hater or a lover until you try it. There's running, jumping, music, some iffy storytelling, and an overall unique experience. I've also heard it's good with VR. Give it a shot, it may just be your next obsession.

Oh lord, this will get downvoted like crazy but I have to be honest and adress the emperor's new clothes.
Half-Life was a milestone in first person shooters that changed the entire genre for better or worse. Everyone who was around back then can tell you how monumental it felt. It was incredibly well-made, balanced, though linear always gave you the feeling of actually exploring the levels, which in a sense disappeared altogether because the whole game felt unbroken from beginning to end, despite the technical limitations of late-nineties PCs that wouldn't allow entire games streamed without load times. The platforming was a nuisance but everything else aged incredibly well and is still worth checking out. I'm more partial to the jedi knight series and the first Unreal but there's no denying Half-Life's status in the gaming world.
With Half-Life 2 I was just never sure what the fuss was all about. Few games deserve universal acclaim and journalists are quick to jump on the bandwagon. Just try to find a review of Final Fantasy VII from back in the day that doesn't praise every aspect frantically for example. There are games  I don't like but get the appeal of but from day one I found Half-Life 2 to be mediocre and despite several attempts over the years I've yet to complete it. You're on a painfully linear progression from beginning to end. Tunnels connecting stationary shootouts like pearls on a string. There's no fun gunplay in the shootouts and there's no interesting discovery connecting them. Back in an era when gaming quickly moved into character-driven open-world and semi open-world territory (mostly on consoles though with the exception of beyond good & evil) this approach to set-piece focused gamedesign felt really outdated. When gaming embraced deeper characterization and atmosphere, a sense of discovery and adventure you're stuck with a mute protagonist shooting anonymous faceless enemies in a gaming world that feels controlled and lifeless. Physics engines were new back then but there's only so many times you can wow me with a physics puzzle that feels like incredible machine for dummies.
Half-Life 2 isn't horrible, I don't engage in hyperbole, but I find it still as unremarkable now as back then when it was brand-new and I can't for the life of me understand why it gets so much praise. Praise the first one, praise Deus Ex, all of them more worthy. Even Half-Life 2's peer Doom3 aged better and it was mocked mercilessly for its dodgy design decisions. Given the same close scrutiny as other titles Half-Life 2 just falls apart.

A lone robot in a dead and unmoving future world, you find yourself amidst the rusted ruins of your robotic peers with only the power of magnetic energy to help you revive these elders to their former glory. Magnetic by Nature is a sidescrolling platformer with a magnetic driven twist, facing the player against complex chains of positive and negative reactions they must properly attract to and repel from in order to reach the end of each thoughtfully crafted stage.
Each of the large robot idols you must revive and unlock play host to a series of refreshingly difficult levels of their own colorful and entrancing environment. Guided by the shimmering melodies echoing with cave-like and natural qualities, droplets of water heard lightly dripping from hanging stalactites in the background. The game has beautiful and engaging surroundings that seem to live and breathe around you, with the glistening surfaces of twisting rock formations with occasional flocks of birds flying by all drawing you into the wonderfully relaxing mood of each differently themed setting.
Mere movement in Magnetic by Nature requires the sharpest wit and the quickest reactions, propelling yourself across wide cavernous gaps and attempting to quickly reverse polarity to catch yourself on another magnet and swing even further. As you learn the ropes of using your magnetic charge to slingshot yourself around each stage with ease, the momentum speeds up and swinging yourself across stages becomes an exhilarating trapeze act.
Often times the game moves far beyond mere platforming and into ingenious and accessible puzzle mechanics, having you push and pull magnetic orbs into proper slots or even through complicated stone mazes. Throughout the entirety of the game I was surprised with how fresh and engaging the new mechanics brought by each level were, never feeling same-y or overstaying its welcome.
The game quickly becomes intensely difficult, but in the best ways possible that offer an accessible challenge which always feels within your grasp.  What starts out as quick and clever manipulations of magnetic force in order to reach a nearby platform soon turns into long and complicated series of chained magnets strung above dangerous obstacles and deadly contraptions.
The retries will come swiftly, as you practice on perfecting the aim and arc of your propelled movements from each magnet to the next, timing your swings between them just right. It doesn't take long to figure out how to wield this unique mechanic, and completing the most puzzling labyrinth of magnets is always an incredibly rewarding feeling.
Magnetic by Nature is a game that deserves to discovered and played by a much wider audience. I'm ashamed I hadn't played it earlier myself, as it has proved to be one of the most pleasantly original platformers of the year. The consistently challenging and unusual mechanic of harnessing magnetic power to slingshot yourself to victory combined with an earthly atmosphere unsurpassed in its natural charm make this absolutely worth the admission.

Let me start with a tl:dr version:
This is a management type sim. Not a game where you get to control a wrestler in an actual match.
This isn't the company's current offering in the series, but the software sold from their website is evil - meaning it's tied to ELicense. So even if you aren't a fan of Steam - be thankful you haven't messed with ELicense.
That aside - this version has well established mods and is plenty of fun if simulations and wrestling are interests of yours.
----
My original review on why I'd recommend it.
Total Extreme Wrestling (TEW) is a fun game if you always wanted to delve into the management side of wrestling.
Management side of wrestling? Yes, the side of the industry where we all know it's story based entertainment, with athletes portraying the roles of actors, all with varying degrees of success. In this game you play the role of the person who runs the company, building the stable of your wrestlers through contracts, defining which talent you'll be aligning to which story line, and who they'll be facing in order to make it all entertaining for the people who come to watch the show.
This is where the challenge comes in, as the best long running plot can fail utterly if you use the wrong kind of talent in pulling it off. For example, you may create a grudge war which pits two of your wrestlers against each other for the fans viewing pleasure. The individual steps of that grudge war can include actions such as one wrestler taunting the other in a pre-match interview. Well, if the wrestler you have give the interview isn't skilled in speaking well, then the fans might not find the taunting interesting enough, and as a result, they'll be cold towards the next event as they begin to loose interest.
The end result you find is it's a management / business sim where you need to hire athletic actors to manipulate the masses by entertaining them and playing with their emotions, which then nets you the money you need to keep the business going.
Also, while some folks enjoy the wrestling universe that comes with the game, I myself find it hard to relate to, so I usually find one of the fine "Real-world" mods that the TEW community has created, so that way I can hire / fire / ruin the career of wrestlers I actually am familiar with.
While this isn't the current version of the game (TEW 2013 is), the current version is only sold on the company website. I've owned both, and found that I put more hours into TEW 2010.

EverQuest --was-- the best MMO that I ever experienced. What people should understand is that EverQuest of old does not exist. There are emulated servers like P1999 that try to recreate the original EQ experience - that alone should tell you how much the current EQ has changed from its inception.
Today, the problems of top-heavy population are very real, and catastrophic for enjoyment of the game. 99% of zones and content are ghost towns, completely unused. 99% of quests and items are obsolete. The game now gives you equipment in "starter packs" that is better than anything you can quest for or loot in the early game. A bad solution to a real problem (no new players), which renders all content except the last couple expansions worthless. 1-75 content is just there to grind levels these days. Maybe even 1-90. If you need gear better than the game just gives you, you won't want to hunt for it. Instead, you'll want to hit the Auction House, which is full to bursting of better gear than you could ever loot for dirt cheap prices.
Agreed that this is not an MMO for new players. Frankly it's not even an MMO for many of us vets, who were around at the beginning. There are still some people playing - three or four chars at a time - but what keeps them going is often the amount they've already invested in the game. Splitting from characters you've invested literally years of your life into is not easy. But few will straight-up tell you that they enjoy the game as much as they ever did.
By all means, give it a try. It's free after all. But don't expect the legendary MMO you might have heard people talk about. That game no longer exists.

Thinking about playing EverQuest for the first time? Don't. Only come back if you've played back in the day and you are returning for a nostalgia run. This is not an MMO you should visit if you've never played before. Why? Well, let's see:
-- The developers have poor communication with the community. They never explain what is happening when the servers are down, they never explain why they decided to take X path instead of Y path, they lock any threads on the official forums if you criticize them, and they don't reply to any threads outside of their own. Unacceptable and completely unprofessional.
-- If you've played back in the day then you'll be used to the graphics, thus you probably won't be too taken aback by how ugly EverQuest looks.
-- You also have the jumbled, unorganized, messy UI the game gives you. When you first log onto your character you'll be surprised how I wasn't exaggerating. It's that bad. I honestly think it's the worst UI out there from any other game I have ever played.
Another developer complaint? Yes! They deserve it. They are in charge of what direction the game is going, and they are always going down the wrong path. Incompetent?
-- Back when the first EverQuest expansion was released ('Kunark') you got 28 zones, that's right
zones to explore and tackle. How many zones in the current expansion of EverQuest? In 'Empires of Kunark' you get....
zones! Hahaha... It's hard not to laugh when you compare the two. This expansion takes place on the same continent of Kunark. You lack 21 zones to explore due to the current lazy developer team. It's quite sad.
-- No maps. That's right, you get very little in-game maps. You need to go to a third-party website to download maps. This shouldn't happen...
-- Speaking of the current expansion, did you know they have the nerve to charge the same amount they charged for 'Kunark' for the most recent expansion 'Empires of Kunark'? With 1/4 the content! How people accept this is beyond me. Actually, thinking about it, they are probably lifelong players who can't take off their nostalgia goggles to see things clearly.
-- Let me explain how things are going to go for you if you are new and/or if you decide to come back:
: "Wow... this is an ugly UI. Um... What do I do?"
: "Ok, I survived the tutorial. I was alone the entire time... Maybe I can join a group once I leave here?"
: "Crescent Reach looks cool! Nice zone.", "Hmm... still no groups even though I'm level 50! What the hell? Where is everybody?", "How did that guy writing that review on Steam know this would happen? Does this happen to everybody?"
: "What the hell happened? Why is it so hard to level up? I'm getting less than 1% a kill and it's taking FOREVER to make progress.", "Also, where are the groups? This game is top-heavy, I guess. Maybe if I keep pushing forward I can finally get a group."
: "Ok, I'm going to quit. The grind is real and it's a real bore. Not even difficult, just killing hundred of enemies for less than 1% EXP."
: "Finally, I'm high enough level to group with somebody!"
You: Hi, level XX [class here], want to group?
Players: No, you're not in our clique, so...
You: ...Damn it! Guess I'll "box"
- Boxing is a term used when a player has more than one account -- usually one or two additional accounts. You do this so you can tackle the games content since the game was designed for you to have a group. If you control three accounts, you can place three mercenaries (computer controlled players) in your party to complete your party. Instead of playing $15 a month, you pay $45 (if you have three accounts total). Depending on how good you are at controlling all your characters you can tackle every single thing in EverQuest besides most raids. Solo content? Obviously. Group content? Depends on what classes you picked and how good you are. Raids? A lot of old raids you can take, however once you reach the 12th (out of 23) or so expansion it nearly becomes impossible due to mechanics and needing 6+ players to enter the zone.
Only come back if you have played before and you want to take care of that itch you have. Don't bother with EverQuest if you are new and want to try an "old school" MMO. It's not worth it. Any other MMO besides EverQuest, is what I suggest. The game shows no signs of improving, terrible developers, not enough content, and most importantly: no players!!
