I needed something to do while I download this game for 800th time, so I figured, why not post a review.  A review?  Well, not really.  More a long the lines of... well, just read it.
You see, EverQuest is the kind of game you can lose your life to and not care one bit.  I know, because I was practically raised in this world.  I started back in 1999, when I was 6 years old.  Watching my Father play, I was captivated the moment I saw it - When I wasn't play it on the computer, I was LARPing it with my Brothers.
I maintain to this day, that I was not raised in Unnamed City, Canada, North America, World.  No, I was Born in Kelethin, Greater Faydark, Faydwer, Norrath.  I was raised and molded by this world, the experiences I had and the people I met.
I haven't, REALLY played in some years, but I still have solid friendships, to this day, that were forged in the Norrathian environment.  I still pop on every now and again, just to catch up.
Every time I do, it's like visiting an old friend.  You haven't seen eachother for a while.  You catch up.  Talk about what is new, get lost n your friendship and despite that you have both done some growing, it's like your friendsip has never changed.
I still get giddy with I hear the loading music.
This game is more than just a game.  It truely is a world in which you may lose yourself in.
It may be dated and have a lot of content that serves no purpose, but, it is there.  Just waiting to be explored.
If you don't mind soloing or have a few like-minded friends - Play this game.
Do not play it for the race.  Do not race yourself through all 115 Level (Maybe there are more now.  There were only 70 when I left)
Do not play it like most enter MMOs, a mad race to get to the top of the world, ASAP.
The expression, "Stop and smell the roses" could not be more true, than in this game.  You will not regret it.  Explore this world.  Breath in it's lore.  Become an inhabitant of Norrath, not sure a player vieing for the best gear.
This game is simply amazing and too fun to play. Don't even ask if you should buy it or not.

Can not recommend this game for a number of reasons. (expanded on 5th August, see below)
Dialogue is florid to the point where I'm already just clicking through the different options and seeing what gets added to my journal afterward. Not ideal seeing I haven't yet left the starting city in any meaningful way.
While I enjoy being able to move items about to set off traps/disable things/work through puzzles, they really could have toned the clutter down a lot. The fifth time I opened a pot or a crate and there was nothing in it was annoying enough, but I guess this is the status quo for the game? If I weren't a compulsive loot fiend I'd probably just skip most of them, which means I'd be skipping both the story and most of the loot. So why am I even playing the game if they've made both those things boring/a chore?
The melee combat is very boring. I do like the magic system, but it definitely feels like they spent way too much time thinking about making that side of combat cool and neglected the rest almost entirely. Casting Rain on a bunch of mobs then electrocuting the bajingo out of the bunch of them is pretty neat, but when that's one of the only things keeping my interest it's going to fall away rather quickly.
Once you start venturing outside the city it's not overly clear where anything is, or what you should be doing. The quests log/journal is terrible at giving you instructions that are meaningful. I'm not looking for glowing arrows pointing me in the right direction, just looking for proper descriptions of what options I have available and where I should be headed.
Additionally, the difficulty of encounters ramps up unreasonably as soon as you start moving outside the city. My party and I have already cleared out everything that it can handle, yet it's still only about halfway through level 4 and being murdered by large packs of level 5 mobs that I cannot separate effectively. Add on to this my earlier comment about combat generally seeming like a chore, and I really can't see myself playing this game for much longer.
One other thing I'll say is that I initially decided to play "upstanding citizen"-type characters, but due to basically EVERYONE in the first town being terrible, annoying, horrible people I regretted the decision immediately and restarted with a couple of rogueish types. About the only fun I've had so far has been stealing all their stuff and selling it back to them.
This game feels like a tech demo that someone else could perhaps use to build a competent game, or perhaps a game that has been pulled out of beta too quickly before it was balanced/had a copywriter look at its dialogue to make sure people speak in a way that doesn't put players into a coma.
** EDIT @ 5th Aug 2014
I feel like I've pushed past the initial difficulty wall (everyone's over level 5 now) but the point remains that if you're not going to allow enemies to respawn so a player can grind up to the level required to get out of a certain area then you cannot call anything that gives you the experience required to continue a "side quest" or optional content. This impacts the replayability of the start of the game, because you need to do every single thing available to you to get the experience to level up and progress. This is the exact kind of game I would normally put something like 200-300 hours into, but if I have to do the exact same thing every time I start then that is not going to happen.
I probably wouldn't be harping on about this quite so much if the devs weren't getting glowing praise from seemingly everyone for this game. I saw one review saying something like "This is a game with little to no hand holding and it does not insult your intelligence by making this game accessible to your five year old sister", but I feel like there's a huge difference between a lack of hand-holding and a lack of a cohesive narrative to the story. Seems like the writers were more interested in making every single character speak in blocks of overly-wrought prose than having a decent storyline underpinning it. It also insults my intelligence in an entirely different way, by making the main characters talk to each other like they are mentally-deficient amalgams of the Lutece twins and a pair of naive, sheltered nobles out in the real world for the first time.
You're dispatched to the town to look into the brutal murder of the councillor, and more specifically to see if the Source was used in the crime, and hunt down the Source wielder and bring them to justice. So what's the difference between a Source wielder and a magic user? Is it just dark magic? It's not really explained very well from what I've seen so far, and a lot of what Madora says further confuses the issue, even though she's supposed to be a retired Source Hunter (who you would assume would actually know a thing or two about the Source). Am I supposed to already know this from previous games? (that I have not played). I've been working on the assumption that it's similar to the difference between WoT's Saidar and Saidin (or perhaps the One vs the True power), or the light & dark sides of the force. It'd be nice to know the background a bit better (without needing to Alt-Tab out and search for a Divinity setting wiki to explain it all for me), especially seeing as both the main characters are supposed to be warriors dedicated to the detection and eradication of one of them, while being free to wield the other.
However, once you get to just outside the town you run across a trio of magic users referred to (if I remember right) as cultists. Are these guys Source users? If so, why aren't they under suspicion for the murder? If not, why are they even there? Are they the reason the orcs have a landing party on the beach outside? Again: if not, why are they there? They seem related, but then the struggle with the orcs is referred to as an ongoing, unrelated thing.
Once you get into the town proper and start the investigation you get pulled into another, completely nut-ball unexpected plot that is really, really badly explained, and not even overly well-written. Then you get to a certain point in the main investigation and run into a roadblock that I still haven't yet cleared, and that I'm hoping I simply have to wait out for a bit while I level up. In addition, I just turned in a character I pretty much know is not the guilty party because I don't know how else to progress the storyline, then I get a whole bunch of attitude from NPCs for doing it.
I'm getting sick of stringing stuff into sentences, so here's a quick list of the rest of my issues (some of which are about the setting itself, I think)
- undead priest mobs casting Heal and Bless on their mates
- orcs being referred to as irredeemably savage, unthinking creatures when the adopted daughter of the town's mayor (who is also the town's librarian and thus meets a lot of people) is one herself.
- low-level mobs having just about every type of elemental arrow available to them from the get-go
- seemingly unrealistic attribute requirements on items (is 10 the highest an attribute can go? If so, why was I finding req str 10 items at level 3?)
- lack of any real strategy to encounters other than finding the quickest/most applicable way to put your opposition's mages & archers into stun-lock (ie: the guys who can do the same to you)
- skeletons who are walking bombs I mean what is this, come on
- why are there these oil, water & poison barrels just sitting about everywhere? Because T-A-C-T-I-C-S !
- why even have a crafting system if it's going to be as badly-explained and useless as the one in this game?
- the bartering system is incredibly daft. Why a town doctor would want half the garbage I've traded to him is beyond me.
The puzzles, controls and graphics are charming. It's a bit slow and major game mechanics are poorly explained. I enjoyed the time I played but I don't think I'll finish this any time soon.

So whether you want a game where you can destroy your opponents with military might, cultural influence, diplomacy or superior scientific application no two games are ever alike and has plenty of replay ability value.

First things first: I love the Divinity universe. I own all of the games, even owning multiple copies on multiple websites, plus Divinity 2: Dragon Knight Saga on the 360. So although I technically could be a bit biased, I am going to try to give as honest a review as possible, featuring both positives and negatives.
Positives:
+ The music in Divinity games has always been phenomenal. Original Sin combines some of the best tracks from all of its predecessors, and WOW was I excited to hear them. Divinity 2 (360 version) came with a full music soundtrack, and that is the only video game soundtrack I keep and prize because the music is supremely beautiful. Many of those tracks are here as well, along with new tracks that keep up with the Divinity standard.
+ The world is lush, beautiful. This game is very colorful while keeping its realism. This is a world you WANT to explore every nook and cranny of, which is great because this game sure makes you do it.
+ The character classes are vast and varied. You can create the character you want (warrior that uses magic, a rogue/mage, etc.)
+ The battle system is FUN, and the battle music is energizing. Original Sin introduces the concept of using elements and environments to make or break battles, so having your mage make it rain over the enemies before shocking them with electricity will give you the upper hand in a battle where you may have been losing.
+ TONS of quests. It kind of gets to the point that is reminiscent of Skyrim, where the player can feel overwhelmed by the vast amount of quests waiting for you in your journal.
+ - Free roaming. You can (and will) run into areas not really meant for you yet, because the game doesn't really block your path of progression. This can be both a positive and a negative. The game can be extraordinarily vague, where you move on to an area that seems correct, only to find out later on (after much searching the discussion boards and guides) that you should have finished part of another quest before you can progress in the one you had been trying to complete.
Negatives:
- Vague/Unclear Quest Progression. This is a game I went into knowing full well what I was getting into. The early access reviews mentioned it was old school and had no hand holding. But oh MY, can this game get frustrating. From the beginning, I have searched for secret areas, read all books, consulted my journal and map, etc. etc. because I knew what others had said about its difficulty. With that said, 20+ hours of my tracked gameplay has been due to backtracking, buying back items from merchants that I had no indication through dialogue or journal that I would need later, or running halfway across maps because I realized that since one quest was "technically" supposed to be completed before another, I needed to go back. I have never played a game that infuriated me as much as this one has in terms of not being able to progress because something miniscule was not completed/kept in my inventory/spoken clearly, etc.
- Aiming in Battles. This is a turn-based RPG, so while you aim your spells/arrows/etc. in battle, your enemies stay in place. HOWEVER, enemies will move/bow/scratch their heads/pick their noses in battle, and when they do, you will find that sometimes if you left-click to attack at JUST the wrong moment, the enemy will move out of your click and your character will either shoot stupidly in the air beside the enemy's head OR walk all the way behind the enemy. I have lost battles over this one flaw, and this was not a one-time thing. This happened quite a few times, and it can screw up your strategy in moments.
- Starting Difficulty. This isn't a negative, per se, but the difficulty in the beginning is much higher than the rest of the game, so it will be a big turn off for some newcomers. Enemies do not respawn, and as you start off in one area, you have to branch out, and all of your options are groups of enemies that are two levels above you, with groups larger than yours.
- Broken Quests. There are a few quests in the game that you will be unable to complete. I have three sitting in my journal right now, forever in limbo. Sometimes quests or the characters involve will overlap, and if you decide to try to complete one quest before another, you may render the previous quest forever incomplete (won't give an example due to spoilers).
Summary: This is a great game, no doubt. I have to say that this will probably be the first Divinity game that I will not replay, however. This is a game that can be great fun, but also greatly frustrating. It is a game expansive and challenging enough to really give you a sense of pride in progressing in, but at the same time, it is not a game you beat. It feels like this game beats YOU. I recommend this game to the fans of the most hardcore of RPGs, particularly the old school RPGs, who have a ton of time to sink into a game that requires you to pay attention to every detail. This game is NOT a game you can just pick up and jump into and out of. Missing or forgetting a detail can be severely punishing to both your progression and your patience, so be prepared to "favorite" a guide. ;)

This is a nice game, for casual or hard-core puzzlers in my opinion. It may be short but it depends on how quick you can solve puzzles.
Pros
- Simple yet nice graphics
- Nice music
- Hidden/bonus levels
Cons
- No speed up button
- No punishment for using the hint button
Plenty of levels to keep your brain going and later one some will make your brain melt.
You get no punishment for using the "hint" system but even though it is there, you are not forced to use it so for those wanting to make the puzzles as hard as they can be, stay away from the hint button.
I don't mind the hint button, you still need to figure out what goes where and it good for those who do enjoy puzzles but don't want to be stressed out by them.
However some "hard" levels seemed easier than others and easier then a few "medium" levels but I guess it is more to trick you into thinking you need a complicated solution when you don't.
I really enjoyed a certain "Cameo" you find later on in the game, it made me laugh, even more when I saw what the cameo actually did to the level. And the level this one brings is perfect for hard-core solvers.
My only problem with the game however is the fact it has no "speed-up" button. Some levels I really wanted to speed up because they seemed to never run out of blocks and just kept dragging on, I wanted to get back to solving, not watching blocks for 2 minutes cross the level, specially when at the last block something happens so I fail the stage so I have to watch them all over again when I think I have re-solved it.
If you love puzzles where you try to guide objects to a certain area, give this game a shot. It is a nice way to pass the time in a relaxing manner and not having to be punished for some hints along the way.

Arguably the best title in the entire series. Building on the basis created by both call of duty 1 and call of duty united offensive, call of duty 2 improved on the graphics, sound and atmosphere of the battles and environments, making a game whose look and atmosphere still hold up to this day. This title refines the early call of duty experience, placing the player as a soldier in the midst of chaotic, intense battles between hundreds of soldiers, and not simply as a one man army. Although the player is technically the 'star of the show' of the battlefield (since you are the player, you would hope to get the most action and impact whilst playing), Infinity Ward cranked up the chaos and danger of battle in this one. In levels such as D-Day and Hill 400, especially on higher difficulties, the game isn't run and gun, but rather slow, tense engagements, where one mistake can lead to sudden panic and intense firefights, that more often than not lead to death in a matter of seconds. Although the much maligned regenerating health first makes its appearance in this game, the levels would not be able to feasibly support the number of health packs needed to maintain a good level of health throughout, especially on the harder difficulties, due to the increases in the number of enemies and dangers throughout the missions. Despite the increases in intensity, the developers wisely refrained from implementing quick time events, over-using of forced cutscenes (only in levels such as D-Day are they used), and instead provides a linear, yet exciting, player-controlled experience free from the faults and shortcomings of the later titles.
Overall, probably the best in the series, and a farcry from the current state of the franchise, especially in the wake of a new WW2 Call of Duty whose "attention to historical accuracy" equates to using stripper clips on scoped bolt-action rifles, allowing for black female German soldiers in Multiplayer, suppressors for sub-machine guns, and having plainly wrong reload animations for some guns. Whilst many will excuse these choices because Call of Duty "isn't serious", or "it isn't historically acurate anyway", just take a look at Call of Duty 2, a game that maintained a great level of fun and intensity, yet had a level of historical accuracy that did not worsen the experience, but rather enhances it.

Boy, this is gonna an unpopular review, but... Nail'd is garbage.
I like this genre of racers-- the tricks, the constant speed, the excitement that so many others manage to capture. Why can't Nail'd do it?
Well, for one, because it's impossible to lose.
Even at the hardest difficulties, I never, ever finished in anything but first place. Even if I constantly crash my bike, I respawn farther ahead than I was before, so it doesn't set me back in the slightest.
I'd still manage to have fun if I could perform tricks, race to awesome music, or at least race on a decent track, but this is just so... boring.
There are no tricks in Nail'd. There's, um... going through gates. Those refill your nitrous. What skill.
The tracks are bland and repetitive. There's really not much else to say, is there? I might as well describe the flashlight on my desk. It's black, but the switch is dark blue. It's more interesting than this game.
The music's better off muted. There aren't many songs, and they all suck.
If you consider yourself a gamer of good taste, spare yourself and buy Mad Riders instead. It has a variety of tricks, a sense of speed, a more exciting soundtrack, and pretty maps. Much less of an eyesore than endless desert.

So what is Magnetic by Nature ?
It's a puzzle platformer centered around one mechanic. Magnetism.
You can attract yourself to these magnets or attract them to you in order to position them properly to pass through the level. You can repel yourself off them or repel the magnet itself into a favorable position. Depending on what series of levels you are doing there are additional mechanics that interact with the magnets to offer more gameplay variety.
How dose it "feel" like ?
How can i describe this to you... it feels.. relaxing...harmonious if you will. It gives off a vibe i only found in Journey (yes i'm willing to go that far!)
The graphics are simple but classy and don't steal you away from the game itself and the music sets the "laid back" atmosphere of the game.
What am i supposed to do ? Where is the difficulty ?
Enjoy the experience, just sit back in the comfort of your chair or couch (fully playable with mouse and keyboard, keyboard alone and 360 controller) and just go through the game without trying to achieve anything, just go with the flow.
Tiered after a long day at work ? had one of those days ? Want to take a blunt object and re-arrange your bosses anatomy ? Fire-up MBN and unwind, belive it or not it can work wonders.
The difficulty dose not come in the shape of "how hard it is to pass a level" but in "how fast can you finish a level".
Story ?
Through a short but heart-warming intro that shows a little robot all alone and sad because he cant reactivate one of his robot friends MBN got me more interested then triple-A 5 minute intros. I genuinely wanted to repower my sad looking robot friend. Can't get that feeling in CoD now can you ?...
That's all i have to say because i don't want to spoil anymore.
In my opinion this is how "lore" should be done in a platformer, short, to the point and effective. Not many people play platformers for the lore, most do it for gameplay... don't you ?
My thoughts ?
It's one of the few original releases i seen all year.
Considering the price, the feel, the look and the new mechanics... It's a no-brainer.
If you chose not to give it a shot then you will be missing out on a great experience.
For clearer view you can check out my first impressions video

Magnetic by Nature is a cool platformer with interesting idea : Usually, in platformer games, you use your jump / double jump to traverse a level and reach your goal, and your success depends on your ability to time your jumps to perfection ... well, not in this one! In Magnetic by Nature you play a metal robot, with the ability to switch it's polarity in order to be repelled or attracted to magnets in the game and that is your most important skill! It takes a bit of time to get used to it and, I'm not gonna lie - it might be a little frustrating in the start, but once you've mastered it, you'll start enjoy the fluid motion and the level design!
There are quite a few levels in the game - by now I have unlocked 5 hubs with 25 levels each. Granted, some of the levels require a couple seconds to beat and in some you need to be really precise in your skill ( read : really really tough, borderline infuriating :p ). In each level there is a bonus objective, that's usually tough to get. If you get the objective and don't beat the level, it will still be there next time, taunting you again, but if you got it and complete the level, you won't see it again. Gladly there is an option to reset all your progress, which I really really like and find very useful (for all the let's players out there <3 ).
Although there are no online leaderboards for the game, there are rankings for each individual level. Your rank for a specific level is determined from the time you need to complete it, compared to other players out there. The fastest time and individual are displayed below your rank, on the level info screen. Now, I would like something done better about this : The time is counted from the moment you load the level to the moment you reach it's goal. I would love, if there was a small countdown, or at least a half a second of get ready - here is where you start moment, as in a lot of levels instant movement is required to achieve a respectable time. Also, if you fail the first time the level is loaded, you'll respawn reasonably fast without the loading screen, but your time won't be reset. So in order to get a top rank, you need to wait for that loading screen and fully reset the level every time you fail, and I think this could be done better.
There are unlockable speedrun game+ , game ++ modes for all you speed runners out there. I've only unlocked the game+ mode : as you start it a timer will appear in the top right corner counting your total time - and you start from the first hub/tutorial levels. As a lot of levels take under 5 seconds to complete, but more than 3 seconds to load on my machine, I would guess, that a fast pc/ssd/ram will have a significant impact on your time, and I don't like that.
The game always shows "press A/Y" to do something, even when your gamepad is unplugged and it took me some time to realize that Esc is the key to replay a level, while Space/Enter is the key to resume. Also I would love to see an option - go back to level hub on that particular screen( replay level / next level).
The controls in general feel good on both keyboard and gamepad, but I stuck to my keyboard + mouse as I found those better suited for me. While experimenting to find out what keys I need to press to replay/go next level, I found out a "secret" ?! : If you press ctrl+F10 you open something that looks like a level designer. I haven't played around with it too much, but if they implement it in some point, the game would definitely benefit from it!
The game is hard, don't kid yourself. There will be people raging at it, for sure ;) A lot of patience will be required, but I still think, it's worth it, as I found it very satisfactory to see myself @ rank 1 on a couple of levels :p

Traded games with my best friend when getting into PC gaming proper, and I got this masterpiece.
Been playing since early access, and WOW this game has evolved so much. Recently, I've been playing it almost DAILY
PROS:
1) Gunplay is so so weighty and satisfying. Each kill FEELS RIGHT. Guns have kick to them, enough that each gun needs some skill to use, and they almost all hold a secret in their alt fire or in how you use them.
2) If you like Demon Hunter, then you'd love this soundtrack. In fact, only recently I turned down the in game music for something a bit more heavy (Cannibal Corpse, Decapitated etc feel much more at home here, you can listen to Hammer Smashed Face WHILE YOU SMASH SKULLS WITH AN EXPLOSIVE SLEDGEHAMMER)
3) Different classes, each having a different role to play in game, and on harder difficulties, you really do need to play your role)
4) TEAMWORK! With a maximum of 6 players in standard, non custom servers, and each class having it's own role, your team composition does matter. It's down to the team, AND THE INDIVIDUAL too, to make it through
5) The gore. Shooting a zed in the face with a shotgun at point blank and watching it disintegrate is amazing. Not to mention Gibs and Fluids, but I can't manage to get those running without massive performance hits (Recommend a 980 to enable both! It's called Nvidia FleX, so AMD users miss out)
6) The difficulty : Normal is for when you want to take 1 perk to level 3 as you learn. After that, Hard and above is the place to go
7) This game can give you an adrenaline rush. Fighting for your life, beginning to get overrun, carving out an escape path to safety only to get separated from your team and you need to regroup. This game gets HECTIC. You CANNOT let your guard down
8) It has PvP! What's better than killling a Zed horde with your friends? Killing your friends while playing as the Zed horde!!!!
9) Maps from the workshop! THANK YOU!
10) The game does look good. Like an art gallery. Where the painter used blood for paint, severed arteries and exploded enemies body parts cover the canvas in blood and gore. Each map starts out looking quite nice, each having it's own themes and settings. As the match goes on, however, the floor and walls and even ceilings start to get coated in blood. By the end of the game, it looks like there's been a bloodbath (which there has!)
11) Playing the game, you level up your perks. This gives you a goal to reach. Then the real game(to me anyway) starts from Hell On Earth when your perk is max level, or Suicidal.
CONS:
1) PvP unbalanced: Seriously, the PvP feature needs work TripWire.
2) Slow updates, they take a very very long time to come
3) Bosses can oneshot you if you're not careful (again, going into the difficulty section of the PROS too)
4) REMOVED DUE TO UPDATE
5) Some weapons are USELESS! (ESPECIALLY the HMTech-201 and the M16 M203. Both are almost always worthless in multiplayer games)
6) The entire Survivalist perk/class
One more con (can't fault devs for it, it's not in their control):
BAD BAD BAD teammates!!! I've lost more games than I have won simply because of bad teammates. This is not a game where playing with randoms is usually a good idea (unless you like dying because someone isn't doing their job right), or nobody is using voice comms, or just salty trolls that when you're calling out "2 scrakes, 3 fleshpounds my end" over the VoIP, the random firebug rages everything and you (medic) get WRECKED. Or the one guy who tries to play on the hardest difficulties on a level 25 perk that was levelled up using a killbox map, and hasn't shot a zed that could attack them before.......
*UPDATE* King fleshpound is now in game OFFICIALLY and as such con number 4 (having only 2 OFFICIAL bosses) is now moot. Also, The Abomination says hello
However if you do find a good squad, you'll have more fun than you'd ever imagine
Definitely recommend this game if you have friends who are willing to learn and actually become good players

Each side alternates a turn for each unit in order, but if you have 6 people on the field and your opponent has 2, they get to move their characters 3x for every time your individual character moves. Hey there, buddy. What's your favorite shape? Is it a cube? Oh, please tell me it is. Does your favorite shape have 12 edges? 6 faces? 8 vertices? Oooooooh, it better. Because I got a nice surprise to show ya, buddy.
The cubes in this game. Look at them. Just look at them. Aren't they beautiful? These cubes are glorious. God cubes, cubes beyond the wildest dreams of cube enthusiasts everywhere. These cubes are the kind of cubes our forefathers strove to perfect. The kind they fought wars over. The kind that would make a man shoot his own father and slap his mom's ♥♥♥♥♥♥s around for. These cubes are beyond the kind of cubes you might be accustomed to. These are the pinnacle of human creation.
You better like these ♥♥♥♥ing cubes, because that's all you're ♥♥♥♥ing getting.
I swear to ♥♥♥♥ing God that's all there is. That's all that's left. Just cubes. Cubes as far as the eyes can see, little buddy. Just lots of God damn mother ♥♥♥♥ing little piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥cubes. Wouldn't you like some? Well here, have some ♥♥♥♥ing more.
Rush is a game all about cubes that you can enjoy on your PC or Wii U. Isn't that ♥♥♥♥ing great? All the cubes you could ever want. 1080p, high definition, 60 frames per mother ♥♥♥♥ing second cubes. Anti-aliasing cubes. Cubes that can make your hair grow back, help your wife rediscover what she ever found attractive in you, and fill your body with youthful vigor. They'll listen to your problems, and make everything all better. They'll even let you get it in. That's right, big boy. Those glorious edges, sides, and angles are all yours for the taking.
All you need to do is tell these cubes where to go and what to do. They'll be all over it. Tell them to go left, they go left. Tell them to go right, they go right. Get your cubes to the end of the level and you win. These cubes take orders. Requests, even. Just like the middle-aged Asian lady at the tanning place. Slip her a few bucks and she'll let you into the special tanning bed out back, which is actually a couple folding chairs and a towel with some nice fluorescent lighting. But that's where the magic happens.
Much like said Asian woman, these cubes don't understand English. So your only way to issue orders is through placing little tiles. And you only get so many per level. It has kind of a Chuchu Rocket or Lemmings feel. You're really not doing much. You lay the orders out for the cubes, and watch them get to work moving their sweet, sweet vertices.
It's a simple puzzle game, through and through. Simple idea. Simple design. Minimalist to the end. Sure, later levels can be brutal as all puzzle games can be. But the core mechanics never change. It's always just a matter of judging three-dimensional spacing, timing, and movement. Like how a really long math problem is just a math problem that takes too long to finish so you just use a calculator because you don't want to waste your precious ♥♥♥♥ing time like this game does.
Just look at how many little godforsaken cubes there are. You're moving cubes around atop cubes, using cubes to guide them to the end cubes, while cubes watch from the sidelines like some kind of barbaric cube sport amidst a sprawling cube universe. It's the geometric equivalent of white people going to their cottage up north to have board game night and watch reruns of Friends. Sickening.
It's actually a pretty fun game. The puzzles are sweet and satisfying, and the art style is actually really nice. Clean, refreshing, and relaxing. And they really are the prettiest cubes you've ever seen. It's visually appealing to watch them roll around.
But there's just so many ♥♥♥♥ing cubes. Too many of them. And it makes me sick. It's nauseating. Watching them squash and stretch as they roll around, like little cubes of jelly. It's ♥♥♥♥ing irritating, dude. All these happy little cubes pisses me off. Makes me ♥♥♥♥ing mad, dude.
You know why they called this game Rush? Because they RUSHED to get this game out and forgot to use some actual objects instead of just cubes. Ha. Ha ha.

Being a fan of the original XCOM franchise, I was excited to hear about Enemy Unknown.  As I learned more about the title, I was more then elated to know the developers took the time to experience the original in order to be as faithful as they possibly could be and it definitely shows.
For the most part, Enemy Unknown stays very close to the original franchise. From the creation of the base to researching new alien life forms it's apparent that they didn't want to stray to far from the original formula but they have taken a few liberties.
Most of these changes happen at the combat level where fitting your crew members with extra accessories has been taken down significantly. With only two spaces regulated toward carrying things such as grenades and weapon enhancements, fitting your crew gets a bit tricky when deciding who gets to carry what.
Gone are the time units that determined movement, attack style, etc. Though there is still a cost in everything you do this process is a bit more streamlined and a lot more forgiving then in the past. Another interesting addition is the squad upgrades as members of your team receive not only extra attributes but soldier classes as well.
These upgrades involve special abilities like fire suppression, headshot, extra movement, and more. As your soldier continues to increase rank, more abilities become available. Another significant difference in this game is the amount of soldiers you can take on a mission. You are regulated to carrying just four soldiers to begin with and 6 total.
While originally I was happy with Enemy Unknown, I felt the DLC Enemy Within was the game that we really deserved. Enemy Unknown tried some new things but Enemy Within honestly set the franchise apart from it predecessor. Enemy within gave us new ground adding to it the ability to augment soldier abilities through gene or robotic development.
It also gave us a different type of threat one that will give players an even bigger challenge then what Enemy Unknown had to offer. I intently suggest anyone interested in checking out this title skip Enemy Unknown entirely and just play Enemy Within as they are both the same game when it comes to progression and story telling.
If you're just experiencing XCOM for the first time, then this is definitely a game I encourage you to play. If you've played the previous XCOM titles you'll be right at home with this next gen offering. While there is still a great deal of elements that are gone from the original, I honestly have no real complaints when it comes to this new offering and I'm just happy to see it come back and get the upgraded treatment that it deserves.

The Banner Saga is a so-so game comprised of a whole lot of very good parts. The story and art are both beautiful and compelling and the lore is really quite rich for such a short game. The combat is pretty much the same grid/turn-based combat you've seen a thousand times with a few quirks. I'd say the game has two major flaws. Firstly it sets up this giant story set in this huge world and the credits roll after you've seen maybe a quarter of it and not done anything about the major evil power established about 3/4 through. It's just too short for the amount we're paying. The second is everything about the character and party system. At times the story seems to kill off main characters with almost GRRM-esque nonchalance. Many of your characters will likely die in ever combat scenario and live to tell the tale, but at seemingly random times the game decides that THAT DEATH was the one time in the game where it becomes permenant. The game gives the illusion of choice while really sending players down the same disappointing path to the same premature ending. If you bought it during the summer sale, you about got your money's worth.

Mount & Blade is a fantastic action-strategy-RPG with the best horseback-based fighting engine I have ever experienced.  Battles can grow very large with 32+ infantry and horse based units racing around in a chaotic bloody mess... with you experiencing the action from an "over the shoulder" perspective.  Strategy elements are managed via a large regional map from which you move your army from place to place accepting quests or following your own agenda.  "Heroes" in you army can be levelled up, like you, and you can purchase new gear or just use the loot from your kills.  Some will think the grafx are a bit primitive, but honestly you will not notice after landing a few headshots galloping across the field.  Also the game does not lead you down any particular path... you will need to explore a bit and just try things.  Eventually you won't be able to stop playing.  The best indie-game ever.

This game is very well made. All the different ships you can use offer different advantages and disadvantages. You'll pick up the basics in one playthrough, and your skills will develop quickly. Warning: It's a Rougelike. That means you're gonna die. A lot. I've played through at least 12 or 13 times, and only won twice. Even when you win, you can't use that ship with all its crew and powerups again. Get used to it, that's the genre. It's a great way to play - you don't have any pressure to do super well on a given run. If you're floundering, you can just see how well you do and try again with a different strategy. It's not like you're going to lose something you wouldn't have lost in a hour's time anyway.

I heard about this game from an NPR special on Austin Wintory's music, and I gotta say you are in for a treat.  Having recently played a stint of next gen games, I was initially put off by the 2D animation, lack of fully animated dialogue, etc.; but they were quickly dispelled after about 10 minutes in.  The game reminds me of the old "choose your own adventure" books I loved as a child, and the rich, evocative text made it feel like I was reading a beautifully illuminated novel, rather than playing a video game.  The music is a  suberb composition that couples perfectly with the sweeping vistas of hand-painted landscapes you traverse.  The art style is clean, and distinctive.  The characters have depth, and give you reasons to be attached to them.  This also makes it hard when they die; decisions you make affect the narrative of the story, and some characters may not survive those decisions.  Combat system is fun, and engrossing; I had more than a few nail-biters.
All in all I give The Banner Saga a 9.5/10.  The 0.5 off is because of the ending.  Believe me, it was a great ending, except it isn't really an ending.  More like, the end of Book 1.  A lot of questions are left unanswered, and major plotlines have yet to be resolved.
To the game developers:  If you are looking to continue The Banner Saga, I will back you on the next kickstarter!  I need to know how it all turns out!

Mount & Blade may be the best game about medieval life ever made. Granted, games about the medieval era are few and far between, but they usually focus on adventure or strategy. In comparison, it's difficult to easily describe Mount & Blade, but it's a bit like a medieval version of Sid Meier's Pirates. It is part action game, where you can ride into battle, swinging a sword to hack your opponents. It's part role-playing, as you control a character that can level up, learn more skills, and even climb the ladder of feudal society. It is part strategy game, as you hire and train a company of soldiers that fight alongside you in battles. And it all takes place in an open world where you choose to be as noble or as dastardly as you want to be.

This is a damn fine ARPG that doesn't insult your intelligence.
Every skill, class combination, and item has value. The Devs have so far avoided micromanaging the number of viable builds down to one per class like other ARPGS (looking at you D3). There's no always-online nonsense to deal with so you can actually play the single-player mode of the game you spent legal tender on without connecting to some corporations' server bank. There is no trade restrictions barring certain augments, which can be stripped beforehand to allow that item to be traded again.
Combat isn't too flashy, which is good because the screen isn't filled with so much♥♥♥♥♥♥you can't see what the enemy is doing so you can avoid it. Skills can still be visually impressive but without the Michael Bay special effects barrage so common to latter-day ARPGs. It fits the artistic and narrative theme of the game while still letting your skills feel impactful but not so overwhelmingly powerful that you can't imagine why anyone would have died to the enemy in the first place. It just FEELS right.
Furthermore, the story presented in Grim Dawn is actually quite compelling especially if you take the time to read through the dialogue and pick up all the scraps of paper left behind out in the world. There is genuine tension in the story as you piece together what happened to Cairn, and how you can help save it. Speaking of which, the world here feels connected and alive, without immersion-breaking nonsense like the copy/paste hero squads with yellow auras just in case you were too stupid to notice them or randomly-generated terrain that looks like someone emptied a jigsaw puzzle onto the table and scrambled the pieces up.
There is even a legit lore reason why you are the only person who can control the teleporters too.
All in all if you like ARPGs this game is worth every single cent of the asking price.

I wasn't entirely sure what I was expecting when I picked up Saints Row IV on the recent free to play weekend. Having heard stories, many of the images that immediately came to mind as I boredly installed the game implied an immature, chaotic, asinine sandbox experience that would turn into a throwaway title or novelty for any serious gamer.
It exceeded my above expectations in every regard but one; you can't put this game down, it is anything but a throwaway, and it remains one of the funnest gaming experiences of the past few years. With a mix of awesome game mechanics (superpowers, need I say more?), a ton of unique bits of content, including great geek homages and ribs, and hours of gameplay, Saints Row IV pleasantly surprised me in a way few games can. The jokes are funny, the craziness is a blast and the whole game has a self awareness that makes the experience that much richer. Any trepidation about this title for what you've heard? Just give it a shot, you won't regret it. Best twenty bucks I've spent in a long while.

I saw this game and had to have it... but not for $60, way too much I thought. So I waited.. then it came on sale for half price over Halloween - now for that price, yeah!
When starting it up I was impressed by the acting and dialog and I felt (like the character) helpless to do anything except stagger around.
After I started the game the combat was clunky, I died a few times, couldn't run very long, and to b honest, wasn't very impressed at the implementation and felt at the mercy of the missions.  I was thinking "maybe this game isn't for me" but I decided to put in a few more hours since I'd already paid for it.
I'm glad I did! After leveling up a bit and extending my runs, getting the hang of combat and how to manuever around the city, this game has turned into a blast!
It's open world is similar to fallout or skyrim with random encounters, side missions and a lot to explore - except this world has a lot more character I feel.  You feel in tune with your character, a decent number of side missions aren't fetchy quest ones and the controls feel good.  Now, the combat is still a bit clunky but now it seems more like a mechanic so I have to plan my attacks a bit more than before, still I feel this is a weak point in an otherwise amazing game.  If I'd known then what I know now, full price would definitely be worth it, as it is, I think I got an awesome game for an awesome price!

Everquest is kind of like being thrusted straight back into the 90s, when your computer could barely run solitare and your mother was pretty hot. I had never played Everquest back in it's hay day, I instead played World of Warcraft back in the Cataclysm days, but it was obvious that when I first started up EQ, that it was the OG of MMORPGS.
It's very complicated in my opinion. But obviously people opt for a different experience over the 'hand-holding' that most MMOs give you nowadays. You kind of feel a sense of 'freedom' when you embrace these mechanics in particular.
Combat is pretty niche, similar to the likes of Morrowind. Honestly, I could only relate to Morrowind as that was the only game that I played that had similar combat mechanics.
Interacting with NPCs was quite profound too. You would have to either press the 'h' key on your keyboard or say 'hail' (hitler) to the NPC you wanted to talk to. From there you have to continue the conversation through the chat box with the highlighted words.
HAHAHAHA no. Simply put, this game is pretty rock hard honestly. I found myself dying in pretty awkward situations and failed to see why the game hated me so much. It obviously takes a lot of time to master what's in game for sure.
I honestly don't know what to say about this game. If you want to feel the rush of nostalgia and cheesy 90s movies and commercials throbbing through your veins, then give it a shot. If you're looking for an MMO to try however and haven't really scratched the surface with online gaming, this game might not be for you.

I was actually playing EverQuest off and on for quite a while since I was 12 years old (so, about 14 years now) -- introduced to it by my parents. I remember back in the day, when it took FOREVER for me to get level 8, and I thought I was so awesome when I finally got level 13, even though my parents were WAY higher level. I couldn't even comprehend getting that high at the time.
There are a lot of ads now in the game, as is expected of pretty much all Free To Play games. They want to hook you in to those micro-transactions. Admittedly, I have purchased a few aesthetic items off of the store. The game, even in it's current free-to-play format, still brings back memories during times of when it was subscription based.
All in all, if you used to like EverQuest back in the day, and don't mind the free-to-play model, then this game is fantastic. If you're looking for something new, then this isn't it. This game is quite old, so nothing really new here. If you liked the combat and gameplay system before, the basics of it haven't really changed.
Personally, I like having to collect bones for my summons, and meditating, or resting, versus how most modern MMOs take such things into account. :)

I fail to see any reason why this game should be considered metroidvania style. All that the character can do is move left and right plus sing and stomp. The character doesn't really acquire new abilities (at least it didn't in my 80 minutes of gameplay). The chicken does learn some songs but those don't deepen the gameplay or widen levels like is usual in metroidvanias.
Because the movement and action is so reduced, consist all puzles from walking to a certain place and sing/stomp and from there walking to a another place and sing/stomp. Positive thing is the form of the puzzles: instead of usual flip a switch or step on a pressure plate puzzles, most of the puzzles consist guiding and manipulating animals. Usually interaction with animals follows formula: singing atracts and stomping scares. How and why singing and stomping should be used differs with every animal.
The biggest problem I had with the game was my metroidvania expectations. I waited something more similar to the first Rayman, which has new skills that widened old levels. In this form I found puzzles of the Toki Tori 2+ quickly boring and after a level is complete, are new aspects of the next level usually quite minor. If Toki Tori 2+ had one or two new animals (puzzle elements) in every level, it might maintain its initial novelty. Another thing that was quite of for a metroidvania was tempo. The character is a fat bird and that gives quite good picture. There aren't really any enemies in a usual sense. They should be considered more like obstacles, like in any other situation with animals. These obstacles are game's so called puzzles. From this it follows that each level could be divided into countable number of separate puzzles (obstacles). Because of this kind of world structure and the crippled movement, for me, the game seemed like a classic Mario game where instead of jumping Mario could only pull or push boxes. There wouldn't be a problem if puzzles were interesting and challenging and there weren't too long gaps between them. Getting forward and completing levels should be much more rewarding than it is now. In essence: combination of level design and gameplay lacks feeling.
I'll admit that my playtime is quite low and the game could get better as it goes on, but for me to find game enjoyable this would require occurrence of some major gameplay or level design changing element. Even if game had more to offer later, it wouldn't erase the fact that I found early game very tedious.
If Toki Tori 2+ interests you and you consider buying the full game, I'll higly recommend trying the demo and then think if my critique could have had any base.

Despite its simplicity, this game is quite fun. It's fun to bounce off of... bouncy bits and throw disc... things against... bumper things to knock that one prick off the stage. I only have a few real gripes with this:
-It can be difficult to find a server to play on
-The aforementioned bouncy bits have varying degrees of bouncyness, without any indication of what that bouncyness is. This means that there will be times when you expect to fly way over yonder when you only go down a floor.
-The additionally aforementioned disc things are effectively two dimensional, so you can't shoot at someone a floor above you, and vice versa. The bumper things are also very picky where you shoot them, so if you shoot your disc as soon as you go off the bumper, it's heading off to the vastness of space.
I found the power-up system to be enjoyable, but confusing to new players. To save you the trouble of figuring it out, I've prepared a little guide.
Note: You can have multiple power-ups and once.
-Power: Red Thingy: Decapitates people when you shoot them
-Fast Shot: Green Thingy: Lets you fire a flurry of discs at your opponent
-Triple Shot: Purple Thingy: Let's you fire three shots at once in three different directions. Useful for ricochet kills.
-Ice Shot: White Thingy: Turns victim into effective turtle on hit. Also seems to have slight homing properties from my experience.

I've never really liked any of the other Divinity games, so didn't think this would would be much to talk about.
However, with torrents of positive reviews coming out one after the other, watching a little game footage, and seeing a few comparisons to Baldurs Gate (one of my fav games of all time), I took a chance.
And I'm glad I did. The game does indeed remind me much of Baldurs Gate, and provides all the tactical combat goodness I could've asked for. While the story was fairly bland, it did its job of moving things forward. Levelling your characters and finding new & interesting ways to make your skills blow up the enemy is what you're really here for, and it's a great time doing it. Spreading out flammable substances over the ground and blowing it all up with a fireball, or bringing the rains to flood the ground and turning it into an electrical mealstrom with a well placed lightning bolt just never gets old!
If I'm going to level a few complaints at the game then it's that it gives you very few clues on how to proceed at many points in the main storyline. There were far too many instances where I had to look up things online, like the somewhat confusing & cumbersome crafting system, and several moments of me being completely stuck only to read in a forum post that I had to find a microscopic switch on a wall somewhere that only turns visible when you reach a certain Perception level.
Ridiculous.
I would've liked to see things like that on side-quests only, but instead the game forces annoyances like that upon you as part of the main plot.
Additionally, I found the early game somewhat frustrating when I had to wander around looking for the enemies with low enough LVL that I could actually fight against without automatically losing, regardless of what kind of enemies they were.
All in all, though, I found the game very enjoyable and played it all the way to the end in just a couple of weeks. It doesn't look like it's very long, but it's actually quite a trek from start to finish (ca 70h for me, doing lots of sidequesting and exploring).
If you like fantasy CRPG's, and especially turn-based combat, you'll like this.

Here’s a quick fact for you; it’s coming up to 12 years since the original release of Half Life 2. Yeah. Let that sink in for a moment.  In that time we’ve had not one, but two new generations of consoles; each with their own breakthrough franchises and classic titles, along with an endless stream of new innovations and experiences. Yet perhaps the most remarkable thing in those 12 years is just how well Half-Life 2 has withstood the test of time – and just how many things it just gets right.
For one, it’s incredible how atmospheric the game remains to this day. The visuals naturally don’t stand up to much scrutiny nowadays, but it doesn’t really matter, as the game still manages to suck you in just by the way it goes about presenting things. For instance, take the very start of the game, where you step off the train to be met with an endless army of faceless guards and flying security cameras, the overseer menacingly staring down at you as bystanders mutter to you desperately...  It really creates a very real sense of hopelessness and oppression, one that becomes satisfying to slowly break down as you play through the game. Thankfully, you slowly tool yourself up with a variety of weapons that all feel satisfying to use from beginning to end. That collection also includes the renowned gravity gun – a physics bending, item-flinging piece of kit that just never stops being entertaining to use. It’s so amazing that given the choice, I’d probably be picking it over a portal gun.

It’s also crazy that no matter how Valve shifts the gameplay around as the game rolls on, each new segment continues to feels as polished as the last. There’s high speed chases with some pulse pounding music, suspenseful scenes such as crawling along the narrow beams underneath a towering bridge, and much more. Even when the game suddenly shifts dramatically into doing horror it does it astonishingly well, as anyone who has played through Ravenholm (And heard the heart-stopping clicking of a poison headcrab nearby) will testify to. There are just so many classic moments to list that you could be there for a long while just trying to get them all down, and that’s not even an exaggeration.
If there’s any negatives, I think it’s fair to say that the story is perhaps showing its age somewhat. There’s nothing actually wrong with it – in fact, it’s still clever and compelling in its own right – it’s just that with so many games doing blockbuster epics or deep narratives so well nowadays, it’s a little jarring to go back to something where everyone just talks and reacts to your voiceless, emotionless husk. The AI, primarily when it comes to the followers you can recruit late in the game, can also prove a little bit of an issue, getting in your way when you least want them to. As far as I recall it’s an issue the game has had since launch day, but still, it’s nothing that will ever stop your enjoyment to any great extent.
Of course, it feels a little pointless to even review Half Life 2 at this point. Everything that needs to be said about it has probably already been said. But if you’re one of the very few that have never played the game... Well, you need to get on fixing that right now. Even if you have played it before, or done so on other formats (like myself), it’s still well worth a play through again, just to marvel at how entertaining it remains. Now all we need to do is wait for the third game to come out. Should be any day now...

I finally played this game the whole way through, as I originally hit a spot that triggered a fatal error continuously, killing any desire to restart.
As this was my first time playing, I don't really have the rose colored glasses of nostalgia that tend to come with your average person that thinks this is the greatest game of all time. With that said, most of the game holds up very well. The gunplay is okay, with very few weapons being accurate at a distance. The gun variety is very good though, so if you want to play it as a traditional duck and cover shooter, that's a possibility. The things that make this game a true joy to play and a cut above the rest are the physics and, specifically, the Gravity Gun. Anything and everything that isn't bolted down can be used as a weapon, so long as it isn't obscenely heavy (a washing machine is about the largest thing you can toss across a room). The physics puzzles throughout are fun and rewarding to complete, and the Gravity Gun adds an extra dimension that features in several of the middle chapters.
As with most First Person Shooters these days, there is plenty of time devoted towards vehicles, which includes an airboat and a buggy, both of which are effectively on rails but are still fun for the limited time and give enough control and leeway to not have rage inducing spots that you just can't get by.
Another facet is the inclusion of squad commander type sections, where you can tell a group of 4 constantly respawning allies to go lay down their lives for Aiur. In some parts it can be very effective, and some parts they just seem to be there for cannon fodder and to get in your way. Alongside this, there is are a few small Tower Defense segments. The variety of gameplay elements in the game has a wide breadth without any segment becoming stale, with the physics and shooting apparent throughout the entirety of the game.

As I didn't play the original Half Life, the story didn't make much sense to me at all. After playing through the game several times in a few days, it still doesn't make much sense, but it was told in a way where not knowing won't cripple your enjoyment of the game. The final boss is rarely mentioned for much of the game, while the overarching enemy is completely faceless, which bothers me. I thought it was interesting, but didn't explain nearly enough for my tastes.
One thing that can't be overstated is that the missions don't overstay their welcome. Some games can just drag on and on and go from being fun to a grueling mess, but Half Life 2 is a solid 10 hours full of interesting content.

It's been a little over 10 years, but Half Life 2 is still a very solid game in this day and age. The gameplay can stand against the best of the FPS genre today and hold its ground, and the Source engine allows the physics elements to shine. The story is okay, neither amazing in and of itself nor a hindrance. I give it a 9/10 and highly recommend giving it a go for anybody like me who hasn't played it yet and is skeptical of all the hype.

I'm not a huge fan of Tower Defense games in general, but Orcs Must Die managed to catch my attention some years back and I'm glad it did.
The game functions like a combination of Tower Defense and Third Person shooter, much like a certain dungeon defending other game that is absolute garbage and will not be discussed in this review. As you make your way through levels, by accomplishing various feats you gain Skulls that you can use to unlock and upgrade traps and guardians you can place in the levels, as well as unlock and upgrade gear for the Warmage Maximillian, who you run around fighting with while your maze does its work.
Every level serves up its own array of challenges but for the most part there's a solid strategy to be found in the basic sort of "put up barricades so there's only one bottleneck, then shove them through as many traps as possible." On Nightmare mode that attitude changes entirely, but for the game's normal mode, that basic strategy will get you through pretty much the entir game with only a few rough spots.
Enemies run the rnage from a bunch of orc types, who just blindly run at the Rift, to kobolds, who ignore everything and just attack the rift, to gnolls, who tend to ignore everything else and just come to kill you. There's also Giants, Trolls,and Ogres who are massive lumbering foes who are barely stopped by any traps and require immediate attention or prolonged trap work to kill. Frantically rebuilding your mazes while hacking and blasting away at orcs is a lot of fun no matter how you slice it.
The game's not overly replayable, IMO, unless you're going to max out five skulls on every single level on both difficulties, but if you do want to do that, there's plenty of playtime ahead of you. If you're interested in score and leaderboards, the game also does have that, but I wasn't personally interested in it. Some of the levels are very challenging though, especially in Nightmare, and unless you suss out the level's specific trick, especially on Nightmare, getting 5 skulls can seem like an impossible task. At this point the game becomes as much a puzzle as it does a Tower Defense hack and slash game. You can also go back to older levels with the new unlocked trap gear and marvel at how your upgraded traps smash through orcs like so many dominos while the Warmage gets to watch.
There's a reason this first game spawned a sequel, a F2P MMo, and even a boardgame: It's because the game is a whole lot of fun. The story isn't anything amazing, and mostly serves as a backdrop for why there's orcs everywhere (You're the guardian of a Rift in a massive castle, and you're shutting them all to stop the Sorceress from sending armies through.), but that's fine. The only real downside to the game is that there's no multiplayer.... but hey, the sequel has multiplayer! So play this one to get the background and get your feet wet, then jump in with some friends into Orcs Must Die 2: Bigger and Better-er. Absolutely recommended.

I've always loved Fire Emblem and Final Fantasy Tactics while growing up, and seeing this game during the steam sale, I decided to give it a shot, as the general layout of the game looked decent, and the story seemed to be solid based on the reviews. It has been amazing this far, and I love the choices available to be made along the way, even if I don't realize the consequences. I enjoy choosing dialogue that matches what I personally feel, and though some of the choices lead to loss (sadly I lost two strong characters in my party), it does force me to be careful with my choices, regarding strategy and character upgrading, lest I stack one character with everything and lose him or her later on. It reminds me of permadeath in Fire Emblem, as I always feel I'm weighing options carefully every time a choice comes up in case I lose one of my party due to a twist in the plot.
Battle wise, I'm finally getting used to the armor/strength system, very different from say, maxing out your general in fire emblem and never taking damage with him in the front lines. Every character can be fragile, and I've had several close battles where I've temporaily forgotten the slight intricacies of the Banner Saga that trip me up (allies can't move through allies, choosing armor vs strength dmg).
Overall, I highly recommend this game, and I'm definitely moving on to multiplayer once I finish going through the rest of the 1 player story; I can't wait to see what happens next.

A much needed return to old-school RPGs from the makers of the well loved Titan Quest series. This new installments offers rewarding gameplay, multiple choice options and an unbelievable amount of content. Like Titan Quest, this game is single narrative, though the amount of side quests and main-quest-influencing guilds, make the game a favorite. Not as big as Titan Quest, it can be a quick game for the avid gamer, not including the amount of radiant quests up for offer. The main downside to this game is the skill options. While made to feel different and class specific, your character and quite easily become generic. Out of 3 playthroughs with two of the selectable skill options (all different each playthrough) it really felt I still had one character going. You could quite easily finish this game without picking any skill options at all, albeit a long and tough time. Regardless, this game is a real gem when it comes to true RPG - freedom of choice, consequence and an engaging narrative. Can't ask for more from this well justified Titan Quest crew.

There is so much that made me want to love this game. However, the strength system is horribly unbalanced heavily favoring units like warhawks while units like archers have little recourse once an enemy is upon them. Couple this with the fact that units you invest in can very abruptly die via text menu decisions and you've laid the path for a brutally unlikable experience. I'm also not terribly fond of the inability to move after issuing a command nor am I fond of chain battles when there isn't any sort of healing. Not being able to move through my own units was also not well thought out.
While you can advance units by spending Renown on them it quickly becomes expensive and the stat points you're allowed to allocate are sparse at best. Couple this with the fact that a unit can leave or die at any time and I have to wonder why anyone would bother. As well, the save system is janky as hell. Want to save and come back whenever you like? Too bad - you're back at the start of the chapter. I guess now you can maybe stop that party member from abruptly dying. Sloppy decisions. It's a shame - the game is beautiful.

One of the biggest freedom online RPGs in existence. You can create your own stories, adventures, quests and so on. You don't have to do what the NPCs or whatever else tells you to do. Sure, doing the things they offer you can give you really nice rewards, but you can also get really nice rewards doing your own thing. There are other games out there that allow you to do this, but it's a lot more limited. Ever Quest has very few boundaries.
This game is purely amazing and it's your choice weather you want to play your own way or not, or both. Both ways are great. I do both myself. So if you’re asking yourself, "Can you play solo and not get involved with people?" ...Yes. You can. However, you can gain a lot of good by teaming up with people for groups and raids, but it's not needed and you can have just as much fun  playing by yourself. I am mostly a loner player and I make and find my own stuff. I wander the vast world, and explore with no quests attached. I do a lot of NPC quests, but mostly I just do my own personal quests, stories and adventures. Playing this game is like playing a fantasy book you wrote.
If you never played this before, and love older fantasy books along with using your vast imagination, I recommend you play this.  The graphics aren't that real looking, but are pretty nice, which leaves a lot of room for you to see it your way and not an already created way. Don't worry about the rating, this game is for you to figure out. The rating will not tell you how you feel about the game. Trust me. It's too unique to go by other people’s ratings. It's not for everyone, but it's definitely for those who always wanted to play a game that's how I described. Here's a big plus too... The character customization is awesome. I don't mean the standard looks; I mean the equipment, stats and advanced looks.
Yes, if you’re new to the game... there will be a lot to learn and takes a lot of time, but it shouldn't be hard at all.

Review @ 100 hours and level 18.
<tl;dr>
Despite having a few flaws this game is one of the most engaging for a long time, and worth the full asking price - don't wait for a sale, get it now!
</tl;dr>
My wife and I play this in LAN co-op mode, we bought this pre-release as we are fans of the genre but did not start playing until a few weeks after release to avoid the inevitable patch-aggrevation.
To gauge whether you have a similar taste to us, we loved:
- Baldur's Gate
- Neverwinter Nights
- Ultima series
- Sacred 1 & 2
- Diablo 1 & 2
- Titan Quest
- Eye of the Beholder
- old-school Sierra Online & Lucasarts games
After 200 collective hours of playing, we have not had a single crash (platform is Windows 8.1 x64) - this is noteworthy for modern games I think.
The things we like most about the game:
- the humour (at times subtle and possibly for older players, however)
- the camera style (not first-person or over-the-shoulder)
- the quests are not spoon-fed
- you are free to develop your characters as you want (no forced classes)
- ALT-tabbing works flawlessly and quickly
Things which have frustrated us at times, but not enough to dissuade from recommending the game:
- mis-clicking during combat due to animation of a mob
- the inventory UI does not feel polished (e.g. after dragging an item out of a container, clicking anywhere will be interpreted as a location for the character to move to)
For the NPC dialogues we can look at whichever screen we need to, but I can imagine the passive player in a co-op game might feel a little lost or left out if not in the same room as the active player.
We have had 1 quest which required a manual hack of a savegame to complete due to it disappearing entirely after selecting "we'll talk about this later" - luckily a quick Google showed us what to hex-edit trivially to reset the quest/NPC status.
We have had no issues with performance, but our systems are not low-spec and not overclocked or bogged down with background processes - certainly no loading screens measured in minutes.
It is good to know that the game uses 1 core 100% all the time, so having at least a quad core CPU is advisable, as well as plenty of RAM, a 64-bit OS, good cooling and no overclocking.

Ok... This is a bold statement... and shouldn't be taken lightly. Divinity: Original Sin is the BEST RPG I've ever played. Nothing can touch it. It's also my GOTY, hands down.
Rarely does a developer put so much of their love and affection into a game. Larian have, and by doing so, they've changed the game, maybe even the rulebook for every RPG that follows. This is the new benchmark, probably for any genre.
Even if you don't like RPGs, D:OS will have something for you. Even if you're a casual gamer, it's so well paced, you could hop in for just half an hour at a time. But you wont.
You'll be drawn into a beautiful, complex and vibrant world of adventure, mystery and more importantly FUN.
D:OS won't hold your hand, or assume you're stupid. You can do ANYTHING from the get go. GO anywhere.
This freedom isn't just limited to what you can do, it's how you do it.
You're offered choices constantly, be it through clever dialogues with NPC's or gameplay itself. The game will know what you've done, who knows about it, and who it will effect and adjust itself accordingly.
I'm not going to offer any spoilers here past the first hour. That would be morally bankrupt. The beauty of this game, is discovering it for yourself.
D:OS doesn't stop you from doing what you want. You can treat people how you want, do quests any way you want and shape the story any way you want. This is role playing at it's finest. Actually *Playing a Role*. Want to be the bad guy with a penchant for stealing fine art from inns? Go ahead, or maybe you want to be the wordsmith that uses their charm and intellect to feed your cheese habit. Real freedom, and from it comes real fun.
If it's there, you can interact with it. You can even do it in combat too...
Combat... oh yeah! There's so much to do that isn't fighting, that I almost forgot! The combat in D:OS, is quite simply, the best turn-based combat system ever devised. I'm not even going to describe it. Words don't do it justice.
The worst thing you can do, is ignore this game. It may 'look' like a generic RPG from screenshots, but once you're in, you're not getting out without loving it.
One thing I wish could be implemented is controller support. Then, this game would be absolute perfection.
10/10 Must buy.

In a word: Janky.
Mirror's Edge is a game around parkour and flow.
It however doesn't flow; not easily.
In story mode, there is very little flow.
The levels are often broken up between puzzle-like climbing sections, where the aim is to get from A to B using the available structures, to arcadish shooter segments, running from A to B whilst being fired upon.
In both you are often funneled down a predetermined path. You must jump from here to here to progress. You must pass these dudes to progress. And very little of this lends itself to speed or flow.
To solve the puzzle you must stop and examine the environment, and to pass the shooters you must either stop and dispatch them with your own gun, or try to run straight at or through them as they fire at you (which doesn't work most of the time).
The best bits of the game are between these two segments, where you have space to move. Or when you are simply chased.
But these are fleeting, and often the physics of the game conspire to ruin these too.
For instance, run at a wall straight ahead and you will attempt to climb it. Run at it at an angle and you will wall run across it.
You can jump onto an object, or automatically vault it plummeting to your doom.
Leap at a guys head and knock him to the ground, or stand on them instead.
Or the most frustrating grab a ledge, or simply not and fall.
Some of these dichomotomies rarely trouble you, aside in small spaces where the difference between the two actions becomes hard to maintain.
But some are confused so often that it just leads to repeated attempts and failures.
Of course maybe I'm simply bad at the game.
There's a narrative too, such as it is.
It is very much a narrative of convenience. Things happen because they need to involve the main character, rather than occuring out of any sort of narrative cause.
Take the premise. You are a runner in a city because the guvment is cracking down on crime. And so the crime lords need stuff transported outside of the city's transport system I think.
These packages you're meant to be delivering? You never deliver any throughout the game. You never work. You are the worst courier the city has seen. But the crime lords are never seen either so I guess they can't be too mad.
Similarly the police have not cracked down on you because of fear of reprisal. Until they do, in the first chapter.
There is race mode, which involves chasing down your own time and that of your friend's ghosts.
You could probably try to beat the leader's too, if they weren't cheats with single second runs.
Still, this feels like a missed opportunity, as a true race mode, competing head to head parkouring around the city, sounds like great fun (and I think is the premise for Speed Runner, which I'm yet to play).
All in all, this game has a good premise with poor, even sloppy, execution.
Which is a huge shame.
A sequel is coming out soon though, so perhaps this will improve in the areas above.
In any case, either wait for the sequel to come out, or buy this in a sale if you're curious.
Wouldn't recommend.
Maybe play like Sonic Adventure 2, or Tony Hawk Pro Skater 2 or 3.
It's not parkour, but the freedom of movement and the straight ignoring of physics to allow the flow to continue are there.
And the flow is all that matters.
