I thoroughly enjoyed my time with Toki Tori 2+. Although admittedly it took a little bit to start appreciating the game. This is primarily due to the lack of instructions or direction provided by the game. There are no tutorials, no dialog, nothing. What the game does do to help the player is provide subtle hints, that I personally missed at first. For example, always pay attention to the little white bird. He will show you how to get to certain areas and even show you song melodies that you can play to do certain things (e.g. fast travel, restart, point out collectibles). Although this lack of direction made starting out a little tough, I ended up appreciating it later on.
What I really enjoyed about the game is how it takes such a simple concept and is able to make complex puzzles. Throughout the entire game, you can only move (not jump), stomp the ground, and make tweeting sounds. You must use these abilities to interact with different animals and objects in order to solve puzzles. From the beginning of the game, you have the ability to get to any area. The only thing you might be lacking is the knowledge of how to get past certain points. Again, the game does not tell you how to do things with dialog boxes, instead it subtly shows you, through gameplay, how to use your stomping and tweeting to progress through the level.

for when you get stuck, and you most certainly will. You may have to hunt through the videos to find where he covers the section you are stuck on, but it is definitely worth it as he shows how to unlock all of the achievements and shows some stuff that I would not have been able to figure out on my own.

Nail'd could have been an average generic racer if it wasn't for a huge flaw: the driving mechanics.
Everything is unpredictable. The way the gravity will react, the way the vehicle is going to respond when landing after a jump, or even if you're going to grip or not. This makes for a very unpleasant experience, not helped by the amount of glitches. Sometimes you can pull one-wheel wheelies because the engine glitches, sometimes you will crash into invisible walls, sometimes you will crash face first while trying to land, and much more. This is why I can't recommend the game.
This is a shame, because it has all the basics for an enjoyable little racing game. The graphics are decent (apart for the ugly and nearly headache-inducing shake filter when boosting), sound design isn't too unpleasant and there are some interesting ride and rider customization options. The game still has the same faults you can find on pretty much every relatively low budget racing game:
- nail'd becomes a bit boring as you start powering through it. The limited amount of tracks (12) compared to amount of races (around 70-80) means you'll be going around the same tracks again and again, which completely nullifies the point of having branching tracks and scripted set pieces. You'll have to learn the optimal line around a track to be able to beat the AI.
- Horrible, inconsistent AI. The AI will teleport itself, it will drive through you, it will do impossible moves. But it will be slow nonetheless. There are only a couple of near end-game events where the AI cheats enough to be challenging. In most races, it's easy to gain a 5 second lead and never let go of it.
- Generic locations and art-style. While I did appreciate the mediterranean caricature, the three other environments are painfully generic. Generic desert area with huge rock formations and a western movie styled town. Generic jungle area with mud, too many trees and some wood bridges. Generic snow area with snow covered mountains. Generic vehicles with generic paintjobs.
On the technical side, since it's running on Techland's engine you'll have to deal with all sorts of bugs and issues depending on your configuration and the moon's phase.

Probably one of the hardest and most frustrating games I have bought in the last year, and thats a good thing! Its a squad centered, turn based game about leading a team of soldiers to combat an alien invation. Squad members have unique classes that level up over time, giving you access to a limited tree of different perks and abilities for each class.
Stategy and tactics is the name of the game here, and blinding rushing your troops into the fog hoping to overwhelm an enemy will only lead to their early demise and a failed mission. The beauty here lies in making smart, practical moves forward and systematically clearing the map using your squads abilities and talents to eliminate aliens one group at a time. Played over a variety of maps (tons more with the expansion), your troops will fight through cemetaries, malls, restaurants, open wilds, and eventually inside the alien's own spacecraft and bases to root out evil where ever it hides.
As you progress, you research new technologies that lead to better equipment and weapons used to fight the aliens. Later armors add specific abilites to your squad, ranging from a grappling hook used to posiition troops on higher ground to stealth armor good for flanking aliens. You are also tasked with building a base from the ground up to help support your research and expand production options, inveitablly leading to more boons in the field, Money is aquired through missions and by building satalites over nations which reduces panic in those nations, and adds to a monthly stipend you collect monthly that will be your primary Or do you want to buy new guns, armor and upgrades to keep your guys alive now? There never seems to be enough money to do it all, so every purchase matters and will have an effect in the future.
This game is engrossing and intense, especially when played on ironman (which i recommend), which forces you to live with each of your decisions, and each of your failures. You become attached to your troops, all of whom are customizable to a reasonable degree, allowing you to personalzie your team. When a squadie that has been with you from the beginning dies because you didnt see that mutton flanking you from the side, you feel it. That sense of permanence and finality draws you into the universe, and makes your think long and hard before every move you make.
TLDR; if you love tactical combat and a real challenge fighting aliens with futuristic weapons and powers, while juggling the last bastion for human defense, and long for deep combat that rewards forthought, this just might be the game for you. Absolutely recommended!

Amazing game! It's extremely difficult, but once you figure out how to attack and defend, it becomes much easier. However, it gets progressively more difficult the farther you move along in space and the final boss is no push over. Also, with the "Infinite Space" mod, it adds a whole new way to play this game. Instead of being worried about being chased by the Rebel fleet (no not the peace loving ones from Star Wars), you can free roam around space until you eventually are murdered in a very crushing way. The only problem with the mod is that it has a weird difficulty spike not too long after you start. The music is also a fantastic part of this game and really adds a something extra incredible to it. It's both intense when you're in combat and very peaceful when just hovering around space. one thing that you should be warned of are the random events that happen through your journey. You may be that guy/girl who really likes to help everyone you come across, but sometimes, if you help that random stranger, you'll either get damaged or you could even lose a crew member, which is devestating. Your crew is your most important part about this, other than the ship itself of course. The best way to win a fight is to assign each person to a specific section on the ship and have them monitor/ repair it. If you don't, well then your weapons won't charge up fast enough, or you won't have enough evade skill to dodge a missile, so it really helps if you have someone at each section or at least the most important ones to stay alive. Overall, I would strongly reccomend this to anyone who really likes a good strategy game with a high difficulty and also someone who has always wanted to command their own ship and fell like somebody out of Star Trek.

basic slashes while running allowing you to speed through corredors and with skill and timing, kill everything in sight without a loss of speed.

You then proceed to smash his statue.

Playing this game is a bit like seeing The Force Awakens first, then watching A New Hope for me because I played Knights of Pen and Paper 2 on my Android tablet first before trying this the first game on Steam. I did that because KOPP2 was free on the app store at the time but the first one wasn't.  I'm glad I came back to the first one and decided to give it a try. The 'Cyber Monday' sale helped me decide though.
Compared to KOPP2, the first one has cruder graphics, a less intuitive interface and tinnier sound effects. Perhaps this was intentional and they were meaning to give homage to the early PC RPGs like the SSI Gold Box games.  Though the game looks and sounds cruder, I'm glad I tried it for the different jokes and campaign. There are some gems here that you'll miss if you only play the second game.
However, I do like a few things about this game better than the second.  I like the less restrictive inventory system where you have no limit on what type of item you can put in a slot.  While the second game's inventory system is a bit more realistic, I do sometimes find it frustrating to have to swap out items so much.
I also like way this first game begins better.  It has one of the most archtypical, classic RPG beginnings to it that will make players familiar with those campaigns smile.  The beginning of the second game is a bit flat by comparison and not as funny.  I found the second one's to be very funny, but now that I've seen the beginning of the first game, it's not quite as clever of an homage as the first one.
Beginning items seem to cost less and there seems to be more variety in them than in the second game.  You also earn less gold per encounter too so it balances out.  Also, spells in the first game seem to be less powerful at level one than in the second game.  Maybe this is to emulate the 'inflation' and  'power creep' that we see between the earlier editions of D&D and the newer ones. :)  Fireball, for example, only affects one creature at level 1 in the first game, but affects every creature in the mob in the second game.  However, in this first game, it does seem to do more damage to that one creature than it does to each of the mob in the second game.  So, there are plusses and minuses when it come to powers and spells when you compare games.
Finally, I like the first game's choices of game player people a bit better than the second one's.  In this first game, there are more varied choices with some truly funny options in there.  One of them, I won't spoil it by saying who, might be an homage to someone the developers know and really like because that character gets a lot of buffs.  Plus, starting the game with three PCs rather than two feels a bit more well rounded of an adventuring party than starting with two like the sequel has you do.

Necrosphere is a great old school platformer with a gimmick.  The game is laid out like a metroidvania-lite.  What I mean by that is that there is one big level and as you gain new abilities as you progress, these abilities let you access new areas, and these areas are designed to use these abilities to their fullest.  The reason I say "lite" is because there is very little backtracking(a good thing IMO), once you finish an area you get warped back to the start of the game and then you can use the acquired ability to reach a new area.
The gimmick of this game is that it only uses 2 buttons, left and right on the keyboard, or L and R on the controller.  The control is super responsive but the odd control scheme may cause some to shy away from it.  When I first started playing the game I loved it, as more abilities became unlocked my enjoyment of the game faltered a bit as I was dying more to the control than the obstacles. I gave up on the game and posted a negative review.
The developer saw my review and we began talking about it, he then messed around with the code of the game a bit and emailed me a version of the game that addressed my concern, and the game played like a dream.  The fact that a developer would take the time to listen to the complaints of a single customer and implement a fix tailored for that customer is pretty mindboggling.  Developers who care this much about their customers are a rare breed and this fact alone is enough for me to want to support him.
Having said that, once the fix was implemented the game played like a dream.  The controls are super tight and the game offers a very nice challenge.  This game is tough, everything kills you in one hit and there are tons of obstacles everywhere.  There are very liberal checkpoints in the levels and instant respawns which means the game is rarely frustrating, it is simply addicting and each death makes you want to try one more time.
Level design in this game is perfect, each level looks unique, and is loaded with unique challenges tailored to that level and that particular ability used to access it.  The variety of obstacles in this game keep things fresh and it never gets boring in the 2-3 hours or so it will take you to beat this game.
If you want a great retro themed platformer with an interesting gimmick, give this game a try.

I Worked through the entire game with someone very close to me, it was ok. this game however has some glaring issues,
1.The Enemy Humans.
This game. probably because of some poor writing, features a very weak antagonist 'force'. Forgive me if I'm wrong but in a zombie survival game you expect to be fighting against zombies. Instead you are fighting mostly against a hostile gang of human thugs. All of which die in one headshot from any gun and have some of the most brainded (hue) FPS AI I have ever laid eyes on.
Fighting these enemies in melee is at first exciting. As unlike zombies they actually block and dodge attacks. however after figuring out a simple early game combo. (which you can do without even using a weapon) they also die in one hit.
2.The Grappling Hook. This is an optional upgrade which may as well be renamed to noclip gun. This thing makes the whole free running part of This game kinda pointless. it has about a 5 second cooldown and makes you zip around the map like Rico Rodriguez of Just Cause fame. it's fun for about 5 mins. Then you realise you are an overpowered genie and there's no challenge anymore. you could throw it away... but the fact is it speeds the game up makes it a bit foolish not to take..
3. Night Time. Day Time.
The fact you are never more than 300 meters from a safe zone. which lets you change the time of day at will. means you never have to go outside at night. Which is apparently dangerous. Personally I wouldn't know. seeing as I can force it to be day whenever I want. which seems a bit stupid
4.Craftable Weapons.
You can make your own throwing weapons, bombs, and even a shield. all of these things cost experience levels and SUCK. they don't scale with level at all. they do no damage.
5. The Ending.
I'll try my best not to spoil. But here's the thing. You have to do the end of the game in single player. which was kind of final nail in the coffin for me.
It's forced. Because the boss battle consists of QTEs. which is lazy really considering there are some true boss batles with HP bars and everything in the rest of the game...
All in all it's not a bad game. it's just not really worth your time. you could play it in co op and spice the experience up a bit. but that ending will leave a bitter taste in your mouth. as you and your buddy/partner/etc. are forced to play it alone.

Toki Tori 2 is, rather obviously, the sequel to Toki Tori. It's evolved from being a pure puzzle game, with limited use of items, to a more fluid platformer puzzle. While the original was pretty unforgiving, and often required surgically precise steps to solving the puzzles, TT2 isn't quite as strict. Most puzzles can be re-attempted without a reset or winding back time.
In TT2, you return as Toki Tori, and you only have two (unlimited) abilities at your disposal : a whistle, and a ground stomp. There are many other creatures and elements in the game, and they will respond to one, oftentimes both, of these actions. Puzzles are solved by using your abiltiies to manipulate your surroundings. It sounds very simple, but there are many, many different creatures in the game, and the trickier puzzles will require chaining their reactions together. The 'core' puzzles that you need to solve to progress through the game are fairly straightforward, but the side area ones are much tougher, and it always feels very satisfying to finally solve them and hear the bonus area background chime.
There are several good points to this game that I want to highlight.
1) It doesn't try to babysit you. The game provides subtle hints to guide you along, but it lets you learn it without butting in obstrusively. The game itself starts off without any kind of narration, and you're left to make your way through the levels. In fact, the only help text I ever remembered seeing, was the hint to sing the Reset song, and even that only appears after you fail to follow the non textual clue. The effect of this is that it increases the immersion of the game, and makes solving the levels so much more rewarding.
2) No need to constantly run to an ingame menu. Instead, Toki Tori can whistle a certain combination of notes to perform certain actions (e.g. reset to last checkpoint or go to the world map). It's a very nice touch.
3) You don't get any new abilities as you progress (with the exception of the songs, but those don't factor into the puzzzles). This means there's no grinding involved. All puzzles are solvable right from the beginning of the game, but on your first try you won't know how. You'll learn several tips and tricks as you go along, and when you backtrack to the earlier to fulfill your masochistic desire to collect all the score items, it will suddenly strike you that you can get one frog to float another frog up.
4) Graphics and music. The art style is very minimalistic, clean and ridiculously cute, and the music fits the game very well. For the most part, it's a relaxing experience, in spite of all the puzzle solving.
As with most platformers, it plays much better with a controller.
Highly recommended.

Sid Meier's Civilization: 5 is a turn based strategy game. The game features scenarios for you to play but from what i've gathered the default mode is most popular. You can customize your game settings before hand to make each game unique and you can put many different challenges in your way besides bot difficulty. This game also offers full steam workshop support which is always a huge plus. You can choose to start the game in a bunch of different time periods and based on which time period you pick itll determine where you start in the tech tree. This will decide if you get swords men or infantry at the start. Every civ will start at the same spot in the tech tree and will progress at rates dependent on their science. Overall Civilization is one of the best strategy games to date and is a must have title.
PROS:
- This game offers endless hours of gameplay each game can last 10plus hours easily.
- There are many different civs to play as each offering a unique play style.
- You can win a game in many different ways.
- You can decide if you're going to be a peaceful civ or a ruthless one.
- Multiplayer where you can play with a friend on a team or against eachother. You can also still have bots in the game as allies or enemies.
- Steam workshop support which makes getting mods for this game very easy which adds even more countless hours of gameplay.
CONS:
- This game is only as great as it is if you get the DLC. So getting the Sid Meier's Civilization V: Complete bundle is a must. It goes on sale from time to time so watch out for it.
- Mods do not work in multiplayer without having to do a lot of tedious work that is not worth it.
- Tech tree is very linear and will feel repetitive after playing a few games.
Conclusion: Civilization 5 is average at best when you play the base game but its one of those games where the DLC really picks up the slack and makes this game a really good title to have. Its sequel Civilization 6 comes out next month and if it is half as good as the civ game itll be worth picking up.

I finally played this game the whole way through, as I originally hit a spot that triggered a fatal error continuously, killing any desire to restart.
As this was my first time playing, I don't really have the rose colored glasses of nostalgia that tend to come with your average person that thinks this is the greatest game of all time. With that said, most of the game holds up very well. The gunplay is okay, with very few weapons being accurate at a distance. The gun variety is very good though, so if you want to play it as a traditional duck and cover shooter, that's a possibility. The things that make this game a true joy to play and a cut above the rest are the physics and, specifically, the Gravity Gun. Anything and everything that isn't bolted down can be used as a weapon, so long as it isn't obscenely heavy (a washing machine is about the largest thing you can toss across a room). The physics puzzles throughout are fun and rewarding to complete, and the Gravity Gun adds an extra dimension that features in several of the middle chapters.
As with most First Person Shooters these days, there is plenty of time devoted towards vehicles, which includes an airboat and a buggy, both of which are effectively on rails but are still fun for the limited time and give enough control and leeway to not have rage inducing spots that you just can't get by.
Another facet is the inclusion of squad commander type sections, where you can tell a group of 4 constantly respawning allies to go lay down their lives for Aiur. In some parts it can be very effective, and some parts they just seem to be there for cannon fodder and to get in your way. Alongside this, there is are a few small Tower Defense segments. The variety of gameplay elements in the game has a wide breadth without any segment becoming stale, with the physics and shooting apparent throughout the entirety of the game.

As I didn't play the original Half Life, the story didn't make much sense to me at all. After playing through the game several times in a few days, it still doesn't make much sense, but it was told in a way where not knowing won't cripple your enjoyment of the game. The final boss is rarely mentioned for much of the game, while the overarching enemy is completely faceless, which bothers me. I thought it was interesting, but didn't explain nearly enough for my tastes.
One thing that can't be overstated is that the missions don't overstay their welcome. Some games can just drag on and on and go from being fun to a grueling mess, but Half Life 2 is a solid 10 hours full of interesting content.

It's been a little over 10 years, but Half Life 2 is still a very solid game in this day and age. The gameplay can stand against the best of the FPS genre today and hold its ground, and the Source engine allows the physics elements to shine. The story is okay, neither amazing in and of itself nor a hindrance. I give it a 9/10 and highly recommend giving it a go for anybody like me who hasn't played it yet and is skeptical of all the hype.

There is so much that made me want to love this game. However, the strength system is horribly unbalanced heavily favoring units like warhawks while units like archers have little recourse once an enemy is upon them. Couple this with the fact that units you invest in can very abruptly die via text menu decisions and you've laid the path for a brutally unlikable experience. I'm also not terribly fond of the inability to move after issuing a command nor am I fond of chain battles when there isn't any sort of healing. Not being able to move through my own units was also not well thought out.
While you can advance units by spending Renown on them it quickly becomes expensive and the stat points you're allowed to allocate are sparse at best. Couple this with the fact that a unit can leave or die at any time and I have to wonder why anyone would bother. As well, the save system is janky as hell. Want to save and come back whenever you like? Too bad - you're back at the start of the chapter. I guess now you can maybe stop that party member from abruptly dying. Sloppy decisions. It's a shame - the game is beautiful.

I was surprised by the jump in quality from CoD1 to CoD2, #2 is such a leap forward that it crystalized everything in the single player which all future CoD games would follow.  The formula is all here: you play multiple random grunts, with continuous side characters who are invincible (unless you kill them), an emphasis on cinematic, high-octane action scenes, regenerating health, highly funneled navigation paths, and repetitive shootout encounters where hordes of cloned opposition troops sit in defensive positions and plink at you 'till you whittle them away. The formula is so well worn that my interest was only held in the environmental details that separated one battlefield from another.
The big problem with single player is you're always aware you are playing a GAME, with game conventions, but the game demands you suspend disbelief and play like it's real.  It doesn't work and it gets tiresome when you know other games let your skill have greater impact on the events.

"I reject your reality and substitute it with my own!"
This would be a fitting tagline for this game. The physics don't make sense, the track design is ridiculous, and most of the things you're going to should be impossible.
In other words - it's nothing but mindless fun. Give your cortex some time off and let your brain stem take over.
Good music (several licensed songs, well chosen), fast driving, acceptable graphics, easy gameplay once you get comfortable with it.
Which will likely take some time - at first you may think the game responds weirdly, and the blurred graphics are disorienting.
Still, once you start jumping down a ledge, down being about 50 meters, or use an opportunity to race atop a speeding train, you'll see the game is well worth the few drawbacks it has.
(The only real drawback is the lack of online play. Once it worked. Now all that is left is LAN, apparently...)
The single player campaign consists of a tournament with quite a number of races. Unfortunately the number of tracks is rather limited (14), and several share segments. After a while they repeat, since they're grouped into regions (for the races).
To offset this, each race has "mutators", which change the way the race works - for example, in one race you may have continuous boost, while in another you can't hurt another player.
Which can be quite a drawback, as the game clearly intends for you to win races, not friends. When someone is trying to overtake you - bump them. Ideally, they crash and you get 30% boost fuel.
Land on someone after a jump? 100% boost fuel!
Don't worry for them, as you'll see when you crash (and you will, believe me), all that happens is that you respawn a few seconds later.
You can customize your vehicle somewhat - by winning races you unlock parts and paintjobs - different parts will give different benefits, so you might want to check that carefully.
The track design, which I described as "ridiculous" above, is actually quite fancy - it just doesn't make any sense whatsoever.
The tracks are clearly marked - you cannot escape the track, unfortunately - but they lead you across an active train track sometimes, or right through a hot-air-balloon festival.
On one track, part of the physical track is held in the air by helicopters even. (They change altitude, btw.)
Mindless fun.
Fast fun.
Fun.

Quick review: It's an amazing game and you should totally buy it worth every cent
Long-ish review: This game is amzing, but it's not without it's flaws.  I'll go over the good and the bad in this review
First the good: The game is extremely addicting you could pump hours and hours into this game as I hope to one day. IT IS HARD, know this going in and be preapred for brutal losses and crushing defeats. Never the less if you are a fan of hard♥♥♥♥♥games than this is the game for you. The combat is fast-paced, but not dumbed down. The game is more action-focused, but it is still a deep tactical game that will force you to make tough decisions and sacrifices. There are amazing stories to be had. I'm not talking about the in-game story (though it is still good) I'm talking about the personal stories. Stories about that sniper who took down three mutons and a cyber-disk single-handed, and the time your "rambo" got killed but took three berserkes down with him. The character customization is amazing, though some is locked to DLC. Finally the game is rewarding. You fell so good as you after a mission where you took no damage and killed like 20 aliens, and when you FINALLY built that plasma rifle and equiped it to your favorite unit. Overall great game but it's not perfect.
The Bad: It is HARD. "Didn't you put this on the good list" you are probably asking yourself. Yes I did BUT this could turn a few players off so be warned. The game has a few bugs, most of them mainly related to graphics but some do affect gameplay. Tha amount of luck involved in the game is annoying. You could have perfect tactics but still lose a few soldiers due to random chance. Overall a few minor problems, but nothing TOO extreme.
Final rating: 9/10. Thanks for reading this review.

Amazing game! It's extremely difficult, but once you figure out how to attack and defend, it becomes much easier. However, it gets progressively more difficult the farther you move along in space and the final boss is no push over. Also, with the "Infinite Space" mod, it adds a whole new way to play this game. Instead of being worried about being chased by the Rebel fleet (no not the peace loving ones from Star Wars), you can free roam around space until you eventually are murdered in a very crushing way. The only problem with the mod is that it has a weird difficulty spike not too long after you start. The music is also a fantastic part of this game and really adds a something extra incredible to it. It's both intense when you're in combat and very peaceful when just hovering around space. one thing that you should be warned of are the random events that happen through your journey. You may be that guy/girl who really likes to help everyone you come across, but sometimes, if you help that random stranger, you'll either get damaged or you could even lose a crew member, which is devestating. Your crew is your most important part about this, other than the ship itself of course. The best way to win a fight is to assign each person to a specific section on the ship and have them monitor/ repair it. If you don't, well then your weapons won't charge up fast enough, or you won't have enough evade skill to dodge a missile, so it really helps if you have someone at each section or at least the most important ones to stay alive. Overall, I would strongly reccomend this to anyone who really likes a good strategy game with a high difficulty and also someone who has always wanted to command their own ship and fell like somebody out of Star Trek.

I have spent the last month of my gaming history pretty much exclusively playing this, and every moment of it was a blast! The game blends RPG elements with Empire building and real-time combat in a convincing and realistic medieval world (extremely rare in the genre!).
Unlike most games M&B doesn't even try to hide the darker aspects of the middle ages but embraces them: women don't have anything to say, the aristocracy reigns supreme and slavery is everywhere. Human life is cheap, and you are a foreigner who has yet to make a name for him/her self when you start your adventure in the fictonal land of Calradia.
You will find no elves, trolls or magic spells in this game. You will find a grim world modelled after Europe and parts of the middle east and Asia in the Dark Ages. The adventruring/empire management interface is clunky, but the battles are truly brutal. Especially castle sieges are good fun. Expect to see your character covered in arrows and gore at the end of the battle!

My relationship with this game brings me back to Dragon Age: Origins. I'm not an old school PC RPG player, so I don't have any stories about Baldur's Gate or Planescape. Regardless, this is probably the best RPG to be released since Origins and has captured more of my time than I can scarcely begin to understand. The gameplay lends itself to thought and thankfully doesn't hold your hand with quest markers, flickering trails to the next objective or obvious build decisions. If you're not a veteran of the genre the game is going to sock you in the face over and over again, but it feels so good when you do finally learn to dodge the punch. Encounters, especially with bosses, seem unfair at the outset when they pit your 2 to 4 man group up against 5, 6 or 7+ enemies. A little element mixing and ingenuity can see two turns tilt a battle in your favor or bad positioning have you reloading in a heartbeat. You can use mages to deal massive AOE damage by combining elements such as fire and poison for huge explosions or catering to a melee character with massive magic buffs to create a massive wrecking ball. There's a certain level of sarcasm and wit peppered into the dialogue along with pop culture references that can bring a smile to the face without really overwhelming. Good music, nice looking areas--it's definitely worthy of all of the great reviews it's been getting. In a few weeks I'll probably have a 100+ hours into this and I'll still be coming back for more. There's even frickin' multiplayer, with rock-paper-scissor arguements that can come up between players on how to handle quest decisions. If you don't have a friend you can set your AI partner's behavior and experience two main characters disagreeing. It's fantastic. Oh, you can rob entire towns blind, too.

This is what a computer game should be - great fun (who doesn't love vapourising a 2 metre tall human look-alike reptilian with a plasma sniper rifle), challenging (oh that floaty alien thing in the red bath robe is inside my head and, oh, did I just shoot my own squaddie?), easy to get into (time in the tutorial until you see a casualty literally shredded :30 seconds - time until you see a body that looks like it lost a fight with a 'chest-burster' from Alien: 45 seconds - time until an ET is shooting super heated green goo at you: 90 seconds) , intuitive interface, variety of things to do (kill, capture, rescue, explore missions, build items and facilities, air defence interludes, upgrade most things, hire, heal, promote and development soldiers etc etc along with a nice collection of cut scenes and 'background' characters.
It's a little bit of everything but at the same time not an awful lot of anything. One of the great beauties of the game lies in its balance of giving you a variety of tasks (military, engineering, scientific and political) to simultaneously carry out when you only have the resources to do less than half of what is needed forcing irreversible decisions to be made and consequences to be faced. Having said that what is required will not take you hours to do. Character development for example is fairly simple, yet rewarding - don't expect a Skyrim type character development tree with myriads of levels and skills to work on requiring endless hours of game time (although I love Skyrim for this!) , the same is true for weapons, armour, air defences etc - the changes and advances you can make are limited in number but significant and amazingly rewarding.
At the heart of the game is the tactical infantry combat pitting your initially small squad  of rookies against a variety of alien creatures bent on wrecking Earth's cities and countryside. Your squad size will vary depending on your rank, training, who is wounded, who is dead and whether or not you can afford or want some new recruits. The maps you fight on are quite varied and largely destructible, and the tactics you use are centred around the concept of finding cover (from the above mentioned super heated green goo). Don't expect COH style detail or grittiness, but there is lot here that is compelling.
The downsides are there - the squad voice acting is probably the worst of it and the maps, while fairly numerous and different, do all have a sameness about them after a while, but these are minor issues.
But enough of my rant. At the end of the day, this game is just pure FUN. It was engaging, varied and a great way to spend a couple of hours when you have an urgent need to vapourise an alien invader who desperately needs it.

I like a lot of what The Banner Saga has to offer. The art, with its elegant simplicity, works well with the lore.  The musical score is superb. The world- unexplored as it is- offers a fantasy setting without resorting to the most standard orcs vs. elves that  we've come to expect. The choices were interesting and the narrative was generally impressive, even if it was also generally linear.
But there are things that don't click with me. First, the combat system. This is bad news, because the player  spends the most actual playing time in combat. The choice to make health the same as strength is interesting and makes sense in a  world where foes bash each other. But the developers departed from most games in another way, in that initiative is  given to each team alternately. When it's six on six, that's fine. But when you've taken out a couple of the  enemies, all of the sudden they're getting a huge advantage in attacks per round. This gaming mechanic has some unfortunate consequences:
- Attrition is unbalanced. Even if you pluck off the enemies one-by-one using great tactics, the remaining two will hammer  your troops at a high rate. You are punished for winning. Furthermore there are enemy abilities that can be used to take out friendlies no matter what the enemy's health level (like that stupid bloody flail). The whole system is artificially biased towards the enemies killing your guys.
- Enemy 'grenade' style weapons become overpowered as there is no way to avoid them since their fuse is based on the enemy's turn.
- The attrition means that the end of a battle, there's a good chance your guys have been wounded. This is made  worse with the 'second battle' option, if you take it (and it's important for resources). Either way, you'll be expected  to fight another battle soon but it's hard with wounded warriors in your roster.
- It makes it very difficult to level up lower units. Using this system having lower-level units in battle is  actually worse than having no extra unit at all. Since you don't get to face the easiest enemies much past the very  early portion you have to game things to make sure your low unit gets the 'kill' since that's the only way to gain  experience (not through wounding, healing, etc). Since units only advance through fighting (AND by spending resources) this messes with the whole thing. I also am not a fan of having the same resources for everything including leveling as it just doesn't make much sense and tends to lead to min-maxing rather than a more organic increase in skills.
The alternating turn is a poor game mechanic that is very counter-intuitive. Instead of isolating and killing enemies the useful  tactic is to wound them down to 1 'strength' so they can't do much damage. This is so 'gamey' that it breaks all immersion for me. The worst situation is when an enemy (or two in the same round!) uses his "Tremble" ability to call for a fully powered reinforcement unit and you can't stop him because of the alternating system.
Aggro is obscured. Some characters have abilities to buff their defense but enemies will just ignore them... unless you get lucky and then everyone gangs up on them. Seems to be random except that the enemy will always try and kill someone if they can (like your squishy archers). Maybe it's just not well explained, but that's a problem in and of itself.
There's also problems with the "supply" system in the game, in that it doesn't seem meaningful except as a money-sink. You have a caravan  you are in charge of, but which you don't really control. You can buy supplies to keep people from starving, but  the only effects of starving are lowered morale and less people in the caravan (which means less supplies needed!).  I suppose you lose if everyone in the caravan dies (edit: apparently not according to other posters), but other than that it just feels like a number with no effect  on the main game. Since you can't know how many days of supplies you need in most cases, it's only purpose is to  muddy the waters and doesn't add anything of use I could recognize except to burn currency that could better be spent strategically on known issues. Furthermore one of the two caravans is ridiculously underprovisioned.
Finally, the plot and characters. I hate to say it, but both feel wide and shallow (especially characters). Some of the  heroes are  well established and fleshed out. The father-daughter relationship in one of the two parties is particularly good,  for example; I made decisions based on it which I otherwise would have avoided. Many of the characters are just a  face and stat set, though. I like the player having more choices (I loved the Jagged Alliance series!) but  in this game it just feels empty to have these fellows with little or no characterization standing around.
As to the plot,  there's a lot of moving parts that might make more sense as the story develops but it feels disjointed at present. A journal is badly needed but missing. This story is largely linear, imaginary 'choices' notwithstanding. One of the most annoying examples was when the game  forces the player to 'play' an unwinnable battle. It might be my pet peeve, but I hate this trope. If you need to enforce cutscene incompetence,  put it in a cutscene and don't make the player bang his or her head against a wall.
Oh, I almost forgot: the save system sucks. It saves at the start of chapters and then has one autosave slot. Hit the wrong button and the game saves? Welp, you're screwed. Didn't realize that a dialogue choice would mean something entirely different than you intended? Screwed. You can go back several battles if you want... and then it'll quickly autosave to make sure you can't reverse THAT either (found that out the hard way!).  I'm sure some people don't want a manual save for whatever reason. Luckily for those people they always have the option to not use it. Unfortunately in this game there is no option to have one for the rest of us who don't have or want to spend hours to replay chapters. Shame on the developers for doing that.
I can't help but be drawn into the story and I really like parts of this game... but there are some basic issues that need to be worked out. The idea that each side should alternate attacks regardless of casualties is 'different'... but being different is not good in this case. The gimped save system doesn't even have 'innovation' as an excuse and is simply unpardonable. I really hope they reconsider these issues for the next game.

Hardcore indie retro platformers and time-attack games have been a dime a dozen for years now, but I'm extremely pleased to share that JumpJet Rex is among the very best I've ever had the pleasure of playing.
To save the Earth from a deadly asteroid, you'll find yourself loose in a number of (mostly) bite-size levels in which you, a space-faring, rocket-boot-wearing T-Rex, must propel yourself through low gravity around obstacles and enemies, passing through a set number of golden rings to unlock the exit. You can combat enemies (and interact with some obstacles) with both Rex's spin attack and, cleverly, the emissions from your rocket boots. You earn stars by completing the level and, optionally, by doing so without dying and/or doing so within a challenging time constraint. The progression scheme is reminiscent of Super Mario 64 - you choose non-linearly from an assortment of levels until you have enough stars to unlock the boss battle, and beating the boss unlocks a new assortment of levels, and so on. Coins scattered around the levels can be exchanged for a plethora of cosmetic items and color schemes for Rex, and easter-egg-style "treasures" encourage pushing the envelopes of the level designs and finding ways to explore out of bounds. Couch co-op (!!) is available if you don't wanna go it alone.
The controls are tight and responsive - Rex does what you input, when you input it, nothing more, nothing less. Controls make or break a game like this, and it's refreshing to feel a game get it so right.
The graphics are of the familiar SNES-era cutesy pixel fare; Rex's design especially stands out as charming and appealing.
The game is both challenging enough (in level design) and forgiving enough (plenty of checkpoints) to appeal to most players interested in this sort of game. But the additional challenges offered are where JumpJet Rex really, truly shines. If you want JumpJet Rex to be
hard, it'll step up to the plate and bare its teeth in no time. The game is fairly short, but earning all the stars in the game is no small feat - no-death level runs and especially time-attack level runs get absolutely brutal, but never artificially so. No random agents of death - what you see is what you get, and if you die it's your own damn fault! Just how I like it! Online time-attack leaderboards ensure that there's always a time to beat, propelling the replay value to phenomenal levels. And if that isn't enough for you, RageQuit Rex mode tasks you with completing the entire game on just three lives. Good luck with that.
Aside from the couch co-op, multiplayer Arena and Dino Race modes are available; I have not yet had the chance to experience them well enough to assess here.
The soundtrack consists of well-crafted true-to-hardware chiptune, which is admirable, fitting, and sounds great. That said, though, to me the tunes were less memorable than I'd have expected considering the notable talent involved. Personal taste only - there's nothing at all objectively wrong with it, and you may well find that the tunes stick with you more than they did to me!
The boss fights that keep the gates to the next levels are underwhelming when you figure out that the devs intend for you to cheese them to get that time attack star, and indeed every boss in the game can be cheesed disproportionately easily. Fortunately there are few of them, and even cheesing them is admittedly fun.
Though the game gives you a radar to locate the rings you must collect, there are a few levels that were designed with what I felt was an excessive amount of non-linearity in order to get you mixed up and lost. Though, again, they are few and far between, they were the only ones I didn't particularly look forward to replaying.
On that note, this game cries out very, very loudly for a level editor. As I understand it, the resources just weren't there, and more than two years out from release, it’s not likely to happen. That's too bad. I certainly can't hold it against the game or its developers.
Overall, do I recommend JumpJet Rex? Well, yes! Very much so. I can't remember the last time I played a game of this genre that was as satisfying and such an apparent labor of love as this one. If you're into this sort of game, absolutely give it a spin!

Robot Entertainment have produced a slick action game here based around the popular tower defence genre. This game follows the traditional tower defence script of building traps to stop a constant stream of enemy foe but introduces player spells and weapons to assist.
Far from becoming confused the game merges the 2 styles effortlessly, there are occasions when building an intricate series of diversions and traps is the order of the day and other times when equipping your poking stick and some fire gauntlets is required to smite the raging hordes.
The game follows a steady learning curve, those new to tower defense games will be handheld throughout the first stages and with the game introducing new skills and abilities as you go along you will never feel overwhelmed at the pace.
The games real charm rests in the war mage himself, the character story is developed via cut scenes between levels, he's equipped with a few witty one liners that he will dole out at various times and you cant help but like the guy!
The graphics are good, the music is solid and atmospheric . Some people will play through it once but with the introduction of the "skull ranking" system many will replay the levels in order to 5 skull them. In this game skulls mean upgrades and upgrades means more dead orcs! ... This game takes its place as one of the best tower defence games available today. With the announcement of a sequel on the way things are looking good for Robot Entertainment.

Even though JumpJet Rex seems like just another indie pixel platformer, its raison d'être is based on its spotless execution regarding balance, gameplay and style. This is a game that noticeably improves player skill without being too easy or too punishing.
The pixel graphics are cute and colourful with beautiful, almost mesmerising particle effects. There are a few visual bugs on walls, making them overlap awkwardly. But apart from that, the art design is clear and only requires some familiarisation with different hitboxes. Apposite to its visual presentation, its background music consists of a set of lively chiptune pieces, rounding off the overall impression.
Gameplay wise, JumpJet Rex manages to hold the balance between moments of frustration and the drive to improve. It's less a game of reflexes and more of timing, evaluation and muscle memory. The controls initially seem floaty, but really are tight, precise and responsive after the first few minutes of play. Most importantly though, there's no random ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Every situation is solvable and learning how to cope with difficult enemies or levels always feels like a great success. The momentum that builds during a run is rewarding in itself.
JumpJet Rex is simply a good platformer.

The expansion introduces a few new enemies, new soldier upgrades (mecs, genetics) by way of Meld, a new enemy human faction called Exalt which is reminiscent of the "Cult of Sirius" from XCOM: Apocalypse, new environments and new government missions.

I wanted to finish it to fully get it off my mind - but it wasn't a pleasant experience, sadly.
If you're sure that you personally would enjoy the game, get it for your phone - game is better in bursts because the gameplay is very, very stale. Little more about this in the last paragraph.
The good: game has countless references, nice (but mostly stationary) pixelart, and makes quite a few jokes about RPG tropes.
On the other hand the game is incredibly grindy, the endgame turns way too slow even if you just focus on taking down the enemy with max damage, and even slower if you cheese it to reduce the health and mana loss of each battle.
And the gameplay solely consists of fighting - move to a location with a chance of being attacked, then get a few lines of text and a quest to protect something (waves of enemies) escort them from A to B (attacked each location) kill X enemies or kill enemies until you get Z loot.
Additionally, as your party won't change during the game (you can get new party members, but they always start at level 1, who is instakilled by level 10ish enemies - mid-lategame scales around level 25-35) each and every fight of yours will be the same. Almost all the time you fight one type of enemies, and the characters of yours have only 2 viable type of damage each tops, so the game's hint about choosing damage based on weaknesses is just bullsh*t.
In my case each fight went druid made an enemy fall asleep for 6ish rounds, mage could stun one for 2 rounds, warrior, and if needed cleric debuffed the attack of the enemy and then paladin-warrior-cleric did some damage, while druid supporting them and mage doing fireball/stun every other round. And this was the gameplay since 1/3 of the game, with exactly zero change.
While other RPGs also offer similarly repetitive combat, the limited 4 hardcoded (and usually 1 being absolutely useless) ability on each role limits tactics, turning the game into oversimplified choices - if they deal too much damage, debuff 3 with cleric. If someone's hurt, heal. If not, smite on the focused enemy.
So again, the game is a flavour-text supported repetitive, unimaginative combat, from the first minute until the last, literally. I can not recommend the game to be played on PC because there are way better games available ; but I do recommend you trying to play KoP&P on your phone on the go. Cheaper, controls better and fits the platform better. Or try the second one - while it's openly free to play with MT. on phones, it has more depth and variety as this one.

What an entertaining game!!!  I haven’t had this much fun in a game for a while.  Not safe to play around the kids, lots of violence and language - but in a hilarious way.  I paid $20 for it, and SR4 was worth every penny.  I definitely will play through it again at a later date to explore more and find what I’ve missed.  I haven't played any of the previous SR titles but after this I want to try them.
SR4 is basically a mix of gameplay from GTA and Batman Arkham City, wrapped up in a Matrix-like story.  You are trapped in a virtual environment, which gives great story-based excuse to randomly destroy stuff, run over people, and also have super powers (as opposed to GTA where you just do it to be an a$$).
The game has an excellent soundtrack, hilariously woven in with the missions and story (youtube: “Saints Row nuclear Aerosmith”).  At a later point in time after rescuing a homie, you and he are battling through hordes of bad guys together to the tune of “The Boys are Back in Town.”
The story itself is fun and quite entertaining, and gives you the opportunity to fight with your superpowers in the virtual world, then without them in the real world.  You get to save humanity, fight aliens, struggle to save your friends, and “romance” (f!ck) them afterwards, if you so choose.  You’ll leap over tall buildings (or run up them), smash into the ground to damage everything in the area, throw fire, ice and shoot electricity, use telekensis to pick up and throw vehicles, and cause general mayhem and destruction in order to crash the virtual simulation so you can break out your homies and take down the aliens that run it all.
Graphics are pretty good, nothing groundbreaking but more than sufficient to make the game look nice.  The gameplay and sounds are excellent.  The voice acting is superb, the characters are fun and believable, and you have a multitude of options for your character aside from the usual physical customizations, including different voice styles and tones.  You can even select “the scroob” (SpaceBalls) as your gang’s “thing” they do to taunt.
One comment about DLC’s – there are tons available for this game, but all they do is add more (themed) costumes and weapons.  The game already has lots of choices for costumes and weapons.  I want to buy a DLC that gives me more story to play through.
The story, gameplay and audio make this game superb.  Its high ratings and reviews are well earned.

This game is great, and it's outrageous value for money. There are only two buttons, left and right (initially just to move in the corresponding direcition, but you can eventually double tap them, and hold them both at the same time, for new abilities as you unlock them).
The game thus has one of the easiest control schemes in PC gaming, but the perfectly tuned difficulty curve quickly makes sure that you will be tapping those buttons like they're going out of fashion. By the end of it you will be pulling off maneuvres that you will look back on in awe, occasionally while being chased by an angry fireball that makes sure you're not getting too comfortable.
It took me around 4 hours to complete the main story (I'm now working my way through the DLC) and according the credits I died 1200+ times trying. But that's not a problem, because the checkpoint placement is great, so even though you will occasionally scream at your screen with rage, you never have to repeat more than necessary for a given section as you try to master it.
Only downside would be that beause there's no map, I did occasionally struggle to work out where I was meant to go next, especially when going back to earlier areas to find some previous obstacle after I received a new ability that would let me get past it. But that's nitpicking, the game is fantastic.
Buy the bundle with the DLC as after you complete the main game you will be wanting more, and the DLC ups the difficulty curve even more, but in line with where you finished the main game.

Below is how I think the meeting went when Saints Row IV was pitched
"Hey, you know how Saints Row the Third was brilliant is it's hilarity and added new characters that people love to bits now?"
"Yes..."
"Well, I think if we added aliens and the ability to shoot fire from your hands, it would be better"
"That's brilliant!"
As a Saints Row fan since the first installment came out, where I'd spend hours of my time picking my way through Vice Kings and Westside Rollerz, I greatly anticipated Saints Row IV's release and when I finally got to play it, what did I find? The exact same game as Saints Row the Third, except you have super powers now and also the Earth blew up. Yes, the ability to jump higher then a squirril on crack riding a pogo stick IS fun, and yes I did find the power to freeze enemies useful when I was overwhelmed, but Saints Row IV was, largely, an expansion pack to Saints Row the Third. Most of the same characters are there, or can be unlocked using DLC content, and there are three versions of Shaundi with a DLC add-on. A past one, a present one and a future one. I get that Shaundi's popular, but I think that went a bit overboard.
Gameplay wise, Saints Row sticks to the way it was in Saints Row the Third, with a third-person outlook on the world so you can admire your character's tushie. The powers, however, are the only thing that really changed. They ad interesting ways to combat different scenarios, but I felt sometimes they were overpowered. I get that you are SUPPOSED to be overpowered in the game, but you at least want SOME challenge. Hopefully. The main thing I had was whenever a spaceship started attacking, I could just hurl a freeze attack at it and it was an instant kill. When I discovered this, I ABUSED the hell out of it like a honeymooner's mattress, but once my powers grew to gigantic levels, combat was too easy, far easier than it should have been.
I did, however, laugh at some of the lines of the characters, particularly those from CID, the floating eye robot. I believe that the characters develop somewhat, and the return of a favourite was a highlight that made me smile my head off, but the characters largely remain the same in Saints Row IV, where Pierce is whiney and Shaundi's a ♥♥♥♥♥.
All good games are built with the following line. Beginning, middle and end. The beginning was great, where you're the President and you get to make decisions about fighting cancer or abolishing world hunger, then the world gets attacked by aliens and suddenly your shooting spaceships in the name of Uncle Sam! The middle was good as well, where it stole elements from Mass Effect in the form of loyalty missions, which if you completed, made the crew super as well. The end, though, really did not feel right for me. If you're one of those people who goes "God damn, why did you spoil it?!", look away now.
(spoiler start)
In the final battle, you go through this spaceship blowing up scene, then you divebomb down into the bad guy's ship, blow him up, then take over his empire. You find the world can't be saved, but going back in time is possible!
(spoiler end)
All in all, Saints Row IV is that alternative to Grand Theft Auto V, where you prefer just doing crazy stuff rather then aactually breaking the law properly (hell, you can drive around in a car that has flamethrowers attached to it). Saints Row IV, though, needed more to be great, it needed to have an ended that made everything worth it, and it needed to feel like a game in it's own right, not just an expansion pack. Still, though, it's fun and you should play it!

Divinity: Original Sin is a Balder's Gate-esque roleplaying game where you are sent to uncover a mysterious killer in the town of Cyseal, but what you find has consequences which affect the entire world.
Divinity is a fantastic game. Absolutely amazing. It has been #1 on Steam since it's launch for a reason: it's incredibly good.
I spent 90 hours fully completing the game, and enjoyed it all.
Divinity is a roleplaying game in the truest sense. When you talk to someone, or learn a new bit of info, it gets added to your journal, but that's it. There's no quest objectives, no drive, it's up to you and you alone to figure out what to do. You wanna investigate the scene of a murder, okay, what do you do? Really, think about it, what's your first move? Then, you do it in-game!
There's no hand-holding, no hints or tips, it's pure logic and it's incredibly enjoyable and satisfying.
There are some bugs, but Larian have been releasing patches almost twice a week fixing the little odds and ends which cause issue. Throughout the entire 90 hours of play, I encountered only 1 bug I would consider "annoying", so I think that says a lot.
Pick up this title if you like the sound of it. I must add the gameplay is fun and easy, the turnbased system. The story is engaging and interesting, with some great and coherent voice acting throughout, and the game just looks fantastic from the get go.

Mirror's Edge is very unique game with really interesting and beautiful setting and premise, scarred by weirdly inconsistent game mechanics and an almost insultingly short campaign/story.
The game takes place in an unnamed city set in the near future with clearly hightened levels of police activity and surveillance. Just by reading the posters/bulletins/public service announcements it is clear that you could describe it as dystopian. It is in this city that you play as Faith, a mysterious "Runner" who left home at an early age after her mother was killed in a protest turned riot. I won't go much further in the story as to not ruin the whole thing.
THE POSITIVES:
The game has an absolutely amazing atmosphere and minimalist aesthetic. It's almost indescribable. For a game from 2009 it definitely has its pretty moments as well. The score is great, including "Still Alive" by Lisa Miskovsky, which you could say is the game's theme (on a side note, CHVRCHES' released "Warning Call", the theme for Mirror's Edge Catalyst and it's absolutely phenomenal) There is something about the setting that really makes you feel like you're in the middle of something important. It's unexplainable but as I played it I really felt like there was something more to the city, and constantly wanted to explore beyond each level's boundaries. There is a fairly modest cast of characters, each with a pretty decent design, at least I felt like they all weren't too samey looking, but at the same time they fit with the game's aesthetic. One thing I would like to say is that despite the game not going very deep into Faith's backstory, something makes me care about her and I really want to learn more about her in Catalyst.
The gameplay itself (When it works, but I'll get to that) is really fun, especially once you get going and get a good momentum. When you really get into it and you're hopping, climbing, sliding, and swinging at a pretty fast pace, it really  makes you feel like some kind of parkour ninja.
The combat *works*, however I have some gripes, and I'll get those it later.  You can disarm enemies as well as take them down with miscellaneous martial arts moves. It feels pretty bad♥♥♥♥♥to run up on 3 or 4 fully armed riot police, activating the slow motion, stealing one's assault rifle, knocking him out, and mowing down the rest, all in the course of a few seconds.
The voice acting is fairly decent, nothing to write home about, but it's far from "bad".
The game runs well on any modern system, however the in game v-sync is virtually broken so you'll have to force it in Nvidia Control Panel or whatever the AMD equivalent is.
I think I've just about covered the bases, now for the bad...
THE NEGATIVES:
DICE made a game with a stunning aesthetic, an interesting setting, and a decent main character. HOWEVER, this game is RIDICULOUSLY short. You can beat this game in like 4 hours. That's right. And if you are really good at it I'd wager you could finish it in 3 hours. Which really sucks because with the setting there could have been so much more done, and the character development is virtually nonexistant besides for a little bite of Faith's backstory. The story itself is very uneventful. I honestly don't have much to say about it other than it's really nothing special. There's a pretty big plot twist about halfway through the game which you would think would be a big deal, but you literally just leave the area and it's never mentioned again at all. I really hate when this♥♥♥♥♥♥happens because it's such a unique premise and again such a beautiful setting but doesn't have a story to match.
As I said, The combat leaves a LOT to be desired. Like it's pretty basic. Run up to enemy, punch until he dies, take his gun and shoot other enemies. Or, run up to enemy, hit Y when the gun flashes red, and rinse and repeat. It would be cool to see them maybe incorporate some of the taketown type melee things from the Far Cry series just to spice it up, but that's just a thought.
Okay, now to gameplay gripes. I can't tell you how many times I lined up a jump, or a ledge grab, executed it, and Faith flat did not grab the ledge and fell to her death, even when I did everything right. It really breaks any momentum you get and gets frustrating as hell after it happens 3-4 times in the same chapter.
The game's broken v-sync was fairly annoying, as I said earlier I was able to fix it but it's still a complaint.
Overall, simply because I'm in LOVE with the game's beautiful minimalistic art style/setting, and relaxing yet emotional ambient OST, I'd have to give it a 7/10. I really hope Mirror's Edge Catalyst dives deeper into the characters and general world-building. Ultimately I had a fun albeit short experience, but Mirror's Edge honestly left me wanting to know more about this mysterious city and the people who live in it.

I like a lot of what The Banner Saga has to offer. The art, with its elegant simplicity, works well with the lore.  The musical score is superb. The world- unexplored as it is- offers a fantasy setting without resorting to the most standard orcs vs. elves that  we've come to expect. The choices were interesting and the narrative was generally impressive, even if it was also generally linear.
But there are things that don't click with me. First, the combat system. This is bad news, because the player  spends the most actual playing time in combat. The choice to make health the same as strength is interesting and makes sense in a  world where foes bash each other. But the developers departed from most games in another way, in that initiative is  given to each team alternately. When it's six on six, that's fine. But when you've taken out a couple of the  enemies, all of the sudden they're getting a huge advantage in attacks per round. This gaming mechanic has some unfortunate consequences:
- Attrition is unbalanced. Even if you pluck off the enemies one-by-one using great tactics, the remaining two will hammer  your troops at a high rate. You are punished for winning. Furthermore there are enemy abilities that can be used to take out friendlies no matter what the enemy's health level (like that stupid bloody flail). The whole system is artificially biased towards the enemies killing your guys.
- Enemy 'grenade' style weapons become overpowered as there is no way to avoid them since their fuse is based on the enemy's turn.
- The attrition means that the end of a battle, there's a good chance your guys have been wounded. This is made  worse with the 'second battle' option, if you take it (and it's important for resources). Either way, you'll be expected  to fight another battle soon but it's hard with wounded warriors in your roster.
- It makes it very difficult to level up lower units. Using this system having lower-level units in battle is  actually worse than having no extra unit at all. Since you don't get to face the easiest enemies much past the very  early portion you have to game things to make sure your low unit gets the 'kill' since that's the only way to gain  experience (not through wounding, healing, etc). Since units only advance through fighting (AND by spending resources) this messes with the whole thing. I also am not a fan of having the same resources for everything including leveling as it just doesn't make much sense and tends to lead to min-maxing rather than a more organic increase in skills.
The alternating turn is a poor game mechanic that is very counter-intuitive. Instead of isolating and killing enemies the useful  tactic is to wound them down to 1 'strength' so they can't do much damage. This is so 'gamey' that it breaks all immersion for me. The worst situation is when an enemy (or two in the same round!) uses his "Tremble" ability to call for a fully powered reinforcement unit and you can't stop him because of the alternating system.
Aggro is obscured. Some characters have abilities to buff their defense but enemies will just ignore them... unless you get lucky and then everyone gangs up on them. Seems to be random except that the enemy will always try and kill someone if they can (like your squishy archers). Maybe it's just not well explained, but that's a problem in and of itself.
There's also problems with the "supply" system in the game, in that it doesn't seem meaningful except as a money-sink. You have a caravan  you are in charge of, but which you don't really control. You can buy supplies to keep people from starving, but  the only effects of starving are lowered morale and less people in the caravan (which means less supplies needed!).  I suppose you lose if everyone in the caravan dies (edit: apparently not according to other posters), but other than that it just feels like a number with no effect  on the main game. Since you can't know how many days of supplies you need in most cases, it's only purpose is to  muddy the waters and doesn't add anything of use I could recognize except to burn currency that could better be spent strategically on known issues. Furthermore one of the two caravans is ridiculously underprovisioned.
Finally, the plot and characters. I hate to say it, but both feel wide and shallow (especially characters). Some of the  heroes are  well established and fleshed out. The father-daughter relationship in one of the two parties is particularly good,  for example; I made decisions based on it which I otherwise would have avoided. Many of the characters are just a  face and stat set, though. I like the player having more choices (I loved the Jagged Alliance series!) but  in this game it just feels empty to have these fellows with little or no characterization standing around.
As to the plot,  there's a lot of moving parts that might make more sense as the story develops but it feels disjointed at present. A journal is badly needed but missing. This story is largely linear, imaginary 'choices' notwithstanding. One of the most annoying examples was when the game  forces the player to 'play' an unwinnable battle. It might be my pet peeve, but I hate this trope. If you need to enforce cutscene incompetence,  put it in a cutscene and don't make the player bang his or her head against a wall.
Oh, I almost forgot: the save system sucks. It saves at the start of chapters and then has one autosave slot. Hit the wrong button and the game saves? Welp, you're screwed. Didn't realize that a dialogue choice would mean something entirely different than you intended? Screwed. You can go back several battles if you want... and then it'll quickly autosave to make sure you can't reverse THAT either (found that out the hard way!).  I'm sure some people don't want a manual save for whatever reason. Luckily for those people they always have the option to not use it. Unfortunately in this game there is no option to have one for the rest of us who don't have or want to spend hours to replay chapters. Shame on the developers for doing that.
I can't help but be drawn into the story and I really like parts of this game... but there are some basic issues that need to be worked out. The idea that each side should alternate attacks regardless of casualties is 'different'... but being different is not good in this case. The gimped save system doesn't even have 'innovation' as an excuse and is simply unpardonable. I really hope they reconsider these issues for the next game.

Here’s a quick fact for you; it’s coming up to 12 years since the original release of Half Life 2. Yeah. Let that sink in for a moment.  In that time we’ve had not one, but two new generations of consoles; each with their own breakthrough franchises and classic titles, along with an endless stream of new innovations and experiences. Yet perhaps the most remarkable thing in those 12 years is just how well Half-Life 2 has withstood the test of time – and just how many things it just gets right.
For one, it’s incredible how atmospheric the game remains to this day. The visuals naturally don’t stand up to much scrutiny nowadays, but it doesn’t really matter, as the game still manages to suck you in just by the way it goes about presenting things. For instance, take the very start of the game, where you step off the train to be met with an endless army of faceless guards and flying security cameras, the overseer menacingly staring down at you as bystanders mutter to you desperately...  It really creates a very real sense of hopelessness and oppression, one that becomes satisfying to slowly break down as you play through the game. Thankfully, you slowly tool yourself up with a variety of weapons that all feel satisfying to use from beginning to end. That collection also includes the renowned gravity gun – a physics bending, item-flinging piece of kit that just never stops being entertaining to use. It’s so amazing that given the choice, I’d probably be picking it over a portal gun.

It’s also crazy that no matter how Valve shifts the gameplay around as the game rolls on, each new segment continues to feels as polished as the last. There’s high speed chases with some pulse pounding music, suspenseful scenes such as crawling along the narrow beams underneath a towering bridge, and much more. Even when the game suddenly shifts dramatically into doing horror it does it astonishingly well, as anyone who has played through Ravenholm (And heard the heart-stopping clicking of a poison headcrab nearby) will testify to. There are just so many classic moments to list that you could be there for a long while just trying to get them all down, and that’s not even an exaggeration.
If there’s any negatives, I think it’s fair to say that the story is perhaps showing its age somewhat. There’s nothing actually wrong with it – in fact, it’s still clever and compelling in its own right – it’s just that with so many games doing blockbuster epics or deep narratives so well nowadays, it’s a little jarring to go back to something where everyone just talks and reacts to your voiceless, emotionless husk. The AI, primarily when it comes to the followers you can recruit late in the game, can also prove a little bit of an issue, getting in your way when you least want them to. As far as I recall it’s an issue the game has had since launch day, but still, it’s nothing that will ever stop your enjoyment to any great extent.
Of course, it feels a little pointless to even review Half Life 2 at this point. Everything that needs to be said about it has probably already been said. But if you’re one of the very few that have never played the game... Well, you need to get on fixing that right now. Even if you have played it before, or done so on other formats (like myself), it’s still well worth a play through again, just to marvel at how entertaining it remains. Now all we need to do is wait for the third game to come out. Should be any day now...
