The most remarkable aspect of this game is presentation. From the soundtrack to the art direction to the interface, everything is immaculate and elegant. Nothing feels rough around the edges or half-finished as far as those elements go. The gameplay is unique- a combination of choose-your-own-adventure style frequent decision-making, an Oregan Trail-like survival and travel element that involves some resource management, and the battle system itself which involves tactical strategy and some interesting components like individual health and defense bars to attack, and the Varl race of characters who take up a lot of unit space in battle but have high attack power. There are so many characters to choose from during battle- as many as 20 are encountered by game's end and even character usage involves some decision-making as characters only level up by not only actively participating, but getting in a number of kills.
Now for some of the downsides- though there are such a plethora of options and routes to go on, nearly all lead toward the same end and plot points seem black and white in nature- you either picked the "right" answer leading to hidden items or a surplus in resources, or you picked the wrong one which can set you back in progress. But making wrong decisions matters little since the difficulty level is low until the end, and the initially interesting tactics-driven combat is actually quite simplified compared to other strategy RPGs. Aspects such as equipment management involve collecting numerous accessories and each character can hold just one. Character classes and stat allocation is similarly straightforward. On the bright side, that makes this title a great choice for those new to the genre and not very interested in micro-management.
The storyline is interesting and involved, but there is not much clarification of the lore. While the character and plot development is nicely done, it can be vague with some side characters receiving barely a line of exposition. While I compared the decision-making to a choose-your-own-adventure novel, it has nowhere near the verbosity of visual novels or many story-driven RPGs. The writing is of an appreciably high standard of quality though and the lack of meandering over any particular element (whether it be storytelling or the various types of gameplay present here) keeps the game fast-paced.
I achieved completion at around 10 hours and do feel there is some replay value here, but the general asking price ($24.99) is very high for this amount of content. I would suggest waiting for a sale of at least 30-50% off. The exception being if the subject matter is particularly riveting to you, in which case I'd say go ahead as it is likely to impress.

I finally played this game the whole way through, as I originally hit a spot that triggered a fatal error continuously, killing any desire to restart.
As this was my first time playing, I don't really have the rose colored glasses of nostalgia that tend to come with your average person that thinks this is the greatest game of all time. With that said, most of the game holds up very well. The gunplay is okay, with very few weapons being accurate at a distance. The gun variety is very good though, so if you want to play it as a traditional duck and cover shooter, that's a possibility. The things that make this game a true joy to play and a cut above the rest are the physics and, specifically, the Gravity Gun. Anything and everything that isn't bolted down can be used as a weapon, so long as it isn't obscenely heavy (a washing machine is about the largest thing you can toss across a room). The physics puzzles throughout are fun and rewarding to complete, and the Gravity Gun adds an extra dimension that features in several of the middle chapters.
As with most First Person Shooters these days, there is plenty of time devoted towards vehicles, which includes an airboat and a buggy, both of which are effectively on rails but are still fun for the limited time and give enough control and leeway to not have rage inducing spots that you just can't get by.
Another facet is the inclusion of squad commander type sections, where you can tell a group of 4 constantly respawning allies to go lay down their lives for Aiur. In some parts it can be very effective, and some parts they just seem to be there for cannon fodder and to get in your way. Alongside this, there is are a few small Tower Defense segments. The variety of gameplay elements in the game has a wide breadth without any segment becoming stale, with the physics and shooting apparent throughout the entirety of the game.

As I didn't play the original Half Life, the story didn't make much sense to me at all. After playing through the game several times in a few days, it still doesn't make much sense, but it was told in a way where not knowing won't cripple your enjoyment of the game. The final boss is rarely mentioned for much of the game, while the overarching enemy is completely faceless, which bothers me. I thought it was interesting, but didn't explain nearly enough for my tastes.
One thing that can't be overstated is that the missions don't overstay their welcome. Some games can just drag on and on and go from being fun to a grueling mess, but Half Life 2 is a solid 10 hours full of interesting content.

It's been a little over 10 years, but Half Life 2 is still a very solid game in this day and age. The gameplay can stand against the best of the FPS genre today and hold its ground, and the Source engine allows the physics elements to shine. The story is okay, neither amazing in and of itself nor a hindrance. I give it a 9/10 and highly recommend giving it a go for anybody like me who hasn't played it yet and is skeptical of all the hype.

Though the artwork and soundtrack are beautiful, it is heavily outweighed by a bland storyline. The characters you meet along the way should intertwine and create a ''rich story'', but I was left bored and waiting for the next fight. The Banner Saga has a great concept, but poor execution. Be cautious when purchasing this game.

To the person who loves this game and has loved it since it first came out, why are you reading a review?
To the person like me who had never played it and is considering buying it: Don't buy it at full price. While it's a fun game, it really isn't "the best game ever" or "amazing" like so many here have said. It's an older game that was, at one time, really unique and fresh but now is a bit stale and cumbersome.

An absolutely brilliant game that is a must-own for almost anyone, it’s endlessly replayable and presents a very distinct challenge. Its complexity doesn’t come from overwhelming the player – all the mistakes you make will be your own fault – it’s just brilliantly designed in that it requires instant critical thinking in battles and a thoughtful approach while traversing the galaxy and encountering unknown or enemy vessels. The perma-death element is what gives the game its replay value – a single session could last 15 minutes to two hours depending on your skill (and luck); dying in this game is really just a learning experience. The unlockables don’t necessarily make the game any easier and the only way you will advance further is by refining your approach. I find myself coming back to the game time and time again to see how far I can make it.

Knights of Pen and Paper is a simple, stream-lined rpg in the style of a table top rpg (ala, Dungeons and Dragons).
This game is a barebones RPG, you have five characters with four abilities to level up and then you fight in turn based combat.  It's a tad slow, a tad simple, and highly repetitive.  Despite this, there are two good qualities: experimenting with all the classes and combinations is quite fun and the game takes some time before becoming grind-y.
In addition to the base gameplay, there are a few other things going on.  A variety of quests which essentially all end up being just fighitng thigns over and over.  Different environments and enemies with a fun style.  A bunch of  flavor in the text.  And a "crafting system" that ends up just being collecting items to upgrade the blacksmith and pouring money into him to upgrade your characters in a very ineffecient method.
With all that said, it may seems like this is a bad game, but in reality rating this game is hard.  It is cheap and the base gameplay is satisfying in that it is rewarding on a very simple way (much like incremental games) combined with almost brain-dead gameplay.
It's definatly not for everyone, but Knights of Pen and Paper has its audiene.  Fans of Rpgs could get a few hours out of it before it beomes too grindy.  Those who enjoy incrimental games would probably get the most out of the game.  In the end its really just a question of what you expect for the price.  I'm giving it a thumbs up, but only for the right audience.

Zombies are just a little very played out at this point. And even with that in mind, Dying Light is one of the best games I've played in a while. To be fair, it plays like a mashup of a few of my favorite games - Mirror's Edge meets Far Cry at its core. The game borrows a fair bit from Dead Island as well, and seems to improve vastly on those bits.
It gives the player chances to feel powerful and fight off zombies while throwing in a select few variants that will thrash you without too much trouble if you don't come prepared. The day/night cycles are nicely utilized, as well. Harran is somewhat dangerous in the daytime, but it becomes extremely threatening at night. Vicious, nocturnal beasts won't hesitate to shred the player, and stealth is critical for traversing the city.
The environments do suffer a bit from copypasted features, there are occasional moments of "am I going in circles?" when you hop across one rooftop and then find its clone a few minutes later. But the map is fairly good sized. And while the features aren't always as varied as one may hope, it doesn't feel like there's any wasted space. There's stuff everywhere.
Lastly, it seems to run well on Linux. It had one random, sudden crash when I paused it in about 14 hours of gameplay, but the autosave brought me back to where I was. I really appreciate the devs supporting my OS. They also seem to do a good job supporting the game in general. Haven't gotten to any DLC yet but they're continuing to produce things, and that's good news. Workshop support is another very unexpected plus.

My second review, yay :D
(P.S. Please ignore all of the grammar and spelling mistakes, I wrote this review when I was waay to tired)
Anyways, I can defenatly recommend this game. At first I was skeptical, since I'm not one for Top-Down view games. Especially when there is turned based combat. But after the first few hours or so I just started loving this game, and I don't think I'm even a quarter through it.
So like I said its a top-down view game, wher you can move your character either by holding the left mouse button and then draging it in the direction that you want to move in, or my simply clicking on anywhere in the area.
The combat is turned baste, which at first was a "meh" thing for me since turned baste games are a "meh" kind of thing but after an hour or two it just became something that was there and I accepted it, so its defenatly not a negative aspect for me. I haven't really figured out what decides the order of when each character goes, but so far my characters were all ways the first ones (yay). Similar to other games with turne based combat, you have AP which decides what and how much you can do per turn. So if you need to move in order to dash at the enemy because a big rock is in the way, both of those things will cost AP. If you level as specific skill from your Characters, you will get more starting AP. And if you just simply do nothing and skip a characters turn, or you do something which doesnt require a lot of AP, the left over AP gets added to your next turn.
Now at the beginning of the game you can go into a Tutorial Dungeon, where you will already get to learn quit a few of the games mechanics, LIKE LIGHTING TORCHES (I love little things like these). You can move boxes and barrels around to find a hidden key under neath that may unlock a chest or a door. You can use the environment to your advantage in combat. For example there are barrels that have poisen in them, you can move them into position so that when you enter combat all you need to do is shoot them with an arrow (or something equivallent) to make them explode. Now of course you could already explode the barrels even before you enter combat, to already deal damage to your enemies.
You also have to look around real carefully for traps or hidden loot.
But even outside of the Dungeons and inside the Towns you can do a lot of stuff. For example, you can brake into other people homes and steal their stuff, all though you have to be carefull because if you get cought there will be consequences.
You can trade with pretty much anyone, and all most everyone will have something to sell to you, or you can sell anything to them. The trading in this game is pretty good to, you don't necessarily don't need to pay for the Items with Gold. If you have some spare equipment that you don't need, you can use that to pay for the Items. Making your useless crap into...something...more...usefull.....yea.
Like someone ells have probably already said, you need to talk to different people in order to get your quests, so no exclamation marker above peoples heads to tell you where a quest is to be found. Which is actually pretty cool and something new. And for me it draws and immerses me more into the game.
You are also able to use your abilities (like becoming invisible) in order to accomblish different things.
When you create a new game you get to customise two characters, meaning you will have two main characters that you can switch between (and later you can also switch between other party memebers that you pick up). Again at first it was a "meh" thing for me but I have gotten used to it and I actually quit like it now since I can have a Mage and a Rouge. Though you can also teach both characters both things, so the starting class that you pick is just more of a specialisation rather then a locked in character class. When you are talking to a NPC and they give you a choice, you sometimes need to defend your choice from your parters choice by a simple game of rock-paper-scissors. And who ever wins, their choice will be take. So if you say "Kill them all" but your partner says "Spare them all" and you play the game of rock-paper-scissors and you win, that means that you and your partner will kill every person/enemy there. There are also stats that influence of how quickly and easaly you can win these little games.
The writing/story of this game, for me, has ben pretty good so far. Though its best if you find that out yourself, or look at a few videos.
I can't comment on the Co-Op part of this game yet, since I haven't played this game with a friend up until now, but I'm sure if you enjoy the single player like me then you will definitly love the co-op. Though I would recommend playing it with a friend that is also interested to hear the story, and not just goofing off killing every body (though in a second play through there is nothing standing in your way of doing that of course).
So do I recomend this game, hell yes. At first I was skeptical about it, with the top down and turn based thing and all, but after a few hours I can definitly say that this game has become one of my favorit games. And the RPG element in this game is pretty awesome.
The level design is awesome, the challenge is real and the music are great! The story is intriguing and each the game is satisfying for people that try hard to pass every situation!

Before I begin, Id like to give you my background in MMO's so you have context to this review. I've played several mmos over the years but the 3 which ive spent the most time in were Runescape (1 year), WoW (2-3 years), and Everquest 2 (2006-today) which is my current favorite. I had always heard stories about Everquest's difficulty and coupled with the expectations of an ugly game with clunky controls that is outdated in every manner, I was left with the impression that this game would not be for me.
Logging into Everquest for the first time I instantly note that the textures look nice despite the low polygon count. Character creation was vast in terms of race/class choice but limited in hair/face models. It offers you an optional tutorial which I suggest you take because I caught on quickly thanks to its guidance. This is the only MMO that I have ever played which forces you to actually read NPC dialogue as you need to respond or click key words to choose dialogue options. Additionally there is no quest helper, but you are given enough details on the quest in your log. Many problems I have with older MMO's is that theyve become a cakewalk. Im the type of player who enjoys the journey more than endgame itself and Everquest is no cakewalk. Granted that its much easier than stories I hear from 1999 but I found myself struggling and needing the help of a mercernary even in the tutorial. The thrill of finding a new item or defeating that one enemy which stumped you several times in the past is there from below level 10 and on. Another problem I have with many older mmos such as Everquest 2 is that it can sometimes be a ghost town, but much to my surprise Everquest 1 is still filled with players. In the tutorial I remember joining several groups and having to wait my turn for a boss to spawn for a quest. The Ui is fully customizable as well where every window allows you to change opacity and shape in addition to font size.
There are several aspects of the game which add additional challenge which I appreciated, one being that you're not automatically given new abilities every time you level but you need to find an NPC vendor in order to learn a new ability. In addition to this you can only use a handfull of abilities at a time causing you to change your loadout depending on which enemy you face. As a paladin I would have to choose which spells I werent planning to use and replace them with spells which were effective against the undead, because without them I would have been toast. When you die your body is left behind holding a portion of your experience, finding it will return this experience to you. Long gone are the days of loosing everything on your character which im half thankful for, but part of me would like to experience this challenge. Probably the most rewarding challenge that ive met so far has been going into a large zone and having absolutely no map, getting lost and having to use my compas in order to find my way out without dieing. In these situations you can always google zonemaps, but I prefer to use the games cartography tool which allows me to create my own map. You can do this by running along roads and borders of the map to create lines or leaving notes in various areas informing you of locations. Crafting is also challenging as well, even at low levels you're required to create several other items used in the process of crafting the item you originally needed. Everquest 2 requires you to play a minigame while crafting and farm random ingredients from nodes (for example blueberries from a blackberry bush). You never know what you will get and I'm glad to say that I prefer crafting in EQ1. Materials fall from enemies, and theres no minigame with crafting.
Currently I am level 27 and I was left with such a strong impression that I felt the need to share my experience. EQ1 is a game filled with personality, which I find charming and sometimes comical. Little touches such as comical loading bars which are basically inside jokes to the likes of; "warning, half elves are now 49.9% elf", "Polishing Erudite forheads" ect. When choosing an enemy, theres no way to know their strength by looking at them, pressing C to consider will give you a readout of their relative strength which ranges from "this can be risky" to "what would you like your tombstone to say?" I probably enjoyed these little touches more than I should, but sadly as a long time player of EQ2, these touches were missing.
My experience with other players has been mostly positive. I've made a few friends and joined a guild right out of tutorial which is filled with friendly players who are more than willing to help me out with my noob questions. Players in zones will ask you to trade buffs with them which I found helpful. My only negative interaction with another player was when I had my zone camped by a higher level player when I was trying to complete a quest but this has only happened one time.
While EQ1 is still challenging to a new player, I have found a few areas of handholding which you may or may not appreciate such as getting a letter in your inbox every time you level up which tells you where you should go. I will probably appreciate this at a higher level though. I also with death consequence was a bit more harsh because I find myself not caring enough to walk the distance to gain the exp i dropped. I am only level 27 though so I cant speak for this in later parts of the game.
In conclusion, Everquest is a game which I choose not to see as outdated by nearly 20 years, but a game which has been refined for much longer than anything else on the market. Its a welcoming experience for new and old players alike. I am currently a free player and outside of the occasional popup advertisement, I do not feel limited in terms of bagspace or character options, however I do hear higher quality spells and armor are restricted to paying members later on in the game.
Enjoy!

This game is pure genius.
In a nutshell, you're a small egg-shaped chick, whose goal is... wait, what was its goal? No matter. You get thrown in the middle of a 2D side-scrolling world, with no tips or hints at all - you just walk to the right, and eventually find things as you walk, like more birds like you, gear pieces, or even the Toki Tori 2+ logo. All you can do (and you find out soon enough) is walk, whistle, and stomp on the ground. And that's all you will be able to do the entire game.
Using just those skills, you will explore the world. A beautiful world, full of different and vivid kinds of landscapes. You will go through a path, it seems, eventually discovering diverse things about the world you suddenly got thrown on, facing countless innovative puzzles that you solve with just the abilities you have at your disposal - again, walking, whistling, and stomping. What you do not know is that it isn't only a path. And that you may actually go anywhere in the world, right at the same time you get thrown in it - you get no additional abilities. The only barrier preventing you from doing so is knowledge of how the different elements of the world work. This, itself, makes the game amazing.
The core, of course, is in the puzzles - it's a puzzle-solving exploration game. The puzzles are very creative, yet not frustrating or particularly hard; you do not need to be an experienced puzzle-solver to be able to complete the entire game, without using a guide. The game may net you 15~25 hours of gameplay to complete fully, gameplay that you will enjoy to its fullest as you travel through the world of Toki Tori 2+.
If you have an inchling of curiosity towards this game - perhaps you saw the beautiful screenshots, perhaps you played the original Toki Tori, perhaps you simply love puzzle games - and you are indecisive and this game is on sale, you should definitely give it a try. The world is even more gorgeous than what you see in the screenshots. The puzzles are much more creative than in the original. I have a hard time thinking of any game that has a similar concept to this one, and it's astoundingly well delivered.
You will be surprised.

Quick note about making this work on modern systems:
1. The default PhysX setting will use outdated software and murders performance when the cops start shooting. There are several workarounds available on the game's PcGamingWiki page. Alternatively, just turn PhysX off.
2. The in-game Vsync did not work (at least for me). I still got horrible tearing even with it enabled on my 60Hz monitor. Forcing adaptive Vsync in the Nvidia drivers worked perfectly.
Once you get those issues fixed, it runs like a dream, and honestly it looks pretty great for a game from 2008. The bright, sunny, whitewashed world is a nice change of pace from the typical grimdark of many recent games. The city feels vibrant despite a relative lack of NPCs. Also, the good anisotropic filtering means that textures usually look pretty good (at least, they're not distractingly bad like they are in some 360-era games). The character modeling on the enemies is relatively weak and probably the biggest indication that this is a last-gen title.
The gameplay itself is primarily first-person platforming with occasional combat mixed in. The platforming is the stronger element - nailing a free-flowing parkour section is exhilarating.
Early in the game, the platforming is quite easy, so you can gain a lot of speed and you start to feel like you're flying. It's amazing. Some later levels have much tougher platforming sections that break up the momentum a bit (at least on your first playthrough), but successfully navigating them is still extremely satisfying (and once you've figured them out you can speedrun them to feel even cooler). There's also one boss fight that's a little bit stupid, but it's thankfully short.
Overall, despite the occasional moments of frustration, Mirror's Edge is a unique and frequently breathtaking game that's worth a buy for both FPS and platformer fans.

An utterly fun game, Orcs Must Die! combines FPS with placing down traps. Probably not a new idea, but that doesn't in any way, shape, or form detract from the enjoyability, so let's get into some pros and cons.
Pros
-It has some story elements (a big thing with me). This game could have gone without story altogether and still been fun, but the developers decided to spice it up! I mean, sure it's a pretty basic story, but, considering the game genre, I'll consider it a pro.
-Responsive and intuitive controls that are easy to learn and get the hang of.
-Normal (Warmage) difficulty getting boring? Try Nightmare difficulty for the challenge you crave.
-Great music and graphics.
-Great replayability across most levels (I say most because the first level, even on Nightmare, will get easy pretty quick).
-Funny commentary from the characters.
-DLC adds new weapons, traps, and levels.
Cons
-No multiplayer. If you're not into that then this point is moot.
-Only one character and set of weapons/traps.
-DLC costs money. Might be a con to some. I wasn't personally bothered by it, but, then again, I probably got it on sale 'cause I'm cheap like that.
So, yeah, that's all I got. So go get it. It's worth its full price, but if you want to get it on sale, that's understandable. Anyways, it's a great game I would recommend to just about everyone.

nail'd is one of those games designed to flick all the "HELL ♥♥♥♥ING YEAH!" switches in your brain. Normally when I play a racing game, I'm super serious. No, that doesn't mean I play Gran Turismo, Forza, Project Cars, or any other simulation. I'm a fan of arcade racers like Daytona USA, Outrun 2, Ridge Racer, and so on. All of my attention is focused on making those expertly crafted turns, weaving past my rivals, and powersliding. I don't care about realism, but games that emphasize your opponent's destruction (Burnout) don't do anything for me.
I have to admit, nail'd flicks my switches real good.
This is an ATV/MX racer, with some vehicle customization. Sim-fans are going to be shown the door immediately, since the first thing they'll notice are stats like "boost acceleration" and "mid-air steering". It's expected that at least 1/5 of the mileage you put into this game, will be spent in the air. Each track is composed of ramps, hills, slopes, cliffs, and other structures designed to get you high. The tracks are also loaded with obstacles such as trees, rocks, trucks, trains, and so on on.
Unlike the arcade-racers I usually play, collisions aren't an automatic restart in nail'd. You're always in the race, and you lose maybe 1/2 a second or so when you crash. However, keeping up with the pack (and winning) requires that you boost. Boost is acquired via certain gates, mid-air rings, perfect landings, wheelies, going fast, and even wrecking your rivals.
That last one actually doesn't come up very often in a race, which is why I love it. With Burnout and its ilk, the pacing starts to become effected when it seems like every few seconds I'm watching a cut-scene of a burning wreck. What was once awesome, gets really tiring. Knocking your rivals out in nail'd works because there aren't any cut-scenes. Everything moves so quickly that it takes you a second to realize "Did I just do that? Holy crap!" At one point I jumped off a ramp and actually landed on someone, destroying them instantly, I was so freaked out I crashed twice in a row. There are other moments like this, like the time I got so much air I actually rode on top of a hot-air balloon.
nail'd is an extreme racer sure, but it also has a touch of subtlety. It rewards players for doing the unexpected. The tracks are designed to accomodate rather than frustrate, giving racers room to look for shortcuts and opportunities to score more boost. This is likely one of those "you already own this" titles due to its appearance in bundles. Do yourself a favor and give it a go.
Also it might be a trick of perspective, but the racers in this game have phat behinds.

This game is great, great fun for those who like platformers.
Jumpjet Rex is level runner, or rather "jetpacker", where your performance is graded in "stars" as you try to beat the levels. Finishing a level gets you one star, for free. If you complete the level without dying and using checkpoints, you get the "no death" star. And finally, if you beat the target time you gain the third star.
The music is all right. It's obvious that the developers are aiming for a classic Mega Man musical vibe, but fell short. The graphics are wholly servicable for the game, and fit the goofy tone of the game's premise. I liked the NES style story cards, and wish there had been more because the developers did a great job with them.
In the levels, there are also collectibles, coins and rubies that earn you "money" that can be used for purely aesthetic reasons. You can buy different heads, scale color, boot color, and jetboot trail color... I suppose this is nice for the multiplayer modes, but I didn't feel compelled to play more just for the coins. My impetus for replay was more so the leaderboards and star system, which make for a fun little exercise in seeing how much you can "perfect" a level.
Anyhow, there's a free demo for this game, if you're still hesitant, try that for sure. For those who do enjoy platforming level runners, grab this game for a fun time.

JumpJet Rex is the hippinest hoppinest dino on booster boots I’ve ever seen.
It’s a retro, almost B.O.B.esque, relatively average skill based 2d platformer taking advantage of an anything but average mechanic – flight. Now, I’ve never seen a platformer built entirely around this one mechanic before JumpJet Rex. Maybe some game has done it in a similar fashion, but JumpJet Rex does so to a level that I have to imagine is greater than most other similar attempts.
It isn’t your average platformer in that it includes a leaderboard for each level making it a race against time, or rather your or the world’s personal best as well as a non-linear level path that forces you to complete every stage to a strong degree. It also includes various multiplayer LAN modes.
Now, I’m speaking completely on assumptions but the thing is that JumpJet Rex is so well polished that it feels as if, well, it could have been a big game Super Nintendo. I grew up with Super Nintendo and thus, as the console that introduced me to gaming, I’ve a lot of experience on this console and games somewhat similar to JumpJet Rex.
What JumpJet Rex does is put you in a new, yet relatively familiar, world. It’s almost as if you’re playing B.O.B. with infinite jetpack abilities. But JumpJet Rex makes it feel as if some new life has been breathed into the genre. To be honest, it feels like a game anyone could have made too which is really cool if you’re an aspiring game designer or programmer. It gives you something to mimic that doesn’t feel out of reach. Finally, I believe this is a game anyone who is interested in creating videogames should try out at least once.
In conclusion, for a score, I’ll give the controls a 7/10, the graphics an 8/10, and finally the gameplay a 7/10. The game could have been better but considering the feel it’s a very good game and is sort of inspiring in its own way. This equates to a 74 out of a possible 100.

Let me just say first of all that this is a free-to-play game and the game (even if it wasn't free to play) is great, and let me tell you why.
To be honest, I'm not big on the uh... pixel games or 8-bit games like this but this is a major exception.
Starting it up I was very skeptical, but it's got a great Main Menu with continues, options and all that good stuff you need. Your goal? Reach the top of the mountain?
Why?
Because you need money.
One thing I didn't like is the quick story that didn't make a lot of sense, which was the holiday hike to make money, the concept is you die... you lose money and you can find money stashes along the way. You also have a "zip-line" rope sort of thing that is incredibly fun to use and to solve puzzles. There are enemies and you can jump on their heads but it won't kill them and even just some of the enemies get stunned for a short period of time. This does give you the advantage to progress or get a quick stack of money. It is difficult! But just the right difficult. Not too difficult but each "part" of the mountain doesn't have a bottom except for a ball with spikes (that's your suicide) and when you drop and can't think of a way to get back up... that ball of spikes is your only option.
Music? It's one song. One of the best parts of the game, literally, while you're playing, you will start humming the song.
(I'm a big fan) of achievements and this game has them and they're pretty easy to get too! Which is a great addition.
There's one quick cutscene at the beginning and you're into the game. No glitches, no mistakes (not from what I've seen).
Sometimes you have to think outside the box, especially with this rope of yours (YOU COMPLETELY CONTROL IT) which means sometimes you have to time things almost perfectly which aims for a greater challenge (see what I did there? You'd have to play the game to get it... :P) Anyways, cool song, cool gameplay and awesome puzzles, achievements, and pretty much a great game and for what price? None. Get it now. Also!!! It only takes 1 minute to download. :D

Surprisingly they did a great job with this enhanced version and it does run much better than before. I can maintain great framerates at amazing graphics!
Lets talk about the game. It is a very fun game with a less-than-interesting singleplayer campaign. Unfortunately, the SP story is kinda lacking emotion and the villain is a bit weak. The voice acting isn't that good, but it is acceptable.
The combat however, is stunning. It is one of the best parts of the game without a doubt. Sure, in the beginning blunt weapons will deal little damage to zombies and they break fast - I HATED THAT! But stick to the game, because the more you explore, the more you find these hilariously overpowered weapons. And once you get THOSE weapons this game becomes ridiculously easy, and thankfully, there are three difficulty settings which actually make sense and are useful if you want a lot more challenge. The free-running is nice too! Easily one of the best freerunning systems in any game ever; probably better than Mirror's Edge (haven't played Catalyst though). Killing zombies was never this satisfying... or was it? No, not really. This game is really unique in that sense.
The zombie genre is a very crowded one, so Dying Light had to be something else. And, thankfully it is something else. But not entirely. If you like having fun, this game is definitely for you. If you like games with deep and intensely interesting stories, you won't really find one here. The story is really dull and overly cliché. Easily the worst part about the game. Everything else, however, is fun and interesting. A large sandbox world filled with things to do. Freerunning challenges REALLY put you to the test though - seriously, those are killer hard at points. Practise makes perfect though!
So overall get the game but come in with somewhat low expectations because you MAY have an absolutely horrid experience or an absolutely amazing one. Surely, the game is not particularly great at the start, but once you get into the second city it becomes so much better.
6/10 to be honest, all the imperfections really add up to make this game an above average game, but not an extraordinary shining example of anything spectacular. Anyway, prepare for bore, prepare for annoyances, and prepare for fun.

Remember those animal things in Super Metroid that taught you how to shinespark? Toki Tori 2 is basically that moment but as a game.
Unlike the first game, which was a puzzle game closer in heritage to Lemmings, Toki Tori 2 is an exploration puzzle platformer with zero in-game text and no ability gating. You have two ways of interacting with the world: stomping and, most interestingly, singing. By alternating long and short presses, Toki can sing big or small notes, respectively. Similar to the ocarina in Zelda games, different combinations of notes will have certain effects. Technically, there is nothing stopping you from using any of these "powers" from the start of the game. You could, in theory, brute force all of them on the opening screen, but that would take a while. The way the game teaches you these powers at the "right time" is through little birds that you'll see around the environment that sing little note combos. Copy these notes and BAM you'll learn what that combo does. There's only five or so powers, which was initially disappointing, but I realized that it would be much more challenging for the developers to fully explore the mechanics. And they've done a great job with that as it is. Admittedly, I'm only about halfway done with the game by my reckoning, but the variety I've seen in puzzle design and mechanical interaction has impressed me.
Toki Tori 2 is one of the most surprising games of 2013 for me. I wasn't a huge fan of the first game, but Toki Tori 2 has blown me away with its well-designed environmental puzzles and storytelling. I wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who likes a great puzzle game.

An easy recommandation for this one. Yes the campaign is short, but the gameplay is so rock solid, that its worth the low price of admission just for the races unlocked at the end of the campaign.
Because Mirror's Edge is at its best when it's all about sustaining the momentum. The rare but annoying enough combat sequences (be it with fists/feet or guns) and the slower/puzzle plateforming moments are, in my opinion, what drives the short campaign to a somewhat mediocre+ experience. The poor story-telling and overall narration, with some of the worst looking AAA animated cutscenes to date, don't help either selling that part of the game.
The arcade part on the other hand, the part that has no attach to anything remotely emotional, that doesn't deal with combat and that, for the most part, is just about running, jumping and landing as fast as you can, this part is a real treat. The game has an amazingly neat body-awareness (the kind that I suppose don't mix well with motion-sickness unfortunately) precise command and requires skill in execution. And when you get to the three stars for every race, you're on top of the f-ing world!

Don't let the appearance fool you. This is not a platforming game. This is not a casual game. This is not a beautiful game.
Well actually it is a beautiful game, but definitely is not a platforming or casual game.
This is a hard puzzle game which rewards patience, exploration and thinking. And if you play by its rules, it is quite enjoyable. Or I should say if you manage to learn the rules, because all the game is built around exploring, looking, guessing the world mechanics and the use it to your advantage. This is a slow pace game in which you learn by trying, but all the solutions are fair and you don't need any platforming skills.
The metroidvania comparison may be a little too far fetched because you don't get skills or objects, only knowledge to access other areas (think Myst). Of the two general metroidvania features (areas that you are allowed to access as you progress in the game and cool abilities/gadgets), you only get the area access, there is no abilities/gadgets.
All in all, if you like exploration and puzzles, this is a very good game. My only concern is that may be you need too much trial and error to test your ideas.

So, should you buy Grim Dawn? I recommend it for anyone who wants to scratch that ARPG itch. This game is all about the interesting characters you can make by experimenting with all the customization options you get. The dark atmosphere and gritty world is a callback diablo 2 fans will appreciate. The audio compliments the gameplay nicely. The game runs well for the most part and loads very quickly. If you’re looking for a grandiose endgame with online ladders and seasons and rift farming, stick with diablo 3. If you want meaningful character customization and you liked diablo 2, Grim Dawn is something you’ll want to look at.

A mixture of Skyrim, Baldur's Gate and Dark Souls, Divinity: Original Sin is a top-down, sandbox RPG with loads of content for the players to explore. Why I made the comparison to Dark Souls is that you will bang your head against the wall.  But when you break through, you will get insta-hooked.

If you liked the first Killing Floor, you will like this too, it comes with many improvements from the first one.
The most important takeaway for me is that this game provides one of the most involved feeling of fighting. This was achieved by creating what is essentially 120FPS animations for guns and weaponswings so that once you go into "zed time" (slow mo), they will be going at crisp 60fps. Additionally, weapons work differently in different situations as it doesn't just come down to headshot/bodyshot difference. You can shoot legs to stumble, you can stun with specific weapons, melee weapons have different direction swings that for the most part actually influence how you will damage someone etc. This is also an FPS that I really recommend playing without crosshairs as it makes the from hip shooting feel more deserved, but also puts emphasis on down the sight shooting for many weapons.
This gunplay and feel is unique and something that is heads and tail above most other FPS and to be honest, almost none come close to this feeling. The weapon variety provides many playstyles and unlike the first game, some of the classes do feel like you have to play a bit differently. With its combat, this game provides the most fun 3d enviroment dodging and fighting of mindless enemies which reminds me of dodging enemies in shmups or descent. Its just a blast to play.
Sadly, this game isn't perfect. Two things hinder it.
Its herritage to an old unreal mod is one of them. Its in essentia a storyless defend from waves of enemies whose (min)game whose design hasn't strayed far from that initial old mod. The grind is still present albeit a bit less tedious than in kf1. The simple enemy AI means that a good round completely depends on the maps design. This means that while there is some support for making your own maps and guns, player made maps tend to just be maps to grind experience on as making a good KF map means being able to make a map that funels the zombies in such a way that its not too hard or too easy. Funnily enough even a couple official maps tend to lean more towards the punishing side by making them too small and restrained. I am looking at you Farmhouse.
The second issue is that somewhere halfway in development Tripwire lost its idea and goal for the game. Initially it was supposed to include more bosses and enemies, probably meant to be more variety. They added exactly one new enemy since launch, which is practically a stronger reskin with a couple new animations, and there's only two possible bosses.
Tripwire also had the idea to pursue a versus mode, much akin to what L4D had, where one side of the players jumps into super versions of the zombies. It was a fun mode, but what made left for deads mode fun was the dynamic maps you run through allowing for ambushing spots and other tactics like isolating players. KF has much smaller and more arena like maps, which makes for a different feel. Also the special player zeds were rather overpowered in this mode, which lead to this mode just not being fun for many players and promptly getting abandoned in like 2 weeks after its appearance.
So Tripwires next move was to create dynamic maps: maps that would change each wave. The map that came out of this experiment is very fun but Tripwire imidiatly abandoned this too and never made another map like this, instead opting to make arena like maps for its further two next patches, which simply had dynamic stuff happen in the background. I can only speculate that making the initial dynamic map, even without making new assets for it, just ended up costing too much development time.
Additionally, leading up to the launch they were having problems nailing down the very last class, which was supposed to be a martial arts one. They decided it wasn't working out and dropped it, which is good, but they decided to replace it with a class that is a jack of all trades and uses everyone elses weapon. For most people this class will simply be useless and just another thing to grind xp for.
Also abandoned was the share weapons through dlc thing that now just gives the claymore that everyone owns anyway.
The weapons added since launch have mostly just been machine guns. Missing are the energy weapons (there was an energy weapon icon in early access) or anything more involving than just shot more bullets, the club and shield being the most inventive thing they came up with since launch.
Now Tripwire is working on a VR version of this game instead of working on the base game. This all just seems to be aimless wandering, trying to figure out something for this game and they seem to not be able to find whatever they are looking for.
This is all just a warning in that I feel they won't invest much further in the base game in the future, which is sad. Good news is that it has an alright enough playerbase/ population (which seems to be becoming a rather sinister problem for newer multiplayer games). The microtransactions are thankfully some of the least intrusive I've seen and work like csgo/tf2 crates but include exclusively only cosmetics, and the game being mostly dark and gritty the cosmetics are kind of rubbish to be honest (the incidental humour of kf1 is kind of lost in 2, they tried to bring back witty voiceacting and weird costumes but its just not the same).
For the price of admission you get a rather good and most importantly unique feeling FPS game that provides adequat, easy to set up coop pve.

For a couple of dollars, I would recommend the game. Anything more and I wouldn't recommend the game.
The game works well and the graphics/sound aren't bad at all. My main critisisms are with the gameplay.
1. The initial controls are wierd. What should be a single-hand setup is instead made awkward. Why:
a) Up/down is to tilt the vehicle forwards and backwards, while left and right turn left and right. Accellerate is shift, boost is ctrl and brake is Z. So a touch typist uses the three main fingers on the right hand, but only the pinky (for three buttons) on the left hand.  Additionally boost can only be activated when accellerating, so your pinky must be pressing shift and ctrl at the same time.
b) recommended setup (and i have no idea why this isn't default) is tilt up/down is W/S, Turn left/Right is A/D. Accellerate is Shift, Brake/reverse is ctrl, and boost is space. This configuration feels a lot more "natural"
2) Forced "resets". If you go slightly off the designated "track" it automatically resets you regardless of whether you could recover from it. For example, one section of the first track you get the option to drive on the top of a train, or on the track beside the train. if you choose to drive on top of the train and fall off the side onto the track, it forces a reset. (even though you could have easily just kept driving on the track). This is also the case if you do a jump, and land on a "pillar" for a moment before landing on the other side of the jump - you get reset, regardless that you were still going to make the jump.
3) Arcade feel. This isn't a bad thing, but it isn't really my style. you can extend jumps by tilting up, and you can change direction in mid air. It also puts some small encouragement to doing tricks such as "wheelies" on your quad bike, which isn't something a racing person would do mid-race. It doesn't really add to the racing feel in my opinion.
All up, the game worked fine and there isn't any significant problems, it just isn't my type of game.

Hailing from the indie developer, Behold Studios;
is an enjoyable throwback for any and all tabletop RPG gamer. It doesn't hold much brilliance in terms of either story or gameplay but makes you play the whole campaign with a persistent smile on your face anyhow. If you have spent your fair share of Saturday nights around a table, creating characters, passing each other various snacks and rolling the dice; you'll find the core concept of the game relatable and fun. If not, most of its content will be lost on you, so you could prefer avoiding this one. Being a chronic RPG gamer myself - both on tabletop and on PC - and still DMing for my various groups at age 30, this one hit the spot for me. It was all too familiar and successful in bringing tabletop humor to a PC game. So if you are an actual role-player - especially familiar with Dungeons and Dragons - go ahead. It's like someone decided to make a hotchpotch out of your regular Saturday night content, and even though you know it’s not the greatest dish in the world, you'd eat it 'cause it's familiar.
I do bear a tradition of presenting an outline of the story in my reviews but here, there really isn't much to tell about - a bit of a disappointment, coming from a game about tabletop RPGs actually. Basically it's Saturday night, and a group of noob players huddle around their Dungeon Master and start a campaign. For the remainder of the game, your table will be the only constant between the game world and the real world. You'll be experiencing constant passages within these realities, as players constantly break the forth wall to comment or criticize the DM. Anything and everything within the game consist of RPG or Fantasy references and parodies, presented both during many out-game squabbles and relevant plot displays. As the storyline progresses DM will constantly bend the game world for it to fit into various RPG clichés. If you are familiar with the fantasy genre even remotely, you'll recognize at least a handful of given references. The baseline of the story is "big baddies are cooking up vile plots, so we gotta beat them and get their loot" pretty much. No depth there, but character squabbles and DM's commentaries on gameplay are funny and relatable. Thus, you keep playing the game even though it is a grind hell. So, this is what all this is about: spot on FRP parody.
The game being a port from the mobile original, graphics are not demanding. It's a pixel run in a fantasy world with 8 bit music, coming from the same three tracks running in the background. It's fun and charming for a while, but kinda gets tiresome by the end. Still, there is some nostalgic spark in monster designs, that much I must agree with. With each new mob monster you'd come across, you'd catch a new reference. Would like to battle a gremlin? A doppelganger? A mimic? A dragon? Or even the Dark Knight? Do not look further.
What about the gameplay? Well, this being a parody it certainly does its job on criticizing the power mechanic of many tabletop games. Everything is really, really basic. During battle, characters do bear 5 simple choices: attack, defend, use skill, use item or flee. That's it. The dice roll is not determinant during battle at all. It is presented only as a way for encounters to appear. There are a handful of classes you can pick, each having four skills which could be upgraded once at each level up. You attend quests - which are basically escort, slay or travel - to get exp, grind on monsters to do so, and pass for the next one. Yah, that's about all. It all boils down to gold, loot and exp, boys and girls. As the game progresses, mobs will get resistances and immunities, but combat mechanics never change. It is simplicity itself. Accompanied with the same 8 bit music over and over again, battles become really repetitive too. Once completed and the humor itself experienced, there really would not be any reason to revisit the game. So, there really isn't that much of a replay value, either.
Well, I haven't shared any grand plusses about the game so far, did I? Mostly, I would say that it appeals to the common experience of tabletop gaming and parodies the DM/Player relationship based upon it. On doing so, the humor is successful, presenting you with many clichés, references and even some laughs. For someone who has never played a tabletop game? Nah, not so much. I would highly recommend for you to grab the game on sale if you are interested with the said humor, 'cause after going through the main game for 20 hours or so once, you won't be revisiting it. Enjoy, nonetheless!

It's unfortunate that, among all of these retro-throwback games, JumpJet Rex doesn't seem to get a lot of attention and is even negatively compared. It clearly has plenty of buyers and players, but it's still seemingly not often mentioned. Even after reading some of the criticism (not that there's much anyway) I am still flabbergasted as to why, because it's easy to see just how much of a labor of love this game is (and I'll note right now that the game controls great, don't know why that was an issue for anyone). Much care and thought has been put into the game, what with the level design coinciding with the strict yet still possible time limits given if you choose to speedrun levels. This is mixed with some legitimately nostalgic aesthetic touches which show that the people who made this game clearly were alive back in the day long enough to know what it was like. This isn't just any ol' imitation, I could legitimately see a game like this having been around back in the 90s on the SNES (not the NES despite the style of the soundtrack; the graphics are too nice for the NES otherwise), and as a child I could imagine this being my favorite game.
Admittedly, as an adult it's not my favorite, as it can be frustrating at times, particularly when attempting to obtain some treasures in the game, though it is due to a legitimate toughness as opposed to any glitches or nigh-impossible fake difficulty. Though the game does get harder, it does become more rewarding to play as you feel like you actually accomplish things when you obtain victories, even minor ones, as the game takes practice rather than luck. This is the case whether you are speed-running, exploring to find secrets, or just breezing through the levels, and it's great that all of those options are available. The game retains its challenge either way since you'll be facing actual platforming (or "platflying") challenges, especially when treasure-seeking. I will say, however, if you do happen to just play through the game in a "Point A to Point B," manner, you are not going to enjoy this game nearly as much since, especially for ten bucks, the game can actually feel like a great adventure (yes, adventure).
Though I said it's not my favorite game as an adult, the passion the developers show here seeps into my heart and makes me love it just as much as they likely did, and so I still find this to be among the greatest games on all of Steam, possibly even the best of the retro-throwbacks I've played (if not, it's damn close). In terms of recommendations, particularly since it doesn't seem well-known or oft-discussed, it comes quickly off the top of my head among my first recommendations.

Lets talk about the game. It is a very fun game with a less-than-interesting singleplayer campaign. Unfortunately, the SP story is kinda lacking emotion and the villain is a bit weak. The voice acting isn't that good, but it is acceptable.
The combat however, is stunning. It is one of the best parts of the game without a doubt. Sure, in the beginning blunt weapons will deal little damage to zombies and they break fast - I HATED THAT! But stick to the game, because the more you explore, the more you find these hilariously overpowered weapons. And once you get THOSE weapons this game becomes ridiculously easy, and thankfully, there are three difficulty settings which actually make sense and are useful if you want a lot more challenge. The free-running is nice too! Easily one of the best freerunning systems in any game ever; probably better than Mirror's Edge (haven't played Catalyst though). Killing zombies was never this satisfying... or was it? No, not really. This game is really unique in that sense.
The zombie genre is a very crowded one, so Dying Light had to be something else. And, thankfully it is something else. But not entirely. If you like having fun, this game is definitely for you. If you like games with deep and intensely interesting stories, you won't really find one here. The story is really dull and overly cliché. Easily the worst part about the game. Everything else, however, is fun and interesting. A large sandbox world filled with things to do. Freerunning challenges REALLY put you to the test though - seriously, those are killer hard at points. Practise makes perfect though!
So overall get the game but come in with somewhat low expectations because you MAY have an absolutely horrid experience or an absolutely amazing one. Surely, the game is not particularly great at the start, but once you get into the second city it becomes so much better.
6/10 to be honest, all the imperfections really add up to make this game an above average game, but not an extraordinary shining example of anything spectacular. Anyway, prepare for bore, prepare for annoyances, and prepare for fun.

I'll start by saying this: The Banner Saga is the most interesting game I've ever played in my life. It's beautiful and a piece of art (beyond just the stunning animated visuals), but it also is the most upsetting video game I've ever played.

Maybe I am just not a very good caravan leader, but my every minute was a struggle for survival. Whether I was running short on food two days before reaching the next town (only to be unable to purchase any food, I might add), or watching some of my best fighters fall, or unexpected twists with both friend and foe alike, every moment was spent wondering about the choices I made; were they the right ones, or the wrong ones? I tended to lean toward mercy, forgiveness, and trust; things sometimes didn't go my way, and I often had no idea what was in store for me. Sometimes I could manage the aftermath of my choices, yet others followed me for the rest of the game. Always, though, I felt a strong melancholy that haunted me. I sort of enjoyed that feeling, however. I'm not used to feeling weak or powerless in a game, and this game truly made me feel the burden of leadership unlike anything else in my life ever has.

The story and world hooked me almost as soon as I opened my map for the first time. The story only kept getting better and better until the game's climatic finale, which had my heart thumping fast. The ending left me surprised, shocked, and I'm still recoiling from the effect my choices had. I can't wait to see where the rest of the story goes, but, at the same time, I can't help but feel regret for all that's happened under my watch.

The Banner Saga is brutal; don't expect any leniency for your mistakes. One mistake isn't going to make the game impossible to beat, but more likely than not, players are going to feel the weight of their choices, and it's not always so easy to shrug off. I can best describe the game as a bit of Oregon Trail (managing the caravan and responding to events while traveling), some of Fire Emblem/ X-com (very tactical game play and sometimes permadeath), with a sprinkle of Mass Effect (choices have a lot of weight; actually, they probably have more weight in this game than in Mass Effect), meets Game of Thrones (if you're used to looming doom and a confusing labyrinth of politics and trust, you'll feel right at home).

All in all, I highly suggest this game. It's truly a gem, and if you're looking for a deep game that will get you thinking, both tactically and philosophically, this is the game for you.

Originally a WiiWare download title called Rubik's Puzzle Galaxy: Rush, the game has since lost its Rubik's licence, being released on Steam simply as Rush, with additional stages and content. Rush is a puzzle game, in which you are given a certain number of directional signs, stop signs or split signs which you can place on the map in order to guide each cube from point A to point B without them colliding or falling off the map. Those stages are grouped based on their difficulty starting with the easy ones, and moving on to the medium ones and the hard ones, allowing you to choose a challenge fit for your experience and get better with time, allowing you to learn from your mistakes, observe how the cubes move once you've hit the green button and rearrange the signs based on what you have seen. There is no sense of advancement since there is no leveling up system and you're not really unlocking anything besides the next levels, but playing Rush more will definitely make you better at it, as long as you keep replaying the same stage, since you're not exactly learning how to play the game better, but instead observing the problems in your sign arrangement; it's more like ruling out the bad solution and eventually getting to the right one, how long it takes to get there depends only on how well you understand the mechanics.
The gameplay is simplistic and intuitive, offering a challenge for everyone and satisfaction to those who dare to give the hardest levels a shot. Placing signs is easy and understanding how they work is the key to solving puzzles, while directional signs are the most encountered ones, using them efficiently is what will get you through as the natural direction of the cube plays an important role in many puzzles, and combining good use of direction movement with things such as speed which can be influenced using a stop sign or a directional sign, and the split sign which will allow you to group cubes based on their color in order to send them in the right direction, all matters in the end. There is also a hint system that will tell you where signs should be placed without giving the exact order, a tool that will come in handy for those who want to enjoy the game without wasting too much time on a single puzzle. There are levels grouped depending on the challenge level, but there's nothing stopping you from enjoying all of them, as the hard ones can be approached using the hint system and the easy ones can be fun even for the pros. Adding all that up, there are more than 80 different stages, with different levels of difficulty, so there's plenty of challenge for everyone.
Rush is a colorful universe, using cubes and their respective colors to create beautiful backgrounds that will often captivate you more than the stage itself. Even though all the stages respect the same rules of color and formation, each one feels unique in its own way, and successfully solving a puzzle often rewards you with a beautiful parade of flawlessly moving blocks.
The electronic soundtrack is in theme with the game, and even though the number of tracks is limited and will become repetitive eventually, you can always play Rush with your own music in the background since there is no dialogue or information given that you'll miss if you do that. The sound effects are okay, yet nothing spectacular to support the colorful movement of successfully guided blocks.
With all its 80+ stages including the bonus stages and the special Portal Event stages, Rush can take anywhere from 3 hours to 10 hours to complete, depending how long it takes for you to give up and hit the hint button, but even so for a 5 bucks title, you get plenty of content to play around with.
Rush is a must play for puzzle fans who want a little challenge, but it still provides a few intriguing levels for the casual puzzle solvers too, so there are enough reasons for everyone to give it a shot and see how well they can guide the cubes.

Toki Tori 2+ is not at all the game I was expecting it to be. The original game was a series of self-contained puzzle levels that were solved using a limited set of items. Toki Tori 2 is not that at all. Instead, the game drops you in the middle of a vast open 2D world and leaves you to figure everything out on your own. There are no instructions, tutorials, levels or items. The whole world is open from the start and you just need to figure out how to get through it while collecting a series of, err... collectibles. Unlike the previous game, Toki no longer uses items to solve puzzles. Instead, your abilities are limited to walking, singing and stomping. That's it. Where the complexity (and genius) comes in is how you can combine those actions with the various creatures that populate the world. For example, you can lure birds to pick you up with chirps, move bugs by stomping, and much, much more. I won't say anything further on that, as half the fun is figuring out the rules of the game on your own. As with the previous game, level/puzzle design is utterly brilliant. So many times you will think there is no way to proceed past an area, only to have the solution click a few minutes later (and you subsequently smack yourself upside the head because of how simple it actually was). That is a sign of good design, and I admire it a lot. I can't really think of any puzzles that were totally unfair, although there were a handful that were somewhat tedious. The singing mechanic is also a pretty neat new feature. In addition to its standard functionality, you learn a series of songs that provide other abilities, such as time-rewind, warping around the map, and more. And oh yeah, the characters are all really cute - especially Toki and the frogs (if you're into that sort of thing as a selling point). It all comes together nicely in a really well-executed package. Overall, I liked this a lot better than the first game, due to the open-ended exploration/collection gameplay and the "complex simplicity" in the puzzle design. It's a fun, laid-back game that should appeal to puzzle fans. A-

20 years ago Lemmings one of the most popular video games of its time saw you guide and eventually rescue cute little suicidal rascals through a plethora of destructible landscapes. Now fully fleshed out in a 3Dimensional take on what made this game so fun has been mastered. Meet Orcs Must Die a somewhat grown up take where instead of adorable lemmings we now have ugly and angry orcs, okay maybe it feels a little more frantic than lemmings. The wit, premise, control, Ui, art style, characters, gameplay, even plot in what is essentially a tower defence game is super superb. I haven't played Nintendo in a long time but this game distinctly reminds me of its charm, knowingness and ability to throw you in the deep end of fun.
OMD hard mode Nightmare offers re-playability to OMD on par with Super Meat Boy one false move and you have to try your best again, I cant think of a better comparison even though they are separate genres. The nail biting choices you have to make as the charming apprentice War-mage with a fully equipped arsenal are many. Usually these choices will make themselves self evident: a little nook for archers where they oversee a choke point or noticing you will be facing fire dragons you choose the ice ring knowing they a vulnerable to it. But sometimes you will be forced to change your tactics in the face of (hard to swallow) defeat. Its a mad house at times: fine tuning, timing and running about building, fixing and fending off the horde until your sophisticated blender of death is running at optimum efficiency. I bought OMD2 also a brilliant game but the feel is a little different due to a new engine. Its also good to see they have thrown in a female playable character, and co-op.

This game doesn't know what it wants to be. It simultaneously attempts to be both a platformer in which you go as quickly as possible and try for the best time, and a platformer in which you hunt down secrets and get all the collectables. Neither of these goals are accomplished well.
The air dash is extremely inconsistent and hard to control, and didn't even work half of the times that I tried to use it. Every trap on the map is on a global timer, which makes sense on paper, but it starts as soon as the level loads; this means that getting the best time will sometimes require you to guess when to actually start moving around so as to be able to bypass timed lasers and moving enemies. This also makes getting 3 star ratings extremely obnoxious to get, and certainly not worth the effort for achievements.
Coins are strewn about the levels, encouraging you to pick them up, but most are far too out of the way to be able to still get a good time. There are also collectables and warp zones (for lack of a better phrase) that are only accessible if you go the completely wrong direction. Some collectables, as far as I can tell, are entirely unobtainable as well, and exist only to taunt you.
Graphically, this game is a fairly forgettable 2D pixel art style. Nothing pretty, but nothing painful to look at either. Music is generic chip tunes, but again, forgettable. Sound effects are all but nonexistent as far as I can tell.
Overall, this game is, as I've said several times already, a forgettable speedrunning platformer. Controls are slippery, most abilities don't work half the time you try to use them, and level design is laughable at best.

In Nail'd you will crash a lot, at least in the beginning, maybe even accompanied with some cursing, but you after learn the tracks, both will be reduced. But lets not jump ahead to the gameplay and continue with the options. There are a lot video option (texture quality, material quality, shadows, texture filtering  and so on) to make the game run on slower machines. The game came out in 2010 and I can safely say it looks decent 4 years later.
I was quite surprise from the audio option. You can manage every sound in the game – engine, music in game and in the menus, environment and so on. As a hole the audio is okay. The engines sound okay and the music is decent, fits really well with the game. Also you can adjust the brightness and rebind keys on the keyboard. And honestly, you need to, because by default they are weird. You can play with 360 controller, but controls are absolutely fine with the keyboard.
After you set up all the option, it's time to choose male or female character, some clothes for them and atv or dirt bike. For your driver customizations are limited just to clothes, but you can change parts on your vehicle. They are unlocked just by playing the game and they have advantages and disadvantages.
The gameplay is arcade. Here the gravity is not the master. What I mean is, you can do extremely ridiculous jumps. And the sense of speed is amazing. This maybe is one of the few games where I don't mind the motion blur. Even if I want to I can't turn it off. In the beginning, before I get used to the sense of speed, I often missed some turns. Interesting thing in the gameplay is the steering in the air and leaning to adjust your jump. In other words – you almost fly.
There are 4 types of races – single lap, 3 laps, time challenge and stunt race. The first 3 are self explanatory. The stunt race is a little bit different. They are not stunts in a traditional sense. In this mode points are given if you drive through fire gates and circles, make wheelie and few others. And of course, here also matter if you finish in first place and how much you were in front of the other players. That way you can win a race, even if you didn't make enough stunts. All of them give you boost. My favorite way of getting it is to fall down on someone or push them in to obstacles. This can happen to you too. Other interesting thing is the mutators. They are constant boost or no collision.
To work everything I said about the gameplay, you need really good tracks. This is the case here. The design is great, even the environments are good – village, harbor, forest, canyon and others. Every track have different routs to take, but not all of them are shortcuts. Also in some tracks there are obstacles like falling rocks, but they are easily avoidable and stop being a surprise after a while.
One of the things I didn't like is the difficulty. I played on medium. The first half of the game I didn't have any problems with the AI. Then the difficulty jumps high for a few tracks. After them I was winning every race again without a problem. But biggest issue here is the repetition. It's kind get boring after a while, because there isn't enough variety. Since this is old game the online multiplayer is dead, but if you have some friends there is LAN, it's such rare thing to see these days.
I never played racing game with such sense of speed and adrenalin. Some compare it to MotorStorm. Even with the repetition, which comes at some point, this is still a solid game. If you have friends to play it gets even better. I recommend it.

A nice little nostalgia trip,this game appears to be made by the same people as the original monster jam game.
(y'know the one. It was on Wii,DS,PS2 and PC. not path of destruction,urban assault,MTM2 or rigs of rods,it was just "Monster Jam")
Or at least these guys are pretty darn close because the handling is nearly identical,as is the soundtrack. Of course,they use newer songs of the same genre,but put on five horse john's missisipi king and omigosh it is nearly the same game.
Of course,you do not drive monster trucks rather ATV quads and Motor Cross bikes. I can't help but see the bikes as the motorcross before the Monster Jam show,and the ATV's as the Monster Jam trucks,but that's probably from the coincidentally similar gameplay styles.
However,the thing that sets this apart from that series is the customization. You can change colors of every part of your rides,making both the bike and ATV have different paintjobs. Then you can edit your driver. Make them male or female and apply one of 8 color schemes. I believe you unlock more as the game progresses.
You have to make a profile for some reason,which is odd since this isn't multiplayer. However,with the "remember my password" just a simple press of the log-in button can have you racing twoards victory in no time. Again,this was a welcome surprise as it sent me on another nostalgia trip as the (what a shocker),ORIGINAL MONSTER JAM GAME did this too!
Sorry for the constant comparison,but i'm seriously curious about all the similarities between this and the Monster Jam game.
Of course,the tracks also show some similarities,some welcome similarities at that! You can fly through the air like in the MJ game,and some of the obstacles are pretty similar.
Of course,unlike that game this time you can feel the power of these vehicles kicking up dirt and rocks,and it's remarkable! A+ on realism guys,awesome job!
Unfortunately,there are one or two nitpicks.
First off,the hitboxes on the tracks are questionable at best. I went flying under a curved,arch-shaped rock and it said i hit it. Then,i flew past a rock with a tire width between me and it and i still hit it.
I wouldn't mind it if they added a damage system. Not like a performance limiting one such as N'14,but one where you hit something a chunk of your vehicle flies off like in the old MJ game this is so similar to.
But one tiny impact and your driver and vehicle graphically burst as the screen fades to black,white and grey and eventually total darkness with some splatters here and there.
And the respawn takes a whopping 30 seconds of in-game time,meaning one crash can absolutely DEVASTATE your lap time. This isn't uncommon among racing games though,so even if it is a minor annoyance this game isn't at fault.
I also dislike you cannot mix colors and paint jobs. If you put on the "graffiti" one for example it makes the vehicle black and red. I turned the ATV yellow but when i applied the decal it switched the base color back to black! Every paint job i try does this. But that's just my customization freak mind,not a real problem in the game.
In the end i gotta give this game an excellent rating of 5 stars. all games have problems,sure,but this isn't ment to be cutting edge i don't think,i think this was meant as a nice little reminder of some of the great racers of the past,and even the LOADING screen gave me that impression.
Any racing game lover HAS to pick this up,it is a gem in any racing game collection!
