This game greatly overstays its welcome. While it's fun at first, and the dialog definitely helps keep your interest, the weakest part of this game is the gameplay. It starts out promising, but within a few hours, you'll have a full party with all (four) of their abilities unlocked, and then the gameplay never evolves at all and every encounter becomes trivial., but still time consuming because every monster has quite a lot of health.
Once you have this setup, there is absolutely no feeling of progression. Level ups raise stats and give you a skill point to level up one of your abilities, but a single skill point seems so miniscule and it increases the mana cost so sometimes it doesn't feel much like a straight upgrade. Enemies never evolve outside of just stat upgrades. They don't get any cool abilities or anything. Some can use skills that your party can, but again, combat is so easy that it makes no difference. It also eventually introduces enemies that are physical or magical resistant, but this feels more tedious than it does innovative because it just means their large health pool just got even larger essentially.
There's also a strange mechanic where you unlock new characters and classes, but they all start at level 1, and your first party of 5 is likely very good at handling any group of enemies, so there is no incentive to swap out your original crew for any new members.
All in all, this game starts out fun and interesting, but after a while, you see how repetitive it is. It seems to bask into its repetitive nature down to the very core, making no effort to hide it from the player. It's a neat idea, but gameplay is kind of important to video games, and this one lacks in that regard.

FTL: Faster Than Light is an awesome game! Unlike many games these days, it is very brutal and difficult to beat even on its easy mode. Really, no progression in this game is easy, all the achievements actually take work, unlike most games these days, unlocking new ships is actually based upon doing work in the game, including some very specific events, and unlocking new types of the same ship requires getting some ship-based achievements. The gameplay is still fun, and there are so many strategies  that you could use that every player can have their own fun experience. Of course, you might not like that FTL is so much more difficult than a regular game, but it makes success, even small ones, like getting a new crew record for skills mastered on a game where you got so close to the boss (which is the mother of all bosses ever) so much more rewarding than any other game. I imagine beating that boss is the most rewarding thing ever. It would probably make you want to try again in a different way, demonstrating another beauty of this game; every run is quite random, yet not too random. You can learn from ship layouts and apply that knowledge to future runs, but not have the exact same ship. I highly recommend FTL, It is a true must have!

ARPG's like Diablo, Torchlight and Titan Quest rely on a couple basic tactics to allow weaker players to overcome harder AI opponents: "kiting", where you hit and run from a distance, wearing the boss down; and "grinding", where you just go replay earlier areas to level up and get better loot until you can survive against the boss. Grim Dawn has largely disabled these tactics by (a) putting bosses in small areas and giving them fast movement so you can't effectively "kite", and (b) always setting the boss level = player level + N, so grinding just makes the boss tougher. I want to play this game, but it's too hard for me. I can't get past the bosses and I've given up.

Being developed by the same team as its quasi-predecessor Titan Quest and using the same engine, Grim Dawn plays a lot like the aforementioned Titan Quest. That is, it is a classic hack-and-slay. As this is written, the game is not releaed yet, so some of the now mentioned points might change until release. Unfortunately, there are severe technical issues contained in the current build (which is build 30), for example local multiplayer not working with 3+ players and a high rate of random crashes. The difficulty is somewhat higher than one might be used to from other hack-and-slay titles but still enjoyable. Apart from that, gameplay is designed quite conservatively. That means one should not expect an extraordinarily innovative gameplay but a hack-and-slay ARPG like many others before. On the other hand, this also means that the gameplay is really great (there is a reason there are so many hack-and-slay titles), so this is not necessarily a bad thing. In general, the gameplay experience is captivating and the atmosphere created in the game does help this a lot. In conclusion, I can really recommend Grim Dawn to anyone who is willing to ignore the troubles of early access (else you should probably wait unitl release and get it then).

Grim Dawn is an excellent game and I had fun playing it. This is a pre-release review so things may change, but unless they replace game data with Superman 64 I expect my review will hold for final release.
These are the things I liked about it:
- Fun top down slaughterfest with addictive gameplay. Blood, gibs, explosions, magic, witchfinder general hats.
- Lovecraftian storyline and very bleak setting during the twilight days of humanity. Lore that will give you chills.
- Black and Grey morality with choices that change who is a friend or foe with factions that don't all get along.
- Fun classes to choose from which you can mix and match to figure out what is right for you.
- Large world lots of quests and many alcoves to explore, and nooks and crannies if you like those instead.
- Optional Rogue-like dungeon crawl for the brave. Veteran mode is awesome for your 1st playthrough.
- Hardcore mode for crazy people. Crafting for crafty people.
- No karma meter to show how "Good" or "Bad" you are.
- A "Throw Feces" ability to let you fling poo at your foes like an ape.
These are the things I didn't like:
- I spent a great deal of time playing the game instead of being a productive member of society.
- I want a sequel or xpac, which will deprive me of more time.

I love puzzle games, but this one's not for everyone.
After the greatly enjoyable easy and medium levels, you're graced with the irritating hard mode difficulty. I felt that solving a lot of the problems didn't involve skill but continuous trial and error.  It ended up overstaying its visit and without tools like slowing down, pausing, or many ways to see what went wrong. In the end, it means you're shuffling tiles, clicking the go button, and then trying agian.
But that's not where my big complaint is. It has a "Beat the level for me" button. If you're stuck, press the hint button. Go on, there's no repurcussion. In fact, click it as many times  as you want. It'll solve the level for you with enough clicks. This might sound like a good thing, but it makes solving a puzzle so unsatisfying. You work for an answer that you can get the same results from just letting the game tell you were to put it all. And (outside of achievements) There's 0 drawbacks. In a game that gives you few tools to diagnose your problem, it puts a bandaid on a bullet wound by solving the problem for you.
My last complaint is that it's just so heartless. Until you get to the glados levels (which are the best part of the game that remove the F***it button and add some flavor to the game) You're playing a game about cubes. Emotionless, boring, cop-out cubes. Minimalistic? Yes. But like modern art, if I have no reason to be interested in these cubes, they're just cubes. I'm just solving puzzles and not engaged with anything put on the screen. It's a very subjective opinion, though. If you're here for puzzles more than engagement, you'll probably like it.
All in all, it's a great game that spikes in difficulty a little too quick and with a few too many tools to help you figure out problems. If you enjoy games that require 1 answer, don't mind cubes, you'll probably enjoy this game. Otherwise you may want to look elsewhere.

The ground fights are pretty good, for the game's time. The voices and sounds in general are well done (when not glitching out), and at times the game performs just like you would hope a Star Wars type FPS would. The player can (and must) make a difference in the battle, but can also die without too much penalty usually... although it's ridiculous on some maps when you have to fight a dozen jedi when only armed with a blaster because you seem to be the only one actually involved in the mission. If the "mission rests on (my) shoulders" maybe I should be able to select something with a useful weapon rather than generic storm trooper. Like some other games I've played this one is unsure if it wants you to be a soldier in the machine or the hero... and suffers for that.
The game should have had a better UI and should pause to allow for an actual review of objectives since they come on the fly and are not always clear. The space battles (which seem awesome at first) are difficult because of counter-intuitive controls and even less in the way of clear objectives.
The game also has unacceptably bad AI, which should be a concern unless you are only interested in playing online. I  have bought this game during the Summer Sales 2015.
"Why not?" I thought, since it was there for a bargain.
And I wasn't dissapointed!
Now, let's get to the game itself.
The goal is to lead the boxes (orange, purple, green, blue, red,  I hope I have mentioned all colors now!) to their dedicated (same colored) destination.
To achieve this, you have a certain number of "direction markers" (among other things) you can place on the field, like arrows that show the direction where it will lead each box that touches it. You can place these direction markers on any spot you like, just make sure you are placing them on the right position so the cubes reach their correct destination.
Oh, and these markers are limited, depening on the level/area. And it's not allowed to let the cubes bump against each other...or let them fall off the field. With logic, you'll make it.
K, now to the music:
I like it. it's some ambient electro stuff, and matching very well to the game.
So yeah, I started it, played the training and finished some "beginner" levels so far.
Since it's a nice looking and fun game, I'll keep playing it more often.
You should get this game too if you like logical games or want to have something to play & relax!
Oh, the animations are nice too. You can move the camera around, so you have a nice overview.
Unfotunately, I didn't see any option where I could have set the speed of the boxes (I can be such an impatient person, no matter how nice the cube animations are in this game). Anyway, I like it so I recommend this game.

JumpJet Rex is a neat little indie game with platforming being left, right and center of the gameplay. It's comparable to games like Super Meat Boy (and might actually be the best entry in the genre since said title). The game has good leveldesign, the controls are on point, the music is great and it manages to capture the spirit of the SNES era quite well. JJR himself with all his customizable features is a likeable hero and quite fitting for a game like this.
However, the designers made one choice that I simply can't get behind:
Implementing three different gamemodes is a good thing, but instead of letting the player chose which mode he wants to play - all three modes are mandatory for advancing through the normal adventure. This decision can lead to the need to constantly replay certain levels, which kills your sense of progression and can get frustrating at times. Even though the way the time challenges are implemented (with ghosts, leaderboards etc) is near perfect, it is never a good idea to remove choice from the player.
But as I said in the beginning JumpJet Rex is still a good game, there is just this one stupid decision by the developers that holds it back. If you are a fan of the the genre I'd say it is still worth its full price, if not wait for it on sale.

I regret to inform you that I write this review without having finished the game. Not for lack effort, but because it's just not feasible. I'll go into why later in the review.
JumpJet Rex is a colourful speedrun game about a dinosaur that collects stars to save the universe. Something like that anyway. There are some 30+ delightful little worlds with each type of world (ice, desolate space base, etc.) seeming to have their own little chiptune to go with it. And these are some damn good chiptunes. I bought the game through Chrono GG so it came with the soundtrack and my god was it worth it. Definitely got some workout tunes out of it (should I ever be finish my selection of podcasts). Really, have a listen to some of them. You can also customize the appearance of your dinosaur, 4 elements. Head, skin tone, shoes, jumpjet particles. But that's dress-up and I don't find it particularly enjoyable.
In each level you collect rings to unlock the gate. Pass the finish line and you've completed it, you earn a star. You can earn up to three stars per level. One for completion, one for not dying, and one for speedrunning. You need to collect some number of stars to unlock the next few levels. Simple enough. I usually settled for completing without dying to grind stars because I only needed to be careful to progress. But some levels are easy to speedrun if you take advantage of checkpoints (and dying). So I took those too. You can also download ghosts within the game of the top players in the world or people near your skill level to see how they do things. So it provides a good improvement tool within the game, well done.
As the game goes on, and certain elements get added to the levels, I saw some SIGNIFICANT frame drops. Like, we're talking 2 fps frame drops. The culprits seem to be certain environmental objects. Patches of thorns that disburse leaves and these globules that travel up and down. And it became a real pain on a particular boss fight called 'Seedmour' in which the level is full of these thorn patches so after maybe a minute of fighting the boss you'd be unable to do anything for several minutes due to the fps drop. Alt-tabbing seemed to help, but I don't know for sure. That boss fight was a particularly annoying because after dropping the boss's health to zero you also had to ground-pound it before it got back up and if you happened to be stuck in 2 fps time when that window presented itself... prepare yourself to have to hit it again because there's no way you're going to do it in time. And this is why I haven't finished the game. Because in the later levels this becomes a constant issue and you kinda need the frames in a speedrunning game if you want it to be fun. (I suspect the issue is some kind of garbage collection or object recycling code).
Other than that though, the game is brilliant. Definitely recommend giving it a go.

It's not a bad game. The experience opens strong, with a humor-rich premise and an uncomplicated-but-fun combat system. Unfortunately, the game leans too heavily on these, and it quickly gets repetitious. Just as important: Because the repetitious combat takes a long time, the game becomes boring.
To see if the game would let me, I decided to take a level 30 quest when my party was level 8. I completed the quest, but it was the last satisfying experience of the game. Every fight was a little grindy: Sleep/stun everything, then focus fire on one enemy. Turn order is the same round after round, so there was no chance of me missing a lapsed sleep or stun. The stun-immune boss required a little more strategy, but it was still repetitious: paladin soaked; druid and witch kept paladin alive; wizard and rogue dealt damage (and occasionally stunned minions).
When I got done with this quest, I thought, "Ah, my party can beat level 30 content. Surely I'll burn through level 20 content like an acetylene torch through butter, so I can quickly advance this light, humorous storyline." Not so. It turns out that I still have to spend a dozen rounds whittling down level 20 fights. The only difference is that, if I let a sleep or stun lapse, the consequences are lower, since the monsters don't hit as hard.
Bottom line: I got some decent entertainment value out of Knights and Pen and Paper. I'm probably not going to finish it, though, and I can't say I would have missed much if I hadn't played it.

I think this is a great platformer but I don't recommend it because of the way new levels are unlocked.
To unlock the next level, you need to achieve a certain number of stars from previous levels. You earn 1 star for completing a level, 1 star for for completing it without dying, and 1 star for beating a set time limit. However, just completing levels is not enough to unlock new levels; you won't have enough stars. Some levels are long and quite difficult to get through without dying. If you need the stars to unlock the next levels (and you will), you will need to restart the whole level every time you die. The game has checkpoints in each level, but you are punished for using them because it means you won't get the extra stars that you need to unlock new levels. The grind to get stars is annoying and frustrating, and I would much rather prefer levels be unlocked as the previous one is beaten, without the need for stars.

The use of scarce resources works really well into the storyline and even more into the player's decisions of what to do. I'm not really much of a tactical combat fan so I was surprised by how much I really enjoyed the game.
The best part, however, are the really amazing visuals (outside of cutscenes). I plan on playing through the game a second time just so I can screencap some of the scenes. And even better than the graphics? The music.
Really the only thing I could complain about is that the end of the game doesn't really feel like an ending. It's more of a resolution to the current situation than a resolution to the entire storyline. Of course, this may mean a sequel in the future!

Seriously, XCOM: EU (and the expansion Enemy Within) is the best turn based strategy game I've played in years. If you know the old XCOM series and liked it, you will not be dissapointet.
You take turns, so naturally there will be no high speed action with explosions and smoke and
bombs flying everywhere all the time. The graphics are good though. What am I talking about, just look at the screenshots.
The Game's main aspect is the turn based combat. Here is where the difficulty setting kicks in, and it kicks in hard! While the lowest setting should be doable by everyone but the weakest of heart, the
-setting will make you question your sanity for putting up with this. (And then you will klick
.)
Most of the combat mission are of generic "there-aliens-go-kick-them" quality, but during (and for) the development of the story there are non-generic missions. While playstyle is the same, those are spiced up by e.g. additional voice acting or special rewards. The generic missions started to bother me a little on my 3rd playthrough, which I consider perfectly normal even for a great game.
While not showing your BattleCommander-of-Greatness-Skillz you don't get to rest! Between alien attacks you have to manage your base. This is less detailed than in the old XCOM games. E.g.: You still have to buy / manufacture weapons for your team, but you don't have to buy Ammo and MediKits replenish their uses after battle automatically with no cost. If this is a pro or con is to you to decide.
Base management can be broken down to the three pillars Money, Engineering and Science. Especially on the harder difficultys there will be though ( = fun, you old guys know what I mean ) decisions.
All in all, some hardcore gamers might be a bit dissapointet, but the rest will find a nice, not too dumbed-down "Base-Manager" that really has an effect on Combat.
Apart from what I already mentioned, the only downside I can think of is that the harder difficulty levels limit the ways you can play (and win) quite a bit. A good chunk of technologies and tactics which a) sound reasonable and b) worked fine on lower difficulty just have to be left out when going for the "Impossible Ironman" (Hardest setting, Autosave after everything you do, no manual saving). I would have liked a little more freedom of choice there, but figuring out a working way to do it was also kind of fun.
It's XCOM. For some thats enough.
The rest of you should buy this for the robust combat mechanics, the replayability (you unlock little 'mods' by winning the game), the occasional WTF moment, the wide range of selectable difficulty, the well made cutscenes and great voice acting, and, of course,
Platformer. Free. Profits. Need I say more?

ARPG's like Diablo, Torchlight and Titan Quest rely on a couple basic tactics to allow weaker players to overcome harder AI opponents: "kiting", where you hit and run from a distance, wearing the boss down; and "grinding", where you just go replay earlier areas to level up and get better loot until you can survive against the boss. Grim Dawn has largely disabled these tactics by (a) putting bosses in small areas and giving them fast movement so you can't effectively "kite", and (b) always setting the boss level = player level + N, so grinding just makes the boss tougher. I want to play this game, but it's too hard for me. I can't get past the bosses and I've given up.

Being developed by the same team as its quasi-predecessor Titan Quest and using the same engine, Grim Dawn plays a lot like the aforementioned Titan Quest. That is, it is a classic hack-and-slay. As this is written, the game is not releaed yet, so some of the now mentioned points might change until release. Unfortunately, there are severe technical issues contained in the current build (which is build 30), for example local multiplayer not working with 3+ players and a high rate of random crashes. The difficulty is somewhat higher than one might be used to from other hack-and-slay titles but still enjoyable. Apart from that, gameplay is designed quite conservatively. That means one should not expect an extraordinarily innovative gameplay but a hack-and-slay ARPG like many others before. On the other hand, this also means that the gameplay is really great (there is a reason there are so many hack-and-slay titles), so this is not necessarily a bad thing. In general, the gameplay experience is captivating and the atmosphere created in the game does help this a lot. In conclusion, I can really recommend Grim Dawn to anyone who is willing to ignore the troubles of early access (else you should probably wait unitl release and get it then).

Grim Dawn is an excellent game and I had fun playing it. This is a pre-release review so things may change, but unless they replace game data with Superman 64 I expect my review will hold for final release.
These are the things I liked about it:
- Fun top down slaughterfest with addictive gameplay. Blood, gibs, explosions, magic, witchfinder general hats.
- Lovecraftian storyline and very bleak setting during the twilight days of humanity. Lore that will give you chills.
- Black and Grey morality with choices that change who is a friend or foe with factions that don't all get along.

Divinity: Original Sin (commonly referred to as D:OS) follows the same style of play as the original Divinity Series, and also to, Divinity Eco Draconis or the Dragon Knight Saga.  D:OS is a role playing game that follows the rules of Dungeons and Dragons probably better than other games of a similar genre - wherein this game features turn based combat.  Explore freely, get attacked, and rather than being completely unprepared for it, you have the time to formulate your strategy
There are very many fun aspects of the game, but the biggest "success" is the fact that you're given the freedom to be who you want to be.  If you want to be the most unsympathetic swine in the world - you can.  Want to kill random strangers?  Go right ahead!  Of course, you'll be hunted down for doing so, but at least the game gives you the choice to do it.
The term "LOL" will apply many times when playing this game - of course assuming you have a funny bone.  I'm sure my neighbours heard me the first time I used the sneak ability.  The main story line is "serious", but I'd say a great many of the side quests have some kind of funny anecdote here and there.  These occasional lapses into ludicrity make the game really enjoyable to play.  You may even find yourself drawn into the game emotionally, feeling really sorry for the plight of the people that you are helping.
Having played this game from it's release date, I've found that I've fell into a lot of pitfalls of this game, and I've had to play it 3 times through before being able to complete it.  I'm an achievement fanatic, and unless you play this game in a very specific way, you won't get 100% achievements, because some options just wont' be available.  To me, this is not a good thing, because it reduces some of my freedom.
Another bad aspect of the game is the lack of quest markers - in fact, quest markers are, to my memory, used only twice within the game.  This is just simply not enough, considering the amount of times I've had to fumble about with the map to try to figure out where I'm supposed to go.
I've spent more time Googling in this game than in any game I've ever played - because a lot of the quest objectives, or maps aren't obvious enough.  The dungeon tutorial also doesn't provide enough tutorial for you to really get to know the game well enough - like for example
.
Thanks to the concerted efforts of the developers to provide bugfixes so quickly after the game was released, I can happily say now that this game will now bring you a lot of hours of enjoyment, with a few hours of frustration.  The good news is that you don't have to stay frustrated for long - just use Google and then you'll find the clues that were nowhere else to be seen.  This game will annoy you - but as long as you persevere, you wil find that the overall experience will be more rewarding.
Prepare yourself for many hours of fun.

Can a game be improved for the wrong reasons?
I enjoyed my time with this game, but it feels like an expansion more than a proper sequel. For instance it take place in the same exact city. Not even a remodeled city, from what I can tell, just the same exact one with some visual differences. There are a few sections outside the simulated Steelport on the alien battleship. It would be cool if it was an explorable area, but those are just linear segments.
IV has the same major flaw as The Third where too much of the game is padded out with mini-game sidequests. You run a race and apparently you took over part of the city. It's as unsatisfying here as it was in the previous game. Like The Third some of the story-line missions are really fun while others are phoned in. Like they ran out of time developing them and had to half♥♥♥♥♥it. They don;t have that bombastic style that you want from a Saints Row game.
So what did they improve? Basically the superpowers further streamline the process of running around the city. That's both a good thing or a bad thing. Part of the open-city crime genre is getting into the city and feeling like you're a part of the streets. You learn how to get where you want to go and you absorb the city's personality. It's nice to just fly in a straight line to your next mission, and I know the storyline makes this not just another open-world game, and yes because you're exploring the same city you're probably notgoing to care as much about absorbing the aesthetics, but I can't shake the feeling that this game is missing the point a little.
Of course, the mechanics behind the superpowers are easy and fun, and the gunplay is solid as ever with lots of satisfying munitions to unload so it's still fun to blast your way through the more uninspired sections of the game. The writing is sharper this time with a better mix of gutter humor and genuine cleverness. Overall it's a fun game to play despite the flaws, but the fact that, despite everything, the game is genuinely fun makes me hate the flaws even more.

You have to guide cubes to exits, but the hardest part is not how to lead them, but to prevent collisions between them. Fortunately, almost all levels have hints, and you can chose between 2 types. In a puzzle game, it's expected for you to solve them by yourself, but this feature can help you if you're stuck. And you will be a lot. And in here you don't need to rush, because first you fit the course for the cubes before they run. This releases pressure and allows you to concentrate on the solution. Overall, it's a nice puzzle game, accessible and challenging at the same time.

Orcs must die is a tower defence game and third person shooter wrapped up into one.
The plot is as simple as it gets. There are two worlds, our world, and the orc world (insert warcraft joke here). They are connected by rifts, which allow travel between the two worlds, and for magic to flow into both worlds. An order has been set up to protect these rifts at all costs, using massive forts filled with traps to stem the hordes. You are a thick beefcake trained by the best old man the order had, before he died, it is your task to defend the rifts and keep back the hordes.
The meat of the game is wave based tower defence, where in you spend mana to set up defences along lanes in order to protect the rift from any nasties trying to get through. You yourself are loaded with weapons as well which allow you to take an active roll in the defence of the rift. You have a set amount of slots with which to select your tools of death and are locked into those until the end of the level. Weapons and traps both take up a single slot, so choose wisely.
Its a difficult but extremely satisfying process, going through each wave and being careful with how you plan everything out, from basic trap set up to the shooting mechanics, every enemy is dealt with in a slightly different way, with no true stratagy to perfectly stop the incoming hordes, you're always moving, always setting up new traps, always doing something. Its chaotic, but rarely overwhelming to the point where its impossible to handle right up until the end when you've failed to make the optimal trap set up somewhere or haven't been active enough in your own personal combat against the creeps.
Visually the game is very cartoonish, everything is very clean and it goes well with the cheesy comedy aspect, really hammering home the fact the game is light hearted, which is fine. The music scores, while not the greatest pieces, are memorable and even weeks later i can perfectly remember the main theme, i personally found them fantastic, but your tastes may differ.
The game overall was a wonderful experience from start to finish, being one of the most addictive games i've ever played in my life, and it was also the first game i ever played on PC, forever bringing me into the folds of the PC master race. I whole heartedly recommend this game to anyone looking for a fast paced tower defence game, or third person shooter with heavy focus on not doing all the work by yourself.

What is The Banner Saga?
The Banner Saga is at its simplest, a hybrid of a strategy RPG and Oregon Trail.  Try to picture playing Oregon Trail that is broken up with turn-based strategy gameplay like that found in Fire Emblem, XCOM, or Final Fantasy: Tactics.  While marching on the trail, many decisions will be heaped upon the player as to what to do next.  These sections are presented in text with options as to what course of action to take.
What is most striking in The Banner Saga is the inspiring hand-drawn artwork and amazing animations.  It is like an exceptionally bloody and brutal Disney movie.  The game boots to a gorgeous title screen that makes it clear that the game is in a class of its own when it comes to visuals.  The game begins with the now typical statement of “Choices matter in this game” thanks to TellTale’s The Walking Dead beginning that trend.  With multiple endings and characters that can be recruited or missed, it feels as though the decisions the player makes do indeed affect the turn of events presented in The Banner Saga.
Pedigree might be something to consider when looking at The Banner Saga.  Stoic Studios is comprised of ex-Bioware employees who worked on Star Wars: The Old Republic.  They also netted the composer of Journey to do the music for the game, Austin Wintory.
The Story
The Banner Saga is a tale of family, trust, betrayal, and survival.  These themes permeate throughout the narrative and the gameplay.  The player is constantly bombarded with decisions about if this group can join the caravan or can “these” types of people be trusted.  Many narrative hooks revolve around characters that may or may not join the party.  The player controls two different sets of adventures as they travel across the countryside in order to fight and run from the mechanical Dredge.  One side is a band of Varl, a race of horned-giants, who have much experience in vanquishing the Dredge; the other centers on a man and his daughter who are humans.  Their respective journeys inevitably collide as the game progresses.  The game begins slowly and very densely.  Like the opening to The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim, the player is assaulted with meaningless proper noun after meaningless proper noun that does nothing but confuse the player.  After two hours, however, the game gets its narrative and gameplay hooks into the player and does not relent until the credits roll.
As the end of the game approached a fear began to run over me: the fear of a cliffhanger. I knew the game was a baby of Kickstarter and that this is part 1 of scheduled trilogy.  This premonition proved false as the game ends quite well, and can end in multiple ways.  Despite the fluidity of the storytelling, the final fight is rigid in requiring the player to use two specific characters. One of the characters that I had neglected to properly level through the rest of the game was worthless at this point.  The absence of a free-battle or place to grind made the final encounter an enormous difficulty spike on what was rather smooth curve up until the end.
Gameplay
The grid-based gameplay is familiar, but has some nice points of distinction.  Every unit has Armor and Health.  Health equals damage.  Attacking it lowers an enemy’s ability to deal more damage, but Armor subtracts from the amount of damage that can be done to Health.  It is a good balance that is explored by differing enemy types.  The Dredge have loads of Armor, but enemy Varl have a ton of Health and can therefore do damage quickly if allowed to.  Turn order is important to remember as well.  It might be wise to leave a couple of weakened enemies alive, so that the stronger enemies will not attack as frequently.  Add in a well-balanced upgrade system, and some special class related abilities and one has a good idea of the core gameplay present within The Banner Saga.
While moving from city to city and balancing the food supply and the caravan’s morale, the player will be tasked with responding to the many encounters the game possesses.  These may range from a simple investigation of a fire, to determining if a group of people may or may not join the caravan, to decisions that result in the death of party members.  The Banner Saga pulls no punches, and is not afraid to wreck the player’s best character after a poor decision.  Another type of encounter is “War.” A number of Dredge or bandits may be spotted and then the player may try to avoid the fight, go in leading the charge (resulting in a harder battle for the player, but will result in less casualties), or lead from the rear (resulting in an easier fight with more potential casualties).  There is also a river crossing section that is clearly a nod to Oregon Trail, where one can ford the river, caulk the wagons, or attempt to find an easier place to pass that could eat up precious time.
One minor critique of the gameplay would be how experience is handled.  Characters level up based on the number of kills they accrue on the battlefield.  Level one characters are essentially useless until they get two kills.  Fire Emblem handles this by awarding experience when any amount of damage is done, but gives much more for the final blow. In The Banner Saga, kills are all that matter.  This is in no way a deal breaker, but a small irritation.
The Recommendation
The Banner Saga is an excellent and engrossing experience.  Every decision is doused in consequence.  The gameplay is intense and it ties wonderfully into the game’s narrative providing a cohesive and full gaming experience.  The visuals and score accent simple but gripping mechanics, and many of the characters are memorable and well realized.  There is startlingly little to complain about in The Banner Saga; a slow start, a questionable experience system, the difficulty spike in the last fight, and a “speed up” option when traveling for additional playthroughs would have been nice.  It is hard not to respect a game that took three of my best characters at the conclusion of one dialogue section.  The Banner Saga is brutal, beautiful, and most importantly hard to stop when has started it.  The depth and care that went into crafting the world of The Banner Saga is evident, and that hard work should be praised.  Those looking for a Kickstarter failure will have to continue to look elsewhere.

Pickers is an incredibly unique game. It's probably the only game that combines economics with hidden object games. But does that mix work or is it just a scrambled mess?
You are the owner of a little shop called Rusted Gold. Everyday you can shop at 12 different "stores" (which will be unlocked one store at a day starting with two) and buy up to 7 items which you can showcase in your store or immediately sell at an auction. Once you've bought all 7 of your items, you're going back to your store.
The goal of the game is to become the #1 picker at the end of 30 days. You will be competing against 9 random pickers and will be compared to them at the end of each day. If competition isn't for you, you can also choose a relaxed mode where there's no competition. Or if you think the game is too easy, there's also a more difficult mode for you.
While buying your inventory, you can haggle with the owner and change their mood. Happy owners are more willing to give you a discount while angry ones might even refuse to sell you anything for the day. You can make an owner happy by buying their junk for double the price and then get them to haggle for the expensive stuff. Their mood changes very drastically with every deal, so make sure you plan your purchases ahead.
The game features a lot of treasure that you can find, combine and sell; original screenplays, dolls, movies, tickets, signatures and even old vehicles. But buy with caution: every day has a new "hot item" category where you're more likely to get much more profit out of your items. Once you've bought something and sold it, it won't respawn ever again.
While the game is actually about a store, you're going to get a lot more profit off of the auction house, especially from hot and rare items. Every once in a while you'll get a "jackpot deal" where you can make more than double the profit. It's important to save your items for "hot" days and only sell expensive items at the auctions.
Now you're probably wondering where the hidden object mechanic comes into play. Well, it really doesn't. Every store has one hidden object area which can be used once a day. From it you get one random hot item that can be found in the hidden object puzzle. This may be a $10 toy or a $4,000 vehicle, so make sure to plan ahead if you want to use this as well. Each hidden object puzzle has a specific amount of items and once you've found everything and received a handful of free items, the spot will be dry and can't be used again.
If you're looking for the usual hidden object game, this game really isn't for you. But if you like basic economics with planning ahead, a little competition and lots of achievements, then you're probably going to have a lot of fun with this one. To me, this game is a hidden treasure.

What it does right: Firstly, the game is beautiful in appearance and sound. The art and animation is very carefully done, and the soundtrack sets the perfect mood throughout. Secondly, it combines an intriguing mix of turn base combat and overworld travel and text based decision making a la Oregon Trail. Lastly, the choices in the game provided a strong sense of agency.
What it does wrong: First, the game ends sooner than you’d expect, and leaves too many loose ends begging to be tied up. While the ride was entertaining up to that point, it magnified the fact that all the choices previous were illusory.  Secondly, with that in mind, many of the tough choices you make regarding your forces or clan in the overworld lack some sort of greater purpose by the end. I even found myself wondering “Does it really matter that my people are about to starve” and an hour later, it turned out it did not (save a small combat mechanic with “morale”). You would be better off buying trinkets or leveling your characters rather than using resources to buy supplies for your people, because the game abruptly ends with simply killing a BBG. Lastly, a smaller detail to nitpick, there appears to be a lot of added content that was designed to make the game appear epically larger, but never is used to actually make it grander, such as the detailed overworld map that you will only ever follow a linear story path on and little history lessons on places you come across.
If you’re big into game design, I’d recommend you try it, because it has a unique feel to it. However, if you enjoy strategy rpg’s, there are better options, because Banner Saga weaves an intriguing tale that gets you leaning closer and closer with a developing plot, then just slaps you the face.

Knights of Pen and Paper is a solid game, but not a perfect one. It has fairly well thought out mechanics and there is nothing you can do in the game that the game itself doesn’t make intuitive to do, but there are multiple points when the difficulty-curve is not so well designed, even going so far as to require you to grind well after finishing every quest in the game save one that is actually HARDER then the last main quest of the game.
It is also very simple. In fact many would probably call this game an RPG-lite and they would not be wrong. Despite the new angle of playing the people around the table instead of the heroes on their character sheets, this game is overall a very simple title… simple enough I was not surprised to see the game is readily available, not just on the PC, but on mobile phones.
This makes for a surprisingly good game overall, but not one designed to be played over long sessions. Rather, it’s a series of bite-sized sessions that will ultimately get you through the to the end, assuming you have the patients to get through some of the later muck.

At this point I don't think there is any 1 direction you "need" to spec yourself out because every skill seems equally viable.  Heck I found myself holding skill points because I simply did not know which way to go and ended up leveling 5 times before spending any!
The mood and atmosphere settings for each locations are wonderfully detailed.   The one complaint I may have is that in some areas it can become extremely dark even with lit torches around.
There are things that happen within the game that will make a profound impact to your game.  Rescuing a survivor from the area he may be at may not be the best idea...
Although the main world you will be exploring are all pre-rendered maps, there are extra dungeons in which are special challenges that are all very much roguelike and different that require a special key to enter.  Trying to find these places are what makes the game that much  more fun to explore and check every nook and cranny for something cool.
I was pleasantly surprised to find sooo much meat on this game to indulge myself with and even after several playthroughs with different combinations of classes, I still found myself having loads of fun.  This game is a must have!

Since i have played Grim Dawn, Titan Quest and Diablo 3 a LOT, here's what i think about this game:
Pros:
- Skill system is similar to Titan Quest and very complex, allowing you to customize your character alot. There are obvious builds just like in D3 (Pet-master, Fire-builds etc.) but you are not limited to them.
- No allways-online, you can in fact play this game completely in offline mode, characters are saved on your harddrive. (similar to Titan Quest)
- Many items with the same system as in TQ where rare pre- and -suffixes can occur on normal items. Also Epic and Legendary stuff (including sets and abilities granted by items)
- Farming: A combination of TQ and D3, boss runs are still effective (TQ) but there are also Hero spawns in normal locations that can be lucrative (D3)
- Simple Multiplayer system, you can either host a game (and others might join you, you can set a password or kick others) or you can join a game yourself (direct join to your steam-friends or browse existing hosted games)
- almost no bugs, the few that are there allways get fixed ASAP
Things i personally dont mind but might be important to you:
- performance issues when ALOT of stuff is going on (R9 290, 16GB RAM, i7 and dropping to 20fps on high settings, can be improved by lowering the settings though)
- Multiplayer MIGHT not allways work, make sure you have administrator rights when searching for games or it can crash (just like in TQ)
- even though they are not popular, you might find cheaters online (since save-files are on your harddrive you can just manipulate them). In that case just host a game yourself and kick them :P
- no voice acting and average grafics might scare you. but keep in mind that crate entertainment is a really small studio ("Crate Entertainment has grown from one man with a dream to a team of ten with veteran developers....") so what they achieved is actually really impressive.
Conclusion: A really good ARPG. not a tripple-A title like D3 with millions of budget, still managed to entertain me more than D3 personally. If you like these kind of games, just buy it!

TL;DR
If you've ever enjoyed playing similar games, then you'll love this. It follows the formula in a fairly straightforward manner, but it's impeccably refined – one of the best, in my opinion.
My bullsh*t:
I'd had my eye on this game for a couple of years, frankly, but the thought of playing an ARPG in delayed, unpolished segments seemed miserable. After reading that the game was 'content complete' with the release of Act 4, I decided to finally dive in (it was also on sale, which was sweet).
To be clear, I love this genre. Diablo, Titan Quest, Torchlight. Loved 'em all. Hell, I even like Diablo 3 (because I think its streamlined nature makes it an amazing local co-op console port, but I suppose that's besides the point). All of this taken into consideration, Grim Dawn, as an all-round experience, is better than some of the most prolific titles of the genre.
To start, it offers a wonderfully refined balance between the min-maxing ARGPs of old and the mash-to-win fair of today: the gameplay is modern(ish), character-building is back-to-formula without being too overbearing (respecs are cheap, and the dual-class system, in addition to being damned fun, provides a lot of versatility), and the questing is considerably deep for the genre (a blend of story missions, side quests, and bounties – there's always something to do). The late-game also incorporates Factions, which adds another layer of (admittedly shallow but nonetheless enjoyable) immersion – and a good amount of gear, at that.
To the benefit of its well-crafted content, level progression is such that you never find yourself grinding, and gear progression is perfectly consistent, even at later levels.  As a result, the game plays fluidly, offering us junkies a true-to-form “Wiki-this” experience whilst maintaining an almost action-adventure pace. This is in part due to the impressive amount of content, which keeps the game from ever feeling wanting for ideas / challenges. Like all ARPGs, the progression is certainly linear, but this game does a better job than most at making its limitations unnoticeable.

Moving on to the artsy side of things, Grim Dawn looks pretty great. Others have likened the tone and art direction to Diablo (going so far as to label it a “true successor” to the series), but I think it's really carved a style of its own. Unlike other games, Grim Dawn never seems overtly “fantastic” - even as you're having your kneecaps mauled by an outer-dimensional being (borrowed straight from the pages of Lovecraft, mind you). As a result, the early, critter-laden environments contrast brilliantly with some of the wierder sh*t down the line. This grounded atmosphere allows the escalating doom-and-gloom to feel genuinely threatening, which is something I haven't felt since my first encounter with D2; however, unlike the Diablo series, I can't say the game ever felt “scary” at any point. Dark, for sure, but never scary.
In line with the game's intriguing atmosphere, there is a clear effort invested in the environments (evidenced by the player's ability to rotate the camera 360 degrees – a rarely utilized but none the less cool and welcome feature). As a result, the environments never feel paint-by-numbers or overtly themed (looking at you, Torchlight 2), and the game does away with the randomly-generated levels of yore that, while intended to keep things "fresh," really just end up being a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ The only bit that I'm not terribly impressed with are the characters, themselves. Player models, as well as most other NPC humans in the game, just don't look that great. Passable, but not great. What's more, the gear, perhaps in keeping with the game's relatively down-to-earth aesthetic, just never pops or impresses the way it does in other titles (a disappointing lack of dishwasher-sized pauldrons, for certain), and because of the necessary mish-mashing brought on by the dual-class system, there's never much visual differentiation between classes.
I know that nobody really reads this crap beyond the “buy it” part, so I'll go ahead and close this off with the usual: 11/10, would die in aetherial fire again. But seriously, if you're a fan of the genre, this is worth a look, especially when it's on sale. It's business as usual, no doubt, but it does everything just a little bit better.
Stray observations:
Other downsides? Maybe crafting. Crafting is always either a miserable grind (every title but Diablo 3) or an oft-disappointing time-sink (Diablo 3), but this game manages to make it altogether irrelevant, minus a few relics. Keep in mind, it isn't necessarily 'bad,' but it's the one thing that feels sort of phoned in.
Also, I'll admit that I haven't dabbled in the multiplayer AT ALL, and I've read less than favorable reviews regarding this aspect of the game, so if you're looking for a more social experience, I'd recommend checking out Path of Exile (which, despite being free-to-play, is excellent in its own right).

I can sense it; you've come here for asylum after getting man-handled and betrayed by other action rpgs, and you lie awake at night wondering, "Will I ever love another action rpg the same way again?"  Don't lose hope, you WILL love again, and your love may blossom as soon as THIS VERY MOMENT.  After all, the night is always darkest before the dawn, and Grim Dawn will make you praise the sun once more!
What's good about Grim Dawn?  I'll try to avoid direct comparisons to other games in the genre, but here are some of Grim Dawn's highlights:
+the game feels impactful.  Every strike against an enemy is accompanied by a satisfying thud, and ragdoll animations send enemies flying all over the screen in tiny bits
+there is near infinite levels of customization.  The game awards you plenty of skill points, but not enough to to able to invest in a wide variety of skills.  You'll have to plan carefully and pick your favorites, which increases replayability.
+There is a hardcore option.
+There is multiplayer
+There is a huge variety of loot.
+Making a functional build requires thought.
+crafting exists.  If you're having trouble finding the item you need, you can either craft one using a blueprint (which you can loot randomly), or by having the blacksmith craft a random piece of gear.
+There are plenty of side areas to explore.  Exploring is almost always worth the time, since you may find unique bosses or Devotion Shrines which grant you points to use in your devotion skill tree.
+multiple difficulties are available to the player.  Every character you make progresses through normal, elite, and ultimate difficulty.  Once you beat the game on normal difficulty, you can play Elite difficulty with that character, and once you beat Elite, you can play Ultimate with that character.
+The world changes in meaningful ways as you play.  Your choices in sidequests have a lasting impact on your game, and aiding the npcs in town may cause them to treat you differently.
+Factions exist in the game.  For example, the first settlement, "Devil's Crossing", will only tolerate your existence at first.  As you prove yourself to the settlers, you will gain access to new quests and new equipment sold only at that settlement.  By contrast, enemies also have factions.  The more that a specific enemy faction grows to loathe you, they'll throw tougher monsters at you.
+the game is moddable
+The plot is extremely good for a game of this genre.
+Last, the developers of Grim Dawn are extremely receptive and transparent.
So what are some of Grim Dawn's flaws?
-drop rates for rarer items are low.  I personally like the droprate though.
-Even on pc's with good specs, some people have framerate issues with lots of enemies.   Some users do not experience this issue.
-stash space is limited.  If you are willing to mod, this is a non-issue.
-it takes FOREVER to reach "nemesis" status with enemy factions (this is the highest status possible).
Overall, the game is a solid 9/10.  If the developers can manage to further optimize the game and improve framerate, I would give it a solid 10/10

A challenging puzzle game with smooth, aesthetically pleasing graphics and a very nice art style. It seemed like a lot of work was put into these puzzles, as some of them were extremely difficult, and took me a long time (and maybe some hints) to figure out. If they take that long to solve, imagine how long it would take to make them!
For completionists, the achievements are plentiful and unique, involving hidden secrets in particular levels or in the level select menus. Most of these secrets are extra levels that can be even more challenging than the normal ones. Achievements can also be earned finishing a level in a specific way, or creating an infinite loop using particular tools. There are even some Portal themed levels, and I won't say much about those except that a familiar 3-D object is included and that the last "test chamber" is one of the most interesting puzzles I have ever encountered both in a video game or other medium.
All in all, Two Tribes have yet again created a fresh and unique game, one that has replay value and challenge, combined with great visuals and an excellent soundtrack.

Rush is a nice little puzzle game that's good for a few hours of play. The only gripe I have is the difficulty. Easy is exactly as it says it is, Medium is a little harder and Hard is for when you want to feel like a dumb ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. The jump in difficulty from medium to hard is disappointingly gargantuan, going from a little challenging to frustratingly confusing. The artificial difficulty lies in the very specific tile placement needed to beat the levels and the little to no clues to help you decipher the solution. Even when you figure out the trick to beating a level, fidgeting with the tiles to find the ONE solution it asks for is somehow both simultaneously boring and frustrating. I felt very disappointed in myself for having to use the hint system, but unless you want to move tiles around aimlessly for hours you're going to have to use and abuse it to win. Simply put, hard difficulty is not fun and felt more like a chore than anything else. However, in the 3 or 4 hours it takes to beat the easy and medium stages, I would recommend picking up this game only if it is heavily discounted. Not worth a whole $5 in my eyes.

It is very addicting as you start from the ancient era and research technologies that move you up through the eras as you build cities, go to war, trade with other nations, and more to hopefully achieve victory. You will need to find a balance on how you want to run your empire while also defending yourself from possible threats of barbarians or other civilizations. Yes. Just yes. So yes.

•	The gameplay is fun and addictive. The vehicles you can drive in the game handle very well. The combat in the game is addictive, not overly complicated and killing enemies with certain weapons can be very satisfying, for example with the gravity gun and the pistol.
•	Fantastic character development. You actually care about the protagonists in half-life 2, characters like Alyx, Dr Kleiner, Eli, Barney and many more. The characters are interesting and interact well in conversation with other characters in the game including Gordon Freeman (Player), who doesn't speak.  Half-life 2 also has a brilliant antagonist as well, Dr Breen.
Probably the best character development I've ever seen in a video game.
•	I loved the futuristic/industrial setting of the game, seeing the combine's technology, but also seeing lots of the derelict buildings and factory's. The game also has a retro feel, especially in City 17 and by the coast. I also liked seeing all of the resistance Graffiti throughout the game as well, very artistic. The levels aren't too linear; there are parts of the game where you can do some exploring. The game still looks good in 2016.
•	There are many puzzles to solve in the game to proceed to the next area and they aren't too complicated and the puzzles are fun to solve.
•	Brilliant soundtrack. I get goose bumps every time I hear certain pieces of music playing in different parts of the game.
•	A great arsenal of weapons. The gravity gun is a very fun weapon to use; there are so many objects you can pick up with the gravity gun in the environment which you toss at enemies.
•	You can drive Vehicles this time round like the buggy and the hover boat, which is awesome, adds more variety to the gameplay.
•	Plenty of secrets to be found. You can find Lambda caches, which contain ammunition and health kits. I've completed half-life 2 many times before and I still can't find all of the Lambda caches, I've only found 40/45 caches.
•	Steam achievements. I got 32 out of 33 achievements.

•	The A.I can be stupid; Alyx and the resistance fighters can block your path and get in the way sometimes. Sometimes the combine can one minute be shooting at you the next looking in another direction ignoring you.
•	So many unanswered questions in the half-life series, which we may never know.
•	Some parts of the can be very tricky, I recommend playing this game on normal to have an enjoyable experience.

It is also very simple. In fact many would probably call this game an RPG-lite and they would not be wrong. Despite the new angle of playing the people around the table instead of the heroes on their character sheets, this game is overall a very simple title… simple enough I was not surprised to see the game is readily available, not just on the PC, but on mobile phones.
This makes for a surprisingly good game overall, but not one designed to be played over long sessions. Rather, it’s a series of bite-sized sessions that will ultimately get you through the to the end, assuming you have the patients to get through some of the later muck.

Fairly lauded for distinctive artistic design and a atmospheric OST. The game sets the pace with impressive animated cutscene reminiscent of the 1978 animated LOTR film/animated Shakespeare, though, sadly, fails to follow up with similar quality in much of the later content. The static animation is of a high quality, but I feel that the storyline and game as a whole suffered as a result of the sparsity of such talented animation. Admittedly, this may have been due to budget restrictions - as this game is said to be the first installment of a trilogy, fans will undoubtedly be able to expect a more polished, invested experience from the upcoming episodes on account of the financial success of Stoic studios' initial sales.
The tactical gameplay has a challenging learning curve, though a tutorial introduces the player to the basics and a 'training' mode will help uncertain players get to grips with the system in short order. If you wish to try it out before purchasing the game, you can play an online FTP version of the battle system called 'The Banner Saga: Factions'. However, the compelling OST, along with a plot-driven investment in the outcome of each engagement, ensures that the single-player product has a (superior, IMHO) mystique of its own.
My only reservation concerning this otherwise well-executed game is the lack of an inherent multiplayer capacity. The FTP online version is evidently designed to satisfy this purpose, though I was disappointed that purchasing the game did not offer any kind of bonus or incentive to get involved with the FTP multiplayer component.
Overall, though, The Banner Saga is illuminated by an absorbing narrative set within an atmospheric and enchanting environment, supported by the foundation of a solid tactical game mechanic.

The Banner Saga is a great story-telling strategy RPG. Although at the beginning it is easy to be confused by all the names and places, it is really atmospheric and will immerse you very quickly. This is definitely at least partly due to the fantastic, fitting music.
You have to make very tough decisions storywise, and you never know whether your choices are correct. For example: You have almost no supplies left, so very soon people will starve unless you find a place to buy food. However, the moral among your people is miserable, and resting for a day would improve it. Can you afford resting for a day, hunted by enemies?
I really like that each of these decisions has its consequences, which are sometimes revealed only much later in the game. Some very likable characters and a fun combat system make you feel like a part of the world.

If you haven't watched Firefly, I suggest you do so now. If you HAVE, however, then enjoy this game, as it is basically as close to Firefly: The Game as it gets. Addictive, fun, beautiful, deceptively hard, and less linear than a swimming pool, even the thought of fighting for the Federation and not the rebels couldn't keep me away!
The existence of so many different systems and so many ways to upgrade existing systems leads to a huge variety of ways to play, with no one right solution to any problem. Don't like to get your hands dirty? Use drones! Shields getting in your way? Use missiles! On a budget? Just board the enemy ship and kill their crew! Want to kill the crew but all you have is this fire-bomb? Use the fire-bomb and watch as your enemies rush around desperately trying to put out the fires that just won't stop popping up in their Oxygen room.
The sheer amount of systems the player needs to manage (with the help of their meager but ever-developing crew) also adds a huge amount of complexity to the game. If a system gets damaged it will no longer function until your crew repairs it. The AI's targeting system is completely random, so you never know if that incoming Artemis missile will hit your door control and do virtually nothing, hit your sensors and blind you, forcing you to turn up your sound to listen for hull breaches, fires, etc; or hit your oxygen room and slowly drain your oxygen until your entire crew suffocates.
The various alien races all have neat little bonuses (yes, even Humans, which were buffed ever so slightly in Advanced Edition so they recieve training in the major systems faster). These bonuses are game-changingly powerful, but each and every one is extremely situational. The Mantis and Rock are the optimal choices for close-quarters combat, for example, with the mantis having increased damage and the rock having increased health and immunity to fire damage. However, the rock are painfully slow when moving and mantis repair at half speed, making them useless on a damaged ship. Zoltan have pitiful health but give 1 permanent power bar to the system they are manning, Lanius have boosted health and are immune to suffocation but drain the oxygen out of the room they are in, Engi are weaker in combat but repair faster, Crystal are slightly slower and tougher and have the ability to lock a room down temporarily, and the slugs have amazing telepathic powers that help them see inside enemy ships.
The game is balanced so that you will always be surviving just by the seat of your pants, unless you get extremely lucky. This expert balance system means that players are kept on their toes the entire game. As you upgrade and develop your ship, the scrap rewards scale up but the enemy ships get stronger. This balance system scales up so well that, especially on Hard mode, almost every situation needs to be carefully weighed, as most combat scenarios (especially late-game) are high-risk, high-reward.
Developing a strategy in FTL is something that happens during a game rather than before it, which is relatively unique in the Strategy gaming world. Yes, each ship's starting layout gives you an idea of how to secure a bit of scrap early game, but throughout the game you will be buying and selling weapons, drones, systems, augments, and anything else you can get your hands on in order to develop your ship into an effective fighting machine for whatever little scrap you may have in your storage. Effective strategies and knowing how and when to use each item can lead to amazing synergies, such as the use of a Glaive beam with a Weapons Pre-Igniter to cut down on its drawn-out charge time, or using ion weaponry to take down shields and then dealing damage with combat drones.
The beacons and sectors are randomly arranged, so no two runs are alike. You can find yourself hopping between civilian sectors one run only to find yourself barely scraping through two Abandoned Sectors and one Rebel Stronghold the next. The pursuing rebel fleet is another brilliant mechanic, as it encourages you to keep moving while scavenging as much loot as possible. The pursuing rebels are tough stuff, too, some even coming equipped with Chain Vulcans and level 4 shields!
Being a roguelike game, FTL likes to mess with the player. As a result, you will die very, very frequently. The great thing about FTL, though, is that it never feels cheap. Your death is always the result of YOUR actions. Not in an in-your-face way, either. You never just die because you forgot to check the corner for snipers or something (like in, oh, say, CS:GO), you always die as the result of a pleathora of factors working together. For example, you took way too much damage in the last fight and had to jump away with a broken shields system and half Hull points, only to jump straight into an asteroid field. The asteroids pelt your ship, damaging systems and hurting your hull while the pursuing pirate teleports a fire-bomb to your Oxygen room and an Intruder Ion drone into your weapons. The drone smashes a hole in the hull and makes short work of your weapons, leaving you defenseless, while the fire spreads from your O2 to the rest of the ship. As you send in your crew to put out the fires, an explosion is heard coming from the Oxygen room. The fires must have caught on an oxygen tank and exploded, and now your oxygen system is completely offline. This becomes a problem, as you had been trying to fight the flames by opening your airlock to vent the fires. Hoping to salvage the situation, yousend your crew to the Medbay and close all airlocks and interior doors. However, a shor from the enemy burst lazer strikes your medbay JUST as the first crew-member enters, killing her instantly. In a panic, you rush two other crewmembers to the oxygen room to put out the fires and repair the system before you all suffocate, and you send your pilot to repair the shields. You cross your fingers and pray, but the autopilot just can't evade the enemy's shots without the assistance of your pilot. You manage to get the pilot out of the shields room just as another fire-bomb incinerates everything inside, but while you were distracted your other two crew-members burned alive in the oxygen room. At this point, the fires have spread to every room but the helm, where you send your pilot in a desperate attempt to save him. At last, the final few laser shots from the enemy sail straight toward an exposed section of your hull, and your last three hull points are depleted. One last explosion rocks your ship as it is torn apart, ending yet another fantastic journey in FTL.
Overall, this game is very well made in every aspect. One of the best games I have ever played.

Game is great, fun to play, good replayability, solid micromanaging and many customization possibilities (even more with the expansion pack).
Story: Well, it's an alien attack, don't expect something exctrmely convoluted, story is ok, not great, but good.
Graphics: They are good 7-8/10
Soundtrack: Ok, nothing remarkable, nothing epic like other strategy games.
Customization: Excelent, you can customice your soldiers a lot, name, nickname, armor, cammo, hairstyle, headgear.
Difficulty: Excelent, highly customizable, from easy to impossible, from short gameplays to very long ones.
Progresson: Good, you don't have to grind, and you can advance at your own pace, however, there are only 3 tiers for items.
Non-Combat Strategy: Great, you must carefully decide what and when to build, what countries you help, how you spend your money, etc.
Combat:
My main complain is here, while combat is interesting, there is an annoying RNG (random number generator), and while you see your hit chance percentage, that number is completely false, if the game decides you cannot hit one unit, it doesn't matter how many times you attempt to kill it, worse, the game works with "seeds" which means every turn every outcome is already decided for every action and you can't change that by reloading a savegame (unless you have the expansion pack), to change the outcome you must try a different action, because the game might decide that this turn your 90% hit chance rocket will miss no matter what.
AI is pretty stupid, so they had to compensate, how do they do it? by cheating of course, the AI knows where your units are at all times, enemies can shoot at units they can't see, they get a free move once you spot them, so they always have the tactical advantage, ambush is impossible unless using an special sniper ability, AI is very defensive, even in missions where they should be attacking, which of course gives the AI an unfair advantage because it can't get bored.
But those advantages doesn't matter, because the AI is really stupid, its prime directive is seeking cover and never leaving it unless moving to another cover, the AI never takes risks and will rarely attempt to flank, most times you get flanked is because you did a bad move, AI only uses explosives if there are 2 or more units together within a 3 title radius, instead of using them to remove cover or to take down a wall for a better line of sight, it has problems with target prioritization, and they'll usually go for the biggest threat instead of the weakest link, even if that threat is so far away they can't even hit him.
Most enemy units have abilities, abilities the AI seems to use at random, I've seen several times the AI using an offensive buff and then retreat, suppressing an unit standing in front of them instead of shooting at his face, throw grenades at the ceiling,  using a reposition ability that leaves its units in the worst spot ever.
Another complain is the "overwatch" ability, basically an unit in overwatch gets a free shot against an enemy unit on the move, the problem is the game makes all your units in overwatch fire at the same time, this can be hilarious, since there is a mission where you get 4 extra units, and sees 10 guys shoot at the same enemy at the same time is priceless, it's like watching the expendables sci-fy version, but pretty much kills the purpose of the ability, which is defending a position, it makes no sense, to use overwatch in several units at a time (unless they are far away) because they'll waste all their shots at the same time.

Since i have played Grim Dawn, Titan Quest and Diablo 3 a LOT, here's what i think about this game:
Pros:
- Skill system is similar to Titan Quest and very complex, allowing you to customize your character alot. There are obvious builds just like in D3 (Pet-master, Fire-builds etc.) but you are not limited to them.
- No allways-online, you can in fact play this game completely in offline mode, characters are saved on your harddrive. (similar to Titan Quest)
- Many items with the same system as in TQ where rare pre- and -suffixes can occur on normal items. Also Epic and Legendary stuff (including sets and abilities granted by items)
- Farming: A combination of TQ and D3, boss runs are still effective (TQ) but there are also Hero spawns in normal locations that can be lucrative (D3)
- Simple Multiplayer system, you can either host a game (and others might join you, you can set a password or kick others) or you can join a game yourself (direct join to your steam-friends or browse existing hosted games)
- almost no bugs, the few that are there allways get fixed ASAP
Things i personally dont mind but might be important to you:
- performance issues when ALOT of stuff is going on (R9 290, 16GB RAM, i7 and dropping to 20fps on high settings, can be improved by lowering the settings though)
- Multiplayer MIGHT not allways work, make sure you have administrator rights when searching for games or it can crash (just like in TQ)
- even though they are not popular, you might find cheaters online (since save-files are on your harddrive you can just manipulate them). In that case just host a game yourself and kick them :P
- no voice acting and average grafics might scare you. but keep in mind that crate entertainment is a really small studio ("Crate Entertainment has grown from one man with a dream to a team of ten with veteran developers....") so what they achieved is actually really impressive.
Conclusion: A really good ARPG. not a tripple-A title like D3 with millions of budget, still managed to entertain me more than D3 personally. If you like these kind of games, just buy it!
