This is the game that's responsible for making me a "gamer". It's the first world that I had become fully immersed in, and I think that all the games I've bought and played over the years since have been in a way seeking to get the same sort of feeling that Everquest had provided for me. I still have the fondest memories of my days as a young Dwarf, finding adventure and misadventure in and around the Butcherblock Mountains; being chased by Corflunk and Zarchoomi; being blasted to bits by a brownie in the Lesser Faydark, and enlisting other low-level guildmates to run interference while I make a naked corpse run to get my stuff back; camping Crushbone forever, so that I can get as many belts as I can to turn in to Canloe Nusback for the faction boost. I remember drowning while trying to find a certain island with mermaids on it in the Ocean of Tears. I remember being beaten to death by farmers in East Karana while trying to seek refuge from a lion that was chasing me.
These days, I'm not much for the MMO experience -- I'm not wild about forced socializing -- so I like to look for games that provide the sort of open, persistent world full of possibilities to explore and adventure, which EQ provides so well. Graphically, I can't say the game has aged too well, although it doesn't look too bad for a 15-year-old game. The best thing is, though, it's still alive! It's still worth playing. The world of Norrath is so incredibly huge, and now that there are elements put into place that makes the game easily soloable, it's worth it to get out there and explore. And, hey, bring a friend along for even more fun.

Are you and Anime fan or a whovian? Yes? Well here is the game for you:
Featuring both England AND Japan you can now dress up your soldiers to be kawaii sugoi Doctors w/ guns!
References: Guns(Doctor Who and animes feature guns!), Aliens(Doctor Who and animes feature aliens!) and of course Japan and England.
Jokes aside, XCOM: Enemy Unkwown is the newest sequel in a long line of strategy classics.  This time it has been simplified to make it more accessible, or at least that's what everyone says. I can't really confirm that as I haven't played the older titles. Let's see how it holds up to the legacy.
Visuals:
The game looks very good, especially for a strategy game, however with the visual fedelity of both game and the impressive cutscenes we also have some problems due(probably due the Unreal Engine). Textures load terribly slowly even for the Unreal Engine. The frame rate also seems to suffer due to the engine, however I am not sure about that.
Sound:
Sound design is actually quite good. Music, sounds, voice acting and of course the general composition of those challenges some AAA movies as it reminds of Alien, and other classics.
Gameplay:
As already mentioned, gameplay is quite simpe. Now, don't get me wrong XCOM is one of those game that is easy to grasp but you WILL get anal probed trying to master it. As it is a standart TBS you move your soldiers in your turn and get #rekt when the enemies turn comes. You have equipment, a small set of skills and different weapons to fight the ET threat. All quite standart but fan. Maybe you have already guessed but difficulty is kind of a thing in this game. Like in BF3 it's also quite weird. Basicly a "difficult mission" can range from "stomping enemies to the ground" to actually "a bit diffucult", then we have "very difficult missions" that can again range from "this makes me sweat a tiny bit" to "oh my god where do those elite mutons come from?". I would recommend to pick the easy difficulty for unexperienced players, normal for TBS veterans and normal+ for XCOM veterans.
Playability:
This games biggest problems are it's bugs and the aggro-system.
You have multiple game breaking bugs that can scramble saves, block your turn(good luck if you haven't saved), etc. And also quite a few glitches.
What I mean by "aggro-system" is the moment in-game where you encounter enemies. That can be random, not only will saving at the beginning of a mission not mean that the enemies come from the same directions(which can be both good and bad), some times you will just be overwhelmed by enemies that throw themselves at you from nowhere.
Final Verdict:
A fun game when it isn't frustrating as hell. Play this if you are a fan of the originals and want a lighter version, or if you want to get into the genre. I would say that it takes some influence from Starcraft 2, so maybe if you like a combination of SC2s style and a TBS with a faster pacing in a "Battleground: Earth" atmosphere then buy this.

Dying was a very promising game that has alot of fun gameplay and interesting freedom of movement. You will LOVE running around at breakneck speeds clubbing anything in sight with a variety of interesting moves and fields to satisfy your penchant for violence with pretty graphics and large explorable environments.
This was done right.
What was done wrong was the game was far too in love with itself to even consider you. What you do in the game world does not affect the story at all. No matter how much of a stonecold slayer you are, Crane will always be a wuss wannabe that turns tail or forgets he has guns in his pockets. The game goes even farther to arbitrarily cripple the player in order to ram it's story down the players throat. While it is interesting and decently suitable for a B-flick movie it is hard to take seriously then instant death is around every corner and the player has most of their abilities taken from them. You go from tiger to kitten in an instant and it's awful, the sharp contrast and unforgiving plot turn points ruin immersion completely and drive the player from what is 'fun.'
Case and point, you get tooled up for a boss battle. All your weapons are removed. You tool up all of your abilities and get some powerful honking weapons and it turns out the end of the game is a glorified quick time event cutscene that is grossly unsatisfying for the horrendous trial of climbing and lazy instant death pits. It will leave most unprepared players listening to the same dialogue many times and focusing on a point on the screen smaller than a key for their keyboard rather than listening to an otherwise decent rant from a madman. All of which culminates in a COD MW2 clone ending (No more than that so no spoilers.) that leaves a poor impression.
If you like the game. For all that is holy, do not complete it.
My opinion of this game went from a 8.5 out of 10 to a 5.5 out of 10 at the ending.
Do not build a game around skills and take them away just because you cannot scale difficulty.
Do not add in a quick time event to make sure your boss is irritatingly difficult when there were no real quick time evens to speak of before hand.
Do not render everything the player does in game completely moot to the happenings around them for it ruins immersion and shows them just how badly put together your game really is. It leave the player shouting at their screen that they have several things that could solve the situation at hand. Case and point, a man pointing a knife at you. You shoot them because you have a gun right? No, you get stabbed instead because cutscene says you don't have anything. It's that sort of in love with it's story.
If you don't plan on completing this game and want to releive stress. PLAY IT. It's fun for that.
If your looking for a satisfying completion and a good rock solid story. Don't bother,

I didn't hear of this game until shortly before its release, but when I saw it in the Steam Sale and watched some gameplay videos of it I was instantly interested in it. An old-school RPG with turn-based combat, a well thought-through spell system (poison + fire = explosion, water/blood + electricity = stun, hitting puddles with fireballs makes them steam clouds, steam clouds + electricity = stun clouds and much, much more) and a huge, very detailed world with many secrets to discover make this game the best game I have played this year so far. I've heard people criticize the lack of a 100% voice-over, but Fallout 2 didn't have complete voice-overs and is considered one of the best RPGs up to this day.
The negative points I have are these:
- more or less bland companions. You don't get to know a lot about them, and both are only relevant for one or two quests overall, but depending on how you chose your main character's classes they complement your party very well. If you want to play "alone" (ie. only with your 2 main characters, there is an extra perk for that as well)
- the story could have had better pacing. For the first half of the game the story makes total sense, you are investigating an outbreak of undeads and some other things on the side, and then suddenly everything gets overthrown and for a while you are left wondering what is going on. Luckily this gets cleared up shortly after, but it was still a little confusing in the beginning
- the fights in the beginning of the game start out extremely challenging, but lose the intensity later-on as more of your characters can learn healing spells and have high resistances gainst the spell schools etc..
- also, money inflation is a problem. In the beginning you never have enough money, but after ~15h played I had so much money I traded items with vendors for free just to get them out of my inventory
However, these negative points are far outweighed by the positive aspects of this game, and it has been a long time since I put 65h+ into game in such a short time (the last game was Skyrim, and only due to mods that I spent so much time with it).
If you like RPGs and you are not put off by turn-based combat or lack of complete voice-over then this is a must buy!

Since so many people who are playing this game are veterans of ARPGs, and many have been playing since the early days of development, I thought I'd offer a perspective from somebody for which neither condition is true.
I have never played a Diablo game.  I played the first Torchlight for about 30 minutes.  I did put a fair few hours into Titan Quest, but didn't finish it.  I am not, by any stretch of the imagination, an ARPG expert.  I do however love role-playing games in general, and have played more than I can readily count, my gaming going back 35 or so years as it does, and my memory not being the best.
I just bought this during the Winter sale after eyeballing it for awhile.  I haven't finished the game, but I'm in Act 3 (and have played up to level 10 with a second character), so I've put enough hours into it to have formed a strong impression.  It's a really fun game.  The soundtrack is rousing, the different environments all look great, and the writing is solid.  I especially enjoy the writing in the various journals scatttered around.  Obviously story isn't the biggest draw of games of this (sub)genre, but for me, the quality of the story on offer here is good enough and plentiful enough that it provides strong incentive to hack my way through another swarming nest of creepy-crawlies.  (note: if you're squeamish about bugs...buyer beware)
I'm never going to be the guy who will test out 100 different builds and tell you the best skills and equipment to max out your DPS or any of that stuff.  I'm not a min/max guy, won't ever be.  I can tell you that the character development choices are plentiful and fun.  Lots of skills, from your class choice, items (which can be upgraded), devotion points from restoring shrines, a million combinations of stats and powers making you feel as if you can experiment and create truly diverse characters.  I started that second, now 10th level character just so I could try some other stuff out, and she's a bomb throwing, gun-toting pyromancer who plays very differently from my heavy weapon slashing, damage soaking soldier.  So that's fun.

Aesthetics: The enviroments and characters are drawn and animated well in a simplistic, old-fashioned style of animation that I personally like. So no, there are no flashy or high-budget scenes of intense action as most people are accustomed to.
Gameplay: The combat system is unique but doesn't work 100% with your characters strength tied to their health; i.e. as you take damage your ability to deal damage decreases. You have plenty of options to avoid fights however. But this goes into the main problem with the game design which is that the same resource (valor) for upgrading your characters is the same one used to buy food for your caravan (and yes you will need lots of it) and for buying items to equip of your characters. This means you have to make the decision between letting your people starve or upgrading them so they don't get clobbered during battles.
Story: The story and character development are very good. A warning, however; don't get attached to the characters (like "A Game of Thrones" they tend to die often). One final thing to mention is that the ending has a major (and potentially tear-inducing) cliffhanger. Fortunately the developer is working on the next part.

I didn't actually beat this game yet, but it's damn good.
Think the Oregon trail meets Game of Thrones meets an actually good game, and you get this one.
A lot of games talk about trying to make all your decisions matter, and a lot of games say they do, but in the end it simply doesn't feel like your actions really matter. Banner Saga is probably the only game I've played where I felt like it was true. When I need to make a decision in-game and someone dies, I feel like their blood is legitimately on my hands. Sometimes the only ones that die are nameless clansmen, and, honestly, that doesn't affect the game much, but one time I made the decision of trusting the wrong guy, and one of my best combatants, a centerpiece of my offense, was just straight up killed.
From what I've seen so far (because I've started playing the game twice), the main plot doesn't change, there are no grand branching paths far as I've seen, but you definitely feel the weight of responsibility as decisions constantly have you weighing morality vs. personal survival, risk vs. chance of reward, and sometimes just posing a genuine question of morality.
(Choices? 10/10. Your move, AAA studios)
Now, without the choices, how about the story itself? The world is nicely built, the story is compelling, the characters are interesting, and there are some really good quotes. It gets trippy as hell, though. Like I said earlier, I never beat the game, so I can't attest to the quality of the ending.
(Story? 8.75/10. Worthwhile.)
Now that we got this girly nonsense talk about "story" out of the way, let's talk about combat. The real men's subject. It's a grid-based, turn-based rpg system, but instead of attacking you decide whether to strike armor or strength. Each does a thing we're not getting into now. How does this effect the gameplay? Enough to distinguish itself. It definitely gives a unique feel, and the tactical question of "Should I attack strength or Armor?" rarely has an obvious answer. So it adds a layer to strategy. It's not necessarily ground-breaking, but it adds a little spice.
(Combat? 8/10: can't complain; pretty good)

It adds just the right amount of spice, really. A classy amount. The Banner Saga is lIke something from a fancy resturant. Just don't actually eat there because the waiter poisons people at random.

Excellent! Simple to play, easy to learn, definitely a one-of-a-kind Third Person Shooter + Tower Defense game. Gameplay is easily summarized - Defend your rift(base) from orcs, with melee, range weapons, magic, traps, and guardians. There're over 10 different types of enemies, and 22 weapons, traps and guardians added up altogether. I would strongly suggest downloading the demo first before trying (I got hooked on the game this way). Maps are playable in 3 different levels - Apprentice(Easy), WarMage(Normal), Nightmare(Explains itself). The game has practically no ending, you can replay your maps as many times as you want. No rewards, but the gameplay itself is rewarding. The only "ending", is probably when you completed all achievements, upgraded every single trap, and 5 Skull-ed all maps on all difficulties. Pretty fulfilling!
Pros
- Graphics are cartoon-ish. Great for casual players. Graphics which are too clear makes me really stressed.
- Gameplay varies, dependent on the type of player you are. Melee, magic, shooter, you choose!
- Achievements are all attainable. Last broken achievement was removed, hence, 27 workable achievements.
- 24 different maps, excluding 5 DLC maps(Might as well get it).
- There's a difference shooting at the head, and at the body. Dealing different damage really draws the line between players who only want to complete the game, and those that REALLY wants to perform. You can't just spam.
- Simple upgrades. Basically you complete a map well, you are given up to 10 skulls per map, then you upgrade it. There is simply no need for a guide on what to upgrade. Just do it. Eventually, all skulls will be used, and everything upgraded.
Cons
- Single player. Might not be too optimal for couples, or a group of friends. Orcs Must Die 2 has co-op though(Recommended as well).
- Despite "Practice makes perfect", some really tough maps are really argh. You would be finding yourself restarting the map many times just to achieve 5 Skulls(5 Star Rating).
- Endless isn't available, so once you're done with the map, you're done. Clearing the map isn't tough, but getting 5 Skulls for it might be a chore for some.
- Too damn addictive. You really can't stop playing!!
On the overall, apart from perfecting this game by achieving 5 Skulls for all maps on all difficulties, even as a casual game, it will not fail to entertain. Definitely.
On a scale of 1-10, I would give it 9.5 (: Lack of companionship in this game kinda killed it for me, but I still completed it nevertheless! Fantastic game!!

At first, I was in love. After you learn the basics, this game completely opens up. It feels good to run, and the mix of strong colors and good visuals help make the experience that much more vivid. Jumping, sliding, running, flying; all of this flows together as the levels go on. I felt like water. The biggest source of grief here is the combat. Forced combat, mind you. The weakest link here feels like a big screeching interruption to the flow. Combat in this game punishes you for being reckless, especially in the later parts of the game. Now, in a game about jumping around, this is exactly the thing you don't want. I think Mirror's Edge mixes up its priorities here. The entire game, you've been teaching me to be as reckless as possible. Why would you want to stop me dead in my tracks?
Next, characters and plot. In order for a fully enjoyable experience of this game, I recommend ignoring all of that. The cutscenes give us very little. Some clever stuff here. Some character development there, and add a dash of world building there. That's all you get. We don't get to know much about anything. And the details we do get are lost in a swamp of bad storytelling. Not that I expect much in a game about running, but this becomes a serious problem. What exactly was accomplished? What were the details surrounding anything that happened? Are any of the characters memorable at all? These aren't questions I should be asking.
If you want a game about running through some nicely designed levels, then this is it. If you want a game that perfectly blends story, combat, and parkour, then look elsewhere. I'd still give this game my recommendation as a good game. Mirror's Edge has some serious flaws, but I'd be lying if I said that I didn't have a good amount of fun with it. In the haze of running and flying around roofs, buildings, and constructions, I seem to forget all of the problems. For just a moment, this game becomes great.

Sooooo, what is JumpJet Rex?
It’s a jump’n run game similar to Super Meat Boy. There aren’t as much levels in it (and they aren't as hard as in SMB) but the length of a stage is much longer than in SMB.
You are a T-rex in space (a dinonaut to be a precise) who has the task to plant a bomb on a meteorite aiming for the earth (to prevent the extinction of all dinosaurs).
Rex is equipped with a pair of boots which allow him to fly indefinitely (dash, rocket and unlimited jump). Of course you can’t just fly how you want. The levels are so designed that you have to carefully utilize your abilities to reach the end of a stage in one piece.
In each level are 3 stars to get: one for finishing the stage, another one for beating a certain time limit and a third one for reaching the finish line without dying. As you collect stars you unlock more stages.
Besides coins you collect in the levels, which you can spend in shops to customize Rex from tip to toe (different heads, body- , jumpboots- and jet stream-colors), you can also find hidden items in each stage which are merely decorative (referring to the gaming society and pop culture) but still nice to have because they aren’t easy to find and give you a feeling of accomplishment.
Additionally to the normal levels are 4 boss levels. Those fights are entertaining and at the first sight very hard. But as soon as you look through the enemy and recognize their weakness you can finish a fight in a few seconds (which is also necessary to get the time star ;)).
The 8-bit graphics are nice to look at; the different themes of the stages are good conversed to the player. As you would’ve thought the music is 8-bit chiptune. There are some tracks that I really like and furthermore none of the soundtrack gets annoying as you might have thought. Certainly the music and the graphics are not for everyone but if you are fond of 8-bit music and graphics there is no reason against JumpJet Rex (regarding the art and music).
I’d recommend the game to those who’d like the 8-bit style, a challenge, and have no problem with doing a level over and over again to fully complete it (For your info: it is not necessary to get ALL stars to finish the game, 2/3 are sufficient to complete the game).

First, let me start off by saying: this is a great, great game.
Lots of time and experience (think the King of Strategy: Sid Meir) went into this game, and while there are some visual bugs, it's quite pretty and eery at times (although the envirorments are not continent-specific whatsover; sometimes you kind of chuckle when you're dropped into a jungle in the middle of Egypt).
It's also hard; really, really flippin' hard.
I would venture to say that in my short span of gaming, this is the hardest game I've played. I'm a casual gamer, granted, but this game...it has infuriated me beyond any other game I've played. It's fun! Really, it's a "one more turn/one more match/holy crap it's four AM" kind of game, and the story line really makes you push yourself (sometimes too quickly) to advance.
But it's really hard.
Now, I actually DO recommend this game - to gamers really good at strategy and tactics (AKA NOT ME). But for the casual gamer who has maybe five hours a week max to sit down and game, this is NOT the game to play. It's honestly ruined a few nights for me because I've had to keep restarting to beat one level - and that's on easy.
Okay, so odds are I suck (95% sure of that). But that doesn't mean I'm wrong. That's also one of the beautiful things of the game, especially when you put Ironman mode on (automatic saves, perma-deaths). It really makes you take ever turn, every decision, every research and engineering project seriously. But it's just really flippin' hard, and as a gamer who wants to be slightly challenged, not frustrated, and experience a good story line, this game doesn't do it. Also, it’s hard in some dumb ways - your guys are gonna miss A LOT of seemingly-super easy shots, only to get murdered the next round.
So, summed up: it's a great game, even two years later - but it's hard, and while I got it for free via a promotion, I would never spend actual money on this game that has visibly upset me for a good few days now.
If you feel up to it, by all means go for it. You might find it worth it. As for me, I'm shelfing it and moving on.

That said, mind you, the game still has a few problems. The largest of them is, I believe, the inventory management. Each character has a separate inventory and moving items between them is a pain. This was most likely done to account for their maximum weight capacity (Strength-based), but since items weigh next to nothing and my mage is currently running around with 30 sets of armour and 40 weapons, without breaking a sweat, I don't think it matters very much and the inventory could just as well have been shared. Another thing is that spell casters are overpowered. Often it so happens that my mages have finished the combat, before the slow, heavy armoured, two-handed-weaponry-using warrior has made it into range. Overall, however, Divinity: Orginal Sin is an excellent game. It's innovative, beautiful, engaging, clearly made with passion, and  a delight to play.

XCOM "Enemy Unknown" and "Enemy Within" are both very enjoyable games.  The risk with tactical games is repetitiveness: move → hide → shoot → rinse&repeat.
XCOM brilliantly manages to avoid falling in this trap by being an extremely well-balanced game: the difficult progression is perfect, skill technology advancements match well the progression of the aliens one, and the story and graphics are compelling.
“Enemy Within” is a cool expansion because it introduce an entire new tech tree (actually two, but based on the same material), a competing organisation fighting against the XCOM,  and radically change the combat dynamics on the battlefield, giving the game a second life.
My only minor gripe, is that story advancements happen upon discretionary actions by the player (accepting a special mission, launching a specific research project, etc...).  These actions are normally well signalled with a “Priority” label, but it is still possible for the player to just postpone them
without any adverse consequence.  On the contrary: the time gained by postponing such missions, typically allows the player to stockpile in skills, equipment and new recruits, dramatically lowering the level of challenge the game provides.
However let me say this again: this is just a minor problem of the game structure, that I encountered by chance, by re-playing it and experimenting with non-obvious choices.  The game in itself is very enjoyable!

This is by far, hands-down the best early access title I have every played. There is so much to like about this game from build varieties to the massive amounts of loot you can get. The art direction has obviously been influenced by Diablo 1 & 2 and has kept it more mature. This visual style is exactly what I wished Diablo 3 would have had and I couldn't be happier.
It has a strong single-player campaign and pretty decent multiplayer (this is where it falls a little flat). Traditional "Diablo-esque" elements such as leaderboards, ladders, etc... don't exist here and if you want that competitiveness, then this probably isn't the game for you. Controls are what you would expect in an ARPG and there are no complaints there.
Game length is good. I've played for about 20 hours now and am partially through Act IV (I like to explore and take my time). Maps are really big with lots of areas to explore as well so you won't get bored quickly. Dialogue in the game is text-based. There is no voice acting for NPC's that I've come across. This can get a little tedious at times, but nothing quick clicking can't solve. Optimization is pretty darn good as I am getting 90-120 FPS (depending on monster density) on my playthroughs at 1440p with a 980 Ti and settings all set to maximum. Achievements aren't working, but that's not a big deal as its still in early access. For those of you running ultra-widescreen monitors, you'll be happy to know that this game natively supports them. Visual elements such as spells and melee abilities can look and feel awesome. Pros:
Hand-drawn animation style
Original, epic reimagining of Norse culture
Challenging, tactical gameplay
Cons:
Resource scarcity
Other:
Opaque choices
When I saw the Kickstarter, I fell in love with the Ralph Bakshi-like animation. The Sleeping Beauty-like parallax side-scrolling was captivating, and I wanted to explore the apocalypse of their reimagined Viking culture that had nothing to do with Ragnarok. The carefully-animated fights are squad-based and reward good planning.
The most frustrating challenge was money management, as there were lots of combat-altering trinkets to purchase, but funds were frequently so short in supply that in an entire game I'd only buy a few and hope that enemies might drop more (rare occurence). Originally the final fight was much too difficult in comparison to preceding fights, but that has been tweaked recently to make it less jarring (I've yet to compare it).
Choices were both profound and sometimes frustrating. They sometimes come down to a best guess, as the result of a choice can be challenging to predict, and come calling a dozen hours after it has been made, often in life-or-death terms. This was especially true when it was not always clear that a choice had been made. This imitates life, and for that reason I think it is both a pro and a con, but it bears saying that even over multiple playthroughs you could miss these opportunities. It was both exciting and anxiety-inducing to wonder after every event whether it could have gone differently, if only.
Overall, beautiful, challenging squad-based tactical gameplay with an epic, mature story.

Let's review the most hyped and over-reviewed FPS on Steam, a game everyone into FPSs has played already, the ones outstanding are those who want to see if it's still good or what the fuss is about (or of course who will never ever play it to begin with). From today's perspective this game has indeed some obvious weaknesses: people might say it's too linear, some parts take too long (driving with the boat), and especially the AIs one has to play co-op with in the later parts are frustratingly stupid. And regarding the so often praised physics engine and puzzles, it's pretty "wonky" actually, it's easy to get stuck here and there, et cetera.
But don't be fooled: This is definitely one of the most enjoyable shooters of all time. The gameplay is brilliant, the pace is brilliant, relaxing parts, exploration, mini-boss-battles, stealth, puzzles,.. there are so many concepts put into one, and the balance is just right. Be it fighting an overpowered heli with an air boat, avoiding stepping on sand to not trigger sand ants, later using them to defeat enemies being their commander, and I just love the mini-helicopter battles. Use the gravity gun to pick up trash and "throw zombies to death", make use of traps, ... the variety is indeed brilliant and every part has its own distinctive feel and atmosphere.
This game isn't flawless, but it brings so much to the table. It's fast paced, brilliantly thought out, and extremely enjoyable. Every few years I find myself returning to this gem to play it through and every time it's a blast.
Not sure if today's youngsters will be able to enjoy it as much, try to look past its quirks and find the (maybe rough) diamond within, cause boy, it's a big one!

I backed this game on Kickstarter and I must say I am deeply satisfied of what I've got up to now.
The gameplay is simple yet fun and the mini games help breaking up the monotony of the standard beat'em up sections. But the greatest achievement of this game is the atmosphere, it really feels like re-enacting the iconic movies of Bud Spencer and Terence Hill.
The two actors and all the iconic characters of the movies are drawn and animated perfectly, but what really shine it's the sound. Being able to play while listening to the original movies score is what make this game unique.
Of course since this is an early access product it needs a lot of polishing, for example:
- Controller buttons need to be explained properly, it was by pure luck that I discover that L1 switch character and R2 make the character run (way better than having to press the right stick).
- I really can't understand what's the meaning of the three blue bars. They seems to be related to the heavy attack, pressing X empty one, but they refill almost instantly after a couple of hit, so what's the point?
- In the western stage during the shooting mini game the button displayed when the target hover on a enemy is the triangle, but in reality the square is the right button to press.
- After completing the dune buggy race the game froze on the loading screen and I had to force quit it. When I restart the game I was able to continue from the next stage.
Also the game seems to be a little on the short and easy side. To be honest I don't think this is really important, this game should be bought and played for its amazing atmosphere and nostalgia effect. But for people out there that are not fan of Bud Spencer and Terence Hill, this is a good and enjoyable game, but you may want to check some reviews and gameplay videos (and maybe some movies too :P) before buying it.
For me this game was a really nice surprise and a great addition to my game library.
Good job Trinity Team, keep up the good work!

There are so many ways to customize your character; lots of goofy items to collect; lots of other characters to run into; lots of buddy characters to fight with. Ah, EverQuest, one of the great-grandfathers of all modern MMORPGs.  I played it when I was younger, but then ended up stopping my account when my PC decided to go out in a blaze of glory.   It took me ten years to get back into it, but to be quite honest, it's still got that same magical spark.
Even with its twenty-first expansion on the horizon, people still play this.  I have a couple characters, but at the same time, it can be really just kind of depressing choosing to roll up a new character, and finding that you're the only person in the starting zone.   To be honest, there's not really a lot of players on the lower-end of things any more- most of your players are essentially those who have still got their high-level characters and are chruning through higher-level content as it comes out.  There are still a handful of players in the lower levels, but to be quite honest, if you like soloing, this is the class for you.  The mercenary system is a godsend for those mobs you can't handle on your own, but you'll still run into quests that you just can't handle on your own. For example, the newbie weapon for Wood Elf Druids requires you to break the throne room of the castle in Camp Crushbone, and even with a merc, it's not really something that you'll be able to accomplish on your own until you get to a level where you can easily find things that outclass the reward.
The graphics are really dated- there are games with much better graphics out there right now, but at the same time, they're not as hard to run on non-top of the line computers any more.   If you're not running a graphically-intensive computer with a three-hundred dollar card in it, no worries- this runs fine on my laptop.
Gameplay is still solid, even after all these years, but at the same time, it's not really changed that much.  The addition of the tutorial is always a plus, but to tell you the truth, it makes for a better way into the game instead of just being dropped into a newbie zone with nothing to do.  You can easily grind up to 13 or 14 here, if you accomplish all the missions, and you can find some decent equipment, too.
To be honest, though, it's free to play, and you can't go wrong with a game that won't tax an older machine.  If you enjoy a trip back to the days of groups looking to hit up the Halls of Honor or the Plane of Disease, download this game- just be ready to do a bunch of soloing.  If you used to play, all you really need is your sense of nostalgia and for your memories to come flooding back once you hit up your old favorite zones and hear that old, familiar music.

JumpJet Rex is a solid casual jump and run.
Unfortunately with a few flaws.
Pros:
- Nice retro setting.
- Nice retro music.
- Good control concept with the jumping jet boots (although it feels like flappy bird sometimes).
- A lot of secrets.
- Weird but nice and supershort story.
- "Super Mario Style" amount of coins. Which you can use to buy skins. Nice!
Cons:
- Engine: One main problem is its performance. I play it on an i7 quadcore with an ok gaming video card.
In a ridiculous resolution (1280x720). And the game lags in huge levels. I even got the feeling, that sometimes when I hit a button it just doesn't react at all. So there seems to be a technical problem in the core engine.
- Speedrunning concept: The developers want you to speedrun the levels. There is a bonus if you finish within a narrow time limit. But you just don't see enough in a lot of levels with your small point of view. So sometimes, suddenly, out of nowwhere, an enemy appears or a big block goes straight towards you. And you don't feel like you had a lot of chances to avoid it, except for learning the level by hard. Wrong approach in my opinion.
- Boss fights: The bosses mostly annoy me, they are hard but not in a good way. Hard to describe.
- Full price is too expensive. I paid 5€ during sale which seems ok, but it is definitely not worth 15€.  Here you have better options (e.g. BattleBlock Theater).
Conclusion:
It's ok to play it in easy mode, casually, then you will have a lot of fun. But I wouldn't speedrun it or try to get every achievement.

Dying was a very promising game that has alot of fun gameplay and interesting freedom of movement. You will LOVE running around at breakneck speeds clubbing anything in sight with a variety of interesting moves and fields to satisfy your penchant for violence with pretty graphics and large explorable environments.
This was done right.
What was done wrong was the game was far too in love with itself to even consider you. What you do in the game world does not affect the story at all. No matter how much of a stonecold slayer you are, Crane will always be a wuss wannabe that turns tail or forgets he has guns in his pockets. The game goes even farther to arbitrarily cripple the player in order to ram it's story down the players throat. While it is interesting and decently suitable for a B-flick movie it is hard to take seriously then instant death is around every corner and the player has most of their abilities taken from them. You go from tiger to kitten in an instant and it's awful, the sharp contrast and unforgiving plot turn points ruin immersion completely and drive the player from what is 'fun.'
Case and point, you get tooled up for a boss battle. All your weapons are removed. You tool up all of your abilities and get some powerful honking weapons and it turns out the end of the game is a glorified quick time event cutscene that is grossly unsatisfying for the horrendous trial of climbing and lazy instant death pits. It will leave most unprepared players listening to the same dialogue many times and focusing on a point on the screen smaller than a key for their keyboard rather than listening to an otherwise decent rant from a madman. All of which culminates in a COD MW2 clone ending (No more than that so no spoilers.) that leaves a poor impression.
If you like the game. For all that is holy, do not complete it.
My opinion of this game went from a 8.5 out of 10 to a 5.5 out of 10 at the ending.
Do not build a game around skills and take them away just because you cannot scale difficulty.
Do not add in a quick time event to make sure your boss is irritatingly difficult when there were no real quick time evens to speak of before hand.
Do not render everything the player does in game completely moot to the happenings around them for it ruins immersion and shows them just how badly put together your game really is. It leave the player shouting at their screen that they have several things that could solve the situation at hand. Case and point, a man pointing a knife at you. You shoot them because you have a gun right? No, you get stabbed instead because cutscene says you don't have anything. It's that sort of in love with it's story.
If you don't plan on completing this game and want to releive stress. PLAY IT. It's fun for that.
If your looking for a satisfying completion and a good rock solid story. Don't bother,

This is a sort-of platformer where you play a dino floating around with rocket boots in space, with an ultimate goal of destroying the asteroid currently heading for Earth. There are about 40 regular levels and a few boss levels, with each regular level involving touching or shooting all the rings before you can proceed to the exit. Stars you collect unlock more levels, and you gain a star per level completed, as well as up to two additional stars for completing a level with no deaths and within a strict time limit. Besides stars there are a bunch more collectables, so there's plenty to do, and my first run through a seemingly short game took me about 6 hours. Collectables include getting 100% of the coins on a level, finding things to spruce up your dinonaut base, and unlocking pieces to customize your Rex with.
After you're done with Adventure mode, there's Speedrun mode (for, well, speedrunning) and RageQuit Rex mode (complete the game with three lives, lose them all and it's all over.)
Overall it's a very fun game. Movement feels nice and fluid. The soundtrack is really great, the background music gets stuck in your head and the sound effects feel good. Some of the artwork is really nice, particularly the boss designs and ending screens... but sadly the in-level graphics are a bit on the bland side. The level design is a little repetitive too, which you notice on your fourth time navigating a twisty spike-filled corridor. Somehow, though. the game still pulls through and manages to be really fun. I'd like to see online co-op and a level editor added in the future.
I give it 7.5/10, WAY better than Radical Rex.

Just to be helpful for wanna be buyers, the short condensed version:
Pro's:

Cons:

- A lot of the conversations are rather lengthy and only suited for hardcore lore fanatics

Personally I would like a tad more fighting and a bit less wandering about in search for a key.
All in all a good game for people that love isometric fantasy games, it delivers what might be expected of the genre. If long ago you enjoyed Baldur's Gate, then this will suit you well.

I wish, as many do, that there were some option between "Yes" and "No" for recommending. Half Life 2 isn't a bad game by any stretch of the imagination, but it blows my mind that the reviews are overwhelmingly positive. It has ups and downs, and I can definitely see why it was such a massive success when it comes out. The story is a little overworked, but compelling. It isn't particularly interesting by itself, but like many before me have pointed out, the levels are beautifully designed aesthetically speaking, effortlessly mixing in-game mechanics like cover or obstacles with an immersive setting.
That said, my single biggest gripe is the gameplay. It isn't fast enough to be a third-person bullet hell like the original, and the levels are waaaaaaaaaaay too long to be enjoyable. The Airboat scene especially comes to mind - I couldn't force myself to get all the way through it (I played it for roughly 8 hours and then quit - mostly offline, hence the low number shown).
It's a solid 7 or 8. Well polished, pretty game, and wonderful for its time. I just don't see how it holds a candle to any of the more recent games.

Half-Life 2 (stylized as HλLF-LIFE2) is a first-person shooter video game and the sequel to Half-Life (1998). Developed by Valve Corporation, it was released on November 16, 2004, following a five-year $40 million development, during which a substantial part of the project was leaked and distributed on the Internet. The game was developed alongside Valve's Steam software. It introduced the Source game engine and, because of Steam, was the first single-player video game to require online product activation.
Some years after the events of Half-Life, protagonist Gordon Freeman is woken by the enigmatic G-Man to find the world has been taken over by the alien Combine. Joined by allies including resistance fighter Alyx Vance, Gordon searches for a way to free humanity using a variety of weapons, including the object-manipulating gravity gun.
Like its predecessor, Half-Life 2 received critical acclaim. It was praised for its advanced physics, animation, sound, AI, graphics, and narrative. The game won 39 "Game of the Year" awards and the title of "Game Of The Decade" at the 2012 Spike Video Game Awards, and is widely considered to be one of the greatest and most important video games of all time. Over 6.5 million copies of Half-Life 2 were sold at retail by December 3, 2008, (not including Steam sales); as of February 9, 2011, Half-Life 2 had sold over 12 million copies.
Like its predecessor, Half-Life 2 is a single-player first-person shooter broken into several chapters, permanently casting the player as the protagonist Gordon Freeman. The sequel has nearly the same mechanics as Half-Life, including health-and-weapon systems and periodic physics puzzles, except with the newer Source Engine and improved graphics. The player also starts without items, slowly building up an arsenal over the course of the game. Despite the game's mainly linear nature, much effort was put into making exploration rewarding and interesting; many optional areas can be missed or avoided.
A diverse set of enemies is present, which usually require being approached with different tactics: some coordinate in groups to out-maneuver or out-position the player; others, like the Manhack, fly directly at the player through small openings and tight corridors; still others use predictable but powerful attacks, while others hide before swiftly attacking the player. Gordon can kill most enemies with his weapons, or make use of indirect means, exploiting environmental hazards such as explosive pressurized canisters, gas fires or improvised traps. For some portions of the game, Gordon can be joined by up to four armed Resistance soldiers and medics, and can send his team further from him or call them back.
Many of the game's new features utilize its detailed physics simulation. Two sections of the game involve driving vehicles. Instead of button-based puzzles from Half-Life, environmental puzzles are also introduced with makeshift mechanical systems, revolving around the player's new ability to pick up, move, and place objects. Solutions involve objects' physical properties, such as shape, weight, and buoyancy. For example, in Chapter 3, Route Kanal, the player is required to stack cinder blocks on a makeshift see-saw ramp to proceed over a wall. Alternatively, the player can use these to build a crude staircase, so sometimes, multiple approaches lead to the desired outcome.
Part-way through the game, Gordon acquires the Gravity Gun, which allows him to draw distant objects towards himself or forcefully push them away, as well as the ability to manipulate larger and heavier objects that he cannot manipulate without the weapon. These abilities are required to solve puzzles later in the game, and can also be used to great effect in combat, as any non-static object within proximity to the player has the potential to be used as a makeshift defense (e.g. a file cabinet) or a deadly projectile (e.g. a gasoline can or a buzzsaw blade).
The game never separates the player with pre-rendered cutscenes or events; the story proceeds via exposition from other characters and in-world events, and ensures that the player controls Gordon for the entirety of the game. Much of the backstory to the game is simply alluded to, or told through the environment.Half-Life 2 presents a dystopian alternate history of Earth, where the resources of the planet, including the human race itself, are being harvested by an oppressive multidimensional empire, known as the Combine. The game is set around the fictitious City 17, roughly 20 years after the events of its predecessor Half-Life.
During Half-Life, the scientists, including Gordon Freeman, at the Black Mesa Research Facility, accidentally caused an inter-dimensional instability known as a resonance cascade and later as the "Black Mesa Incident", when an experiment on an alien crystal sample went wrong.[1] Alien creatures, such as the Vortigaunts and headcrabs, from the borderworld of Xen, flooded into the facility. Gordon fought his way through them and the government cover-up response combat units, making it to the Facility's Lambda Complex. There, the Lambda scientists helped Gordon teleport to Xen, where Gordon destroyed a large alien entity keeping the rift open. Gordon was then suddenly extracted by the mysterious G-Man, who had been watching Gordon over the course of the game. Impressed with his ability to survive against all odds, the G-Man offered him a job before placing him into stasis, which Gordon had no option but to accept.
Some time after the ending of Half-Life, the instability at Black Mesa had attracted the attention of the Combine empire, and they invaded Earth. Humanity surrendered at the conclusion of the resulting "Seven Hour War". City 17 became the home of the gigantic Combine Citadel, and Dr. Wallace Breen, the Administrator of Black Mesa who had negotiated the surrender, was appointed representative and Administrator to supervise the survivors on behalf of the Combine.[2] Unable to breed due to a Combine suppression field, humanity matured. The Combine implemented a brutal police state of Civil Protection officers and Overwatch soldiers by recruiting and biologically assimilating humans and other species. Meanwhile, an underground "Lambda Resistance" of humans and Vortigaunts, now working together, was formed. This saw Freeman as a saviour who would lead them to freedom.20 years after the Resonance Cascade, the Combine emerge from the portal with advanced technologies, enabling them to conquer the world in 7 hours. Gordon Freeman is brought out of stasis by the G-Man, who inserts him into a train arriving at City 17.[3] After arriving at the station and eluding Combine forces, Gordon joins Lambda resistance members including Barney Calhoun, a former Black Mesa security guard now working undercover as a Combine CP officer, and Alyx Vance, the daughter of one of Gordon's former colleagues, Dr. Eli Vance. After a failed attempt to teleport to Eli's resistance base known as Black Mesa East from Dr. Kleiner's makeshift laboratory in City 17, Gordon, re-equipped with the HEV suit and a crowbar, is forced to progress on foot through the city's old canal system. After obtaining an airboat, he battles his way to Black Mesa East, several miles from the city.[4][5]
Gordon is reintroduced to Eli and meets another resistance scientist, Dr. Judith Mossman.[6] Alyx introduces Gordon to her pet robot D0g and gives him a "gravity gun", an instrument which allows Gordon to easily pick up and move large objects. Black Mesa East comes under Combine attack, and Eli and Mossman are taken to a Combine prison, Nova Prospekt. Separated from Alyx, Gordon takes a detour through the zombie-infested town of Ravenholm with help from its last survivor, Father Grigori. After making his way through the town and a mine, Gordon arrives at a Resistance outpost. He uses a customized dune buggy to travel across a crumbling coastal road to Nova Prospekt.

TL;DR
Pros:
A lot of variety regarding levels.
Jet boots offer a fun variety of moves.
Fair learning curve.
Nice soundtrack.
Rex Controls very well for this type of game.
Cons:
Looking back that game feels a bit shorter than expected.
In JumpJet Rex you take control of Rex through a series of platforming challenges that can range from simple to pretty crazy (especially when going for specific stars.) The length of levels are about on par with 'The End' in super meat boy being ~45 seconds, however some maps can be upwards to 2+ minutes long featuring a multitude of paths to take or being a long path filled to the brim with traps.
The main mechanic of the game are the Jump jet boots Rex wears. The boots allow him to jump anywhere in the air as much as he'd like, but if you wanna go fast, you can dash sideways, stomp down for faster falling speed, or boost upwards which is faster than spamming jump, but is initially much slower. Overall I love those boots, it's surprising how creative you can get with some obstacles and saving a lot of time on a nice chunk levels.
The goal of each level isn't necessarily just beating them either, Like Super Meat Boy there's a par time that they push you to complete under, in my case they seemed pretty fair with a few curve balls they throw in to catch you off guard and force you to think out the box. Then there's deathless runs, which can be absolutely brutal on the late levels that can be ~2 minute long runs of non-stop pain for your Dino. There's two other goals that aren't necessary for getting the ending, grabbing all coins, and finding all secret loot stashed in the levels, so if you're a completionist, expect some hunts for specific coins or treasure.
All in all that games pretty great, albeit a little short for my tastes. I'd definitely recommend it to fans of challenging platformers, there was a lot more fun than frustration and I thoroughly enjoyed the experience.
As of this review I've completed the game, 3 starred all missions, and collected all secret items so feel free to use that for a reference for the length of the game, although the game definitely has high replayability, and if you're crazy about getting those small times to earn nice spots on the leaderboards, then expect a lot more hours invested.

Divinity: Original Sin is a throwback to what Action RPGs used to be.  When I was a young adult back in the late 90s early 2000s we had games like Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale, Planescape Torment, and Nox.  These games, while real-time based (technically based on DND rules), flowed well and the envrionment was at your disposal.  Divinity should not be compared to any of these games as the gameplay itself may be similar but some of the major elements are still missing.
Divinity is a turn based action RPG based in the Divinity world.  You don't need any former knowledge of the series but you will see some appearances and references to other games.  The world is, in my opinion, a medium sized world that captures your attention and makes it feel much larger due to several factors.  First, everything is usable or can be modified from one state to another.  Some of this comes into play during combat.  In fact, some battles that could not normally be won until a later level can be won earlier if you play your battle correctly.  Oil barrels that explode upon getting hit by a fireball, poison barrels that lay poison onto the ground which can be ignited by fire, and water that can be electrically charged, stunning everything in its area.  These are all aspects of a battle that can be turned against you or the enemy, don't forget, blood conducts electric too, so that blood puddle isn't something you want to stand in if a mage is slamming bolts everywhere!
The one thing that really intrigues me as well as adds points to the game is the difficulty.  This game, as said before, is a throwback to the old school games of the early part of last decade.  There are no quest markers or hand holding.  You need to figure things out for yourself and this could be a turn off to the new generation of gamers.  Please don't take this as an insult but most newer games step you through the entire game, Divinity does no such thing.  The map is useful for markers that you can place, town areas of interest, secret boxes marked on your map, and waypoints.
With no handholding you are left to fend for yourself, this often entails you wandering for a few minutes until you get your bearings.  Walls of text that can get in the way and have no meaning to the current quest line can get annoying but are there to help you immerse yourself.  Quests can often go either way, kill the troll or let him live.  Sometimes you find friends in the strangest areas, so before you go blasting into combat make sure that the skeleton you get your eyes on isn't a friendly.
That brings me to the combat which is extremely well designed.  Everything is turn based meaning that each character goes and does what he/she does for their turn and then it is the next characters turn, friend or foe.  Action points make up your characters ability set and define how many things they can do in a given turn.  Walking, attacking, casting most spells, and drinking potions all consume action points.  The good news is, if you want, you can save up your action points to a certain amount and unload three, four, or even five attacks in one turn.  This adds an element to the combat that makes it strategic.  Some spells cost so much that you need to wait one turn to even cast them while other spells have a cooldown regardless of how many action points you have stored up.
As you level your characters you quickly learn how to lose professionally.  Enemies two levels above you can completely pulverize your party unless you got a trick up your sleeve.  However, the level difference begins to get a little easier as you get more powerful.
Character creation is somewhat of a detailed job that you can easily spend an hour getting right.  The classes presented to you are merely templates as you can modify them to be anything.  Want a geomancer with pyromancing abilities? Go for it.  Want a mage that can wear heavy armor and cast spells?  Sure, go for it.  You do end up sacrificing some things over others as going the latter route will undoubtly have you suffering in one aspect or the other eventually but it is still a viable jack of all trades class.  I am a personal fan of the Red Mage play style so when I can get a party to have a red mage I do it.  On a final note on character creation, you have to create two as the story line does entail two protagonists, so your other two party members will be whomever you choose as you go throughout the game.
As far as the graphics go, the game is good enough.  Nothing stellar but it was never designed in that fashion.  The music rocks and the voice overs are nice.  The game can run on high end systems with no issues and even on middle and low end systems fluidly.
Now with every review comes a few of the bad things.  First I would like to point out that you need to read the manual.  This isn't a flaw or a bad thing for me but again, the newer generation wants everything done for them as games are designed in this fashion.  Another flaw is that sometimes you intend to attack an enemy via melee but your character moves around them instead.  I have had this happen a few times and it gets irritating to say the least.  I haven't lost a battle because of this but it drags out some battles an extra turn when it could have been over earlier.  My other complain is the walls of text I referred to earlier.  Sometimes you end up reading a page out of a book from one conversation before the point is made.  While this adds depth, doing this to often gets tiresome, especially when you are eager to go out and whoop some butt.
Overall, Divinity: Original Sin does the old days justice.  It captures what made games so good back then and then amplifies it to another level.  I was really hoping for an open world in which I could go anywhere and do anything.  While you can do as you wish, some areas are just way to powerful for you and you get spanked.  The story has a set path that you will be at certain points at certain levels, give or take one or two.  I don't think this is bad but enemies don't respawn so other than retracing steps to get some older quest complete or a secret dug up, there is little reason to go back to old areas of the map already explored.

It's like Dead Island with parkour for 60% of the game, then it turns kind of interesting for some time when you reach the second area. Ultimately the game has a decent pace, but ridden with flaws that create a frustrating player experience.
Here's a list of the worst offenders:
- Controls (gamepad) are sluggish and unresponsive. They are also unintuitvely placed and cannot be changed save for a few configurations.
- Combat is frustrating. Enemies are basically walls of health that come at you. Weapons don't feel rewarding and never deal enough damage or seem to damage enemies realistically. Zombies almost always get up even after getting hit multiple times, making combat mostly a chopping simulator. Stronger enemies are basically never worth fighting because of lacking weaponry and because their abilities are tedious to deal with. Not fun.
- Missing design language for in-game objects. Explosive barrels are unmarked. Sometimes in linear level section I still got lost because it was unclear which way I was supposed to go and what part of the level was background/fluff. Ledges and other climbable objects were never highlighted, which in many cases caused death by falling.
- AI behavior and abilties are imbalanced and the fact that different AI attacks can synergize to create a devastating effect for the player seems to have eluded the developers entirely. It's not fun getting thrown off buildings just because a zombie swings its arms or receiving death by rebar sledgehammers when you're in a biter lock.
- 60% of the world is basically Act 2 from Dead Island. Second location is more interesting, but ultimately there is too much time spent being in sewers, in projects or other boring places.
The only real fun in this game is the parkour rooftop gameplay, which is great in the second location, but lacking and uninteresting in the first location and all side locations (sewers, inside buildings etc). I would be more lenient if I didn't have to spend €50 on this; it is definitely NOT worth the money. Go get MIrror's Edge if you want parkour. At this point it's both cheaper and a better game in this genre.

I've had this game on my wishlist for quite some time, since it was in early-access. When it was fully released, it went on sale, so I decided to pick it up. I was skeptical at first, but I didn't regret it at all.
The thing you'll be doing in the game is just getting to the exit of levels. To do so, you can jump an infinite amount of times with your jet boots, dash left or right, hold a button to fall faster, or hold a button to fly upwards faster than you could jump, although this is difficult to control. Projectiles shoot out of your jet boots each time you jump or dash. If you jump, they shoot downwards, and if you dash, they shoot out in the opposite direction you dashed. These can be used to attack enemies and bosses, which makes boss fights unique and interesting. Although, there are only four boss fights. There are 37 regular levels, not including the final level. To unlock the door that leads to the level exit, you need to go through rings scattered about the level. Sometimes this just means finding them once and moving on to the next one, other times it means all the rings are on the same screen and you need to go through the same ring up to three or four times; there's an amount of time that must pass before you can activate the ring again. The level design is overall pretty creative, and many levels have their own little quirks.
It isn't as simple as getting to the end of the level, however. Three stars are available to be earned, depending on how well you do in each level. You can earn a star simply by completing the level, another by completing it without dying, and another by completing it in a certain amount of time. Completing a level in the target time is usually the hardest thing to do. Other levels are unlocked by stars. You can't simply just complete levels or you wouldn't earn enough stars. However, unlocking other levels is fairly easy. You can earn a total of 123 stars (of which I have earned 109). If I didn't want to, I wouldn't even have to complete the last levels of the game, since I had already unlocked the final level. The amount stars required for unlocking levels is very low, so don't worry about having to unlock every single star; some of them are very difficult.
Scattered throughout some levels are hidden collectables. Each time you find one, it is shipped to Rex's space base. It's neat to see the walls become decorated with various different things, although they serve no function. Also scattered throughout levels are coins and giant rubies worth 1000 coins. Coins can be spent at shops to customize Rex's appearance. You can customize the color of Rex's boots, the color of fire or whatever it is that comes out of his boots, his body color, and even his head; there are heads that make him look like Rambo, a ninja turtle, and even Megaman (this is the one I use).
So now for the little things. The music is... lackluster. There are probably around 10 tracks, and none of them are memorable. They're simply mediocre at best, and if a glitch occurred that would have muted the music, I probably wouldn't have minded. Graphics are decent. I'm disappointed that yet another developer chose to go with the pixel-art route, however. I'd like to see more... wholesome graphics. Controller support is good; if you use a controller with Xinput, button prompts change. I have 9 hours in the game and I have 109 of 123 stars. I'm not going to try to get the others, as the're simply too hard. For what you pay for this game, that's a pretty decent value for your money.
There's not much else to say, really. It's a simple game that does what it does well. I highly reccomend it.

An absolutely amazing and fresh, turn based Role Playing Game, reminiscent of the Black Isle days when games like Baldur's Gate and Planescape Torment captivated our imagination and free time.
Combat requires a high level of strategic decision making, utilizing your characters to the max and taking advantage of the environment. There is a huge, beautiful world to explore, with loads of secrets and sidequests plus a variety of different ways to approach different quests. Exploring the world, talking to people(and animals) and searching everything is something i strongly recommend that you do as the game doesn't really hold your hand and you're expected to discover everything your self.
The classes feel very different from each other and restarting the game with different ones makes the game worth a second playthrough. Add to the mix the co-op mode, and the editor where you can create your own missions and share them with other players and the replayability value goes through the roof.
I disagree with the claim that this is a classless game. Each class can start spending points in any ability and attribute they wish. A mage could spend points on single handed weapons and the strength attribute for example, but by allocating their points on many different abilities they may spread their power to thin. I would instead say that the game offers very flexible class customization options but you have to be intelligent about it.
The only issues i have with the game are minor and they haven't affected my overall gaming experience. I initially didn't like the inventory system and some of it's functions, but because the game is built for co-op as well, i understand why there are some minor inconveniences.
If you're a fan of the genre this is a must buy. I give it a 9/10 and it is definitely on my list with the top RPGs i have ever played.

I've been playing ARPG's since Diablo, am a firm believer that Diablo II: Lord of Destruction is the best ARPG ever made and Diablo III: Reaper of Souls is not a true successor to the series. Besides that I've also put time and effort in Torchlight II and Path of Exile, which I both found to be better than Diablo III but which still couldn't satisfy my ARPG need. Now I've purchased Grim Dawn early on but due to performance issues I was unable to play it at that time (which have been fixed) and I left it until recently.
My experience comes from playing Act I in Hardcore Veteran mode, both solo and with friends in multiplayer. The difficulty at Veteran -which is a modifier to Normal difficulty, increasing the amount of "Hero enemies" and the rewards that you reap from them- is very solid. You will roughly level from 1 to 18-20 during Act I, during which I got the feeling that this game is quite well balanced. Sometimes you will feel weak, but most of the time that is to be fixed with reassigning your skills.
The overal look and feel of this game is, like the name implies; Grim. It's dark and "serious", like Diablo II and Path of Exile. No cartoon art-style as Diablo III or Torchlight II. Personally I find this to be a big plus, seeing as this gives the game a more serious presentation.
The unique point of this game is that you start the game without choosing a class, called masteries in Grim Dawn. Once you reach your first level you gain the option to select one out of six masteries; Arcanist, Demolitionist, Nightblade, Occultist, Shaman, Soldier. Each mastery has an unique and fun skill tree with enough skills to keep you trying out stuff for a while.
Just like in Diablo II you will have to assign attribute points to either Physical (health), Cunning (melee) or Spirit (mana). A lot of gear you will find will require X points into Physical and either X points in Cunning or Spirit, depending on the kind of gear (weapon type, heavy or normal armor).
This goes on until you reach level 10, at which the game presents you to choose a (optional) second mastery. You can choose to combine masteries to supplement your character with additional skills that would otherwise be impossible to get, or to ignore this and go deeper into your previously selected mastery. Based on the combination of masteries you've chosen, your character class title will change to something else. The option of adding a second mastery will stay definitely once level 10 has been reached. The current level-cap is 85.
All in all this game feels refreshingly good and comes close to the feeling I've got while playing Diablo II: Lord of Destruction, but without the bots running all the games. If you need something different from Diablo III, Torchlight II or Path of Exile, this is it.

My buddy and I started a new game, a couple of wayfaring adventurers looking to make a living 'n what not. Our first quest is to investigate the murder of a counselor.
In the midst of our investigation, we determine 4 suspects - one of which being the town healer's apprentice. We went to go question her on the matter but found her in the middle of treating two patients in dire condition. She had a strange stone in her possession that could possibly heal one of them of all ailments, but we would have to choose which one would receive the treatment. My partner and I discussed it, and after a rousing game of rock, paper, scissors, we decided that the younger of the two should be spared an early death.
After the healer's apprentice used the stone, it suddenly went haywire and transported my partner and I to another dimension where we were greeted by an imp claiming to be a historian - an archivist on all of time. He mentioned he had finished recording all of history, and told us to look through his giant looking glass. We peered through, and witnessed the end of all things. The universe being sucked into a void. After seeing this, the imp told us he wants to stop time from ending - save the world, y'know. Then he took us to a woman who had a giant, golden tapestry behind her.
This woman was time itself, and wove time together within that tapestry. She told us that neither of us were bound by time, that we instead, create time, and are the keys of saving time itself. After accepting a quest to gather "Star Stones to save time", we were given a teleportation pyramid that we could use to leave the dimension we were in and return to our own.
Upon using it, we found ourselves back in town, in a woman's house, where said woman was taking a bath and screamed at us to get back. My partner initiated rock, paper, scissors to convince her we're here for a good reason, but lost sorrily, and we immediately vacated the premises and continued our investigation.
On top of all that, the combat is complex, yet simple. Easy to understand, but just really deep in strategy. We got into a fight with about 7 monsters that happened to be a couple levels higher than us and we decided to make a tactical retreat while having our wizard character consistently teleport enemies and electrify pools of water for them to run into until we could get them close enough to the city gate where we could call upon some of the town guard to help us so we wouldn't get our butts reemed.
Character customization is what you'd expect from a classic-style RPG such as this: Multiple appearence alterations, and complete freedom in choosing what stats to put points into. My partner is a geomancy using wayfarer who also uses oils and poisons to incapacitate enemies, while I, being a knight, run around with a giant weapon crushing the skulls of my enemies, but have foregone most of the healing abilities set in the begining to up my power in combat.
The game truly came alive for me when I started to have that "Baldur's Gate experience." Where it wasn't just another RPG, but it felt more like an adventure. The possibilities still seem endless, and even though we haven't seemed to make much progress, it hasn't become a chore to run around and talk to NPCs, barter with each and every one of them to see what loot they might be willing to part with, or see what the latest gossip is, yielding other quests to be found simply through exploration and inquiry. And the amount of player interaction found not only between the players and the enviornment, but also the players themselves (should you play co-op) is absolutely fantastic.
Divinity: Original Sin is for those who are looking for a good, well developed, in-depth classic CRPG that fans of D&D and Baldur's Gate can appreciate. And with custom campaigns being available, the game has a near limitless potential.
