Half-Life 2 (stylized as HλLF-LIFE2) is a first-person shooter video game and the sequel to Half-Life (1998). Developed by Valve Corporation, it was released on November 16, 2004, following a five-year $40 million development, during which a substantial part of the project was leaked and distributed on the Internet. The game was developed alongside Valve's Steam software. It introduced the Source game engine and, because of Steam, was the first single-player video game to require online product activation.
Some years after the events of Half-Life, protagonist Gordon Freeman is woken by the enigmatic G-Man to find the world has been taken over by the alien Combine. Joined by allies including resistance fighter Alyx Vance, Gordon searches for a way to free humanity using a variety of weapons, including the object-manipulating gravity gun.
Like its predecessor, Half-Life 2 received critical acclaim. It was praised for its advanced physics, animation, sound, AI, graphics, and narrative. The game won 39 "Game of the Year" awards and the title of "Game Of The Decade" at the 2012 Spike Video Game Awards, and is widely considered to be one of the greatest and most important video games of all time. Over 6.5 million copies of Half-Life 2 were sold at retail by December 3, 2008, (not including Steam sales); as of February 9, 2011, Half-Life 2 had sold over 12 million copies.
Like its predecessor, Half-Life 2 is a single-player first-person shooter broken into several chapters, permanently casting the player as the protagonist Gordon Freeman. The sequel has nearly the same mechanics as Half-Life, including health-and-weapon systems and periodic physics puzzles, except with the newer Source Engine and improved graphics. The player also starts without items, slowly building up an arsenal over the course of the game. Despite the game's mainly linear nature, much effort was put into making exploration rewarding and interesting; many optional areas can be missed or avoided.
A diverse set of enemies is present, which usually require being approached with different tactics: some coordinate in groups to out-maneuver or out-position the player; others, like the Manhack, fly directly at the player through small openings and tight corridors; still others use predictable but powerful attacks, while others hide before swiftly attacking the player. Gordon can kill most enemies with his weapons, or make use of indirect means, exploiting environmental hazards such as explosive pressurized canisters, gas fires or improvised traps. For some portions of the game, Gordon can be joined by up to four armed Resistance soldiers and medics, and can send his team further from him or call them back.
Many of the game's new features utilize its detailed physics simulation. Two sections of the game involve driving vehicles. Instead of button-based puzzles from Half-Life, environmental puzzles are also introduced with makeshift mechanical systems, revolving around the player's new ability to pick up, move, and place objects. Solutions involve objects' physical properties, such as shape, weight, and buoyancy. For example, in Chapter 3, Route Kanal, the player is required to stack cinder blocks on a makeshift see-saw ramp to proceed over a wall. Alternatively, the player can use these to build a crude staircase, so sometimes, multiple approaches lead to the desired outcome.
Part-way through the game, Gordon acquires the Gravity Gun, which allows him to draw distant objects towards himself or forcefully push them away, as well as the ability to manipulate larger and heavier objects that he cannot manipulate without the weapon. These abilities are required to solve puzzles later in the game, and can also be used to great effect in combat, as any non-static object within proximity to the player has the potential to be used as a makeshift defense (e.g. a file cabinet) or a deadly projectile (e.g. a gasoline can or a buzzsaw blade).
The game never separates the player with pre-rendered cutscenes or events; the story proceeds via exposition from other characters and in-world events, and ensures that the player controls Gordon for the entirety of the game. Much of the backstory to the game is simply alluded to, or told through the environment.Half-Life 2 presents a dystopian alternate history of Earth, where the resources of the planet, including the human race itself, are being harvested by an oppressive multidimensional empire, known as the Combine. The game is set around the fictitious City 17, roughly 20 years after the events of its predecessor Half-Life.
During Half-Life, the scientists, including Gordon Freeman, at the Black Mesa Research Facility, accidentally caused an inter-dimensional instability known as a resonance cascade and later as the "Black Mesa Incident", when an experiment on an alien crystal sample went wrong.[1] Alien creatures, such as the Vortigaunts and headcrabs, from the borderworld of Xen, flooded into the facility. Gordon fought his way through them and the government cover-up response combat units, making it to the Facility's Lambda Complex. There, the Lambda scientists helped Gordon teleport to Xen, where Gordon destroyed a large alien entity keeping the rift open. Gordon was then suddenly extracted by the mysterious G-Man, who had been watching Gordon over the course of the game. Impressed with his ability to survive against all odds, the G-Man offered him a job before placing him into stasis, which Gordon had no option but to accept.
Some time after the ending of Half-Life, the instability at Black Mesa had attracted the attention of the Combine empire, and they invaded Earth. Humanity surrendered at the conclusion of the resulting "Seven Hour War". City 17 became the home of the gigantic Combine Citadel, and Dr. Wallace Breen, the Administrator of Black Mesa who had negotiated the surrender, was appointed representative and Administrator to supervise the survivors on behalf of the Combine.[2] Unable to breed due to a Combine suppression field, humanity matured. The Combine implemented a brutal police state of Civil Protection officers and Overwatch soldiers by recruiting and biologically assimilating humans and other species. Meanwhile, an underground "Lambda Resistance" of humans and Vortigaunts, now working together, was formed. This saw Freeman as a saviour who would lead them to freedom.20 years after the Resonance Cascade, the Combine emerge from the portal with advanced technologies, enabling them to conquer the world in 7 hours. Gordon Freeman is brought out of stasis by the G-Man, who inserts him into a train arriving at City 17.[3] After arriving at the station and eluding Combine forces, Gordon joins Lambda resistance members including Barney Calhoun, a former Black Mesa security guard now working undercover as a Combine CP officer, and Alyx Vance, the daughter of one of Gordon's former colleagues, Dr. Eli Vance. After a failed attempt to teleport to Eli's resistance base known as Black Mesa East from Dr. Kleiner's makeshift laboratory in City 17, Gordon, re-equipped with the HEV suit and a crowbar, is forced to progress on foot through the city's old canal system. After obtaining an airboat, he battles his way to Black Mesa East, several miles from the city.[4][5]
Gordon is reintroduced to Eli and meets another resistance scientist, Dr. Judith Mossman.[6] Alyx introduces Gordon to her pet robot D0g and gives him a "gravity gun", an instrument which allows Gordon to easily pick up and move large objects. Black Mesa East comes under Combine attack, and Eli and Mossman are taken to a Combine prison, Nova Prospekt. Separated from Alyx, Gordon takes a detour through the zombie-infested town of Ravenholm with help from its last survivor, Father Grigori. After making his way through the town and a mine, Gordon arrives at a Resistance outpost. He uses a customized dune buggy to travel across a crumbling coastal road to Nova Prospekt.

It's another Telltale Walking Dead game. There's a lot of quick time events, a tiny bit of exploration, a lot of sitting back and watching the story unfold, and making a few choices that affect how the story unfolds. The problem with all of the Walking Dead games except for the first one is that there are no relatable or likable characters. Further, this is a prequel to the show so obviously nothing is going to happen to Michonne herself and thus there's no tension. What the first WD game lacked in challenging puzzles it made up for with heavy emotional decisions that had to be weighed. This one just feels like I'm the subject of a laboratory experiment to see how cruel I will be given the opportunity. The story itself was ok. There's another group of humans that Michonne and her group have conflict with and there are hordes of zombies that attack when the plot calls for it. The sub plot has Michonne dealing with the loss of her two children. There are lots of flash backs spliced in with the main story showing how her guilt for losing her two children affects how she processes events going on in the present. This didn't really work for me. It just made Michonne seem like a shell shocked basket case that was in desperate need of a lot of rest and relaxation instead of as being a bad a.ss warrior. The game takes around 4 hours to complete all three episodes. The cel-shaded graphics style used in all of  these games still looks nice. The animation can look a bit stiff at times, betraying that it is indeed a video game and not a cartoon. I'm hoping that Telltale will make a Walking Dead game in style of their Sam & Max series. Those were the days when Telltale games were firing on all cylinders. Taking the puzzles solving out and relying on pure story can work, but what sinks this game is that it just made no emotional connection with me and there were no mentally stimulating puzzles to keep me engaged otherwise.

Amazing action tower(traps?) defense gameplay bound together by a great theme and execution.
You're given great customization options on what to use to slaughter thousands of orcs. Fireball them from afar, push them into lava with a gust of wind, slice them with your bladestaff or mash/mince/grid/slice/incinerate/freeze/mind control them with any combination of traps you  desire.
Level variety and design are also good. Each level feels different and presents you with its own set of challenges and you have to figure out where best to set up your killing fields. Some levels also have some "consumable" one-time traps, that you have to trigger manually and have a powerful effect.
Sound design is good, dialog is funny, soundtrack is tense and epic and really makes you feel like you're the last bastion of defense, protecting your home from an invasion of orcs.
Overall great game, lots of fun, good challenge for those who seek it, so get it and start killing some orc!

I’ve just finished playing The Walking Dead: Michonne mini-series and I’m really baffled by the extent and amount of negative criticism, not to mention some of the reasoning. Obviously people are entitled to their opinions but for example, I have read a fair few complaints about the length of the game in comparison to other Telltale titles, I mean c’mon guys, the clue is in the name- it’s a mini-series!!
I’ve also seen criticisms aimed at the fact that at certain points of the game the element of choice is reduced and the direction is somewhat dictated, unless the expectation is an unending game with infinite possibilities then of course there have to be defined, critical points in the narrative! I also saw some mention of clunky controls, I didn’t have any issues with this but Telltale games are amongst the few I play with a controller rather than keyboard and mouse so maybe the latter is bad but I couldn’t really say.
I’m leaping to its defence and it’s not a perfect game by any means (does such a thing exist?) but I read the description and checked out a few reviews; I knew what to expect and enjoyed the game. The story is good, though for what I thought we’re obvious reasons it doesn’t get as in depth as the other walking dead games; the same applies to the characters.
I wasn’t sure how well Michonne matched up to the Michonne I know from the series; she seemed a lot more emotional and open but this could be because she hasn’t been through as much yet or simply because this plays out from her perspective? I also haven’t read the graphic novels so if the TV series deviated from her character it’s not something I’d have a clue about! The supporting characters we’re diverse, well-constructed in their minimal screen time and I thought the dialogue was well written for the most part.
I have 6.7 hours played but I was playing late at night, procrastinating and being generally very slow and I’d imagine 3-5hourws is probably a more accurate expected playtime. There are things I wish I’d done differently though and I’m interested to see where other choices lead so it definitely has replayability.
I bought this in a recent Humble Bundle so paid less than the regular asking price on Steam of £10.99, which I’m not sure is relative to the price/experience of the main Walking Dead titles (£18.99) but if you’re particularly interested or can get it at a reduced price I would definitely recommend playing it.

RUSH is a solid puzzle game, unique in the way that each one needs to be. The basic mechanic of using directional and other controlling pads to direct blocks of various colors toward their respective goals is an intelligent and compelling one, if slightly more so on paper than when playing. I give my compliments to the developers for wringing as much life as they have with RUSH out of a few simple pad types: up, down, left, right (no cheating - the pads rotate in tandem as you rotate the camera), alternate-direction (this one's my favorite, particularly with the puzzles that having blocks approach the pad from different directions creates), conveyor (shifts a block over one space while preserving its direction), and temporary-stop. Use of warp points, while a bit of a design crutch, adds more variety so I'll give it a pass. The game does get tedious, though, when you have to fine-tune your pathways so that blocks don't run into one another. In moderation this would add welcome depth to the gameplay, but as it is, it shifts the balance a little too far from creative problem-solving to drudging trial-and-error. Another, less frequently visible flaw in the game mechanics is that the number of blocks you must allow through your system is inconsistent - I once noticed that, due to the way I had my alternate-direction pads set up, my solution wouldn't have worked if one more block of each color had been expelled. The general feeling of designing cycles, however, is quite relaxing, so the gameplay is still well in the positive zone in my eyes.
There's not much to be said about the aesthetics. The music, while extremely repetitive, somehow scarcely gets annoying. The visuals... exist. My only complaints tangent to a discussion of aesthetics here concern the camera: you can't zoom, and the overhead expanse of blocks in the "crocodile" (or was it "alligator"?) level is a needless hindrance. Not impossible to work around, but not pleasant.
Overall, RUSH is an enjoyable, if imperfect, piece of work, and I'd recommend picking it up if you want something to occupy a few minutes (or longer) here and there as needed.

Speedrunning used to be a small genre within the gaming scene. You’d take a game, preferably one with action/platforming aspects, and simply attempt to beat it as quick as possible. Within the past five years, speedrunning has become a genre entirely of its own. While most speedrunning games still harken back to their platforming and action roots, they usually also feature a timer, a time to beat, and enough speed to make a cracked out Sonic drinking Red Bull get jealous. JumpJet Rex exemplifies speed. Paired with a colorful aesthetic and a bevy of extremely varied levels, you will be shaving seconds with pleasure in an attempt to see what comes next. Will JumpJet Rex speed it’s way into your heart, or crash and burn? Let’s take a closer look at JumpJet Rex.
The controls in this game feel extremely smooth. Most people haven’t played as a dinosaur in rocket-boots before, but let me tell you that it’s surprisingly much easier than it sounds. Hitting X will send Rex rocketing in the direction you are currently facing, with reckless abandon. This is the primary ability used to get through stages, along with your levitate ability which is activated with Y. Pressing A will allow an itty-bitty jump, and B will have Rex tuck his legs and butt-slam his way to the ground. You will need to chain all of these abilities effectively in order to avoid enemies, obstacles, and traps in an attempt to reach the end of the stage. Just reaching the end is enough to win a star, but each stage has two additional stars. One awarded for not dying. The other can be won by completing the course under the par time.
There are also three different game modes, so once you bumble your way through the story mode you can come back again and rage as you attempt to complete the entire game with only three lives. Finally in time attack mode, you can attempt to complete the entire game as quickly as possible and try to dominate the global scoreboard. Your efforts in game are always rewarded, usually with cosmetic upgrades but I can tell that even dinosaurs like to play dress-up. Currency is found in every level and, as with any good game, will usually lead you where you need to go. Level design is varied from arenas to sprawling mazes, and new mechanics (such as breakable blocks) are periodically introduced, which keeps things interesting for the player. As I stated before, the aesthetic is colorful and helps enhance the fun nature of the game. The music is good for the most part, though some tracks do slide into questionable listening material.
The sound FX get a bit repetitive after an extended period of play, as I’ve found with most speedrunners. The story is also pretty generic and serves basically only to get the game started. Some stages are quite confusing, and you are sure to never get three stars on your first try. That seems to really be about it. There aren’t a lot of negative points to JumpJet Rex, and while it could do with a bit of polish, I think what is offered currently is extremely solid if you’re into fast-paced platforming with a winning aesthetic and a ton of replayability. I’d like to thank TreeFortress Games for providing us with a review copy, and we look forward to seeing more releases of a similar caliber in the very near future.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown, where to begin?
This game is the game I never knew that I wanted. It's a perfect blend of a strategy simulator, mixed with a tatical RPG.
In this game you play as the commander of an elite taskforce known as XCOM. XCOM was created in response to the alien threat, and only your team is equipped to handle these things.
The game has two distinct phases of play. The first phase is the strategy simulator, in which you build your base, monitor alien attacks, research new things, build new items for your troops to use, and customize your troops.
The second phase is where you put to use all the upgrades and modified troops and it becomes a tactical RPG, in which you play a deadly game of cat and mouse with a (up to) 6 man squad exterminating the alien threat in a variety of maps and missions. Some you just go in and kill everything, others you have to save civilians, and some you even have to capture some of the very same aliens who are trying to kill you in order to perform more research.
The two phases work in complete harmony with one another, if you do bad in one phase, you'll do bad in the other, and vise versa.
Some of the biggest highlights of the game come from customizing your troops. As they participate in battle and kill aliens, they will go up in rank and earn new skills (the 4 categories that your troops can become are: Heavy, Support, Sniper, and Assault). But along with earning new skills you can also customize each individual soldiers facial features and even change their name and give them nicknames. This whole level of customization that the game offers makes it just that much more personal. Try going in with a soldier named after your brother, who you've leveled up to the final rank, just to watch him die in front of you, it's heart wrenching. That's another thing, death in this game is permanent, so permanent in fact that you can go to the barracks and view the wall of fallen soldiers.
This game will test you in no way a video game has before. It will teach you one way or another to plan out all your moves and be careful with your troops, because once they die, they won't come back. XCOM is unforgiving and rewarding all at the same time, and worth every penny and every minute of your time.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding cheese cake recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1 cup digestive plain sweet biscuit crumbs
3 tablespoons sugar
3 tablespoons melted butter
40 ounces softened cream cheese
1 cup sugar
3 tablespoons flour
1 tablespoon vanilla
1 cup sour cream
4 eggs
Directions:
For The base:.
If you're using a dark pan, preheat the oven to 350. If you are using a shiny pan, 375.
Combine the crumbs, melted butter and 3 tbsp sugar well and pat onto the bottom of a 9 inch springform pan. I also like to very very lightly butter the sides of the pan so that the cheesecake will not stick later on.
Bake for 10 mins in your preheated oven and remove. Let it cool while you prepare your batter.
For the batter:.
Make sure everything is at room temperature.
Combine sugar, cheese, flour and vanilla in a big bowl and mix on medium speed till well combined. Don't forget to scrape the bowl as you're doing this.
Mix in the sour cream till its incorporated well. Then, add the eggs one by one, mixing well after each addition.
Pour the batter into the springform and let it bake for 1 hour and 10 minutes After the baking time, turn off the oven and leave the door ajar. Let the cake cool in there for about 1 1/2 hours.
Remove the cake and let it cool thoroughly. Refrigerate overnight.
Release the sides of the springform.
Eat.

RUSH, also called Rubik's Puzzle Galaxy: RUSH on Wii, is a puzzle game in which you have to guide colored blocks to their applicable exit points to complete levels.  Blocks are guided by placing markers on the ground which change the direction of, speed up, or slow down blocks that pass over them.  Later levels also offer conveyor belt markers which can shift blocks to the side without changing their direction.  Losing any blocks off the edge of the level or having blocks collide fails the level.
Levels vary from trivially easy to frustratingly complex and difficult, though most of the levels are pretty reasonable.  In levels where streams of two different colored blocks need to cross, you will often end up making lots of small adjustments to the position of markers to avoid collisions which can be rather frustrating, especially when everything seems to be going perfectly only for the last two blocks on the level to collide.
Overall a very enjoyable puzzle game.  It makes me sad to see Two Tribes closing.

Both whimsical and incredibly complex, Divinity - Original Sin has a multitude of everything. Evolving your characters' personalities as they go, moving and adjusting nigh anything that isn't nailed down to the ground, a crafting system that's both intuitive and incredibly complex... and a story that I found myself thoroughly enjoying.
I admit that I missed Divine Divinity, back in the day. Beyond Divinity was fairly dull and repetitive, so I gave up on it eventually, even though it had a fair share of complexity. Divinity - Dragon Knight Saga... it was nice, but only the expansion truly showcased what the game could have been, in terms of deep dialog and character design, complex questlines, and interesting gameplay.
But here... here I got an RPG that was amazing. One that features no level scaling, one that does turn-based combat incredibly well. One that nailed down things like complex, multi-layered effects to one's choices even in battle.
It's not perfect. A few areas could have been even more complex, sure. And I was never a fan of Diablo-style item randomization, preferring instead the more personalized and deep feel games like Baldur's Gate provided.
But this is a masterpiece. And it deserves respect! Play it!

First I will start off with a disclaimer. I am a huge fan of the isometric dungeon crawler genre, but I know it is not everyone's cup of tea. Also this is my first review ever.
With that being said this game in my opinion is hands down the best ARPG released since D2 LOD. If you are a fan of titan quest you will feel at home with how the core game feels as the same engine is used. The story is dark and gritty with an alternate world that has recently expierenced an apocalpyse of sorts. Needless to say there are plently of monsters that need slaying.
Pros:
+Excelent skill trees with meaningful passives. ( I miss passives that actually change your build, and I am happy to see the return to form, very similar to D2)
+Items are meaningful, uniques and legendaries feel just that unique and legendary. This is one of the most important factors in the genre, and I feel comfortable in saying this game has the best item attributes around.The items in the game can dramatically change your build. Like D2 One of the great features of this is granted skills from items (another feature missing in many of todays arpgs)
+Plenty to do after and during the story. While many arpgs simply have you killing monsters in the hopes of getting loot, this game adds a couple of new layers to the loot grind. The first is a reputation system, that allows you to buy specialty items and recipees. Which brings up another neat feature which is crafting. Crafting in this game is actually very useful and can help create unique builds, especially through relics (items that you can equip in a relic slot granting specific bonuses and a new skill). There is also a roguelike dungeon in the game that if beaten grants a reward of treasure chests galore. There is plenty more I have not mentioned like the Nemisis system, and devotion shrines.
+Both offline and online
Cons:
-Graphically speaking it does not push the boundaries, but that is to be expected in the genre.
-Combat while not bad, is typical of arpg's. Nothing boundary pushing here. Basically the combat is near identical to titan quest which is no surprise. Still the combat is on par with any other arpg out, and the build possiblites pretty much gurantee a style for you. I only put this in the cons because some people may not be a fan of the basic combat style of arpgs.
-Some people may be turned off by the large number of passives in the skill trees (I myself love passives)
- There is no serverside online. Meaning the characters are saved to your computer allowing others online to modify/cheat their character. (This can be mitigated by playing with friends, but it would be nice to have anti cheating measures)
Overall:
This game is a must for arpg fans especially those that enjoyed titan quest and d2 lod. While the combat may not be as smooth as d3 or the trade community as active as PoE, I beleive that it more than makes up for it in the sheer number of awesome items (once again one of the most important parts of an arpg) and the many builds you can make. With devotion shrines to be found or reputation to be gained, there is plenty to do, and you will not have to worry about only grinding the same area over and over. If you are a fan of the genre this game is for you, if not then you will most likely not enjoy the game. This is a game that caters very much to people like me, that is to say the developers bring back the feel from the late 90's early 2000's that I loved so much.

Cons:

We had the game bug out and put the second player off the map and unable to get back in early in the game (before we had could port out) in the first 20 mins of gameplay.  Within the first 5 hours we had the game kick the second player nearly 10 times, and hard crash (had to close and re-start) 3 times.  We've had less bugs since the last patch and are still playing (gameplay is that good), but if you're looking to play co-op don't be surprised if you run into more than a few bugs.  Save Often!
Verdict:
Though I greatly appreciate the game for what it is, I don't think I'd recommend it to someone looking for a co-op-only play through.  I'm not one for critical reviews, but I want to make sure our experience has been noted by the team at Larian Studios.  I'm looking forward to a patch that fully addresses the co-op bugs so I can change my "No" to "Yes".

Half-Life 2 (stylized as HλLF-LIFE2) is a first-person shooter video game and the sequel to Half-Life (1998). Developed by Valve Corporation, it was released on November 16, 2004, following a five-year $40 million development, during which a substantial part of the project was leaked and distributed on the Internet. The game was developed alongside Valve's Steam software. It introduced the Source game engine and, because of Steam, was the first single-player video game to require online product activation.
Some years after the events of Half-Life, protagonist Gordon Freeman is woken by the enigmatic G-Man to find the world has been taken over by the alien Combine. Joined by allies including resistance fighter Alyx Vance, Gordon searches for a way to free humanity using a variety of weapons, including the object-manipulating gravity gun.
Like its predecessor, Half-Life 2 received critical acclaim. It was praised for its advanced physics, animation, sound, AI, graphics, and narrative. The game won 39 "Game of the Year" awards and the title of "Game Of The Decade" at the 2012 Spike Video Game Awards, and is widely considered to be one of the greatest and most important video games of all time. Over 6.5 million copies of Half-Life 2 were sold at retail by December 3, 2008, (not including Steam sales); as of February 9, 2011, Half-Life 2 had sold over 12 million copies.
Like its predecessor, Half-Life 2 is a single-player first-person shooter broken into several chapters, permanently casting the player as the protagonist Gordon Freeman. The sequel has nearly the same mechanics as Half-Life, including health-and-weapon systems and periodic physics puzzles, except with the newer Source Engine and improved graphics. The player also starts without items, slowly building up an arsenal over the course of the game. Despite the game's mainly linear nature, much effort was put into making exploration rewarding and interesting; many optional areas can be missed or avoided.
A diverse set of enemies is present, which usually require being approached with different tactics: some coordinate in groups to out-maneuver or out-position the player; others, like the Manhack, fly directly at the player through small openings and tight corridors; still others use predictable but powerful attacks, while others hide before swiftly attacking the player. Gordon can kill most enemies with his weapons, or make use of indirect means, exploiting environmental hazards such as explosive pressurized canisters, gas fires or improvised traps. For some portions of the game, Gordon can be joined by up to four armed Resistance soldiers and medics, and can send his team further from him or call them back.
Many of the game's new features utilize its detailed physics simulation. Two sections of the game involve driving vehicles. Instead of button-based puzzles from Half-Life, environmental puzzles are also introduced with makeshift mechanical systems, revolving around the player's new ability to pick up, move, and place objects. Solutions involve objects' physical properties, such as shape, weight, and buoyancy. For example, in Chapter 3, Route Kanal, the player is required to stack cinder blocks on a makeshift see-saw ramp to proceed over a wall. Alternatively, the player can use these to build a crude staircase, so sometimes, multiple approaches lead to the desired outcome.
Part-way through the game, Gordon acquires the Gravity Gun, which allows him to draw distant objects towards himself or forcefully push them away, as well as the ability to manipulate larger and heavier objects that he cannot manipulate without the weapon. These abilities are required to solve puzzles later in the game, and can also be used to great effect in combat, as any non-static object within proximity to the player has the potential to be used as a makeshift defense (e.g. a file cabinet) or a deadly projectile (e.g. a gasoline can or a buzzsaw blade).
The game never separates the player with pre-rendered cutscenes or events; the story proceeds via exposition from other characters and in-world events, and ensures that the player controls Gordon for the entirety of the game. Much of the backstory to the game is simply alluded to, or told through the environment.Half-Life 2 presents a dystopian alternate history of Earth, where the resources of the planet, including the human race itself, are being harvested by an oppressive multidimensional empire, known as the Combine. The game is set around the fictitious City 17, roughly 20 years after the events of its predecessor Half-Life.
During Half-Life, the scientists, including Gordon Freeman, at the Black Mesa Research Facility, accidentally caused an inter-dimensional instability known as a resonance cascade and later as the "Black Mesa Incident", when an experiment on an alien crystal sample went wrong.[1] Alien creatures, such as the Vortigaunts and headcrabs, from the borderworld of Xen, flooded into the facility. Gordon fought his way through them and the government cover-up response combat units, making it to the Facility's Lambda Complex. There, the Lambda scientists helped Gordon teleport to Xen, where Gordon destroyed a large alien entity keeping the rift open. Gordon was then suddenly extracted by the mysterious G-Man, who had been watching Gordon over the course of the game. Impressed with his ability to survive against all odds, the G-Man offered him a job before placing him into stasis, which Gordon had no option but to accept.
Some time after the ending of Half-Life, the instability at Black Mesa had attracted the attention of the Combine empire, and they invaded Earth. Humanity surrendered at the conclusion of the resulting "Seven Hour War". City 17 became the home of the gigantic Combine Citadel, and Dr. Wallace Breen, the Administrator of Black Mesa who had negotiated the surrender, was appointed representative and Administrator to supervise the survivors on behalf of the Combine.[2] Unable to breed due to a Combine suppression field, humanity matured. The Combine implemented a brutal police state of Civil Protection officers and Overwatch soldiers by recruiting and biologically assimilating humans and other species. Meanwhile, an underground "Lambda Resistance" of humans and Vortigaunts, now working together, was formed. This saw Freeman as a saviour who would lead them to freedom.20 years after the Resonance Cascade, the Combine emerge from the portal with advanced technologies, enabling them to conquer the world in 7 hours. Gordon Freeman is brought out of stasis by the G-Man, who inserts him into a train arriving at City 17.[3] After arriving at the station and eluding Combine forces, Gordon joins Lambda resistance members including Barney Calhoun, a former Black Mesa security guard now working undercover as a Combine CP officer, and Alyx Vance, the daughter of one of Gordon's former colleagues, Dr. Eli Vance. After a failed attempt to teleport to Eli's resistance base known as Black Mesa East from Dr. Kleiner's makeshift laboratory in City 17, Gordon, re-equipped with the HEV suit and a crowbar, is forced to progress on foot through the city's old canal system. After obtaining an airboat, he battles his way to Black Mesa East, several miles from the city.[4][5]
Gordon is reintroduced to Eli and meets another resistance scientist, Dr. Judith Mossman.[6] Alyx introduces Gordon to her pet robot D0g and gives him a "gravity gun", an instrument which allows Gordon to easily pick up and move large objects. Black Mesa East comes under Combine attack, and Eli and Mossman are taken to a Combine prison, Nova Prospekt. Separated from Alyx, Gordon takes a detour through the zombie-infested town of Ravenholm with help from its last survivor, Father Grigori. After making his way through the town and a mine, Gordon arrives at a Resistance outpost. He uses a customized dune buggy to travel across a crumbling coastal road to Nova Prospekt.

The Banner Saga is an almost perfect game for me.
Initially, the art style is welcoming and beautiful, and stays consistent during travel, cutscenes, or combat.
Gameplay itself is part Oregon Trail, part Final Fantasy Tactics, and part Point and Click,
-The "Oregon Trail" bit is fun the first time through, interesting the second time through, and unfortunately predictable after that. There are no "random" encounters, everything occurs on a schedule. It is definitely an interesting attempt, but unfortunately weakened by the lack of a random element.
-The "FFT" parts are my favorite, though not without flaws. Combat is extremely tactical, where you have to use your characters' skills intelligently, while manipulating your opponents into using theirs poorly. There are enough characters to keep this fresh (though I would love many, many more), and there is even a matter of fatigue -- damage doesn't completely heal on its own after battle, meaning drawn out engagements can go very poorly for you. The downside of tactical battles are that the "maps" are almost all the same -- a flat grid. The art is different (and wonderful), but there is no terrain or obstacles to speak of, barring a map or two. Even minor touches here would greatly enhance gameplay and strategy.
-The "Point and Click" bits come when you enter towns and areas, and works well enough. They missed some opportunities with making different things happen based on the order you click on areas, and there are no "secrets" of any kind, but it serves its purpose well.
The story, characters, and even the enemies are interesting. I very much want to play the sequel, or at least see some additional content added to this title soon. Having heard no news on either front, I'm going to cross my fingers and home something is in the works and coming soon.
I rate this game an 8/10 and recommend it especially to folks to like Tactical/Strategy games, similar to Final Fantasy Tactics or X-COM: Enemy Unknown.

Quick Summary: Orcs Must Die is a combination of third person action and tower/trap defense, similar to Sanctum but with humor and medieval weaponry. The game is a lot of fun, but unlike the sequel, there’s no co-op gameplay :(
You take on the role of a cocky student war mage trying to hold back the onslaught of orcs coming through into our world. The hero is pretty dumb, but fortunately the orcs are even dumber and their paths through each level are almost completely predictable. With your magic traps and artifacts (for casting spells) you need to make sure as few orcs as possible get to the end of the level and enter the rift (sometimes there’s more than one rift to defend).
The game is broken up into individual levels, each with a different map, and on each map can be multiple orc entrances and exit rifts. At the start of each level you are given unlimited time to run around and see the layout, as well as set up your loadout (which traps or spells you can use during the level). Once you’ve started the game you cannot change your loadout, you’d have to restart the whole level. You have a ton of traps to choose from, although a few of them aren’t much use and you’ll likely be sticking with the basics like wall arrows, tar pits, and barricades for most of the game. You’ll be facing only a few different kinds of orcs (fast runners, arrow shooters, ogres), but they’ll be coming in large numbers so the key to beating each level is channeling the orcs into choke points where you can use fewer numbers of traps. The traps cost money so you can’t just fill the map with them (and unlike many other tower defense games, you cannot upgrade the traps during the levels).
The biggest difference though between Orcs Must Die and traditional tower defense is the fact that you the hero are on site blasting enemies alongside your traps. You’re armed with a reasonably powerful rapid fire crossbow that’s able to kill small numbers of the slow moving orcs, or the really fast runners that die in one shot. Your traps usually have cooldown times so you cannot rely on them to catch every orc. For example, a spike trap might only trigger every 5 seconds, and during those 5 seconds, more orcs might run over it. It’s up to you and your trusty crossbow to fill them with arrows while waiting for your traps to be ready again. Every level you beat unlocks a different trap type or spell (like fireball or lightning) so by the end of the campaign you’ll have a massive arsenal to choose from.
Pros:
+The difficulty ramps up slowly and gives you a chance to learn various strategies for tackling levels. In the meantime, enjoy the humor. “Oh no he di’nt” – Orc, as he’s knocked into lava
+You can go back and replay levels with your newly unlocked traps and spells. The game tells you the top scores for each level that your Steam friends achieved. I’m not that competitive though, I just wanted to finish each level and see the story.
Cons:
-I mentioned the difficulty ramps up, and by the end some of the levels seem practically impossible to get max score if you’re trying the Nightmare difficulty.
Overall, Orcs Must Die is a little known gem. The metacritic score is high, but nobody really talks about it. Some of the Steam achievements require mass grinding though, which is a little annoying. 9/10

XCOM: Enemy Unknown, where to begin?
This game is the game I never knew that I wanted. It's a perfect blend of a strategy simulator, mixed with a tatical RPG.
In this game you play as the commander of an elite taskforce known as XCOM. XCOM was created in response to the alien threat, and only your team is equipped to handle these things.
The game has two distinct phases of play. The first phase is the strategy simulator, in which you build your base, monitor alien attacks, research new things, build new items for your troops to use, and customize your troops.
The second phase is where you put to use all the upgrades and modified troops and it becomes a tactical RPG, in which you play a deadly game of cat and mouse with a (up to) 6 man squad exterminating the alien threat in a variety of maps and missions. Some you just go in and kill everything, others you have to save civilians, and some you even have to capture some of the very same aliens who are trying to kill you in order to perform more research.
The two phases work in complete harmony with one another, if you do bad in one phase, you'll do bad in the other, and vise versa.
Some of the biggest highlights of the game come from customizing your troops. As they participate in battle and kill aliens, they will go up in rank and earn new skills (the 4 categories that your troops can become are: Heavy, Support, Sniper, and Assault). But along with earning new skills you can also customize each individual soldiers facial features and even change their name and give them nicknames. This whole level of customization that the game offers makes it just that much more personal. Try going in with a soldier named after your brother, who you've leveled up to the final rank, just to watch him die in front of you, it's heart wrenching. That's another thing, death in this game is permanent, so permanent in fact that you can go to the barracks and view the wall of fallen soldiers.
This game will test you in no way a video game has before. It will teach you one way or another to plan out all your moves and be careful with your troops, because once they die, they won't come back. XCOM is unforgiving and rewarding all at the same time, and worth every penny and every minute of your time.

RUSH is a 3D indie puzzle game by
. It's their second Windows release after the successful Toki Tori. In RUSH, the player needs to guide colored cubes to the appropriate exit points. This happens by using items that are unlocked through the progress of the game, such as Conveyor belts, Warps and more. The player places the items in advance and needs to imagine how they will affect the cubes' process through the level.
I don't have much to say against this game, just one suggestion: a level editor would be great. After completing this game once, I have nothing more to do and there's no motivation for me to play it anymore. If there was an option to download community-created levels (for example through the Steam Workshop) and designing own levels, it would definitely raise the replay potential for me and probably many other players.
Other than that, this game has great, tricky levels, for those who want a challenge, or if you want to set your mind at ease or are just stuck at one level for a while, there's a hint system that makes your life easier. The environment looks neat and clean, which contributes to the game's calming and relaxing feel along with a chill music and simple drag and drop controls. Everything about this game says "No rush." (such irony). On a gameplay level, I like the idea of the game, it's really simple but they did a good job implementing it, the levels have interesting and creative patterns, the items used to control the cubes are decent.
Overall I'd recommend this game if you're a puzzle game fanatic or if you just want a calming game to free your mind. If you're none of these two, you might not have as much fun with the game as I did, but it's worth a try.

Space/Sci-Fi rogue-like RPG. If you're not familiar with "rogue-like", it means there's no save feature to speak of. If/when you die (or in this case, your ship's crew dies) then you have to start over. The story is fairly simple, but the possible negative outcomes make every choice a bit more nerve wracking. You can play through the story in about 2 hours. Less if you don't read any of the text. But the variety of aliens (both on your crew and the enemies you fight), the way you spend "scrap" to upgrade your systems, the different equipment modules, and unlockable ship types all with primary and secondary variants give it a lot of replayability even after you finally beat it. You'll pretty much never have 2 play throughs go exactly the same way. Simple but clean 2d graphics. It relies more on its depth of gameplay more than any bells and whistles to keep you engaged and entertained. All in all an excellent diversion when you want something less action based and requiring a little more thought than most other games these days. *On a side note, they're releasing an updated version sometime in 2014 to everyone who has already purchased the game. And while not officially supported there are mods which you can find links to from the official website's forums.

The Definition of Repetitive
Knights of Pen & Paper has a nice theme going for it.  You are a bunch of people sitting down for a game of D&D.  Unfortunately, you have a terrible DM who fills the game with references and memes and little else.  It makes the story not only irrelevant, but obnoxious.  As an example, Nabe Gewell tasks you to get a crowbar because reasons.
Moving into how the game plays, you start off being able to select a few characters and classes for you to control; more get unlocked later in the game.  Each character has their own ability and every class gets four abilities, some active, some passive.  You only get one free character to make but you can spend gold to get the full party of five.  It is recommended you do this as soon as possible since you always start at level 1, forcing a grind for them to catch up since they will easily die and dead characters gain no experience.
This is where the whole repetition comes into play.  You go to an area around your level (moving areas involves clicking the area; that is it), select how many and what monsters to fight and go at it.  There are quests to complete but they are almost all kill X things or collect X things from monsters.  The rest are escorts that force a battle on every move you make, even if you vastly outlevel the area.  This is what you spend the entire game doing, even for the main quest.
Good combat could have salvaged this but it is very basic.  Everyone gets a turn order slightly modified by your initiative and you end up spamming one ability per character until victory.  It is barely above the original Dragon Quest in how things operate.
Even after all this, there are further glitches and issues the game has.  The quests all have levels so you can tell when they should be done, except there are several that require you kill things greatly higher than the quest level suggests.  Sometimes the quest level will even jump mid-quests, forcing you to abandon it and redo the parts you already did later.  I had level 6 quests task me going into a level 20 area as well as a level 40 area.
While minor, even leveling up your own skills are slightly glitched.  I noticed several times where the game claimed leveling up a skill would give it four damage only for it to get three.  It gets even worse any time decimals are used where the game seems to forget about them in later skill ups.
Knights of Pen & Paper had potential but it was ruined with its tedium and nonsense.

First things first, this game does not compansate for the hype it created. Consider this while reading my review.
During first few missions you will feel like you are playing Dead Island. In fact, fighting mechanics feels like it until you reach a certain point in Power Tier. Then it becomes more and more interesting.
What makes it more different from Dead Island Series is not only more advanced graphics and night-time gameplay but also the aspect of free-running (parkour). There is almost nowhere that you cannot jump to, climb to or run to. Moreover, there is an Agility Tier where you can improve your character's parkour abilities.
Regarding story, I can easily say that there was just a few moments that shocked me. Other than that, the story is quite linear and uninteresting. However, there are two major maps and one minor map which have lots of points of interest and things to explore. Side quests are not very varied and mostly consist of "go there, get that, bring back" missions. All these combined, if you do not rush finishing the game, you can play it for a long time.
Weapons and tools have a good variety and combinations but when you figure out which combinations make the best weapons and which tools are best to use, you will keep sticking to the same weapons and tools setup throughout the game. Ranged weapons, however, are just a few rifles and pistols and useless against zombies.
Night-time play is so much fun if you happen to lay your hands on a very good weapon. You can try to fight volatiles which is quite a challenge. If you like a bit of scare, try out exploring Harran at nighttime.
Multiplayer, in my opinion, sucks. Co-op is quite a nice option but if other players are not near you, you cannot progress quests, which is quite a problem. A player joined my early game and gave me an overpowered end-game weapon. It broke near the end of the game, so I was able to use it most of the time. Be the Zombie Mode and Invasions also suck. I had to turn off invasions because my quests were so often interrupted and that becomes a pain-in-the-bum after a while.
Unfortunately, there is not a really interesting or worthy DLC available at the moment. Bozak Horde is a major DLC and feels like "oh yes a stryline" but it turns out to be an extremely difficult series of challenges you do as a puppet of a madman. It merely seems like a storyline and almost impossible to beat solo.
As a result, if you like "parkour style, beat the sheet out of zombies with a lot of melee weapons and tools" game, go for it but I strongly suggest waiting for a %75+ discount, though.
Edit from Heavens: With latest updates, Devs show that they still care. Hope they keep caring this gem.

Grim Dawn is among the best ARPG games around and at currently 14 bucks cheap as hell. It has long been in the making, but it was definitely worth the wait. The Devs have continously listened to the community and made good decisions on how to design the game.
Despite not having random maps as other ARPGs out there, the game yet offers endless replayability by giving the user the possibility to combine two classes with distinct set of skills to create a completely new character that plays very differently from the ones you had before.
Also item drop rates are very rewarding as well as an abundant amount of usable loot that you can use to equip your characters. In many ARPG games, end game characters very often used the same gear all around and if you do not have a specific part of equipment you are basically doomed. Not so in Grim Dawn: Playing self-found only can work for many kinds of possible character builds quite smoothly. I even managed to find complete sets in this game, a feat I have not managed to accomplish in other games of this kind.
The overall world and story is exciting and consistent. There is a lot of lore and other background information to be found. Travel ways are short and a town portal function is available. The game mechanics are logical and well documented in the game. The interface is easy to use and does not force the user to exuberant micro management. And lastly, the guys at the official forum are very nice and helpful if you have any kind of question.
So, I'm approaching 200 in-game hours in Grim Dawn which is a lot more time than I have ever put into a game in recent years. Highly recommended!

It might be easy to dismiss OMD! as a FPS/tower defence variant reliant on its tongue-in-cheek humour and simple gameplay to appeal. While these are two of its key strengths, there is far more to OMD! however; it has very well designed levels, plenty of weapon choices and types of enamy, as well as many different potential styles of play. Nightmare difficulty (available after the campaign has been completed) requires particular dexterity and speed of thought and adds further longevity to the mix. All that said, the real reason this game is recommended by so many people is that killing the titular orcs is immensely good fun. Eviscerating an orc wondering whether its parking has been validated as its friend explodes a day before it is due for retirement (the back stories courtesy of the grumbles the orcs utter as they amble towards you) frankly never gets old. Having just completed Nightmare with over thirty thousand kills to my name, I can safely say I would happily sign up to melt, crush, shoot, detonate, squash, burn and generally mangle the little gits all over again. Given this was released in 2011 it comes on sale quite often and is definitely worth a go.

Note that I write this review after i get the 100% completion, so the game is around 33.5 hours.
Knight of Pen and Paper is actually just a role playing game. By "role playing game", i didn't mean those RPG games when you fight monsters and explore lots of places. By "role playing game", I meant the more traditional RPG, when you act as a character, imagining that you are in a different place, and do whatever you want. There are battles, of course, as it's crucial to this game.
The first thing from this game that catches my eye is the art. I am a fond of pixel graphics games, and this one satisfy me. The pixels are made in a great detail. All of the assets are great looking, and the most important thing, there is no "recolored" monster at all (or i just didn't notice it), and fyi, there are tons of area to explore in this game, with different environments and monsters in most area. The music itself accompanies so well with the art, and i am never bored to listen it for long.
There are tons of characters that you can choose, and tons of classes to play with, creating a party for up to 5 people, Each character has their own advantages, and each class has their own roles (dps, support, healer, tanker). You can costumize each class to your own preference because their skills can be raised with skill point which is gained every level ups. Because of this, choosing your party member can be crucial, because you can finish the game quickly or slowly depends on your setup. Also, some classes and characters need to be unlocked first, which limits your choice even more on your first playthrough. If you want to do a 100% completion, i advise you to make multiple saves, because the gold carries on each save. You can have up to 3 save slots, and although the gold is carried between saves, the accessories, equipments and levels are not.
As for the battles, it's quite easy on the first part, and it becomes tougher and longer later on. You might need to grind a little or a lot depends on your setup, so make sure you get it right. Accessories also matters, because you can boost your characters quite well if you choose the right one. You can't really choose your equipments, but you can upgrade it with a success chance (well, don't worry because you can boost the chance to 100% if you have the money).
Pros:
- Tons of characters
- Tons of classes
- Tons of battles
- Almost none random encounters; you can set up your own battle
- Tons of maps
- Tons of stories and quests
Cons:
- Long battles
- Tons of grinding
Should you buy this game?
If you love to grind and doesn't mind with the long battles, buy it.
If you don't, then don't because it can be frustating.

The settings themselves are rather basic, but that is passable in this case due to the basic nature of the game.  Despite being basic, this game WILL kick your bum time and time again if you are a casual player.  It is because of this that I recommend the game only to cautionary players who are aware of it's potential difficulty.  It is one game which is hard but in fair ways, so pros at games like Dark Souls may not be phased, but normal players can expect a challenging game with much to find and more awaiting for those patient enough to wait for each update.
*****That said, THIS GAME IS INCOMPLETE and therefore I advise extreme hesitation as you may not get your money's worth if the project fails.

Update [Spoiler Alert... Skip to Early Access section to avoid]: I beat the game in speedrun mode, took over two hours straight for me to do. I was behind in the race I was doing at first, but I quickly took a lead in the earlygame as I went through all the levels I knew beforehand in a flash, giving be this big star lead over my friend.  But when I finally did get to the home stretch, my friend took the lead and ended up getting to the asteroid before me. I managed to catch up within 10-20 minutes, and I actually found the path before him, but I gave up on the path as I assumed it was the wrong one... Then he ended up just telling me because we were both taking so long on the level.  We both took a snack break, pausing our games at the same time, and after we continued, I lost.  I kept going though, as I wanted to see how long it would take me to finish my run.  Yeah... I actually liked the experience, but the fact that a single mistake would cost me anywhere between fifteen seconds and nearly a minute really added up.  (Anyone else just kept jumping into spikes? I know I did. Alot.)  I'll be playing through the regular mode 100% before I modify this to be a full review.
Before we go to early access section, just remember this.  IF YOU GET THIS GAME, IT WILL BE TOUGH.
[Below was in Early Access, before the first boss was moved and some modifications to levels were made.]
Jump! Dash! Jump! Dash! Die! Repeat until level is complete!
Yes, this is a 2D classic-style platformer with a lot of hidden references.  I'll warn you this, it gives you infinite jumps.  Now you may think that's overpowered, but remember, the obstacles get pretty hard, and your afterburners are your only way of dealing damage other than ramming your head into some of the enemies.  One hit and you die.
This game is EASILY speedrunner friendly, and unique.  Heck, they even let you test out the controls on the title screen!  I love it when games let me do that.  Gives me a convenient way to warm-up pre-run.
You can customize the T-Rex you play as. (Spoiler alert: Mine already has a Megaman helmet!)  From colors, heads/helmets, boots, heck even to your boots' trails, it's all customizable.  The shop mixes up every 15 minutes of playtime after you leave the Dinonaut Base, so be ready to rush to the store and check it out if you have 2000 coins or so already!  (This timer includes time used resetting the level, from what I can tell, only time spent in the shop seems to not count.)
The difficulty? Oh, yeah, it's quite unforgiving, but only if you want that no death star...  Otherwise you respawn at checkpoints... UNLESS you play on the harder mode--it even has rage quit in its name... Listen, that mode gives you 3 lives and no checkpoints for the ENTIRE game if I understand it correctly.  I've only played up to the first boss so far, though, so I don't know exactly how hard it'll get.
From what I can tell, it gives you 3 singleplayer save files, so you atleast don't have to delete all progress files every time you restart the game.  Not sure if the files are seperate in Coop or not yet.  The controls are VERY accurate.  Once you input a control, it feels basically instant responses, atleast with the Xbox 360 Controller that I was using.  Oh yeah, did I mention?  It supports controllers directly!
The soundtrack is excellent, infact if the soundtrack doesn't come with the game, I'll probably go ahead and pick up the soundtrack if it's cheap enough.  It's not often that I actually listen to the game's music/sounds if I'm not streaming my run, excluding certain games of course...  But this game easily passes to a point where I'll probably barely ever not listen to it.  Infact, this is probably one of the first platformers to make it on that list of mine.
You can directly challenge the WR IL times if you wish, thus if you just want to try to hit a IL record, you can easily get ready to do so through that.  You also can challenge your PB--infact it does so on its own if you already have beaten the stage before apparently.  It took approximately 1.2 hours for me to get through the first set of levels and the first boss in total, if you include trying to get the 3 stars in most of the levels and the time spent shopping/adjusting to the controls. (Which I got in all of them except the boss!)

text:
XCOM: Enemy Unknown, a game that I have a good time playing so here is everything to know about the game.
Story:
The year is 2015, and it starts off with an alien pod being dropped onto the Earth's surface. The pod obviously attracts attention of the people in the area, and soon, the people around the pod die. In response to this, the world leaders have started what they call "The XCOM Project." You have been chosen to be humanities last hope.
Gameplay:
The game is an RTS (Real Time Strategy for those who don't know). The tutorial explains pretty much everything you need to know about the game. Now let me be clear about this, THIS GAME WILL NOT HOLD YOUR HANDS THROUGH IT. You also can have up to 99 soldiers that you can edit to your hearts content. You will be forced to make decisions on who to help as you can only help one country at a time, so the country you help, panic will go down, but for the countries you don't help, panic will increase. There are a few different types of mission types but I shall only go through a few. The first one is where if you manage to shoot down a ufo, you can send troops (up to a maximum of 6) to attack the crash and eliminate the surviving aliens. The next mission type is where you have to go into a city that is being terrorized by the aliens and have to go in and rescue the civillians. And the third mission type I will explain is where the aliens plant a bomb and you have to go in and defuse it. There are many mission types for you to do, but you never get to pick which it will be. Enviorments always change so you can never give yourself an advantage of knowing the area. And there is also PERMA-DEATH. Thats right, you get one of your troops killed, and thats it for them, but there is a small chance of them becoming critically wounded. And now for what will be in the base. There is researching and  autopsies. Those should not need explanations. And then there is the foundry, pretty obvious what you can do in there isn't it?
Controls:
The game controls are smooth to say the least. Your mouse is all you really need but there are hotkeys if you fancy them.
Video & Audio:
This game has some of the best cutscenes and audio clips I have ever seen and heard from in any video game. Even on the lowest quality you put it on, the game still looks beautiful. Does video need to be explained further? Now for sound, there are no sound cut-outs which is always good.
Misc.:
The game does happen to take up a lot of space so if you want this game, you will want to make sure your computer can hold all of its data. Your soldiers will go a bit crazy for one turn if they witness a soldier dying, so that's another reason to keep your men and women alive. No bugs that I have seen so there is another plus. I can't really think of anything negative to type about this game.
Final Verdict: 10/10 with Angry Joe's Badass seal of approval.

I bought this game in June of 2014, gave it a quick 20 minute try to see if I would enjoy it. I liked what I saw then but I knew the game wasn't complete. So I waited for it to be completed. And sure enough, slightly close to two year later and the game is content complete. I decided to give it a try and have loved nearly everything in it.
Let's start the actual review.
Story:
The story is interesting to say the least. Some big apocalypse happened and a multitude and ♥♥♥♥♥torms sprung up from it. Through quests and lore tidbits you can pick up and read, you find out the various aspects of how hard the♥♥♥♥♥♥hit the fan for different areas. The factions you'll meet have interesting lore behind them and collide with each other in interesting ways.
Music:
The most defining aspect for music for me is that I want to actually keep it on, instead of just turning on my own playlist to listen to. For this game, they nailed it perfectly. Ranging from area clips that feel just right, to returning to your hub world of Devil's Crossing and hearing that soft music kick in. The soundtrack feels great and I love it.
Combat:
Now, I've given every singular class a try, haven't yet had a chance to try them all crossed but I've done a handful of them crossed and I must say, combat feels great. The early game is a cake walk, you smash through enemies like they're cardboard and it left me feeling a bit underwhelmed at first. Until I reached more irregular units and finally heroes. The basic enemies mostly serve to flood you, while irregulars do the heavy damage. I have to say, my first boss fight I died quite quickly and was surprised. Late game though, I can tell the difficulty has jumped and I like it, with my main character, a Sorcerer (Demolitionist+Arcanist) I have to often run and gun as I fight hordes of what have you.
Classes:
Mentioning them in my last sentence brings up the important aspect, your classes. So you have six options available to you. Soldier, Demolitionist, Occultist, Arcanist, Nightblade, and Shaman. Soldier is your classic tank. Demo is a mixed ranged/magic. Occultist is your summoner/curse dealer. Arcanist is your straight up mage. Nightblade is your sneaky stabby guy. And Shaman is a damage dealing tank. Now what gets interesting is, at the beginning you make your character and you start at Lv. 1 as nothing. One you hit 2, you choose your class. And then at Lv. 10, you have the option to choose a dual class. Every class can mix with another, the only limit being you can't mix same classes. No Soldier+Soldier+Uber Soldier silly crap in here. The name changes are purely for flavor, Arcanist+Demo=Sorcerer is just a name change, you still retain those two seperate classes and level them together.
Devotion:
Ok I'll be honest, the Devotion system confused the hell out of me at first. Scattered around the world are these shrines that you can restore. That's the easy part, do what you need to restore it and you're rewarded with a Devotion point. Looking a the Devotion page, you're confronted with a page of constellations, starting with the 5 pointed crossroad. From there you choose your direction and upon actually reading different constellations it becomes clear. The constellations each have stars in them, each star is bought with a single devotion point. You start with the crossroad, for example maybe you start with the Eldritch crossroad and from there move to I believe the Fox constellation which gives permanent buffs to your Cunning. Take my word for it, it becomes a lot more clear once you take a moment and read it.
Overall:
This game was a surprise to me, I wasn't sure whether or not I was going to fully enjoy it or not. Once it went content complete I decided to give it a try and was surprised when I realized that 10 hours had passed by. I was even more surprised to find out I was still in Act 1 of the 4 acts, this game has so much to offer and I can't wait to fully explore all of it.
This game is a solid 9.5/10 and for it to reach that 10/10 for me, I feel like it could use some balance in the beginning, make your character less strong so that you're not smashing through everything to easily.

Glorious ARPG knigts of yesteryear have returned to form Crate Entertainment and laid waste to the competition with their first game. Grim Dawn is "built" on the same engine as Titans Quest so this game feels right at home to anyone who has laid hands on that gem of a game. The graphics have been improved over Titian's Quest too. Add in good physics and ragdolls, particle effects and post processing, all add to the modern look on an  older but solid game engine. Even though the game hasnt officially released yet, the optimization of the engine is better than most games who are years into their full release. The content is amazing so far. Even though the enviroments are NOT randomly generated, something I thought would really effect my enjoyment of the game, so far, I cannot imagine a time I wont want to replay this game. The depth and scale of even the earliest of areas makes Diablo 3 timidily pee itself in the corner while I drool at Grim's amazingly sexy climes. Loot is ample and extremely interesting. Lots to explore when leveling up too. Multiple paths, skills and even more customization from the Devotion system, which you gain points from finding hidden shrines throughout the game. As if you weren't already starting to go "wha?", there is also dual class system. Similar to the way they handled things with Titan's Quest, once you reach a certain level with your first class, you get to choose another. Now, when you level, you have to choose even more carefully where you want your precious skill points to go. On top of all that, you are also give Stat points too, so you can break you characters in so many ways, it's rediculous and I'm giddy as a schoolgirl about it. No hand holdy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t here folks. They have ample guides and helpful tip in the game. Read them if you don't know. But don't get mad if you don't and your character is gettting ♥♥♥♥ing owned at higher levels. I don't want to go on a huge long spiel about how much I love this game. Been watching it's progress and lurking in the  comments for a long time. I had very high hopes as it forged it's way along the Early Access path. When it emerged as content complete I knew it was time. I have not been disappointed. Five Star quality from an 10 man dev team (smaller than that for most of its development), you can't beat the value you will get from this game, even if you bought it at full price. Can't wait to see what they add to it and support it going forward, as even though they announced it's content complete, the game is still in early access for the time being so they can continue to polish assets and gameplay balance. The time is now my friends, get this game before you're sad that you missed out.

The atmosphere of The Banner Saga is incredible. It's oppressive and depressing, and helps you become part of your party as they desperately seek solace in a world that is slowly ending - being consumed by an ancient darkness.
Gameplay is split between turn-based strategy with an interesting Armor/Strength dynamic that will effect your approach and strategy to every situation, and overworld politics and diplomacy as you try to lead your party, maintain provisions, determine the speed at which you travel, and help (or abandon) passersby.
The Banner Saga is a slowly paced game, and I mean that in the best possible way. It gives you time to absorb the world, and hammers in the weight of the decisions you have to make for the caravan and your allies. And these decisions matter. Critical characters can live and die based on the decisions you make, and there is no auto-saving to get them back. Choices are gray at best, and it's solely up to you, the player, to decide what you feel will best serve the caravan.
Visually, it is beautiful, with smooth gradients of color behind swathes of silhouetted foreground, and a fitting soundtrack for you slow trek through the end of the world.
Highly recommended for anyone looking for a story-driven game or a different take on turn-based strategy. The Banner Saga is oppressive, overwhelming, and exhausting. And it's incredible for it.

Space/Sci-Fi rogue-like RPG. If you're not familiar with "rogue-like", it means there's no save feature to speak of. If/when you die (or in this case, your ship's crew dies) then you have to start over. The story is fairly simple, but the possible negative outcomes make every choice a bit more nerve wracking. You can play through the story in about 2 hours. Less if you don't read any of the text. But the variety of aliens (both on your crew and the enemies you fight), the way you spend "scrap" to upgrade your systems, the different equipment modules, and unlockable ship types all with primary and secondary variants give it a lot of replayability even after you finally beat it. You'll pretty much never have 2 play throughs go exactly the same way. Simple but clean 2d graphics. It relies more on its depth of gameplay more than any bells and whistles to keep you engaged and entertained. All in all an excellent diversion when you want something less action based and requiring a little more thought than most other games these days. *On a side note, they're releasing an updated version sometime in 2014 to everyone who has already purchased the game. And while not officially supported there are mods which you can find links to from the official website's forums.

An excellent turn-based strategy game.
Visually, it is a beautiful game. The art style fits well, and the animations are well done. The "animated painting"-style backgrounds add lots of subtle detail that really shows the team put a lot of effort and thought into the visuals.
What audio there is is excellent. I realize that voiceover work is expensive and time-consuming, and that this was funded through Kickstarter, so it's understandable that it's not there in the final product. Would have been nice if it had been possible.
The gameplay doesn't stray particularly far from the traditional turn-based strategy standards. Most gameplay elements are intuitive, though I personally would prefer on-hover tooltips in addition to the help menu system as they have implemented it the game. The game is difficult, and would be especially so for players who aren't as familiar with turn-based strategy games, but not overwhelming, and I never got the sense that I was constantly losing outside of the very early stages of the game. The gameplay itself had a sense of progress in terms of how good I felt at the game.
The setting is intriguing, and it shows the developers were planning ahead for further games set in this universe, as there is much left unexplored and unexplained. The story itself usually resists the urges of the usual fantasy tropes--especially when it comes to the portrayal of women, and really comes across as a mature endeavor.
Overall, I would recommend this game. Visually, it is a work of art, and gameplay-wise, it is a challenging, but not frustrating. The story is deep and engaging.

Best MMORPG of all time, but if you haven't played it by now it is likely too late as the game might be hard to get into since it is so old now and has low population and old control mechanics that are hard to adapt to.
They just don't make MMOs like this anymore. MMOs where the game was about exploring new locations, the lore, and slow steady progression. MMOs today are just hubs littered with thousands of mind numbing quests to level 1-Max in a month, grouping not required. MMOs today are about getting to end game and raiding endlessly. EQ had its fair share of raiding, but when I think of EverQuest that is not the part that I think of. My initial character that took a long time to level up (probably a year to get max level) and slowly progressed from zone to zone and the different people I met along the way that I grouped with is what I remember most. No other MMO has had a similar experience since because they just go by too fast and too easy to get people to the end game, and with instance queues (usually multi-server) there just isn't any sense of server community in current MMOs.
At the end game EQ was similar to what we know today in MMOs, nothing that special, with the primary difference being competition over spawns since there were no instances. This was fun and not fun at the same time. It formed different guild rivalries if we stole a spawn or they did, but sometimes you would have to change plans due to not being at the right place at the right time. The more proactive your guild was in monitoring spawns and mobilizing quickly and efficiently the greater chance that your guild would be the strongest on the server. It was a different mechanic than current MMO raids, but ultimately that isn't where EverQuest shined to me.
The EQ lore is what kept me playing. The locations and the story lines were there, but you had to find them, they weren't laid out for you with giant exclamation points. EQ has some of the best zones in any MMO I've played and I would recommend playing it today just to get a chance to experience certain zones and dungeons, but again this game will be hard to pick up at this point with its age.
There are still people that play the game, but they're all at end game raiding. I would recommend this game still today as a single player experience to just experience some of the zones and game lore, but it would be hard to recommend it to play end game with all the catching up that would be required.
A new EverQuest comes out in 2015 (probably) called EverQuest Next so be on the lookout for that one, it looks to be doing some really great things in the MMORPG genre..
