At first glance Orcs Must Die! looks like a Tower Defense game. In reality if you rely solely on towers to kill enemies you will lose very quickly. It's more of a hybrid Over-the-shoulder 3rd person action and Tower Defense game. Yes, increasingly difficult mobs lumber brainlessly toward an exit, but they may also try to kill you directly. Around half of your kills will come your main character using his trusty crossbow and spells than by the towers themselves.
This is generally a good thing but if you're looking for a pure Tower Defense game this isn't it. It does however keep the action fast as you sprint around each level where you need to help bolster defenses on various ends of the map. You can't just "set it and forget it" for most levels.
While the different traps are fun, they generally come in 3 flavors: Single use (the worst, dead after one trigger), episodic worse (deals damage and then cools down), and constant (best, constant damage to all enemies that traverse it). As later levels and difficulties feature tougher and more numerous monsters, you will have no choice but to use traps that deal constant damage, of which there are a limited amount. This makes many of the more entertaining and flavorful traps pushed to way side. There are at least 3 traps I never used.
Regardless the game is still fun. Planning how to handle each wave and setting up a circuitous kill zone is extremely satisfying. The whimsical art style and humorous protagonist also helps things immensely. There's tons of replayability with multiple levels, 3 difficulty settings, and a decent expanion pack to boot. Well worth the sale price.

JJR is flippin' hard, but flippin' rad. Seriously. Think old school 8-bit intense gameplay paired with speedrunning and avoiding life-ending obstacles. There's also boss fights like Mega Man and you gotta use your dino-jetpack to fight them.
Levels? It's got a whole bunch. Each level has certain objectives (finish without dying, complete under a certain time frame, etc.) and you earn stars as you complete them. Earn enough stars, you unlock more levels and bosses and progress through the game. Don't fret though, you've got as many tries as you'd like to complete the levels, theres no "game over" waiting if you're not quick enough. But for real, be prepared to be frustrated on certain levels. Sometimes you'll repeatedly make the same mistake of boosting into a laser beam....and yeah, you'll get annoyed. But it's still fun!
The variety of level design keeps the game fresh as you play on and the cleverness of being a little dinosaur keeps it fun. If you collect enough coins while playing, you can buy aesthetic upgrades to change the appearance of your character and customize it to your liking.
So could I keep talking about the game? Sure. But ultimately you should really give it a shot and see how you like it. If you're at all interested in games that challenge your skills in a fun speed-run/platformer way then I think you'll like this game a lot. 8/10 (needs more dinosuars)

As an avid platforming fan, I am often very cynical/analytical when it comes to playing new ones. I'm stuck in the past, rarely do I find a platformer that I feel can stand up to the SNES era.
JumpJet Rex though, took me totally by surprise. I didn't expect to fall so hard and fast for this game.
I always look for specific things in a platformer, a formula for perfection if you might:
Difficulty - Is the game challenging? Will it make me shout profanities but still make me eager to go back for more? Check. JumpJet Rex is no easy ride, though the difficulty curve put in place is sublime. Not too fast, not too slow, excellent pacing.
Controls - I can get really wound up about clunky controls in platformers. There is a certain "feel" that needs to be reached. I have no qualms about the controls for JJR, very reponsive, reactive and creative.
Replayability - Will I feel like playing through the levels again? Will I get attached to the world the developers present to me? JJR hits this mark splendidly. Not only can you complete the levels, there are plenty of collectables in place. You are graded on each level out of 3 stars. Completion, not dying and time. You need a certain amount of stars to prgress onto further levels, so you will find yourself revisiting levels, and I wa absolutely glad to every time!
Appearance - Is the game easy on the eyes? How is the level design? Seriously, JJR is one of the most beautiful modern platformers I have played. The graphics are fun, edgy and cute. You can also customise your little dino, LOADS of options available. You can buy customisation items from a store, with currency you earn IN-GAME, or find them hidden within levels.
Boss Fights - Will the boss actually challenge me? Will I feel the rage build up as I am slaughtered over and over again and feel like a champion when I overcome them? JJR delivers this. The bosses require you to figure them out. There is zero hand-holding.
Music - Will the music match the theme of the game? Will the music egg me on as I play through? JJR again, passes with flying colours. I usually game with my own music, but for JJR I absolutely love the soundtrack, it gets the heart pumping! Beautiful.
In summary, I can't reccomend this game enough to anyone, epecially if you enjoy platforming! Seriously, it's a little dinosaur with jet-pack shoes. Buy it, you wont be dissapointed.
Yours sincerely, an absolute platforming snob. Hahaha

I bought this game in June of 2014, gave it a quick 20 minute try to see if I would enjoy it. I liked what I saw then but I knew the game wasn't complete. So I waited for it to be completed. And sure enough, slightly close to two year later and the game is content complete. I decided to give it a try and have loved nearly everything in it.
Let's start the actual review.
Story:
The story is interesting to say the least. Some big apocalypse happened and a multitude and ♥♥♥♥♥torms sprung up from it. Through quests and lore tidbits you can pick up and read, you find out the various aspects of how hard the♥♥♥♥♥♥hit the fan for different areas. The factions you'll meet have interesting lore behind them and collide with each other in interesting ways.
Music:
The most defining aspect for music for me is that I want to actually keep it on, instead of just turning on my own playlist to listen to. For this game, they nailed it perfectly. Ranging from area clips that feel just right, to returning to your hub world of Devil's Crossing and hearing that soft music kick in. The soundtrack feels great and I love it.
Combat:
Now, I've given every singular class a try, haven't yet had a chance to try them all crossed but I've done a handful of them crossed and I must say, combat feels great. The early game is a cake walk, you smash through enemies like they're cardboard and it left me feeling a bit underwhelmed at first. Until I reached more irregular units and finally heroes. The basic enemies mostly serve to flood you, while irregulars do the heavy damage. I have to say, my first boss fight I died quite quickly and was surprised. Late game though, I can tell the difficulty has jumped and I like it, with my main character, a Sorcerer (Demolitionist+Arcanist) I have to often run and gun as I fight hordes of what have you.
Classes:
Mentioning them in my last sentence brings up the important aspect, your classes. So you have six options available to you. Soldier, Demolitionist, Occultist, Arcanist, Nightblade, and Shaman. Soldier is your classic tank. Demo is a mixed ranged/magic. Occultist is your summoner/curse dealer. Arcanist is your straight up mage. Nightblade is your sneaky stabby guy. And Shaman is a damage dealing tank. Now what gets interesting is, at the beginning you make your character and you start at Lv. 1 as nothing. One you hit 2, you choose your class. And then at Lv. 10, you have the option to choose a dual class. Every class can mix with another, the only limit being you can't mix same classes. No Soldier+Soldier+Uber Soldier silly crap in here. The name changes are purely for flavor, Arcanist+Demo=Sorcerer is just a name change, you still retain those two seperate classes and level them together.
Devotion:
Ok I'll be honest, the Devotion system confused the hell out of me at first. Scattered around the world are these shrines that you can restore. That's the easy part, do what you need to restore it and you're rewarded with a Devotion point. Looking a the Devotion page, you're confronted with a page of constellations, starting with the 5 pointed crossroad. From there you choose your direction and upon actually reading different constellations it becomes clear. The constellations each have stars in them, each star is bought with a single devotion point. You start with the crossroad, for example maybe you start with the Eldritch crossroad and from there move to I believe the Fox constellation which gives permanent buffs to your Cunning. Take my word for it, it becomes a lot more clear once you take a moment and read it.
Overall:
This game was a surprise to me, I wasn't sure whether or not I was going to fully enjoy it or not. Once it went content complete I decided to give it a try and was surprised when I realized that 10 hours had passed by. I was even more surprised to find out I was still in Act 1 of the 4 acts, this game has so much to offer and I can't wait to fully explore all of it.
This game is a solid 9.5/10 and for it to reach that 10/10 for me, I feel like it could use some balance in the beginning, make your character less strong so that you're not smashing through everything to easily.

This game is intense and incredible. I'll admit, I save-scummed to get through it on medium difficulty (I really like my superteams and impregnable fortresses). Still, the game's emphasis on hard tactics and choices against tough odds makes you feel like you're in the best urban warfare story ever, with hostile aliens. My friend and I tried this game on a hard setting without save-scumming, and couldn't even pass the first mission! Dayum!
Many people say the combat is "fair", and I agree. Being a game, you get to play it again if you fail, and going through successful and failed missions is the only way to learn what works and what doesn't. The occasional impossible shot the aliens make on you is balanced out by the awesome sniper/grenade vengeance that you can dish out to them.
I started imagining "percentage-of-success" signs over everyone's heads for a day after I finished this game. Like when I was asking someone out, or going for an interview. Sometimes you just have to take the shot and hope for the best, but it helps if you know your terrain and your options.
Update: Enemy Within DLC makes this game even more awesome. The MEC troopers and Gene Mods add tremendous variety and replay value. They are expensive in more ways than one (casualties from fast play due to the Meld timer, money, training time), which balances out their distinct advantages. The EXALT enemy and additional story missions also add interesting new challenges. The overall effect is to make this a significantly longer and more complex game, which is a good thing.

Glorious ARPG knigts of yesteryear have returned to form Crate Entertainment and laid waste to the competition with their first game. Grim Dawn is "built" on the same engine as Titans Quest so this game feels right at home to anyone who has laid hands on that gem of a game. The graphics have been improved over Titian's Quest too. Add in good physics and ragdolls, particle effects and post processing, all add to the modern look on an  older but solid game engine. Even though the game hasnt officially released yet, the optimization of the engine is better than most games who are years into their full release. The content is amazing so far. Even though the enviroments are NOT randomly generated, something I thought would really effect my enjoyment of the game, so far, I cannot imagine a time I wont want to replay this game. The depth and scale of even the earliest of areas makes Diablo 3 timidily pee itself in the corner while I drool at Grim's amazingly sexy climes. Loot is ample and extremely interesting. Lots to explore when leveling up too. Multiple paths, skills and even more customization from the Devotion system, which you gain points from finding hidden shrines throughout the game. As if you weren't already starting to go "wha?", there is also dual class system. Similar to the way they handled things with Titan's Quest, once you reach a certain level with your first class, you get to choose another. Now, when you level, you have to choose even more carefully where you want your precious skill points to go. On top of all that, you are also give Stat points too, so you can break you characters in so many ways, it's rediculous and I'm giddy as a schoolgirl about it. No hand holdy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t here folks. They have ample guides and helpful tip in the game. Read them if you don't know. But don't get mad if you don't and your character is gettting ♥♥♥♥ing owned at higher levels. I don't want to go on a huge long spiel about how much I love this game. Been watching it's progress and lurking in the  comments for a long time. I had very high hopes as it forged it's way along the Early Access path. When it emerged as content complete I knew it was time. I have not been disappointed. Five Star quality from an 10 man dev team (smaller than that for most of its development), you can't beat the value you will get from this game, even if you bought it at full price. Can't wait to see what they add to it and support it going forward, as even though they announced it's content complete, the game is still in early access for the time being so they can continue to polish assets and gameplay balance. The time is now my friends, get this game before you're sad that you missed out.

XCOM Enemy Unknown is best described as a smaller scale, futuristic,and right-to-the-action version of Firaxis' another excellent turn based game, Civilization series.
Does it make it a bad game? No, far from it, it's so damn addicting and awesome! I love how Firaxis can make a game like this, I mean.. it''s innovative, refreshing, and familiar (if you're a fan of Civ) in the same time.  Since I bought the game with the Enemy Within DLC and installl The Long War mod right away, my review won't be "purely" about XCOM EU alone, its based of my experience with those 3 games combined, and yes if you want to buy XCOM, you should buy it with Enemy Within and I highly recommend the Long War mod, for a better, longer, more varied, and more challenging experience.
Story (10/10)
You are a (unfortunate)  commander of goverment's secert anti alien project, XCOM. Your mission is to defend earth from alien invasion, and learn their secrets through research. You, and your XCOM crew has a long way ahead, to defend earth, With limited cash and resources, you'll have to protect humanity, while you, yourself is in the edge of panic. That's the basic premise of the story, the story itself told in form of various missions and progressions of alien-neutralizing missions. You have been picked up by The Council, so pay back their trust to you. Simple, isn't it? Well, no, not at all. It's not as simple as you think.
Gameplay (10/10)
XCOM is a  combination of turn based-tactical game and real time management. In the battlefield you'll control your desired squad to neutralize the aliens. You're in charge of keeping your soldiers' life safe, since there's the "permadeath" system. Straightforward combat isn't effective, at all. You're, strength and armory wise is weak compared to the aliens. Soldier's positioning, patience, tactic, are essential to wipe out the aliens. Flank them, trap them, ambush them, outsmart them. Don't be an easily tempted nuthead who will sacrifice cover for a 100% hit, 100% critical chance, split up, regroup, retreat, attack, and repeat. You'll find yourself going back and forth, and around the map. Do whatever it takes to keep your soldier's life safe. Yes, your soldiers isn't just a "flat" soldiers. You'll level them up, assign new skills, invest all you got to make them a better soldier, when you lose them in battle, you'll regret it, forever, especially in harder difficulty setting. This game is unforgiving, even in the easiest setting possible. You'll find yourself short of money to build facilities and items. You'll have a hard time deciding what research you wanted to do first, you'll take at least 10 minutes to gear up your team for the  upcoming mission. You'll have to decide what your priority is, decision..deccision. Every decision has their own advantages and disadvantes, you'll be unsatisfied on whatever deccision you make. Even from the start, when you have to choose the base location, you'll have a sense of satisfaction and regret in the same time. This is a massive alien invasion, everyone is on panic and frustration, and Firaxis want you to feel it. Yes, its frustating, but thats what make it so addicting, its unforgiving, but its for the sake of realism. Oh, and don't name your soldiers name with your best friend's name, because..well, they'll die a lot.
Graphic (9.5/10)
Its pretty, I don't even realize its made by Unreal Engine 3, no I don't say that UE3 its bad, it just..out of my expectation. I kove the blue tint of this game, make it feels more sci-fi ish. I can't say much about the graphic. The atmoshpre is spot on, graphic is decent, the destructable environment is fantastic, the map are varied and an example of well designed tactical battleground. I just hope for a better and more varied soldier customization tho, the hairstyle and face isn't too diverse, but its a really minor problem.
Sound (9.5/10)
Can't say much about the music tho, too addicting that I don't notice it. The sound effects are amazing, combined with the fantastic voice acting, make this game even more immersive than ever.
Conclusion and Enjoyment (10/10)
Addicting, immersive, fun, frustrating, brain-draining, and clever game, that's it. Firaxis never dissapoints. Oh yea, this game's UI is probably one of the best, most intuitive, friendly UI in a tactical game, of course without sacrificing its challange and complexity at its core.

As a turn based RPG, The Banner Saga does a competent job, if somewhat shallow, with character leveling and strategy. The art style is good and the story is epic in proportion, however, as a game, it has some minor-major issues that hold the game back from a enjoyable experience for me:
- There virtually no aggro control for the majority of the game, rendering tanks useless and the only strategy becomes pretty much free for all.
- Although the art style is good, the game spends a considerable and unjustifyable ammount of time in loading screens, regardless of your PC specs.
- The game saves automatically, which makes a short chain of defeats the first step in a dimishingly enjoyable sequence of battles. By what I take to be the middle of the game, I could not win a battle without losing at least half a party. And it just got progressively worse from then on.
- By the time you hit one of the main bosses, you may not be strong enough to beat him regardless of your lineup and strategy. This leaves you with two choices: a) start the game over, which may take a dozen more hours to get to the same point or b) choose an easier difficulty setting. Both options represent a pretty evident flaw for the game design for me, and I find myself unwilling to choose any.
I wanted to like this game a lot, and enjoyed part of it thoroughly, however, it simply refused to let me like it without wasting a lot of my time. If you're thinking of buying it, I'd recommend reading a guide before starting a game (one other option that I would not have chosen).

+ Great art and animations
+ Some recognizeable music (Austin Wintory + Dallas Wind Symphony)
+ Recognizeable characters
+ Feeling of deep lore
+ Alternating protagonists to control, different views on the events taking place
+ Some freedom which paths to take and which fighters to let join (or leave) your group. When resting at villages/cities or when the caravan is moving events pop up giving you multiple choices, often difficult ones as either your caravan, your integrity as it's leader or the people in the surrounding area may suffer from your choice (like your supplies are low - steal from these peasants or pass by letting clansmen in your caravan starve?)
+ The combat situations you are getting into are reflected in the actual combat fields you are fighting on (you are not randomly thrown into some generic landscapes; the areas are visibly designed accordingly to how they were previously described, and have fitting assets like buildings, corpses or passive fighters of all the participating factions observing the events).
~ Final boss battle can be frustratingly hard (at least on any other difficulty than "Easy")
~ Story is not finished. It was promising as long as it lasted, but ended rather abruptly, I didn't expect the game to end where it did. I guess this is where the line "Saga" comes into play. Stoic is apparently outlining or already working on the sequel. If you expect a conclusive story from this single installment you will be disappointed.
~ There is a feeling of deep lore. There is a big world map, and literally any place, landmark and terrain formation you can click at to get a description of it's history or naming or whatever. This alone deserves some respect in my opinion. But not all - perhaps naturally - is used in any gameplay-related way. The worldmap itself only serves as an overview as to where you are, and where you will be going, to get an understanding of your journey. You can very well never look at the map and still get along.
- Only very few voice acting, and never during character dialogues (the launch trailer falsely suggests there to be more).
- Hostile AI is occassionally doing some strange moves, sometimes hurting their own combatants more than yours.
- No idea if it's me but sometimes the game glitched a bit. I was clicking around the combat options of one of my fighters and somehow the game ended the turn of that fighter despite me never wanting to do that. In one occasion I noticed my fighter was teleported on another combat field too. It didn't happen >that< often, but often enough for me to notice, and in some instances it prevented me from finishing some combats as I had hoped to do.
- Special moves of the fighters are sometimes a bit difficult to understand. A full explanation you can only look up before a battle. When in battle there is only a reduced description which sometimes lacks important details. So you either need to learn these moves beforehand (there are training battles in cities/villages and when resting with your caravan) or do trial and error (there is some room of error as long as you aren't a perfectionist, fighting on "Hard" or on "Normal" against the final boss). This could possibly have been made easier by allowing you to look up the full character profiles (and special move descriptions) during combat too.

This game is RAD.
I'm not the kind of person that likes to play platformers - I usually get bored and frustrated by them really quickly.  This, however, is GREAT.  It's like Super Meat Boy met Flappy Bird and gave birth to a dinosaur with jetpacks on his feet.  "Eww, Flappy Bird! That game is soooo stooooopid!" You may or may not have just said. "That also came out in 2013!! Are you stuck in the past, grandma?!" Haha okay there buddy, but seriously, hear me out!
In my first dive in I found that the game was very easy to pick up; the controls were very responsive and so easy to grasp that within minutes I was literally flying through the levels like I was DINO-PETER PAN!  It feels like its at the right speed too - not too slow to make it feel clunky, and not too fast to make it overwhelming.
The art style is super cute - I just love my lil' Rex with his lil' cyborg eyepatch - did I mention you can dress up and customize Rex?  Yeah, you can DO THAT. And it's AWESOME. I may be just biased though because I'm a GIRL.  Who sometimes plays into GENDER STEREOTYPES.
Aaaanyways, the levels are quite diverse and I never knew what to expect going into each one, which is fun! I love mysteries! I mean it's not exactly Jump Jet Agatha Christie but y'know, it's cool.  In all seriousness though, the level design is tight. There's also no forced tutorial but rather a main hub where you can learn basic mechanics and manoeuvres either yourself or through training, which is a nice option.
This game, despite being so easy to pick up, is very punishing - something that it openly advertises, so that's probably what the devs were going for.  I found myself getting a little frustrated with the first boss battle after I died a ton trying to figure out how to beat it.  The problem with this one battle was that the pacing was so different from before - I'd been trained to just GO GO GO as fast as I could throughout the previous levels while in this battle I had to wait for the right time to attack - it was actually easier to stand still than to keep moving.  Despite this I've still really enjoyed JJR and heavily recommend it to anyone that is looking for a strong platforming game that you'll not only have a ton of fun playing but will also challenge you. Even a filthy casual like me enjoyed it! Support your the indies, guys! :)

Knights of Pen and Paper is a blast. I love turn-based RPGs and this game is an excellent one that has a solid mixture of gameplay, humor and replay value that took me by surprise. To start off with, if you enjoy turn-based RPGs then this is worth buying. Read on for a more in-depth review.
In Knights of Pen and Paper you play as some friends sitting around a table and playing a Dungeons and Dragons-like game. You pick out your party and set up their class before the game begins which I thought was pretty cool. Typically new characters are introduced throughout the game, so it's interesting that we get to create our own dream team to play with. That's not all. You'll still find more characters throughout your time in the game. They'll offer new classes to use which you can switch out whenever you're not in combat. I found the cast of Knight of Pen and Paper to be nothing less than diverse and clever.
The gameplay is pretty basic at far as turn-based RPGs go. Each party member and enemy will get a turn, and you're given a bar showing who's turn is when so you can plan out your turns accordingly. Leveling is a lot of fun as you get to unlock new abilities and see how each of these characters evolve.
For me, the true appeal of Knights of Pen and Paper is its presentation. The story isn't groundbreaking--it's about as generic as any quest in Dungeons and Dragons could be. However, the characters themselves are entertaining as the story plays out. The developers did a great job of portraying all the party members as human beings who with personalities. Sometimes someone will question the logic of something absurd happening and is quickly told to shut up by the game master. I also remember one character being jubilant in defeating a boss and the text-based dialogue was perfect. Whenever I saw the speech bubbles appear I got a little excited.
Knights of Pen and Paper is a solid game. It's got a classic feel to the gameplay, it has amazing presentation and it doesn't take itself seriously in the least. Even if you've never played a turn-based RPG, this is a game that would be the perfect entry to the genre.

Steep is a game I would love to hate. There is always online-DRM, microtransactions shoved in your face and dodgy DLC, but the game scratches a very certain itch of mine that hasn't been scratched this way since Skate 3. I really enjoy exploring the mountains, finding cool spots and lines and wondering if I could succesfully spin 1440 degrees down that cliff. I really enjoy some of the challenges, especially the ski orienteering and freeride ones. The games varies nicely between atmospheric relaxing and controller-gripping "one more try"-anger. The skiing and snowboarding are where it is at for me, I couldn't care less about paragliding and wingsuiting. There is a little bit of Red Bull EXXXTREME DUDEBRO stuff going on, but I was delighted how well the game generally captures the feel of freeskiing. Snowboarding and skiing feel good too, at least on a controller. The graphics are also pretty impressive and it runs pretty well on my machine. I was skiing through a forest, tall and impressive mountains as a backdrop, orange sun shining through the forest and glimmering on the snow, relaxing music at the background, nice lines to carve on the snow and I really enjoyed myself.
There are small issues that really annoy me at times, like totally unnecessary long ragdolling after a while which gets really annoying when you have to restart a challenge because your character fell for a minute and slid slowly past a checkpoint, or clunky controls on the Mountain view. If the game didn't feel as good as it does or didn't have the right feel for me, those little thing could cumulate to be a dealbreaker for me, but with all the good stuff I can overlook it. If finding your own fun on skis or snowboard in a great, snowy world is something that appeals to you, I would recommend Steep.

TL;DR Best ARPG on the market.
After the untimely demise of Ascaron studio with their Sacred series (everybody agrees that sacred 3 is pure sh*t right? :)), diablo 3 and PoE being what they are, and no other seriously themed ARPGs on horizon, Grim Dawn is the only hope.
1. Iron Lore' previous game - Titan Quest - is on my "best ARPG ever" list. I bought GD in early access (beta 16 or so) and it had non-stop stream of updates (monthly), so it's rare game developer that doesn't scam you (unlike bugbear with their Next Car Game for instance). So the devs are good.
2. The setting is superb. Somebody may think of it as generic, but in my opinion it's not. Dark gloomy fantasy world, after the cataclysm, with humanity on verge of extinction, but fighting back, with magic AND gunpowder - by far, it looks very compelling to me. There are hidden quests that are quite good and emerge you into this game world even more. So let the storyline unfold a little and you will see this dark world at it's best.  The devs say that this game won't be the only one in this setting.
3. Core gameplay is of a typical ARPG. Very good ARPG to be honest. Skill system is what i like here the most. Classes are not generic, you have to mix them in pretty interesting ways to get a good toon. You can make different toons for years and they all will play different.
Say, i've got semi-passive retaliation warder, you just run into bunch of mobs, put totem and wait till everyone around is dead while your hp bar never goes below 70%. Want action? Enter the assassin blademaster - you have to move around as you're squishy, but damage output is tremendous. Or you can just take your trusty revolver, summon hell beasts and watch as they tear everything apart.
Also, skill enchantment wih devotion system? Also, skills from items and item enchantments?
4. Item system is very good i think. Also got craft with dropping recipes and multiple ways to upgrade items.
5. Game balance is quite ok for the moment, no super overpowered classes, no super underpowered, monsters are also good balanced.
6. i've played some coop with my friends and there are couple of downside to it.
Faction selection - if server owner plays for different faction it's kinda bad for you, as you cannot complete your quests and obviously you cannot help each other fighting different factions.
Also when game owner
quits other players just crash to desktop.
Nevertheless multiplayer is fun. Also pvp to death on hardcore ultimate? :)

REASONING / SPOILERS BELOW: Don't read if you haven't played SRIV for at least a few hours
-----------------------------
I enjoyed my time in the virtual world of SRIV but the same things I liked are what make it a bad sequel.  Within the first few hours of play, the current world of saints row is blown up in an attempt to keep up with the power creep of each release.  In SR1 you fight for the streets; SR2 for the city; SR3 for the island; SRIV for the world; SRV for the universe?.  So thanks to their increasing of the stakes, SRIV had no where to go but up in terms of size/wackiness but they went too far and destroyed the world
of Saints Row in favor of a more configurable reality.  This new 'world' is one that allows for super powers and other things to occur without it being 'law-defying' but this new mechanic overshadows and effectively ruins the established gameplay mechanics from the older games which they still tried to cram in.
- Tons of fun to find your ride and trick it out.. This is made useless thanks to super speed/Jump-gliding
- Super powers do more damage and use a regenerating ammo. After a few hours you can essentially stop using guns altogether.  (Ammo becomes infinite much later)
- Same as shooting, super powers upgrade and become practically infinite.
- Now this one they actually did a good job on.  They integrated the new 'super powered' melee moves that you could augment with later powers.
If they spent time and thought it out, I bet they could have found a way for the super powers and old mechanics to co-exist better but in the end they left them there to rot.
Now if they would have marketed it differently, I may have let it slide.
As an Expansion: It would have just been viewed as a refreshing change to shake up the gameplay
As a 'titled' release (EX: Saints Row: The Power-ing): Same as expansion
As a 'NUMBERED' release: It is an unwanted revamp to an already fun formula.
The reason why a numbered release pisses me off is it implies the events of the game are of the main story and not some side branch.  This means the next game will have to continue where SRIV left off and honestly, the SRIV devs did SR5 no favors in terms of a lead in. They could ignore everything that happened in IV and treat it like a side branch or a dream or something but doing so would just prove the previous game should have never been 4.
-----------
All ranting aside, for ~20 bucks for ~16 hours is a pretty good deal and definitely worth the purchase if you like the crude humor of Saints Row and the crackdown-esque gameplay.. just ignore that it is a Saints Row sequel if it bugs you as much as me.
(Also hunting orbs is too damn addictive)

Spoiler FREE review.
The visuals and music are beautiful and so it's the concept. But gameplay?
First let's get to the core of the game,The Turn Based Combat System!:
The turns are like a chess board game, let me use an example:
Le's say you have 4 guys and your oponent has 8.
This means that each of your guys will get to move at least 2 times by the time your oponent has managed to move it's entire team, this is ofcourse if you didnt slay any of them. If you did then, things can get reversed until you reach pillage mode.
When you reduce your foes numbers to just one, you will go into "PILLAGE MODE!" To put it simple It just sounds cool and the turn mode becomes like those of any Fire Emblem Games. Meaning everyone gets one turn per round, including your opponent. This can help you set up the kill for the hero that needs to level up, or simply for the next wave of enemies.
It is an interesting concept but could had been done more justice.
The enemy will automatically go next - even if it just moved in the previous turn - and will do what this game does best, search for your weakest guy and try to bring it down.
I understand that this was so that if you had 5 guys left and your oponent just one it wouldnt get to move every time your oponent does, otherwise it would be crazy!
But anyways, do you get a reward for pillaging? Do you get to burn stuff? No, you dont, Unlike real life Pillaging.
In real life the last unit would flee, do a last stand or surrender . Not search for the weakest and going on a programmed kamikaze mode. But this is what this game does.
I often wonder if the programmer or the “Creative director” ever bothered on playing fire emblem or final fantasy tactics or doing some research on other strategic war games.
And talking about the  A.I. of your enemies, It is ridiculou! It’s like you are fighting terminators that know exactly every specific movement that you will take and that will ALWAYS have more bonuses than you and will charge at your weakest unit no matter if other units are closer to them.
They are like Kamikazes that will search for your weakest guy no matter if it's behind a giant maze. So get ready for an intense challenge.
The Story and Writting ELEMENTS! choose your dialogue wisely:
First and Foremost be aware that every dialogue you choose can mean the life or death of one of your heroes. Even at the very beggining of the game.
So unless you want to save it, you will have to redo the battle all over again and explore for the proper dialogue option. Sometimes it is often the most cliche one the one that saves it.
However it appears that at some point the programmer or writter got aware of this "save scamming" as they like to call it. And very early on the game you get a choice and you will take consequences near the end of the game depending on that choice.
An extensive dialogue tree will be presented and no matter your choice of dialogue or any other thing that you have done in this game, you will loose at least 3 characters that may be some of your strongest ones.
Meaning you wont be exploring their relationships anymore and you will be heavily outmanned when you get to the last combats.
This was Lazily implemented and poorly written, many players consider it BS yet the programmers think its cool and even compare it to The Game of Thrones Death of Ned Stark. Which doesnt make sense because that is the predetermined story, it is very well written and its not an option just to screw the honest players.
Suffice it to say that if you want to save them, you will have to restart the game or edit the game save files.
The Renown!
Renown it's the currency and blood of the game. With it you level up, improve your skills, purchase items and most importantly get FOOD!
It is extremely scarse you can only get it after battles or after certian actions so be very greedy on it, unless you have to level heroes or purchase food supplies.
But why food?:
In this game you are the leader of a caravan, as each day passes your people will consume food "supplies" and if you start running out of it then the morale will go low and they may ended up dying out of starvation. You have the option to set a camp and rest in order to improve morale, and morale helps you A LOT when it comes to battles.
Items can be found and obtained after war simulated battles or visiting places and interacting with them. Others can be purchased with Renown. I personally didnt like that Renown and currency where the same thing in this game, because you either have to choose wether to level up your character or purchase food or a cool item.

The tutorial it’s extremely basic and leaves you to learn the new abilities by yourself. The game doesnt like rewarding you and it's always trying to make you miserable or frustrated.
In Short, the game doesnt like to reward you but will try in a constant basis to screw you and make you miserable. Maybe it wants you to understand how frustrated the main heroes of this story feel, I dont know.
Visuals and looks:
Bloody Gorgeous, reminds you a lot from the Sleeping Beauty and all those animated movies from old disney and  the knight and medieval movies Like Ivanhoe. Even if it's Norse Mythology based.
Definitly the selling point of this game. The art and coloring it's just pure eye candy and even sometimes eye protein too. You can spend a good amount of time just examining screens, horizons, forests and even the battle scenarios.
The music it's really beautiful too, and sometimes very inspiring.
If you are a hardcore Turn Based Strategy Game Player that loves to play It's Fire Emblems in hard mode. Then you are on for one hell of a ride!
If you are just going to enjoy the ride, I suggest you to play it on easy unless you are up for some frustrating times or a real challenge.
Thank you for reading through this sincere review, as always no boot licking.

Overall I have been very pleased with this game.  I played the original BG and NW series, Icewind Dale my favorite.  This game brings a lot of those rpg and turned-based 4-person squad elements with a fresh take on the open world / roaming environment that feels similar to playing the Ultima series for me. I'm not very far at the time of this post, maybe 15+ hours, and I've enjoyed every moment of it.
The graphics are easy on the eye at ultra settings on a modest machine.  It defaulted to those on a AMD FX 6300 / Radeon 6800. UI is pretty standard as the come.  The only thing is the, rather important, button on the right which is how you teleport.  Wish that one was more evident... sadly responsible for 30 mins of my play time.
The way you can split you party is very cool imo.  At one point one of my two main characters was about to die in combat on the next round (surrounded).  If both of your two main characters die you lose and load. (lots of f5/f8)  I fled with my other main character and one side character back to town and was able to regroup in real time while my other main character stayed in combat awiting their return.  I ran the other two back into the fight and was able to prevent his death.  While some may see this as a cheap way out or breaking game mechanics there is also the possibility that those returning character run into another mob and I would have two seperate battles to wage, or manage to merge them back into one.
Your characters have conversations with the party that you control. Doesn't really have a place in the SP mode (although it does change stats in some cases) and you can turn it off in the options but in MP mode it comes into play as if you don't agree with the person your playing with you can argue and try to intimiate/charm/reason with them.  And finally a draw will bring rock-paper-scissors to decide it all.  Another new element that I am indifferent on but for the record have yet to play multi.
Crafting is a nice addition.  You learn your recipes by book reading and from there it's a drag-and-drop process mostly.  However keeping all the ingredients can get messy in the inventory.
Soudtrack is quite enjoyable and the audio is well done.  VOs are ok, but honestly very few make it immersive.  The main story is not bad so far but I've been bouncing all over the place with side quests and have much more to do.
It's one of those "what's over there?" games that makes you hate the next day at work from lack of sleep.  I would give it a 9 or 10.  I bought it at $40, I'd do it again.

A must have for any puzzler enthusiast's collection.
RUSH is a 3d puzzle game involving simple logic skills. There's colored entrances and exits, and as soon as you believe you've finished the puzzle, blocks will teleport into existence and follow a straight line across the map, only turning right when they bump into walls.
You, as the player, have to place special movement pads on the ground that influence the path these blocks take, allowing you to divert block traffic to help all of them reach the exit without colliding or falling off the map.
While this premise sounds really simple, in practice it can get really complex because of this simplicity. There's 4 direction changing pads, a direction switcher that switches back and forth when blocks use it. A pause pad, as well as a conveyor belt pad. While their effects are simple, it's the entire contraption and combination of switching and redirecting traffic at the right place that turns out to be the big puzzling question in this game.
The game divides the puzzles in a few difficulty settings, starting with tutorial/easy puzzles that only involve a few pads, up to hard and 'special' puzzles that require great insights and rational systematic analysis of the paths the cubes take to find out the solution. As such, pretty much anyone should be able to get *something* out of this game, and the more you practice, the better you'll get, allowing even the weaker puzzle fanatic to grow and progress to the harder areas of the game.
RUSH also features a slightly upbeat ambient track that is fun to listen to, and it really fits with the sounds of blocks squeaking their way throughout the level.
So if you like puzzles, if you like 3d puzzles, if you like logical thinking. Get this game! It's definitely worth the price.
As a sidenote, if you liked Chu Chu Rocket: This is the exact same thing, except it uses cubes.
Sound: 3/5
The sounds are simple but fitting, though some people might get tired of the Sqeaky Cube noise after a while.
Graphics: 3/5
The graphics are again, simple, but fitting. Everything is cube shaped and the ambient lighting gives the entire game a soft look and feel. The cubes themselves are a bit more shiny. There's not much to say due to the simple graphics, but they look good for a puzzle game.
Gameplay: 4/5
Great puzzle fun, though there's less replay value once you've finished them all, unless you forget the solutions to the old ones. Controls are fluent, game mechanics are simple to understand and logical.
Overall: 4/5

Steep is a bit like Star Wars Episodes 1-3: If you can ignore Jar-Jar Binks and the other outright obnoxious parts, it's pretty enjoyable.
So first the good parts: the graphics are beautiful and the concept is great. It's been years since there has been a good winter sports title, and I'm really glad to see someone take a stab at it, even if it was Ubisoft and all of their misguided product designers. Steep is a challenging game and overall lots of fun, even if some of the sports and events are more interesting than others. That said, there is more than enough content to keep one entertained for hours. As somone who grew up in Colorado and spent every winter both skiing and snowboarding until I moved away for college, this game gives me that warm fuzzy feeling of being on the maintain again. (That said, please Ubi, PLEASE make a DLC for the Rockies! The Alps and Alaska are nice but so cold and barren).
Now for Jar-Jar! So, what are the annoying aspects of this game?
First and foremost, the designers of this game have failed to understand one of the key elements about winter mountain sports: they are not social activities. Any seasoned skier/snowboarder knows that there is nothing more wonderful than the spiritual solitude of the mountain, and nothing worse than long lift lines and crowded hills. Even if you go with friends or family, you only see them on the lifts, not the way down. Well congrats Ubisoft, you managed to digitally recreate the annoyance of a mountainside full of acne-faced pukes. Steep's mountains are filled with random, stupidly dressed idiots with lame gamertags, polluting the beautiful scenery (at least you can't run into other people, thank god). It's easy enough to ignore other people and their pointless friend requests, except for the morons who use the smoke trail accessory with the wingsuit. Seriously, screw those guys for ruining my visibility and making me restart a run.
Also, all the game characters are idiots. The "A" button is dedicated to the sole function of making your character holler something embarrassingly stupid. The dialog tries so hard to be "hip" and "cool" that it comes off sounding like Poochie the Dog from the classic Simpsons episode. Fast-travelling to a location also triggers this feature, so even if you avoid pressing the A button you cannot escape the moronic things that occaisionally come out of your character's mouth. But again, this is easy enough to ignore.
The music is also horrid, though I guess this is more of personal opinion. Basically, if you like white-boy rock bands where the chorus of every song is just oooooh-ing and ahhhhh-ing, then I guess you'll choose to keep the music on rather than mute it and run Spotify in the background like everybody else. Also, the game has a pretty annoying feature wiping out causes the music to a stop like a turntable brake, then restarts the song from the beginning if you restart your run. Given how often this happens it gets to be pretty annoying (especially for everything involving the wingsuit and also most hard events for skiing/snowboarding), but again, is easily counteracted.
The "stories" are tedious and silly and best and irritating at worst. Fortunately, all cutscenes are skippable, so again, easy to ignore. It's harder to ignore the stories which involve other people (that is, more "Poochie the Dog" characters) who talk to you while you do a run. Almost all dialog in this game seems to unintentionally parody snowboarding/skateboarding/surfing culture.
So yeah, lots of annoyances, but they are possible to ignore. The gameplay and scenery alone make this game worthwhile though.

I'm just gonna go ahead and answer what you're thinking right now. Is it as good as Diablo 3 or Path of Exile? The answer is yes.
PROS:
+Fantastic Talent Tree/Devotion Tree system (more about that shortly)
+Dual Classing and combining different abilities is fun and rewarding
+Respeccing is easy and works well (Looking at you POE)
+Itemization is customizable and satisfying
+Lots and lots of quests to do and hidden areas to explore.
CONS:
-Game is still buggy and the friends I play with including myself crash frequently for no reason.
-Hosting Multiplayer games works sometimes and other times not so much
-Some spell/ability effects from enemies can be hard to see in the clutter of everyones abilities going off. It's very easy to take damage and not know where it came from
-Quests should be shown on the world map
OTHER NOTES:
One thing that stood out to me is the game isn't randomly generated. Everything is meant to be where it is except for a few "rogue" special dungeons. This works well because they've hidden a lot of things in the corners and nooks of each area. Everywhere is worth exploring.
Lets talk about respeccing for a moment. You get Stat points you can level up (Physique, Cunning, Spirit) these are requirements for gear so depending on how you build your character you just allocate points according. These are not respeccable. After you pick both your classes you have to use your talent points on either talents or mastery points. Mastery points allow you to pick up talents further down the tree. These are NOT respeccable.
Throughout the game you find Shrines. you'll either need a component or have to kill enemies to clear them and you receive a Devotion point. Devotion points are spent on these Constellation mini talent trees. This is where i'm pleased with how much I have available to respec. I can respec talent points and devotion points so all I really have to be certain about are my Attributes and Class Mastery points. This is a great system and only slightly restricts your character. It allows me to play with different builds but still have to make important decisions on if I'm going to raise my mastery with a class for that one talent, or just dump those points into something I already have.
I find myself playing this for hours on end with friends and this is the perfect ARPG escape when I've already dumped a few hundred hours in other ARPGs.
Happy hunting gentlemen.

Where to even begin with?
Well for those who are in love with the platforming genre, stop reading my review andbuy this game immediately.
Now for the other I'll detail it a bit more ;)
Jumpjet Rex is a very fun, old-school yet modern platformer, but not your typical platformer. If you really need a comparison with other title, it would be a merge between Super Meat Boy and Fenix Rage. It's medium-paced, which makes it moderately "hardcore". By moderately hardcore I mean the kind of hardcore everyone can play, even casual players ;) So even if you're a casual player, don't be afraid by the trailer or the images !
In term of gameplay, you have infinite jumps and dash to the sides, with various hazards to avoid. Each levels contains 3 stars to get, the first one is obtained by finishing the level, the second one by beating a time limit, and the third one by not dying more than a set number of times (for the first levels it's zero of course).
Last but not least, the game has a heavy customization aspect. If like me, you like a good game in which you can over-customize your character in quadrillion of possible ways then this game is definitely for you. Each customizable piece of the rex has many parts available. The pieces are head/skin color/jetboots trail color/boots color. That really makes for a big variety.
**CONCLUSION**
Couldn't recommend it more. I hesitated for a long time, and I was awfully wrong ! Grab that credit card of yours and add this game to your cart right now (you even get a free extra copy to give to a friend if you buy it during Early Access).

REASONING / SPOILERS BELOW: Don't read if you haven't played SRIV for at least a few hours
-----------------------------
I enjoyed my time in the virtual world of SRIV but the same things I liked are what make it a bad sequel.  Within the first few hours of play, the current world of saints row is blown up in an attempt to keep up with the power creep of each release.  In SR1 you fight for the streets; SR2 for the city; SR3 for the island; SRIV for the world; SRV for the universe?.  So thanks to their increasing of the stakes, SRIV had no where to go but up in terms of size/wackiness but they went too far and destroyed the world
of Saints Row in favor of a more configurable reality.  This new 'world' is one that allows for super powers and other things to occur without it being 'law-defying' but this new mechanic overshadows and effectively ruins the established gameplay mechanics from the older games which they still tried to cram in.
- Tons of fun to find your ride and trick it out.. This is made useless thanks to super speed/Jump-gliding
- Super powers do more damage and use a regenerating ammo. After a few hours you can essentially stop using guns altogether.  (Ammo becomes infinite much later)
- Same as shooting, super powers upgrade and become practically infinite.
- Now this one they actually did a good job on.  They integrated the new 'super powered' melee moves that you could augment with later powers.
If they spent time and thought it out, I bet they could have found a way for the super powers and old mechanics to co-exist better but in the end they left them there to rot.
Now if they would have marketed it differently, I may have let it slide.
As an Expansion: It would have just been viewed as a refreshing change to shake up the gameplay
As a 'titled' release (EX: Saints Row: The Power-ing): Same as expansion
As a 'NUMBERED' release: It is an unwanted revamp to an already fun formula.
The reason why a numbered release pisses me off is it implies the events of the game are of the main story and not some side branch.  This means the next game will have to continue where SRIV left off and honestly, the SRIV devs did SR5 no favors in terms of a lead in. They could ignore everything that happened in IV and treat it like a side branch or a dream or something but doing so would just prove the previous game should have never been 4.
-----------
All ranting aside, for ~20 bucks for ~16 hours is a pretty good deal and definitely worth the purchase if you like the crude humor of Saints Row and the crackdown-esque gameplay.. just ignore that it is a Saints Row sequel if it bugs you as much as me.
(Also hunting orbs is too damn addictive)

EverQuest is a very old game. Well, sort of. It predates most of the MMO market by a few years, especially a certain other exceptionally popular game anyone remotely familiar with the genre will instantly know. In its heyday, it was one of the most popular MMOs, with about 100,000 subscribers, give or take. The epic scale of the raids still hasn't been replicated to this day.
But has it aged well? Sure.
EverQuest has always been about change. Sure, you can't have a dynamic influence on the world in most cases, but the game has always been changing. Where once you couldn't do anything without a group unless you were a specific class, now nearly everyone is capable of soloing for experience.
Don't get me wrong, the game is still old and looks old, but there's a wonderful charm to it that other games really haven't come close to replicating.
Oh, and it's HUGE. In the old days, it used to be said that it took six hours to run from one end of the map to the other on foot. Well, the game has gotten bigger since then, to the point that they've added a number of hub zones to make travel easier. The down side to this truly epic size is that very few zones are consistently occupied by players.
There's also a bit of a disjointed aesthetic to the game. While many older zones and models have been updated over time, just as many have not. While Freeport and the surrounding Commonlands have received overhauls to the point it's almost a joke in the community, Qeynos and the Karanas are mostly unchanged from the time of launch, barring a few new quests that make you visit there.
Now, let's talk about the sound. It's dated, sure, but that little factor hasn't stopped people from loving music before. And EverQuest has some real goldies. Kelethin, the sea approach to Freeport, Rivervale...great music that will stick in your mind forever. It's unfortunate that some of this music, such as the Rivervale theme, are in places you'd never normally visit, but sometimes it's worth it just to hear it.
It's not all rose colored glasses, though: The UI is cluttered beyond belief, to the point you'll be glad you can alter it to your liking. The previously mentioned disjointed graphics can also be rather jarring when you compare newer cash shop aesthetic outfits with older, standard armor. Everything works, but unlike most MMOs these days that are like receiving a new toy with karate chop action, EverQuest is like receiving one of those totally awesome playsets...with the words "Some Assembly Required" etched on the front.
But if you ask me, it's worth it.

The amount of content in this game is nothing short of staggering. So many raids, monsters, items, secrets, spells, skills, races, cities, towns, dungeons, lore and everything else you'd expect from a huge RPG like this. If you end up enjoying it, your patience with the game will go long before you ever even get close to seeing all that this game has to offer. In many people's opinions, this was/is the absolute pinnacle of the MMO genre.

Now here's a charming tidbit of experimental gaming. A player pretending to be players role playing a game. It could have gone so wrong, but the developers understand that brevity is the better part of expression, and choice representations of tranditional pen and paper role playing cement this as a must play for anyone curious enough to give this a second look.
It may take you that long to realize just what's happening, but once you do you'll probably be hooked ensuring your Grandma has her 17th level Paladin wearing fully upgraded equipment. The biggest drawback is the titles in game currency, which on iOS translates to real world microtransactions. Fortunately you can quest your way through earning all of the gold you'll need to pay for all of your upgrades.
This is an addictive game, and the pixel art style has its appeal, through does not appear to scale well to all resolutions. A minor gripe, as the gameplay is the most compelling aspect. You'll want to grind away so your players can have the leveling high. There's no doubt this is a niche experience, but one you'll no doubt remember. A little pricey solo, I'd suggest buying the bundle of both Knights of Pen and Paper I and its sequel in one package (available via either of the games Steam pages).

Let me start this off; This game is fantastic.
When I started it up I expected crap, I've been burned a lot by Early Access recently and this was going to be my last EA game for awhile, I am glad to say that it has given me hope once more.
A simple version of describing this game is this; D2 + Titan's Quest = Grim Dawn
It takes the atmosphere and "feel" of diablo 2 and grabs the skill/class and stat system from Titan's Quest.
Overall this game feels great, it feels fantastic. Everytime I kill a hero I get a nice rush of YESSS I JUST DID THAT! Every level up makes me feel stronger and able to kill tougher enemies. Each class, once you get about five levels in, feels vastly different.
The biggest Pro for this game? To me it's exactly what we SHOULD have gotten with Diablo 3, I adore it.
A few cons, however.
Using Titan's Quest skill/class system, or an implimentation of it, makes it so it takes quite some time before I feel any class diversity.
Not enough "class" dependant armor types. Everything requires a base of physiquie, except for chest armor and some hats that are caster focused.
More Skills, or rather more variety to fill up the bar and give us a variety of tools to face the challenges in the early game.
This is, at the price of 14.99 a damn must have in any ARPG lovers Steam Library!

JumpJet Rex is an arcade platformer designed to be rewarding and satisfying at any level of play. There is no difficulty option; you're set on course with all the necessary tools at your discression to simply have fun with the game, or make it a competitive speed runner to climb the leaderboards against your friends.
Each level has a prime directive which is to get to the goal at no matter the cost, however you're awarded extra stars for completing a level with out dying, or reaching the goal in record time; however, like any good retro-inspired platformer, you're rewarded in your efforts for exploring and collecting coins. Scattered throught out most, if not all levels, there's secret warpzones and costumes for you to collect and buy to decorate Rex in your own fashion.
The art is top notch, and each level is a vibrant landscape that you'll probably come back to multiple times again to beat your fastest time, and earn coins, and the music is excellent that - you'll probably get a few tunes stuck in your head in the same fashion Strike the Earth from Shovel Knight has become an instant classic much like the classic theme from Mario Brothers and other games.
JumpJet Rex is a solid platformer that everyone should try regardless of the title of "early access" being plastered on it's store page. Support TreeFortress and their games, I'm thoroughly excited for what more this game will offer.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown
Or
How to survive an alien invasion 101
Good morning class! Welcome to your new “optional” class of this semester. In light of the recent alien threat we will be going over how You can contribute in defending this muddy patch of dirt called Earth!
Step 1 – People will die
Since you will be commanding the elite unit that is supposed to be the first and last line of defense, it is a good idea to complete the tutorial. Regardless what kind of veteran you consider yourself, getting used to the new control of your units is always useful, especially during a mission with no real stakes. Even if you think that’s below you, the tutorial will remind you of a small fact: soldiers die. As a general advice don’t get used to your buddies too much, unless you are playing on the lowest difficulty – in which case you can leave your man card on my desk on your way out. Oh and one more thing; people who fail my class get promoted to rookie status, get awarded with granddad’s old rifle and army jacket, and can go prove themselves on the front lines.
Step 2 – Dig a hole
While your less intelligent classmates are fighting on the frontlines, you will be sitting in the comfort of the anthill you call your base. Using all the technology available to man, the faceless representatives of Earth’s nations have decided to dig you a hole on a continent of your choosing, with different advantages. Europe for example will allow you to maintain your research facilities at lowered costs, while Africa will make sure that any unfortunate extraterrestrial you manage to bring home will spill their secrets much quicker. Later on you will have to dig deeper to expand your new bachelor pad. In order to give you a chance in your ongoing fight with the seemingly endless alien armada, you will have to build additional manufacturing, research and training facilities, all the while making sure you have enough energy to run the whole thing.
Step 3 – Sun Tzu says…
Knowing your enemy is half the battle. When fighting aliens with vastly superior numbers and technology that makes the Silicon Valley look like the arts and crafts class from fourth graders, it is pretty much the entire battle. The way ahead lies in collecting as many alien artifacts as possible, bringing back their corpses and even live specimens as time goes on. The German ex-mistress turned scientist Dr. Vahleen will “probe” these poor animals and provide you with new technologies, while the obligatory generic Japanese Dr. Shen will manufacture whatever comes out of her twisted mind. As you fight the new specimens of the alien invaders, their remains will let you upgrade your weapons and armor, produce better aircrafts, or even unlock special abilities for some of your soldiers. Falling behind on these will decrease the already small chance of survival of your faithful bullet sponges, causing you to fail essential missions.
Step 4 – The coin is mightier than the sword
Even though the world is about to end, nothing is free. While the visitors from outer space managed to turn back inflation by about 70 years, everything you build or develop will cost you money. Your afternoon world saving club is financed by 16 countries who are willing to pay and provide you manpower if you provide them protection. This extortion racket works as long they are actively protected. To translate, you will get payment from countries you watch over with satellites. If they get too many unregistered visitors they will “panic”. Every month the council will evaluate your performance. If the panic meter is full at the end of the month, the country will leave the project, and fend for itself. This is something you should try to avoid at all costs, because you will lose potential income and the bonus provided by protecting an entire continent. Should you get low on the almighty mulah, you have multiple options; you can sell alien parts or some of your weapons to other countries, or if they give you one, complete council missions. Managing your finances is very important even in the face of total annihilation. Running out of money while not the end of the world, makes the game a lot harder.
Step 5 - Time to get technical
Defending Earth in XCOM is a tough but fair experience. While the game will give you equal opportunities to smash your mouse against the wall, or shout victoriously as that damn alien’s head blows up, it is not without its flaws. Shooting through walls is common. While this is understandable with some of the later weapons, it is painful to watch as your soldier executes a fatal shot through walls they can’t even see through. The camera sometimes takes angles where nothing is visible, and no amount of rotation or zooming can make it better. Aiming with rockets or grenades is a pain to say the least, often making you miss perfectly valid shots. Needless to say, these are almost always critical situations since using explosives means losing alien artifacts. The system otherwise is fairly easy to learn, and while certain useful tricks, such as the importance of constructing the same type of buildings next to each other are easy to miss, the game tries it’s best to explain everything.
Three stage plan: 1.We engage the aliens. 3. We liberate Earth and celebrate. Easy right?
The road to victory will be long, and undoubtedly challenging. I can’t promise anything but blood, toil, tears, and sweat.
The multiplayer option allows you and your friends to choose sides, and use those nasty alien powers on each other, while equipping everyone with that mega laser rifle you could never afford in-game. While sometimes laggy, the multiplayer works fine 90% of the time.
In conclusion, for anyone who likes turn-based tactical shooters, this alien shooting, Earth defending, base building 2K creation is a must. A true spiritual successor of the original, the game will satisfy the hardcore fans of the original, as well as newcomers to the franchise.

65 million years ago dinosaurs ruled the earth and then suddenly vanished.... so we thought.
Dinosaurs have actually lived among us for millions of years on a small tropical island called Isla Nublar. What was once believed to be  a hollywood movie, "Jurassic Park" turned out to be an actual real documentary about the events that took place on the island and documented the attempts that humans  tried to gain control over these dominant creatures.
Due to unlawful experimentation the humans were able to give the dinosaurs extreme human like intelligence. It would ultimately be the downfall of mankind. Ever so tired of the villany of the humans, the dinosaurs rebeled against their captures and soon regained control of the island. Any attempts to reach the island were met with failure.
For many years the dinosaurs planned a way to rid the world of the human race. Once unleashed , the virus quickly spread; wiping out the entire human population. Dinosaurs once again ruled the earth.
Over 5,000 years have passed since the virus wiped out humanity. As time went on the dinosaurs intelligence continued to grow as did their techonology. To overcome their problems with moblity they designed space ships and rocket boots that allowed them to move with great ease. It wasn't long after they started to colonize space, setting up many space stations and offworld colonies. The second era of dinosaurs looked bright.
Alas  not all was well in the universe. A dark long forgotten force had grown angry at the dinosaurs. In it's anger it summoned a huge meteor to crash on the dinosaurs home planet earth hoping to wipe them out from existance.
Now as a first responder: JumpJetRex, you must save your home planet from annihilation. Using your wits, and of course your rocket boots; you must overcome the many challanges that face you ahead. The fate of the planet rests in your hands.

VALVe's mostly unknown experiment with the GoldSrc engine. This platform-esque shooter was the source of VALVes most hated projects, condemning it's ridiculous concept and lack of support.
The gameplay is platform-based first person shooting as (and might I add eerily) same vain as Tron, the famous sci-fi film. You must knock each other or shoot discs at the head to score points for a kill or knock them off the platforms to also score a kill/frag.
Fast, reflex based combat with a focus on bouncing discs across jumping platforms keeps the game pace action-packed and feeling of Tron's aesthetic shines through.
One map is literally all there is to this game, so variety becomes a serious issue for a paid game that is for £4.00. Due to it's lack of popularity, this game never developed very well nor did it evolve with modifications to it's Goldsrc counterpart, it is quintessentially a dead game, often used mockingly to name a certain "third project" VALVe is doing. VALVe themselves do not like the game and the inflection given suggests this game will never get a remaster.
The game only has 1-5 players playing since the last edit I made to this review which means it is highly possible that it is a dead game. Don't believe me? Go to the server browser if you own it.
Rigid movement system and the Steampipe broke the any chance for modifications that were developed before it.
Latency on some servers is extremely high, at about 100-200 mS ping. This arguably makes the game almost unplayable when network jitter occurs. So hosting one might be recommended.
Unpolished textures, very rough on the eyes.
Apart from a few screams and moans and the gun's sound effects sounding like something out of Tron. Extremely empty of anything else.
Aim and fire disc with the mouse or deflect them off bars to hit them off the platform to their barren, empty doomed lives! As it's name suggests, if you 'ricochet' the disc off the walls and hits an opponent, I believe more points are added.
Utilizes GoldSrc's detailed MIPMAPPING, colourmaps, skeletal animation giving impressive animation (for the time). Atmospherically dark with a focus on contrasting magenta on black. Very tron-esque.
Jump from platform to platform, watching that you don't fall off or decelerate enough to fall into the abyssal plane! Shoot discs at other players. Some platforms may spawn or generate an ability to fire triple discs, to increase the likely hood of attacking and pushing several players off, a decapitation power up which deals out a one-hit kill disc that slices through your victims head and rapid fire disc power ups which spam out 3 in quick succession!
It's matter of you against everyone. Fight
The Source version (which is that of a modification) of this using the Half Life 2 base is on Mod DB and improves on the formula whilst removing it's weaknesses so buying this game is utterly pointless by this point in time unless someone at VALVe is a nostalgiafág.

The core gameplay is satisfying but there isn't enough that complements it and keeps it interesting.  The majority of maps are static and non-interactable (you can't climb ladders, lots of objects aren't destructible), the design is the same; layout with multiple entry points and some doors you can weld shut.
The classes have perks that differentiate them a litte, but really, they all do the same thing.  I don't feel like the medic is any less proficient at killing than a berserker, and really I often see medic and support classes with the highest number of kills.
There's a severe lack of content.  I've seen comments complaining about this that date back 9 months, with people saying "There are only two bosses?  Don't worry they'll introduce more in time."  Well, at this stage, it seems unlikely.
They seem to be relying on user made maps to fill the content gap.  Meanwhile, their microtransaction cosmetic store is full to the brim with hilariously over priced hats and costumes.  Gee, I wonder what's going on there?
After a few hours you'll start to realize that all matches pretty much play the same.  Everyone clumps up and slaughters everything.  Maybe some strategy is required in the highest difficulty settings, but playing on "Hard" everyone seems to do fine just running in circles and blindly killing everything.  It's repetitive and dull.
At full price this game doesn't justify its cost.  Maybe on sale.

The Walking Dead has been very dear to my heart. The Telltale ones, I mean.
The length is usually 2-3 hours per episode, 5 episodes. This game changes the formula however. This time there's 3 episodes with a total runtime of 200 minutes or so.
The length should've been longer with there being 4 episodes instead of 3 or just had the episodes be the standard length. The lack of time made it so that literally no character was properly fleshed out and instead you're left guessing why a certain character would do something. The personalities aren't really the obvious archetypes either, so it's obvious that they wanted the characters to be more than just bags of flesh that Michonne could interact with.
There's this extremely annoying subplot, which you could probably already guess if you're familiar with the show. Michonne keeps seeing visions of her past, in specific her family. While this was an interesting way to start off episode 1 as a quick way to show everyone a quick recap of her past, it starts becoming annoying after the first episode. During episode 3's culmination. The events that are supposed to be the crecendo of the whole story, is cut off with her boring past. Now, don't get me wrong. I love me some mentally unsound protagonist as the next person, but it's repetitive. You either see Michonne thinking that she's in her old apartment while actually being in the real world or you see her two kids that are very shadowy. It was a good scare twice for me (and I'm very easily scared) but it fell off after they showed it every 5 minutes or so. The sub-plot never actually developed and during the whole 3+ hours, we just managed to find out that the kids were supposed to be at their aunt's and that Michonne had a choice of either staying home or walking out on her kids.
Now, call me a ♥♥♥♥♥baby, but that's in no way enough of a sub-plot to dedicate around 10 minutes in the 20 minute long end scene and 40 minutes in a 3 hour game.
Now that we've got the story out of the way, let's talk about the elephant in the room. Telltale has been cherning out the same formula with the same clunky engine with the same animations. The engine and the formula aren't the things that bother me. Neither does the notion that they haven't upgraded their graphics at all.
Instead, the only issue I have is the animations and the way they convey emotions. Animations aren't fluid at all and the facial animations literally change from shocked to exhausted to mad in a matter of 4 seconds. I literally counted it during  episode 1.
I've really hammered on this game during this review, but in reality it's a good game. It's just that the parts that I didn't like really stuck out like a sore thumb. Regardless of these issues, during episode 2, I truly got hooked. I wanted to know what happened next and I managed to finish, wanting more from this story. It's not another TWD Season 1&2. If you don't expect this game to be that, then I think you'll enjoy it.
Buy it at sale price.

This is an amazing ARPG.
It has been a while since I have achieved that Diablo-II-esque high of loot and progression. A lot of games have tried - Diablo III failing pretty hard straight out of the gate - and have not even come close. Path of Exile was hit or miss with a lot of people, as the game engine is rather basic and only recently has the desync bug been resolved. Grim Dawn is the exception to all of these blunders.
You feel like you're discovering something new around every corner. When you find a unique item, it's actually very powerful and rewarding. The progression systems are also very cool. Since it's modeled somewhat off of Titan quest, it really is a build-your-own-class type of character progression. However, it's not too complicated - such as, say, Path of Exile's skill tree system - so you can jump right in without feeling the need to read a bunch of guides on optimal tree paths.
Without beeing too shallow in comparisons, it's not exactly a modernized Diablo II, but it definitely captures the intrigue and skinner box glory of old. Highly recommend if you are a fan of the action RPG genre.
