I dont usually do reviews just read them, but this game is one that I just had to give an opinion on.  I have so far played through this game twice and it is just awesome, the decisions you make can be brutal and decieving but that is what makes this game so good.  Sometimes characters will die never to be seen again and other times new characters will join you and it all depends on the choices you make.
The tactical side is also a great feature, you have the giants who take up four squares and are strong but arent very mobile, then you have the humans who only take up one square and are more agile but are slightly weaker in strength and armour.  The game is turn based where the player takes a turn and then the enemy takes a turn in that order always until you manage to get the enemy or yourself to one character,  this is when you enter pillage mode.  In this mode basically you get to move all your characters before swapping turns for instance we have the enemy down to one character left so now I can move all my characters before he gets a turn.
Each character has a class and they all level up differently and have different skills such as a warhawk who can do a massive aoe attack on every friend and foe around him.  The level cap is five for every character but in most cases you will need to rotate characters in and out of your team due to injuries so you shouldn't concentrate on leveling one team but instead try to spread the levels around.
As for story you follow two sides the Varl (the Giants) and the humans both who are fighting for the same cause to rid the world of the dredge armies.
overall great game definately recommend this turn based strategy rpg.

In a game that makes me think of mashing together Assassin's Creed, Farcry 4, and any Zombie game ever - you play Kyle Crane. As an undercover operative for the GRE your goal is retrieve stolen information that could be dangerous to the world in the wrong hands. The game takes you in a solid story through the streets of Harran, where the Harran Virus has hit with devastating effect. While the virus can be suppressed with medications, no known cure exists. And of course, as with anytime people are in a crisis, someone is taking advantage of the entire scenario to run their own show. Watch out for thugs and infected as you apply your talents to help the survivor's grasp hope, while keeping the Government at bay.
The game starts out good. The infected are all completely OP compared to you at first, and the difficulty takes a slight decline quick. Gameplay speed increases as you get more familiar with your abilities and those of the infected. Dynamic gameplay gives you different gameplay at night vs. day. With loads of side missions and over 100 customizable weapons, brush up your skills to survive. Incorporating stamina into running and fighting helps keep the player from becoming too OP against the infected, and gives the infected a defined advantage that sticks through almost the entire game. Even the weakest of infected don't get tired. While the game plays and feels like a FPS, the main focus is melee weapons. The environment and the threat of infected gear the player to treat every step as a puzzle-trying to maintain the high ground to reach the goal.
The graphics were top notch, as they should be. Good effects and no issues with rendering the environment or buffering problems.
I have to say the gameplay reminded me of any FPS style game. But the multiplayer Co-op was what really made this game top-notch to me. Unlike other games there were no limitations on other players such as weapons/experience/distance. You and your friends can play the game, thats it. The only missions that were different were the beginning missions and the end mission. Having 4 players doesn't ruin the gameplay experience either. I found that while we were obviously harder to kill as a group, we were more liable to get a little ballsy during gameplay. Not to mention, some missions still killed the entire team more than a couple times before we were able to complete them.
To top everything off, Techland is celebrating the success of the game with plenty of additional content including new maps, quests, weapons, game modes, and more.

I apologize if this review doesn't seem accurate, or if you think it could have been written better. This is my first one, so feel free to let me know how I can improve this review, and I'll do my best to keep your advice in mind when writing future reviews, Thanks!)

When I played Grim Dawn in its very first iterations and act one, the content didn't exist, the itemization wasn't as in depth but as this game updated I sat silently until beta 29, content complete.
The only permanent choice is your two classes and the base points you put into them, all abilities within that class can be refunded for points to reallocate, or to put into your second class, if you chose one.
Itemization is nuts, you are constantly making tough choices between use abilities, procs, percent damage and all sorts of fluff. Its really in depth between components that you can slot one of on an item that only fit on certain item types, and aguments which are bought from factions that are seperate but go on certain slots as well. You are constantly looking for synergy between moves.
Do I need more fire damage, or should I stack more physical? Should I stack cast speed? Whats my energy regen like? This component gives a fireball on my gun, this would change everything!
Gameplay is similar to Titan Quest, but its better. It isn't as well, almost bland I felt Titan Quest could be at times. The enemies have a good mix between easy to kill lighter ones, and tougher enemies out of a crowd that youll learn to hate. I've been playing on Veteran difficulty, the second difficulty in the game which you can play on your first playthrough. Its very enjoyable, a challenge, and there are "roguelike" areas built into the game that you require rare crafting materials to create a key of sorts, and if you die inside said area you are kicked out.
This game has been an amazing coop experience full of challenge, choices, sharing, crazy item drops and being slammed by pain in the♥♥♥♥♥enemies.
My only gripes:
We had netcode issues where my friend would desync from me and not be able to see me.
Items would sometimes "float" for him in the air instead of being on the ground
A few crashes, especially bad on a one-time openable chest.
Medium settings are great, but High FX is poorly optimized and way too straining to run.
When you are done with certain quests where you have 0 uses for a quest item, they remain in your inventory until you throw them out - where they disappear before hitting the ground.
The worst one is there is no feedback for certain debuffs. Like being stunned. Its very bad in a ARPG with a hardcore mode to not even give you feedback on total control loss of your character!
All in All, I reccomend this game as someone who played Diablo II, Torchlight and Titan Quest. Its enjoyable and reminds me slightly of POE, without the worry of totally ruining your character with a bad build. There are definitely tough choices - but you won't have to destroy your character because of one ability!

Rush is a 3D puzzle game that requires high level perception as well as cognitive thinking to solve its overabundance of puzzles. In rush you used direction tiles as well as other types to guide cubes to exits. One of the top reason to buy Rush is the fact that there is no competition in this game. There is no clock to time you, there are no scores to obtain, it’s just your mind against puzzles. All these factors combined with a very soothing tune and you’re in for a very zen-like period while playing. This game hits perfection almost everywhere, the pacing is fantastic, the controls are intuitive, and the art direction is very relevant to the game. However, the game completely lacks replayability and all the puzzles have very limited solutions. This is because each puzzles have a fixed amount of tiles and in almost every scenario in Rush, you will end up using them all. Regardless, the game is very high quality and for such a cheap price replayability is a non-issue.

The Banner Saga is a game with an original concept that I would describe as a union between consequence heavy strategy games like Final Fantasy Tactics and a pioneering simulator like Oregon Trail where you have to manage resources and make hard decisions that effect your journey in unexpected ways.
On paper, this sounds amazing, especially when you start to be engrossed by the powerful artwork and storytelling of the designers.
Unfortunately, I've reached a kind of personal impasse with The Banner Saga, which ironically is due at least in part to the orginal intent of the designers.  The journey these characters are taking is meant to be bleak and arduous, and playing the game feels like an extention of this as the days slog on: you have been starving for weeks, the characters you've invested the most resources in have died inexplicably, and on top of it all, you face the endless hordes of monotonous battle vs the same enemies over and over and over again.
So for now, for my own sanity, despite my admiration of the creators intent and craft, I can't go on.  I can't help wondering if this is a personal flaw and not one of the games design.
(note:  the designers have a patch planned which will lower the difficulty of the notoriously difficult last battle)

I've gotten through the first boss and have really enjoyed it so far. The first boss was fairly straightforward once I realized I could shoot lasers from my boots, but still quite a challenge to beat without dying.
Which brings up the most interesting aspect of this game: The DIY difficulty. Any level can be completed by simply hammering through it and dying endlessly (all items collected are saved), but you'll only get one star. The other two are for not dying, or doing it under a certain time. I really liked this because it gave me a reason for going back, but also didn't halt my progress when I encountered a particularly difficult (for me) level. It's also much better than the seemingly arbitrary stars given out in Angry Birds.
As far as the mechanics go, I can safely say this game plays great with a keyboard and mouse. The controls are tight, and when I die it was annoyance with myself for rushing and not being careful, never with the game itself for being unfair.
Definitely recommend to regular and casual players alike, but if Super Meatboy is more your thing, this game (thankfully imo) is not that level of difficulty.

Having played through once around completely, I can honestly say I will hit it again in the future.  Being a fan of strategy games in general, this one has thus impressed me the most (even though it's been out for a few years).  But, let me sum it up:
Pros:  Just about everything, from the personnel and base management, to the strategic selection of encounters, while balancing out the needs of the planet vs the needs of the base.  The battles themselves are a test of your thinking skills to the highest degree - what do you need to kill first, who can you use to bring it down, how many other enemies are there, how many shots left til you need to reload . . . this is the unsung epic of warfare:  strategy and balance.  Music scores and event sounds are excellent, conveying a definite sense of desperation from mission to mission.
Cons:  This is more about the little gripes as opposed to anything that really stands out.  While the playing fields are good, there doesn't seem to be much camera control when you're shifting levels (ie moving from base floor to roof/next floor) and the viewing gets a bit confusing or clunky.  An interface to select what level of the field you're viewing would be beyond helpful.  Same with units, cycling or selecting units doesn't always give you a full idea of everyone's status at once (tabbing through your team can get tedious, and sometimes the click on unit function will get wacky with the level issues too).
Overall, after playing through this game, I finally understand how frustrated LT. Gorman was in ALIENS . . . and even though you get a few disasters through the missions, you realize that to stop fighting is the only true death.  Good luck, Commanders.

The core gameplay is satisfying but there isn't enough that complements it and keeps it interesting.  The majority of maps are static and non-interactable (you can't climb ladders, lots of objects aren't destructible), the design is the same; layout with multiple entry points and some doors you can weld shut.
The classes have perks that differentiate them a litte, but really, they all do the same thing.  I don't feel like the medic is any less proficient at killing than a berserker, and really I often see medic and support classes with the highest number of kills.
There's a severe lack of content.  I've seen comments complaining about this that date back 9 months, with people saying "There are only two bosses?  Don't worry they'll introduce more in time."  Well, at this stage, it seems unlikely.
They seem to be relying on user made maps to fill the content gap.  Meanwhile, their microtransaction cosmetic store is full to the brim with hilariously over priced hats and costumes.  Gee, I wonder what's going on there?
After a few hours you'll start to realize that all matches pretty much play the same.  Everyone clumps up and slaughters everything.  Maybe some strategy is required in the highest difficulty settings, but playing on "Hard" everyone seems to do fine just running in circles and blindly killing everything.  It's repetitive and dull.
At full price this game doesn't justify its cost.  Maybe on sale.

This is the true spiritual successor to the Baldur's Gate series.  Earlier reviews, such as those of SunsetAmethyst and Darkreaver1980, detail what that means.  I won't repeat their analyses.  Moreover, the game developers seem to be constantly tweaking and expanding the game in ways that improve an already outstanding product.
I had never heard of this game or Larian.  I stumbled across the game a few days ago while randomly searching through popular games on Steam.  After reading several reviews I purchased it, and was astonished (in a good way) soon after I started playing.  I loved the combination of character development, story quality, and rich combat strategy in the Baldur's Gate series, and had never quite found it again until now.
But to simply equate this game with that earlier all-time great is a bit of an injustice to Divinity: Original Sin (DOS).  Combat in DOS is very environmentally interactive.  Spells interact with one another and with the environment in creative and powerful ways, somewhat like Bioware tried to accomplish with Dragon Age, but much more comprehensively and with much greater fluidity in DOS.  DOS also is somewhat open world and rewards the player for exploration.  I say "somewhat" open world, because even though you seem to be able to go anywhere at any time, your party will die quickly to a higher level enemy if you venture into a wrong area too early in the game.  Enemies seem not to scale to the player's level (which is very good in my opinion), and I haven't yet been able to beat a group of enemies more than a couple of levels above that of my characters.
Finally, I have grown very tired of the stale, uncreative, possibly lazy game formula based around the "trinity" of tank, damage dealer, and healer.  I've been pleasantly surprised to find that I can play this game equally well either with or without that formula, which makes for what I think will be almost endless replay value.
I have no major complaints against the game.  The gameplay itself is great, the sound effects and graphics are well done, and the voice acting is outstanding.  The camera on the other hand is sometimes annoying.  I can't rotate it sufficiently to see items along some corners and walls (the game does allow the camera to be unlocked, but advises against doing so).  That's fixable by switching to the overhead camera, but still it's annoying.  The layout of some of the buttons also could be better.  Some of them are extremely small, and others are in odd locations in the interface.  For instance, I thought that it was impossible to delay a character's action during a turn until I finally saw a tiny button near the flee from battle (retreat) button on the edge of the screen, rather than near the bottom of the screen with the other buttons that control combat actions.  These are minor though, and have not detracted from my enjoyment of the game.
If that's not enough, they've released the tool set they used to create the game.  I've tinkered with it a bit, and can't wait to see (and play) what talented people develop with it.
The folks at Larian rock.  In the game manual, the head of the company states that this is the game that the company always wanted to make, but was prohibited from doing so by its publisher overlords.  If this is an example of the type of product they'll be producing, then I'll be buying everything they release from now on just to support them.

Short & dirty: This is a FUN and short indie platformer with some arcade style thrown in.
The game doesn't pretend to be anything else and runs smooth. The characters don't bring much difference except in maximum stats. Would have been cooler if certain weapons were restricted and that certain ways to complete levels were character restricted but hey that's what a sequel is for :P I enjoyed it.
Long & clean:
What really appealed about this game was it was NOT a zombie game. It was about plant based monsters. FInally a sub-genre in the monster genre that has barely been touched. Apart from Triffids most people don't see Monster Plants as a threat. When was the last time it was used? Mario? What they did here was great.
You only see about 8 or 9 monster types but still they are fun to fight.
The graphics aren't anything to rave about but they do the job and look great for the platformer. Runs fine on both low and high rigs. Didn't notice any graphics glitches or bugs and did not encounter any invisible walls or such.
The sounds are decent enough. After a while the smash & squash sounds tend to become repetitive but realistically it doesn't distract that much and I was more focused on getting combos than listening to see if the splatter noise was going to repeat this time.
The gameplay is fun. At first it feels a little meh and annoying but the replayability is what brought me back. As I gained new skills and weapons my combos got higher and higher and I wanted to push myself to see how fast I could finish the level or how high my score could be.
The level design is decent but it IS repetitive. You get 2 x Subway levels, 2 x Theme park levels and guess what... yep 2 x School levels. The tutorial level wasn't too bad and I would have liked to see more as you pick up guns and get more wacky skills it would have been cool to have a mini-tutorial level instead to teach you how to use them effectively.
Good luck getting all the achievements. Not sure how anyone is supposed to get 200K point combos. I've read there has  been a lot of hacking and cheating and if that's what people have to do I guess it's their way... except all they've achieved is cheat... they didn't gain anything. Because you know getting Steam Achievements is totally going to get you laid and a high paying job. Losers.
Anyway I liked it a lot. I got it cheap on the sales and suggest the same for anyone with budget concerns but otherwise totally get it and play with friends it's a lot more fun and easier.

This is an amazing ARPG.
It has been a while since I have achieved that Diablo-II-esque high of loot and progression. A lot of games have tried - Diablo III failing pretty hard straight out of the gate - and have not even come close. Path of Exile was hit or miss with a lot of people, as the game engine is rather basic and only recently has the desync bug been resolved. Grim Dawn is the exception to all of these blunders.
You feel like you're discovering something new around every corner. When you find a unique item, it's actually very powerful and rewarding. The progression systems are also very cool. Since it's modeled somewhat off of Titan quest, it really is a build-your-own-class type of character progression. However, it's not too complicated - such as, say, Path of Exile's skill tree system - so you can jump right in without feeling the need to read a bunch of guides on optimal tree paths.
Without beeing too shallow in comparisons, it's not exactly a modernized Diablo II, but it definitely captures the intrigue and skinner box glory of old. Highly recommend if you are a fan of the action RPG genre.

One of the best games I've played in a while.  The combat system is simple but not boring, and not too easy (plus you can change the difficulty).  The characters you build, what traits you improve, and how you use them, are important in each battle.  You might feel you perfect the battle system after a while but I ended up getting to the end of the game, and unable to win the last battle.  I was not wanting the game to be over so quickly anyway so I just started again.  Every decision you make will have real consequences - sometimes even ending the game.  And as I saw when starting again, the decisions really do make a difference...it's not a cosmetic feature.  Although there's almost no voice acting, the story is good, the animation is great, the music is fitting, and I found myself enjoying the characters and not wanting to stop playing.

This beautiful game draws a lot of inspiration from Norse Mythology, being set in a frozen continent, inhabited by humans and a race of horned giants called Varl. It's a world where the gods disappeared and the sun stopped moving. You play as a couple separate groups of people, traveling from place to place in this world, coming into conflict with and trying to outrun an army of sentient stone statues called The Dredge who have started invading from the north, and trying to survive in what many believe to be the end times.
The name of the game comes from a recurring motif within the game's story. Every clan of people in this world has in its possession a magical banner, which has been enchanted to continue spinning and weaving itself of its own accord. In its own body, it weaves words and pictures, telling the story of the clan who carries it. Many of these banners have been passed down from clan leaders over generations, and thus have grown very long. Due to story events, you are now tasked with carrying your clan's banner, and all of your deeds, good and ill, will be woven into its body. What kind of saga will your banner tell?
Gameplay combines elements from several different genres. Combat is reminiscent of tactical RPGs, such as Final Fantasy Tactics or Disgaea. Combat is turned based and takes place on a grid. You can decide which characters from your party to use (all of which have unique classes) and equip them and level up their stats as you see fit.
Story sections are more reminiscent of Japanese Visual Novel games, or Bioware games like Dragon Age or Mass Effect, with static character images conversing with each other, and branching dialogue trees. You hear it advertised all the time, but this is one game where the choices you make really do have consequences, sometimes even life and death consequences for your party members which you may not see until much later, so take your time and choose wisely.
Finally, the sections in between story and combat take inspiration from, of all things, The Oregon Trail. Most of the time you and your caravan will be traveling between major cities and settlements, and it's your job to keep your party well-fed and happy, amidst a number of random events happening on the way. The more of your party you can keep alive and in good spirits, the easier your time will be in the other game sections.
The one resource in the game is renown, gained by performing great deeds in battle and in life. This is what you will use to level up your characters, buy items for those characters, and buy supplies for your caravan. Because of this, you have to balance how you spend your resources. If you spend too much in one area, the others will suffer. If you buy too many items for your characters, you won't be able to level them up, and if you spend too much on leveling them up, you won't have enough to buy supplies at the next town, and your caravan may run out of food and start to starve on the way to its next destination (which may lead to the death of some of your characters). This makes gameplay challenging and interesting, and lends itself to a lot of replayability.
And finally, the Don-Bluth-inspired artwork and orchestral soundtrack are both simply gorgeous.
So yes, even if the game isn't on sale at the moment, it's well worth the price.

The quickest way to describe the gameplay would be a cross between FTL and Fire Emblem. When you're not engaged in turn-based combat a la Fire Emblem, you travel through the overworld of the game in a caravan, in which you must keep track of supplies and morale, choose when to rest, choose when to fight and when to run, etc, sort of like traveling in FTL. While traveling in the caravan, you'll be confronted with random events, to which you can choose from a list of responses which may have great effects on your game, such as permadeath of a playable character, or an unexpected loss of supplies and subsequent starvation of NPCs, which will make combat harder in the future. I found out during my second playthrough that the majority of these events are not actually random, but it had little effect on my opinion of the game. The events that aren't random are scripted so as to better serve the storytelling, which is the main attraction of this game. The art and storytelling are beautifully done. The dialogue has subtleties and develops the characters well, and the constant threat of losing characters as well as the setting and conflict of the game (which I won't spoil) create a very convincing sense of desperation as you attempt to survive. The story is not very long, but it is high quality and will be continued by two future titles, I believe. There are some parts of this game that are unpolished, such as a few quality of life features that are missing from the combat sequences, and, occasionally, text that doesn't match the events taking place. Overall, if you're looking for an immersive single-player experience filled with colorful and relatable characters, this will be worth your money. If you're looking for a deep turn-based strategy game, this is not it.

I would say almost better than the first with some exceptions.
tl;dr KF2 is worth it if you liked KF or if you want to try something similar to LFD2
I can't really say one is better than the other but if I had to pick one, I would say KF2. KF has more content simply because it's been out since 2009 and KF2 has CSGO style of case-opening so there's a point for the original 'Floor..... But I wouldn't say that's necessarily a good thing.
The classes that existed in the game are not truly better or worse in this game as the class-specific weaponry seemed to be more enjoyable in a couple of ways... Commando, for example had more variety it seemed in weapons; tier 1 being the starting weapon: bullpup (L85a2), tier 2 having 4 weapons (DLC dependent :c) (M4, AK, Thompson SMG, Thompson Steampunk), and Tier 3 (FN FAL and Scar Mk 17). KF2 closes the content gap with its new and improved leveling system where the weapons are more heavily affected by how you outfit the class through perks.
I enjoyed the M4 and AK so when I learned the M4 became a pistol-caliber varmint rifle, I hung my head in sorrow. But where this game lacks in pain-staking (in)consequential detail, it thrives in the dynamics of the class compared to the first. KF had singular leveling, levels 1-6 increasing in level by doing determined damage or specific zed kills (like Commando had to reach certain Stalker kills, Support needed door-welding, Sharpshooters needed headshots etc.). KF2 has 25 levels with perks gained every 5 levels. These perks add more interactions to the zeds (KF didn't have ZED-Time specific bonuses or special interactions like parrying attacks) so I would say it's an improvement overall. It also has "time-specific" perks like upgrades to knife and pistol to buff your first 3-4 waves at the expense of some buff to stronger weapons.
This is just one example, but I would say that 90% of this game is the first game's charm but improved on a technical level.

The gameplay storyline is rather short compared to Saints Row III, mainly trying too hard to get players to link back from the past to end off the main antagonist. Shops now doesn't requires money to own them, but rather solving puzzles through hacking. Only certain story quests allows for Co-Op missions, and few activities. There's lots of jumping tower quests that seems too mundane. I spent more time jumping into the air for travelling than gunfights.
On the technical note, I sense this game was published too early. Ragdoll system are too bugged this time round, compared to the SRIII. Especially when there's a warp portal between them, models starts to go haywired and stretched. Making you unable to aim their heads perfectly.
If you like funny open-world gameplay with superpowers, you will like this. If not just go for GTAV instead, with a more logical realistic gameplay. I'd recommend buy Saints Row IV, only if there's a Saints Row III and IV bundle at a cheap deal.

A good way to describe RUSH would be to say that it's a cross between SpaceChem and EDGE (except, of course, that it predates both of those games). It has a similar emphasis as the former on what's essentially visual programming, and also features the latter's basic gameplay mechanic of cubes rolling around on a 3-dimensional playing field. The result is an enjoyable puzzle game that can keep you occupied for hours. While the puzzles are much less open-ended than the ones in SpaceChem and thus provide less replay value, the solutions can, at times, provide considerable satisfaction from just looking at them, with large numbers of colourful cubes rolling around in sync with each other. Recommended for all puzzle game fans.

If World Keepers had some voice acting and a half-competent script, then it could have been an awesome hidden object adventure: gameplay is challenging, there are plenty of interesting locations, and the puzzles are fun.
World Keepers: The Last Resort has only one problem, but it is a huge one: it feels like as if a little kid wrote it. The story cannot keep any focus as we wander from place to place, while reading dialogues that were likely cringe inducing even in their native language, let alone this butchering of the English language of a translation.
Ironically, the plot itself is good: we play as a female pirate captain who embarks on a quest of stopping Ancient Evil (its actual name), which serves as a good excuse to visit a plethora of interesting and beautiful locations.
The gameplay also shows several signs of great design, especially with the difficulty of the point ‘n’ click segments and in the puzzle variety. It falters a bit at hidden object scenes, since there are only seven of those, but the rest could easily make up for it, if the story would not constantly ruin the mood with its horrible lines.

This is one of those casual games that is technically considered a Hidden Object Game, but is trying to hide it as much as possible - it's a lot more adventuring and environmental puzzles with only a minimum of HOG screens. It's very cutesy (the World Keepers are little animated Kewpie dolls that look a bit like sackboy and have more personality than you'd expect for this style of game). Many recent Indie games I tried felt like unfinished, half baked products by lazy developers who've been trying to ride a trend for some easy money and fame, leaving me feel cheated and disappointed. Not The Banner Saga, though. This game looks like a lof ot talent, effort and hard work had been poured into it, and that alone, in my book, means a lot.
The Banner Saga is a tactical Strategy RPG with a deep, intense story. The graphics and soundtrack are great, but what I like the most here, is the story. The atmosphere of the game is really dark, as the story is about a violent and bloody war. There's a lot of death, injuries, bloodshed and grief. Some people might consider such a setting to be problematic or even inappropriate for such a game, but I kind of like it. It's a refreshing look on things, at the very least. Just don't expect too many rainbows and unicorns. :)
Another good aspect of the game, in my opinion, is the choices. Some people complain they don't have enough influence on the game. While I agree that it would be great if the choices had more weight, I think they do offer enough replayability value. Going through the game just once hardly feels like all there is to it, as I know if left me quite curious to play again, make different decisions and see where it leads me.
As for the strategy part of the game, it's certainly one of the better parts of the game for me. The battle system is simple to learn (should be almost intuitive for anyone who's ever played such games before), but seems to have enough depth and balance to be appealing and interesting. It kind of reminds me of the battle system in Expeditions: Conquistador (another great tactical RPG, btw).
As of now I haven't beaten the game, but I did get to the final battle. I ended up losing quite a few times, after which I simply got frustrated and gave up. I restarted the game, got kind of half-way before losing a mid-game battle and getting a 'Game Over'. The reason I'm describing all this, is to point out what I consider to be the only two real problems I have (or used to have) with the game:
1) At the time, the difficulty level of the final battle was much higher than anything else you encountered during the game, and I don't mean "slightly" or "moderately" higher (which would make sense, considering it's the final battle), I mean it was REALLY much more difficult. I know many people have been complaining about this, enough to have the developers address and fix this issue, which probably means it should be okay now.
2) The game is somewhat vague regarding the consequence of losing a battle. In most cases, if you lose a battle you can still continue playing, but you suffer some negative consequences. In a few specific battles, though, losing means getting  a "Game Over". It means you can get back to your last save and try again, but you don't get to continue playing despite the loss, as you would after losing a normal battle. This wouldn't be a problem for me, btw, if the game was clear about the rules. I'd expect to get at least a clue, that I'm facing a critical battle that I must win in order to survive. Well, the game doesn't give you anything to indicate there's a difference.
Despite those two problems, I really like the game. It's one of the better games I encountered during the last few years. I'm kind of disappointed I didn't get to beat the game yet, but I did really enjoy playing it, regardless.
EDIT (March/31/2016): By now I've managed to win the final battle and beat the game on 'normal' (the medium difficulty level). While I'm happy to have finally succeeded, I still feel the spike in the difficulty level was too much.

Turn-based combat RPG with interesting story, decision-making and combat system.

The combat system involves armor and health/strength. Losing health diminishes the strength of a character, and losing armor means they are more vulnerable. If strength is too low itll be hard to attack an enemy with higher armor level. First time Ive seen such a system in a game and it makes for more thoughtful and careful play. As I began figuring out the system my enjoyment of combat increased a lot as I began to make the right decisions and win more battles. For example, archers arent very strong against armored enemy, but they can plink away at armor whilst the melee character moves in - once both have broken they can both finish off the enemy quick.
Also theres a practice battle option which provides random set of enemies. It doesnt improve or injure your heroes, just practice. These are usually harder than what you face in the normal game, allowing you to improve a lot and learn how to beat the odds. Playing on the hardest difficulty is essential I think otherwise you might find it too easy. If you like the game's combat is a good addition and adds a bit more to the game's challenge. You can also change how many heroes you go into the battles with so that can make it more of a challenge and make you a better player.

In a game that makes me think of mashing together Assassin's Creed, Farcry 4, and any Zombie game ever - you play Kyle Crane. As an undercover operative for the GRE your goal is retrieve stolen information that could be dangerous to the world in the wrong hands. The game takes you in a solid story through the streets of Harran, where the Harran Virus has hit with devastating effect. While the virus can be suppressed with medications, no known cure exists. And of course, as with anytime people are in a crisis, someone is taking advantage of the entire scenario to run their own show. Watch out for thugs and infected as you apply your talents to help the survivor's grasp hope, while keeping the Government at bay.
The game starts out good. The infected are all completely OP compared to you at first, and the difficulty takes a slight decline quick. Gameplay speed increases as you get more familiar with your abilities and those of the infected. Dynamic gameplay gives you different gameplay at night vs. day. With loads of side missions and over 100 customizable weapons, brush up your skills to survive. Incorporating stamina into running and fighting helps keep the player from becoming too OP against the infected, and gives the infected a defined advantage that sticks through almost the entire game. Even the weakest of infected don't get tired. While the game plays and feels like a FPS, the main focus is melee weapons. The environment and the threat of infected gear the player to treat every step as a puzzle-trying to maintain the high ground to reach the goal.
The graphics were top notch, as they should be. Good effects and no issues with rendering the environment or buffering problems.
I have to say the gameplay reminded me of any FPS style game. But the multiplayer Co-op was what really made this game top-notch to me. Unlike other games there were no limitations on other players such as weapons/experience/distance. You and your friends can play the game, thats it. The only missions that were different were the beginning missions and the end mission. Having 4 players doesn't ruin the gameplay experience either. I found that while we were obviously harder to kill as a group, we were more liable to get a little ballsy during gameplay. Not to mention, some missions still killed the entire team more than a couple times before we were able to complete them.
To top everything off, Techland is celebrating the success of the game with plenty of additional content including new maps, quests, weapons, game modes, and more.

Ricochet is truly an underrated masterpiece.
You play as an unnamed warrior, sent into outer space with no weapons or supplies, leaving you to scavenge loose discs left from broken ships. You learn to use these discs to fend off against enemies. The thing about this game, though, is its primary theme of isolation. Rarely will you encounter other forms of life, creating a lonely, brooding atmosphere, perfect for the game's outer space setting. For its price, I highly recommend Ricochet. Definitely Valve's greatest achievement.

Saints Row IV has came back from the previous storyline, now overthrown by alien community. The gameplay storyline is rather short compared to Saints Row III, mainly trying too hard to get players to link back from the past to end off the main antagonist. Deep Silver has used by the same Steelport map, just minor asset changes. Saints Row IV still maintains its cheeky humour jokes as the story unfolds. The game can seem rather repetitive after you have maxed up most of your superpower skills to dominate the towns. The superpowers are overpowered, even without the weapons fully upgraded. For example, owning a vehicle now seems meaningless, with unlimited stamina speed and glide mode.
Shops now doesn't requires money to own them, but rather solving puzzles through hacking. Only certain story quests allows for Co-Op missions, and few activities. There's lots of jumping tower quests that seems too mundane. I spent more time jumping into the air for travelling than gunfights.
On the technical note, I sense this game was published too early. Ragdoll system are too bugged this time round, compared to the SRIII. Especially when there's a warp portal between them, models starts to go haywired and stretched. Making you unable to aim their heads perfectly.
If you like funny open-world gameplay with superpowers, you will like this. If not just go for GTAV instead, with a more logical realistic gameplay. I'd recommend buy Saints Row IV, only if there's a Saints Row III and IV bundle at a cheap deal.

I both love and hate this game. I really didn't think I was going to get it at first simply because the turn based combat was a red flag for me. A friend of mine ended up gifting me the game and I can say that I'm very happy for that. My initial concerns about the combat disappeared after a few hours and I got used to it. The game has a huge amount of qualities which make it very interesting and fun. To list a few: Skill combinations inside and outside of combat, unique uses of skills, rewarding exploration, interesting side quests, rich lore, absolutely zero hand holding, and I can go on.
If you have no interest in reading, having to remember details, writing down reminders for yourself or simply want an easy game to quickly beat and mark off the list... well this game isn't going to be for you. Many aspects of this game are very rewarding, but it also punishes you.. secret traps, games of chance, and a wide variety of other insta death mechanics are virtually everywhere in the game. There is a feeling of ambiguity which envelops the entirety of the game, this is something I enjoy a lot but many people seem to hate; a prime example being the completion of hard puzzle which the rewards at the end are completely trash.
Now the game isn't without problems. I've run into many bugs, issues of movement, and not all of the billions of lines of dialogue are interesting. There are faults to be had, but there is something about this game which keeps you playing. A feeling I have not felt in a long time.. even the more boring content is bearable. I often found myself going to a new area, and spending hours talking, reading and exploring.. and at first it wasn't very exciting but something about the game gives you a special compulsion to carry on and unlock all those hidden bits of content. The game is still a little rough around the edges, but once you look passed that it is a very nice game which lives up its universe.
Overall I would give it an easy 8/10, which some bug fixing it could probably reach a 9. I feel many of the issues I have in some game designs will probably be solved in future patches or mods.

The first half or so of the game I loved the experience. Then the realism of what was going on hit me, a big fat smack of nostalgia. DOS has some redeeming qualities, and way more issues. If Larian fixes them, it could be a great game, but as it stands right now, the game is riddled with bizarre design decisions, frustrating mechanics (like the clearly broken rock-paper-scissor argument system), and progression blocking issues. The most infuriating of these was the final battle, where an NPC is with you and places herself at the front lines, where the final boss will launch a salvo of attacks and can kill her before you're allowed to do anything, losing the game.
Then there are countless other annoyances that make little sense, and terrible balance. Numerous skills have literally no use to the player in any difficulty, while others are so vital not having them can make the game unmanageable. The crafting system is a neat idea bogged down by it's borderline worthlessness. Clearly not enough thought was put into many systems, and this game needed more time in beta to work out the kinks.

RUSH is, with ease, one of my favorite puzzle games. It brings nothing groundbreaing to the table, but it has no major flaws and avoids most things I don't like in a puzzle game, the biggest one being time constraints. It's a basic game where you direct the paths of cubes in a 3d enviroment, guiding them to a path and preventing collision. The wall mechanic is a clever addition that gives the little extra depth to push it over the top, adding an unexpected level of complexity. I like the graphical choices they have made a lot, and there is enough puzzles to keep you playing for a while. The difficulty of the levels vary a lot, and should have something that will challenge anyone. There is a group requirement to access the bonus levels, which is something I'm not terribly fond of, but the rest of the game is stellar. The music is also great.

This casual point-and-click adventure is not great, but is enjoyable. There are only a handful of easy hidden-object scenes, and the puzzles are for the most part trivial -- expect one that is brutally difficult in “hard” mode (I had to switch to easy for that one).
The good things going for it are some adorable characters (no voice acting, just written dialog) and a pleasant narrative flow. Unfortunately the graphics are rather mediocre, and there is a weird resolution glitch: the scenes are all too big for the screen, so you have to scroll up and down with a mouse click. It's very easy to click and drag by mistake and create a nausea-inducing effect. There is nothing hidden up or down, so this annoying “feature” provides no gameplay value.
There are better games in this genre, but this one is nice enough.

Mirror's Edge is a beautiful game and a great concept set in a futuristic society bordering on dystopia. The world is incredibly stylized, the controls are fluid, and the puzzles are great. There are even quite a few moments that will get the adrenaline pumping. The only place it falters is with the flat characters, it seems like a shame to waste such a potentially rich overworld on a somewhat bland story.
That being said, it was a fun game and worth the price considering I picked it up on sale. I would suggest it to anybody looking for a challenge that is completely fresh that isn't looking for a 60+ hour affair.

The Banner Saga, is an imersive tale steeped in the mythos of Nord culture. The game thrusts you into a world in which your decisions have weight effecting the story and the events that ocurr, creating  real emotive connections with the charachters. The beauty in the animation of the game, comparable to the old disney classics, especially The Sword in the Stone, is unique and imediatly intregues and grips the player. In terms of gamplay the chess like combat sequences are tense due to the weight they have, which occurs due to the foundation of imersion. Although to an extent repetitive there is enough charachter progression and variety to keep the player gripped, however the real stregth in the Banner Saga is its mythical setting, aethetic design and overall imersive feel which keeps the player wanting more. The game feels like an old nordic saga, a saga which has not yet been written, a saga in which the player still controls his fate.

Awesome game anybody who likes story driven games must play this. The game is gorgeous to look at with simple yet interested combat however its main strengh lies in the art work and the emotional story.

The story is silly but interesting. It has many inconsistencies but it's fine as a whole. The gameplay is OK(ish). There are quite a few bugs but they aren't very annoying. You can solve everything without having to use any hint and you don't feel the need to skip any puzzle. In general, the puzzles are logical and quite straightforward with a few exceptions.
IMPORTANT HINT:
There is an issue with the last puzzle involving a clock where the position of one of the clock hands is not where you might think it is supposed to be and many people end up skipping that part and fail to get the achievement for finishing the game without skipping any puzzle.
That puzzle is solvable. It's just that the smaller clock hand must have a small offset to the right, from the 12 o'clock position, so the arrow doesn't point towards the golden dot but rather towards the right segment of the stone portion that is above it. This is not a bug. If you have an analog clock around, set the same time and have a look at the smaller clock hand position and you'll see the hand has the same offset in reality.
All in all, the game was enjoyable and I recommend it.
TL;DR: It's not a "must play" type of game but rather a "might play" one. In other words, if you play it, chances are you'll have some fun and you won't feel like you wasted your time for nothing.

Ricochet to me at first was that game VALVe made that they didn't like to talk about. That they wished people didn't remember. I could see why; it was a really small, simple, low def game. in other words to some people, trash. I'm not really sure when I got ricochet, as it was probably included in a counter-strike pack of sorts. I recently held a LAN party with 2 of my friends and we didn't really have any multi-player games to play, so jokingly I said "Hey guys, let's play Ricochet!" As luck would have it, they had the game too, so we installed and played it. My first impression of this small, 3-map game was "This is gonna suck" but as time went on, we all had a blast laughing at the low-quality screams of falling into a huge pink spinning vortex after being hit in the face by a high-speed disk. If you choose to buy Ricochet, get it in a pack where it's just an included game and don't expect any online servers; rather, play with some good friends and I assure you you'll have a great time.

is a side-scroller beat-em-up game that combines platforming, horror and button-mashing. Better said by R.L. Stine, " Viewers Beware, You're in for a Scare!" this game follows the misadventures of four different protagonists, characters and their story through a high school reunion. The stakes are high and fulfilling objectives does come at a great cost. What is that cost exactly? If you guessed monsters that aggravate you until you want to tear your eyes out, then indeed you were right. Will you choose to play as either Brutal Joe, Nathan, Cassy or Sean? Brutal Joe is a former quarterback for his high school football team that has the size and strength to take on the big brutes. He is just your normal high school jock that likes partying, probably hanging with women and is good with mano-a-mano (hand-to-hand) combat. Nathan is your common nerd that enjoys computers and other technology while keeping up with the latest tech that comes out.
Likewise, of most geeks, he was bullied in school. His advantage is explosives instead of melee weapons as a result. Cassy is the only female of the group, I know, odd isn't it? She is your normal red-head priss queen that cares about her looks, is a great dancer and loves close-range and long-range combat whom dresses in denim jeans, the kind that is boot-cut or loose with a street punk look. Sean on the other hand loves guns but prefers long-range more. Unfortunately, we don't know much about his characteristics nor personality. Welcome to Final Exam, where if you don't make it, it will be your final exam.

When you begin, the music on the main menu serves as the preface for the theme and exposition of the game. It gives you a hint of what to expect and leaves you wanting more before you delve into the actual content of the game.
soundtrack on the main menu, the first song, has a very illuminescent, old-school horror style theme characterized by teen high school horror films of the mid to late 1990's. I love it, it has a
vibe but instead of more calm, synthesized piano ballads at first, it adds a touch of harder drums, metal and then purports itself toward a nice bass with a calm array of 1980's , 1990's horror American goodness without it being overtly oversaturated throughout the other tracks chosen as background music for the game.
The graphics are presented in comic-strip format, something you will see in any modern-day comics. It uses cutscenes after you fulfill certain objectives to progress the storyline along. It is linear going from area to area such as the subway to the amusement park and so on. I am thankful for this addition because it works well for the beat-em-up genre. If the story was non-linear, the game's score would be ruined because it would not fit well. The story tells us more about what has happened to the group, band of misfits we play as in order to understand why we are placed in the setting, objectives and environment we are currently located in.
Local co-op is your normal co-op where another player can join in for couch co-op or you can play the single-player missions alone by yourself. 2-player local is where each player is given separate lives as normal. This means if your partner dies, you can revive your partner when you are down. 2-player local co-op works the same as 4-player drop-in/drop-out co-op does.

The objective based missions are the selling point of this game and where it shines the most. Sure, the story is nice but let us be honest, most of us that look for a good game to play in the beat-em-up genre will be more focused on the controls and environment, gameplay than we will the story. Even if the story was taken out, this game would still be fun and could still be justified at its current pricing point as an arcade beat-em-up. The objective based missions are so perfectly aligned, that they tie into the whole story (e.g. Usually you will be escorting someone that has some type of trade such as repairing doors, garages or working well as a mechanic etc... then you will also have to save hostages at times across different levels). Based on the short amount I got done right now, I can't say if this consistency carries over to the other missions. I would believe so since majority of the game is rescuing people, escorting people and interacting with objects; lifting and picking up objects to move on to new areas(missions).


I used a controller, Xbox 360 controller to play this so I can't say how well the keyboard controls work. The controls with the controller work very well and are responsive. The only thing I have had some problems with is going downstairs because having to press the left control stick and then B, it can get confusing until you get used to it after a while.

The mechanics are the same that you would expect from a normal beat-em-up game. You need to perform different combos in order to execute different moves and eliminate enemies quicker. If you have a large horde of enemies coming straight for you, at times, it is better to dodge then going full front-line in the thick of the battle. You have ground based enemies, kamikazes which are exploding enemies and enemies that can fly such as the catcher, splitter and hornets. You are given medipacks sometimes when defeating enemies which is represented by a hamburger and fries. You are given a total of three lives, so, if you don't survive for long you can go through these rather quickly.

RUSH is one of those games that sneaks up on you in terms of difficulty. It starts out simply enough- here's some cubes, get them to the exit, here's some arrows to make them go in directions. By the time you realize it, you're threading slower-moving cubes between waves of advancing ones with precision timing, tossing cubes down holes with no visible exit, teleporting around with wild abandon, and even solving a puzzle in complete darkness (check the bonus levels, it's really there). If you like puzzle games, give this a shot, if only for the catchy soundtrack.
Heck, if you're going to get it, go for the whole Two Tribes pack and enjoy Toki Tori and EDGE with it.
PROS:
Great soundtrack
Difficulty scales up nicely over time
Hints for those puzzles you just can't figure out
Cheap
CONS:
No hints for the Actual Challenge levels (but then again, this was part of the Potato Sack ARG, so that would make it too easy.)
Limited replay value (unless you really want to shoot for cheevos)

First off, this game is amazing. Great visuals, great story, combat system that is fairly entertaining (not terribly deep, though the character abilities can really change up your playstyle), and a score that, while it isn't as expansive as I would like, is fantastic. Don't read a walkthrough your first time through the game, just pick the decisions for story/random events the way you think is best. These decisions you make may not change the grand scope of what happens, but they leave you agonizing over which decision you think would be best, and they do have an effect on who lives and dies, and many other factors. Characters are fantasic.
Now, I need to mention the things I disliked. While I liked the oregon trail aspect of keeping your caravan going, it is annoying that, outside of story events or random events, you can only get food using the same currency as you use to upgrade your troops. Would have preferred an additional option to get food along the way, maybe go hunting or something, idk. Just felt there wasn't much proactive you could do on that front.
Also, the music, as mentioned above, is excellent, but there isn't enough of it. Tracks do get repeated, though not so much that it got on my nerves. And again, it is great music.
The story ends at a good enough point to have some conclusion before the next installment, but I can't help but feel it ended a bit too soon.
The clansmen were really just a useless number. I kept them alive and fed because that's what I wanted my character to do, but there seemed to be little incentive to save people besides "be a decent person". Maybe that was intentional? Fighters and Varl only matter in battles, which is kinda lacking, but it still rewards you for keeping your warriors alive so that your subsequent battles are easier.
I also encountered a few bugs. Nothing serious or game breaking, but one is at the end, to activiate an ability that is needed to advance, I fulfilled the requirements (reduced the target's armor to the point that I wouldn't miss), but it wouldn't let me use it. Reloaded and tried again, worked just fine. Another happened only in battles I had Egil in, but the character it happened to wasn't constant. I would order a character to move or attack, and suddenly they would move in the OPPOSITE direction and end their turn. This only happened to me rarely, but still irked me.
Still, I loved it. Played it twice (three times if you count when I lost my save data [my fault] and restarted).
Edit: A few things I'd like to add. First, the lore is fantastic, a lot of thought went into creating the places, people, and things in the world.
Also, if you like Fire Emblem, I'd highly recommend this game. I like it better than Fire Emblem, because characters don't permadie if they fall in battle. I felt like having that happen in Fire Emblem necessitated restarting the chapter, as you'd miss out on any character specific convos, endings, etc, all because a stupid enemy critted a 11% chance to hit, 3% chance to crit. Banner Saga, if people die, it's because of decisions you made.

This is an amazing work of art, for starters. To keep it brief as can be, it's Oregon Trail in terms of "Watch something move across a horizon while waiting for♥♥♥♥♥♥to go wrong that needs your attention".
It isn't as ruthless and esoteric as the problems you would face in Oregon Trail, but it doesn't pull its punches. People will die, it will be your fault, and you will struggle with the guilt and shame to the very end. "Could I have done better? Could I have saved so many people's lives?" is a question that lingers with me after completion.
That's a good point to say the game is brief. It's part 1 of a trilogy. I had no idea until a google search pulled up that information. In regards to a first act this is quite the package. It ends so abruptly, but it couldn't end on a more painful and lingering note that demands you look forward to sequels.
Aside from the scenarioes requesting your tense attention, there are several tactics-RPG style combat episodes. Enough to not feel like the game is void of tactic content, but also scattered enough to feel it does not take the role of being a tactics game first, before good story telling. The tactics depth in this game may not be as diverse as titles like Disgaea in terms of units and customization, however it is a brilliantly done experience. You'll find yourself forced to pace out a battle rather than simply focus-firing down targets in quick succession. Balancing weakening your opponents to prevent more pain dealt to yours, and preparing them for the decisive blow to end them- and most importantly the When.
8/10. If this game was delivered as the whole package, it would easily deserve a 10/10 for its remarkable content and storytelling, especially with the agency you have within to feel the guilt and consequences continue to burn down through the course of your adventure. The gameplay, the story, and visual/audio art comes together into an experience that could not have been delivered better, save for the whole deal.

This game was a major breakthrough in the gaming world. Parkour hasn't been addressed much in any game until Mirrors Edge came out. There are a few ninja games (or splinter cell games) that had a bit of these abilities available but it wasn't until this game came out that parkour started exploding (besides the youtube videos). I beat this game on xbox 360 and here I am again for more.
You are a girl named Faith running through a city that is poison for runners (as her kind is called). These runners are pursued by "police" relentlessly until a potential mayoral candidate is found assassinated at his desk with Faith's sister (who is a police officer) right besides him. The story starts lifting more questions than any wrestling sitcom ever would.
The
itself is fairly good, especially for it's age (released 2008). Controls include jump, slide, punch, kicking while sliding, disarming, time distortion (slow), turning 180 on a press of a button and another button for hint. Sprint happens gradually as you gain momentum and hold LS all the way up. RS will allow you to move your head as you'd like even when climbing a pipe or ladder. Some of the grab controls feel clunkier on PC than they did on xbox. By that I mean you have to be very direct in where you point and how you jump. If, for example, you are jumping ledge to ledge and decide to jump from a diagonal, you may encounter issues in Faith grabbing the ledge. Sometimes it will catch (depending on where you're facing). Other times, you will fall miserably to your death from hundreds of feet. Besides that little hiccup, most of the game feels right on. Besides zip lining and running and jumping on ledges, the player can jump from some insane heights, run along the wall to reach another ledge and even combine sliding (crouching) and jumping under and over obstacles. All these mechanics put together with the pressure of evading bullets really combines for a neat and exhilarating game.
To help the player figure out where to go, pressing B will point you in the right direction. It can be a bit confusing at times as not knowing what to use to maximize your parkour skills can be difficult. Fortunately, the developers chose to go with a simplistic graphics scheme. This simplicity does not take away from the game. Rather, it accentuates what's really important about it. The
using a minimalist design not only helps the player recognize tools they may use, but also gives the game a unique personality. Concerning the animations, they aren't the best but certainly aren't the worst. Some disarming scenes may feel a bit funny to watch. Would have been nice if they gave you more control in this situation! You will see faiths hands or feet appear on the screen as you jump (which is a great addition).
and effects are pretty good. You'll hear Faith pant when she gets tired or a clunk when she misses something (or a big thump when she falls to her death). I think they could have done a little bit more with the sound to incorporate more of an ambiance.
Overall, this game is definitely recommended. I'm not sure how it's predecessor will live up, but this is the game that made parkour "famous". The physics in this game were definitely a break through and a lot of other games have attempted to emulate such movement. When it first came out, it was easily an 8.5. Due to it's age...
RATING : 7.5/10

Knights of Pen and Paper +1 wasn't really the game I was expecting to go through. I thought it was actually worse than it is, and I'm glad I ended up buying this title and playing through it's 9 hour-ish campaign. The basic premise is, you are a group of friends that are playing the much known fantasy tabletop role-playing game, and your adventures are depicted both through pixelated landscapes/characters and from what the D&D players are actually saying, or actually the dungeon master. Much like in the main idea from the movie Inception, you are playing a game in which the characters are playing a game. So, gameception?
KoP&P (Knights of Pen and Paper) is an RPG, and most features you expect from one are available in this title. Leveling up your characters, giving them new items, armor and weapons, upgrading your character's abilities, questing your way through until the very end, or until New Game +, in which your able to replay the whole game, with the same characters, but everything is harder. It didn't really attract me, since the main campaign features a bit of grinding and I didn't want to go through the same. It's useful for completing the achievements, though.
Soundtrack fits the theme of KoP&P, but can actually become boring after a few hours of gameplay. Another interesting feature is the abundance of references to tv shows, movies, etc.
The 4th wall is also broken lots of times.
Probably my favorite game of all time.

If I were to describe ME in a single word, it would be elegance.
ME is another one of those rare gems where the gameplay takes a backseat and the art and story telling take center stage. Revisting the game here recently (no doubt because of rumblings of a ME:Catalyst reboot), I was curious as to how well this left-field venture from DICE circa 2008 has held up. Analysis? I believe ME has held up quite well. Props to DICE for gifting this gem to us.
Then again, maybe I'm a sucker for aesthetics. Admittedly, the straight-line parkour gameplay is ME's true weakness, but I seem to easily forgive that important detail given the phenomenal overall experience. I don't know if its my love for the whitewashed world of ME, the engaging electronic music, or the likeable (albeit few) characters making this dystopian world believable. Reflecting back on my original impressions in 2008, maybe the story seems a bit paper thin by today's standards? I have a feeling ME:Catalyst will solve that.
Oh, and did I mention I absolutely love the soundtrack? Still Alive is such an amazing piece to roll credits on. I get chills everytime...
ME is elegant. ME is beautiful. ME is art.

As I write, my eyes grow blurry with tears of joy, awe, and woe. From what I heard, "The Banner Saga" was an Oregon Trail clone with vikings. I could have been more mislead.

The dialogue, while well written and having no typos, was anachronistic. It didn't match with the feel of the rest of the game. Your milage may vary, but seeing a giant viking warrior say something like "So, yeah..." was more than a little off-putting for me.
The combat, while manageable at its best, nail-bitingly tense at its worst, had just the right level of complexity to make you think about every move you make. Every character class has its own unique ability in combat. Furthermore, each member of your party can be equipped with an item. You can obtain items throughout your travels. Careful though: if one of your character members dies, they take the item they had equipped with them to the grave.
The rythym and rhyme (let's put aside the comment about the dialogue for a sec) of the game's story performs flawlessly, providing deeply impactful choices that must be made for the survival of your clan, and the world. The story is partialy told through dialogue trees, but much of the story happens on the caravan trails. The characters of this world are all engaging and have their own stories to tell. Help you, hinder you, betray you...it all happens in the game. You have to decide who will accompany you, and who gets left behind.
The music of "The Banner Saga" is worthy of praise from even the most jaded musical connoisseurs, delivering hair raising, spine tingling croscendos, moving wind solos, and profound vocals.
The art, likewise, is enough to engage one in this game. The 2D style is colorful, even though many scenes in the game are of winter landscapes. It is a kind of understated beauty that is seen in so few video games.
These three factors - story, music, and art - coalesce to create a truly unique and powerful tale of honor, couarge, death, and kinship. It is a game you should pick up if you like a good story

Antichamber is sort of like a minimalist surreal first person puzzle game, which I found to be an interesting concept.  In execution, though, it's a little clunky.
The traditional layout for a puzzle game is you're introduced to the rules, are presented with a problem, and have to figure out how to solve the problem within the established rules.  That's not always the case -- as some puzzlers can have you discover the rules as you go, and even change them partway, but it's usually the basic premise.
Antichamber turns that on its head, and the first thing it teaches you is that there aren't really any rules.  Walking down a hallway takes you somewhere you don't expect, and falling down a hole takes you right back where you came from.
Which, while interesting, just led me to frustration.
Rather than working through a problem with logic, I found myself just trying every conceivable thing until I found something that worked.  You cannot predict the way anything is going to behave, because there are no established rules, which means you have an endless gauntlet of experiments and banging your head against a wall.  It felt like puzzle by brute force, which wasn't very engaging or satisfying.
Admittedly I gave up on this game pretty quickly, as I got frustrated pretty quickly.  Maybe the game gets better as you get further in, but eeeehhhh.

Dying light has been out for a while now and I picked it up when I was able to get it on sale, like many people this is why I use steam. For the most part this a very good zombie FPS, so many things are done just right and there are not too many issues with the things done wrong. The critiques I have are few;
1)I wish there way more of a stealth game here, later in the skill tree you can do sneaky kills but it is nearly impossible to use a real stealth strategy for a majority of the game.
2)The crafting is a little shallow, lots of stuff you can make really easy in fact too easy. All of the ingredients for crafting are easy to acquire and commonly available there is rarely a need to find any ingredients as you will most likely have them in your inventory already. Takes some of the "survival" feeling out of the game.
3) Climbing is a little too variable, it can be hard to maintain a climb and some climbing surfaces require you to hold the spacebar, or tap the  spacebar, or don't even touch the spacebar. Expect to fall to your death for doing something that worked somewhere else fine just a second ago.
Now some stuff that is done well:
1) The game interface has a semi steep learning curve but once you get a handle on it you can expect to nearly fly over the rooftops of the city; quick, fun and well done.
2) Zombies are dangerous! Really, you get in melee combat with more than one or two zombies and you can expect to get eaten like twinkie in the hands of a 2 year old kid. Pick lone targets or use ranged weapons if you want to live.
3) Night is dark. Really dark. If you are well prepared you can do some good stuff at night for a good XP bonus but if you just decide to make a quick jaunt across town in the black of night you will end up zombie food before you can even figure out where the hell you are.
Looking for a good zombie FPS? You should really  take a look at Dying Light, while it is not a classic in the making it is a damn good game and worth your $$$.

Original Sin is every bit the old-school RPG it set out to be. Reminiscent of Baldur's Gate, Planescape Torment, Icewind Dale, and all of the other classic turn-based fantasy RPGs of old. Boasting beautiful isometric graphics, and a stellar character development system, Original Sin kept the best of the old, and created something all new for hardcore gamers to min-max at their leisure.
When it comes to the difficulty, Original Sin doesn't play around. Even on normal difficulty the game is incredibly challenging and will no doubt leave many gamers rage-quitting after forgoing a quicksave when caught up in a particular story arc. Be warned ye who enter: checkpoints are very few and far apart, and the game encourages to save often for a REASON.
With a campaign that spans well over its asking price, fans looking for a long, epic trek shouldn't even hesitate to grab this, even at full price, it's a steal.

Across the myriad titles released in this game's generation and beyond, there has never been one quite as unique, quite as diverse, as Ricochet. In both style and execution, this game exceeds what the players, and, I think, the developers, had in store for the experience. It brings you into its world and immerses you in its culture from the very title screen, urging you to play more, to investigate, explore, and really see your environment from the viewpoint of your character. It does this not by throwing you into lengthy, drawn-out cinematics, but with control and movement unparalleled in any game to date, graphics unrivaled by even the largest of studios, and combat so immersive, so unmatched, that no other game can quite compare. No matter what advancements may visit videogames in the future, it's quite certain that Ricochet will always be a masterpiece, a paragon of ground-breaking gameplay and graphics, right up there with Dongers 3: The Revengening and Hello Kitty Island Resort: Uncensored Version.

There's a few points that sully this game.
Massive SPOILERS to follow, so be aware.
FIrstly, the gameplay is solid. I don't like Zombie games in general, because I find them a chore more than anything else. However Dying Light made zombies a real threat, rather than an inconvenience. The addition of parkour elements really helps boost the survival feeling and the variety in zombie types made for some strategic combat choices.
Once again though, there are serious problems when it comes to some aspects of combat.
It's drilled into you from the start that firearms are a bad idea. They are loud and attract infected to your position, making them a serious 'last resort' weapon. Sticking to melee is recommended and indeed is where the fun is.
So why make human enemies carry guns and cause hell for no reason? It's not impossible to melee enemies armed with guns, but it does destroy the pace of combat when you have to play 'hide and seek' with enemies with guns.
This isn't too bad later on, but early in game it spoils the melee focus of the game, I feel.
Storywise, well...meh.
Typical standard fare of 'hero white man inserted into ethnically diverse region to save them from doom'. Sure they try to play some kind of philosophical message about free choice, in a direct rip-off of Bioshock, but ultimately the bland story still rides on tired tropes and I'm disappointed overall. I'm usually all for story being important, but in Dying Light, the story gets in the way,and is so poorly written it might as well not exist anyway.
I have to mention the treatment of Jade here too. What the f**k? In a scene toward to end, Jade held her own against 4 heavily armed and armoured men and took them out rapidly (something that even the player cannot do at max level) and efficiently, and this bad♥♥♥♥♥moment is ruined by her turning? Oh come on, that's lame by anyones standards, and shows seriously poor storytelling ability. Jade should have been treated MUCH better as a character, but instead is thrown away in some cliched redemption/sacrifice story arc that makes little sense to anyone with a brain.
There are fan-faction writers putting stories out for FREE that can write better than this cliched junk. These people got PAID to write the biggest tropey schlock out there and people are giving this a pass? Poor effort, guys.
Gameplay wise, there are some huge improvements over Techland's earlier work with Dead Island (so thankful they didn't tie kicking to stamina again) and while there are some oddities (screw physics, you can fall from nearly any height so long as you deploy your grappling hook in time, Just Cause style) movement within the game is great fun. When you unlock new abilities, it only amplifies things, creating a parkour playground, and they capitalise on this with free-running challenges all over the map.
The weapon system from Dead Island returns too, only more streamlined. Melee weapons are fun to use, and the attention to detail with mods and such truly makes crafting weapons an actual desire, rather than simply another chore to do.
Look, this is one of those games in which I really can't recommend it, but I can't not either. The Yes/No system is too restrictive but I have to err on the negative side here. I simply can't let this tripe of a story get away with it, and in my opinion this game falls hard in that area. Of course, if you're not interested in story and just want to kill hordes of zombies, then you're going to have a blast here. It's satisfying killing hundreds upon hundreds of zombies in a myriad of creative ways, or traversing the city in quick bursts of free-running but anything outside of that and this game just doesn't bear up. Mechanically it's awesome, but ifd you're looking for more than that...look elsewhere.
