Orcs Must Die! is a fun, addictive game that combines twitchy, arcade shooter goodness with tower defense mechanics to hold back the neverending tide of Orc invaders.  The levels are well designed and the traps are some of the most unique I've seen in the genre.  From bubbling pools of lava, to spring boards that launch enemies into ponds of acid, as well as the classic spike and arrow traps, you'll have more options than you know what to do with.  The story is basic but complimented by funny banter from the main character and is told through voice over and still images.
Perhaps the games greatest strength relies in the the 3rd person shooter elements.  You're not relegated to simply laying traps and hoping for the best.  Instead, you can fight alongside your machinations, whether it's with a spear, crossbow, or magic; you yourself lend a hand in achieving victory.  It's fun and fast paced and keeps the player engaged in each level as well as providing room for error when setting up traps.  This is something, I feel, the genre as a whole is in need of.  Too often in these style of games, the player is relagated to one or two winning strategies that are only uncovered through tedious trial and error.  In Orcs Must Die!, the player can create endless combinations to achieve victory precisely because they can shoot and stab the orcs alongside the traps.
In the end, it's a fun, addictive game with 3 difficulty levels and plenty of replay value.  There's also a sequel worth mentioning.  So if you like tower defense games, this is a must buy.  If you don't, I'd still check this out on the cheap during a steam sale.  It just might surprise you.

The second installment of the Tales of Alltynex shoot em up trilogy, RefleX is widely acclaimed for its unique defensive gameplay mechanic and cinematic sprite puppet show, which builds to a finalie that rivals Super Metroid's legendary climax for those who have seen it.
Only so much can be said about RefleX's bleak interplanetary war without spoiling its greatest setpieces though, so I'll be focusing on the gameplay here.
RefleX, aka Reflection X, is built around a unique shield and parrying mechanic which allows you to deflect enemy bullets back at opponents by summoning a circular shield of light around yourself. The shield's use is limited, but recharges when not in use. Refraining from firing altogether causes it to recharge even faster.
Armed with this unique ability, RefleX aspires to be a game thats simoultaneously more chaotic and frantic than most bullet hell shooters, thanks to your ability to nullfiy vasts swathes of fire power, but also more accessible. The game succeeds at this, visually, but play is more of a mixed bag.
RefleX's main weakness is that reflection makes the game a bit too defensive. Once you get the hang of releasing fire to double your shields recharge rate, a "play it safe" strategy begins to dominate bosses, and the games balance of risk/reward goes out the window as the difficulty curve plummets.
That's not to say it's bad, though. The creativity and epic scale of many of RefleX's setpieces, alongside its aforementioned worldless storytelling style, still lends the game a gravitas and compulsion to push forward that will insure you never get bored. And when the level design does rise to heights that can uplift the game mechanics and give the player genuinely exciting and challenging choices to make admist its apoctalyptic fireworks, its sublime.
Perhaps the most flawed of the trilogy overall, but in many ways the most special. RefleX is certainly worth the time for 2d enthusiasts.

Overall, this game is quite good, but it's not perfect. This game is very much in the vein of old-school RPG's like Baldur's Gate.
The characters are interesting, the combat is refreshingly challenging, and you're never quite certain what's going to happen next. Unfortunately, it inherents many of the flaws of old-school RPG's.
The crafting system is very complex. Almost anything can be picked up and crafted into something. You're encouraged to experiment and hopefully stumble onto a useful recipe or piece together the cryptic clues from optional recipe books. Unfortunately, it practically means only a handful of recipes are useful and most people will revert to Google to look them up. Coupled with this is the fact inventory management is a nightmare. You're never sure what items can be safely sold and you're either stuck with 10 pages of junk flavor items or forced to hunt down the random vendor you accidently sold a plot-critical diary to.
Creative solutions to puzzles are encouraged. Can't find a key? Bash down the door, pick the lock, or teleport around it. 90% of the time you're free to be flexibile in your problem solving. This flexibility makes the remaining 10% quite glaring. This makes the times you can't "think outside the box" VERY frustrating, and the worst part is the solution is generally a soul-sucking pixel hunt for a stupid switch.
The game looks and sounds gorgeous. The characters are well modelled and everything is bright and beautiful. There's a good mix of beaches, jungle, forest, frozen elemental planes and forbidden mines.
Combat is where this game really shines. The game is very unforgiving, but at the same time 100% fair. Deciding when to burst down a target, or when to setup the proper crowd control combination becomes critical to your combat success. And the rules are very fair. With very few (but reasonable) exceptions, no one is immune to any spells. Fluff skills like loremaster give you the elemental immunities and absorptions and the rules are consistently applied.
Overall the game is quite good, but it carries with it some of the baggage from old-school RPG's that prevent it from being easily approachable by new players. This game requires significant investment to get past some of the user unfriendliness and quirks. But get past that, and you have an amazingly well crafted game.

95% of this game is beautiful. The writing is great, the art is gorgeous. They do a fantastic job of just letting you play the game. You make a choice, you deal with the consequences. You're totally immersed. Only a few other games (Walking Dead) have made me feel regret for choices I've made. Not in a 'oh I played the game wrong, and I regret that' sort of way. But more like in a 'I wonder if...' sort of way. Looking wistfully back down the road, thinking about the path you didn't take, the person you hurt, the hard choice you had to make, but knowing you have to press on.
And then they throw all that beauty out the window on the final battle. Turns out, you should have been min/max'ing the entire time. Turns out you are going to be railroaded into a very specific strategy with very specific characters. Oh you wanted to play the story your way and chose not to use Allette so she's still level 1? That sure does suck for you! Because you MUST use her in the final battle. Through the game, the combat was challenging, I never finished a fight without a few knock-outs on my side. I even lost a few. But choices you made on the battle field affected the story. It felt like a struggle, but one that you were getting through. You never restarted or replayed a battle, you just made due with the consequences of your good or bad decisions. I loved that! Which made the bizarre try-hard 1337zor final battle all the more upsetting.
I still can't beat it. Not with the character selection I ended up with, the choices I made in the game set me up *terribly* for the final battle.
Just restart and play it again, this time with the final battle in mind? To me that just completely negates everything that I loved about the game in the first place.
I would still recommend the game. It's beautiful. With these two caveats: Level up Rook and Allette, and put all your points in Armor-break.

TL/DR: if you are a fan of Action RPGs, then you should seriously consider buying this game.
The longform review:
I've only gone through the early parts of the game - just completed the first major main quest, and a major sidequest - but Grim Dawn promises a wonderful romp through a post-apocalyptic, steampunkish world that has zombies and the suggestion that you'll eventually go up against some of Cthulhu's cousins.
I think what interests me more than the story is the skill tree. You start off classless and get to pick your first class with your first level. At level 10 (a pretty fast occurence), you get the option to dual class. You don't have to pick a new class immediately, but you can anytime after the 10th level. Like what it says on the tin, this promises a lot of... interesting ways for dealing with the threats this world has to offer.
There's also the atmosphere. Post-apocalyptic gothic steampunk. If you want a change in scenery from all the D&D cloned magic-medieval worlds, this may be the game for you (especially if you don't want the cartoon-y look of my other fave Action RPG, Torchlight).
The game isn't perfect - lighting can get bad, especially in the dungeons (how realistic, though) - but remember that this was created by an 8-person indie team. Given how good it is, that 8-person team has done the amazing.
And, yes, it's an indie. So for those of you looking to support more indie game studios and devs, this is a very good buy.
Looking forward to revealing more of this world. Easily the best buy of the lot during Wintersday 2015

I'm going to go ahead and recommend this game in the uhhh... Ummm, I guess "spirit" of having more sports games on PC. But this game is, well, rough. That's about the nicest way I can put it.
A quick note; I only played single player, and only played with mouse and keyboard.
It took a single game to learn the passing mechanics which is far and away the highlight of this game. Using mouse for passing like it does with something as simple as "short click lob" and "long click bullet" is brilliant. You can lead your receivers and all that fun stuff. It feels great and intuitive. Once I figured it out though, I won my second game 62-14 and unlocked most of the achievements. By the end of this second game I had also figured out how to return kicks for TDs with relative regularity, thoroughly exploit things on defense, and found a kickoff glitch to almost always recover the ball. And this was on the hardest difficulty.
Simply put, if you have put any serious time into football console games in your life you will absolutely murderously dominate the computer in this game within a single game. Two max. I'm years and years removed from owning a console and this was never a challenge. There's games of the 8bit and 16bit eras with much more depth and AI than what you'll get here.
But there is still some fun to be had if you don't expect anything. Hunting down the achievements got me to week 3 of the season. The names of the players are phenomenal. You'll spot anything from a LB for New England named T.Castle with #54 (Obviously a Blue Mountain State graduate) to A. Silva and a bunch of other MMA names. Ran into a Falkner and Romanov too. The announcing is bad in a good way but then bad again. I had to mute it after a half. None of these things bring any substance to the shallow gameplay but made the experience worthwhile and made me feel like I like the developer. The game feels like something my buddies and I would end up with if any of us had an ounce of talent or knowledge to make a game. It was fun in that regard. If that makes sense.
Like I said, this is just a thumbs up in the "spirit" of more sports games on PC. I miiight finish out the season just to get the championship achievement but the game really doesn't offer much past a game or two. I feel like there's something here though. Especially the mouse passing. It has great potential. As far as I can tell poking around the forums, the developer is planning a sequel and while I still wouldn't set my sights high or get hopeful in it taking the leaps and bounds it needs... Who knows! This could evolve. It pretty much only has one direction it can go; up! I got it in a bundle but think its worth supporting.
End of the day, I've seen worse. Don't expect much. Happy Superbowl Sunday!

Coming into this game, I really had no idea what to expect beyond the FFTactics-style combat and the stylised anime-ish visuals. So it came as a pleasant surprise to discover that not only is the game quite fun to play, but it also features a rich and complex world of characters and creatures all of which has a decidedly viking feel to it.
The games strengths are largely in the combat system and character progression, where each of your fighters 'level up' based on how many enemies they've killed. Battles are always on a grid much like old-school tactical rpg's and almost always involve each side alternating turns. The visuals as well are quite nice to look at and the voice-overs are done well and never feel cliched or cheesy.
The only negatives I can think of are that you are thrown in to the deep end almost from the start without much to guide you in the intricacies of combat or strategy. You're never really told whether a character will perma-die if they die in combat or if any of your decisions have any direct influence on how the game unfolds.
Besides those small details, The Banner Saga is a solid tactical rpg and is well worth the price of purchase.

Grim Dawn is the quintessential sequel to Titan Quest. This is because most of the UI is eerily similar, as is the dual-class leveling system and even the augments.
Where Grim Dawn succeeds is in the graphics and audio departments. There are several improvements to the graphical API, there are plenty of new sound effects and those that are re-used are at least altered. The day/night cycle returns with lustrous appeal and even adds in some weather effects.
Where Grim Dawn falls short is that it fails to be an evolution in the gameplay department. The pacing is very slow and the environments, while very well designed, don't change enough over the first 20 hours. The crafting system looks very nice, but it takes way too long to farm out the materials you need for the first set of items. The gameplay mechanics for Titan Quest were top-notch for the time, but other ARPGs that came out later (like Torchlight and Diablo 3) lay out a streamlined experience that Grim Dawn fails to learn from.
If you've never enjoyed another ARPG after Titan Quest, then Grim Dawn is right up your alley. I would also recommend giving it a go if you're aching for a dual-class leveling system that works. But if you don't think you'll be able to put up with a slow-advancing game or clunky combat, then you won't be missing out on anything.

I've had an itch for over 15 years that I cannot scratch. An itch to play a decent football game on the PC. When the original Front Page Sports football faded away many years ago, I thought that some other title would carry on the torch. It just didn't happen.
Now we have this entry. We are instructed by other reviewers not to compare this to Madden. Unfortunately however this is exactly what this game tries to be, an "arcady" twitch game. Since this game cannot compete on this level with the aforementioned game, one would expect other areas to be better developed, but sadly this is not the case. If this game had tried to be more of a Front Office football with graphics, it would have fared much better.
There is simply no simulation value to this game whatsoever. There is a "coach" mode, but this is simply the same game only you do not control one of the players. Since this game is all about action, this mode makes no sense. The action itself is not very satisfying. Often, players being blocked will just stand there, not moving. You can find the one or two plays that will always work, regardless of how good or bad the team you are playing is. As an example, after 4 games, my team's rushing defence has given up negative yardage. My opponents simply cannot run the ball against my team. However, once in a while they will get off an 80+ pass play since their receivers can always outrun my defenders (again - regardless of how good or bad the opponent team is). So every team you play feels exactly like the previous team you just played, only with a different coat of paint.
There's also alot of missing elements from actual football. There are no leagues or divisions. All teams are thrown into the same standings with the top 12 teams going to some sort of post season play. There are no quarters in games, only 2 five minute halves and there is no changing this. Stat enthusiasts will be very dissapointed as there are no league leader displays. While in a game, you can see the stats of your individual players, but outside of a game, all you can do is view team totals.
If you want to support one of the only options in PC football, then by all means do so.  I wished I hadn't however. We do have a very large hole in the PC Football genre, but this offering does nothing to scratch that football itch. If I enter a fruit cake into the county fair, and my entry is the only entry in the fruit cake division, of course I'll win the medal, but that doesn't mean it's a good fruitcake. This may be the only football game on steam to date. Is it the greatest? No. Does it provide the basic elements of football? To an extremely basic extent. Does it have local co-op to justify a purchase? Yes, at a price. Is this a game of football you can enjoy for at least a bit? Yes.
Axis Football 2015 could have maybe been quite the miniature football game. Though simplistic in nature, the game does provide for an arcade experience. I absolutely love how they made throws possible (even though it is supposed to be done with a keyboard, a game pad works just as well). Holding down "throw" will bring up a circle in the middle of the field just above the touch line. This white circle can be moved towards any player you wish. Alternatively, you can press Y to zoom out and see which player is assigned which button (such as RB, B, A etc...). The players catching ability varies and some players will actually fumble the ball if their not on a proper path to catching it.
The
itself is relatively smooth and decent, but it's the specifics where this game lacks. Take tackling for instance, there is no specific button to tackle. You simply run into another individual to take them down. This bothers me the most as the timing of a tackle and where a player makes contact with another players is extremely important. Furthermore, there is no sprint button. I'd like to assume all players run as fast as they can but having that little feature can get anyone out of a tight spot. Another issue : there isn't anyway to incorporate tricks or moves around opponents. Off a kick-off, your player will receive the ball. A second or two later, you'll notice every moves as if it's Play Action Football for the original GameBoy. Instead of spreading out, everyone forms into a cone, then into a line to make their tackle. Sometimes it'll be easy to bypass the entire team while other times you'll have the ENTIRE team chasing you. On defense, you are able to move some of the defensive lines around. On offense, there are ample amount of plays to choose from which are actually quite decent. There is a seasons mode but it is nothing extremely substantial. Some players may find the halves a bit too long.
The
are not bad but the crowd is horrible. The
is at best decent and the announcer is okay. Extremely neutral on this topic as some of the yelling from the players is nice. Although, they just end up standing there like pylons with no attitude after a play. The menu may be a bit difficult to navigate at first as the player may have no idea how to. You really need to pay attention to what the screen is telling you as pressing start simply won't stop the game.
Although the game does a good knockoff teams of NFL teams, it just doesn't hit the spot when it comes to a proper game of (American) football. This game, more or less, is for someone who would like a football game on their library list and have a bit of a breakaway from traditional gaming. It has it's moments where it will entrap you. Soon enough, you'll be wanting more and Axis simply cannot deliver it.
Definitely not worth $17 but on a sale under $5... probably.

XCOM is a game which allows you to take on aliens in turn-based combat, recover their corpses and the remains of their technology, and use it to develop your own weapons and armaments against them.
If you are a turn-based strategy enthusiast, I cannot recommend this game strongly enough.  The combat is deep and engaging, the base management is interesting, and the level of customization of your troops is exceptional.  It even has a solid story and some excellent "challenge" options.
But where the game really shines is ironman mode, where all your choices are permanent.  It is because of this mode that I would recommend this game to absolutely anyone.  You might not think a turn-based game could be intense, but I have never encountered adrenaline-pumping situation in any game like I have in XCOM Ironman, where one move could brilliantly win the mission, or cause devastating defeat.
I got this game for free with Bioshock infinite and decided to give it a try.  Now it's my favorite strategy game of all time.  Give it a try.

The other two Tale of Alltynex games don't have this issue (nor do any of my other shmups), but RefleX is definitely buyer beware, given the absolute refusal to fix even game-breaking bugs.
To those of you marking these facts "unhelpful", I'm glad you were fortunate enough to receive a playable game, but I can't recommend a product that doesn't work, and buyers should know that if it doesn't work for them, it simply will not be fixed.
Addendum: Adding dgVoodoo 2 will work around the broken graphics code.  I'm leaving this thumbs down because the product is still sold broken and the developer and publisher refused to do anything to fix it, but I wanted to note that fans at least have a third-party workaround now.

For those who played, loved and miss epic DnD games like Balder's Gate I &II, Icewind Dale, Temple of Elemental Evil etc you are in for a treat. Divinity captures the spirit of those great games and takes it all a notch further. D:OS reminds me more of ToEE than any other; you are very weak to start and must re-play some battles seeking a better strategy. The game also ( like afor mentioned predecessors) refuses to "hold your hand"....there are no convenient quest markers for NPCs, very few map markers, and most clues to quests are given via dialogue. It should also be noted here that while combat is turn-based, you explore the world in real time. In short:
The Good-
> Battles are fun again! Using your enviroment to your advantage is a huge part of average strategy.
> Voice acting is very well done.
> Humor; the developers are a naughty bunch.
> Complex character development...spend points wisely!
> Tons of hidden objects, easter eggs, areas, and just fun stuff.
The Not-So-Good
> The basic UI ( ie un-modded) can be a tad clunky.
> Battles against foes at least one level above yours can often be a disaster..plan accordingly.
> Not many "skins" for starter characters; very bland choices.
> May not appeal to non-readers! Most (98%?) of dialogue is text...and there is ALOT of it!
I highly recommend this game!

Divinity: Original Sin was an unexpected delight that I did not see coming.
A friend recommended it after he tried it, then I casually bought it and  tried it out. Little did I know that the hours flew by so fast than any other game I played  in recent years.
Divinity: Original SIn consist of an immensly rich world with a ton of content with everything from interesting NPCs, beautiful envirmoents, engaging roleplay mechanics and the ultra-creative quest solving. The story itself is pretty straight forward, but it's the quest you do on the side pared with the world itself which creates the game's excellent atmosphere.
This game goes way back to the old roots of old school RPG's where it doesnt necessary tell you exatly what to do, neither does it give you a generic quest marker to follow. The game wants you to figure out things out on your own and doesn't hold your hand for one moment. This is a game where you really have to use your brain and immerse yourself in the world to understand what to do. Sneaking, pickpocketing and crafting are also feautred in the game, and lots more minor things which help make Divinity: Orginial Sin an immense game.
Early on I noticed the combat was spot on. Divinity: Original Sin uses a turn-based combat mechanic and to be honest I was never particulary fond of turn-based RPG's, simply because I always felt the action went rather slow and never really felt as engaged as other genres. This is NOT the case in Divinity: Original Sin.
Unlike other turn-based games, Divinity: Original Sin is a bit much faster paced and uses the elements such as: Air, Earth, Water and Fire and utilizes it perfectly. Do you want to create a blizzard in the middle of your enemies? Do it! Feel like shooting out poisenous gas and then igniting it with fire to create an immense explosion? Do it!
The amount of possibilites in this game is staggering and learning new tactics is a continous process.
One thing that perhaps the casual audience may not find so appealing is the lack of help, lack of forgiveness and thinking that this is another Elder Scroll or Diablo. In terms of scope and content it definitely matches the big dogs in the business, but it's not a pick-up and play title as others.
I recommend this game to the fullest and I wish everyone who plays this to please partcipate in the community and provide feedback to the developers.

Divinity: Original Sin is a beautiful game, everything from the look of the water, to the sound design is top notch in my opinion. What really makes it awesome, is that it relies on a sort of "old school" methodology when it comes to combat and questing. I think that is what sets it apart from so many other games, and in a good way. This game is not easy, but at the same time, I wouldn't say that its unfairly difficult. As long as you take the time to understand the mechanics, it won't be too bad. It really makes the player analyze each encounter, and use that knowledge to be better prepared for future fights.
The game's combat is turn base, so that might put some people off, but I personally think thats part of the reason the game is so great. It gives you the freedom to stop and think instead of rushing into a fight.
Another point I mentioned, was the questing system. This game is totally free of hand holding, so you really need to use your head to figure out the quests, you actually need to talk to the NPC's and explore the environment to have any chance of completing them. (Get petpal ASAP!)
"Player choice" and "Freedom" are terms often used to describe games, but usually I feel, most games fall short of allowing the player to really play the game how they want. With Divinity: OS, this is not the case, you really can play the game how you want. If you want to kill the starting NPC's that give you the first quests, you can do it. There is no set path that you are supposed to follow, you can really play the game how you want.
Lastly, I just want to mention that somethings are hard to figure out when first playing the game. For instance, you will want to save up ability points so you can unlock better skills instead of spending them right away. Certain things like this can be tough to figure out, so I would recommend reading some beginner guides online first. There are some great ones on Steam already. Past the basic stuff, I wouldn't read anything else online though, part of the fun of this game is figuring stuff out on your own.
Honestly, this is one of the best games I have ever played. I don't think I've been this engrossed in a game in years. If you like RPG's and rewarding/challenging games, please get this game, it really is amazing.

This is a horrible football game.  It takes the worst parts of Madden and then sprinkles its own special flavor of bad on top of it.  I wish game designers would stop trying to copy other games.  Madden is really a poor game and we're stuck with it.  But instead of trying out new concepts and aiming a little lower (think 2D animation) this game attempts to take on the giant using a small rock.  The rock misses the giant and comically bounces back to harmlessly hit the developers of this game square in the head.  There's no reason for anyone to own this game, it's not going to get better than what it currently is - a poorly designed, poorly thoughtout pile of wasted time (and my money).
Advice for the developers.  Go back and really THINK about the kind of football game you want to make.  Is a 3D animation similar to Madden really something that market needs right now?  Nope, and you're never going to comepte with them.  So why not make a game based more on strategy and less on graphics?  Why not make a thinking mans game?  Why not develop something that requires less "throwing it deep" and more "let's free the right defensive tackle and run a trap play up the middle because the guy is unblockable and is in our backfield every play anyway!".
Dear developers at large, THIS is what the football genre is missing.  Not more Madden nonsense.

Like many reviewers said, this is NOT MADDEN.  It's a solid Indie effort which currently highlights a great aimed passing feature.
Pros:
- All 'official' pro cities represented but for obvious copyright reasons, I thought the dev was very clever with each team name.  You will have no trouble identifying each game team's counterpart in the big leagues.
- As mentioned before, the aimed passing feature
- on easy, the AI is too easy but seemed to get challenging on the harder levels
Cons:
- On all levels AI needs a little more beefing up.  Have AI adjust to player's preferential play style during the game which would force the player to quit using plays that 'always work'
*Rather than list the below items as 'Cons', I understand the game is still being developed so...
Needing:
- At 1920 x 1080, I feel the status bar gets 'in the way' of the view during the receiving portion of a kickoff or punt return.  A way to alleviate this would be to get dev to move the bar down a little bit.  Have not tried lower resolutions
- Color blind features needed - namely for the ground 'target' circles. Being partially color blind myself, I have gotten used to noticing the circle during passing plays but still have a hard time seeing the target circle when about to recv. from a kickoff or punt.
- REAL time 4 qtrs of play.  Maybe have a mode where one could do a quick game (the way it's set now) then have a more official mode using the official clock times
- Some of the Madden features for being able to throw off blockers - hitstick, etc  Maybe a quick view change once a pass or kick is caught or after a ball is handed off where one could look from the player's POV while running the play after the catch or hand. *OR*
- Keep the same view since I get that you want 2 players to be able to share the same screen (friend at a friend's house sort of thing) then maybe slow the game down a little bit.  I think all the AI players noticeably all run around the same speed >> FAST.  Greater variability on each individual AI and player controllered players so that some run faster, some slower.  Some defenders block and pass rush better, some don't.  etc..  By slowing the game down some, a player can read the defense a little more, maybe find the holes to run through.
Otherwise it's a FOOTBALL GAME FOR THE PC!  I think it's worth it.  If you're tight with the money, maybe hold out to see what the new 2016 version will be about.  I bought in now because the dev needs to earn a living too, and so I gladly supported his efforts for this 2015 edition and will most likely shell out some more moola for the 2016 version.  I'll become a 'lifer' supporter if I see great improvements in the 2016 version because that's usually a good sign that the dev is in it to win it!

Axis Football, I was really hyped when I saw an American Football Game on Steam which was non simulation, so I decided to buy this game. I heard this game was built on a 500 dollar budget, the game was very robotic and seemed like it was simply made. I then launched the game and played, it's what I expected basically, no NFL licensed official teams, unis, stadiums etc. But I was shocked on the lack of modes in this game, yes Seasons and Head to Head is nice, but where is the Online and Roster Editing and a place where you can share your mods (ala 2k share) When I first played I noticed the Controller controls were stiff, and the passing with the controller was hell, it is a great feature but just doesn't go with the controller(hard to get used to) The running was another thing, the players just took off, it didn't even look like the center hiked the ball to the qb to hand off to the rb, it was like that animation was skipped, I always noticed how the players ran moving awkwardly, and again stiff. I always have had problems with defenders teleporting to my QB, and On Kick Return there is another player who stands out of bounds (KR2?) The graphics are like Madden 01. It lacks a soundtrack, and most importantly CREATE A PLAYER MODE. The commentary is not very exciting, with it's repetitive lines, and in fact it's very cheesy, but what do we expect from 1 guy producing all of this game. I believe that this game has potential, but definitely should be treated as a beta, not as a finished product. This game is a flop but definitely has some potential to become a big hit on the pc if it fulfills its flaws and the developer puts in some more money into the game. I cannot recommend this game, but I do recommend you keep an eye out for future games. 30/100 but has potential for upcoming games

After owning the game for a while I'v finally decided to make a review
Killing floor 2 is of course round based zombie gameplay where you blast "Zeds" and earn money each round for more guns. Why does is this game different from Cod zombies or other zombie games?
Pros
The gunplay is extremely fluid and when combined with bullet time makes for extremely satisfying killes
The special zeds if you call them that vary a lot from the large boulder crushing zeds to the invisabled screeming zeds that sneak up on you it can feel very Unique and interesting.
There are also a large arsenel of weapons from assult rifles to shotguns to katanas that can shred each and every part of a zombie
Another unique thing there is the makes it different from other zombie shooters is that there are classes you can pick that specilize in certain weapons but they really cant do anything until you are a higher level
There are custom maps that can enhance the expeirence as well as a commuity workshop that can let creative people make things for the game if you into that type of thing
Cons
The gameplay can feel very reapetitive as the maps dont do anything to create a unique experience
There are only 2 bosses in the game so you will end up with one or the other every time you play
As mentioned before there are classes which are a great thing to make you unique but until you are a higher level the class you play does not actually matter in a game
Overall the game may not feel worth a full 30 dollars depending on your likes but at 20 dollars or less it is definitaly a good title to pick up. On a scale on 1-10 I would rate this above averge with a 7

A good old classic. BFII is a great game that can take any Star Wars fan back into that old Star Wars mood. The classes are fairly balanced and the maps have a strategic, compelling and memorable structure that can make even the person who only knows who Darth Vader is happy in the knowledge that their sci-fi combat interests are satisfied. My only three problems with this game are the online, AI and map changes from Star Wars Battlefront (the original). The online is fairly barren, but the remaining community are friendly, jumping into random games and starting conversations in the chat log, so it’s not all bad, but it can be annoying if you're looking for a big match to get that 'battlefront' feeling (if you are into that and would not mind a less sci-fi based experience then I would recommend battlefield 3 or 4). The AI, although not terrible can be repetitive in its actions, and through that, advantageous to the player who will rarely need to change tactics in combat no matter how many enemies he or she is going up against. This can be even more of a predicament if online with friends as the AI are merely fodder for both sides which can result in unfair bias depending on player skill, map setup etc. The last problem I care to put some extensive thought into is the changing of the original maps (Geonosis being the key one). Some of the Battlefront maps are far cooler than the Battlefront 2 ones which makes it annoying for the players of the original, however it doesn’t really matter too much if you haven't played BF 1 as it’s merely a conservative viewpoint and also my opinion, although I do have other friends who agree.
All in all this game deserves 4 stars due to the great improvements from the original and the star wars vibe you can get from playing it. If you like sci-fi combat or more importantly, are a star wars fan, then I recommend this game to you.
I could go on about the good bits to this game, but being a fanboy to the original BF I'd rather look to explaining the bad (which I've already done), so I'll simply state the best good points:
- Space combat
- Galactic Conquest
- Hero battle
- Single player campaign
- Music
- Lore/fan friendly (factions, maps, ships, units, skins, guns, vehicles etc.)

Some games you can tell are going to be good from the first 10 minutes of playing them. Orcs Must Die is one of those games. From the moment you start playing, its slick presentation becomes very apparent, ranging from a charming artstyle, to nice fast-paced music, and a comedic tone.
But presentation is not the only thing where the game shines. As a tower defence game it has some pretty ingenious trap ideas, such as trapdoors that release scorching flames, spring pads that launch orcs into the air, as well as acid bombs and even knights and archers. The level designs are also very well made, at times providing very obvious spots for where traps are ideal. And in addition to traps, you also unlock weavers, which are sorceresses that provide you with passive skills for the duration of the level. Upgrading these skills makes either your abilities or your traps/guardians more effective at what they do.
At the end of each level, you get a score (which is shown against scores of people on your friends list) and a rating out of 5 skulls. You can then use the skulls to upgrade some of your traps.
Overall the game was loads of fun. I've had a blast. Perhaps the only minor criticism I have is that when starting a new level that has more than 1 enemy entrances, it's often impossible to tell where the enemy is going to come through first. But it's a very small nitpick. The game is fun. If you like tower defence genre, get it now.

If you like RPGs, especially older Western ones like Baldur's Gate and (obviously) Divine Divinity, give this game a go.

Instead Of Writing A Full On Analytical Review I Have Written A Short Curatorial Paragraph On What I Believe To Be The Best Aspect Of Half Life 2
Hypothetically Speaking Half-Life 2 Doesn't Consist Of Any Technical Implementation Of Pacing. Whereas Instead The Game Symbolically Toys With The Player ''You'', By Using Your Instinctive Ambition To Control The Consistency Of The Pace. What Controls Said Ambition Is The Teased Objective Presented During The Introduction Of The Game, Witch Is To Reach Obtainable Ground To The Citadel. This Objective/Goal Drives The Player Immensely To Want To Win. For Winning And Achieving Satisfaction In A Video Game Is How This Media's Inauguration Hasn't Changed In The Slightest. In Other Words The Citadel Is Half-Life 2's Symbolic Representation Of The Infamous Flagpole.

Options include Subtitles (OFF by default), Subtitle Size, Resolution (800x600 up to 1920x1080), and separate sliders for Master Volume, Music, and Brightness.
Gameplay is the same as you would expect if you're a Telltale fan... It's an interactive movie where you make decisions that affect how things play out. It seems like there were a lot more QuickTime Events in this installment of the series than I've seen before (haven't played Season 3 yet).  I don't know whether they're easier this time around, or if I've just gotten better at gaming ;)
If this is your first dip into the game version of The Walking Dead, you can play without fear - Michonne contains no spoilers for Seasons 1 or 2 (and I'm guessing not for Season 3, either).
I am a huge zombie fan, but I've yet to see TWD TV series - nor have I read the comics - so I don't know if Telltale did Michonne justice or not.  I CAN say that her character is a badass with a compelling story, and that the devs did just as amazing a job with choreography, mannerisms, and facial expressions as in their previous games, and the voice-overs are excellent.
There are 21 achievements, but they are all obtained by simply playing the game.
The game took me about four hours to complete (I did not re-play any of my decisions), so it's not very long, but it's also $10 less than a full season of TWD.  One of the antagonists reminded me a lot of a character from Season 2, which threw me off a bit, but overall I'd say that the story was pretty solid, leaving me teary-eyed at one point.  It kept me interested throughout, and I only took one short break during my play-through.
What can I say except that I loved it?  Definitely recommended!

With a name light "Knights of Pen and Paper" and with a UI designed around the table top, I expected to have fun with this game.
That was not the case.
One of the big problems with this game right off the bat is that each character has only 5 things they can do. Each of them can attack and then each class has 4 upgradable abilities, but some of them are passive. The problem here is that with a small margin of exception, there's no strategy to the fights. You either hit attack or you use abilities until you run out of mana.
The problem with the skills themselves is that the level scaling is frankly horrendous, so if you don't focus on one of the 4 skills, you'll quickly reach a point where you can't play the game anymore because you'll just get trounced during every encounter. This means that you really need 4 characters for each class by the end of the game because if you have a level 20 fire mage and you're up against fire resistant creatures, then you're probably going to get your party killed.
Another problem I have is the grinding. For a game that's supposed to be just a short cute DnD knockoff, there is an obscene amount of grinding. Example: "Collect 20 green apples". Well, green apples only drop from venus fly traps that take off half your health per attack and killing one isn't a guarantee that they will drop. So to get 20 green apples, you'll probably end up playing 12 encoutners against 3 venus fly traps. And that's just the beggining.
The upgrade system is also based on grinding. You need to visit special areas where upgrades can be found (usually caves) then you need to roll a 20 sided dice and hope you get lucky just for the chance of getting an upgrade item. Once you have about 5-10 upgrade items (for your first upgrade) you then take it to a blacksmith who gives you a %chance that your item will be upgraded or he'll just waste your upgrade items. You can upgrade the blacksmith himself so that you're more likely to succeed, but that requires double or even triple the number of upgrade items you already needed, so now you need go to back to grinding in the caves. Plus, each character has 2 items (clothes and weapon) and when you remember that you need multiples of each class, you understand that you'll need hundreds and hundreds of grindstones just for a chance of upgrading your party. You'd think you could just ignore the upgrading, but because the level scaling is so unbalanced, you have to upgrade to proceed.
Its just an awful time waster with no sense of progression and I'm glad I bought it on sale because this is literally a ported mobile game.

This reminds me of the old arcade-style games where I'd probably be spending a lot of time in. The last football game I played was on the PS1, which was NFL Gameday 99 and that was a long time ago. Never played Madden since I pretty much stopped buying consoles/console games after that. The game size does remind of me the early 00's where I used to buy it off from the store as a CD and it was the full version altogether.
Anyways, on to the game itself. It has plenty of rough edges that can be fixed, I liked the way the ball can be passed but sometimes it certainly doesn't work really well as expected, so I pretty much rush than pass and it works for me in such an environment. The AI can be really challenging especially in close games since it always forces me to an overtime which really puts the pressure to play even better but sometimes I feel like it's not trying at all when it can't chase any further. The teams do remind me of how it was back then in the arcade, renamed teams that represented a city so that the developers will not have to deal with copyright issues. I did notice the team named Atlanta Hawks, it rings the same bell as the actual NBA team but I guess since it is football we can get away with it somehow. The stats are also interesting especially in Season Mode which I've recently started on, at least it does feel like how I watch it on TV.
Granted, I have no first-hand knowledge/experience with football especially in my country where it's not really that well-known but on a personal level this sport is interesting and I've always wanted to play a game like this at least on the PC. I think the announcer is really funny, but perhaps a few more sentences can be added since I've pretty much kind of memorized everything he was saying. The crowd does look a bit dead probably because of how they were rendered and maybe a louder crowd would at least hide that. The announcer was talking about the ref...I don't see the ref, or maybe I'm missing something here.
Anyone who wants to at play a football game on PC should get this but the caveat here is don't expect too much. This isn't Madden, it's Axis. Was it worth for me? I can say yes, because since I don't really play on consoles so I pretty much spend it here in Steam and this is pretty much the first football game I played ever since 99. Will it be worth it for someone else? Well, that depends. Try it on your own time.

I was skeptical at first in regards to this game, but I was quickly won over within five minutes of playing it.
The Banner Saga is what you get if you combine:
1. The multi-perspective first person narrative of Game of Thrones/ASoIaF, and on a scale seemingly just as grand.
2. Norse mythology and old Viking epics.
3. A wonderful soundtrack with grade A voice acting.
4. Turn based grid combat right out of classics such as Fire Emblem and FF: Tactics.
5. An Oregon Trail-style overworld with scenarios around every corner.
6. Gameplay where each and every choice alters the story in a multitude of different ways, right out of a very well thought out Choose Your Own Adventure story.
7. Classic Disney style animation.
Highly recommended if you like Vikings, Game of Thrones, old epics, Oregon Trail, Final Fantasy: Tactics, Disney movies, or games that value story substance and branching decisions (such as BioWare games).

First off I would like to say that I think the passing mechanic is the best innovation to the football genre in over a decade. I just wish that the rest of the game was as well fleshed out. Don't get me wrong, I've had fun with the game, but it feels like it should be in early access or a promotional tool to get a kick-stater going and not something being sold as a finished retail product. Also, it's awesome that this game supports Xbox One controllers.
For me it just has too many issues to recommend it at $20, which puts it in the same class of competition as games like Rocket League and SuperMega Baseball. But at a discount it is worth checking out but bear in mind it does have a few glitches and bugs here and there.
A few of those that I've encountered are:
I've had multiple instances of kickoffs out of bounds resulting in touchdowns being awarded to the AI. I've been rewarded touchdowns on successful two point conversion tries. Dropped lateral passes aren't counted as fumbles. There are some ballance issues with certain teams being pretty OP (you can easily run for 1,000 yds a game with Seattle). The A.I. throws far too many interceptions (I've had as many as 12 in a single game) and takes too many sacks (I've had as many as 39 in a single game) on higher difficulty levels.
I hate having to give this a negative review. I think this is a great starting point, the dev has some really good ideas, I'd love to see him get a serious backer because with proper resources and a team he could make an amazing game, but this isn't a $20 product. Again if you can get it at a lower price, you should give it a try, just have level headed expectations. This isn't a Madden-killer yet. Maybe in 2016.

and

This game is glitchy and the interface is terrible.  Much of the game is based on To Hit Percentages, that seem to be completely random, as it can give 100% to hit through a brick wall with a pistol, and a 15% to hit percentage with your target standing in the open 10' away.
The aliens use tactics that can only be possible if they can see where every one of your units are, while you can't so much as guess where they are, even if you have a clear view of them, meaning the aliens can basically hide in plain sight, while your units are totally exposed at all times.
When you spot aliens, even if they had no idea you were there, they get a full move action during your turn to take cover and/or hide offscreen.  One of the key abilities your characters have is called "overview," which allows you to ready an attack for the first enemy that comes into line of site, which would mitigate this extra move, if the attack ever actually hit.  Out of 50 uses of the ability, I connected twice with shots.
On top of that, the time your units spend hospitalized for minor wounds is a minimum of 3 days.  This is even assuming some of their health bars represent armor.  Then, critically wounded characters are taken out for a max of 10 days, which if you do the math, means the units heal unbelievably slow...unless they are dying, then they have superhuman healing abilities.
Next is cash flow.  You get about 500 credits a month.  This sounds like a lot, except you are supposed to buy each and every item you research.  While research itself is free, upgrading these discoveries costs you money, and past purchases do not automatically upgrade to the newest tech.  Also, in the course of a single month, you will experience 25-30 various alien encounters, and game time clocks time passage to the game second.  While you can fast forward to the next alien attack, the rewards for succeeding are extremely stingy, if any at all.
This leads to you not being able to afford anything but the basic gear in order to maintain an ever more advanced and dangerous enemy, whose technology seems to be free and infinite.  While this level of complexity would be enjoyable if you, also, got to advance your technology with recovered items, but instead, any weapons you collect are damaged beyond repair and can not be outfitted to your units.  With cash reserves strapped, you have to keep outfitting units that are not leveling as fast as your enemies with fewer and fewer resources.
On top of those strict financial issues, there is upkeep costs on your vehicles and stronghold upgrades, a limit to your power reserves for your various stronghold upgrades (which are vital to keeping tabs on the enemy, research new techs, and fabricating equipment), and you have to pay to replace your soldiers as they are wounded or killed.  It leads to an understanding that while the world governments want to prevent an attack on earth, they aren't willing to pay for any of it.
I would guess that you'd have better cash flow if you could get your soldiers to work at the local McDonald's for minimum wage, and your scientists and engineers, too.  The game overcomplicates in a way that oversimplifies micromanagement of your resources.
All in all, its a frustrating, time sink, and when you are done, you wish you could get that time refunded.  Do not invest in this game.

Perhaps the definitive zombie-survival game to emerge during this zombie-themed game craze we've been experiencing lately (however I say this without having played DayZ - but I've played just about all the others on offer I think).
From the creator's of Dead Island comes a very visually-polished game set in an open world zombie apocalypse.
The game world consists of a city that is under quarantine due to an outbreak which (you guessed it) has been turning people in to zombies.
Part of a military outfit and sent in alone to conduct missions on behalf of their interests; your character spends the game exploring the quarantined city and conducting missions on behalf of survivors and the various groups left in the city, in order to earn their trust and also a bit of scratch to upgrade your zombie-mashing gear.
A perk levelling system exists which is quite deep and varied - keeping interacting with the world fresh, and the game is also heavily parkour-focused... making traversing the environment at high speed with a horde of zombies pursuing behind pretty fun.
It does suffer from some of the same problems as the Assassin Creed series... sometimes you jump to ledges you never intended to, or it tries to intuit where you wanted to go incorrectly - however I found this still to be much less of an issue in this game than the AC series.
A great feature is the multiplayer whereby you can progress through the storymode with mates, and when setting marker destinations on the map etc, the game prompts you with an option to create a competition out of reaching the destination first - there are a few prompts like this which are welcome and keep the momentum going.
Overall, the price is steep but the game is good - definitely head and shoulders above the Dead Island entries. 4/5

A fantastic open-world snowsports simulator that allows you to head out and find your own lines and runs as well as compete in a bunch of events for the various sports. With the paraglider and the rocket wingsuit especially getting around is easy, and you can warp to any unlocked point on the mountains. With what's included in the base game alone you end up with the equivelent of what must be 100 or more runs that you'd find in a game like 1080 or SSX (to give a sense of content scale), with the longest runs being a good 10+ minutes. Whether you want steep and rocky or shallow and powdery, and whether that be smooth or covered in trees and hunks of ice; snow parks the lot - it's all here in droves.
The riding is satisfying and thrilling without feeling too unrealistic. The 'G' system keeps everything in check and is intuitive and natural, other than that there are no meters. The points system works really well, with the multiplyer being based on riding without a fall, it doesn't decay through normal riding so you dont have a pressure to be constantly pulling off tricks - and freeride points can be accumulated through normal riding like riding crests and near misses with trees. This means that you're rewarded for exploring the full scope of riding and making the best of the lines, you don't have to constantly do the same thing.
The one thing I wish Steep had is character/player progression. For better or worse there's no character levelling or gear stats, you just pick from one of the handful of stock characters and dress them with gear you like. Some people will love this - but grinding out an epic character is something I tend to enjoy in extreme sports games. On the other hand there's no 'pay to win' or much of a need to grind. So it's not all bad - the skill comes from you the player - but there's no sense of career or personal development. There is an account levelling system which just opens up more events as you go - it doesn't really have much impact on the game. Completing events also gets you cash and gear.
It does feel haflway to a simulator in that regard - the game aspects are almost a bit light, half baked almost - but if yu want the open world stuff there's nothing that compares to it.

I have both OMD1 and OMD2 and I must say that OMD1 still holds up very well. The graphics and playbility remain strong today despite the fact OMD1 is now 4-years old.
OMD1 and OMD2 is all about killing massive numbers of orcs, ogres, and all manner of creatures in a fun, cartoony-violent way.  Yes, the game has a large amount of "gore and violence" but it is "fine and acceptable" because of the "fun" way the developers render the graphics.  If the graphics were done "realistically", the "gore and violence" would make it unacceptable for kids and even many adults who have queasy stomachs.
For example, I find it funny when you kill an ogre, you see slices of meat / chopped meat to represent the killing than a rendering of what a mutilated ogre might look like "realistically". It is also funny to watch all the orcs "suffer" and otherwise react to being tortured and then killed. I know it might sound really bad when you read this but it is really a credit to the developers who pulled off this magical feat (no pun intended) of making all the killing and violence fun and amusing.
Ultimately, this is meant to be a fun, humorous, and fast-paced game where one can escape to kill hundreds of digital creatures.  And as of the game and the DLC's wasn't fun enough, I bought OMD1 at a steep Steam discount.  When you play a fabulous game for dozens of hours and you buy it for a steal, it just doesn't get any better for a gamer.
OMD1 is a winner.  When you get done with OMD1, go to OMD2.  So much fun!

Gameplay: Solid mechanics, can't get more basic than this. A controller is reccomended though. Timed button presses will make you or break you when playing this.
Humor: It's South Park. If you don't like South Park's humor or didn't really like the show, you won't like this game. References are everywhere and they range from great to "Oh yeah, I remember that."
Visuals/Graphics: This game perfectly recreates the show's art style to the point where as many reviewers have said before: "It feels like you're playing an episode of the show!". You shouldn't need a powerful or fast PC to get enjoyment out of this, but you might not want to play this game if you're running on a potato. Stick of Truth takes a page out of the book of Mario RPGs, in that timed button presses can affect the flow of gameplay entirely. So a PC lacking in power could make the game a bit less enjoyable.
Overall: I wouldn't say its worth the full price of $30, but as of when I'm writing this, the game is about $7 which is well worth the price of this gem of a title. If you enjoy the sickening, but often intelligent humor of South Park, then by all means buy this game.

Disappointing. Not worth $20. But if a few things are FIXED, this game would be pretty good.
First, the bugs:
1) That little white passing target circle ("aimed pass target"), works about 50% of the time. When it doesn't work, the white circle appears STUCK about 10yds down from where ball was snapped. Moving the mouse does NOT move the aiming circle. That needs to be fixed.
2) Kickoff the ball to the sideline; if it goes outta bounds, the opposing team gets a TD. That needs to be fixed.
3) In 1 of 6 games I played, had to quit and restart due to a looping animated sequence; after opponent was tackled, the opponent player gets up, then falls, then gets up... repeat. It was in a loop. Had to quit and restart.
Now for the disapointments:
1) The side view isn't a PLAYABLE view. Only for coach mode. That needs to be fixed. Tecmo is played from a SIDE VIEW. If this game is gonna play like Tecmo, can we at least PLAY it in the Tecmo-like SIDE VIEW?
2) More camera angles would be nice. The up-field Madden camera is fine but can we at least lower, raise or even tilt it? (Same for a playable sideline view).
3) No defensive audibles. Wow.
4) Some wind effects on kicking would be nice.
5) AT LEAST have a button for SPIN (offense) and DIVE (offense and defense). Again, like TECMO, all we can to is change player and guide player. That's it! OK, if this is gonna follow the TECMO model, give us a playable SIDELINE view.
6) Cannot exit, save and continue a saved game.
7) Cannot change difficulty DURING A SEASON. This is really LAME. It took me nearly 3 hours of playing to discover the only realistic way to play this game is to play on the highest level, using one of the better teams. The other easier modes are just too easy. So why not let us change difficulty BEFORE EACH GAME, DURING A SEASON!?
8) NO VIEWABLE schedules. WOW....
9) No coin toss to determine who kicks and who receives. No big deal but found it strange I can decide to kick or receive every game.
10). Modding; not interested in obtaining special graphical software just so I can mod this game. I guess I need cross my fingers that other people can post their modded files somewhere, that REDO the logos, making these teams look like NFL teams with correct NAMES and LOGOS.
That's it for me. Personally, I enjoyed the experience. I'll probably play 1 season and delete this game. Worth $20? Not really. In short,
is like a 3-bite snack to the original TWD game's full course meal.
Each episode is about 90 minutes of play.  While it wisely sticks with the formula of action mixed with dialogue, its biggest problem is there isn't enough time for character development.  The game says "Pete will remember that," but you don't get caught in webs of lies later, or build someone's trust over time based on what you say.  Whether you open up to someone or say nothing, confront them or acquiesce to them, your choices don't seem to matter.  You don't see relationships develop step by step from start to finish, the way it did between Lee and Clementine.
Who are you supposed to care about here?  The boat crew you see for a few minutes before separating from them?  Your kids that you only see via flashback?  Just because the game tells me I should have a bond with them, doesn't make it so.  At least you don't have to keep people you don't like around for long.
In fairness, I haven't read the comic book.  But in the original game, that wasn't necessary.  I won't spoil the final, climactic choice, but note that over 90% of players made the same decision.  I think that demonstrates that the game failed to set up a real breaking point, where each option had merit on moral, philosophical, spiritiual, or
kind of grounds.
I can only recommend
for people whose hunger for more TWD content is fierce, and even then I'd only buy it on sale.

FINALLY an American football game on Steam!  The gameplay is fun, the game is simple (a good thing in my book), and the games are quick enough that you can pop in and play for 15 minutes at a time.  I enjoy the season mode a lot as it is not too complicated.  I also enjoy seeing your combined margin of victory along with your W/L record. My biggest dislike is that all the teams are NOT equal.  If you want to play as your favourite NFL team (erm, city?), you're out of luck if you don't like Green Bay, Pittsburgh, or a select few others.  Only about 1/4 of the teams are actually playable - the rest are just too difficult to bother with.  I imagine this can be changed a little by modding the rosters, but it's a little silly to be forced to edit your team just to make it a viable option.
Overall it's an enjoyable football game with decent AI and fun gameplay.  Yes it's short on features, but it's priced accordingly.  For an arcade football game, you won't be disappointed!

You can balance it yourself by starting with more or less characters. I would strongly recommend starting with 5 players because the endgame is very hard otherwise.

But some people call this 'lacking in depth' and I guess they're right too. They do re-use certain backgrounds and let you grind from level 32-37 and 1 mission later 37-45 at the end of the game, so they definitely rushed through the end trying to add some 'gameplay' without putting in work sadly. That level 50 mission is optional btw. Throughout the rest of the game there is rarely a need to grind though. Do note that the game has some large bugs. Some achievements are broken, some missions are broken, DLC doesn't work for some and there's graphical glitches. This seems like a hasty port honestly. And then there's the fact that if you want the Deluxier Edition you have to buy it at once. You can't upgrade. If you already have Normal edition or Deluxe edition (extra's, but no DLC) you're screwed. Also they just wiped everybody's saves trying to emplement the (not fully working) cloud save. Then wiped all saves again when reverting to the old build.
So the game is very fun, but beware that this game is published by Paradox. As long as you're lucky enough to be in the 90% for whom most things don't break you're good. But if something goes wrong there's no support and dealing with Paradox is like talking to a 3 year old and when they realize you're right they just ignore you.
I only recommend this game because it's unique. It's very money-grabby, too expensive and the publisher is unethical and clearly doesn't care about it's customers, but the game is so much  fun and most people don't care about what happens behind the scenes. And if I'd downvote it the fanboys would downvote this review and you wouldn't be reading about the downsides of this game right now.

Finally an American football game on Steam! And yet, this review, at best, is a neutral review.
Don't get me wrong, it can be entertaining! And I dont regret the purchase. And the dev is great! Very friendly, and seems really dedicated to the game. Its just so....lacking. Literally.
I'll list the cons first, then the pros, to end the review on a good note!
The season mode feels so basic. There is no stats, schedule, nothing. In fact, it feels more like it just randomly generates a matchup to play after each game played. To show what I mean by generating a matchup after each game, this is an experience I had in my season. I was the New England Volunteers( New England Patriots, fyi) and I had to play the New Orleans Crusaders( New Orleans Saints.) I played them as the road team, on, Week 4. On Week 6, I again played the Crusaders, in the Crusaders stadium. The endzones had the Crusaders name in both games. One was played in clear weather, the next in the rain.
Next, the playbooks. Ok I love to strategize about football. One thing I love about Madden video games, is to look at the playbooks to see all the different plays, formations, etc. Axis football, instead has a tiny playbook. I counted the plays. Offensively, there is 45 plays, counting Speacial Teams plays. There are 45 defensive plays, counting the special teams, again. Not much variety. The game is broke down into two(2) 5 minute halves. With limited plays, you'll probably use the same play anywhere between 5-20 times A GAME. For me, most second halves are dull. But, hey, thats just me. Just needed to point it out.
The Ai needs a whole new overhaul. Really.
There isn't probably, a game that you dont eventually know how to defeat and counter the Ai. But this, this Ai is so simple and easy to beat. Even on the hardest setting, I still won and even earned an achievement from it! In this case, it was for the Comeback Kids achievement. Gotta overcome a 21+ halftime deficit. Even on the hardest possible difficulty, I  had to goof off for the first half, just to ensure the Ai was ahead by 21+ points. I won 36-35, even with the clock bugging out, and not stopping when it should have! On another football game, I would've lost. On Axis Football 2015, I dont think its possible for the Ai to win, unless you play horribly, or your team's ratings are lower than the Ai, but thats still winnable.
Next the price. For what they're asking for it, this game lacks in. I bought the game during the promo sale, with 10% off. The game is not worth $20. Given the current state its in, 5-7 bucks is its worth at max. Maybe $10 since its the only one on Steam.
Bugs abound, but none seem to be game-breaking, thankfully. How many times has the playbook glitched after an interception, or kickoff, showing offensive plays, when Im on defense? Its super annoying. And, the worst case of it struck AFTER 1.4 came out! Most of the second half for me, I was stuck using my Nickel formation, since every other formation showed my offensive playbook. Still won, and not game breaking, but still.
I'll now list the few pros:
Creative take on the team names.
A step up from Backyard football.
Good dev, even if experience is a little lacking.
Final thoughts.
Not a bad game, not a great game. Way too easy, even with the new passing mechanic. The game also lacks way to much in game modes. Not even a practice mode(greatly needed) kicking game is wild, and even the roster modding seems to have gotten off to a rocky start, according to some comments in the community hub.
The store page says this is a great alternative to playing Madden. Playing this, it greatly increases my desire to dig out any of my Madden games and play them. Or any of my other football games, for that matter, though none are on the PC and obviously not on Steam.
The dev also says hes in this for the long haul. However, its already been noted that next year, Axis Football 2016 will be available for purchase, so its up to you to decide if the long haul means this game, or if whether in a few years Madden will have a rival football game to compete with. Actually, I believe when I saw game play of this game, it was on Axis Football 2014, so it would seem each year equals a new release, with, presumably, more game modes, etc.
The achievements are also easy to achieve. My first game with 100% achievements, and I earned them all in 9.0 hours of gameplay exactly, according to Steam.
There are plenty of cons, yes. But, I still recommend to at least try it out. If anything, you can learn about the game of football. Or experience a decent dev. Or relive the early days of football video games.

Dying Light was a blast to play and I am happy I did.
Story: 9 / 10 - The voice acting and writing was sometimes a bit silly but an otherwise climatic experience with lots of rewarding moments.
Sound: 9.5/10 - Incredible music really enhances the experience. Sounds are really well done in this game. I would give 10 but the survivor sense was kind of an annoying repeptitive sound you constantly need to use.
Gameplay: 10/10 - Combat was refined and the free running was outstanding. Your character develops really well through the skill trees. I loved all the side content as well. I never once felt bored playing Dying Light. Night time is scary as hell.
Graphics: 10/10 - Fantastic graphics. Nice PC port that ran smoothly from start to finish. Fairly demanding, you will need a decent PC to fully enjoy the beauty of this game.
Controls 9/10 - I used keyboard and mouse and found some things a bit clunky at first but is easy to learn.
Overall 9.5/10 - I put Dying Light up there as my favorite zombie survival/horror/action experience. The mechanics were amazing and I felt very challenged at some points. It's everything the Dead Island games should have been.
Completion time: 40 hours of main story/side quests but I still have challenges, collectibles and other minor things to finish.
