An absolutely fantastic game.
[GAMEPLAY]
Looking back on Dead Island & Riptide, after playing this game, it seems like the developers really have learned from their experiences. Instead of picking a character already focused on one type of combat & upgrading from there, you are free to customise your character as you see fit, which can lead to creating a character that not only fits your play style, but will influence your strategy in surviving in the game world. The game rewards strategic thinking.
It also rewards skill. The lockpicking from Skyrim is here, but without the unlockable character upgrades that can make it easier to open harder chests. It is simply down to your skill. Similiarly, gun-use does not require an unlockable upgrade, which if you play FPSs is hartily appreciated, as you don’t suck at guns for the first half of the game. What does upgrade is your bag, your free-running, your capability with hand-to-hand weapons - their use & their mantainance, your crafting & your health. You gain upgrade points by completing missions or helping random strangers you come across for SURVIVOR uprades, fighting for POWER upgrades & free-running for Agility upgrades, which can lead to you one-hitting zombies or sprinting along walls Prince of Persia style. And you are rewarded for combinations of jumps, landings, attacks & timing, which creates a REAL feeling of progression, as you see what is benefiting you.
Every time you run into something that might get stale, you find the developers have dropped in new elements to keep things fresh. Every now & again you will run into a new type of zombie as the story progresses, which will force you to find new ways to fight them, or to focus on different upgrades or weapons to even the odds. Also, halfway through the game you gain access to a new district, akin to Shadow of Mordor but, unlike SoM, the area has changed so much that your approach to playing changes as well, requiring a slightly altered style of play; a fresh challange against which to pit the skills you honed in the last area.
There is also the day/night cycle. You are rewarded a boost to XP for Agility & Power at night &, not only are certain enemies more powerful, but new faster, stronger & more durable enemies appear. Meaning you can sleep through the night OR you can choose to go and about trusting your agility to guide you through, or just wade in when your feel yourself strong enough. And crafted gadgets like firecrackers & flares (which ward off the big bads) make this actually do-able, when at first it seems like a mad prospect!
The game is very well put together, providing well-balanced & varied enemies so that you cannot just climb up high or run really fast & expect to breeze through & avoid danger, you have to engage with it & REALLY play the game. Similiarly, if you don't want to play at night, you don't have to. But there are parts of the story where you are forced to act against your inclinations & embrace night running, presenting you with the hard opportunity to either just run, praying, or think about it strategically, should you ever be caught out again. (The camouflage ability came in really handy for me in those situations, which was a strategic choice I didn't have to make and, without it, I would have needed to play very differently to survive.)
The free running mechanic is also extremely well-polished &, after a little while, you get a sense for what distances you can cross, what ledges you can make it to, & this also presents an interesting way to approach quests, since you can approach enemy camps from above as well as below. Finding your own way, via your own ingenuity is extremely satisfying.
[GRAPHICS]
The graphics for the game look brilliant. The faces for some characters could be better done & there is the occasional cloning of very minor npcs, but the regular, major & critical NPCs look well, individual & everything from weapons, to gore, to the city itself looks great. The atomsphere is very well done indeed: rain is wet, the world & you will be soaked. Get soaked at your vision will be compromised. It looks & feels exactly like it should. Also, the night is daaaaark, like it should be.
(I ended up in a really nerve-wracking area & found myself telling the character to wipe his bleeping eyes already so I could see! All of it works to heighten the tension. Similarly, at one point he was exhausted and his breathing was loud & heavy, & I found myself worrying that the undead might actually hear it, since they react to all kinds of sounds in the world, which leads us to...)
[SOUND]
Thunder, water, rain, impact sounds, sloughing guts - it all sounds like it should, pulling you in. The undead also make different sounds, which will have you turning about looking for the extra dangerous one you just heard shriek as it spotted you. There are ambient sounds of distant fires, fighting, monster & human screams - when you are moving about through a dangerous area & someone (there are a number of different types) screams distantly "HELP ME!", or just cries out in terror, you hear it but the way it is generated leaves you wondering what direction it came from, giving the city a feeling of living terror that is constantly shifting and moving, and it fits superbly.
The music too is fitting & some tracks are great to listen to. The menu music alone had me sitting listening for a few moments every time I loaded up the game to get me into the feel of it. I still listen to it after having completed the game.
[STORY & CHARACTERS]
The main characters, from the kid who you worry isn't old enough to take charge, to the guy who rallied the first survivors you meet, to the woman you run with (trying to avoid spoilers), and practically across the board, all have their own back stories & many have stories that have influenced the city in some way, you cross posters for some, & meet random survivors who have met or know of others. The stories are nuanced as well, & aren’t rammed down your throat, you get a sense of the person from your time with them & from what others say, which allows you to not only bond with the characters you like but also to fill in the pieces of their back story specifically left out because it isn't pertinent to what they are saying at the time, which feels more realistic.
While there has been the occasional complaint about the main bad guy being something of a stereotype, his backstory (discovered in-game) reveals that he was a very different man up until a short while ago, and even when first the quarantine first arrived. But, now, he is exactly the type of person this crisis would create. Someone who's mind has shifted to see things differently, aiding his survival.
And the story is strong enough, with both your own mission and the added element of the people you get to know and need to protect, that it keeps the momentum up. Regular breaks with new orders from your bosses outside the quarantine give you an actual moral tie to the game and the people you are either helping or putting in danger with your actions. And the fact that side missions tend to build on themselves, creating new issues that arise from other missions make it feel like a more vibrant and alive experience.
[OVERALL]
This is solid game that anticipates the lulls that exist in open world gameplay & actually addresses them to keep things fresh. It is fast, and rewarding and has just the right amount of everything to keep you playing. The peaks and troughs that exist in open world games are a shadow of what they were. The peaks are still there, but you don't feel like your are are wasting time with busy work until your next story mission. It is definitely one I would recommend. I'm already feeling its absence now that I've finished it.

Amazing game. I loved this game, although some parts were hard.
Pros:
Super trippy. You're in one place one moment, then when you turn around, you're not there anymore.
Cool puzzles. Puzzles that make you think alot. Some require leftover resources from the previous puzzles.
Every puzzle is unique enough that it doesn't seem like you're doing the same thing twice (although you may have to return to a puzzle more than twice).
Slow, calm pace, with ambient background noise which gives the environment a very soothing feel.
Cons:
For as decently long as it is, it feels short, leaving you craving more.
Confusing puzzles that require a bit of thinking and consideration before solving, possible turn off for people who like straight forward games that directs you exactly where to go.
Sometimes you find yourself returning to the same puzzles. Returning through older rooms might help give a clue on where to go next.
Basically, Antichamber is an amazing game that I highly recommend if you enjoy puzzle games. It's trippy as balls, and it is an experience you can't really find in many other places.

A good old classic. BFII is a great game that can take any Star Wars fan back into that old Star Wars mood. The classes are fairly balanced and the maps have a strategic, compelling and memorable structure that can make even the person who only knows who Darth Vader is happy in the knowledge that their sci-fi combat interests are satisfied. My only three problems with this game are the online, AI and map changes from Star Wars Battlefront (the original). The online is fairly barren, but the remaining community are friendly, jumping into random games and starting conversations in the chat log, so it’s not all bad, but it can be annoying if you're looking for a big match to get that 'battlefront' feeling (if you are into that and would not mind a less sci-fi based experience then I would recommend battlefield 3 or 4). The AI, although not terrible can be repetitive in its actions, and through that, advantageous to the player who will rarely need to change tactics in combat no matter how many enemies he or she is going up against. This can be even more of a predicament if online with friends as the AI are merely fodder for both sides which can result in unfair bias depending on player skill, map setup etc. The last problem I care to put some extensive thought into is the changing of the original maps (Geonosis being the key one). Some of the Battlefront maps are far cooler than the Battlefront 2 ones which makes it annoying for the players of the original, however it doesn’t really matter too much if you haven't played BF 1 as it’s merely a conservative viewpoint and also my opinion, although I do have other friends who agree.
All in all this game deserves 4 stars due to the great improvements from the original and the star wars vibe you can get from playing it. If you like sci-fi combat or more importantly, are a star wars fan, then I recommend this game to you.
I could go on about the good bits to this game, but being a fanboy to the original BF I'd rather look to explaining the bad (which I've already done), so I'll simply state the best good points:
- Space combat
- Galactic Conquest
- Hero battle
- Single player campaign
- Music
- Lore/fan friendly (factions, maps, ships, units, skins, guns, vehicles etc.)

At the time of writing this review, I have 129 hours in Steep.
Steep is a very interesting game made by people who really understand the winter mountain life. No matter what you do in the game, you can be rewarded for it. It has a lot of heart while also having a lot of ridiculousness. In my honest opinion, there are at least 3 things in this game that any kind of player will enjoy, from racing down slopes at breakneck speeds to enjoying the views from the seat of your paraglider. This is a wonderful go-to game if you are looking to just chill out and avoid the things that make you salty. There's music of many genres and lots of customization that you can earn through progression. The game is like a day out with good friends, whether you just simply hung out at the park or sparred until somebody is bleeding. There is the chill, for fun side where you may just be freeroaming and finding nice lines with buddies, and the competitive side that always subtly pushes you to try again and be the best. Sure, there are some frustrating things in the game, I will admit that. But overall, this is simply a solid game and a wonderful experience. There simply isn't anything truly like it on the market right now. I recommend this game, ESPECIALLY if you are into winter/mountain sports yourself.

I love this game. I still haven't beaten it, and I'll try to update my review when I do, but so far, there is very little about this game that is not fantastic. I bought it for the atmosphere, and I was not disappointed in the slightest. The amount of work that went into making a cohesive and interesting world is impressive. After playing for only a couple hours, I had learned enough about the world to become attached to it, but I still feel as if I've seen only a small part of a grander picture, and I'm enjoying the process of discovering more about the world immensely. There are a few jarring elements, the speech sometimes feels a bit off, and distances and travel times are hard to judge. But overall the characters, the world, and the events of the game create an atmosphere that make this game fantastic all on their own.
Speaking of the characters, you will probably get attached to them. It's difficult in a game like this to strike the right balance for the main characters between blank slates, acting only according to the whims of the player, and fully developed characters who make their decisions regardless of what the player wants. The Banner Saga does a good job with that, the characters have identities of their own, but they are faced with choices where they could reasonably go either way, so the player can still influence them to some degree. You're never in complete control of them, and there might be times when their character prevents you from making a choice you would prefer, but you always feel like you are influencing the story.
I spent a lot of time agonizing over the choices I've had to make throughout the game. I was surprised by how much I cared about the characters as they journeyed across the continent, and it sucks when a seemingly harmless choice ends up hurting them. Sometimes you can recover from a bad decision with particularly good strategy in the next fight, sometimes it's just a matter of making the best of what's left, but it all contributes to my inability to stop playing this game.
I like the combat system but don't have a lot to say on the topic. I've definitely never had this much trouble with a strategy game before, but it's (almost) always winnable. It took some getting used to, but the strategy part has started to make more sense.
The art and music are great, of course, but you know that already.
The only things I've found that I don't like are:
You can't see movement range when setting up units
You can't see enemy move order when settng up units
You can't change your own move order when setting up units
You can't change equipment while setting up units (or more importantly, when selecting your party before the fight)
I find myself misclicking a lot. It would be nice if you could undo moves if you haven't actually taken an action yet. This is especially annoying when I have a ranged ability, and I can see the range from my starting position, but I miscount the number of spaces I need to move before the enemy is in range, and then I can't change my move, so I'm stuck doing nothing.
All in all, the game is great, and you should buy it. It's definitely worth the price.

-Most important..: This is *not* a simulation; it is an arcade game, where you control the QB /ball carrier on offense, and a key player on defense; each "half" is 5 minutes in (more or less) real time.  Moreover, while you can control a player using the direction keys, there are no special moves (e.g. juke, stiff arm, hard tacklee, etc.) a la Madden.
---There are no NFL teams, despite marketing to the contrary....I played the 'Green Bay "IceMen"
---On offense, there is limited play selection; without the ability to design routes, the selection is actually rather limited.   There are an impressive number of defense plays available, based on the number of linemen you put up front.
---The clock/clock management is a mess (no hurry up, each play takes only a few seconds off the clock,)
---since it is an arcade type game, there are waaaaay too many big plays---it's all sacks, interceptions, bombs and long breakaway runs....in one game, my HB had runs of 88, 49 and 38 yards---IN ONE HALF.
---Penalties...: there are none.
---Fumbles...:way too few; Interceptions: way too many
---Injuries: none


A few other observations:
---The graphics are upgradeable, and on my high-end MacPro at maximum resolution, the animations are pretty good
---There is a live announcer, although his calls are limited and quickly become repetitive,
---There is a 'Season' mode, including single-game elimination Play-offs, but no career mode.
---The AI is too easy to beat. There are four difficulty levels; after two "practice" games I started an entire season and went 8-1 before getting bored and giving up.
---There is local multiplayer support (good) but no online MP (bad)

There are so many absent or missing features I would personally consider this an early beta.  To emphasize,the game is strictly  an arcade-y experience---there is no "coaching mode" available---and so perhaps some of the missing features mentioned above are less important---but this is no Madden, and given the availability of other, better American football simulations on other platforms I can not recommend the game in its current state.
Bottom line:  the game costs about a third of what EA chareges for each Madden seasonal title, and has about the commensurate level of quality.

BTW, for those people who, like me, love American football and have been yearning for a realistic and fun coaching sim. game, the best football game I have "ever" played---going back 40+ years to the board-game days of All-Pro Football, Strategy, Scrimmage; through the days of MircoLeague and Playmaker, to NFL Quarterback Club and Blitz; to the modern era and the yearly incarnations of NCAA and Madden---is "Pro Strategy Football," which is (unfortunately) still only available for the iPhone and iPad...if you have never tried it, you owe it to yourself to play it, then bug its devs. to port it to the PC.

the word rouge-like gets throw around a lot. It seems there is a bigger craze for "indie rouge-likes" now more than the DOOM clones of the 90s. Rouge Legacy, Legend of the Dungeon, Sword of the Stars, Dungeon of the Endless, Angband, tales of Majisomething, Spelunky, Paranautical Activity, seriously, like this stuff stacks up quick. Although FTL is one of these rouge-likes, it stands unique and apart from the others.
FTL is a beautiful space exploration game with a very well done art style and good ship design. The randomized elements keep each play through fresh, which is good, because you will have several run throughs trying to beat this game. it took me 21 hours and 50 something tries to beat the game once on easy. While that sounds insanley difficult and frustrating, the shortness of each run through (the victory took 2 hours, while most runs were 30 minutes) stops most of the frustration. In fact, dying 30 minutes in gives a nice little taste of gaming. Busy? Hop into your starship and run a few sectors before being blasted apart by slavers. or borded by mantuis. or being cooked alive by a dying star. or being trapped behind enemy lines like the millenium falcon in the empire strikes back.
A great game, great stories, good combat. not much more you can ask for.

An absolutely fantastic game.
[GAMEPLAY]
Looking back on Dead Island & Riptide, after playing this game, it seems like the developers really have learned from their experiences. Instead of picking a character already focused on one type of combat & upgrading from there, you are free to customise your character as you see fit, which can lead to creating a character that not only fits your play style, but will influence your strategy in surviving in the game world. The game rewards strategic thinking.
It also rewards skill. The lockpicking from Skyrim is here, but without the unlockable character upgrades that can make it easier to open harder chests. It is simply down to your skill. Similiarly, gun-use does not require an unlockable upgrade, which if you play FPSs is hartily appreciated, as you don’t suck at guns for the first half of the game. What does upgrade is your bag, your free-running, your capability with hand-to-hand weapons - their use & their mantainance, your crafting & your health. You gain upgrade points by completing missions or helping random strangers you come across for SURVIVOR uprades, fighting for POWER upgrades & free-running for Agility upgrades, which can lead to you one-hitting zombies or sprinting along walls Prince of Persia style. And you are rewarded for combinations of jumps, landings, attacks & timing, which creates a REAL feeling of progression, as you see what is benefiting you.
Every time you run into something that might get stale, you find the developers have dropped in new elements to keep things fresh. Every now & again you will run into a new type of zombie as the story progresses, which will force you to find new ways to fight them, or to focus on different upgrades or weapons to even the odds. Also, halfway through the game you gain access to a new district, akin to Shadow of Mordor but, unlike SoM, the area has changed so much that your approach to playing changes as well, requiring a slightly altered style of play; a fresh challange against which to pit the skills you honed in the last area.
There is also the day/night cycle. You are rewarded a boost to XP for Agility & Power at night &, not only are certain enemies more powerful, but new faster, stronger & more durable enemies appear. Meaning you can sleep through the night OR you can choose to go and about trusting your agility to guide you through, or just wade in when your feel yourself strong enough. And crafted gadgets like firecrackers & flares (which ward off the big bads) make this actually do-able, when at first it seems like a mad prospect!
The game is very well put together, providing well-balanced & varied enemies so that you cannot just climb up high or run really fast & expect to breeze through & avoid danger, you have to engage with it & REALLY play the game. Similiarly, if you don't want to play at night, you don't have to. But there are parts of the story where you are forced to act against your inclinations & embrace night running, presenting you with the hard opportunity to either just run, praying, or think about it strategically, should you ever be caught out again. (The camouflage ability came in really handy for me in those situations, which was a strategic choice I didn't have to make and, without it, I would have needed to play very differently to survive.)
The free running mechanic is also extremely well-polished &, after a little while, you get a sense for what distances you can cross, what ledges you can make it to, & this also presents an interesting way to approach quests, since you can approach enemy camps from above as well as below. Finding your own way, via your own ingenuity is extremely satisfying.
[GRAPHICS]
The graphics for the game look brilliant. The faces for some characters could be better done & there is the occasional cloning of very minor npcs, but the regular, major & critical NPCs look well, individual & everything from weapons, to gore, to the city itself looks great. The atomsphere is very well done indeed: rain is wet, the world & you will be soaked. Get soaked at your vision will be compromised. It looks & feels exactly like it should. Also, the night is daaaaark, like it should be.
(I ended up in a really nerve-wracking area & found myself telling the character to wipe his bleeping eyes already so I could see! All of it works to heighten the tension. Similarly, at one point he was exhausted and his breathing was loud & heavy, & I found myself worrying that the undead might actually hear it, since they react to all kinds of sounds in the world, which leads us to...)
[SOUND]
Thunder, water, rain, impact sounds, sloughing guts - it all sounds like it should, pulling you in. The undead also make different sounds, which will have you turning about looking for the extra dangerous one you just heard shriek as it spotted you. There are ambient sounds of distant fires, fighting, monster & human screams - when you are moving about through a dangerous area & someone (there are a number of different types) screams distantly "HELP ME!", or just cries out in terror, you hear it but the way it is generated leaves you wondering what direction it came from, giving the city a feeling of living terror that is constantly shifting and moving, and it fits superbly.
The music too is fitting & some tracks are great to listen to. The menu music alone had me sitting listening for a few moments every time I loaded up the game to get me into the feel of it. I still listen to it after having completed the game.
[STORY & CHARACTERS]
The main characters, from the kid who you worry isn't old enough to take charge, to the guy who rallied the first survivors you meet, to the woman you run with (trying to avoid spoilers), and practically across the board, all have their own back stories & many have stories that have influenced the city in some way, you cross posters for some, & meet random survivors who have met or know of others. The stories are nuanced as well, & aren’t rammed down your throat, you get a sense of the person from your time with them & from what others say, which allows you to not only bond with the characters you like but also to fill in the pieces of their back story specifically left out because it isn't pertinent to what they are saying at the time, which feels more realistic.
While there has been the occasional complaint about the main bad guy being something of a stereotype, his backstory (discovered in-game) reveals that he was a very different man up until a short while ago, and even when first the quarantine first arrived. But, now, he is exactly the type of person this crisis would create. Someone who's mind has shifted to see things differently, aiding his survival.
And the story is strong enough, with both your own mission and the added element of the people you get to know and need to protect, that it keeps the momentum up. Regular breaks with new orders from your bosses outside the quarantine give you an actual moral tie to the game and the people you are either helping or putting in danger with your actions. And the fact that side missions tend to build on themselves, creating new issues that arise from other missions make it feel like a more vibrant and alive experience.
[OVERALL]
This is solid game that anticipates the lulls that exist in open world gameplay & actually addresses them to keep things fresh. It is fast, and rewarding and has just the right amount of everything to keep you playing. The peaks and troughs that exist in open world games are a shadow of what they were. The peaks are still there, but you don't feel like your are are wasting time with busy work until your next story mission. It is definitely one I would recommend. I'm already feeling its absence now that I've finished it.

Cartoony, and humorous slap-stick style turret defense with added fps elements.  Extremely fun and engaging from start to finish. You are the guardian of the warp-gate thingy... baddies (orcs, trolls, bats, goblins, etc) spawn at a specific location and traverse the map to get to the glowing blue pillar of light that must be protected at all costs. The AI isn't amazing but it will alter its path if there is one of lesser resistance, or even move to attack you directly if you're close enough to them. Your task as the guardian is to stop them by any and all means necessary. be it shooting them with arrows, magic, or traps that you've cleverly placed along their selected path. All the while upgrading your skills/traps along the way to improve your chances of preventing them from escaping.
In short, Orcs must die! like, a lot...

This game is simply amazing. 6 out of 5 stars.
Pros:
Very good story; deep, emersive, and intriguing.
The voice acting is realistic and believable. Unlike other games the devs seemed to have gotten actual professional voice actors and not just recycled the same 5 voices.
The dialog is realistic and entertaining, with your conversation options feeling realistic and lifelike. As well as your relationships with NPC's and the other members of your party.
The game play is fantastic, intuitive, and open.
The amount of quests open to the character are seemingly limitless.
The combat is very well done, cinematic, and challenging. For instance you can use magic to make it rain on the battlefield, then cast an ice spell on an enemy to freeze them because they were soaking wet from the rain.
The graphics are spectacular, bright, clear, and beautiful.
Put simply this is the closest video game I have found that comes close to being as open as a table top Dungeons and Dragons game, with how your choices effect everything and how each battle varies and is affected by the environment.
Cons:
Not all dialog is voice acted. Some portions of quests related conversations can be really lengthy, and with not all conversations being voice acted this leads to a lot of reading.
During combat it is very easy to click beside an enemy rather then on the actual enemy; causing your character to waste action points walking up to the enemy rather then attacking.
When moving from one area of high altitude to low altitude or vice versa, the camera will often get stuck zoomed extremely far out (due to being stuck at the high altitude areas height) or extremely close up (due to being stuck at the low altitude areas height).
All in all this is a fantastic game and I highly recommend it. Some adivce (seems obvious) would be at the character selection make sure complimentary characters are picked, if your characters dont have complimentary combat abilites you will be in deep trouble.

I didn't think I would enjoy this game but I do. I'm hooked.
I thought that the fast-paced strategy would be chaotic and difficult to master. I was pleased to find out that you can pause the action at any moment and give orders, and that the mechanics are very simple and easy to understand. That doesn't mean that FTL is an easy game: plenty of choices and their consequences, as well as the random-generation make it quite the opposite. The game is never unfair to the player, giving many opportunities for upgrades and pacing the zones quite well.
Critical thought and planning ahead are as important as combat in FTL; saving some "scrap" (the games spending and upgrading currency) could mean the difference between bribing a hostile pirate or having to engage in combat. Spending your "scrap" on ship upgrades could mean that you run out of fuel later in the game, or it could be the bump that saves your crew's lives.
The most aesthetically pleasing thing about FTL is the way it can be played with only a mouse. Pausing the action is bound to the middle mouse button, leaving your other hand free to grab a snack, pick your nose, or stratch that itch. More often you'll find yourself chewing on the nails of your free hand, as the action in FTL can get extremely tense in the latter stages.
Overall, I would recommend FTL to anybody who enjoys difficult strategy games. Being a roguelite is also a huge plus for me. The art is great, the music is great, and there is a fairly high replay value with unlocks and achievements.

Cons:
- I can't seem to find any season stats in season mode.  I can only assume that it's also missing career stats as well.  That would really help the feel of continuity and give an incentive to keep playing.

This game is a cute tribute to D&D, and it's a nice novel game. But there are some glaring issues with it that I plan to dissect.
Pros:
-The game has a bunch of cute references to D&D/RPG game mechanics.
-The art style is nice. They pull off the pixel style very well.
-Even though the story is somewhat mundane, it still kept me interested because of the nice art and clever jokes.
Cons:
-Within 20 minutes of starting the game, you can unlock every ability. So that means the combat from then on is exactly the same. You battle strategy is set extremely early, which will make you frustrated because...
-The game requires an insane amount of grinding. Plus, the difficulty curve is artificial, since the only difference between high level and low level enemies is how long it takes t kill them.
-My final problem was that my copy of the game randomly erased my save file. After 14 hours of grinding, it was gone. So I gave up.
Final verdict?
If it's on sale, it could be a nice way to spend your afternoon, but don't spend more than $1 on it.

Perhaps the definitive zombie-survival game to emerge during this zombie-themed game craze we've been experiencing lately (however I say this without having played DayZ - but I've played just about all the others on offer I think).
From the creator's of Dead Island comes a very visually-polished game set in an open world zombie apocalypse.
The game world consists of a city that is under quarantine due to an outbreak which (you guessed it) has been turning people in to zombies.
Part of a military outfit and sent in alone to conduct missions on behalf of their interests; your character spends the game exploring the quarantined city and conducting missions on behalf of survivors and the various groups left in the city, in order to earn their trust and also a bit of scratch to upgrade your zombie-mashing gear.
A perk levelling system exists which is quite deep and varied - keeping interacting with the world fresh, and the game is also heavily parkour-focused... making traversing the environment at high speed with a horde of zombies pursuing behind pretty fun.
It does suffer from some of the same problems as the Assassin Creed series... sometimes you jump to ledges you never intended to, or it tries to intuit where you wanted to go incorrectly - however I found this still to be much less of an issue in this game than the AC series.
A great feature is the multiplayer whereby you can progress through the storymode with mates, and when setting marker destinations on the map etc, the game prompts you with an option to create a competition out of reaching the destination first - there are a few prompts like this which are welcome and keep the momentum going.
Overall, the price is steep but the game is good - definitely head and shoulders above the Dead Island entries. 4/5

Spiritual successor to Titan Quest, this game has its own ARPG feel.  Don't expect a bunch of similarities to Diablo or even Path of Exile, although there are some.
Story is far better developed and written than D3. and it doesn't have the near snuff film level of charnel-house horror that Path of Exile has going on.
Gameplay wise, it is again, very similar to Titan Quest.  There are 6 Classes and you can pick any combination of 2, leading to a wide variety of skill combinations to suit your preference.  On top of this there is a "new" (for Titan Quest) Devotion tree, which lets you further customize your character by activating shrines and unlocking special active and passive skills in a large group of sub-skill trees that are independent of the main classes.
Normal mode gives you enough leeway to play around with what you want.  IMO, powerful builds will cruise through Normal and really only start to face serious challenges in harder difficulties.  Non-optimized builds can still have loads of fun in Normal mode and enjoy the game.  However if you're looking to push the Elite tier, you will need to seriously focus on building a character as optimal as possible.
IMO in the end, worth the money if you like ARPGs or want to get into them and don't want "Babby's First ARPG" Diablo 3, or if you don't want "Futility Simulator 2015" Path of Exile

Once a Civilization player, always a Civilization player.  I played them a loved them from the first game in the early nineties, so this game was predestined for me to like and it didn’t disappoint.  If you are a book reader and are familiar with expression “page turner”, meaning a book that is hard to put down, well, this game is a “turn turner.”  I would sit down for a causal game after dinner just to try out different tactics with different civilizations, and end up playing till 1am, just wanting to see what the next turn would bring, just this battle to finish, just this city to conquer, or even just this final fog of war area to explore.
I could write pages and pages about the things I love about the game, but instead I’m just going to mention several that I see as flaws.  Far for it that it turned me off from playing the game (you can see the hours I spent on it), but maybe things that could’ve been done differently.  It’s worth saying, that many of those things existed in previous Civ games, and also found in other similar type games.
1.	Achieving any victory other than Domination (eliminating all other civilizations) often feels like unnecessary hard work.  It’s easy to get a strong army and crush everyone, and depending on the game difficulty, it will happen sooner or later, but definitely way earlier than any other victory type.  So, winning different type of victory requires a lots of patience, which I don’t always have.  I like getting Steam achievements as much as the next guy, but I’m not chasing them.  Saying this, I didn’t play the game on very hard difficulty levels, maybe in those cases it gets too hard to just crush everyone, so getting other victory type becomes priority
2.	Bonuses that different civs get.  Although I applaud to the great variety of civilizations available, I’ll never choose to play as some of them.  The reason is that I find their bonuses a bit useless.  It could be just my style of play, but this is my personal review, not an unbiased expert’s opinion ;) For example, I always fancied Mongols, but I think that City States offer more as friends and allies, than enemies, so all the bonuses that Mongols get for fighting City States are useless to me. Or Celts’ bonuses from non-improved forests – I never leave a single tile not improved.
At the same time, bonuses that some other civs get are just too good.  If you play in archipelago type world, Vikings and Polynesians have huge advantage.  If you are focusing or quick building of a big army, Germany is great with their chance to absorb units from barbarian settlements they defeat.  Even if supporting big army becomes an issue, you can disband the unit for some gold on your territory, so you still get something out of it.  So, although I understand that the whole idea with the variety was to cater for different player styles, I wonder if some civs get chosen at all, other than as a challenge.
3.	Unfair starting position – and yes, I understand that the challenge is to win no matter how tough the start is, but sometimes total lack of balance is too unfair.  It especially shows on the archipelago type maps.  Once I ended up on this little island with no resources, second time I was stuck on a slightly bigger island with Polynesians (which as mentioned above have huge advantage on archipelagos), third time the island was of average size, had two resources of dyes and one stone and iron, but had no horses, or anything else.  That last time, playing as Germans, I still managed to build a big army from respawning barbarian settlements, and invade the neighbours, but If I wanted to play peacefully, I would’ve been at a huge disadvantage.
4.	AI when defending – not sure if this changes with increased game difficulty, but when defending a city, AI always attacks an already damaged unit.  So, what I do is get a unit with good defence (with ranged defence selected perk or generally tough), and get some damage on it by attacking a weaker opponent.  I put it within the city attack range and it takes fire from the city and any ranged units within the city (sometimes nearby melee units).   That way I divert attack from my siege engines that are the real danger.  Sometimes I scarify the unit, sometimes I am able to move it out the range and heal, but the city falls easily.
5.	Late game drag – which is probably the reason why I prefer dominant victory. So you have a big army, you know you can crush everyone, but now you have to move them to the other part of the world to do it and it just takes so long, whether it’s on the land or via the sea. I wouldn’t mind an option popping up “Your army is invincible at this point. Do you want to keep playing or take Dominant Victory?” Mind you, this is probably the thing that bothers me the least.
But like I said, I really love the game and none of the things above prevent me from playing it.
For the end, just want to tell you what my favourite unit is – a scout that finds superior weapons in ruins and gets upgraded to an archer.  The combination of crossing any terrain without penalty and ability to destroy units from afar is just too good.

This game is overall great.
Took me a moment to wrap my head around the concept that even though an area is accessible the enemies aren't necessarily beatable yet.  I had to recreate my characters 3 times to get what I felt like was a decent composition, but that was part of the fun since there's so much to choose from.  Of course part of the problem is you're setting a large amount of customization before you even see waht the world has to offer.
Sort of like Turn-based Diablo meets Dark Souls meets Baldur's Gate meets Dungeon Siege.
Lots of inventory management, lots of different things to customize, lots of challenging battles, lots of interesting combat situations.
For instance, if there is poison on the ground you can blow it up with fire, and you can then put oil on the fire to make a black smoke archers cannot see through.  You can make it rain and then chill someone in order to have a chance to freeze them.  You can use the rainwater to strengthen your electricity spells instead, etc etc etc.
Worth a shot if you're into the genre.  If you're a super casual player, I'm not sure if I can recommend or not.

Orcs must Die! is a third person action Tower defense game and probably the best when its about the gameplay. You play as a War Mage who needs to defend Gates from ugly Orcs. To do this task you can use Traps and Weapons as well as some envoirmental stuff.
The Gameplay is pretty straight forward. The first Wave and every 5 Waves you have unlimited Time to decide what to Build. Between each other wave you have a time limit until the next wave starts. You can purchase Traps with money. You get money for killing Orcs and you get even more money if you kill Orcs with more than one Trap. The trick is to get as many traps on one place as possible. You need of course something to fight for yourself. For that you can use a magical crossbow that can shoot bolts very fast or a Sword. You can also use magical items to shoot fire or ice and with the DLC you get some interesting items like a pot full of acid which you can throw on the orcs to kill loads of orcs with one attack. All items have a secondary attack that uses mana (In case of the Acid pot it always costs mana to balance it). You can refill your mana at the Gate that you need to defend. Or you can use a magical contraption that refills your mana if you stand next to it. Later in the game you get the wavers, which sell upgrades if you have a spare coin for them.
The grafics are nothing special but the artstyle is great. I always considered that the artstyle is more important than the grafics of a game and Orcs Must Die! is the best example for that. The medival comic look fits nicely with the theme of the game.
The Soundtrack is pretty good. It is mostly medival rock music and fits perfect to the artstyle and the Gameplay.

Okay, so I finally got the opportunity to spent some hours on this. After 13 hours of playing I still have very mixed feelings, but now mostly negative ones.
At first I was completely terrified, what the hell happened to X-com - only one fixed base, some sort of backstory and RPG-like dialogues, resources, scientists and engineers granted as rewards for missions, soldier stats reduced to health and accuracy, combat system from some boardgame probably...
On the other hand, soldier perk trees and the backstory are nice lements for this arcade.
Then I got a bit deeper into it, rejected it as an X-com title and took it as some simple regular arcade game (I was often feeling like playing a game on tablet, rather than a PC game), that worked - it was fun...until glitches, bugs and annoying stuff started to outweigh the fun and good stuff.
Creating more complex tactics in combat is completely impossible, choosing the shortest path usually leads to disposing your troops to enemy interrupts, since they usually take the dumbest way. One unprecise movement click can jeopardize the whole mission.
The flanking is fun at the begining, but becomes a bit annoying later in the game. Aliens are usually walking shooting and seeing through obstacles or even several walls and houses.
All the physical objects in the missions are just eye candy, because when someone is flanking you, he's just flanking you, no matter how many concrete blocks, metal plates, cars and objects are in his line of fire.
Soldiers are sometimes unable to throw grenades, scanners and whatever properly, in combination with weird flowing camera it's a great pain.
Frequent cutscenes and dialogues becomes annoying after time.
The necessity to choose only one mission at a time, leading to failure at some other fronts is a bit annoying and the game itself feels a bit rigid, probably because it's also made for consoles.
Of course there are some bugs present, no need to talk about them much here, but there was one thing that actually forced me to stop playing the game. It just ceased creating savegames for me. Only the autosaves were executed, which made missions quite impossible to finish. I then started overwriting my older saves, but when those started to disappear from the load menu as well, it was too much for me...
It does not deserve to bear a title of X-com game, should have been named
or something...
To summarize this, X-COM Enemy Unknown would be nice arcade, if the bugs were fixed.
But in fact it's just making fun of the original X-com series, here the "X-COM" is just a nice shiny sticker on a package of tampons.
If you want to play some real X-COM again, the
is probably still the best way to go.

To my surprise and subsequent delight, this little side scroller beat-em up appeared in my games library seemingly out of no where a while ago...
Saving it for a rainy day, I paid it no mind until I became tired of the standard FPS and MMO fare that I've become so burnt out on...
Expectations low, I installed this little "2.5D" title and after a silly cliche intro and pretty half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥attempt at a "story", jumped right into the action...
What I found, was a surprisingly fun, albeit simplistic gem.
The  premise is simple, slash, smash, bash, and shoot your way through a level not-so-chalk full of monsters... Completing your standard "go here and flick a switch" or "go here a grab an item" type objectives, all while trying to pump your combo meter as high as you possible can in order to achieve the best score possible.
While the concept sounds pretty boring and uninspired, the execution is surprisingly well done in what I can only describe as a sleeper title.
The graphics are actually pretty nice, the sound, not too bad.  The music kicks in at certain times and has a decent amount of energy to it to keep it relevant to the action on screen.
A rudimentary skill system is present, as well as passive/active abilities to enhance your beat-em up style game play.
Lots of options for high-hitting combos, air juggles, charge-up attacks, throws, explosives, and ranged gunplay.
Skill and ability points are awarded based on your performance, as well as upon mission completion and on your ability to locate and track down 7 hidden objects throughout the maps.
Character selection boils down to 4 cliche types, the melee specialist, explosive experts, gun master, and a jack-of-all trades/master of none.  The character you choose affects the allocation of your starting skill points, and I believe, although am not positive, you get a different skill tree based on your selected character's expertise.  It's a nice touch, but it seems like the majority of your attacks are going to be melee based, so an explosives expert really seems to be the odd man out in terms of usefulness.
The level design is simple, yet large enough to keep you engaged.  It does lack a mini-map, and due to the repetiveness of some of the levels, it can be a bit difficult to keep track of where you have been at times.  I will say that one glaringly obvious flaw is that the levels simply do not have enough monsters/enemies.  You will find yourself running around from one end to the other of a decent sized map, encountering very little in the way of resistance, making some tasks really kind of boring and banal.
Controls are decent, allowing you to use mouse/keyboard or a controller...  Normally I am a mouse+kb kind of guy, but I think this game would benefit more from a controller given the type of gameplay that is encouraged.
I have yet to try out the multiplayer, but I think if you managed to coerce a buddy into joining you, whether online or locally, many a good times could be had.
All in all, I would give this game a solid 7.5/10, as it does has some charm.
Worth checking out if you want a little bit of nostalgic gameplay.
TLDR
Pros
-nice graphics, especially the animations, for a side scroller arcade-ish game
-soundtrack flows with the action
-combat/combo system
-multiplayer
-gameplay and control works excellent
Cons
-story (what story?)
-level design - lacking in enemies
-cliche character classes
-cinematics

An interesting find among games for the casual videogame player, "The Banner Saga" seems to be a mix of genres that aren’t to common. Part RPG, part turn based tactics, part survival simulator that seems to have nostalgic roots in the Oregon trail series, this game is complex enough for multiple play-throughs yet simple enough for players with an intense daily schedule to pick up, play and run off again on a whim.
With a story setting in alignment with harsh Norse legends, the story centers around two perspectives for most of the game. One a war band of ice giants attempting to discover return to their homeland as an old enemy starts spontaneously growing in power and a band or human war refugees trying to outrun the same enemy and find a safe haven. Each group has a bandleader who must make difficult decisions in order to keep their own bands alive and in a feat of excellent imagination, each decision has consequences that can be felt later in ether story perspective or in the efficiency of your fighting strength. It’s very interactive for a game that mostly involves watching over a traveling band of people. The art surrounding this is crisp and beautiful with older hand drawn styled animation television cartoonists would use.
The gameplay is divided into three major parts: One is the survival sim. The player watches over their banner caravan as it slowly travels from one destination to the next, encountering obstacles, managing resources to keep people from starving, and setting disputes among your more colorful caravan members. This part has a huge impact on combat when your band must defend itself from an enemy. The second is turn based combat. In chess like fashion, you select certain members of the caravan to defend it by placing each unit on a grid and taking turns to issue them commands. The third part is route customization, choices you make can change the story, therefore battles will change and your fighting units with it.
As far as downsides go there was very few; there are a few bugs regarding turn based battles, but nothing anyone with any sort of patience would find hard to ignore and some story decisions seem to get so tangled that it’s possible to miss important plot devices. The ending also seems abrupt and unexplained, your it is hinted that there may be two opposing villainous forces facing off, only to fight a boss that seems unimportant to ether side and the whole game ends…it’s a bit confusing.
All in all I recommend “The Banner Saga”.

I've read a lot of reviews on here that talk down on the gameplay side of The Banner Saga, and frankly, I say they have missed the point. This is the story of a journey across a harsh land, where people can die at any given time. If there was an option to disable the turn-based strategy combat, and issue orders much like in the War sections of the game, I would. Combat is not the focus of the game, it is the characters and the story.
Other people complain about how despite winning every fight, they still lose characters in the dialogue. I think that is one of the most interesting parts of this game. In a fight, someone could die and it could just be because the enemy is stronger than you, or because you made a mistake. Fairly simple. But making a mistake in how you judge a situation or a threat, and losing characters you've just spent the last hour investing promotions into, makes the game a lot more exciting. Every sentence could be the last you say to this person. For good or for bad.

Basically, buy it because it's cheap might eventually lead to Mighty Rocket doing an Obscure 3.
Core gameplay is fun, the beat 'em up parts work pretty well, the characters are samey but have slight differences. Mostly, one "Always on" skill and some special moves, and the damage they deal with specific weapons. It's more fun with friends, but so is anything up to and including getting slaughtered by an ax-wielding maniac. Even the weapons are pretty samey, but it's fairly straightforward to start whacking enemies and never get touched, stringing S combos together in no time.
Not much in the way of story here, generic characters go to town on zombies because zombies are in the way of generic characters, eventually they run into token savior scientist. (Named Adam, no less! Only Heinrich beats that for cliche points!) Should mention that much like Corey from Obscure 2 was a Derrick Whitley expy from Sum 41, Sean is Jarle Bernhoft from Span, which is pretty cool. Although he's browner, for some reason.
Music holds up, although you might wanna pop the youtube repeat on. Horde music is always the same.
Overall, the first five levels hold pretty well, but here's the thing: It's an 8 level game with 4 effective levels, AND it's padded over that. Once per episode, your characters must stop beating people up to do something completely unrelated! Hey, let's toss boxes at this guy while we chase a train! Let's ride flyers and hit other flyers while we're at it! Let's play space invaders! Why? Cause... Those games were 2D too...? The minigames come out of left field and most of them do NOT fit well. When it's not minigames, it's lugging stuff around. Apparently Leafmore has a booming business in demolition. You can tell from all the nitro boxes laying around unsupervised.
As mentioned, you get new levels on 1, 2, 3 and 5, and the rest is repeated. You will surely be familiar with splashy world by the end of this game, tell you that much. It doesn't work against itself as much as you'd think: Being able to get a grasp on the levels quickly means you can blaze through them while racking up your combo the next time you're there, which you'll probably want to do.
You know when Obscure 1 pulled a bait at the end, and it was awesome? When you've just beaten the final boss, your character injects the vaccine, and then, in broad daylight, the final boss comes creeping back up to try and fight you until the very end? That underlined his human nature and the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ situation he was in, a man who had lost what very little he had left? Obscure 2 tried to do that, and... It brought back that one puzzle from 1. Hey, even then, my thoughts were "Hey, more game, cool." Final Exam tries to do that, with a cool minigame, followed by an okay boss, followed by another boss, followed by ANOTHER boss, followed by YET ANOTHER GOD DAMN BOSS ARE YOU KIDDING ME followed by EVEN ANOTHER BOSS ARE YOU EVEN oh it was a bait cool then.
So yeah, it keeps the Obscure formula, if a little mislead at times, it still makes for a fun game, and the best selling point would be that it's pretty cheap. Don't expect any of that caustic humor or videogame references they promise, though. Caustic humor never gets past "Fat guy dies ridiculously" and videogame references can be summed up as "Gordon Freeman had a crowbar, the cake is a lie."
Despite my tendency to underline the negative, I'd say grab it if it's in a sale. Or even if it's not and you like beat 'em ups. On it's own, it's a good game, and I'd say actually being tied to obscure, specially obscure 1, hurts it by comparison.

I didn't think I would enjoy this game but I do. I'm hooked.
I thought that the fast-paced strategy would be chaotic and difficult to master. I was pleased to find out that you can pause the action at any moment and give orders, and that the mechanics are very simple and easy to understand. That doesn't mean that FTL is an easy game: plenty of choices and their consequences, as well as the random-generation make it quite the opposite. The game is never unfair to the player, giving many opportunities for upgrades and pacing the zones quite well.
Critical thought and planning ahead are as important as combat in FTL; saving some "scrap" (the games spending and upgrading currency) could mean the difference between bribing a hostile pirate or having to engage in combat. Spending your "scrap" on ship upgrades could mean that you run out of fuel later in the game, or it could be the bump that saves your crew's lives.
The most aesthetically pleasing thing about FTL is the way it can be played with only a mouse. Pausing the action is bound to the middle mouse button, leaving your other hand free to grab a snack, pick your nose, or stratch that itch. More often you'll find yourself chewing on the nails of your free hand, as the action in FTL can get extremely tense in the latter stages.
Overall, I would recommend FTL to anybody who enjoys difficult strategy games. Being a roguelite is also a huge plus for me. The art is great, the music is great, and there is a fairly high replay value with unlocks and achievements.

If you are hesitating to buy this game... Read this review.
Let me start of by saying this first. If you are new to the telltale series and games, don't start with TWD:M. Read my other reviews for the other series and rather go with episode one to get a feel for the game in the right way.
There... Now that that's done and over with. Let's get down to you whom I presume are owner of the previous games.
TWDM is a complete side story which is in no way connected to the previous titles what so ever or the TWD TV series (correct me if im wrong here.) This means that it is not necessary to have watched the show or played the previous games to understand what is going on in the story.
I am presuming you are familiar with the setting and the type of game this is. If not, its a modern point and click with some quick time events... in a short sense.
The game itself, as the title implies, revolves around Michonne and her quest with a bunch of new people on a boat. Obviously they run into trouble at various locations and areas and your choices will lead where you end up (sort of). The main problem of the game comes down to length and character development, which after playing the first two excellent entries in the series, this one just comes up very short, and it's a shame too, since Michonne obviously is a fan favorite character in the TWD series.
I usually hate to clock a game or complain about content, since what is mainly important to me personally in a game is the atmosphere, the feeling and the sheer joy you get from playing it, not by completing every little side quest in the whole wide world just for the sake of it. But unfortunately the game is a tad bit short for it's own good and hence the game is not worthy of your hard earned dollars.
Here comes a bit of mini semi spoiler (you can still read on, it wont ruin the story for you just a little notice about the story telling)
In stories if there is one thing I do not like is the many flashbacks and suggestive story telling. If it really and I mean REALLY doesn't enhance the games mechanics, then why introduce them, as they are boring and similar things have been done so many times in so many movies previously. This was honestly a deal breaker for me personally, and if you also feel the same way about flashbacks, then this game is not really for you, as it will irritate the S**T out of you those sequences.

I am a big fan of Telltale games. With this said, this is by far the worst of their recent attempts to create an engaging and immersive story. The biggest letdown stems from the fact that it seems like this was written by someone with split personality. You have a very cohesive main plot, albeit not groundbreaking by any standards, that is constantly ruined by idiotic flashbacks/allucinations that hardly make any sense. Every time you start enjoying the story, Michonne starts tripping, while you ask yourself "what's the point in this cheesy drama?". By the end of the third chapter you realize there's no point whatsoever, and you consider replaying Tales from the Borderlands just to cleanse your soul after such a disappointing experience.

Between Steam and the Android version, I've surely logged 40 or 50 hours on this game. It's great fun, and the game-within-a-game structure makes for some funny moments in the main quest. While the gameplay can get a little stale after you've maxed everyone out (not hard to do), it's still a fun diversion from time to time. I can wholeheartedly recommend KoP&P, but at the same time ... it's game that's also a tremendous missed opportunity for something greater.
My big complaint about the game is the lack of additional content. The one DLC, "Haunted Fall," is a mere sliver of addtional content, and hardly worth the price. This is the kind of game that SCREAMS for a rich set of adds ons and expansions, particularly for high-level gameplay. After two years, however, we have one lackluster, overpriced expansion that would have been a free upgrade from most other publishers.
If it had Steam Workshop support, it could easily become one of the best pick-up-and-play RPG games out there. But, again, we have nothing like that. Just a great core game and some tantatlizingly untapped potential.
That said, at $10 it's a touch on the pricey side. I picked my copy up on sale for perhaps $5, and when the DLC was maybe $3. It's a great deal at $8, but I'm not sure I'd feel the same way at $20 for the Deluxier version. If you can get it on steep sale, you won't regret it. Otherwise, stick to the much cheaper mobile version,

Made by reknowned doujin circle Siter Skain, RefleX is generally considered to be the best out of the Alltynex Trilogy of doujin shoot-'em-ups, with the other two gmaes in the series being Kamui and Alltynex 2nd. RefleX features a shield system where your ship can activate an impenetrable shield that not only protects you from enemy fire, but also redirects certain enemy fire back to the enemies! However, energy for the shield is strictly limited, and can only be replenished quickly by not shooting. As such, the game demands that you know when and when not to shoot, shield, and send lasers back, and that demands practice.
Thankfully, the game gives you extra continues whenever you get a game over, so you will eventually see the end screen if you persevere. However, we all know that that's not how shmups are meant to be played - and the game will only record your high score if you don't continue, in line with that "one credit completion" mentality. So practice, persevere, go beyond your limits and post that 1CC hi-score for all to see!

(Note: I've "completed" RefleX on a copy Kickstarter backers received from Nyu Media, so the hour meter by this review is a bit inaccurate.)
RefleX is so far the best shoot'em up I've played on Steam. Danmaku Unlimited 2 comes in even or close, though. It's challenging, it hits the risk-reward balance for high-score competition, the visuals have the OOMPH! to it (that is, enemy ships don't go down with a whimper but a boom) and good playability with something of a twist in the gameplay mechanics at the end.
First off, there are no powerups in RefleX and only one weapon. The main trick the game has is the "reflect shield", which will turn blue enemy shots to hit the enemies instead. Homing beams (what a weird term that is) seek out enemy ships whereas beams and "unguided" bullets just bounce off the shield, allowing proper positioning to aim the bullets at the enemies.
The score multiplier increases by these "reflected" bullets hitting (or destroying?) enemies. The multiplier will reset after the "combo" of destroying enemies ends.
The shield system shouldn't be overused either; the less shield power you have, the weaker your own weapons are. The shields will also regenerate faster if you're not shooting all the time.
Alas, SITER SKAIN, the game's developers, decided against a Steam-integrated highscore table, or so I have understood. This would've made the score attack goals by far more interesting.

Finally the renowned doujin Shoot'em up trilogy "The Tale of ALLTYNEX" is getting released on Steam. Starting with RefleX the second game in the series.
Gameplay:
Polished and intuitive, the key mechanic of the game is your ships relfecting shield. When activated the shield reflects bullets, but your ships energy is drained fast and when it gets low enough the shield stops working and even your weapons get weaker. So using the reflector-shield requires timing and strategy, mastering the game requires a lot of pattern recognition, good timing and knowing when to use the shield.
Sound:
The sound design is spot-on, catchy electronic retro music. With nice sound effect feedback from explotions and hits.
Graphics:
Looks basically like an Arcade game from the early 90's. But with some modern effects like lensflares and transparencies. It's pretty good looking for a low resolution 2D game, but the animation is somewhat lacking. The explotions and lazer effects look however satisfying.
Overall:
Impressive for a Doujin game, this could have passed as an professionally produced Arcade game in the 90's. I would recommend this game for any veteran fans of the Shoot'em up genre, the gameplay and music is top notch. But the graphics do look dated, and it is a shame that the developer did not allow making modifications to the game, so it is missing Steam achievements and leaderboards. Also the game lacks configuration options in-game, you have to find the config executable in the steamapps/common/RefleX directory.
For people completely new to the genre, out of the games available on Steam I still recommend starting out with Ikaruga. The only reason being it looks modern and has a great well polished PC port with full Steam features. However RefleX is likely more fun and easier to grasp than Ikaruga for beginners, but not everyone will accept the dated look.

The best way I can describe Steep is like a winter-themed skate 3. You're given a massive, detailed mountain from which to ski, snowboard, paraglide, or wingsuit from. There’s a plethora of challenges to do, lots of areas to discover, and a lot of points from which to just do stuff from. The game leaves a lot in the hands of the player and how they feel like approaching it, which feels very refreshing. The amount of detail in the world is stunning, the mountains are gorgeous to look at from the mountain view as well as up close. Steep straddles the line between being a serious sport sim to an easy-going arcade fairly well. The only real letdowns I had were with the online aspect and the lack of a cohesive story. Its MMO features simply don’t seem necessary. It’s fun to run challenges with friends or other people online, however…there just aren’t enough people playing this game, nor is there a real lobby or area to meet people to play with. There also isn’t much in the way of plot, which would have been nice to have to give the game a foundation, or give it some character.
Overall, Steep is a pretty great game that hits nearly all of its ambitious marks. I find it very easy to recommend when its on sale. It’s a great way for me to wind down after a long day.

Long have I searched for an RPG that captures the nostalgic feelings of Baldur's Gate that innovates and improves with modern technology and game design. My search has ended.
Divinity: Original Sin provides a compelling atmosphere with a lengthy list of party customization that allows you to build an effective party based on your own, personal whims. Want a caster who can also get up in to melee range and go to town? Done. Want a ranger that casts spells alongside her arrows? Done. All you need to do is learn some of the basics and figure out what abilities will complement one another and you're good to go.
On that note: This game is not (typically) easy. Be prepared to save and load games frequently! The tides of battle can and often are easily decided on your tactical decisions, and sometimes incapacitating an enemy at a crucial moment really does mean all the difference.
The game also allows you to build two very different characters in terms of personality. Your characters can have conversations with one another and your choices during these conversations will help shape how that character is at their core.
If all that wasn't enough to interest you, then I'd suggest looking to the company themselves. They have a very clear understanding about what makes this kind of game enjoyable, and their commitment to go from KickStarter to launch proves they are willing to support this project going forward.
TL;DR: If you enjoy tactical based RPG games such as old school Baldur's Gate then you'll probably really enjoy Divinity: Original Sin. If you want a game you can just blast through without much thought, you may be disappointed.
