The gameplay mechanics regarding the city and property management are okay, and I want to like it because the city building and logistics part of the gameplay is so interesting, but the rest of the game is just not there yet. Nothing in it is fun to *do*, except maybe building and interacting with other players:
-No effort has been put into any aesthetic detail in this game, the only evidence you need is to look at the basically unanimated rectangle men that occupy the city and the out of place vehicles they ride around in. It's only fitting that they're so unanimated and undetailed because they don't seem to do anything at all but run into walls or look at you and shoot. Unfortunately the community doesn't seem to understand that improving the graphics by any degree wouldn't result in the implosion of the world so they will vehemently argue against any talk of graphical improvement. Why bother when you can just do nothing at all? What an outstanding attitude. Fortunately, the developer is saner than his community.
-FPS combat is a major part of the gameplay, but it is absolutely the worst and most unfinished part of the game - next to the driving. It's a game that has absolutely not been built for this, or at least, the time hasn't been spent here to make the gameplay fun or interesting. Avoid fighting NPC's at all costs.
-NPC's don't do anything, and look like garbage.
-Cars aren't fun to drive, which is a basic game mechanic for a game about driving around town. Also, it's impossible to see if a car is inhabited so it is possible to accidentally carjack, and there's nowhere to purchase vehicles.
-Example of a small aesthetic detail that is of poor value: Dropped objects are sprites, an unfinished detail so old and out of touch not even Minecraft renders things this way anymore.
Anyways:
This game looks so bad it shouldn't have even been put on steam in this state. The textures that aren't part of the free model pack used for these vehicles were obviously drawn in MSPaint. Everything looks, sounds, and plays like trashbaskets. Cars drive like unfinished vehicle assets, guns shoot like unfinished weapon scripts, player models move around like ghoulish haunted scarecrows hand painted by a 4th grade class, textures, buildings - it all looks like s***. What doesn't look like MSPaint scribbles looks like purchased or free models,
and the sound effects were apparently harvested from a windows 95 bargain bin game and run through a bitcrusher. Even the crosshair looks like some comic-sans childs idea of what a crosshair should look like. It's huge, it covers like 5% of the screen, it's like I'm looking through a dollar store toy's scope.
Ironically there are paintings you can buy and put in your builds, which look *exactly* like children's drawings. Because they are a child's drawings.
This game could almost be good:
Multiplayer 1st person simcity sandbox. The citybuilding gameplay is pretty dense and interesting. The city is a huge functional environment, and works a lot like simcity, where the players are their own business leaders. Properties can be purchased, zone, built upon, profited from, sold. You can go to little stores and see people walking around, albeit, into walls and onto furniture. The gameplay here is starting to lush out, though there's not much to do other than grow an empire. What's neat is that there's a gamemode where the AI controlling the enemy factions is aggressive and threatens to knock other players out of the game - much like an RTS. This is incredibly fascinating, there simply is not another game like it. It's everything I want in a game, I still sometimes play SimCity2k Network Edition, online SimCity is all I ever want. Now if only you could build buildings out of something that didn't look like trash and populate the world with something that didn't resemble crayon drawings.
This game offers A LOT of potential, being the only game of its class. Unfortunately, that is literally the only thing it has. You're going to find the graphics nearly intolerable. The models, the sprites, the voxels - everything looks BAD. It's unacceptably bad, and this game should set new standards - not adhere to lows.

Highly recommend for old school RPG fans.
The game doesn't hold your hand like most other games these days. There are no quest markers for npcs with quests, autopathing, giant indicators on your map, nothing. You have your journal and npcs to talk to, you use your brain to logically figure out what to do next if it's not entirely clear.
The game just throws you in there, explains a few basic mechanics like fighting and stealth and that's about it. It's up to you to find and solve quests, the game wont do it for you and hand you the answers. The game is VERY heavy with dialogue and reading, if you don't like that and want everything voice acted, this is not the game for you.
The game uses a mostly fixed perspective camera (you can rotate a little bit by default, and zoom in (although I don't see why you would aside from screenshots)) but you can completely unlock it in the options menu. Although if you do you will notice some poor terrain in certain places (usually it's abruptly cut off) because the game simply wasn't designed to accomodate a free camera, it was built for that specific fixed one so just be wary of that.
Combat is turn based, if you don't like turn based combat perhaps this is not the game for you. Movement is realtime only combat is turn based. You can chain spells for some very fun and effective combinations. Oil+fire, water+lightning, poison+fire, etc... It makes for more dynamic and interesting combat.
The game is classless. When you create your character you will have templates to choose from (knight, mage, wizard, witch, etc...) but you can change absolutely everything about them skill-wise. The only thing you can't change are the weapons. So if you select the mage preset but you want to make them a knight with armor and a sword and shield, you can't. You will start the game with your mage staff and have to get the knight equipment later on. This may result in some incredibly gimped characters starting out and you might want to just start over and remake the character.
The visual customization leaves a lot to be desired. While it may not necessarily be bad, it's by no means good. There are a very limited number of hairstyles to choose from (maybe 10 or less) and they're pretty... bland I suppose. A quarter or half of them are joke hairstyles that would never fit into the world and the rest are "okay" at best. I know this is very subjective so take it how you will. There are NO options to change your facial structure or your body type (slim, athletic, fat, or a mix). I'm not asking for hundreds of sliders, even presets would be nice to get away from the default look. The only face options you seem to have is some sort of makeup and warpaints which again, I feel are pretty bland and boring.
The co-op. By far my biggest problem with the game. I'm so disappointed with how this was executed since I was looking forward to it the most. There are a few scenarios here:
- You join someone when they're creating their character and you can create your own character as well and play with it in their game. You CAN NOT then play with that character you created in your own single player game or any other multiplayer game.
- You join someone's game in-progress. You CAN'T use your own character, you are stuck with the character they made at character creation and therefore you likely don't give a crap about the character at all and may not even like the build or setup they have for it. This makes it almost entirely pointless to join people you don't know.
So basically, if you create a character in single player you can only use it in single player. If you create a character in multiplayer, you can only use it in the players' game you created it in. This basically means if you want to play with multiple people you have to either constantly create new characters or you have to play with a bunch of random characters you know nothing about. To me this is a huge problem and inconvenience regardless of the reason they chose to do it this way.
People with PC specs far above the recommended have reported huge problems with loading times and sluggish, almost unplayable, performance. Personally I have had no issues what-so-ever and my PC is fairly low to mid range. AMD FX 8320 cpu, not overclocked, Radeon HD 6770, win 7. Even on max settings I get at least 30 fps and with all the annoying crap turned off like bloom and some post processing things I get well above that. I don't know if it was intentional or a mistake but the game seems to utilize only one core most of the time. So if you plan on purchasing it just do your research and see if anyone with your hardware has performance issues.
I know this sounds like a ton of problems but in the end most of them are very minor and don't impact the gameplay at all. Co-op arguably does and while it is annoying, it's not a deal breaker imo. The performance problems are the biggest issue but fortunately, I am not one of the unlucky people who has those problems.

The Banner Saga is a Norse mythos inspired story with mixed elements of Oregon Trail and turn-based strategy.  For much of it you are switching between two groups travelling through lands being overrun with giant monsters called Dredge and you can lead as the type to fight on the front lines or as a tactical advisor with many fights being avoidable. My initial impressions were it was a strong story with interesting travel choices and somewhat weak combat, but the more I played the more I realized there were quite a few layers of strategy to employ well beyond simply trying to beat down your opponents.
The story is stupendously engaging, and even knowing one possible outcome I had to go right back in and do it again - with less screw ups! Even though you are constantly strained, on the run, and it is overall rather dour, there are moments which remind you there can be glimmers of light in even the darkest of times. I felt for the characters who were largely a ragtag band doing all they could to survive as their world fell apart around them.
Even with its simpler game play, the art and audio fit great, and there's nothing like suddenly noticing the panorama is filled with skulking monsters bearing down on you. The soundtrack was a great addition to my playlist unlike anything I had before.
Overall, it's challenging (especially on hard) and I've never been so engaged by a game where I was constantly on the edge of losing and if you remotely enjoy random event games or turn-based strategy then TBS is a must.

I stumbled upon this game by accident, but as a fan of turn-based combat, Xcom-like management and a steep difficulty curve I bought the Banner Saga right away. I am not at all disappointed. The game tells a story of varl (giants with horns) and humans as they struggle to survive in a dark time of dredge (stone-like figures) invasion. The player controls a handful of heroes leading a caravan that just tries to make it in the harsh reality of war. During the struggle the player faces myriad of difficult (often lose-lose) choices that are presented in a form of options in the dialogue box. The main characters also frequently engage in dialogues so we can learn their history, motivations and opinions. As a caravan leader, you must manage supplies (boy are they scarce!), morale of the entire group, the roster of fighters and how to spend renown points - the only currency in the game used to buy enchanted items or supplies and level up your fighters. Renown points are gained through winning battles and making dialogue choices. The combat is turn-based with a twist - the turns are always your character-enemy-your character-enemy and so forth, no matter the numbers. So you can have 6 fighters (maximum you can) against 3 enemies and it's always an even distribution of turns: you-them-you-them. I haven't made up my mind yet whether I like this system or not. It has both its advantages and disadvantages. There are five attributes: Health (the amount of punishment you can take and dish out. Lesser the health, lesser the damage output). Armor (block damage. your strength - their armor = damage). Willpower (points that grant a slight damage bonus, further movement or use of a special ability). Exertion (the amount of willpower you can spend on an action). Break (the amount of direct damage you can do to an enemy armor). Each stat is equally important and enhances the tactical aspect of the battles. The fighters come in different shapes. Varls are giants that take up 4 grids on the battlefield and humans are smaller and nimbler. As for classes you can have a spearmaster (can attack one grid away from the enemy and has the ability to impale), shieldmaster (attackim him drains armor), archer (for every point of armor the enemy lost the health damage increase), a mage even (called menders) and so on - each class has a special unique active ability (for instance taunt, which forces an enemy to attact the taunter) and one passive ability (i.e light step, which allows a character to swiftly move between big varls). The graphics are hand drawn are a pleasure to look at. Animations of the characters are very fluid and have a Disney feel to them. The music is definitely one of the highlights of this game - composed by Austin Wintory (known for the soundtrack to Journey) it sets a tone for the harrowing experience and fits perfectly to the snowy lands the game takes place in. I heard people complaining about how short the game is, but I can't really say that myself. The first playthrough took me 11 hours and I didn't even finished the game - I died in the beginning of the last chapter. Furthermore, I think the game has replay value, as you can make different choices and end up with a significantly different roster and problems along the way. But probably the biggest upside of this game is its atmosphere and how easy it is to immerse yourself in the bleak reality of Banner Saga. Very much recommended.

A beatemup spinoff of the Obscure games.
Graphics:
The graphics are stylized, cartoonish and funny.  The character's bright colors help them stand out in the mostly dark and drab locations.  All the enemies are bight green and easy to spot, as well.  The graphics also look quite nice, all in all.
Sound:
The sound is limited in both effects and music.  There is very little variation and the characters have few, if any lines, outside of story cutscenes.  Most in game cutscene dialouge is told through picture bubbles, slapsick, and grunts.  I ended up ignoring most of the sounds while playing.
Controls:
The controls handle quite well with a gamepad, which is VERY reccomended, but there's no real impressive combos, just standard button mashing, which a few jumps or special attacks thrown in.  Guns, when found, are also easy to use.
Gameplay:
The game, consisting of several story levels, involve running around and slaying monsters while compltely objectives, such as finding keys or npcs, esccorting npcs, etc, with horde waves thrown in to change it up.  The special attacks of each character are kinda unqiue, but they all share the same basic skill tree, that seems to have been thrown in as an afterthought.  The hilarity of the characters and enemies is almost overshadowed by the bland and monotinous combat.  In fact, aside from certain specials, the characters play the same to me.  There are hidden items sprnkled through out the levels, but aside from an achievement, serve no purpose.  The weapons you can get are also hidden throughout levels, but once found, can be selected in the inventory screen before a level, and they feel somewhat different, but none feel like they have any weight to them.  A few times I have nodded off playing this game.
It's a mediocre beatemup, but if it's on sale or you're a fan of the Obscure games, then get it.

Bought this since it was so cheap during the one-day sale.  Glad I did.
When it first came out, I wanted to get it due to the description of what this game was all about...space ship management!
But then I read reviews saying it was extremely difficult and a bit confusing, so I passed on it.
It is difficult, no doubt.
It is confusing only for a while as you get used to the mechanics and little quirks...which I am still in the progress of accomplishing.
But it is also VERY addicting.
You basically try to advance as far as you can without being blown to bits or having all your crew die on you.
There are a lot of things to level up with the currency called 'scrap'.  Managing your scrap is key and at the core of the game.
Advancing through the game is kind of like those choose your own adventure books - you pick points to "jump" to, and a new suprise is waiting for you each time you do so - some good, most bad.
Battle is fun - but it will probably end your game quite often at first. Okay, so this, along with the rest of the Tale of ALLTYNEX trilogy, is widely regarded in shmup circles as one of the best doujin (Japanese indie) shmups ever, and it really is very good. The gameplay revolves around your ability to produce a reflective shield, similar to Giga Wing. If you kill an enemy with a reflected bullet, you get a score multiplier for a little while. If you continue killing enemies with reflected bullets while the multiplier is still active, it goes even higher, to a maximum of x64. You can't just keep the shield on all the time, though, as you have a limited amount of energy for it, which recharges while you aren't using it, and does so more quickly if you aren't shooting. Speaking of shooting, your firepower is tied directly to how much shield energy you have left. As an aside, you don't get a traditional lives system in this game. Instead, you have a health gauge which is fully repaired at certain points. Whether or not you will prefer this to a traditional lives system is subjective.
As for the presentation, the music, graphics, and story are top-notch. I have nothing more to add there. My only real complaint here is that this version of RefleX doesn't have the Steam overlay (even though ALLTYNEX Second and Kamui will), so you'll need something like Puush if, say, you want to take a screenshot of your personal best score. There are also no online leaderboards (also something the other two games in the trilogy will have). Overall, though, if you haven't bought this yet, go ahead and do so. It's awesome.

Short Answer:  Yes, this game is amazing.  Buy it now!
Long Answer:  I picked up this game last year from Nyu Media's website, and I'm glad it finally made it to Steam.  Yeah, I've got a few buddies I'm going to corrupt with some Alltynex goodness.
There's a great sense of design behind this game.  From the way the levels flow into each other, to the progression of escalating boss fights, everything looks in place.
Even the unique bullet colors have consistent meanings; some can be absorbed, some can be reflected, and some can be shot down.  Knowing when to shoot, when to reflect, and when to just let off the fire button and recharge, is the key to victory.
The scoring system comes naturally.  Use the reflect feature well, and get big multipliers.  It's great fun sending off a mass of reflected bullets and homing lasers, followed by some giant x64 kills.  Or for those who just want to play to the end and enjoy the spectacle, continues are awarded on a regular basis to aid progress.

In Space Hotel, your main objective is to find four colored keycards and make your escape via an on-board spaceship. While on a trade route, one of the engines on your ships breaks, forcing you to land at this location in the star system of Merope, in the constellation of Pleiades. Little did you know before landing that a massacre had taken place, and the killer is still lurking through the dim corridors.
See what just a minimal amount of creative writing can do to set the mood? Space Hotel sounds pretty alright, huh? Don't let the above description fool you, as that's all the backstory you get regarding this title, and absolutely none of it is located in-game. Actually, you aren't even told what your main objective is, you just wander around until you end up finding your first keycard and you go from there. The monster has a set path, and he never strays from it; meaning that unless you're directly in his way, he won't bother with you. If you do happen to die, it's back to the very beginning because the supposed save system was never implemented.
There's no ambiance, no soundtrack, everything is way too dark, the graphics are okay at best, the flashlight and stamina meters disappear if you ALT+TAB, the monster is a lurching axe-wielding ogre... which brings us to the next point; the video on the store page must be from Space Hotel's alpha state, as it is not an accurate representation of the current build of the game. The video shows a glowing, humanoid figure, plus some small cutscenes and scripted events that do not actually occur. It needs to either be updated, or removed entirely, as it's misleading.
Lasting 10 minutes per playthrough at best, Space Hotel is another drab sci-fi horror game with a stealth twist that just doesn't get it. Not to mention, it feels like you're wearing side-blinders for the entirety of the game since everything outside of the flashlight illumination is pitch black. It's definitely not the worst that's out there, but it's far from the best and a total waste of time and money; but hey, surprisingly there are no performance issues.

An amazing tactical game, with plenty of strategic gameplay as well!
Tactical aspect of the game is top-notch, with a huge variety of maps to fight at. And as XCOM features humanity’s struggle against a “coalition” of invading alien species, the enemies you face highly vary in both abilities and tactics. Similarly your own soldiers belong to one of four distinct classes, each with different set of perks that determine soldier’s role in battle – and being able to choose between two perks at most ranks give further customization to your soldiers within given class.
Tactical battles aside, the game features strategic gameplay as well: between battles you research new technologies, build up your base, plan your satellite network to minimize panic spreading across the world, and overall decide where to apply your very limited funds.
Graphics is astonishing: both environment and character models are very well designed, and game provides a lot of cinematic-esque close up shots on characters to show that off.
In short, XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a must-have for anyone who likes tactical games!

The difficulty will go up and you'll be stuck trying to research LASER weaponry while turtling so hard. So damn hard... - For those not in the know, "turtling" means inching your squad forward, then setting up overwatch focused on kill lanes that cover all directions and ideally also cover the majority of your squad members; i.e. snipers OP. - Don't get attached to your soldiers the first playthrough too even if you play amazingly, because of how the skills are set up you could lose out lategame simply because you "picked wrong"; as in didn't match the proper skills to be useful. And yes there's proper skills. Or rather "proper" skill trees.
On the plus side Enemy Within exists. It vastly improves the game, adds a ton of content, balances everything out, fixes some of the skill nonsense, adds in base raids (as in your base gets raided, have fun) and makes vanilla XCOM so not worth playing. I still recommend it for turn based squad combat fans but do yourself a favour and get Enemy Within. And don't trade away your plasma weaponry.

What this game lacks in story and longevity is filled with brain-twisting puzzles, engaging mechanics and a very unique atmosphere. The different puzzles present challenges that will give your brain a workout and occasionally get you to gawk at your monitor (in a good way). If I had to guess, the puzzles and some of the game mechanics are drastically different than 90% of what you've probably encountered in other games.
If you enjoy atmospheric games like Journey and/or puzzle-heavy games like Myst, it's a good bet that you will enjoy this. You'd also like it if you enjoy exploring, as there are a decent amount of secrets to be found in this game. The devs did a fantastic job at throwing curveballs and hiding certain content.
To keep this short(ish), while Antichamber isn't without it's flaws (the one irking me most is the lack of

The gameplay is similar to fire emblem if instead of knights, mages, and wyverns it was large half-man half-beast human type things with horns, knights, and heavily armored stone enemy things. Also vikings. Think chess mixed with a western rpg for a good comparison. It's a turn by turn strategy game that is a lot deeper than it may look at the start. Each class has a special ability and every character can be leveled up, but leveling up requires the use of your "renown" which is limited and, depending on how you play, can easily be depleted as that same resource is used to buy items and food for your journey. The battles have a very interesting armor vs strength mechanic that is great to play with. Essentially you have health and strength represented by the same stat and armor represented by another. You can choose to weaken the armor so you can do more damage or attempt to go straight for the health. This adds a very unique dynamic to the battles that I never had experienced before.
The story, which is a "choices-matter (but not really)" type game, starts out rather small like many games do. You start out on a simple escort type mission. Playing as a Varl (the half-man half-beast giant things) you are escorting the prince of men on a trip back to the human capital, but along the way there something happens and the story expands from there eventually ending with a "fate-of-the-world" story. It is very reminiscent of Bio-ware games or RPG's in general as that's what they're known for. The majority of the game takes place in battles while the second largest part will be eaten up by waiting for your caravan to reach a marker or town. Along the way there you will get random encounters with story and decision that directly effect your caravan and what happens down the line too. These decisions may not effect the main story at all but seeing little sub-stories unfold based off my decisions was a really good feeling and reminded me a lot of dragon age: origins (one of the best games ever I might add but that's a different discussion.)
The art and animation for this game is absolutely beautiful and literally bleeds the emotion and feeling put into the making of it. Overall the game is great. The combat takes some getting used to and the fights can be unbalanced but adapting and learning is part of the fun. If you have the money to spare get this game! You won't regret it

This is one of the greatest games I have ever had the pleasure of playing. It gives the feeling that you're playing Grand Theft Auto and Minecraft together, both combined with dozens upon dozens of mods. There is barely a thing you cannot do in Voxel Turf.
-You can build and interact with almost anything you place.
-You can build anywhere and then drive around or destroy what you built.
-If you're not the creative type, there's premade lots that you can place.
-You can load up randomly generated cities.
-You can build your own from scratch using the premade lots.
-Workshop support allowing for custom made lots from other players, plus extras.
-Missions, diplomacy, shopping, plus more.
-Earn money by protecting neutral businesses or residences and make money, do some missions and collect a profit. Build up your empire by buying out land/properties. Raid bandit bases for loot and sell it at various stores to purchase other things.
-Play with other AI factions in a race for city domination or however you please.
-Play with unlimited funds, pick what to start off with, choose to play alone with no AI factions, or just play the default way. Choice is yours.
-Destroy ANYTHING! Spawn a tank and drive it through a building? No problem! How about create massive holes in the street or a building? Sure! Insure your property to protect it from all damages and hit the repair button to restore it to its former glory!
-Weapons, weapons, weapons! You can add up to two (2) upgrades on weapons to either add zoom, make bullets explosive, or have armour piercing rounds.. Whatever you wish. If you want to drive around in a car and do a drive-by, that's possible. You can also fly a helicopter and do a fly-by! But let's not forget about the tanks.. If you thought a huge cannon strong enough to punch a huge hole inside a building wasn't strong enough, why not do a tank-by! Use your weapons while inside of a tank.
-There are also police in the game, watching you. Be careful as their unique system puts the GTA police to shame. :)
-The biggest pro is that the developer is heavily dedicated to his game and is working NON-STOP to bring us the absolute best experience humanly possible. Not to mention the game is well worth the price tag!

is not the type to focus on its lore or story more than it's necessary. There's a legion of baddies out there and it's up to you and your ridiculously generous array of traps, weapons and spells to stop them. The simple and funny cinematics and voice acting cover the rest. The protagonist is witty, easy-going, wise-cracking, and arrogant to the point of annoyance. And as such, I lovingly refer to him as Bruce Campbell.
The HUD and menus are minimalistic and have been built for easy and simple navigation with a gamepad. Even so, using a keyboard is in no way inconvenient especially when considering that all of the action is paused while looking through the menus.
The graphics are in no way elaborate or any form of high definition but they are far from being poor or shoddy. Considering the high level of action and running around required, they are quite appropriate as nobody wants to have to restart a mission because they got overrun by orcs while looking at the pretty walls. The sound effects fit with the visual style amazingly well, the music is very fun and needs a lot of time for the repetitiveness to become annoying, which sadly cannot be said by the quippy voice acting which does get old pretty fast.
The controls rarely feel awkward and only become a problem for perfectionists (such as myself) who wish to align all their traps perfectly. The heat of battle on higher difficulties makes for split-second perfect placement which when failed might require users to restart the mission. The Options menu is quite modest but fitting to the purpose of
. The Achievements don't ask too much from the user and completionists will get almost all of them by the end. In regards to the Leaderboards, some of the higher scoring users got there with cheats that allowed absurd numbers but ranking among friends works just fine and in real time.
I installed
and played through the first two difficulties with a constant smile on my face, pretty much bewitched by the fun combination of traps and spells I could use during each mission. I refused to let it go until I beat it on the hardest difficulty and got all the achievements. I give this game five skulls (and a horned helmet to boot)!

Wow, just wow. The Banner Saga blew me away. Incredible art and animation, and a fabulous turn-based strategy game with RPG elements in general. I couldn't stop thinking about this game for days after I finished it and I normally don't even like turn-based strategy games (or it has to be something like Advance Wars).
This game is deep, as far as the story is concerned at least. You'll be losing plenty of people over the course of the game, and it's not necessarily because you made the wrong choice. It's because the choices *are* tough and there usually isn't a right answer to begin with. The game autosaves so you can't go back and try it again, and you can't save manually.
The artstyle and animations are just beautiful. I appreciated it, and enjoyed it, for the entire length of the game. There's just so many detail. The characters and the environments, especially when you're fighting. Normally all you see is empty looking environments with a tree or something, but here you have dead bodies lying around and destroyed villages. Nothing looks the same (as far as I can see). They put *a lot* of love in this game.
It also feels, and is, incredibly polished. It's simply amazing. The UI is small, clear and unobtrusive, but some things could've been explained a bit better. Some things are a bit unclear if you go to the character management screen, for example. It could benefit from more and better explanation. Still, no biggie.
One other thing that stuck with me are the difficulty spikes. These are random but annoying. However, you can change the difficulty on-the-fly so it's usually just a matter of pressing a button.
The game itself can take about 9-12 hours to complete, so it's a pretty big game. I personally never got bored of it.
Now I'm anxiously awaiting the sequels, because man, this one set the bar pretty high for me. If they can maintain the same quality and polish it will be awesome, even if they decide to never add any new features.
Absolutely recommended !

Orcs Must Die is a drama of apocalyptic dimensions. You’ll run around killing them with a mixture of clever traps and third person shooting but this tower defense game is really the story of the poor Orcs that you decimate. Every Orc’s story is told with a hallucinatory intensity, whether they were tossed off a cliff by a spring, slowed by tar before being perforated by poison arrows, burned to a crisp by ground based fire traps, or stabbed to death by the merciless protagonist. Orcs may not be real, but their trials and tribulations have taught me more about the fragility and splendor that we call life.
I can’t express how transformative this masterpiece is. Let’s be clear, it’s not just a masterpiece of the tower defense genre, but of humanity itself.  Orcs must die has turned me into a better person. As a result of this game I’ve decided to clean up my act. I will no longer leave spike traps on the floor lest my future offspring trigger them. Also, I will try being friendly with strangers rather than freezing and shattering them.

After completing this game once here's the best way to describe it:
Breathtaking.
Now I don't mean that in a lame metaphorical way specifically, but suffice it to say that there will be times where you will be caught completely off guard by the plot, and the fact that you had direct influence on it. I immediately started playing again, not for the sake of acheivements or even getting a "best ending" but just wanting to do things a little differently.
I'm not really a connoiseur when it comes to music, but unlike other games I never listened to my own music on top of the game's.
Visually this game is amazing. Boiled down, yea its a bunch of simply cycling illustrations, but those illustrations are brilliantly done, and never make you feel like you're watching some dumb gif loop.
In line with that it is one of the only games I can play on my laptop's fan run like a jet engine, which is to say, it is in no way demanding for any computer to run.
That said, assuming that the place where my first game ended is in fact the ending of the game, I think the loose ends did catch my attention. That didn't at all take away from the overall experience, and if anything it makes me think that they will (hopefully) be releasing a sequel, what with the girth of lore that was given to the game. Over your travels within the game you travel not even a fifth of the presented world, but it never feels like you're missing anuything. In actuality it just made me wish I could go farther, which is probably the right way for a game to make you feel.
The combat is fantastic. I was amazed and enthralled with Factions, and the minor tweaks that were made to pre and during combat gameplay was done with this game in mind, not bending to any sort of predesigned border. Such a thrilling experience during every battle.
A small thing that I really did appreciate was that RNG was in the hands of the player. Only by equipping certain items did RNG ever come into play, which is something I wish a lot of Tactical Strategy RPGs (or what have you) would do as well.
TL;DR,
A game with the smallest of blemishes that left me wanting more, 9.5/10

I mean, I know it's a "beat-'em-up", but cooooome oooooon!!  Things can be a little less relentless/tedious than that.
It also has an inordinately large number of "escort" missions, some of which are admittedly very amusing - carrying a candy dispenser to get the fat kid to follow you, or scaring another kid in the direction you want them to go by wearing a giant rabbit head and going "boogie woogie"! - but having to constantly make sure they're keeping up with you, when the game is already a race against time to make it that extra ten feet before you have to stop/drop everything for yet another same-ish battle DOES get a bit tiresome.
Having said that, the escort missions are perhaps the things which give this game much of its "character", as without them, it really is just running around pummelling or shooting things.  Bit of a catch-22 somewhere there, one suspects...

Look, the graphics are lovely, the sound is fine (even if the groovy/spooky music gets a tad repetitious, like everything else), and the gameplay is fun enough in small doses (a notion not exactly helped by the fact that you can't save in the middle of a "chapter", and have to see the whole thing through in one sitting unless you feel like starting from scratch again next time).  I found myself quite unable, in any case, to play for much more than an hour or so at a time, as it really does get a tad "old" kinda fast.
Mostly recommended for the die-hard beat-'em-up crowd...for the rest of us, we'll probably "get the idea" within the first couple of hours of gameplay, and be sufficiently satisfied by that.  I know I was...and that's probably why I'm giving up about half-way through the game (which I may not have done, granted, if I were able to jump into it for only twenty minutes at a time, but the aforementioned save system nixes all that...in all other regards, however, this is the very definition of "casual" gaming).

One thing I will say in the game's defense is that it really IS meant to be a multiplayer game, so I perhaps partly have myself to blame for playing it solo.  Just the same, a bit more variety wouldn't have hurt either the single OR multi-player mode (heck, even reducing the endless amounts of "back-tracking" may have done wonders)!  Recommended, yes, but only for the right kind of people, in the right kind of numbers.

Verdict: 7/10.

If for no reason other than it being from the same developers/publishers, and featuring the same high school and some of the same characters.  And that's about where the similarities end.  It's a strange world, sometimes...)

This is a review that will describe a lot of in game features without spoiling the game or giving my own opinion. My opinion of the game is at the bottom of this review.
The game looks a lot like the other 'The Walking Dead' games, it didn't change much in that way. You can still change the texture quality to a lower or higher level, depending on what your computer can handle. There were few graphical bugs, sometimes the background tweaked a bit, but that's one of the only cons i've managed to find.
The game uses new features to control Michonne, the in-game protagonist. Featuring (more) click and drag moments and pressing on your keyboard arrows. The old 'Press Q' or 'Press E' features are still frequently used in this game. The controls are - in some moments - very hard to use. For example: sometimes the game needs you to press the right keyboard arrow, although they only show this 3-5 seconds after you could've begon pressing it. This often results in  in-game death. These errors do never occur in battle moments though.
The designers tried to make a complex storyline for Michonne. Through using flashbacks and hallucinations they try to make clear what happened in the past. The story is well worked out, the antagonist is well made. The protagonist (=Michonne) is well worked out as well. The other characters are likable, although you don't really know them as much as you do in other Telltale games.
-Season 1: Starts off slow, but it picks up the pace soon after.
-Season 2: The choises are getting more and more difficult from now on. The story keeps continuing at a fast pace.
-Season 3: The climax of this game is very much like other season finals from the famous 'The Walking Dead' series. It still gives you very tough choices.
The story isn't packed with many moments where you have to wander around and find objects and talk to people. This game keeps going and going, gives you choices and basically throws you is an interactive movie.
This side story was ejoyable. Michonne's flashbacks and hullucinations are a bore after a while, but they're good elements in the whole story telling experience. I was only attached to one character in this game (not including Michonne), while in other games you usually care about your whole group.
These 3 seasons gave me a good overall experience although it was short. I'm happy i bought this game during a sale, i might've been less content if i hadn't done that.

This game has a great storyline, and it allows you to do somethings that are not seen in most hit shooters, for instance you can pickup objects on the ground and throw them at an enemy (Or use them as a makeshift riotshield thingy.) You can also kill friendly NPCs (As long as they aren't a main character.) Another aspect that I really enjoyed is the reactions that NPCs can express on their faces and how well their reactions coorespond to the events happening around them.
There are many other great things about this product, however it would take to long for me to list them.
10/10 Would playthrough again.

The gameplay is extremely solid with a great feel to the combat.  You can kite very effectively, using your mobility to build clusters to aoe.  Areas like a goblin camp will be packed full of monsters. This gives map areas a living feel, rather than just as a backdrop for random spawns (cough cough Diablo III).
There are a huge variety of possible ways to play since you can mix classes.  The art is fantastic and provides a very dark atmosphere.  Fighting abhorrent abominations in a beautiful field of golden wheat that becomes scarred with the effects of combat is incredible. I am playing as an occultist with a raven and a hellhound.  Whenever I pass near my raven in a cavern, it casts giant dark bird shadows over the entire area.  Worth playing the class just for that!  Mushroom sprouts also cast shadows for each individual stem.  These small details really show how much care went into designing this game.
The sounds are very visceral, e.g. the firearms have a nice meaty bang to them.  The background ambient noises are mixed well. For example the swamp sounds give just the right feel without being too noisy as in some games.
All of the basic systems of a modern ARPG including a shared loot chest, forging, enhancing items, etc are all present and fully functional as far as I have seen.  One of the few downsides is that the quests are few and spread out, but quests are not really necessary for this type of game other than to help encourage you to advance through the zones.
Overall, this is the best ARPG I have seen in quite a while. Frankly, the price is probably too low for what you are getting, especially if it is on sale.

I enjoy the premise of this game, the core idea that it tries to emulate with a twist, a DnD session where you can customize and control the players and the room that the game takes place in, even the dungeon master.
I will say that the game does have charm and has a good art direction, though I would say that there should have been more effort in the pixel art. However, it has both condensed and distilled the core elements of pen and paper gaming to a level which is far too simplistic for me to enjoy. The combat is shallow, the quests are repetitive, and the stats and perks are shallow and hardly feel like they matter. The UI is also highly simplistic and does not even provide important information efficiently or at all.
I am sure that this is a fun bathroom game on a mobile device or something on the go, but the flaws of this game impeded my enjoyment of this game and cannot recommend this game to people who want an enthralling experience.

You can have several parties going at once and share earned gold across parties which can make for interesting progression styles. There are permenant upgrades to your table and the room you're playing from that really change the way the game is played and I felt that was a very nice touch.
The DEV team was bought out so there's no real support for the game anymore, it has some odd bugs in it still and can occasionally break if you do some things too quickly.
Overall 100%ing this game was fun and a steady challenge it took me just under 30 hours.

Especially if your party composition is unable to overcome an obstacle, you may have to start a new game to support your main party.

I am undecided about this one. I like many things about it, I hate as much. I think it will be great for many people, but you should take some warning.
Do not play this game for the plot. It is not terrible, but it is unoriginal, plagued with clichés. Nothing really to play for. Nothing you will hate either.
Gameplay is great... when it works. It sometimes works at transmitting the "parkour feel", and it feels great. But there are some aspects that kill it. Playing this game means doing the same thing over, and over, and over again. No breaks. Just the same stuff from start to end. Good games break the game dynamic to make it feel fresh every second you are playing. Here they fail at this. I think back on the game and I can only remember one very long level. All levels even look the same!
Checkpoints are an issue as well. There are a few frustrating jumps in the game, and they often make you repeat the previous boring section over, and over, and over, and over again. Bonus points for when a fall resets an older check point!
What I find most disappointing about this game is how empty the world feels. There is no reason at all to explore. There is nothing to find (well, you can find "stashes", which are just 3 bags in every level. They tell you nothing, they do nothing). And even worse: how can a game about parkour be so limited in the paths you can find? This game would be 30 times better if you had some real freedom finding your own way. Sadly, this is not the case. They even paint structures in red so you know the "good way". Talk about breaking immersion.
There are no characters with which to interact. And enemies are not very interesting (they are either boring or annoying).
This game feels to me more like a developer's exercise to test a new idea. And this can be great (Portal 1 is just that). But it seems like they did not really bother with the details here. It looks more like a beta version of a game.
Bottom line: the game is not really bad. And it is short, which is good given the circumstances. But only play it if you believe the points I raised above will not be an issue for you.
PS: I give it a down-vote not because I hate it so much, but to balance opinions. I am actually 50-50 about this game.

text: I don't like puzzles, but i enjoyed antichamber so much. Usually i give up and google some solutions, but this time i finished the game [almost] by myself, because challenges offered by the game are really interesting.

The controls are clunky, and despite free running being advertised as being fast, smooth and loose, it's more like a constant stop and start, as you try to find your way around the levels or even try to free run, since jumping, climbing, or sliding brings your speed to a halt. You die constantly and each time you fall to your death it plays a very loud, ear shattering vibration and train noise.
Combat is very so so. You have the option of doing nonlethal disarm takedowns, making the game TECHNICALLY pacifist friendly, which I usually love in a game, but I do NOT RECOMMEND DOING THIS. In the later stages it starts to get virtually impossible, and it is 1000 times easier and more fun to just get a gun and start shooting. Otherwise, Faith can barely take a few bumps before dying. Also, grabbing a gun out of your enemies hands is something you will be doing very often, but it feels ridiculously hard since you'll have like a fraction of a second to grab the gun, and sometimes even with slow-motion the gun just won't highlight until it's too late to grab it and you get smacked anyway.
The story is also terrible. I won't spoil just for the sake of not spoiling, but it's very cliche, and extremely predictable. It will tease you with a mystery for hours even after you've already figured it out. The voice acting's not terrible, but the dialogue certainly is. Most of what the main character says sounds like something an edgy teenager would say. For instance, when asked if they read the news, they respond "The news is just advertising!" They also have a totalitarian government but provide almost no evidence that it's actually that bad, you're just told it sucks because the city used to be dirty but 'alive'. Every twist in the game is 100 percent predictable, except for the very ending, but only because it's so out of place, random, and stupid that you wouldn't guess they'd stoop that low. It's also short, providing a meager 6 hours, and that's going slowly. The majority of the cutscenes are animated, but the animation quality is very low, with characters faces behaving strangely. It reminds me of Invisible Inc, but very much not as good. The ending is a big fat anti climax that will leave you feeling deeply unsatisfied.
The most constant nag I have is that many of the in game actions feel entirely up to luck or how the game feels. Often you will do a jump, it will fail, then you will do the same jump the same way and it will succeed. Or, you'll be running at or away from enemies and whether you get shot down in 2 seconds or don't get hurt at all is entirely up to chance. It makes you feel like skill ultimately does not matter, luck does.
Also, you VERY often have NO idea where to go in this game. If you hit alt, SOMETIMES it will show you, but it only points at the ultimate end goal, even if it's behind a wall or 8 miles away. Often, this has nothing to do with what you're doing at that moment, leaving you to figure out where you're supposed to go by yourself, knowing only that the objective will be complete 'somewhere in that direction'.
Mirror's Edge is an experiment, and I commend it for that. A game that tries something new and fails is better than a mediocre game that tried nothing. But it is a failed experiment. And if you like experimental games, by all means, go ahead, but you won't be missing anything if you skip this.

Star Wars Battlefront II. Star Wars Battlefront II. This is a game that was second to none for me on my Playstation 2. This game stayed on the top played lists for the original Xbox on Xbox Live for years after it's release. This game is a phenomenon and a classic in the eyes of many, and that should be all I have to say.and It is a game that combines many aspects of the films into a first or third person shooter enviroment. You can play as Yoda on Dagobah, or fly an X-Wing against the Imperial fleet over Hoth. This game justified the exsistence of the prequels for me, as the majority of the maps are prequel movie maps. The game has a surprisingly active community, with an average of anywhere from 200-400 online on normal days. The graphics pushed the boundaries systems like the Playstation 2 and Xbox (and to a lesser extent, PSP) could provide, but now it looks only servicable. There is a total of 24 maps (space and land) included with the purchase, although the active modding community has ported the original Xbox DLC maps and made brand new ones for the PC version. There is also a single player campaign that serves a a nice tutorial to the game's mechanics, and various single player mode such as instant action (pick a map or setlist of maps and start playing), galactic conquest (control one of the factions in moving a ship, managing resources, and eventually controlling the galaxy). This game is more than worth well more than it's $10 price tag, as the content avaliable at the start along with the modded content and active community create a great ecosystem for anyone who buys this game. Star Wars Battlefront II is an excellent title that provides no reason NOT to buy it.

This game could be the very definition of "fun"...if it wasn't also the very definition of REPETITION.  Beat up some monsters, pick up the bulky key item you just dropped and move another ten seconds or so in the direction of your objective before being forced to drop said item yet AGAIN to beat up some MORE monsters!  I mean, I know it's a "beat-'em-up", but cooooome oooooon!!  Things can be a little less relentless/tedious than that.
It also has an inordinately large number of "escort" missions, some of which are admittedly very amusing - carrying a candy dispenser to get the fat kid to follow you, or scaring another kid in the direction you want them to go by wearing a giant rabbit head and going "boogie woogie"! - but having to constantly make sure they're keeping up with you, when the game is already a race against time to make it that extra ten feet before you have to stop/drop everything for yet another same-ish battle DOES get a bit tiresome.
Having said that, the escort missions are perhaps the things which give this game much of its "character", as without them, it really is just running around pummelling or shooting things.  Bit of a catch-22 somewhere there, one suspects...

Look, the graphics are lovely, the sound is fine (even if the groovy/spooky music gets a tad repetitious, like everything else), and the gameplay is fun enough in small doses (a notion not exactly helped by the fact that you can't save in the middle of a "chapter", and have to see the whole thing through in one sitting unless you feel like starting from scratch again next time).  I found myself quite unable, in any case, to play for much more than an hour or so at a time, as it really does get a tad "old" kinda fast.
Mostly recommended for the die-hard beat-'em-up crowd...for the rest of us, we'll probably "get the idea" within the first couple of hours of gameplay, and be sufficiently satisfied by that.  I know I was...and that's probably why I'm giving up about half-way through the game (which I may not have done, granted, if I were able to jump into it for only twenty minutes at a time, but the aforementioned save system nixes all that...in all other regards, however, this is the very definition of "casual" gaming).

One thing I will say in the game's defense is that it really IS meant to be a multiplayer game, so I perhaps partly have myself to blame for playing it solo.  Just the same, a bit more variety wouldn't have hurt either the single OR multi-player mode (heck, even reducing the endless amounts of "back-tracking" may have done wonders)!  Recommended, yes, but only for the right kind of people, in the right kind of numbers.

Be aware that you are going to play this game for about 8 hours and absolutely love it, and then you'll be left dumbfounded by the direction it suddenly takes.
As I said, you'll love it; that is if you like the idea of a role-playing turn-based strategy game in which almost every character has their own unique abilities, and thus worth to a battle. Characters level up like in typical RPGs and you can equip them with stat-enhancing gear (only one though, and the highest level is 5). You'll quickly decide your front 6 and rarely deviate from it.
You will also learn that this game outright hates you, dealing you pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥ cards when you are called upon to make a decision. Not always ♥♥♥♥♥♥, however - some lead almost nowhere. But this where the story is primarily told, and because of these infrequent horrible decisions, and the occasional story-affecting choices, the saga feels like it's yours. I'm quite confident that someone out there has done precisely the same things as I did in this game, but, whilst I was playing it, it didn't feel that way.
The art style is pretty. Think 50's-80's Disney style stationary art with basic movements programmed in for battles, but with the minimal, yet highly appreciated, foreground and background falling snow to give it an easy 3D effect. Nice all around.
My only beef with this game is it's story, particularly the ending. It just ends to soon to put it plainly. Any self-respecting storywriter (who knows or does not know that they may be writing a trilogy) would not have ended it in this way. So many great and interesting angles are left unexplored and hardly explained! The Gods are dead (not much of a spoiler as it's right at the beginning of the game) and yet no explanation is offered. The sun has stopped moving (again, beginning) and no explanation is offered. The (apparent) main boss is introduced 2/3 of the way through without any previous hinting of how significant he's going to be. Why? Because his significance is paired with his existence. Very poor. And it's not even like he's a good main boss: there is a literal earth-shatterer that would have made for a killer main boss!
The storywriters need firing for this one. Actually, just fire the ones who argued that it should end in this way because they need to go back to junior school. I don't care if a trilogy had been in the plan the whole time, a good story does not introduce a key aspect of the storyline and then just do nothing with it.
I do recommend this though. It's a great game. The tone is excellent and it really feels like your saga. When you finish in a day (if your dedicated enough) you'll see what I mean by just how ♥♥♥♥ing disgraceful the ending is.

Imagine a city built up and ruled by protection racketeers and gangs, where you fought for territory and built up your territory for cash.
That would be this game. You can build custom buildings, then zone them as one of several things such as industry, commerce, residential. You can build up a base or convert a building into one as well. And the dev is updating often and with updates people actually want to see, unlike some other games I've seen recently where people playing like them but then the devs inexplicably start altering things people liked and putting in things nobody asked for. If you liked the gameplay mechanics from Saints Row: The Third (and possibly Crackdown), you will most likely enjoy this title. It seems like the same basic game engine and assets were used from SR3 with little to no modification. The character customization is virtually identical to what was in SR3 with the addition of new outfits and possibly hairstyles.
The story borrows heavily from a certain popular sci-fi trilogy, but I still enjoyed it. The voice acting and dialog are both very good in my opinion. The voice actor for Zinyak in particular is outstanding. There are a lot of parody nods to other game franchises which I felt were done tactfully.
The superpowers were the best part of this title for me, but they essentially made vehicles unnecessary to the point where I only used vehicles when they were required for missions. The radio stations are available outside of vehicles, and the music selection is OK. The classical music station is definitely worth listening to for at least one loop just for the host.

As a huge Telltale fan,
is a nice addition to The Walking Dead series. Albeit it has absolutely nothing to do with the Telltale rendition of the story since Michonne is an actual character in the comics, the spirit of The Walking Dead games is captured perfectly in this miniseries.
There's really not that much to say about this one. If you're Telltale/Walking Dead fan you're most likely to enjoy 'Michonne'. The characters despite the short length of the game (~4 hours) are actually richer in depth than many other games which have a significantly longer duration. Playing a Telltale game is all about the story, the characters and the choices you make and TWD:M succeeds in a being a proper title of the studio. Regardless I'd be a liar if I didn't mention the few technical issues that still plague this game a year after release. Some horrendous loading times (on SSD but with cloud saving on), a few crashes, some graphical glitches. It really boggles the mind how this came to be since I can hardly remember any of those issues in previous Telltale games, at least in that frequency.
Nonetheless there are some improvements compared to previous titles. The quick time event combat feels improved (that felt weird to say actually), there's a part where you combo buttons and it actually felt really satisfying to watch the carnage unfold against the walkers. There's a more 'cinematic' feel to the game, a good type of feel actually. Slowing down in combat, letterbox, music score, animations, I gotta admit it feels very polished and I'd love to have more of that on the Season 3 series.
Again, it is really short but if you enjoy Telltale games and especially The Walking Dead series, getting this one on a discount is a nice way to spend an afternoon.

This game is amazing.  It's extremely difficult, it's very random, and it actually requires thinking.  Recommended for anyone looking for something new that won't give them a seizure.

The gameplay is extremely solid with a great feel to the combat.  You can kite very effectively, using your mobility to build clusters to aoe.  Areas like a goblin camp will be packed full of monsters. This gives map areas a living feel, rather than just as a backdrop for random spawns (cough cough Diablo III).
There are a huge variety of possible ways to play since you can mix classes.  The art is fantastic and provides a very dark atmosphere.  Fighting abhorrent abominations in a beautiful field of golden wheat that becomes scarred with the effects of combat is incredible. I am playing as an occultist with a raven and a hellhound.  Whenever I pass near my raven in a cavern, it casts giant dark bird shadows over the entire area.  Worth playing the class just for that!  Mushroom sprouts also cast shadows for each individual stem.  These small details really show how much care went into designing this game.
The sounds are very visceral, e.g. the firearms have a nice meaty bang to them.  The background ambient noises are mixed well. For example the swamp sounds give just the right feel without being too noisy as in some games.
All of the basic systems of a modern ARPG including a shared loot chest, forging, enhancing items, etc are all present and fully functional as far as I have seen.  One of the few downsides is that the quests are few and spread out, but quests are not really necessary for this type of game other than to help encourage you to advance through the zones.
Overall, this is the best ARPG I have seen in quite a while. Frankly, the price is probably too low for what you are getting, especially if it is on sale.

I don't know where and when I got this game...
But... This game...
This game is awesome!
I liked the overall parody feel about it while it has a strong and solid work about delivering action and plot in moderation, getting some loud laughs from me here and there. The battle is unforgiving, so you always have to be focused, despite it being turn-based. The difficulty is adjustable in a manner "How frisky you are today?", taking on anything between 1 and 7 rats or elite monsters. The open-ended way the characters are presented lets you use your imagination. I do feel like playing a table top sheets'n'pens while playing this. Yes, the feel of every character is an illusion, but it's a very-VERY well made illusion.
Another point is the building difficulty: Items give you stats that you barely see. Levels give you damage that you barely see. Hp and Mana regen is earned by tears and sweat dripping down your inner thigh. All this while enemy shamelessly uses lifesteal and applies crazy bleeding stacks. Some battles will be so tight that you will stain your undergarments a bit and still lose because of the enemy randomly preferring your rouge to your fully buffed granny paladin. You will put a sleep on a DoT'ed enemy and lose your healer because of that, and you will spend 4 times the money you earned in that battle to revive your team. You will even spend 2k on upgrading your sword and still get nothing in return because you are a looser and you will have no money to leave the god forsaken town.
But... You know... That's what's good about this game... That's what's your adventure is. And you should not just accept it, but have tons of fun while at it!

Visually stunning but hardly the best game in the Xcom franchise, still enjoyable once you work past its faults.
If you have played previous Xcom games the first thing you will notice is how annoyingly streamlined this game is. Anything you could do tandemly in previous Xcom games has been reduced to one instance at a time. No researching multiple things no launching multiple Interceptors or Skyrangers. Gone are the multiple independant bases, tho you can station interceptors at various fixed locations around the globe.
Instead of having soldiers with stats and using those to determine how you outfit them, there are now fixed classes. Soldiers are (seemingly) randomly promoted to a class after their first mission (or automatically once you buy the foundry upgrade). Time units are gone so there is no more deciding what to do, you can either take an action which will end the turn for all classes except Heavy that have taken the skill that allows them to take a second action if their first action was to shoot. Otherwise you can move and take an action or sprint which ends your turn. Unless you are an Assault using Run & Gun which will allow you to sprint and fire your weapon. Time Units let you do whatever. move and shoot, shoot and move, shoot, throw a genade and move etc.
The real problem I had with the streamlining of soldiers was the sniper. In the original Xcom if your soldier had the sort of stats that fit a sniper you could eventually work them into that position while still using them in other capacities if you needed to. In this itteration of the game BOOM your soldier is a sniper they will only ever be a sniper and snipers for me were dead weight through the first part of the game. They only really start becoming useful later on when you unlock a bunch of technology and manage to get them sufficiently promoted, selecting the appropriate skills.
When the game says Alien Activity what it really means is you havn't run into a scripted event yet. They start off cool but they get old sorta fast. Effectively what happens is you walk to a point where the game spawns in aliens and it does so with a quick but not quick enouhg (when you hit the 30th+ time) in game cut scene where they go from standing around  apparently gossiping to dashing for cover. Where as previous games Alien Activity meant there was an alien somewhere on the map actially doing something with or without you there to watch it doing said thing. That said I'm not 100% sure how terror missions work because you still get the same spawn in effect but civilians in areas you can't see will die if you don't make your way to them fast enough.
I don't quite get how a 9GB+ game can't seem to acomplish the same depth a game managed to decades ago and clocking in at only around 30MB. Still it really does look nice and if you never played the original Xcom you probably won't even know what you're missing. At the end of the day this is probably as close to a revival of Xcom as we can ever really hope for.

I really, really want to like the game... But damn it's infuriating, so around 20 mins and I'm ready to break my keyboard, and delete it.
tl:dr
The Core idea is great, sadly annoying enemies can make this a stressful affair and at least for me kill the enjoyment. So be prepared to be stressed and frustrated.
In a bit more details
The Good part
- Great graphic style: The views and style of the city is amazing
- The Navigation Puzzle: Finding the correct route and best route is fun and can be a nice little brain tease.
- The running flow: When you hit a string of perfect jumps and Faith is blazing through the obstacles
The Okay part
- The Story: I'm almost done with the game and it okay not great in anyway
The "I'm about to go Hulk mode"
- The save points: The game doesn't save in every room, so be prepared to redo the same boring jump over and over.
- The trigger points: The amount of times I have fallen through a Pipe or similar is insane. Faith basically breaks her nose on the object you are trying to hit, but she fails to grab onto it, is absolutely infuriating
The What the Hell part
- Gun/Ninja's play: This is the biggest and most annoying feature for me. Like a bad version of a time attack and its usually the main reason why I want to break something.
The idea of a running game, where you have to navigate a (sometimes) complex environment is fun - but then add a constant pressure of being shot at or trapped. It's a stress factor of bullets flying around, giving you little to no time to figure out your route. You have no chance of hiding or sneak around them, as they always know where you are and have an amazing aim.
Of cause you can pick up a weapon, but it feels off for Faith to shoot and kill people - plus it feels really basic to shot and is unenjoyable.
I wish they had made a "No Enemies" version of the game, and made it possible to be a pure navigation puzzler.
So why am I still playing this, well I'm an idiot and want to complete it. Eventually I will, but for the 15 time I'm going to leave this alone for sometime - the annoyance is just too great.

Be aware that you are going to play this game for about 8 hours and absolutely love it, and then you'll be left dumbfounded by the direction it suddenly takes.
As I said, you'll love it; that is if you like the idea of a role-playing turn-based strategy game in which almost every character has their own unique abilities, and thus worth to a battle. Characters level up like in typical RPGs and you can equip them with stat-enhancing gear (only one though, and the highest level is 5). You'll quickly decide your front 6 and rarely deviate from it.
You will also learn that this game outright hates you, dealing you pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥ cards when you are called upon to make a decision. Not always ♥♥♥♥♥♥, however - some lead almost nowhere. But this where the story is primarily told, and because of these infrequent horrible decisions, and the occasional story-affecting choices, the saga feels like it's yours. I'm quite confident that someone out there has done precisely the same things as I did in this game, but, whilst I was playing it, it didn't feel that way.
The art style is pretty. Think 50's-80's Disney style stationary art with basic movements programmed in for battles, but with the minimal, yet highly appreciated, foreground and background falling snow to give it an easy 3D effect. Nice all around.
My only beef with this game is it's story, particularly the ending. It just ends to soon to put it plainly. Any self-respecting storywriter (who knows or does not know that they may be writing a trilogy) would not have ended it in this way. So many great and interesting angles are left unexplored and hardly explained! The Gods are dead (not much of a spoiler as it's right at the beginning of the game) and yet no explanation is offered. The sun has stopped moving (again, beginning) and no explanation is offered. The (apparent) main boss is introduced 2/3 of the way through without any previous hinting of how significant he's going to be. Why? Because his significance is paired with his existence. Very poor. And it's not even like he's a good main boss: there is a literal earth-shatterer that would have made for a killer main boss!
The storywriters need firing for this one. Actually, just fire the ones who argued that it should end in this way because they need to go back to junior school. I don't care if a trilogy had been in the plan the whole time, a good story does not introduce a key aspect of the storyline and then just do nothing with it.
I do recommend this though. It's a great game. The tone is excellent and it really feels like your saga. When you finish in a day (if your dedicated enough) you'll see what I mean by just how ♥♥♥♥ing disgraceful the ending is.

This game is hard to define. I would describe it as a board game RPG as you gather your party, choose which ones are going to battle, level them up but you never get to change the armor or sword they use.
This game shows the story of caravans running away from their lands due to invasion by external forces. You spend most of the game travelling or talking with the members of your caravan. Those talks can boost or decrease morale. Besides the morale of your caravan, controlling food is a crucial travel element.
Whenever you get into battle, which is the second main element of this game, the game displays a board to you allowing you to position your party members and fight much like a turn based strategy. Each hero has health and armor. Health is the same as any other game. Higher armor helps those heroes receive minimal damage therefore it is crucial to decrease as soon as possibile the armor of your enemies in battle.
Besides managing your caravan and fighting there is not much else to do, however the story is quite interesting and succeds in transporting you to this medieval mithological world.
I enjoyed playing this game and even though this game is a complete experience (not based on episodes), it appears that this is only the beggining of the story (may be a trilogy??).
I recommend this game. 8/10

At first glance, Voxel Turf may look like GTA in Minecraft, but there's quite a lot more to this game beneath the surface. Yes, it is a Voxel based game with guns and missions, block building/destroying, and to be fair those mechanics work quite well for the most part. But what sets this game apart is its sophisticated simulated economy; this game also brings SimCity into the mix. I would call Voxel Turf a GTA-esque Minecraft-esque SimCity-esque voxel sandbox of chaos. That may sound like mayhem, and it is! It genuinely works.
The graphics are reminiscent of another certain blocky game, and here they can look quite nice especially amidst a dense metropolis at night. However most of the time, the visual style looks bland and lacking style even for a blocky game. The effects are also quite boring, with bullet trails looking incredibly odd, and block destruction disappointing (especially with no gravity). The explosions aren't too bad, and I can't say I've played many open world city-based games where I can run around wielding a rocket launcher and blast holes into anything and everything. The sounds are quite dull and low quality, and multiple police sirens are terribly cacophonous. However, the audio is saved by an incredible soundtrack, which is a great joy to listen to whilst playing.
There are multiple customisable gamemodes to choose from, but the 2 main gamemodes would be the full sandbox Free Build mode, and the Turf mode. In Free Build, you start from a blank canvas but have unlimited resources to build a fully functional city of your dreams. For me, the real fun is had in Turf mode. By default you spawn in a very large (size is customisable) procedurally generated city, where you start with nothing but a few blocks and cash. Pressing tab yields you the completion of your first mission, and from there you will be completing hundreds of missions to gain reputation and money. Establishing protection rackets on properties costs reputation but garners an hourly income, which you can use to purchase your own lots and eventually work towards achieving the monopoly.
It's not that straightforward though, there are other AI factions that own portions of the city, and they are simulated as thought they were real players. They have their own net worth, reputation, emotions towards the player, etc. You can complete missions to damage their reputation, and you can also bargain with them to befriend them. There is great mission variety in this game, and these range from street races, to damaging property, to saving civilians from thugs and even driving an ambulance driver. There are mission chains you can complete, but also completely random missions that pop up around the city. The city feels very lively, and every action has a consequence. Committing crimes damages the safeness rating of nearby properties, which can cause them to lose business, so you have to be thoughtful of your actions.
Also present is functional shops, where you can buy guns, placeable blocks, health rejuvenating items, armour and other items. After you're stocked up, you can go on raiding enemy bases which yield weapon mods, or even better-than-shop quality weapons. Weapon mods can be fixated to any weapon; put a scope and explosive bullets on a golden SMG if you want! You can also level up, and upgrade certain attributes such as health, and even pick special perks which give you even more bonuses. The UI isn't great, but it functions fine and the inventory is straightforward (but you have to press 'n' to open inventory, what!?). There's also tanks, and tanks are awesome.
Overall, Voxel Turf is a visually bland, but mechanically fun sandbox game which delivers a surprising amount of content for it's small price. I give this game an 8/10
