Alright I had originally reviewed this game, but now I am going to do it again because of some convictions I had. (Yes you heard me convictions... Hear me out)
DISCLAIMER-
This is my opinion. I am stating it for the readers benifit.
I know there are several people out there like me who have certain morals when it comes to video games. So please understand I also get it that there are other people who could care less.
So yes, I understand everyone's morals vary, but I am going to share mine here so that people can see if this game fits into their morals before buying it and perhaps finding out they will never play it.
So first up. This game is DARK. Hence why it is called GRIM DAWN.
It is dark in several different ways.
I will share those ways below while hitting on the points where the game just went to far "for me".
-------PLEASE NOTE------ I do say a few things you will encounter in this game. So small spoiler alert.
1.DARK SCENARY
The whole beggining of the game is nothing but dark screenplay.
If you are a person who likes green grass and flowers with cheery colors you will not find it here.
There are some different biomes, such as snow, dessert, and a few mossy caves though.
However most of the game will be the same dreary, foggy, and battlescared landscape all         throughout.
2.DARK PROPS
Next, the props. This is where my convictions start kicking in.
While roaming around grim dawn's dark world you will see mutilated bodies, skulls, skeletons, dead babies lying around in the streets (these are somewhat hidden but they are there), torture chambers, tortured victims, and tons and tons of fleshed dead bodies with various parts of them chopped off and thrown around in a bloody mess.
For me the baby thing really started getting to me.
I know some would say "well that's why it is an M rated game." to them I say you are correct, but me saying this may help someone make their decision with a little more knowledge.
I understand games like this are violent, but I think that the reader can agree that some M rated games do not actually have that much blood/guts to them.
3. WITCHCRAFT, DEMONS, SATANIC SYMBOLS, SATANIC REFERENCES, OCCULTIC RITUALS......... I REALLY COULD GO ON.
Seriously though if you are the kind of person who does not care for this stuff. Take my word for it. STAY AWAY.
This is the reason I don't think I will touch this game anymore. It is just to much of it for me.
I have played games with magic in it where you could tell the dark magic from the light.
This game is to blurred for me. Good and Evil seem so be blended in a very odd way...
Right from the get go one finds out they were possessed by a demon like influence. Only to be saved by occultic magic.
The enemys will cast spells on the character leaving the pentagram symbol surronding them, but then the player can cast the pentagram symbol on their enemies too... So?
One will run into a man with hits inner guts spilled out in a sacrifice to a demon. The player's character's storyline will lead them to fight against the ones who did it, yet the player's character can choose to be an occultist for their class which draws their power from a witch... And not a nice on from it's description.
One will find countless demons taking the form of a human, or possesing them completly, but then many of the character class selection's skills have to do with being possessed or filled with some demon/god.
The story line is littered with witchcraft, demons, and satanic symbols.
Although Satan to my knowledge is not named in the game (other then the main town being called Devil's crossing). It does not really matter. It more then makes up for the lack of his name being mentioned.
4. CHARACTER CLASSES
Character classes almost all have their own diety that they are connected to.
One class choice has a witch for a diety and it is heavily hinted that you serve him, and draw power from him if you play as the class. The classes name is Occultist.
5. ENEMIES
They are almost all demonic or possesed in some way. They will cast spells and curses on the player. The player will fight the undead a lot. Undead everything.
6. LOOT/ARMOUR/WEAPONS
This is probably one of the main reasons people like games like this. And this game has tons and tons of loot.
However my problem with it was with the names of the higher lvl loot.
I forget the exact name, but i remember getting a chestpiece that was called something like chestpiece of perdition.
So much of the armour is named after some pretty dark things as well.
7. STORYLINE
*Warning* SPOILER ALERT ABOUT ENDGAME
As i kinda hinted it is a dark storyline. I beat the game. I won't say to much about the ending, but I will say the getting there just felt odd.
The game gives you moral choices along the way such as choosing whether or not to kill a man or save him, but in the end of the game you end up saving the world...
It just goes back to good and evil being blended together in a wierd way again.
Overall I did love the gameplay mechanic, but I hated the clothes put on it.
-----SHORT SUMMARY-----
1. DARK GAMEPLAY
-Very dark setting
-Not for people who like colorful gameplay
-Lot's of gray tones, fog etc
2.DISTURBING GAMEPLAY
-Will see lots of mutilated things which includes babies
-Will see fleshed bloody bodies mangled, cut up, and thrown around
-Torture and human sacrifice are very clearly seen
3.SATANIC/DEMONIC/OCCULTIC
-Almost all character classes serve a diety
-Almost every enemy in the game is possesed by a demon
-Good and Evil is very blurred and blended in a weird way
-Many many many satanic symbols are incorperated into the game
-Dark and Light magic are not defined at all
So to close, I would not recomend this to someone with morals that are in opposition to the things listed above.

TLDR: It has significantly dumbed down the concept, but does deliver it in a package that is still enjoyable and conveys a strong atmosphere. The general gameplay, story and ending are excellent. I wouldn't pay full price. Get it on a 50% off offer or better.
The Good
- A fluid, well designed aesthetic.
- The base design concept is a nice spin off the classic.
- The story is well written and the ending is very satisfying, while admittedly a little cliche.
- General gameplay is enjoyable and scales well. Despite the simplification, it doesn't get old quickly.
- Combat mechanics and the UI are well done.
The Bad
- No sign of the classic base defense missions that UFO/XCOM series have had almost uniformly.
- Little depth in equipment. Soldiers start with a stock 'assault rifle', 'shotgun' etc rather than varying options (eg MP5, G36, AK47 and so on) allowing variance between fire rate, penetration, clip size etc like featured strongly in games like UFO: Aftermath. This leads to a big part of the 'dumbed down' feeling.
- No control over soldier speciality. A unit you developed with a great marksmen ability might suddenly get shunted into a support role, when you desperately wanted her for an elite sniper. You can end up with a dozen assault class but very few/none of the other classes.
- Little customisation for soldiers. You pick between fairly limited appearance options and most voices are basically american accents. Try getting used to that with soldiers meant to be from China, Russia etc.
- It feels like the base game was kept dumbed down to allow them to sell DLC. While a first playthrough is enjoyable, you'll want the DLC to render replays worthwhile.

I've played every Saints Row since the first and all of the additional DLC so you could say I'm a fan of the series. So imagine my disappointment when I load up the "Inauguration Station" to find the same graphic style, same clothing/hair options, and more of the same. It completely turned me off to the game and I hadn't given it a second glance until it recently dropped in price for the weekend.
Boy was I wrong. Rather than being a rehash of the third game, this iteration takes the series in a completely new direction and adds super powers to the game. What many people have failed to mention (including the actual game page) is that this is a hyper-realized world that constantly breaks the fourth wall without holding back. This game at the core is similar to the previous games, but it's definitely a unique contender on it's own.
This game has made me laugh time and time again as well as blow my head off with witty reference one after the other. The game is very streamlined and anything you want to do in the game can be done within seconds. Wanna play with a friend? Hot Seat Co-Op is available and very functional. Want to hop in a mech and wreak havoc on the city? Head over to the Mech Mayhem mini-game. This game has so much available that it's easy to forget that this was originally an expansion for the third game.
So while you're still in the same city, with the same clothes, hairstyles, and most customization options for that matter, the game still shines as a "have fun no matter what" title that I've rarely seen before. You'll quickly stop picking at the graphics and driving physics once you realize you can shoot people with rubber band guns while flying around naked with pearlescent green skin. Maybe you want to just drive around and customize cars? Try to solve jumping puzzles, play the extremely well-written story, or see how long you and a friend can volley a car back and forth to one another.
Is it polished?
No

TL;DR - This game in my opinion is easily the #1 in its genre and there is very little reason to skip it. Offers fun gameplay and combat with good variety.
If you want an open-world zombie ''survival'' game, this one is the best in the market. Hell, even if you just want a game that contains zombies, this is the best one you'll find.
Now, i put ''survival'' in quotations (or whatever its called) because you collect things around the world to craft bombs, weapons, med kits and all that. It's not entirely survival and if anyone claims so, i would disagree. It is sort of post-apocalyptic which makes it look survival, but there is no nutritional crisis, where you'd have to go look for food before you starve, so in my opinion its not a survival game.
The game is well-ported in my opinion, i have a pretty bad PC and can run it quite fine, and the graphics are quite pleasant too (you need to know what settings to tune down though).
What can be annoying for some here is that all weapons are degradable and will be destroyed to uselessness as you use them. You can repair them, but only for a fixed amount of times. What's good with this system however, is that it keeps your weapon variety going and keeps the game interesting in combat to a slight degree (This becomes less of a struggle as the game goes when you can obtain really good stuff too easily).
The zombies are really braindead, but you have some empowered ones that can be pretty tough at times. At night time, you'll have some extremely hard monsters to deal with and its almost never recommended to be out at night unless you want a huge adrenaline rush because it can be insanely hard, sometimes scary. In a nutshell they're really fun to fight.
Story has some plot to it but i assume its nothing special, since people never take stories in open world games seriously as far as i know, but i enjoyed the story. It was nice to follow it along, and it made you feel pretty important, though you're more like just a running slave.
The side-activities arent as interesting but if you want to punch more zombies, they're quite nice. Some involve parkour and gathering aswell.
This game supports lots of mods, and there is even custom games where people create their own maps. As soon as we get more content in on this, this could be tons of fun with others or just alone. I'd say this the core ''end'' game you'll be spending your time with after you complete the story, unless you wanna mess around some more over there.

Another year, another Telltale adventure game, with zombies! TWD: Michonne details what went on when a particular mary sue left the adventuring party and did her own thing for a bit. It seems the writers for this particular game were obsessed with breaking the “invincible female” archetype by introducing flaws in the form of mental illness tied to grievance to the point where Michonne becomes a walking liability. I’m not kidding, she basically has a psychotic episode every 5 minutes and it’s a wonder that she can even function at all let alone accomplish any goals in the storyline.
Considering how Telltale games are 90% story 10% gameplay, there’s really not much room for error when writing the story for the game. So making it as obnoxious as possible to play a well-known “strong” character really just isn’t a great strategy for entertainment. Going to have to recommend giving this game a pass and/or just watching a let’s play instead.

***At the time of writting this only 2 out of 13 negative reviews for this game are inelligble for a refund... What do you have to lose? One hour and fifty-nine minutes of your time?
So i actually have been enjoying this game quite a bit. Public MP is a waste of time right now without 24/7 server's. Coop MP is awesome. SP is what I got my hours in.
Pros
-----------------------
-The real-estate/racketeering system is pretty amazing.
-Tons of default building/decor/base designs.
-Ability to save your own custom designs and build them instantly at the material cost price.
-Minecraft build style with more block types.
-Some blocks are worth more depending on the material allowing you to increase a designs worth/profit.
-Every building is enterable and NPC's are spawned inside.
-Tons of GTA styled missions to gain XP/reputation while you await your real-estate profits.
-You can rob/heist most of the comercial buildings in the game. They will have safes in the back.
-RPG Perk/Stat system. Progression is felt for sure.
-Honestly the music is pretty catchy at times.
-A vast array of vehicles which actually feel pretty good. Races are suprizingly fun.
-The abillity to develop land and expand the city limits and population.
-Sim city style residential/comercial/office/industry supply and demand system.
-Steam Workshop support.
Cons
-----------------------
-Performance/optimization sucks atm. Easy to improve game just came out.
-Cop/enemy combatant AI sucks atm. Very predictable pathfinding/reactions.
-Guns lack weight. Better sound effects+blood particles would improve this ten fold.
-No ramps for cars means your city is flat. Adding ramps for road height changes and vehicle jumps would be awesome.
-Car damage is generic. Adding hitboxes to vehicles(engine/wheel) would drastically improve this.
-No way to fish-tail a car. Add a handbreak.
-Where is my vehicles radio? Lets get some different radio stations too!
-Lack of enemy types. Armored swat members could be cool. Maybe attack dogs.
-No melee weapons/enemies.
-No drug dealing. If he added a drug wars buying/selling system mixed with Crazy Taxi delivery system.. OHMAGaWD! GOTY!!!!!!!!!!!!!!
-Lack of voice overs. 25% of the GTA atmosphere is all of the vocal chatter. This would make this game like 1000x bettter.
-Navigating the city can be a little bit difficult. Better GPS system would be nice.
So there you have it. Most of the cons can be easily improved and the pros are pretty awesome/groundbreaking! Even if this game never gets improved its still worth a purchase because the concept and game design is so freaking slick. If the game is popular L Twigger will be forced to improve it or someone will steal his idea and make millions. Both these outcomes are in your favor ;D.

First of all, as one can see I play the game and obviously like it. It has smart dialogue, quest are diverse and the general idea of combining different attacks in combat is great. However, after all the great reviews and hype, the games lands as a little disappointment.
My biggest problems with the game are:
1.) The basic game mechanics are not explained anywhere: crafting, skills, different combat mechanics and for example selling are things to find out for yourself. There is tutorial, but it would be understatement to say its basic.
2.) The UI is a mess. Selling has to be done separetely for each character resulting switching items to one inventory to another all the time, identifying, picking locks, crafting etc. are all clunky and small things like finding out which item is good for each character is more than time consuming. Most of my game time has been spent in running from point to point, googling for how everything works or organizing inventory.
3.) Small problems with slow reactions to commands, sudden deaths, some weird logic with skills and combining them and unevenly balanced character types.
I know someone is now saying that doh, you idiot, this SHOULD be a hard game for HC gamers and indie developer cannot do everything perfectly. BUT, making a working gameplay is not diminishing the game's HC mentality or difficulty of a combat. Whether the game is hard or not, should be not be measured by how the player interacts with the game but rather how enemies react to you, how to solve a puzzle, what tactics you use etc.
For a 40€ game with a long (beta) development period, the gameplay should be solid and the level of quality of the little details in dialogue and story should also be applied to the rest of the game to make it pleasure to play. Therefore I can only recommend Divinity: original Sin to be played by person who understands he is buying a indie game with quarks. Try the game first, if possible.

A few years back I used to play a game called Ace of Spades with my friends. Two teams would spawn into the world and had to defend their flag from the other team by building a base and fighting it out. That game quickly bored me, as it had a very limited building system, no vehicles, etc.
This game seems to be exactly what I wanted Ace of Spades to be. More blocks, decals, wiring, more detailed combat, vehicles, and so on. From the bit I played, it's still VERY rough around the edges, but with constant updates and additions, I have no doubt that this game has the potential to be the next big sandbox game.
There are a few issues. A lot of it's indie-ness I find to be charming and nostalgic, but there are some things (such as chat text overlapping with HUD text and taking up a third of the screen if someone spams the chat) that really do need to be fixed.
Seeing as it just came out, it's still fairly impressive. If by the end of the year nothing has changed, however, I will have to edit my review, as it would be a waste for such a great concept to go unupdated.

I don't think I can express enough how much I absolutely love this game. I've been playing games from Sid Meier since the beginning, from the original Civilization (played on a Commodore 64) to now. And I still love them all.
At first I was unsure about the "unstacking armies" situation, but after playing I completely agree with the change. The stacked armies of the past were really OP and unrealistic, whereas the current setup makes you have to carefully move and strike with your armies.
The hexagonal map is an amazing idea. I've seen it used in pen-and-paper role-playing in the past, and enjoyed it there, so it really had me excited for this game, even before it was released.
My only complaint is the lack of modded multiplayer. That was a key PRO to Civilization IV, and I really miss it.
So overall: 9/10. Would be 10/10 if they would patch in Mod Support for Multiplayer.

I like it. It's no Diablo killer at all, but this game is for sure a pretty damn fun game.
First: The combat is really fluid. I've only tried two classes, but both speccs required some amounts of kiting, and I could do it efficiently while dishing out damage. I've even had to make tactics of hit and run, force one specific mob dead because it gives a ridiculous buff to nearby allies, bosses and elites are legit hard. Combat gets a 8/10 because some mobs in hard mode deals a bit too much damage for my liking, but it's not a big issue.
Second: The graphics are gorgeous. For a topdown ARPG, the feeling it gives me takes me back about 10 years when I was balls deep in Diablo 2, but it also looks really really good. The atmosphere is calming, but when♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan, you're not so calm anymore. Graphics get a 10/10 from me because of nostalgia.
Third: The loot system is actually pretty meh. There are some mini-bosses here and there, and I can farm them over and over again, so I tried doing that for a little while, but after like the third kill on the rock monster in the tunnels, he just stopped giving me green quality loot. It kinda kills the grind aspect that you can't kill bosses over and over, but I understand it since so I'm not in full blue gear on level 20 or some♥♥♥♥♥♥ which would kinda kill the game a little if I could, and even if I do get something green or better, it's not guaranteed to have either my main stat, or even usable to me. Which I guess promotes alting more than you would. "Oh look, I got this blue quality hat from this boss I can't use unless I'm a spellcaster, I should probably make an alt so it's not wasted." I'm neither for or against this, but I don't really like getting ♥♥♥♥ed from a good weapon because of bad RNG. There are also enchants that you can put on every slot of your equipment. Stat buffs, resistance buffs, added spells, %damage enhancing, debuff auras to enemies. I like these because it gives the game a lot of depth imo, as they have random buffs so you gotta grind specific mobtypes to get that perfect Boiling Blood, or what it's called. I give the loot system a 4/10 because I got a blue weapon with spellcaster stats on my witch hunter, who really needed a new weapon.
Fourth: The skill tree is godly. This is what makes me consider this game to be better than Diablo 3. There are a lot of spells for each class to get, combining classes to get even more choices in spells, lots of theorycrafting to consider the spells with each classes and figure out if they go well enough together to make a valid specc, passive on-hit abilities with an x% to procc, to make it a little bit more RNG. My favorite so far is Shadowblade/The Rogue class (New PC not installed this yet I can't remember the name) + Summoner thingy. I give the class system + skill tree a 10/10 because it has everything that Diablo 3 doesn't have, which it needs, and everything Diablo 2 had, but cut the unneccessary stuff, like being able to point a skill to infinity and it has just the right amount of skills and talents for me to actually have the patience to look everything through and give them thought and weigh them up.
Fifth: The story. I've never been interested in story at all when playing ARPGs until I level an alt, and last I played I had just started playing the second act/arc. I give it a ?/10 since I don't want my indifference to story to ruin the score for the game.
Overall scores:
Combat: 8/10
Graphics: 10/10
Loot: 4/10
Skill/Talent tree: 10/10
Story: ?/10
Overall score: 7/10 this game can be perfect, if it just takes the idea from Diablo 3's nonRNG loot system into the game somehow. Don't misjudge me, I love the game and I don't think Diablo 3's loot system is perfect, but it's better than this games'.

Antichamber is a very fun and innovative puzzle game that challenges the player's perception of space and requires outside-the-box thinking to make progress in the world. Don't try to map out this game in your head, because rooms and corridors connect to each other in ways that defy three-dimensional logic. But don't worry about getting lost, either, because you can freely warp to any room you've previously visited.
Many puzzles require you to stand in a certain place or look in a certain direction, and others involve manipulating small blocks with a special gun in order to form bridges or obstruct laser beams in order to open doors. Some of the block puzzles can't be solved until you find upgrades to the gun, so you need to keep those puzzles in mind and save them for later.
The perception and block puzzles are both creative and enjoyable, although the controls for the block puzzles can be finicky on occasion. Sometimes you'll move blocks forward or backward instead of up or down, and you may end up accidentally erasing a whole line of blocks that you didn't mean to. This is only a small complaint, though, and it doesn't spoil the fun of the game too much.
Overall, I'd recommend this game to anyone who enjoys challenging puzzles.

A good combination of first person shooter and tower defense game with some low brow sarcastic humor.
Pros:
+ It is not an easy game on the higher difficulty levels and in later stages of the game.  You will have to know your traps, choose your traps wisely, and get good at quickly placing them.  Be prepared to lose often and a whole lot on the Nightmare difficulty.  However, I do feel like I earned the win after I have been getting my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me on levels that I have had trouble with.
+ Sound effects, music, and the voice overs from the orcs are cute though a bit repetitive.
+ Graphics and level design are nice to look at.
+ While a single set of traps can get you through many levels, some levels have a design that occassionally forces you to rethink whatever strategy you have settled into.
Cons:
- When using the crossbow while the monsters are at point blank range, I often shoot through a monster.  Not sure if this is a bug or a feature to force you to use the melee weapon.
- While there are a variety of trap types that are unlocked as you progress they seem to fall into categories of use that make them seem like "upgrades" of older traps instead of a new unique trap.  For example I found that I pretty muched replaced the Spike Trap with the Tar Trap and the Wall Grinder replaced the other wall traps when making my trap selections.
- The Gnoll Hunter moves through barricades without breaking them first.  This might be a legit ability of that monster but with their speed and ability to poison it feels like this is less "increasing the difficulty" and more "cheating."
- Some issues with the camera that I mostly notice when backing up against a wall that has a small alcove and when standing under the Swing Mace Trap.
- Some of the spash screens that pop up while loading do have some scantily clad characters that could cause some awkwardness.

I wish there was a neutral 50/50 option. Instead, I'll have to choose one which does not fully represent my impressions.
To me this games looks more like a proof of concept, a competent experiment, rather than a full-fledged game. Its mechanics are rather simple, but it does not make the game easy. It has a full-on story, which is somewhat grim in contrast to stunning vibrant visuals. Oh, the visuals... Mirror's Edge looks gorgeous even in 2016, to me at least. Use of colour is brilliant and artists surely knew what they were doing. Music is great too, by the way, and complements the action greatly.
So why did I choose to not recommend this game?
From a parkour simulator I expected a bit more flow, a bit more uninterrupted motion. Due to level design choices it's only possible(at least it was for me me) when you replay the levels you have beaten previously, which is frankly not the thing I'd like to do. But then again, first-person platforming is not as well developed of a genre.
And lastly, combat. The game actively discourages you from engaging in unnecessary sombat, to the point of being unfair, like deleting all loose guns and removing the one you held in your hands upon loading a checkpoint(checkpoint placement could be better in places, too). But still, for some reason I used every opportunity to kill 'blues' that I could. To me it was much more fun than avoiding them, and it clearly wasn't the intended way to beat this game.
Still, if are interested in such sort of game and the pros outweigh the cons - go for it. It's a competent product overall which you might enjoy far more than I did.

{Copied from my Infinite Air Review}
Alright so by now i got Infinite Air, Steep and Snow.
So let's compare quick!
Gameplay:
IA("Realism") > Steep(Arcade) > Snow(eh...)
Variety:
Steep(+DLC, which is partially free now) > Snow(awful snowmobiles count i guess....) > IA(Only one sport, even with the editor...)
The Mountain:
Steep = IA(again the Editor is great if you have some time) > Snow
Challenge:
IA > Steep = Snow
Character customization:
Steep(lots and lots of stuff to buy and unlock) > IA > Snow(lots of stuff behind huge paywalls)
Soundtrack(subjective but important to me!):
Steep(Different playlists, good music) > IA(So/so music, no playlists.) >>>>>>> Snow(Cut the new age Downtempo crap pls...)
Replay Value:
IA(Get to grips with the editor and build your own mountain) > Steep(Compete in multiplayergroups in real-time) > Snow(Servers crash frequently, the challenges don't give enough rewards...)
So in the end, i would say:
If i want to experience something as close as possible to snowboarding, something fun and challenging, i boot up Infinite Air. The Editor is a bit clunky, but once you realize its potential you can customize a huge mountain all to your favour.
If i want to have some quick fun with a lot of variety, i boot into Steep. The arcady tricksystem is a bit of a letdown, but the mountains are amazing and more varied than those in IA, with a lot of stuff to do. Looking forward to the Olympics DLC(if it's ever up for sale...)
If i want to feel guilty forever since i payed 20 bucks for a buggy early access title back then, with a cash shop where you pay up to another 20 bucks for some clothings, enjoy horribly disfigured animations and bad music... Then i would kill myself before starting SNOW again.
oh and HEADS UP!:
Playing either Infinite Air or Steep for a while will ♥♥♥♥ up your muscle memory once you play the other game again ;)

This is one of those 'good but flawed' games that pretentious ♥♥♥♥s like me keep going on about. Mirror's Edge was one of the first games to really experiment with first-person parkour, meaning this is the grandmother of titles like Dying Light.
This game has some good points, and some bad ones.
Good point #1: Gameplay. Although this was kind of an experiment in first-person parkour, the devs really pulled it off. The movement feels satisfying, the controls have great feedback, and the levels have a great sense of flow. It's damn pleasing to experience, as you jump across gaps, clamber over fences and run across walls.
Bad point #1: Combat. A game like this could have some interesting opportunities to use the environment as a weapon, but instead every encounter reverts to poorly implemented first-person shooting. The guns are as satisfying as a wet slap to the face, there's no way to tell how much health you actually have, and the fighting only gets in the way of the freerunning. Thankfully you can often ignore enemies (or run right past them) but the parts where you are required to pick up a gun are terrible.
Good point #2: Nice aesthetic. The artists deserve a pat on the back, because the game looks beautiful, despite its age. Most of this is done through use of colour, and looking out across the entire city is simply breathtaking.
Bad point #2: Story. The plot of Mirror's Edge is generic and forgettable. It's a bog-standard conspiracy story, which never explains why the villains are after you, and which has plot twists that are both completely predictable
nonsensical. Eventually I gave up on trying to follow what was going on, and instead tried to ignore the various info-dumps.
Good point #3: Level design. A parkour game without good level design is a bad game, but this game has great level design. The positioning of walls, fences and obstacles is intuitive, with a real cohesive feel. The use of colour also helps to draw the player's eyes towards certain points, and the methods of getting from A to B are logical and enjoyable.
Is this a game worth playing? Yes.
Is it a perfect game? No.
Will you enjoy it if you play it? Probably.

I played a lot of tower defence games in Warcraft 3. But Orcs must die sets a new level in this genre.
Combining a 3rd person action game with tower defence, it created the ultimate action survival game.
Set in a fictional fantasy universe, you have to defend humanity against hordes of orcs from another dimension. For that, they built big fortress' around the portals, you have to defend.
For that, you not only have weapons and spells, but a big arsenal of traps and mechanical defend systems, from ordinary spike traps to big swinging clubs, burning pits and big brutal mechanical grinders.
Every level is made of one or several floors with one or several directions the enemys can spawn. You have to defend the rifts to the normal world, so the orcs dont conquer it.
Using the right collection of traps, wisly using your abilitys and being a tactical genius desides about victory and defeat. The game doesnt take you lightly. With the first levels being easily understandable and mostly fast to solve, some maps are difficult beyond everything encountered before. Some maps need tricks you have to find out all by yourself, some just need you to be fast like sonic, defending two rifts at once.
Having a small storyline, mostly living from comedy, the campaign is really fun to play. After one playthrough you unlock another difficulty, that is a serious challenge (and was a real pain for me).
It isnt a real game for casual players, but a good game, for tacticans, that not only want to think but slay their way through their enemys.

I've played every Saints Row since the first and all of the additional DLC so you could say I'm a fan of the series. So imagine my disappointment when I load up the "Inauguration Station" to find the same graphic style, same clothing/hair options, and more of the same. It completely turned me off to the game and I hadn't given it a second glance until it recently dropped in price for the weekend.
Boy was I wrong. Rather than being a rehash of the third game, this iteration takes the series in a completely new direction and adds super powers to the game. What many people have failed to mention (including the actual game page) is that this is a hyper-realized world that constantly breaks the fourth wall without holding back. This game at the core is similar to the previous games, but it's definitely a unique contender on it's own.
This game has made me laugh time and time again as well as blow my head off with witty reference one after the other. The game is very streamlined and anything you want to do in the game can be done within seconds. Wanna play with a friend? Hot Seat Co-Op is available and very functional. Want to hop in a mech and wreak havoc on the city? Head over to the Mech Mayhem mini-game. This game has so much available that it's easy to forget that this was originally an expansion for the third game.
So while you're still in the same city, with the same clothes, hairstyles, and most customization options for that matter, the game still shines as a "have fun no matter what" title that I've rarely seen before. You'll quickly stop picking at the graphics and driving physics once you realize you can shoot people with rubber band guns while flying around naked with pearlescent green skin. Maybe you want to just drive around and customize cars? Try to solve jumping puzzles, play the extremely well-written story, or see how long you and a friend can volley a car back and forth to one another.

Banner Saga is a unique approach to a primarily story driven game. You make tons of decisions that can end up rewarding you or punishing you and often in ways that may seem mundane decisions or are obviously important. What will grip you the most from beginning to end is the beauty of the cartoon-like graphics.
Combat is fairly simple to pick up on, though definitely has room to be improved. You take turns in a way that logically deteriorates: one of your characters go, then one of the enemy's. Where that breaks down is you can be punished when you have more characters in the arena - if I have 6 and the enemy is down to 2, those 2 will go over and over again, while I have to wait 4 extra moves before I get to a specific 2 of my 6 characters again. Then when you get them down to their last character you enter "pillage" mode where all your characters go and then they go - I believe this was probably added to balance things, but fell short. It falls short primarily in that this can be a huge disantage in some battles causing one of your heros to fall in battle, which can take days for them to heal from (normal mode+). In addition, the battles do get a bit repetitive and special abilities are often not needed or very "special."
Overall it was a creative spectical full of rich sounds, music, characters, storytelling, lore, and beautifully done landscapes and scenery. It's exciting to see a game like this come out and I hope it inspires the creators (or others) to mimic this style - only with a few combat improvements.

Released this week on steam for $9.99 (or $29.99 for a four-pack if you happen to have four friends to play with) is a “2.5D sidescroller” smash’em up: Final Exam from Mighty Rocket Studio. A slick looking online multiplayer supported smash ‘em up to make the tried and true transition from Xbox Live and Playstation Network onto Valve’s Steam.
So four characters that look like they should be featured in a ‘where are they now?’ of The Breakfast Club are on their way to a High School Alumni Party. The Jocky Football guy, artsy chick, nerdy boy, and token minority (not sure which, but his skin is darker than the others) happen to be adequately trained with martial arts, explosives, and the use of several types of firearms. Since this is not a game about awkward realization that everyone else in high school has moved on with their lives and become adults instead of trying to relive their glory days into their late 20′s their car runs into a hoard of monsters, you grab a pistol and baseball bat with nails driven into it, and start a swinging.
Each character specializes on a few key skills, Jock is the big melee bruiser, nerd is the tank / explosives expert, Artsy chick is good with firearms and melee, while token guy is good at guns and explosives. Gameplay is smooth and well polished. If you’ve played any 2d style smash ‘em up since River City Ransom you know how this all works (even down to enemies dropping food, ammo, and grenades for some reason when they die). Go from objective to objective smashing things as you go. It’s certainly done well with beautiful polished levels sporting impressive backdrops along the way. If anything the levels are TOO well detailed as some areas can have quite a bit of clutter in the background but overall the game does a great job of offering you plenty of eye candy and a never ending stream of monsters to smash.
As you progress through the game you earn skill points to unlock special moves and such as well as character points to add to your character’s abilities. Basically it improves damage dealt and how much hp you have. It’s an interesting RPG element designed specifically to add longevity to a rather simple and straight forward smashing game. While it certainly is nice to make your character more powerful and makes you want to scour every level for every collectable and weapon to get all the unlocks, the abilities are actually counter-productive to their longevity cause. See with all the new weapons you find and new abilities and stats you get your character becomes too badass and frankly the combat starts to get too repetitive and dull.
The game is broken up into several missions at the end of which you are rewarded for how well you completed it. More points means more skill points. I think though the missions are just a bit too long as some of them really start to wear on me and often times I was just hoping it would hurry up and end. Also the objectives in each mission are pretty much typical copy and paste stuff that feels rather dull and uninspired. After having to fetch crap (be it gas cans, weapons, machine parts, lab assistants, or children) every single mission you get rather tired of it after a while. And while the game has a pretty cool and perhaps a little edgy (and chuckle worthy) style the story is just so inanely pointless I have no investment in it or the characters to care enough to keep playing.
I was ready to praise Final Exam, for the first few hours I played it was fun, fast, furious, and a fresh break from the usual slow paced games I play. Online was likewise even more fun and a great fast paced romp with random strangers. But after the sixth mission I just hit a wall and suddenly I didn’t care anymore. I’ve killed a thousands of these dang monsters, only have a faint idea why and really don’t care if I save the day or not. Just about every mute NPC that I’ve come across in my journey who helped me ended up dying in some kinda humorous way (usually squashed by a mini-boss) and I was just tired of the game.
This game made me seriously consider just how long should a game keep me entertained? Obviously it should do so at least from beginning to end, which sadly Final Exam fails for me. But even if it did keep you satisfied to the end you might replay the game again just to get all the unlocks. But then what? Once you’ve filled out all the skill and ability trees there’s really little to do unless you’re the kind of person who wants to get their name up on a high score list. This is clearly a throw-away game at best that you play through once or twice maybe with a couple friends and then forget it ever existed. It’s almost sad really, as the developers did a great job of making a crisp clean and pretty fighting game. But repetitive boring mission objectives that have been used a million times in MMO grinds (go here, collect, bring back. Go here, escort, bring back. Go here, kill, kill, kill, kill, keep killing, and kill some more.) ruined an excellent fighting game. Combined with a completely uninteresting generic carbon copy story that gives me absolutely no connection or reason to keep going and we have a game that really falls up short.
If you like smash’em up games I might suggest giving it a try but don’t expect anything life changing.

What with the excellent art, cool theme, interesting story and, initially, quite tight and interesting combat, I was very excited about this game. This only served to make my disappointment all the more crushing when I discovered that, whilst superficially polished, the rest of the game is a mess. Here begins the list of insanely frustrating shortcomings.
The two early-game parties are ridiculously disparate in power level and difficulty, meaning that I spent the first half of the game alternately getting massacred when using puny human party and walking through waves of ineffectual mooks when using overpowered varl (big smashy giants). The only effect of failure in combat is no XP gain at the end: you don't reload from a previous save, just keep going (with negligible effect on plot and none on gameplay), meaning that once you start loosing encounters you will continue to loose them. No, there's no way of grinding up a few levels if you're falling behind. Although this loss-streak changed once the human and varl parties united and the varl took charge, massacring every enemy for the rest of the game up to the final boss while the puny humans looked on in awe. By the bye, using the same currency (Renown/XP) for levelling up and for buying  supplies was intensely frustrating, and meant that for most of the game I had to choose between starving and levelling up. At the time, I assumed that not starving to death was more important that self-improvement, but how wrong I was! Starving simply reduces the size of your caravan, and after about half way through the game, it's completely irrelevant how many of your caravan mooks survive. On the other hand, even if there are literally zero people surviving in your caravan, your party will be just fine, and overlevelled to boot! Intuitive!
Thus, in the end, it turned out that despite plowing through every encounter in the last third of the game using varl, I was actually massively underlevelled for the final encounter, which demanded that I use two pathetic humans, one of whom I had not used the entire game on the basis of her class ability being complete rubbish, and who was thus level one. Further, it turns out that, counter to every other encounter in the game, the final boss fight isn't simply an all-out massacre, but an engagement where you have to bypass large numbers of mooks to focus down a brutal boss. Turns out, 4-square-occupying varl are really really bad at moving past tightly packed front lines of minions, and thus almost completely useless in the boss fight. That didn't stop me almost killing the boss: I had it down to about 2 armor and 3 HP when Miss Uselessly Underleveled unleashed her Underpowered Arrow Of Boss Slaying. "Well," I thought, "that was pretty tough, but I'm through now. That arrow will hit, I'll smash the remaining 3HP off, and we're golden.". Little did I know that when the boss gets hit by the silver arrow of boss slaying, he is not, in fact, slain. But rampages through your lines, grabs the puny arrow shooter, murders her (what a loss, I know), and then restarts the combat. At full health. Apparently it's actually an arrow of health restoring or some♥♥♥♥♥♥ But don't worry, you get your characters back. Mostly! I mean, arrow-shooter is dead, so you're one man down, and the ones that died fighting predviously are back but now wounded, therefore at about two thirds strength. And there are now even more random mooks in the fight, some of which are actually competent. Becasue why not.
I didn't finish the boss fight, mostly on the basis that I didn't want to replay the game from scratch so that I could laboriously level up my puny humans this time. I was brutally disappointed with this game. It was so promising, and it let me down on almost every level. Almost certainly the worst 20€ I have spent in the past several years. Thumbs firmly down.

TL;DR - This game in my opinion is easily the #1 in its genre and there is very little reason to skip it. Offers fun gameplay and combat with good variety.
If you want an open-world zombie ''survival'' game, this one is the best in the market. Hell, even if you just want a game that contains zombies, this is the best one you'll find.
Now, i put ''survival'' in quotations (or whatever its called) because you collect things around the world to craft bombs, weapons, med kits and all that. It's not entirely survival and if anyone claims so, i would disagree. It is sort of post-apocalyptic which makes it look survival, but there is no nutritional crisis, where you'd have to go look for food before you starve, so in my opinion its not a survival game.
The game is well-ported in my opinion, i have a pretty bad PC and can run it quite fine, and the graphics are quite pleasant too (you need to know what settings to tune down though).
What can be annoying for some here is that all weapons are degradable and will be destroyed to uselessness as you use them. You can repair them, but only for a fixed amount of times. What's good with this system however, is that it keeps your weapon variety going and keeps the game interesting in combat to a slight degree (This becomes less of a struggle as the game goes when you can obtain really good stuff too easily).
The zombies are really braindead, but you have some empowered ones that can be pretty tough at times. At night time, you'll have some extremely hard monsters to deal with and its almost never recommended to be out at night unless you want a huge adrenaline rush because it can be insanely hard, sometimes scary. In a nutshell they're really fun to fight.
Story has some plot to it but i assume its nothing special, since people never take stories in open world games seriously as far as i know, but i enjoyed the story. It was nice to follow it along, and it made you feel pretty important, though you're more like just a running slave.
The side-activities arent as interesting but if you want to punch more zombies, they're quite nice. Some involve parkour and gathering aswell.
This game supports lots of mods, and there is even custom games where people create their own maps. As soon as we get more content in on this, this could be tons of fun with others or just alone. I'd say this the core ''end'' game you'll be spending your time with after you complete the story, unless you wanna mess around some more over there.

You're going to be making decisions for a lot of people and some of them are going to get hurt.

I'm really, really looking forward to what the next chapter will bring.

A non-biased quick look @ the game:
A cool twin stick shooter to rival classics like Geometry Wars.  Tachyon Project is a dual stick shooter heavily inspired by classic shoot'em ups. We’ve combined many unique enemy types, a large variety of weapons and power-ups with innovative gameplay to ensure a long lasting challenge and discovery at every new level.
In Tachyon Project you take control of Ada, a software program that has taken conscience and that was designed to hack into the most secure servers on Earth. After some rather mysterious events, Ada is thrown out of the test server where it was living and out into the Internet, but when she tries to go back there she finds she's unable to. She'll then start a journey to uncover the truth behind what happened to her creators, which she considers her parents. In the process she'll find out that things were a bit more complex than she initially thought.
The game provides an interesting story mode where you go unlocking new weapons, secondary weapons and perks as you progress and uncover the story behind Ada's creation. But you can also play on challenges that present you with unending hordes of enemies to try for the best score and compete in leaderboards. You can play these challenges either alone or with friends in up to 4 player local multiplayer co-operative games.
Tachyon Project also brings new ideas to the table, presenting a new stealth mode in some levels where you have to pick carefully when to shoot to avoid being discovered too early and keep yourself disguised. - Highly Recommended!

My Quick Look of Tachyon Project:
Essentially, it's a Geometry Wars-like.  The scoring method is inversed.  So instead of shooting things to increase your score and picking up their gems to increase your multiplier, you shoot things to increase your multiplier and pick up gems to increase your score.
I kind of prefer the way scoring is handled in vanilla Geometry Wars, but this way is completely valid.
The parts that expand on the Geometry Wars formula is with the ship's configuration.  You need to advance in the game to unlock new weapons and augments, but essentially you can create a custom loadout for your ship, which is also pleasantly necessary as the game progresses (instead of just being a thing you can do with no purpose).
For instance, instead of your standard mini-spread gun pattern, you can opt for a more narrow but faster shot, like a machine gun.  Or you can go even tighter and with a higher frequency and have a laser.
Vanilla Geometry Wars gives you Bombs, Tachyon Project gives you bombs as well.  But they aren't level destroyers, they just do a spread of damage.  It doesn't necessarily have to kill your enemies, just injure them.  Or you could opt to do one set of bombs and one set of proximity mines, or freezing bombs.
Additionally, you get two augments to complete your loadout.  Augments such as fire faster, do more damage per shot, your ship goes faster, etc.
The last thing I want to mention is the timer.  The timer has two mechanics attached to it.  One is that it's your health.  You can gain health/time by defeating enemies.  The second is your bombs/secondary weapons use 1 second per use (each secondary weapon has a cooldown, so you can't just spam it forcing yourself to die.)
Bottom line: Tachyon Project is a well done Geometry Wars clone, mechanics-wise.  The visuals and sound are not up to par though.

Disclosure – I was given a review copy by Eclipse Games.
Tachyon Project is a dual-stick shooter with many different enemy types as well as many ship upgrades.
Graphics
The graphics are very colorful and vibrant. Each enemy type has a distinct look. There are various particle effects when you fire your ship’s weapons and when when enemies explode. The backgrounds and menus also look great.
Audio
The sound is quite good. The ship and enemies and your weapons have different sounds depending on what you’re using. Also the music can be quite relaxing. The music ramps up during the more intense parts of the game. The electronic music soundtrack fits well with the game and sounds great.
Gameplay
Tachyon project is a very solid dual-stick shooter. The game features full controller support and the controls are very responsive. The game is also playable using a keyboard and mouse but I would recommend using a controller. I played using a wired Xbox 360 controller. The game is split into two modes, a story mode and a challenge mode. In story mode you complete waves in each chapter resulting in a final wave. The waves in each chapter leading up to the final introduce new enemies. Each wave has a goal that must be achieved before moving on. These goals range from defeating a certain amount of a particular enemy type to surviving for a set amount of time. There are also cut-scenes in the game featuring a graphic novel feel with very good artwork.
Throughout the game you can unlock different upgrades for your ship. These include new weapons, increased speed, increased health and so on. I like that mines are one of the possible upgrades. The proximity mine is especially fun to use. Drop one near a large group of enemies to wipe out a ton of them with one attack.
The challenge mode is fun as well. These challenges include a limitless mode where you try to survive for as long as possible, a stealth mode as well as a timed challenge. Online leaderboards are also included.
Overall
Overall Tachyon is a very solid and competently made dual-stick shooter. Whether you want to play a quick challenge or dive into the story there is something here for everyone. The game works for both short and extended gaming sessions. A great addition to the dual-stick genre.

This is one of my favorite games tbh. I beat it on my phone twice, then saw it was on steam and immediately scooped it up and I'm well into my third playthrough. My only wish is that the PC version took advantage of the platform and added some improvements.

Another I'd like is very minor, I'd like it if windows such as your character screens were closeable by just clicking outside the window, instead of needing to click the x. Or at least move the x to the top right instead of bottom left, it only makes sense down there on a phone game for ease of clicking, on PC it's just needlessly different.

Combt is difficult, and to succeed you'll need to learn how to control the battlefield with poison ooze, electrified water (or blood, if you or enemies have been bleeding), or firey embers. Each element interacts with the others, which allows for sweet combos—But your enemies have the same tools as you do and they don't make your job any easier.
The co-op role-playing is also excellent. You can either play with a friend, in which case each of you controls one of the protagonists, or solo. Will you agree with each other, or will you need to turn to rock-paper-scissors (assissted by your charisma) to resolve your differences? Solo play is also perfectly viable, though keeping two different characters in your head at the same time can be dizzying when you end up role-playing both sides of the conversation.

"Baldur's Gate 3, But Only If You Give It A Lobotomy First"
Please note: I play offline. I actually have 28+ hours of play time under my belt.
This game is very hard for me to recommend, which is why I'm not going to do that. It fails my most basic of tests, "Would I recommend this over a long line of other games?" No, I would not. Play Divine Divinity, play Beyond Divinity, Might and Magic series, Final Fantasy series, Fallout 1 and 2, and etc. The reasons it fails this simple test is because it doesn't truly engage the audience on a storytelling level and the RPG aspects are, well, sub-par. Many other games offer a better quality product than this game *cough* Baldur's Gate *cough* and don't skimp where it counts.
Plenty of other reviews already go through most of the pros of the game,* so I won't do that. I'm going to focus on the cons. Please realize I do enjoy this game, it just isn't something I'd recommend wasting 15+ dollars on (note the actual price tag of the game).
The first item that really destroys this game is the 'trait' system. While this was very innovative and intelligent the implementation has broken single player. The traits award certain skill bonuses, which means that specializing the main characters, especially along trait lines means constant infighting. This, in turn, breaks immersion. The rock-paper-scissors mini game does not help with this. While a neat thought (maybe for multiplayer) it just breaks immersion for single player so completely that we'd be better off without it in the first place. An easy fix would just to break away from the binary system in dialogue and offer multiple dialogue options, such that you can get an altruistic materialist agreeing with a egotistical spiritualist. This could make character interaction and quest rewards more interesting, and giving us ways to opt out of pointless (self)bickering.
The second item which makes this game unrecommendable for me is the plot and setting. We are supposedly in a city besieged (for all intents and purposes) by the undead and the orcs. My question to you is this: Where the f*** are the dead? Small groups lay past the city gates, though no real 'threat' is presented to make me think that the Legion, a standing military, should have had this much trouble for 2 years (in fact, why are they just now getting around to scouting out the other guy)? This coupled, with the fact that there is only one man starving in this whole city . . . You know what, Larian? Just go back and look at Divine Divinity. You did the siege right there.
Though, of course, I'm assuming the Larian writing team has that same spark of talent, which isn't obvious in this product. After the introduction to the Homestead, Zixzax, and the weaver I couldn't help but think that it was something on par with fourth grade writing^. 1) The homestead needs foreshadowing and 2) Just cut the weaver's whole line of text. Her text, along with the some of the other dialogue between the main characters just felt like . . . Insincere flattery. It made me feel like I was watching a porno (without the porn). This on top of the linear progression of what should be multilinear quest lines is just sad.
And then there is balance. Too much power in the warrior and mage skill-types, while the rogue and ranger just felt horribly under powered. Additionally, a lot of repetition in the magical schools. Bring all the elemental-type magical abilities under one skill and do a lot of cutting. Then add in some more unique spells that allow for more interesting environmental interactions. I really feel like the focus of magic in this game should have been about taking advantage of the terrain and controlling the flow of the battle, with a degree of focus for rogues being to extend environmental surfaces (like oil) instead of investing that into the mage class as well. Meanwhile rangers could act more as snipers.
And yes, it is just a game, but games are narratives. They're stories. Part of the reason some of us play them is because of the way all these elements fit together. You shouldn't have to 'settle' to pay 40 dollars on a product that seems half-a**ed.
Again, if you're looking at (or like) this product I do heavily recommend looking into the Baldur's Gate series, the Icewind Dale series, Might and Magic 1-8, Divine Divinity, Beyond Divinity, and an ungodly number of other games.

One of the best city builder games of all time. 100+ hours worth of gameplay, the tone is more serious than Zeus by comparison.
Pros:
- Detailed gameplay, with potential to build massive, hugely developed cities
- Probably the Sierra city builder with the most intricate cities to build, and the longest levels
- Huge amount of voice acting, much of which provides levity during long levels
- Makes great use of its setting, with gameplay focused on utilising the Nile, benefits of Egyptian gods, and building a city with resources such as papyrus, linen and figs, and the opportunity to create world famous Egyptian monuments such as the Pyramids of Giza and Sphinx.
- Expansion pack adds further missions and gameplay additions, and variety.
Cons:
- Some features of gameplay not as polished as in later Impressions Games titles - trying to navigate walkers and ensure industry access to workflow is a bit unrefined
- Gameplay can be a little formulaic - once you figure out how to construct a working city, you will follow similar formulas each time with only minor variations
- At times the game can seem a little unfair, especially on higher difficulties. Compared to later Sierra games, the inability to request goods from other cities or conquer them when they can do the same to you can be a little grating.
- Features from expansion are not present at all in base game - while playing Pharaoh, Cleopatra may as well not exist.
Overall, I would strongly recommend this game to fans of strategy games and the ancient world alike. Pharaoh is a deep and varied game, with a fascinating setting Impressions Games makes good use of.

TLDR: It has significantly dumbed down the concept, but does deliver it in a package that is still enjoyable and conveys a strong atmosphere. The general gameplay, story and ending are excellent. I wouldn't pay full price. Get it on a 50% off offer or better.
The Good
- A fluid, well designed aesthetic.
- The base design concept is a nice spin off the classic.
- The story is well written and the ending is very satisfying, while admittedly a little cliche.
- General gameplay is enjoyable and scales well. Despite the simplification, it doesn't get old quickly.
- Combat mechanics and the UI are well done.
The Bad
- No sign of the classic base defense missions that UFO/XCOM series have had almost uniformly.
- Little depth in equipment. Soldiers start with a stock 'assault rifle', 'shotgun' etc rather than varying options (eg MP5, G36, AK47 and so on) allowing variance between fire rate, penetration, clip size etc like featured strongly in games like UFO: Aftermath. This leads to a big part of the 'dumbed down' feeling.
- No control over soldier speciality. A unit you developed with a great marksmen ability might suddenly get shunted into a support role, when you desperately wanted her for an elite sniper. You can end up with a dozen assault class but very few/none of the other classes.
- Little customisation for soldiers. You pick between fairly limited appearance options and most voices are basically american accents. Try getting used to that with soldiers meant to be from China, Russia etc.
- It feels like the base game was kept dumbed down to allow them to sell DLC. While a first playthrough is enjoyable, you'll want the DLC to render replays worthwhile.

This will be the first half of our review for the Orcs Must Die! series. This is the review for the first game, the overall score of which will be averaged with the overall score of Orcs Must Die! 2 to give us our final score for the series as a whole. So far, it’s prospects of a solid score are looking fantastic. Let us begin.
I – Story [7/10]
Orcs Must Die! is a third-person tower defense game from Robot Entertainment, in which, the player assumes the role of the Hero; an otherwise unnamed character and the last living member of the Order. The Order is an ancient and powerful guild of War Mages who have taken it upon themselves to guard Rifts (magical portals that connect the human world and the “Dead World” which also provide a source of magic throughout both worlds.)
The Dead World is home to a faction known as “The Mob” and is comprised of various creatures such as gnolls, ogres, and (of course) orcs. The Mob is lead by a former student of the Order known as the Sorceress. During the course of the game, the Hero is fighting to keep the Mob at bay despite their every increasing aggression and frequency of attacks.
Spoiler Alert: In the end, the Hero steps through a Rift and closes it forever by means of a spell. Although he saves the human world from destruction at the hands of the Sorceress and her limitless legions, he also destroys the source of magic for both worlds. The human world, now dependent upon magic, begins to steadily deteriorate. The Sorceress, stripped of her powers, is trapped in the Dead World with a gratuitous amount of angry monsters.
The of OMD! should be thematically familiar to the vast majority of gamers, moviegoers, and readers alike. It is tried and true and it worked wonderfully for the game. That being said, it has still be done before.
II – UI [9/10]
The user interface was great. It was simple, the minimap worked like a charm, and I kept pressing the “ready” button long before I was actually ready. (Please note that that was not the game’s fault, it was all mine. It felt necessary to talk about it though.) In-game HUD was very user friendly and all of my stats/currently equipped traps (towers) and equipment were easy to refer to. However, the menus seemed to feel a bit clunky. Maybe it was just me, but I felt that they could have used a little tweaking.
III – Gameplay [10/10]
As I mentioned in a previous article, I wasn’t always a fan of tower defense games. In most cases, I’m still not crazy about them. But, every now and then, one comes along that attaches itself to my heart like a parasite and sticks with me for the long haul. Orcs Must Die! is one of those special little parasites.
The vast majority of the maps are incredible free form as far as defensive strategies go. The game starts you off with fairly easy maps and they continually increase in complexity as you hack and slash your way through the campaign. As someone who is (in general) not very good with strategy, I weirdly loved this. It gave me a good chance to brush up on my defense skills and figure out what needs to be where so I’m not eyeball deep in orcs in a few minutes. Should I build outward or inward? Do I need to worry about aerial a-holes or not? Loved it.
As far as using your character in combat, the third-person perspective was implemented expertly. A reticle is clearly displayed (and not easily lost) so that I can wade straight into the action if need be or snipe fools out from afar. Primary and secondary weapon functions are easily used and easily mastered. Movement is very fluid and the character’s sprint speed is comfortable fast.
IV – Content [10/10]
Orcs Must Die! has a lot of content, especially for a tower defense game. The core game has 24 maps, 6 weapons, 19 traps and minions (in total), and 11 different enemy types. Not only this, but any upgrades you purchase for weapons, traps, etc. are permanent and stay with you throughout the entire game. This is fantastic, in case you were wondering.
There are two different DLCs for OMD! (Artifacts of Power and Lost Adventures) and both add their fair share of extra content as well. Really though, if you end up purchasing this game, you’ll probably end up picking up the DLC at some pint as well because you’re going to want more.
V – Visual [10/10]
Every last graphical detail of Orcs Must Die! is enchanting. Character and enemy models are very well done and have a charming, cartoon-esque quality to them. The environments are wonderful and every map has something new for you to ogle in your downtime. When you’re not setting traps or slaying orcs, it’s really worth it to take a few minutes to just explore your surroundings.
VI – Audio [10/10]
Seldom has a game had a more fitting soundtrack than Orcs Must Die! does. Seriously though, just phenomenal. You can annihilate thousands and tens of thousands to this epic score and never grow tired of it. That goes for the annihilation too. It has a very metal feel to it on the whole and I’m sure that War Mages the world over could happily crush skulls to it all day long.
On top of the score, the voice acting is absolutely superb. The Hero is hilarious and you’ll find yourself laughing at his one-liners and his celebratory dance moves map after map.
VII – Overall [9.3/10]
Overall, Orcs Must Die! is a great game and a true testament of what a tower defense game should be, in my opinion.

When this first came out I was excited to play it, me having played the previous Walking Dead games, and I'd say that I personally enjoyed this game, although some people seem to not like it.

All in all, this is a fun game from TTG and I rate it a 8/10.

Star Wars Battlefront II is the sequel to the highly successfull Star Wars Battlefront developed by Pandemic Studios and released in 2004. While the concept is similar to DICE's Battlefield series, the gameplay is more casual and thus, less skill-based, with a lot of emphasis on Third-person shooting (it can be played on First-person) and rolling to avoid enemy fire and proyectiles. Due to the game being released after Episode III came out, the game's content is mostly based from that movie in terms of new maps and story with a clear lack of EU-based maps unlike Battlefront I which can be disappointing.
A new addition to the game is Space Battle in which players spawn in their respective side's commands ship and must use fighters, bombers and transports to rack up points by destroying enemy fighter and/or destroying the opposite side's command ship's appendages.
Unfortunately, the game have optimization issues that may cause crashes or permanent Framerate drops on newer computers, especially on Windows 7.
Pros
> Star Wars as its finests.
> Both Third and First person mode.
> Galactic Conquest, a good time killer.
> Instant Action: A very customizable botmatch with several gamemodes.
> Very moddeable, allowing for new community-made maps and conversions.
Cons
> Annoying and/or stupid AI from the computer-controlled units.
> The game doesn't run smoothly as Battlefront I
> The new maps feel less creative than Battlefront I
> Galactic Conquest lacks some needed depth to make it less stale.

This is one of those 'good but flawed' games that pretentious ♥♥♥♥s like me keep going on about. Mirror's Edge was one of the first games to really experiment with first-person parkour, meaning this is the grandmother of titles like Dying Light.
This game has some good points, and some bad ones.
Good point #1: Gameplay. Although this was kind of an experiment in first-person parkour, the devs really pulled it off. The movement feels satisfying, the controls have great feedback, and the levels have a great sense of flow. It's damn pleasing to experience, as you jump across gaps, clamber over fences and run across walls.
Bad point #1: Combat. A game like this could have some interesting opportunities to use the environment as a weapon, but instead every encounter reverts to poorly implemented first-person shooting. The guns are as satisfying as a wet slap to the face, there's no way to tell how much health you actually have, and the fighting only gets in the way of the freerunning. Thankfully you can often ignore enemies (or run right past them) but the parts where you are required to pick up a gun are terrible.
Good point #2: Nice aesthetic. The artists deserve a pat on the back, because the game looks beautiful, despite its age. Most of this is done through use of colour, and looking out across the entire city is simply breathtaking.
Bad point #2: Story. The plot of Mirror's Edge is generic and forgettable. It's a bog-standard conspiracy story, which never explains why the villains are after you, and which has plot twists that are both completely predictable
nonsensical. Eventually I gave up on trying to follow what was going on, and instead tried to ignore the various info-dumps.
Good point #3: Level design. A parkour game without good level design is a bad game, but this game has great level design. The positioning of walls, fences and obstacles is intuitive, with a real cohesive feel. The use of colour also helps to draw the player's eyes towards certain points, and the methods of getting from A to B are logical and enjoyable.
Is this a game worth playing? Yes.
Is it a perfect game? No.
Will you enjoy it if you play it? Probably.
This is a game that I think really needs a sequel (and we'll be getting one soon), because there is actually some real gold in here, and it would be worth going in to try and make it shinier. Maybe they can also wash off the♥♥♥♥♥♥while they're at it.

Normally twin stick shooters aren't really my thing. I've gotten decently into a few of them (most notably Beat Hazard), but I'm not the sort of person who can top leaderboards, and twin sticks are usually all about efficiently racking up the best possible score. I suppose you could say I'm on friendly terms with the devs though, so when they (full disclosure here) gave me a key for the game to test something for them I decided I'd put the game through its paces and let them and you all know what I thought about it.
The first thing that stuck out to me was how well-designed the enemies are. A lot of twin stick shooters end up feeling the same to me because the enemies are usually few and the strategies to handle them are similar. With this game, however, they constantly throw new enemies at you, some building on old concepts and some introducing radically new approaches. I'm far from an expert on the genre, but I've played my fair share of these games and I've run into some particularly novel enemy behaviors I've never seen combined in quite the same way before. One of the early types that stood out to me was the Bull, a large ship that takes a few seconds to lock on before charging at you in a straight line, exploding if it hits a wall. Depending on the situation you might want to shoot it down, get in close and use the Explosion ability to make shooting it down faster, or just avoid it entirely and let it crash into the wall. Each enemy is usually handled differently, and the way they constantly evolve enemy variety and group up enemies in different combinations keeps your head constantly in the game without leaving a second to get bored.
One of the cooler curveballs the game throws at you is the stealth servers. There's an enemy type that will track your movements so long as you fire, and will go to your last known location when you cease firing. They start you with this one basic element, then start adding enemies that can reveal your position if you get close, or be able to come after you once enough time has passed, similarly to a Bull. Mixing in normal enemy types allows for even more possibilities. Running around while the whole world is coming down on your head, finding an escape and letting all the enemies gather around your last position, then gunning them down as they whirl back on you is incredibly satisfying.
With all that said though, the game's certainly not perfect. For example, in Level 4 you're thrown against a boss that more-or-less requires one specific loadout. I threw my face into its fist a few dozen times before I gave up, quit out, changed my equipment and went through the whole level again. The boss features one to three (they get added as you hurt it) spinning invulnerable rings with holes to shoot through. I went into the stage with the starting loadout, but the regular gun shoots too wide to be useful against the small holes (I switched to the more focused Machine Gun), the ship moves too slowly to get around the boss sometimes (switched both perks to ship speed), and the timing to get a shot through all three barriers by the end  is extremely tight (I switched to the Freezing Bomb to hold it in place). With the loadout tailored to the boss I was able to deal with it with much less frustration.
I also found that I don't really like most of the equipment the game has to offer and usually stick with the most basic options. For the main gun especially the standard weapon felt the most effective. The others seem to offer a better risk:reward ratio and higher skill ceiling, but (in my hands at least) they don't feel as potent, nor have the same kind of variety the enemies do. The machine gun and missiles, for example, seem to be practically the same thing.
In a lot of ways I feel Tachyon Project is similar to Super Toy Cars, the dev's previous game. It had some rough edges,
. In the case of Super Toy Cars, they absolutely nailed handling, making the driving experience fun and engaging. Here we see much the same thing: there's a strong focus on the mechanics, in making sure that every single second of gameplay keeps the player hooked. There's a story, but honestly it's entirely skippable (both figuratively and literally). The art is passable, does its job and little beyond that. Music's okay too, though nothing really spectacular. But what really sells this game, and why you should play it, is because it's just
. I've never played a twin stick shooter that felt more active and alive than this one.
If you like south park and turn based rpgs, you'll like this game.
