If you can look past the console influence (like the UI, menus, it's so awful) and the derivative, contrived leveling/unlock/progression/crafting/objective type system, this is actually a pretty good game. It's better than I expected really. I overlooked this one when it first came out, read a few reviews and watched a few videos and thought it was probably not worth getting. I mean c'mon, it's zombies, another zombie game?
I finally broke down and got it on sale and you know what, it's actually pretty good. The leveling/unlocking/progression/crafting/objective system is a blast really. You have three different skill trees you level up in depending on how you play and what you do: Survivor is mostly centered around loot, crafting, shops, and environmental awareness type abilities. Agility is centered around running, jumping, climbing, and dodging, with a few awesome acrobatic moves you can pull off during combat. My favorite is the flying Kirk kick, it never gets old! And then Strength, which influences your use of weapons, unlocking powerful swings and special moves using different types of weapons.
The crafting is fun too, letting you combine different types of items to upgrade weapons. Weapon durability is still an issue, like in Dead Island, and you can only repair a weapon so many times before it's broken forever. Depending on the base quality of a weapon, you can usually repair it 2-5 times before it's unusable. But you can unlock different perks that make weapons last longer or adding a chance that repairs won't consume one of the weapon's repair slots. You can also get upgrades that make a weapon more durable or add even more repair slots. There are other fun items too like grenades, molotov cocktails, ninja stars, throwing knives, flares, UV lights, etc. You can also craft boosts, basically buff potions.
Co-op is fun, if you can look past the concept that everyone playing is playing the same character. Cut scenes are done first person and your camera is locked, so you can't see your co-op partners. There's also no clipping for other players so you don't have to worry about people taking up doorways or standing on ledges or walls you need to get to.
The climbing/parkour mechanics are intuitive and fun. It works a lot like Assassin's Creed or the Batman games, except it's all first person. It gets a little dizzying sometimes, the camera bobs a lot and you will only grab ledges you're aiming at. There's a FOV slider which helps, but I still wish this game had a 3rd person option. It's down to taste really but personally I prefer 3rd person. There's a little character customization in the different outfits you can choose but they only show up for other players, or sometimes if you look down you can see your arms or feet.
The story is a little meh, but that goes for almost any open world game. The mechanics and gameplay more than make up for it. The game reminds me a lot of Far Cry 3, and as mentioned before Batman and Asassin's Creed, but it's unique enough you're not going to be rolling your eyes about playing yet another re-skinned AAA game. The quests and side missions are interesting and varied, although sometimes you'll notice a few patterns, just like any other game. As you progress you start seeing more and different types of enemies. The standard zombies eventually cease to become much of a challenge but now you're seeing more ferals, spitters, ones that explode, and things like that.
It's really disgusting. That's probably my biggest complaint, it's SO gross. I don't like the zombie genre because I'm grossed out easily, and this game wallows in it. Guts, gibs, blood, severed torsos and limbs, flies, vomit, exposed organs, it's all there in full HD with squelchy sound effects. At least your character never throws up or complains about the smell but you know if it was real life a normal person would barely be able to function. If you've ever had to move or bury a dead dog that's been decomposing for a while you know it's a huge undertaking just getting past the smell.
People complaining about performance issues, yes, it does take some tweaking to get it to run well on most systems. I didn't have any problems but I keep the view distance at about 1/5 and I have fairly conservative settings on almost everything except texture quality and a few other settings I consider essential. On an i7-3770k and Geforce 980, I get 100-130 FPS, with occassional dips down to the 70-80 range, and it looks really nice.
There are a few weird glitches with the sound, sometimes it cuts out during cutscenes, but I guess that's why they call them cutscenes? It's probably a multiplayer thing, I've mostly played co-op so far. Maybe it's lag. It never has issues out in the world running around though. The music is very understated and subtle, mostly providing ambiance. It's just droning mood music really, no strong themes or melodies.
tl;dr
This game's a blast and if you like action games with fun combat, movement, and a sense of progression (becoming more powerful) you need to get this game. Also, it's the only other game I've ever played that lets you kick enemies off ledges or into spikes like Dark Messiah: Might and Magic. (If only it had the destructable environments.)
It's a killer game. Just like L4D in better.

Stories: The Path of Destinies is an isometric hack ‘n slash with pleasantly simple combat,  RPG skill trees, beautiful graphics (Unreal 4), great soundtrack and voice acting. The repetitious mode of story-telling can quickly bore if gameplay, not story, is your focus. Still, given all the positives, easily worth a buy at 33% off, and it frequently discounts much lower than that. Recommended.
Total size on my hard drive: 1.8 GB
+ Beautiful comic-book-style graphics (Unreal 4).
+ Beautiful soundtrack.
+ Excellent voice-acting. The narrator carries almost the entire burden of the dialogue, and he is more than up to the task.
+ Narrator’s monologue is funny and engaging. From funny observations upon death (“Where’s the cake? I was told there would be cake!”) to wry self-congratulation after a perfect combat sequence (“Such a pity there were no cameras to record that!”), the narration kept me smiling. The commentary pool for non-story-related actions is large, too, so repeated phrases are not a concern.
+ Good skill-tree. Talents make a big difference in gameplay.
+ Full controller support.
+/- Frame-drops in a few areas (the desert / lava level in particular), but otherwise runs locked at 60fps maxed @1080p on my RX 470.
+/- Isometric. Camera angle is usually handled well enough, but the usual frustrations of poor angles in tight hallways is still present.
+/- Combat flows well enough once its tricks are learned. Targeting is sometimes weirdly inaccurate. The hero is easily staggered, leading to near-helpless death at times. Other times, the action queue gets clogged. Remember that combat is timing-based, and you’ll be fine. Button-mashers will die often.
+/- Story is decent, but nothing special. Save a kingdom from its evil, power-hungry ruler. You play as a fox, who is in love with a cat. Ravens are the enemies, while the scientists are toads and the rogues are rabbits.
+/- The story is divided into 5 chapters. At the beginning of each chapter, a choice is made regarding where to go next. The choices are mutually exclusive. Reach the end (in about an hour), and the story returns to the first chapter, where you can play the story again and make choices you didn’t make the first time. It’s cool to discover what happens if you choose choice B instead of voice A, but you’ll still be playing the same levels (with small variations) throughout.
+/- Crafting is rudimentary, simple, and only for crafting swords.
+/- No waypoint marker. Can result in missing chests and side-loot. Not a major worry, as chances are you’ll be playing the level again.
Stories: The Path of Destinies is a fun if repetitive experience. The developers do their best to hide the repetition in a variety of finely-wrought trappings, and for the most part, they succeed. A solid 7/10.

Dying Light is without a doubt the best zombie playground to date. It has very smooth combat which is instantly familiar to the dead island games, a very fun and well done parkour system and an awesome enviornment to try out your skills in.
The Story in Dying Light follows Kyle Crane, a GRE agent sent to investigate the infection and to steal a very important file from the villain Rais. This is a very intresting plot to begin with but as the story progresses, the plotline becomes predictable and manages to hit every cliche. The only characters I found interesting were the person you play as (Kyle Crane) and Jade. The rest of the characters were very dull in my opinion and when Rais talked it almost made me mute my audio in the cutscenes as he is just annoying to listen to. Overall the story began interesting but then drops about 5 hours into the game (The story will take you around 10-12 hours to complete).
The Gameplay is very fun and is split into  sections- Melee and gun play, and Parkouring. The Melee combat like I said before is instantly familiar to those who have played the Dead Island games. But it is a lot smoother and a lot fluent then the Dead Island games, YES in the beginning your weapons are weak and don't do much damage and you will feel powerless but DON'T WORRY! As you get into the game and find better weapons and upgrades you feel badass, but be careful because your weapons do have a finite number of repairs until the weapon fully breaks and you cannot use it again. Gunplay is also very smooth and fun to do as weapons appear a lot more frequently giving you oppertunitys to try out guns from Pistols to Rifles and finally to Shotguns. Although Shotguns are very underpowered and instead of you blowing zombies to bits in 1 shot it takes about 3-4 shots to kill 1? Shotguns are not really good so you will instantly go back to using pistols and rifles. Parkouring is EXTREMELY FUN! It is probably one of the best parkour mechanics I have ever played in a video game. Parkouring is really useful for either experimenting and being badass in combat, jumping around the rooftops to get to your objectives, or running away from zombies and finding hiding places. BUT AS SOON AS YOU UNLOCK THE DROPKICK ABILITY THEN YOU ARE GONNA HAVE THE TIME OF YOUR LIFE!
The day and night cycles works to be a guns blazing or sword swinging game in the day, and a stealth game by night as "Volitile" zombies appear at night who are extremely powerful, fast and can climb walls and will destroy you if you get spotted by them at night, and it does get really intense at night whenever you are chased or you are trying to sneak past zombies and it really does add to the atmosphere and it brings tension into the game.
The Skilltrees are seperated into 3 catergories- Survivor, is your main system which upgrades what you can craft, your backpack space and other useful survival skills which come in handy. Agility is to do with your movement. Upgrading your movement will increase your climbing speed and jump distance in parkour. it also has some cool skills like being able to jump onto zonbies heads and leaping off them to gain momentum and to avoid getting hit by enemys. And finally Powerhouse is everything to do with combat, increasing your powerhouse level gives you the option to improve your weapon damage, weapon durability and much much more.
The online mode "Be a zombie" I haven't really played much but from what I have played it is only fun to play with friends as random players tend to leave striaght away and games become impossible to find.
Co-op is the main reason to play the game and having up to 4 friends parkouring together, killing zombies together is a lot of fun and you can have such a blast with your mates.
OVERALL SCORE: Dying Light lacks in its story and its characters and quests, but the gameplay and co-op experiance hold this game up and make it a ton of fun to play, I reccomend this to anybody who is a fan of free roaming zombie games but I reccomend grabbing a friend to play with as singleplayer may become a bit boring.
Final Score:
Alone- 7/10
Co-op 8/10

Overall, this game is a great time killer for mindlessly clicking things. You may as well play a mobile phone app. Looks deep, then you dive in and get overwhelmed with disappointment.
Battle System
---------------
P&P has a fun little take on the D&D system but taking advantage of the two worlds that you would see this in. The fantasy realm and the player realm. Which would have been absolutely amazing if executed better.
The battle system is pretty basic. You've got your skills both active and passive, plus whatever bonuses that your player has. Real easy. What's nice is that you can for the most part control the curve of difficulty. You want grindy? You can have it. You want to breeze through? You can have that too. I like that.
If you're looking for something that isn't too terribly distracting to play, this battle system is it.
Story
---------------
The story for this game is abysmal. It's not engaging and the NPCs are boring. There's no sense of urgency or plight. King and kingdom is in trouble because some stereotypical mage is doing suspicious things and cursing people. Oh boy. How quaint. Let's go murder all the things to fix it. Whoo.
With a mindless battle system, you HAVE to have the story element to draw you in. It's definitely not there and I gave it quite a chance.
Characters
---------------
This is where I had the highest hopes. At first glance, you'd think each player would act out their character differently and there would be lots of fun banter between characters. Nope. All dialogue is cut paste across all characters. This broke my heart. Basically all the player characters are just one personality with different skins. The bully could have been a jerk who begrudgingly helped the party, ET could have misunderstood things and made things hilarious, but nope. Gotta have the one character to rule them all.
tl;dr Mindless click game with generic story. So disappointing I had to write about it.

As a disclaimer, I got this game with the humble bundle.
At first I thought this game looked interesting. Jokes baout tabletop RPGs? Yes! Good pixelart? Oh my yes! Turn based combat? Eh, not my favourite, but there's worse.
When I started playing the game was allright. The story wasn't nearly as good as I thought it was going to be, but the gameplay wasn't as bad as I thought, so that kept me going. The difficulty of the game kept going upwards, which is understandable. I did enjoy it.
For a while.
Then I hit a pay wall. Yes, this game has in-app-purchases for gold, which the whole game revolves around; with enough gold you could pretty much beat the whole game while using a first level character. The whole game is constructed around selling this gold, at least seemingly; although the grind times were long at some points, I didn't mind since games like these always have long grind times. However when I spent a very long time grinding for a single fight, I realized that the game is geared toward trying to get you to buy gold.
Good game. Bad business model. Not worth 10 dollar. I'd say buy it for one or two if the concept interests you, and as always, veer as far away from making in-app-purchases in a game you already paid for as possible.

I wanted to write a quick review to answer some of negative reviews, which almost caused me to not buy this game. I am loving this game myself. Yes, it doesn't hold your hand, and it is true that the world is not very open: these critiques are accurate.
On the other hand, the complaints about the main quest being too difficult, too much text, too much difficulty, and very vague systems are not true unless you are looking for a really simplistic game. The main quest is quite good, the text can be easily skipped through in most cases if that isn't your thing, and the only really vague system is crafting, which is  fully optional and has clue books spread over the world.
What the game offers is some really challenging battles, a beautiful world that is loaded with interactive elements, and many hours of fun for anyone who wants a challenge and is sick of hand holding. It isn't perfect, but it is the best CRPG I've played since Baldur's Gate II: Shadowns of Amn.

In what is arguably a more necessary Steam title to have in one's libary than Team Fortress 2 or Dota 2, Half-Life 2 holds up magnificently as a first-person shooter over a decade since its 2004 release as the first title which required Steam to install and play. The game follows an arc similar to most forms of media, especially film media, with the player seeing highs, lows, and an excellent climax as through the eyes of Gordon Freeman.
As stated above, this game remains an amazing title and experience, both in gameplay and in plot, with a great deal of effort directed at character development and map and AI design. You could be told this was released a week ago and would believe it, as both its graphics and physics engine remain top-notch and put to shame those of most other shooters, both at the time and now.
The game follows M.I.T. graduate and Black Mesa Research Associate Scientist Gordon Freeman, who, after being placed on a train heading to City 17, faces off against the oppressive Combine Empire that controls the city and the planet. With the help of the resistance movement and old and new friends alike, Gordon fights the Combine as they launch continued assaults against him, viewing his return to be a serious if not the single greatest threat to their dominion.
The game is an outstanding example of storytelling, with the arc being one of my favorite in any game released - period. Without a word coming from Freeman's lips, the universe and history of City 17 and Earth in general is greatly explained, and through events the player grows to despise the Combine Empire, which in turn grants extra reward to the player when they succeed in trading blows with it.
With an excellent soundtrack composed by Kelly Bailey, the game's means to convey emotion increase, action scenes become more epic, horror scenes become more terrifying, and emotional scenes become more deep and impactful. The game uses its soundtrack in a masterful way, reintroducing old tunes and beats from Half-Life 1, and introducing a new soundtrack that perfectly fits the situation.
The game is also masterful at finding a blend of pleasing and challenging a player; Most concepts are introduced by some form of training to help open the player up to them, rather than forcing the player to learn skills on the spot, though the game makes sure not to help the player too much to keep the challenge going.
If you haven't bought this game yet on Steam, I strongly suggest you do so. It's an excellent title that has everything a good game should have: Interesting Plot, well-written characters, interesting and fun mechanics, a fitting and enjoyable soundtrack, good map design, excellent world-building, and so on. It stands 12 years since its release in most majestic fashion with the means to challenge most AAA titles♥♥♥♥♥♥out to the market with its first chapter alone.

If you are the one who doesn't like stories and always skips introductions, prefaces, videos and sometimes even the tutorials, then this game will not give you problems because the story is told as you do the levels and only has a few cinematics so that you can focus on the main task, killing orcs !!!
The only thing I dislike is that if you play in offline mode it won't let you use the orc slayer costume with the double sword, which although pure aesthetic makes you see like a badass XD
Finally in short, a great game, plus the sequel is also very good, if you find any of the 2 games on discount, don't hesitate to buy them, you will not regret it.

I honestly could've stopped at my first sentence but there's definitely more to this game that I haven't mentioned.

The reference point for this review is the usual quality of Telltale games, and in comparison TWD Michonne falls behing a lot in various departments - feel free to skip on this game, or buy it with a deep discount.
The game is plagued by bad design choices, and sub-par production values. Did the usual storywriter team go for a vacation, and interns wrote the story and script for the game?
The game was completed in 2016, 4 years after the first game, and yet it still have same problems - black screen on start if controller is connected, invisible then popping textures (like a gun in a hand) and flickering actors. But Michonne topped this with incredible amounts of continuity problems, forced "cinematic" black bars during action sequences, mind-numbingly one-dimensional cliché characters - the badass protagonist, the naive good hearted sidekick, "the Governor", the sociopath, the overeager footsolder who starts a fight, the angsty teen, etc etc. At one point you can save one of your friends, and I thought I need to choose one of the 3. I couldn't even name 2 out of the 3 and I couldn't tell more than 2 sentences bout the third one either. They are cardboard cutouts.
The story in short: teens steal stuff, people in power go after them to take their stuff, so now they are the bad guys. At one point the thief girl called out the "baddies" as aggressors and why they can't leave them alone. Yes, this is the level of storywriting in the game.
Also the playeable character repeatedly teleports during actions (look at an item from the left, manipulate from the left, scene ends and you're standing 3 metres to the right.) so the programming department also made their mark on the game. I really can't recommend this game. Story is stale, characters are nonexistant, and the game wants to convince me that I should care about TWO groups of people, while the 3 chapters are not even enough to get to know them, not to mention to spend time and bond with them.  TWD: Michonne is average as an adventure game, but a despicable mock of a proper Telltale game. XCOM: Enemy Unknown is one of the most addictive games you will ever play.
Your role is to organise and prioritise Earth's defense against an alien invasion. To do this, you have to build and train a squad, manage air defenses, delegate R&D,  and command squads of men against alien landings in a turn-based manner. But don't worry! It is not as drab and uninvolved as it may seem.
You will become attached to your soldiers, especially if you give them names and faces. And your decisions are critical. One little slipup could get your squad killed. Another will lose you the battle, especially on higher difficulties.  But the joys of making a right decision, or a risky gamble are difficult to describe.
When starting this game, open with Normal. Don't open with Classic. The game is much much more brutal on that difficulty and higher, and really is recommended only for experienced players.
Oh, and play on Iron Man. Makes the losses mean so much more.
Good luck, Commander.

Perfection from start to finish.  I write this as a massive fan of the show, so obviously the humour appeals to me, but aside from that the gameplay was joy, the characters spot-on, the plot engaging, the soundtrack beautiful, and the graphics appropriate.  Most of all, when I reached the end of the game and there was no more, I felt an ineffable sense of loss and emptiness.

I will start by warning all the people who care about the price/time ratio; even with some alt-tabbing and exploration of branches that didn't bring much to the table, it took me a little over 7 hours to beat the game.
Now, with that being said, what is Stories? A tale of a not-so-bright freelancer-rebel fox, who gets his paws on a magical book that lets him explore the varied possible futures. The end goal is to kill the evil Emperor and save the Rebellion (well, that sounds a little like Star Wars) but the path to it is windy. As the game starts, there are two main branches of the story to explore, splitting further down the road. Over time, more choices will appear based on the knowledge of possible futures. The main idea is to collect the four Truths, crucial pieces of information otherwise unknown to the character and player alike, that will let to chart one's way through the story - and achieve the true ending.
Which also happens to mean there are 23 ways to fail in more or less spectacular ways and one road to victory.
The game relies on its Bastion-esque storytelling of a witty narrator voice but conveys much more dialogue; which, amusingly, is also recited by the narrator through slightly modified voice. This reinforces the feel of having a book read to you, and does a fantastic job of reinforcing the presentation. This is paired with charming environments and a great soundtrack - here is my first complaint, though, while the game looks nice and highly stylised, the fact that it was hard to keep it on stable framerate at a High level of detail feels a little bit... odd. This is no Doom or Witcher to demand this much horsepower, so likely the optimisation could be a little bit better. Granted, this happens mostly during flashy sequences or with environmental effect on the final island.
Stories has you "backtrack" a lot through the same segments of the story. This is mitigated to a degree by maps having two variants (at least some of them do), several segments where choosing one path leaves the other to be explored another time, and by sprinkling special doors throughout. A door is opened with a proper sword, which needs to be crafted. Materials are best found through exploration, so the game opens up a little bit. Different swords mean different powers, you can also find gems that power your hero up in various ways. After a while, you will know the maps pretty much by heart, though, and this is where another good thing about exploration comes in. The swords-doors often open shortcuts that allow to chop down the length of a level. This is very important.
The other main component of the game is combat, something I would call "indie Arkham combat" done right; there is much less reliance on actually big jumps between enemies (in fact such ability is unlocked as you level up) and more on stationary combat combined with pulling enemies together. Or throwing them, because you can do that as well. The bestiary is not terribly big, amounting to 4 enemies, two of them featuring buffed-up variants.
Now, combat will be a make-or-break for your enjoyment of the game. There is a lot of it, and the system is pretty simple. If you don't find yourself enjoying the steady flow of comboes and dancing through big groups of enemies, the game will bore you as well. I personally found it beyond amusing and an absolute joy to slash through - it also never quite gets easy.
There are only two problems. One, the time-slow effects and perfect-hits that increase combo faster are locked at first, you need to spend skill points on them. Why is this bad? Because the combat feels incredibly meaty when you have all these slight slowdowns and added visual effects on well landed/crutch hits. I heartily recommend unlocking this as much as possible.
The second problem is... some effects are a bit too flashy, making the combat situation a little hard to read, especially given the affinity to bright colours in everything, including exclamation marks warning you of a counterable attack starting. There is not much one can do about it, and it certainly can be adjusted to, but I still find it a miss-step on the developers part.
I consider Stories to be a great game if you want to just get through the story enough times to unlock all the Truths and get to the Happy End; for that, several hours will suffice and you will easily reach a sensibly high character level, find secrets and forge all the weapons. It might become a bother when played over long stretches of time to unlock more/all endings, but your mileage will vary here, heavily depending on how much you will like the combat.
But I didn't manage to find the game any repetitive in my playthrough. Keep in mind, however, that as a fan of roguelites of many kinds I am quite used to the incremental gameplay and fully embrace it.

Truly a choices-matter game with divergent plots dependent upon your decisions.  There are 25 different paths in the game.  You are able to beat the game after discovering 4 of the endings (the 5th one then finishes the game).  If you care to do so, you can then play more to discover the other 20 possible stories, or you can discover some of those 20 before getting the victory ending.  Your choice.
Each area has multiple paths to reach the finish, so playing through the stories multiple times will not feel identical until after the 4th or 5th time through, which I admit does happen rather quickly.  I think Dragon's Crown actually does divergent level paths better, as the paths in Stories all merge together instead of letting you experience different elements every time.
Major downside is that most players will not play more than the 5 stories required to beat the game.  I played 6 stories and at that point felt that I had seen enough.  I had no desire to continue trying to see the other story lines.  I unlocked all the swords and gems, but not all the skills, and I had visited each location multiple times, though I didn't see every possible story at each location, and that was enough for me.
Great narrator comedy throughout the game.  If you've played Victor Vran, expect similar one-liner comedy here but more of it.
Even though it's the prequel, it stands up pretty well to Tribes: Ascend.

Final Edit: And I'm back. Someone asked me about this game, and I said ya know what? About time I finish my review.
This game sucks. Now let's explain why. The first thing that irked me right off was their choice of control schemes involving the middle mouse/right mouse button. See, you get a shield ability, but in order to even use the damn thing requires you to use both the right mouse button and middle mouse button at the same time. On any ordinary mouse, this is an uncomfortable and painful process.
Next you've got their always online nonsense. You can set it to friends only, but guess what? It'll still keep blathering on about what completely random strangers who are not on your friends list are doing.
And then there's just the general game play. It's an awful, repetitive grind with a laughable challange. Basic zombies aren't even worth mentioning, their special zombies are annoying at worst, and those "supah scary warry oooo" night fiends? I was killing them for bored sport, just because I could and they were the only thing that could possible threaten me.
Lots of little issues too. Fatin and Dulin speak each other's lines with their face animations, I was killed by forced character animations (went to loot, pivoted around and stood in the fire - box crashing through ceiling animation trapped me and killed me). And oh the challanges. UGH. There's this one limb hacking one, where you have to jump down in order to complete it, and they don't give you the slightest clue where to jump down (they have a specific location in mind) and I had to find it through trial and (fatal) error. And then there was one where the host, Jeff, starts yelling and jerking your attention away right in the middle of it, when he was supposed to yell at the end. Do the devs even know what polishing a game means?
The rag doll physics are awful, the items are hit and miss at best (Firecrackers, for one. You'll get maybe 2-4 zombies, where as you can bang your weapon on a pole and get 12, which will also kill your weapon's durability too. Great! /sarcasm) and honestly? There's no point to this game. Dead Island was better, and that's a hurtful comment right there.
I did have some good moments. One of my screenshots is of some interesting scene decorations, the letters on the ceiling. If you kill the goons in the school, they're the zombies in a later mission, which I thought was a nice touch. And when you get talking to this one fan girl of the female lead, she will very suddenly drop the issue of her dead sister on you. Caught me off guard at least.
So it shows that there's some talent in this developer, but they've got a lot of glaring weaknesses. If you reallt, really want to give this game a go? Pirate it first, and then ask yourself if it's worth the price tag.

Very neat game from a one-man team. It's a concept I've been wanting to see implemented: GTAV and Minecraft elements.
Of course, as the game is indie to the max, you shouldn't go in expecting the complexity and dev time those multi-million (and -billion) games have.
Being able to build a city, run missions that will wreck havok on it, and then rebuild (or leave it looking like a warzone) is pretty cool.
It's nice to see the care applied to building each of the game's buildings, especially on Special, unlockable buildings.
It's also great that the game has multiplayer from the get-go. You click it and it just works. It's a surprise, given the hell I usually go through to get servers up for indie games.
Going from struggling to make a few bucks, to making thousands of money per minute is really satisfying.
With workshop integration, patches and modding, the game has potential to live on, past its release capabilities.
For the price, there's definitely enough content to be enjoyed!
As always do watch a few videos to see if it's your thing.

Hands down one of the best RPGs in a very long time. The best part: It doesn't take itself very seriously. It's filled with witty occurences and characters, even some of the enemies are hands down ridiculous, which gives the game so much character. The reactivity of the game, the physics of it all is probably one of the more impressive ones I've seen in gaming thus far, how different types of matter reacts with one another, especially how you can strategize that during the turn based combat system is really in my opinion quite mindblowing, and one of the first times I have enjoyed a turn based system of this kind. A definite, and HUGE bonus is that the game doesn't tell you what to do, and in many occurences you actually have to guess that something is actually a quest, even though you will never get a quest log or quest marker for it, you may still at the same time get experience points for completing them. That kind of intuition in a game is something I've long saught after, all the way back to the days of arcanum, baldur's gate and fallout, as gamers we have become bereft of good RPG gaming experiences for a long time now and I am so grateful for this game and how it really brings so much fresh and old material together into the game of the year thus far. It remains to be seen what Wasteland 2 and Pillars of Eternity may achieve, but for the moment this is my favourite game in years, and definitely of this year.

I only have just over 100 hours into Grim Dawn and I'm only level 60 and only in act 2 Elite, but I now have a good understanding of the game, I guess.
I'm big into ARPGs, they're my favorite games. I played them all, I still remember picking up a gaming mag in the mid 90s that had a CD with game demos etc. One of these came with Diablo demo. I was totally blown away by this game.
Fast forward to 2016, I have played them all. Honorable mentions go to games like D2, Sacred, Sacred 2, Nox, D3, PoE, Titan Quest, Torchlight, Dungeon Siege 2.
Enough about my history, let's talk about the game in hand, Grim Dawn. This is probably my favorite ARPG out atm. It takes a lot of good things from many other games mentioned above. What I love the most, surprisingly is the persistent world. It's one big world with underground zones. This is how Sacred games were laid out and it worked. It makes everything immersive. Best thing is you get to learn the world and know where things are in the world. You need a few Ectoplasms? Sure, head to the Spined Cove. It will always be in the same spot. No random running around getting lucky (or unlucky) with the cave spawn. You get rewarded for knowing the world.
Another big plus is the class system. I'm not going to go into details, but it's basically identical to the system used in Titan Quest. It works. You'll have to make some decisions on what skills to take and how far to level them. You have to think about what you want to do with your build. Part of the fun will be sitting in front of the Grim Calc, picking a class, finding something that looks like fun to play and then working out all the other skills around it.
I've waffled on and on about Grim Dawn. It's great. It's a must buy for evey ARPG fun. I hit that awkward spot in game at lvl 45-50, after finishing normal, where I was quite weak to do fast BoC or SoT runs and even weaker to start Elite. But then at around lvl 55 I started Elite, and sure, I still felt a little bit weak but now I'm in act 2 and it's ever so rewarding.
I only have a few negatives to say about this game at this moment. The performance drops at times, in busy areas. Also the game seems to be crashing for people from time to time. There could be more music in the game. The soundtrack itself is great, only there could be more to it. Some will argue the game needs ballancing but games like this will never be perfectly ballanced for every class and player ability.
So overall, great game. Buy it guys!

The freedom this game provides is incredible. Think of it as a kind of mix between The Elder Scrolls, Baldur's Gate, and XCOM. The art style of the game is bright and the game in general looks very good. Almost all objects can be interacted with, and almost all NPCs killed. You can have a party of up to 4 people, with two main characters and two henchmen. Two players can play in one game, one controlling each main character. The gameplay is a mix of exploration and turn based tactical combat. Each character can be customised and leveled up as you see fit, given new abilities and traits. There are no "classes", and you can upgrade whatever you want, no matter how the characters start off. One of the great things about the game is elemental interactions. You can electrify water, burn oil, create steam clouds, and explode toxic gas! I would recomend starting with at least one wizard in order to take advantage of the elements. However, there is one thing i really dislike about this game. The puzzles. The puzzles are almost all variations of "push these 4 buttons in the right order to progress". It just seems tedious, especially when great puzzles could have been made using elemental interactions.
Pros:
Interactive environment
Difficult and fun combat
Awesome elemental interactions
Absorbing world
50+ hour story
Cons:
Terrible puzzles

Although comparable to Final Fantasy Tactics or Fire Emblem, both of which are games I enjoy immensely, the Banner Saga surpasses the two by combining realism and fantasy in a way that makes it a completely unique tactical RPG.
How the player sees and interacts with the world of the Banner Saga, that's the fantastic aspect of this game.Yes, there are people that can wield lightning. There are also gigantic humanoids with horns. ...and moving statue-things that threaten the world as it is known. The artistic and musical portrayal of these details, the stylistic choices in regards with character design and interface, made the narrative blend seamlessly with gameplay.
The Banner Saga's realism shows in the limitations emphasized in the gameplay. Each playable character is unique and has its own predefined capabilities. They can gain levels and improve, but only to a certain point. The player's choice of which characters he uses becomes more crucial because of this. In addition to that, time constraints and logistical pressures add a sense of urgency and weight to the story and the choices made by the player.
As fun as FE was because of it, you can't just train your characters until they become completely over-powered. You don't have the time nor the option. In spite of the endless possibilities that FF Tactics provided with its class-system, you can't change a person's job on a whim. Unlike what many optimists may have you believe, individual people aren't pieces of clay to be molded into any shape or form.
TL;DR The Banner Saga doesn't leave everything up to the player. This game is clear about what it wants to convey and how it wants to convey it. Did I ever wish I had more control over a situation when I played it? Dear lord, yes. That didn't stop me from enjoying the fact that my decisions mattered.

So, I've played about 8 hours and reached the end of what's planned to be the first of three chapters.   Is 8 hours worth $30?  Normally I'd say no, but Banner Saga might be the exception.
As I'm writing this, I'm slightly shaken.  It wasn't the ending I hoped for, though certainly the ending I earned.  The fact it had such a powerful emotional impact should tell you how good of a role-playing game this is.
The combat system is..different.  Some call it bugged, but I like it.  Where the game really shines though is the dialogue boxes.  The choices you make WILL change the game's results.  You also find yourself getting to know and becoming attached to some of the characters.  The story isn't the most original I've seen, but I've seen far, far worse.  The world itself is very well detailed.
The 'economic' system is also unusual:  You earn renown for certain feats or defeating baddies.  Renown is used to level your characters up....and buy magic items...and buy food, which your caravan is going to need if it's to survive.  This forces you to make some hard decisions:  My caravan starved for two days because I wasn't thinking and used my precious renown to level up a character.
It's a great RPG.  As I said, quirky combat system, but the storytelling is superb.

To begin, the good points: the artwork and the music. If The Banner Saga were a coffee table book and an album of Scandinavian folk music, it would be gorgeous. However, it is sold as a game, and that is where it falls short.
You will fight the same battle, against the same 4 enemies, on the same battlefield, over and over again without any need to change your strategy or adapt to new conditions. Every battle in the game is depressingly interchangeable up until the final boss battle, which is as frustrating as it is unrewarding. I can say confidently that I have never faced a game with such an unbelievably ridiculous difficulty spike in the final boss encounter. I came very close to leaving the game unfinished, before I realized that the game difficulty can be changed midstream. There is no shame in a quick switch to easy mode.
You will confront numerous scripted events during the course of your caravan's travel - and indeed, much of the playtime will be spent staring at an attractive cutscene of your little band traipsing across the landscape - where a wrong answer will result in the death of a party member. Leveling your party costs Renown, which is in limited supply and cannot be ground for. No matter how much Renown you have invested into a character, when an event hits, if you pick one of the three wrong options among the four presented, that character will die and will never come back. The game gives no indication whatsoever what the right answer is. That's not replayability, that's cruelty (or more likely incompetence). There is no shame in constantly alt-tabbing over to a walkthrough. Oh, and did I mention that you can't save the game at will?
You will find features that are obviously unfinished - the Map screen is one such, which presents a vast world filled with places and lore (rife with grammatical and spelling errors) that you will never ever get to see or interact with in any way. Commanding your caravan's warriors in battle is another, where your options boil down to "fight a battle with your party" or "lose the game." Of course, these real outcomes are obscured by the game presenting 5 opaquely-described options to you when you have an opportunity to fight one of these battles.
You will constantly wish that there were more to do in this game. The character customization options are very limited, the caravan portion of the game is pretty much automatic, the battles are monotonous, and the events are both arbitrary and unfair. This game is not worth the $25 Stoic is asking. A start-to-finish playthrough will take you 10 hours if you're a slow reader and lose battles constantly. There is no replay value, and indeed, looking back on my experience, I find there to have been little play value in the first place.
The Banner Saga makes me worry about the games I've personally Kickstarted, because it is a disaster mitigated only by its lush artwork and soundtrack.

Stories: The Path of Destinies is a game where you play as Reynaldo, a Fox who finds himself in the situation of reliving the same stretch of time over and over again until he chooses the correct path. Not necessarily the most original idea, but one that I rather enjoy myself. You'll be playing through X out of 24 different stories, each takes about 20-35 minutes to play through. In about 5ish hours I was able to play through 7/24, and get the True Ending. You'll be trying to find out the 4 truths that will help you survive through everything.
is pretty simple, you have 4 swords that each have a special ability (3 relate to damage output, 1 is an inefficient heal that you'll rely way too much on), a skill tree that you won't even halfway complete (the xp scaling gets extremely high), and some gems that add various damage related bonuses (there's only 1 that deals with sustain and that one's garbage). These previously mention elements are a little frustrating (way too much damage options, too few sustain options), but the best thing about the combat in Stories is that it's not frustrating, and extremely fluid. Once you get into the grove of things you'll feel like you're running through the level and it feels nice but it's not at that point where you're overleveled, because the enemies do a good job of punishing mistakes you make.
isn't anything to write home about, but it's not bad in any sense of the word, simply good enough not to complain about and bad enough not to compliment. The levels get a little boring towards the end because due to the nature of the game you're going to be running through the same enviroments time and time again.
was the best part of the game, there were a few memorable characters, the narrator does a great job of bringing you into the story, he is truly the greatest aspect of the game. It feels like an uncle or grandfather expertly weaving a tale with a book on his lap as you sit and watch in wonder. He does most, if not all, of the voice acting, simply changing his voice to fit the character, but every voice is distinct. You can tell when he's doing Reynaldo or Lapino. There were some Good Momments (I laughed a few times, felt a few heart strings tug, felt genuine worry for the characters in the game). The True Ending leaves a bit to be desired, but one of the best parts about this game is that you can spend 15 or so minutes following that path where YOU end up with the ancient weapon and decide to burn a path of destruction. There are a ton of different paths to choose from.

Stories has a lot of potential and charm, but it's ruined by a tedious gameplay. Basically, it's a 'Choose your own story' book made into an adventure videogame: the idea is neat, with a single narrator doing all the voice work, many paths to choose and a very approachable fighting system. The downside, it gets boring quickly, you have too many variations of the story and everytime it goes bad unless you unlock the elements for the true ending...
It's kinda frustrating, having to re-do the same 10 (uninspired) levels, picking different choices only to see how your character will be screwed in the end. They try to add some depth, with a crafting system to create different swords to open new doors, but in the end it doesn't change much, it usually gets you some loot that, after you maxed everything, is pointless.
The crafting system seems redudant, honestly I've never felt the need to use different swords. Same thing goes for the Skill Tree, you get some neat things in the beginning, but after the first few skills you can't feel 'growing', it just refines the skills you got by adding extra numbers (extra damage, extra health, extra mana,...)
Overall, all the gameplay part feels rushly attached to the whole idea of 'Choose your own adventure': as I said, great concept, poor execution. If you're lucky, you can get to the true ending in minimum 4 playthroughs (which, luckily, are not that long and the more you repeat the stage, the faster you can get through them), but it's more likely you'll need 8-10 of them... I believe that a good number, makes you enjoy the game without annoying you. But if you're a completionist (like myself) you'll get utterly frustrated by the number of endings, turning a cute and harmless adventure into a borefest.
Better luck next time developers... Try to pick a different path, won't you?

buy this game if:
+ you fancy a simplified  "Arkham style " combat paired with an skill upgrade system
+ you like story driven games with a strong choice component
+ you're ok with replaying from the start several times (20+) to see and check all possible choices and endings
don't buy this game if:

- you can't stand repetitivity
- you don't enjoy an external "almost-omniscent" voiced narrator
- you like and expect deep lore, stories and originality. They're all equally absent.
Verdict 5/10, shallow game plagued by an unbearable repetitivity
Time required to 100% the main game: 12+ hours (?)
Time required to get the real ending : 4 hours
The game has so many flaws that will become more and more evident as u'll play and replay the game:
1-
there's a single voice actor (covering all characters) who's not able to properly represent the spirit / the idea of this whole story.
I'm not saying he's bad or incompetent, far from that, it's just it doesn't fit AT ALL. Emotions such as rage, jealousy, madness and so on are completely botched. Same deal with the characters' icons in the story's dialogue boxes, that are not well made to represent their emotions.
2-
most of the skills u can upgrade are extremely predictable, unoriginal and most of the time only grant a stat enhancement. Moreover, the more you'll level up, the longer it will take to level up, making the grinding way less enjoyable and meaningful, as enemies won't stand a chance against you anyway and the only reason to lvl up is just to get all the achievements.
3-
the game does a really good job in keeping you entertained for the first 4-5 hours but then  it gets lost as Sunday afternoon. Short examples:
- absent enemy variety (4-5 different enemies)
- total lack of bosses or unique interactions (even if the story had many chances to put them in)
- unoriginal story and characters ( you'll see a bad mashup of Shrek, Star Wars and World of Warcraft)
- alternate endings are often forced -> example: You did this to XYZ. XYZ didn't like that choice and killed you. The end.
- side characters are cheesy and as original as a Xmas Coca Cola's TV commercial: the old friendzoned friend, the envious fellow from childhood, a magic weird-4ss magical gifted princess and all that load of stereotypical nonsense.
TO SUM UP:
Play this game and replay it until you'll get the real ending, after that, leave it be where it belongs, which i'm not even sure where it is to be honest.
Oh yeah, buy this game on sale as it's not worth more that 2$.

Accidentally cancelled out of my own review, so I'll just put the short version up for now :x
So far it's really neat, and while no one part (combat, driving, property management, UI design) is spectacular, it's neat to see all of these ideas coming together and interacting. As a criminal, you get to see the damages and other effects of your criminal empire on the world itself, and as a property investor/developer you get to explore your city and see/interact/build with the interiors and people in each buildings. After doing some missions eliminating bandits and doing some experimentation in my own base, I was able to purchase and customize my own office building, and it's fun to work on that while being able to see people and cars moving around in the streets below (and sometimes going to the nearby skyscrapers for rooftop sniper battles when the bandits cause a ruckus).
The price is cheap for how ambitious the project is, and the devs have been active so far in fixing up game issues, and they even created templetes for various types of gamemods for the steam workshop. If the idea of being able to explore and mess with a world with a lot of moving parts, or anything else I've mentioned above, sounds interesting to you, I would definitely check it out. If you're like me and want to learn more about what you can do in the game, the devs set up about 12 or so articles on indiedb (I think you can access them from the updates list, but I don't want to accidentally delete my review again while checking) explaining all of the various mechanics.
Also I couldn't find a place to put this in my review, so I'll just mention here that the music is pretty amazing. It shows up sparsely, but when it does (usually when building or in combat) it's a real treat.

In what is arguably a more necessary Steam title to have in one's libary than Team Fortress 2 or Dota 2, Half-Life 2 holds up magnificently as a first-person shooter over a decade since its 2004 release as the first title which required Steam to install and play. The game follows an arc similar to most forms of media, especially film media, with the player seeing highs, lows, and an excellent climax as through the eyes of Gordon Freeman.
As stated above, this game remains an amazing title and experience, both in gameplay and in plot, with a great deal of effort directed at character development and map and AI design. You could be told this was released a week ago and would believe it, as both its graphics and physics engine remain top-notch and put to shame those of most other shooters, both at the time and now.
The game follows M.I.T. graduate and Black Mesa Research Associate Scientist Gordon Freeman, who, after being placed on a train heading to City 17, faces off against the oppressive Combine Empire that controls the city and the planet. With the help of the resistance movement and old and new friends alike, Gordon fights the Combine as they launch continued assaults against him, viewing his return to be a serious if not the single greatest threat to their dominion.
The game is an outstanding example of storytelling, with the arc being one of my favorite in any game released - period. Without a word coming from Freeman's lips, the universe and history of City 17 and Earth in general is greatly explained, and through events the player grows to despise the Combine Empire, which in turn grants extra reward to the player when they succeed in trading blows with it.
With an excellent soundtrack composed by Kelly Bailey, the game's means to convey emotion increase, action scenes become more epic, horror scenes become more terrifying, and emotional scenes become more deep and impactful. The game uses its soundtrack in a masterful way, reintroducing old tunes and beats from Half-Life 1, and introducing a new soundtrack that perfectly fits the situation.
The game is also masterful at finding a blend of pleasing and challenging a player; Most concepts are introduced by some form of training to help open the player up to them, rather than forcing the player to learn skills on the spot, though the game makes sure not to help the player too much to keep the challenge going.
If you haven't bought this game yet on Steam, I strongly suggest you do so. It's an excellent title that has everything a good game should have: Interesting Plot, well-written characters, interesting and fun mechanics, a fitting and enjoyable soundtrack, good map design, excellent world-building, and so on. It stands 12 years since its release in most majestic fashion with the means to challenge most AAA titles♥♥♥♥♥♥out to the market with its first chapter alone.

This CRPG is one of the best out there. The game is played in real-time but the battles are turn-based, with great elemental and landscape interactions. The world itself wonderfully drawn--a nice combination between pretty landscapes and cartoonish monsters. The music is awesome and I enjoy the voicing (I talk to the rats more often than necessary because it makes me giggle). The price is well worth the amount of content for the game ($40). (Edited to add--finished the game at ~91 hours. Awesome value for dollar). The story is engrossing and you make many choices along the way that affect your gameplay. In fact, beware; choices are permanent and have consequences. If you choose to shoot an NPC in the face with a fireball in broad daylight...well, I recommend you save often in case you need to roll back after some instant regret.
The puzzles in this game can be hard, and the most difficult aspect is likely the fact that you have to pay attention to EVERYTHING--there's a lot of story and the game expects you to listen and learn. If you get confused or lost (which happened to us...erm, often....) you might get a little frustrated. Consider all of your actions, pay attention to story and quests, put care into where you put your skill points, and you'll be fine.
My complaints are small: inventory can become unwieldy, and some of the puzzles are hard (or require patience levels that I don't possess). However, the sheer fun of this game more than makes up for the small bugs and there are a lot of surprises waiting inside this game
I give it a 10/10 for co-op.

I feel like other reviews have already stated everything wrong with this aspect of the game, so I will be short:
Not. Interesting. I couldn't even
myself to finish the game! All the characters (including Michonne) are bland, the plot is boring and the writing is subpar. It's a shame really, but it just felt like a chore to participate in dialogues and watch cutscenes, which should never happen in this type of games.
Also, why is that Michonne uses a machete and not a katana? Perhaps it is explained during the last episode of the game, if not - add another point to the list of why the story is so poorly made.
Now onto something I feel like people don't often mention, but it's probably as important:
Following up poor storyline, QTE were the biggest issue I've had. Seriously, I have a higher success rate in any competetive/skill-based game than in TWD: Michonne fighting events. They are just too inconsistent,you either have all the time in the world to press a certain button to perform an action, or you get killed instantly by failing to press "E" in a splitsecond which you were given. And even at the 2nd try, you might still fail, despite knowing exactly what is going to happen.
TellTale knows how to make quick-time events right, The Wolf Among Us had one of the best fighting scenes I've seen, they felt so natural and intense, especially those "boss battles" in last episodes of the game. TWD: Michonne is the complete opposite and it makes the second biggest chunk of the game yet another chore to play through. Devs know how to do it right, but they didn't care enough to make it reality.
Another thing worth pointing out is that sometimes you don't even press anything and the character still performs an attack as if you didn't f### it up. I feel like they were just too lazy to add another "branch" to the scene which is why sometimes you get killed with no second chance if you don't press the button fast enough and other times your character will go on and execute anyway. By the way, Telltale are starting to get notorious for this (Batman Game, looking at you). This is not acceptable and completely ruins the immersion.
If the story is boring and the fighting is terrible, is there anything else left in the game that is worth the praise or bashing? Well, yes, there is:
- Poor sound-design that made me lower the volume anytime someone gets hit by a machete or any other sharp weapon.
- Clunky animations.
- Awfully familiar faces (for example, they reused an old model of Brenda for the new character called Norma).
- Dialogue lines interrupting one another.
- Poor controller support.
- A couple of bugs that made me actually restart the game.
- Bugged out cloud sync wasted my save file further discouraging me from finishing the game.
- Shortness and emptiness of the game in relation to the price tag.
I don't see any reason to recommend this game.
As I see it, if you are a Telltale Games fan - you will be dissapointed, if you are a fan of the movie series or comic series - you will be dissapointed, if you are new to the genre - pick something better, if you are a fan of the genre - you will be dissapointed.
The only reason this game exists is because developers simply wanted to cash in on fans of previous TWD titles and movie series of said franchise.

So, in the entire time that Path of Exile's extreme skill customization was a nice change to the Diablo 3 habits of hand holding style. With Diablo 3 and Path of Exile now being moreso known as the top two of these kind of games, there's in between Grim Dawn.
Grim Dawn for one, has the same customizations like the old Titan Quest, you don't have any skills to start with and you have no class, you make your class by progress. What makes that so special, is that there isn't a single class to choose from, one character can specialize into two paths(You don't have to).
Surely not all will be fully suitable for another, but it takes a little curve in knowing what to choose and why. Rather then a path being chosen for you, you can make yours from scratch.
Along with this in terms of skill customization, the game features a nice amount of loot, along with the entire factions offering you their items for trade as well, given you are on their good side. As for the looks of the game, its like the name suggests. Its grim, dark and grimy. Nothing in this world is given to you on a silver platter, and don't think you'll be quick to make friends.
Along with the nice bit of gunpowder skills and weaponary given to you, it gives another feel to the usual magic and swordplay world that is like PoE and Diablo 3, the combat is nice and beefy, strikes feel like they hit hard and enemies are plenty, either to be vaporized by magic or chopped to bits by a gaint sword.
Having played this game a fair bit, I can say it bring back the old feel of Titan Quest, in a new and fresh setting, unlike the PoE and Diablo 3 universe.
I can surely say, to those that enjoyed Titan Quest back in the day or want something different from the two big boys that are Path of Exile or Diablo 3 to check out Grim dawn, its not done yet, and its not perfect. But its a really nice change of pace and well done so far I can say.

The game is reminiscent of a newer version of Syndicate.  It's a turn-based combat simulator, with troop ranking, and a headquarters you can build-out as part of your tech tree (equipment, research, power, satellites, etc).
There's a rudimendary economy, where you can sell collected artifacts if you're short on cash.  Primary income is through member countries and missions.  Expenses are maintenance, equipment, and facility costs.
You play the role of the "Commander" of the "X-COM" forces.  You're fighting aliens.  You manage all of the HQ build-out, but it's strongly suggested that you do certain things.  It's pretty obvious what you need to research, or build.  Not much flexibility.  As for combat, you also serve as a remote command officer.  You direct where each unit goes, what they do, etc.  You'll learn quickly to send in your expendable rookies first, because some of the enemy contacts spawn in a way to surprise and cause the most damage.  They're reactive.  If you go to one place, they'll spawn off your flank.  If you go somewhere else, they spawn elsewhere to be off your flank.
GOOD:
* Interesting concept
* Interesting graphics
* Good-enough voice acting
* Graphics are half decent
BAD:
* Missions and flow are highly scripted.  You're not leading a mission so much as being lead through a mission.  There are opportunities to get everyone killed, but basically, you're a rookie Lieutennant, and treated that way, but called Commander.
* Tutorial actions are very highly scripted, to the point that you're not allowd to explore the interface without being pulled away or locked into the script.
* Missing closed captions for at least TUT_HangarBegin_02.
* Sometimes "Confirm" and similar button clicks beep, but do nothing until clicked several times
* In the beginning of the Arc Gun recommendation, the UI got stuck and forced changing the research track due to no other buttons working.
* In the middle of the Arc Gun recommendation, the UI got stuck, and insisted I go to Mission Control, but I was already there.  The UI was zoomed in, and no buttons were clickable.  I had to just press enter, and it processed the input for scanning.  After that, everything was normal.
* During combat, the cinematics reset your camera position and zoom constantly.  After the cinematics, which are 2-3 times per turn, it does not return you to the same view, nor does it return your zoom when it sticks with a different character.
* AI is pretty restricted, and is also scripted.  Aliens will run towards one of your units, and hide next to that unit after being shot at.  Rookies will panick when someone gets killed, but may run towards the enemy.
* Death stats are weird.  Rookies are more likely to die , because experience in the field allows you to be shot full of holes and somehow dodge internal organs.  Realistically, if someone were shot, they would be pretty likely to fall, not stand there and take more hits until they died.
* No performance penalties for being injured.
I'll put in maybe 10 hours on the game, but I don't think I like it.  Play a free trial, or buy it on sale.  Don't pay full price.

Character damage is based on his HP and each side's turn is over after only one of his character moves.  This means the optimal strategy is to get an opposing character down to 1 hp rather than kill them.  Playing optimal strategy ends up being very annoying because of this.  Instead of applying rational strategy like most other strategy games you spend a lot of time trying to figure out how to best keep all enemy characters just barely alive.  It is counter intuitive and just plain annoying to do.
A problem with this game is that you just end up staring at long cut scenes which cannot be skipped.  There isn't much to look at and a few times they go on for minutes.  It is just your caravan walking toward a hill or whatever.  Really feels like it wasn't game tested... surely somoene would have suggested to skip these.
When starting a battle you often have the choice of how many opponents you will face.  The battles are completely random and there is no information to predict which option to choose.  The exact same numbers of army sizes can be given but the number of enemies you face could be double.  The problem with this is that many fights are going to be too easy, yet if you set the difficultly to hard then some become pretty much impossible.  It is just unpredictable and pointless.  Worse, you can't even manipulate the game to make it a reasonable challenge each time - often you cannot save between each fight.  So you end up spending 10 minutes mowing down a super easy fight and the very next one is impossible because you chose all the hard options... then you have to redo the easy one.
I faced a total of just a few different enemy types after maybe 40 battles.  Human melee characters that are mostly the same, the armored enemies with a big and small version for melee, and a ranged version of them.  The difference in strategy between fighting these characters is extremely limited... after about 15 minutes you'll have it figured out and be bored.
tldr: The game play sucks - I've played many free flash games with better game play than this.  Overall it is just a frustrating experience.  If you wanted a slowly told story with politics and moral choices to be made... then I guess you could set it to medium mode and get through the game, though.

The best description I read for this game was: "Game of Thrones meets Dinsey and Vikings". That tells a lot about The Banner Saga. It is a rpg set in a well-made viking world, with disney-like art, full of different (and really hard) choices to make.
The game has, basically, three main features:
(1) a good storyline, in which you follow different characters and make your choices on how the story goes;
(2) a viking caravan to maintain, in which you have to manage supplies, morale, number of clansman and fighters;
(3) a turn-based strategy combat (like Final Fantasy Tatics), with different classes, skills, level-up and items.
The combat system is so enjoyable that they have an on-line version of it, called The Banner Saga - Factions (free to play).
The only bad thing I found for this game is that it feels really short (aprx 10 hours). It claims for its sequels.
So, in general, the game is so enjoyable that the only bad thing is that it ends too soon.
ps: if you're in doubt if it is worth to pay for it, try the free-version (The Banner Saga - Factions) first as a test =)

Well this is a tough one to review.  I had to give it a not recommended, when it is it has to be said on some level, a well crafted game.  But then again that's hardly going to hurt the very positive rating of this game.  So let this review be a warning to others interested in getting this game.  You have to not mind repetition.  On one hand, it's seemless blending of cute and fuzzy looking cartoon animal with massacres, evil rituals, soulstones, and turning kid rabbits into little kid-rabbit-shaped piles of ash has to be applauded.  However, as time goes on I found myself less and less enamored with the game world.  The overall objective is to find 4 unique truths by going through the same 30-60 minute campaign with 20-odd different endings depending on your choices, with each of those endings split into one of the 4 unique truth groups, so that you can then find the ultimate true ending.  I was enjoying the game initially.  However, on my 4th run through I started to notice I was losing my zeal a little bit and the repetition was starting to ramp up.  Then to my horror I realised upon finishing my 4th run that I had unlocked the same truth twice, so would need to go through the game again and make different choices.  When your reaction is horror to the fact you need to keep playing the game, that's not a good sign.  I basically likened it to the feeling of losing 40 odd minutes in another game because I hadn't saved.  So then I had to consult a walkthrough as I no way wanted to go through the whole thing again a sixth time.  And lo and behold, when I did it the fifth time and got my 4th truth, then to get the true ending, I had to go through it all a 6th time.  And by then I was so done with the game that the little additions to the story that the final go round introduced just passed over me without much impact as I was just glad to be done.  How people stick around to unlock all endings is beyond me.
The reason for why I'm so turned off by the whole experience is it's just that everything is so thinly spread and repetitive, and even though I only played like 6 hours it seems longer.  Everything seems a little pointless and unnecessary.  You unlock swords by collecting ore to find secrets routes through levels, but it's still all basically the same levels over and over.  And you never really use these additional weapons in combat as you will likely have the one you start with equipped to use for healing.  And you also unlock and improve gauntlet gems as you go to gain bonuses, but most I didn't use and those that I did use didn't seem to add much.  And each time you level up (which by the by, seems to take excessively longer to level up again as you go on) you gain skill points, but most after the first couple of upgrades don't add much, as all you really need to extra health and hook-shot shield disarm.  And the enemies seem to go up with your levels in amount and health so I never felt like I was getting more powerful, so hitting things that I had vague impression had higher "numbers" using things with higher "numbers".  Which brings us to the worst of the games sins.  The combat.  It basically boils down to hammering quick attack, and occasionally using your hook shot to disarm shield wearing enemies and that's it.  And there's only like 4-odd types of enemies which you fight constantly, and no boss fights or anything to bring variety.  It just gets so boring so fast, and I came to see it as just a distraction which was keeping me from powering through to the end of the level to progress to the next bit of story.  And the penalty for dying is very minimal so it doesn't encourage cautious play.  It's seems that crafting a very intricate and multiple-path story has got in the way of everything else, in particular combat.
So yes, if you get it, you will get some fun out of it.  It's got quite a charming presentation, a well voiced narrator who throws out some comical dialogue (funnily enough, the funniest bits seem to be thrown out randomly on occasions that have nothing to do with plot advancement), and some nice choice-making which initially seems to change up the game experience and have an impact.  But weak combat, token RPG and crafting systems, and wearing repetition  is what brings this down in the end.  I'd give it a 5 or 6/10.

When it comes to gaming, it takes a lot to get me to actually finish a game. Usually I play a decent ways through, get bored, drop the game for a few months, and then if I try again I have to start from scratch because I don't remember what I'm doing. Mirror's Edge, however, broke the pattern: This game seriously captivated me start to finish and honestly I would've still been hooked if it went twice as long.
You can't access hard mode until you've played through the game at one of the lower difficulties, so I went ahead and made it more challenging on my own by turning off Runner's Vision and refusing to shoot a gun. This was so much fun: Without Runner's Vision suddenly every room was not just an obstacle course but a puzzle where you had to figure out where exactly you can grab ledges or scurry up walls to get to the exit. And without grabbing a gun I got the satisfaction of punching a bunch of enemies in the face repeatedly, even if I died a lot because it's still "fists vs bullets" after all.
The story left a bit to be desired in my opinion. The plot twists were rather predictable and I would've liked a little "hint of the future" at the end of the story rather than an abrupt "Welp, that sure happened." It keeps the story open-ended, certainly, but nevertheless it just felt unsatisfying. I also think it would've been good to have more red herrings about where you're supposed to go with additional pointless ramps or some such, but that might just be because my favorite part was the puzzle of not using Runner's Vision and I like challenging puzzles.
All in all, this is a fantastic game that I heartily recommend. It feels so real without a visible health bar or constant background music that you will be suddenly convinced that jumping between buildings in real life is a good idea. I also heartily recommend turning off Runner's Vision especially for your first playthrough, since it makes things a lot more fun than just allowing the game to tell you where to go.

Oh dear christ the things EA will spit on.
Old game, especially at this point, but still it's necessary to understand what exactly is good and bad about it, and why it succeeded in some ways and failed in others.
What we have here is a first person Parkour game: you play as a woman named Faith, a woman who has the task of delivering sensitive, usually illegal, information to people around the city without detection, which involves running on rooftops and tossing packages from runner to runner, while avoiding the police and law enforcement. Story wise, intriguing. I was compelled to try and get through the game to figure out what was going on. Basically a Film Noir storyline set in Somehwere-In-The-Future. A good start.
Visually stunning. Even as far as graphics have come, this game is still pretty gorgeous. Low graphics kind've kill it like any other game, but even then it's still pretty to look at and the amount of detail in the game (even in areas you never interact in) is well thought out and active. Points for that.
Voice, sound and music are fine enough, good simple tunes and interesting track notes for the game's setting. What I found most satisfying were the sounds in general however; every footstep, every grab, every leap, the panting of Faith's breath, the crunch and sickening smush of bone, flesh and muscle when you don't stick the landing and/or fall to your death, every single movement is punctuated with a powerful, realistic sound. Impressive there, so overall the feel of the game is great!
It's just a shame it's absolute garbage gameplay wise.
Controls are janky and unwieldy, like wrestling with an SNES controller in a game it's not designed for. Using a regular controller helps immensely, but even then there's a lot of slow responses and unpleasant fiddling. There's also the issue that the Jump command for the game is also the Grab/Hold command for hitting ledges. So spamming it kills you, but mistiming it kills you.
Actually trying to get through the game is a nightmare the first, second, third, and respectively incrementing times. Normal mode gives you Runner Vision which highlights the way to go forward, but even with direct guideposts it's infuriating to try and find out which way to go and just what's going to progress you, rather than kill you brutally and viscerally.
The game also cannot decide whether it wants to be a brawler or not; combat comes into the game occasionally, usually with policemen using guns. Now you can use the environment to Prince-Of-Persia your way past enemies (or into them for a punch up), as well as generally flip and spinkick around folks to disarm and smack them about. This sytems is -awful- oh my GOD the combat is disgusting. Jarring, breaks the pace, untrustworthy and just overall hateful, you're not meant to fight but the game forces combat on you anyway.
Overall it honestly just has the same problem most modern AAA titles and the average barfly have: really, REALLY pretty to look at, but you start fiddling with it and you realize that it buckles under pressure and starts flailing its arms about begging to be left alone.

Wow! Valve has done it again! From the creators of the Half-Life and their amazing expansion Half-Life: Opposing Force, I am proud to say that Valve has set a new standard for the gaming industry.
The first time I started Ricochet I was mesmerized by the visuals, the dark tone, and the sounds! I felt very immersed in the universe of Ricochet and the backdrop of space is truly amazing.

Overall I give this game a 9.2/10, it really has shaken the industry with revolutionary design and gameplay, but lacks character development with some side characters that I wanted to know more about.
