This is almost a Yes to recommend, but not quite. I paid $30 and feels too much. I am writing this review at about 7 or so hours into the game. Most of my complaints so far are small nitpicks but in some cases are really annoying.
First person shooter with lots of weapons, enemies, and pretty much everything you saw in Dead Island. In fact the game is nearly the same.  If you liked DI, you will likely enjoy this. The parkour system is fun and most of the time works. You start off with melee weapons early on (I have yet to get a gun). You can craft and repair weapons which is fun if you are into that sort of play style. The day/night cycle reminds me of games like crackdown where combat changes or gets tougher. You also have safehouse areas that you can optionally clear throughout the city. You have sidequests and different skill trees to level up. I am 7 hours into the game and I don't even have 1% of the story completed so lots to do. You also find random encounters where it is nothing but some guy telling you a story, to rescuing a person trapped in a room or things like that. Sometimes you get rewards or xp. As of Sept 2015, the game plays smoothly on my old machine and still looks great.
A sturdy lead pipe would never break in most situations, but after 50 hits against squishy zombies, it does. Repairing is extremely tedious. It is fine for flimsy weapons but not for heavy ones. Instead of breaking, the item should simply become unusable or lower the damage output as you use it. It seems that main weapons can only be repaired a set number of times. This also means that modifications you scrounged for need to be redone on a new weapon.
You have more than enough stamina to jump off ledges or hang there indefinitely, yet a few swings and you are too tired to do fight properly.
After being thrown, they disappear. You can't recover them!?
Humans block throwing weapons at least 80% of the time, even when weilding a pocket knife. Humans also seem to take far more damage than zombies; a lead pipe to the head 3 times and they still run around fast.
Little variation in how they look. As I leveled I saw stronger ones mixed in, but the combinations were very formulaic. I would have loved to see such a huge swarm of wimpy zombies too numerous to fight. Until they see or hear you, most zombies do not move around much; it would be cool to see a swarm shablimg around the block together. They are very predictable in movements and fighting styles.
Just like Dead Island, you play fetch. Run around and set these traps, or collect that medicine.
Some doors look like they can be opened, but you can't. It goes through an unskippable animation only to find that the door is locked and cannot be interacted with again. This is where you should be able to pick or force the lock, or even physically break the door with your weapon.
In some situations, a zombie may grapple or incapacitate you and you have to rapidly tap a button to get out of it. I find that getting damaged during this is random even with the same number of button taps.
I find that certain textures and building fixtures (such as refrigerators, mirrors and chests) are repeated far too often.
There are 3 different skill trees and each one takes different action to level. Pulling yourself up from ledges levels up one tree, while attacks level up the other. A base set of points per level to spend whereever you want would have been better.
You CAN turn off film grain in the game settings. The basics of parkour here are fine and should be available in more games. However, it can be a bit cumbersome with a keyboard and mouse. Occaisionaly during a fight, there will be a little animation showing bones breaking. However, this does not seem to affect zombies in any way. Break their leg? They get back up and walk toward you. It has no real function other than eye candy. There is lockpicking in this game but to be honest, I am getting sick of it. They either need to give you a lot more interaction with the world, or cut it back - lockpicking here just feels tedious. As you level up, stronger enemies start appearing, but you don't often find better weapons in the open world. You generally have to buy them or craft them instead of relying on drops
At first the game felt fun, but it is already getting repetitive after 7 hours. I played Dead Island 1 and Riptide only once through the campaign and I will likely do the same here. Other than the parkour features this game is too much like Dead Island. I am sure I will eventually put a fair amount of hours into this game, but that is only because I can't return it now and will want to get my moneys worth out of it. This is basically Dead Island 3 and feels like the same tired game all over again.

Crappy Community- Play with friends because the random folks are worthless or annoying. They never have mics and when they do it's some kid with his Mom screaming at him from the background. Positives!
Great first person mechanics- Everything from climbing to clubbing to shooting feels nice.
Good action- a fight that you think is handled can develop into something else quickly.
Scary as hell at night!- Seriously, heart pounding stuff until you get the hang of it. Misteps when being pursued cost dearly.
Good RPG mechanics- abilitites, health, and speed all get better, which is good cause you are a whimp at first. But the best part is that the game scales the zombies up too. When you get better more virals come, and more armed enemies appear, and so on.
Good quests- Mostly errand boy missions, but they were varied enough to keep me playing.
I think that's all I have, and my sausages are done boiling. (boil then fry, always) Get some friends and give it a try, play in a dark room, and survive the night.

D: OS takes the likes of
that will have a person lost in the world for many enjoyable hours.  Your ability to steal almost anything, kill almost anyone, and still find ways to beat the game are an enjoyable (if not frustrating) way to play.  Personally I went along with the story, even if I refused a 'main character' and went with a henchman instead, all because of something he said that I didn't like.
I'll admit, this game wasn't the easiest or most friendly, having me frustrated at many intervals because of a TINY switch I was oblivious to or a pressure plate I didn't think to look for.  I also have to say, playing on Hard, the game was pretty hard to a certain point in terms of battles, got easy, went back to hard, then evened out.
The difficulty, however, may have stemmed from my lack of knowledge of the game, where I wandered the 'wrong' way.  But, that was part of the fun!  I'm not one to choose SUPER carefully, but I'm not stupid either.  I know many people have stated their lack of knowledge of the game led to a restart after many hours played, but that would have taken away the fun for me.  And, despite my 'bad choices', I did very well.  My main damage dealer was a 2-Hand user with Witchcraft skills; how was I supposed to know that my lack of the Intelligence stat made it so half of my Witchcraft skills would be hard to land?!  But, that made the experience that much sweeter, because I worked around my choices to develop a great character who utilized her skills masterfully.  Summon that skeleton; only have a 70% chance to land that spell; works for me!
The game has some minor flaws.  You'll un-immerse yourself sometimes when you've done quests out of order only to realize your characters ask for information from an NPC they already have.  But hey, that's part of the fun, in the freedom of discovering things without clues.  You'll also probably get frustrated many times with puzzles, going to Google for the answer to something you should have seen but forgot to look for.  But, that frustration subsides as you enjoy the game in its entirety.  The quest log is just...a log of what you know and what you've found out.  It won't tell you where to go, but what you know.  No hand-holding, no arrow pointing the way.  The game yells at you..."GO WANDER AND FIND OUT STUFF!"
Worth playing?  Yes.  Replayability?  Sure, but maybe not RIGHT away.  After 100 hours, it's hard for me to pick it back up immediately.  Although, I haven't touched certain skills or ways to play, like Backstabbing with Rogue-like characters.
However, once people work out the kinks of the editor (which looks like it has AMAZING potential, even if it's going to take a long time to lean), or Larian gets out more content, the replayability will be there.
: Great game, akin to Skyrim+Diablo+Turn-Based Strategy+DnD.  Potential to be even greater with mods and user-created content.  Worth $40, especially to Larian.

It has weight and the pacing is just right IMO.  Not overly swarmy and hectic like Torchlight 2 and not quite as tame as Titan Quest (though I love both games).
The atmosphere is dark and twisted.  More in line with the original Diablo than any other ARPG.  If you're a ARPG fan then you need to own this game.
The only complaint I can come up with is that normal mode seems a bit too easy and while veteran mode feels much more satisfying overall, it can be a tad grindy for solo play - especially at bosses.  Still for fans of the genre I will recommend veteran level.  Don't bother with normal or you might be bored, unless of course you prefer ultra-casual faceroll difficulty and outleveling content.  Veteran provides that need to grind out a level or two and gear up a bit more while still enjoying the story and side quests.  Personally I would make normal easy mode and veteran normal mode.

Divinity is easily the best RPG I have seen in years, and a breath of fresh air. It mostly sticks to classic conventions: Branching dialogue, dice rolls, turn based combat. Where it breaks though, it does so exceptionally well. Dialogue between party members is a fun way to roleplay. While there are consequences to your decisions, you never feel like you will be punished for doing what you think is fun, or for not going consistently down one moral path. In fact there is no Good/Bad morality system here, which alone is a pretty big change from most western RPGs. Interaction with the environment is kept to a simple few rules and interactions, but they are used often for everything from combat to puzzles, and there are often creative solutions to both.
The game is polished exceptionally well and feels responsive, but there are some downsides. First, the loading times. They aren't too frequent, but they can be very long. Balance seems alright, but a few classes seem less than worthwhile, and you could end up picking a character that overlaps completely with someone you get about 20 minutes in. Also, if you aren't the kind to read dialogue this is probably not the game for you. (But you are reading this so hey.)

D:OS is my new addiction.
, I have equal time spent in both the single player and co-op aspects of the game.  Here's a breakdown:
+It's nice that both characters are the star here.  One is no more important than the other, and you'll spend equal time commanding/leveling both.
+You can now set the AI up, so this means the characters will respond on their own (corresponding to the AI you gave them), or you can choose to make them have none and you have control.
+Control both characters how you want: send one into the battlefield to start a fight, and leave one behind to flank or ambush.  Send one to town to sell while one stands behind to teleport you right back to where you were.  There are even environmental puzzles that make use of this lovely feature.

+Drop-in/drop-out works effortlessly.
+As a strategical turn-based game, it works beautifully co-op.  One controls one character, and one the other, and each take turns and controls their summons and whatnot.  It works SO well... better than I had hoped it would.
-BIG CON HERE:  You don't bring your own character into someone else's game- you play their other half.  Basically, unless you are friends with that person, and they will create a character for you around your visual/skill likes, you're sort of their lackey.
The game is beautiful and highly addicting, and adding a friend to the mix only makes this already enrapturing game even better.  The "no hands held" approach to their quests may be off putting to some, but is overwhelmingly refreshing to me in this day and age of huge set piece action and predetermined paths.  I also love the traits that you can pick up through dialogues with your partner and choices made in the world.  And, the best part?  LOOT LIKE A MUTHA!  I haven't had a good lootfest in quite sometime, and this game delivers it hamfistedly.  All of this is the recipe for the perfect RPG/Co-op experience that is well worth the price!
There is more game here for $40 than I've seen in some games that are $60+.   If you like loot, and you like RPGs, you will have a ♥♥♥♥ing blast with D:OS.

Brilliant cRPG, highly recommend it. Larian have done a terrific job bringing old school RPG into 2014 without compromising or dumbing it down. Pretty much everything you know and love about cRPG is there. Complex character stats, inventory management, wall of texts and no quest marker.
Combat is all turned based, using the action point system. What makes it interesting is the area effect and how the different element interact with each other. Cast a spell to make it rain and enemies become more susceptible to stuns (electricity) or frozen. Drop poison gas or oil and follow it up with a fireball and the gas/oil blows up causing more damage to the affected area. It's going to suck now playing other RPGs and not being able to remove or use hazards to your advantage.
Game was made to be played co-op but if you want to just play it single-player (I did), it'll pretty much play just like any other RPG except you'll have an option to roleplay both characters. A recent patch added personalilties that you can set on your 2 main characters which will let the AI control the other main character you aren't controling in conversation should you want to automate either character's responses.
The story is probably the only real weakness of the game. It's pretty generic fantasy stuff (with a humorous undertone, especially on side quests), but it did keep me engaged enough for the 85 or so hours it took me to finish the game with all side quests done (great btw). The puzzles are, in most cases done pretty well. Some of them might not be obvious right away. You'll have to look around your environment, reading books or talking to the right person for clues. There was 1 or 2 that was convoluted, which lead to trial and error.
The game isn't perfect but I did not run into any game breaking bugs and Larian is constantly updating the game on a regular basis. There's a free toolset that comes with the game so hopefully, we'll be seeing quality user generated content that will keep the game alive for hours after finishing the campaign. We've got 3 more cRPGs coming out (Wasteland 2, Torment and Pillars of Eternity), Larian was the first out of the gate and it has set a pretty high bar for the rest to follow.

I hate to do this, but I have to say thumbs down. After experiencing the fantastic gameplay in the free multiplayer version, I was really looking forward to the single-player campaign. What a huge disappointment!
The combat is still great, but everything else is mediocre to bad. You find yourself struggling against a game that gives you too little information, and you are constantly being arbitrarily punished for decisions whose ramifications often make very little sense. For example, apparently when you tell people they can join your caravan, it also means they have free access to your food supply and all the guards you posted earlier in the game get the night off for some reason.
Even worse, it seems you are supposed to try to get to wherever the hell you're going (and you're given very little reason to care where that is, as you have ZERO agency in any of this, despite a bunch of silly choose-your-own-adventure questions) without losing too many clansmen, I guess?  But once again, it's really hard to care about saving these people since they are mostly just a number that starts to tick down when a fight goes badly or you run out of food.
The writing itself could have used a firmly wielded editor's pen, both in the basic English and in the weak attempts at what I will call "epic fantasy-speak." You can tell what effect they were going for, but it all comes off looking shabby and lame because in the end it's just too obvious that it was all written by gamers, not professional writers.
So I guess if you are willing to ignore all of the actual campaign bits that are supposed to hold together the campaign, maybe go ahead and get it for the interesting combat. But I'd definitely wait for a deep discount -- no sense paying for the bad parts you are better off ignoring.

The Banner Saga really impressed me for the majority of its duration. Great artwork, an interesting world inspired by Norse mythology, a interesting but sad story full of interesting characters and unique, enjoyable combat. I began to genuinely care about many of the characters, they are well written and some have distinctive personalities. You will often have to make walking-dead style decisions where you must weigh risk versus supplies, morale and your available fighting force. Later in the game some of the choices you must make are quite difficult and make the story feel like your own.
The combat is turn-based, with you moving your selected squad members about using different abilities to damage enemy armor and health, which also serves as strength. Weakening armor allows you to do more damage to strength, while damaging their health/strength reduces the impact of enemy attacks. I found the combat difficulty to be well balanced if not a little bit easy for most of the game, I only failed a battle once but often I was down to my last guy when I won.
Sadly things fall apart a bit near the end of the game. The story becomes a bit contrived with the introduction of a certain character, and the final battle is problematic. You are forced to use a specific character in this battle despite making a big choice regarding this character right near the end that in my mind should have left her out of the battle. I had not leveled this character up at all, she was weak and unhelpful in combat and this made the final encounter near impossible for me on the normal difficulty level.
Apart from the last hour or so of this ten-hour game, I really enjoyed the Banner Saga and would put it on part with The Walking Dead in terms of story, characters and meaningful choices that have surprising results. one caveat is that there is no voice acting for most of the dialogue, so if you dislike reading you might not enjoy this game as much. I personally would take no voice acting over bad voice acting, but for some this might be a deal breaker.

Its got a very interesting take on the "Choose your own adventure style" of game, mixed with combat we've seen done in the likes of Batman's Arkham games and more recently the Hand of Fate series.
Story: 8/10
The multiple pathways and continually evolving narrative as you unfold the truth behind Stories is suprisingly engrossing. The story itself on the surface is not entirely interesting though it is novel, and the narrative can sound like a bad fanfiction at times ("And then they kissed and it was the best kiss he'd ever had" - You guys KNOW that line was cheesy)
...and yet, I find myself enamored with it. The characters had just enough depth to establish who they are in the admitedly short time you get to know them, and the game does a great job of showing that you have choices, but while establishing your character would realistically have very little reason to do that. And yet the narrator will make it work anyways. Speaking of, The narrator is easy to understand and plesant to listen too, and I appreciate the attempt of distinction in character voice so I can always tell who's talking.
Gameplay 6/10
Its fluid, and the upgrade system is nice, but there really isn't much to talk about here. We've seen the gameplay style before and it doesn't deviate from it enough to be worth any note. To get an "ending" in the game takes around 45 minutes, but that is because the game is not truely over at just any ending, but one specific one. A great game to play in short spurts even if the story doesn't quite hook you.
Soundtrack: 7/10
I'm of two minds about the soundtrack, it makes great ambiance, but it really isn't anything special on its own. Where the game shines in audio is the narrator. If you're looking for an OST that rocks every track, you won't find it here, but you;ll be pleasantly suprised by the ambaince.
Graphics: 7/10
The areas look gorgeous but the art style may not click for everyone as well as it did for me. The game shows you exactly what you're getting, so make sure you check the screenshots and see if the graphics are your cup of tea.
Overall: 7/10
A nice, refreshingly solid game with a decent story and great narration that weaves a tale just clever enough to get you interested and leaves you fufilled by whichever end you choose, and if you aren't fufilled, you're determined to go find another pathway through the story to hopefully find the one you're looking for. With solid combat, good replay value, well thought out level design, and a fantastical story that just manages to hook you in, Stories: The Path of Destinies, for the price of $15, is a game you owe it to yourtself to play if you enjoy story driven action games.

It's a decent enough game held back by the poor combat.
And I don't mean poor as in "Oh it's just mindless assassin's creed/batman combat".
I mean poor as in ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t design and infuriating enemies. If you can overlook this, the game is pretty enjoyable, but it really irritated me to the point of wanting to stop at times.
Enemies notify you of their incoming attack with an exclaimation point appearing above their head. This works perfectly fine until about halfway through the game where you get enemies with particle effects shooting out other particle effects and laser beams and just eyefuls of color. While it looks nice, it makes it nearly impossible to tell when an attack is coming because there's too much going on. When there's 12 enemies around you all glowing and putting off these crazy effects, it's hard to notice a plain white exclaimation mark appearing above their head for half a second.
Even worse than this, the exploding suicide enemies are entirely broken. They're a fine idea, but the lockon system makes them into death traps. I'd constantly end up swinging or running into them accidentally right as they were primed to explode because the game for some reason gives them priority over other nearby enemies. This means my only choice when dealing with them is to either purposely avoid doing any combat near their direction, or to just eat the damage which isn't really a viable option since they're one of the most damaging enemies in the game.
Ignoring this, the story is cute enough and servicable to be an interesting experience. The weapon upgrading and loot system is a bit infuriating with how easy it is to miss a chest thanks to being forced up an elevator. It's overall just a very okay to decent game held back by poor combat. I can't reccomend it at full price but on sale it's worth a buy.

The Banner Saga is a story lover's game. The narrative is introduced bit by bit with each player decision altering some future event in the game. This piecemeal while impactful delivering style makes is seem like one that can be retold in the oral traditions of old with is perfect for this game inspire heavily by Norse mythology.
The artwork, inspired by Eyvind Earle (if you play long enough that name may seem familiar) and is bright, colorful and deceptively minimalist which lends itself to this mostly Flash game. There's not a lot in the way of cutscenes but some of the stills are so moving that they don't need much animation.
There's a lot of praise I can give to this game and if you play it, I think you'll find plenty of enjoyable moments that will make you wish for more. However, I have some major criticisms. The battle system seems  not completely balanced. While I love that a battlefield is randomly generated, I don't love the lack of grinding opportunities means you can be really tied down in what characters you use. Having played the multiplay game, I like to level up each different type of character so I can play a battle with different lineup. While I understand the Training tent is supposed to fill this role, those battles don't give renown so it really doesn't accomplish what I'd like, especially when some of my main team's heavy hitters are injured.
Finally, the end....The end was beautiful but I don't have a problem with the aestethics of the game. I would have liked to have more lead up to the ending.

Star Wars Battlefront is a game that shall never leave a place in my heart. It's buggy, it's glitchy, it barely has a campaign, but it's just oh so satisying to destroy an X-Wing that your buddy just got in, blow up 5 storm troopers with a thermal detonator, learn the art of fighting as a Jawa fighting Tusken raiders, and become Darth Maul and absolutely murder Chewbacca. There is only ONE game where those things can occur, and THAT game is Star Wars Battlefront. With the continuing powerful mod community, an active online community, clans,  a wealth of modes, maps, and options for playing however "YOU WANT". It is simply a game that anyone can stroll off the side of the rode and play, and I recommend that everyone do so.

So, in the entire time that Path of Exile's extreme skill customization was a nice change to the Diablo 3 habits of hand holding style. With Diablo 3 and Path of Exile now being moreso known as the top two of these kind of games, there's in between Grim Dawn.
Grim Dawn for one, has the same customizations like the old Titan Quest, you don't have any skills to start with and you have no class, you make your class by progress. What makes that so special, is that there isn't a single class to choose from, one character can specialize into two paths(You don't have to).
Surely not all will be fully suitable for another, but it takes a little curve in knowing what to choose and why. Rather then a path being chosen for you, you can make yours from scratch.
Along with this in terms of skill customization, the game features a nice amount of loot, along with the entire factions offering you their items for trade as well, given you are on their good side. As for the looks of the game, its like the name suggests. Its grim, dark and grimy. Nothing in this world is given to you on a silver platter, and don't think you'll be quick to make friends.
Along with the nice bit of gunpowder skills and weaponary given to you, it gives another feel to the usual magic and swordplay world that is like PoE and Diablo 3, the combat is nice and beefy, strikes feel like they hit hard and enemies are plenty, either to be vaporized by magic or chopped to bits by a gaint sword.
Having played this game a fair bit, I can say it bring back the old feel of Titan Quest, in a new and fresh setting, unlike the PoE and Diablo 3 universe.
I can surely say, to those that enjoyed Titan Quest back in the day or want something different from the two big boys that are Path of Exile or Diablo 3 to check out Grim dawn, its not done yet, and its not perfect. But its a really nice change of pace and well done so far I can say.

One of the best ARPGs I've played since Diablo 2.  One of the best ARPGs ever!  Although I do like Diablo 3, Grim Dawn IMO feels better in every way.  The maps are larger and far more detailed, the story is better, the variety of mobs are more dynamic, and the combat has a lot more "oomph" to it, as in heft, kind of like Destiny vs Borderlands.  It has weight and the pacing is just right IMO.  Not overly swarmy and hectic like Torchlight 2 and not quite as tame as Titan Quest (though I love both games).
The atmosphere is dark and twisted.  More in line with the original Diablo than any other ARPG.  If you're a ARPG fan then you need to own this game.
The only complaint I can come up with is that normal mode seems a bit too easy and while veteran mode feels much more satisfying overall, it can be a tad grindy for solo play - especially at bosses.  Still for fans of the genre I will recommend veteran level.  Don't bother with normal or you might be bored, unless of course you prefer ultra-casual faceroll difficulty and outleveling content.  Veteran provides that need to grind out a level or two and gear up a bit more while still enjoying the story and side quests.  Personally I would make normal easy mode and veteran normal mode.

This was exactly what I expected from the newer Telltale games.  It is heavily focused on the story, has a lot of dialogue choices and simple interactive cutscenes, and has very little regular gameplay in between.  The gameplay that's there is decent and the story is interesting, so it works well for what it's trying to do.  Like the other Telltale games, the choices affect what other characters say to you, but most of the choices get canceled out by the end.  And each episode is less than 2 hours, so the overall game is not that long.
Michonne is one of my favorite Walking Dead characters so it was awesome to have a story focused on her.  I understand that Telltale was basing her more on the comic version, but I think the actress who plays her on the show is absolutely perfect so it was a little jarring for me to have Michonne in the game look more like the comic version.  Once I got used to that, it was a good story.  It was a little simple and I didn't get as emotionally involved as I did for the first two seasons of the game, but part of that is due to the nature of this game (obviously Michonne is safe because she appears after this in the comics).  Still, I enjoyed the game overall.  It provided some interesting backstory for Michonne and it was a nice side-adventure.

Not worth the price. People are styling this game after Portal since it is a first-person puzzle game, but it falls far short of that. There isn't an interesting adversary or, in fact, even a story. I like that the game just kind of throws you into it, but I need some incentive or goal to keep me interested. "Solve all the puzzles" well, okay, let's go with that.
The thing is, the game is non-linear. Normally that's praiseworthy, but it turns out in Antichamber there are special guns you gotta find, and you might find yourself facing a puzzle that requires these guns, and have no idea that you're missing anything. So you can easily waste a lot of time trying to solve an unsolvable puzzle. With the non-linearity, you also don't get much sense of progress until you return to the map hub and see what did or didn't get unlocked from your last forway into the puzzle world. Sometimes a puzzle just leads to a dead end. The hub is a nice idea but you end up relying on it a lot because you can't tell if a puzzle has multiple paths without it. Even with it, I got lost pretty easily.
My least favorite part is that your "reward" for solving a puzzle is a little poster with a pretentious phrase that tries to sound profound. For example: "Sometimes you have to go backwards to go forwards." It was kind of cute the first time, but as I played through more puzzles, I was expecting a purpose to appear. No luck. Not only that, the pictures that go with the posters are just... unappealing? heteronormative? More than one poster of a guy getting rejected by a girl. One was a pregnant woman with the phrase "Good things come to those who wait." Like ??? okay??? what does a pregnant woman have to do with the puzzle I just solved? Are they trying to relate the solution of these puzzles to everyday life or something?
Perhaps I didn't play far enough. I didn't want to. The bare white walls began to hurt my eyes. I'm all for minimalism in games, but this one is kind of ridiculously minimal. There isn't much scenery, just white chamber after white chamber. There isn't much music either. Some areas have some sound effects of like nonexistant birds chirping that quickly get on your nerves as it loops.
Finally, when you launch the game, the icon is just the UDK logo, rather than a unique logo for the game. Gonna have to take points off for that.

The Banner Saga is one of my favorite games I played this year. (To put that in context, other games from this year are Skyrim and all DLC, Deus Ex Human Revolution, DmC: Devil May Cry, and Metro: Last Light.) The Banner Saga is a model for what indie, crowdfunded games should aspire to--straightforward but nuanced, artistic but accessible, and engaging but not heavy handed.
The best description for The Banner Saga that I've heard is still Oregon Trail meets Final Fantasy Tactics with a dash of Skyrim. The game's lore is intricate and smart, creating a world where the gods are dead and the creations they left behind--man, varl, dredge--find themselves at war. The main characters are well drawn--from Hakon, who finds himself a reluctant general and diplomat, to Alette, a young girl forced to grow up too quickly.
The combat is easy to undertstand, but difficult to master. On the Hard setting, winning battles is satisfying--and defeats are crushing--because it's easy to see where tactics could have changed the outcome: Should I have broken enemy armor first? Did I expose my archers/ranged characters too much? Should I maim a tough enemy or kill a weak one outright? Should I save willpower or use a character's special ability? The leveling system deserves mention, too, because it allows players to mold characters more towards their playstyle.
In between battles, your party travels from city to city, and it's up to you to make decisions about both random and scripted events that occur. Your decisions are integral to the game, as they can affect your caravan's supplies, morale, or even cause main characters to die or leave the party. In turn, those things may make your battles or less difficult.
As you can see from the screenshots, the game is beautifully drawn. The animations are generally good, even if they lack variety. The music and sound are standouts, although there's very little voiceover and some will complain about how much reading the game involves--I don't think more voice acting was necessary, but I could see why some people might prefer it.
Overall, The Banner Saga should be taken as a model for elegance: It's a game that does important things like combat, art, characterization, and making choices matter really well, but doesn't try to stretch itself for more than that.

This game is very good at what it sets out to do.  It delivers an interesting story and thought provoking setting, encased in beautiful 2D animation.  I've played through it several times and I can stand by the statement that it is a very polished, and enjoyable experience.
However, in my opinion there are 2 main faults of the game.  Without spoiling the ending, I will warn anyone reading this who hasn't bought the game that this game is not finished.  It is the first part of a trilogy.  The ending is shockingly sudden and does not resolve anything.  This would not bother me except for the fact that this game's Steam page does not indicate this in any way.  If they wanted to be accurate they should mark it as Banner Saga part 1 or they should say something in the description.
The other complaint that I have is that the ending is an A or B choice.  The choices you make along the way to the end do radically affect your journey, although they could have doubled down on that as well.  However, at the end you have to make a simple decision, and you have no further control over the ending.
I recommend this game to RPG fans, with those two disclaimers in mind.   If you want to know more about the ending before making your choice, there's no shortage of forum discussions on the topic.

This game is spectacular. It has everything.  You can build cities via the mapmode.  The cities are functional in the sense that it is the world you are playing.  Building placement is about what works best for you.
The economic design is solid.  Vanilla settings permit you a healthy set of options in the beginning.  Complete a few early missions to boost your progress.  You can make an impact on the game if you have a focus.
Earn some money.  Build some things.  Balance the RICO and perk buildings. Use the money to do more.  Build bigger.  You could spend all day making the ultimate apartment building.  Or, you could create a meat grinder of enemy AI vs your AI.  Turn the local area into a pot marked hellscape.  FUN!
Combat.  This game is about management.  You are managing simple soldiers fighting simple enemies.  They won't get all "tactical" on you and execute complicated maneuvers.  Enemies charge and shoot until you or they are dead.  Simple.  Yet, the management aspect of the game is where the strategy lies.  Want to conquer a base?  Sure, you can be all stealthy and tactical if you want to play John Wayne and take the world on by yourself.  But... it is more fun, IMO, to surround the enemy base with a few of your own bases, fully fortified.  Use some rockets to shell their compound while your AI minions fight them.  Numbers.  Have two bases or more.  Maybe three or four for those big bases populated with missile soldiers.
While they do that, go jack a car.  Get the missile spawning perk.  Charge the base and strafe it with missiles.  I do this for hours, laughing maniacally.  I don't know if they have a name for what's wrong with me.

The above-mentioned game features many of the core elements as this one, minus the city-building portion. I only use it as a comparison because it’s entirely free to play vs. the $7 tag this game has.
When you take the difference between the two games, what you essentially get is a $7 voxel city building game, minus the management aspects of Sim City, for your money with this purchase. And even though $7 isn’t much, it’s hard to really justify spending that much on a game that only has one difference from a free to play game of the same genre.
Pros: ability to create your own city; ability to play in the world of your city, interact with residents, purchase land, etc.; freedom to act however you like in said city - rob a bank, build a house, own a business, blow holes in office buildings, etc.
Cons: The destruction advertised feels more like accidentally hitting the delete key when you build something in Minecraft - the blocks vanish and that’s about it; cars don’t respond to any damage and just keep driving like nothing happened (minus falling in a pothole your grenade created); driving is ultra-unrealistic and the controls feel more like playing a 3d game of PacMan, than driving an actual car; cars also lack anything but the most basic of physics relating to being hit by other cars, other than swerving a bit - don’t expect any pin maneuvers or noteworthy crashes; gun fire sounds, looks and feels more like shooting a pellet gun; targets are ridiculously hard to hit, as people just go flailing around wildly when you shoot and they take an insane amount of damage to kill; AI police are also a special level of stupid, failing to go looking for you inside of buildings, even if you never leave the scene of the crime.
Even for an EA game, the list of cons combined with the lack of original features of similar games so far, leaves this game coming up short of what you’d probably expect..

After nearly 4 hours of gameplay in "Dying Light" I'm suffering buyer's remorse.  This game is a good example of what's wrong with current game design and the game press as well.  There is much about this game that is simply frustrating, which is always a bad sign.  There's a mechanic that allows the player to climb utility poles, but NOT if there's equipment you need to get to mounted on the pole.  So you can shinny like a monkey up a bare pole, but can't climb one with equipment on it that could reasonably make the climb easier.  Makes sense, right?  No, I didn't think so either.
Yes, so far the game fulfills the promise of open world, and that's good, and the parkour works fairly well, however the mechanic for timing your jumps doesn't feel right.  Looking down at a soft landing pad, I find myself letting go of the jump control when it looks like my trajectory is good to hit the pad, and it seems the physics just drops you like a rock at that point.  Its as if inertia doesn't exist once you let go of the key, so you plummet to the hard surface adjacent to the pad and take damage.  God forbid you make this mistake jumping for a perch at any decent hight, as missing your target can easily kill you, or take your heath down to such a low point that any random hit from an opponent will finish you off.
Then there are bait and switch setups that have you believing a building you are seeking to enter is a safe zone.  I came back to one I'd found on an earlier mission the day before which was clear of infected then, only to find it had been infested with the creeps when I got back later.  This sort of con is not at all what I'm happy to see in a game I paid good money for.

The main knock against this game is the grind that ruins the entire experience. The whole game seems like it's built to try to get you to buy gold for real money with micro-transactions. Everything from the meager drops from enemies to the fact that you have to pay gold to upgrade the blacksmith to the fact that upgrading weapons and armor always has a failure chance requiring you to spend even more gold. Even the in-game methods of boosting your gold gain almost always come at the expense of experience which in turn prevents you from mitigating the one thing that you're most likely trying to escape from: the grind. The whole time I was playing this I could feel it reaching for my wallet... in spite of the fact that this feature has apparently been removed from the game.
And this is really a shame because it's not a bad game in any other aspect. The combat is the core of the game and, while basic, it's pretty solid. I never found myself feeling overpowered or like there was no aspect of challenge to it; nor did I ever feel like the game had pushed me into a corner where I was helpless. Even though you have very few abilities to choose from, there is depth and strategy in how they're use. The pixel-art backgrounds are good and contain a lot of cool references. It's kinda cool and chilling when you go to an area to level-grind and notice after an hour that slenderman has been standing there the whole time. I personally found the humor a bit flat and irreverent... though also occasionally spot-on speaking as someone who's played the tabletop RPGs this game is supposedly an homage to.
Bottom line: If you like level grinding or have a high enough tolerance for it to see the rest of the experience though then this is the game for you. For me, I've found the game too tedious to play at length and it's not worth spending hours farming gold for the meager amounts of story and the occasional chuckle. Maybe it gets better later on, but it doesn't feel worth it to me to spend the time slogging through it.
And for anyone who says "This is SOOOoo much like D&D"... no, it's not. At least, not if you have a good DM it isn't. ;)
Spoiler alert/warning: Do not side with Marc "I am the wrong horse" Antony. Invest in snake antivenom.

This game requires a little bit of patience.  There will be no hand holding, no quest markers, no arrow pointing you where to go.  You have to explore carefully and thoroughly to make progress.  The beginning in particular will have you poking around town for a good hour or two before you get out to kill undead.
That being said, what a fantastic game.  Remindes me a lot of the old DnD games like Baldur's Gate and Temple of Elemental Evil except you don't need to have the DnD players manual memorized to make reasonable characters :P
The story is an engaging mystery with well paced discovery.  Even the side quests fit well, they never feel repetative or grindy.  You don't walk into towns and just click on every SoB with an exclamation mark over his head, no no.  You actually have to talk to everyone, find out who needs things done, then figure out how to do it.  It's usually much more vague then "bring me 10 bear paws" and many have more then one way to get the job done.
I've never really liked crafting in these games, though the systems here seem fairly robust.  The UI isn't perfect, combining items that exist on different pages of your inventory can require a few clicks, but the combines all seem to have a very natual feel to it that makes sense.
The combat system is fantastic.  The action point system and they way unused action points carry over to the next turn is really good and not something I've seen before.  No one has mana or energy bars, everything boils down to action points and cooldowns.  Normally I dislike playing wizards in RPG's since they tend to just nuke however this game has some great options for support wizards.  I have a wizard with something like 15 spells and only one is a nuke.  Lots of interesting mechanics you don't see in other games, I won't go into too much detail, but as an example, I never thought rain would be such a useful spell.  RAIN?  What other game do you think, hmmm.... I think I should cast rain, in the middle of a fight?
The multiplayer seems pretty slick too, for playing with friends.  I imagine playing with random people would be frustrating as all hell, but great for playing with people you know.

TL;DR
The gameplay is bad, the fun mountains are locked by level requirements,the apparel is pricey, and the gold edition gives you few points for basic customization.
27 minutes and I'm already beyond done with it. Typically, I'd stick through an hour before leaving a review, but this game doesn't bother hiding the plethora of flaws. The biggest? It's Deceitful.
I'll cut right to the chase before going on a bit of a rant. This game tells you that it is all about exploring and finding the best ways to get places, but this is complete and utter garbage designed to lure you in. From the beginning, you notice you have "Helicopter Tickets", which let you get UP mountains....so you can go DOWN them, which is the point of the game. Weeellll those are things you have to buy. You start out with 10, and it costs 4000 points to buy 20, which is the cost of 1 shirt and a low-tier beanie, so it isn't cheap. The biggest and most prominent issue is how EVERYTHING that would make the game fun is locked behind levels. Even a mid-sized mountain is locked behind an xp wall forcing you to be level 20. Rather than giving players the free-to-explore, open environment they're continually told by the game they'll get, they get a small and very bland opening outside of the tutorial. Sure, you could do Missions, but I wanted to do that thing that they even give you points for...e x p l o r e. From level 1, I couldn't even access an area that allowed me to Wing-suit...all the mountains of interest for that were locked by levels.
With that blatant lie out of the way, onto initial impressions.
After an unskippable and dreadfully worthless tutorial that taught me I can indeed use a controller and that my controller does indeed have buttons, I'm finally put into the actual game. The first thing I decided to visit was my character customization, considering I bought the GOLD EDITION, so one would imagine it would come with a few decent things. Not really. I had enough points to buy 3 items that were far from special, and suddenly all my bonus points were gone. I started with about 10 choices of bland jackets and a few decent pants. I had a few beanies to choose from...brown, brown and, oh! Grey! Helmets? Oh look, a lot of things that I need to buy, lest I want the default.
I'm truthfully unsure if you can get the points to unlock things from playing or not, but I'll give it the benifit of the doubt and not really knock it down for this...but considering I got the GOLD edition, which is 60 dollars USD, one would imagine they'd get more.
Let's talk GAMEPLAY.
It's trash.
It is horrible garbage.
The tutorial is typically what you'd want to polish the most to make sure people are sucked in by a false sense of quality...props to this game for just being honest with how awful it is. I live in a snowy place with mountains that almost always are white, and though I'm far from a professional, or even someone who can flip myself through the air, I know how to ski and snowboard. This game doesn't capture the feeling of that in the slightest. Even with the "Safe Trick" option turned off, your board sticks like a magnet to curves in the snow, and the motions in the snow just feel off. It's a lot like when you look at a picture and just know that something is wrong, but can't quite pin what's missing initially, but after looking at if for 5 or so minutes, you realize that the picture is on fire. Something just isn't right.
I'm not one to play games where you snowboard, ski, and so on, but this one offered a lot more than just that, so I figured I'd give it a shot. Much to my dissapointment, I couldn't do anything other than that considering the seemingly endless level locks on a game that so triumphantly claims to be FREE-TO-EXPLORE. Nothing in this game stood out positively except the graphics, and judging it on that would be the same as judging a book by the cover alone. "Wow, great cover art, this is my favorite book! No idea the content, but I adore it already."
TL;DR
The gameplay is bad, the fun mountains are locked by level requirements,the apparel is pricey, and the gold edition gives you few points for basic customization.

Grim Dawn is a very well made ARPG, currently on Early Access.
Graphics : the game is very detailed and good looking, but a bit too dark, I had to increase the gamma just a bit, it's the first game I ever did this. It runs pretty well on my system (i5 3570, gtx770, 8gbs ram) but it has some fps drops which I believe are related to loading from the hard drive. I guess installing it on a SSD would eliminate this.
Sound : not much to say, just average.
Story : well...you are some guy..that has to kill everything on his way! yeah, the story isn't something that got me interested to read any of its lore. Its campaign is quite long though, which is a plus.
Gameplay : it doesnt play any different than the other ARPGs that are out there, you move around killing hordes of enemies, mostly using AOE skills, looting a load of items (dont loot the white ones!), clearing many dungeons,etc. It's a bit tougher than the average, but not much.
Characters : You can choose from 6 classes and after lvl 10 you can choose a subclass, so you have 2 skill sets to spend your skill points on. Combined classes make a new class (eg. Occultist + Arcanist = Warlock). Every time you level up you get 3 skill points and also 1 attribute point to spend on your physique, cunning, spirit and change your stats. There is also the 'devotion' system which adds more skills, mostly passive ones. You can equip your chars with whatever gear you prefer, as the items are not class restricted.
Items : There is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of items you can get, with random stats but they are a bit weird...often low level 'yellow' ones are better than higher level green/blue items. Still waiting for the purple 'Legendary' items to get added to the final game, maybe the rest items will make more sense at the final release.
Crafting : So far, I didn't really feel the need to craft any items, I will take a better look on crafting system once the final game is out.
Overall I would recommend this game to any fan of the genre, it's a really good game without any major flaws and it runs very stable even if its an early access game. Just don't expect to see anything really new that you haven't seen before!

An endearing little choose-your-own-adventure book wrapped into an isometric action-RPG. Your task is to guide the hero, a sword-wielding fox named Reynardo, to something resembling... not a horrible death. And yes, due to the way the game is structured, you will get many great failure endings, some of which may also involve the end of the world. Each playthrough ends with Reynardo's doom, but you keep the character progress as well as the knowledge of your failure to the next. The game alternates between the choose-your-adventure selections, where you choose Reynardo's path, and the actual gameplay sections, where you wander through some exploration areas and carve up the occasional bad bird.
The choose-your-adventure structure is a rather delightful approach, especially given the game's dark yet playful comedy. You'll get to watch all sorts of horrible ends for your hero, albeit solely through the  Unfortunately, though it may seem they had eschewed the traditional march-to-inevitable-victory approach, the game ultimately guides you (through guaranteed failed playthroughs) to a victory playthrough. Nevertheless, you'll have some fun picking up the pieces of what went wrong, then applying those lessons as you go. This also applies to the exploration sections, where you'll have multiple branching paths (depending on how you reached the area) in addition to some locked doors you may not be able to open until a later playthrough.
The combat is a bit of a mixed bag. On the positive side, it's fairly quick and generally not unresponsive-- in particular, the important parrying ability will cancel actions to ensure that you don't get caught on the wrong foot-- er, paw. However, the actions do have some delay afterward, which can feel somewhat awkward if you've been trained over decades to hammer the attack button as quickly as possible. In addition, while it technically works, the decision to essentially make combat 3 buttons (attack, the occasional attack buff trigger, and the the rare grapple) can feel both too automated and too unforgiving. When a large number of attackers pile around you, you're at the mercy of the camera as to whether your attack button press parried the incoming blow, or whether it attacked the nearest opponent and left you open to damage. They had more than enough button real estate to do otherwise, which certainly feels like a missed opportunity. Opponents also lack variety-- there are roughly four enemies in the entire game. Each is quite unique, but there are only so many ways to carve up a mook bird. That's not to say it's bad; it's just not great.
The game is fairly short-- about 5 hours from start to victory state-- but doesn't overstay its welcome. The short and repetitive nature makes it an enjoyable weekend experience, though not earth-shattering. If you want a fun little diversion with a clever narrative conceit, you could do a lot worse than Stories.

Solid character writing, art, sound, and classic turn-based tactical gameplay.  I LOVED the art.  I'm halfway through my second playthrough.  The plot was confusing for a while, with many characters and locations introduced in quick succession, but I got into it after an hour or two.  Waay too many loading screens. Character and inventory management is simple.  Lots of character classes, each with their own unique power, which keeps the combat fresh throughout the game.  The "caravan" mechanic is unique and interesting but shallow.  There are several events that only occur if your caravan has high/low morale, and "war" battles are easier or harder depending on how many fighters you have, but that's pretty much it.  The game has a pretty short campaign that ends abruptly with no resolution to the major plot threads.  There are some unexpected plot twists and upsets and hard choices where the outcome can be permanent loss of characters in your party.  I enjoyed the story so I didn't care, but I could see getting irritated when you lose a character you like because of a single dialogue choice.  You have no warning about what characters are going to show up in later parts of the game, so you will likely waste points leveling up characters who will disappear later.  This game doesn't even visit half of the locations listed on its large detailed map. I only played single-player.  I hope they release followup campaigns.

I would have very likely overlooked this game completely if not for its promotion on
. That is my major bias out there for all to see. But another bias I have is a love for turn-based RPG titles that first bloomed with the original Jagged Alliance.
Even after reading reviews, watching videos and listening to a lengthy discussion of the title, I admit to being unsure as to what sort of game to expect. The gorgeous art style and the fact that it is a turn-based RPG are the only two things I really knew before purchasing the title. Nonetheless, I was almost immediately impressed and addicted soon after.
The Banner Saga is a minimalistic title that some may more bluntly call simplistic. This would be a fair criticism but the game presented a satisfying challenge throughout and most importantly, encouraged me (the player) to live with the decisions I made. This is where the simplicity ends and the nuanced and often dark morality of the title plays out. There aren't really any good or bad decisions to make and I was careful to police myself in accepting the consequences of my actions. This is something that is encouraged with recording progress being restricted to an autosave feature.
Many of the design choices that may superficially seem unsophisticated became sensible after experiencing them. This is true of everything from the combat to the progression system. What was most important to me was that every little choice truly seemed to matter whether immediately or much later in the game.
This certainly isn't a title for everyone but fans turn-based games and especially RPGs are certainly in for a unique experience at the very least.
I eagerly anticipate the sequel.

The Banner Saga: a good game that could've been great (tl;dr version at end)
Don't let that give you a bad impression; like I said, it's a good game. The turn-based combat is satisfying and provides a nice balance of challenge and complexity. The soundtrack is sweeping and epic. The visual design is absolutely gorgeous, very reminiscent of early 90's Disney. The writing is pretty good too, with an pretty interesting and varied cast of characters, as well as a pretty cool setting influenced by Norse mythology.
That said, I felt the setting was a bit clumsily introduced: the game throws a ton of lore and proper nouns at you without adequately explaining a lot of them (for the first half of the game, I had no idea what the hell a "Mender" or "Valka" was).
My biggest complaint is the way the turn system worked: rather than having one side move all their units, then the other side move all their units, it alternates between the two: you, enemy, you, enemy, you, enemy, etc. This means that if you have six people active and the enemy has three, those three will be getting two moves each for each one move for your own people. It's kinda hard to explain in text, but the game essentially punishes you for doing well in combat by giving the enemy more moves the more you whittle down their numbers.
The save system is pretty frustrating too: You only get one uncontrolled autosave file. That's it. No manual saves or multiple save files. Is that too much to ask for, especially in a game like this that features so many different outcomes based on your choice?
tl;dr Great combat aside from the crappy turn system, damn gorgeous visual design and soundtrack, pretty good writing and setting, albeit one that was clumsily introduced. Would benefit greatly from having manual saves.
I still give it a solid recommendation in spite of its flaws

The Banner Saga was a wonderful turn-based strategy game. It's probably one of the more challenging games within the genre. I personally had to play it a little over 2 times through just to get a better foothold on the combat system.
Here are a few observations I can make after playing over 30 hours of the game:
Pro:
- The game is VERY challenging. The jump in difficulty between easy to hard is extremely high and there is a very small room for error in most battles.
- Great visuals. The characters (from the animation to actual design) are amazing. The landscapes are gorgeous and you get to experience them in full as you travel to the final destination.
- Numerous tactical possibilities! When you finish the game for the first time on Normal, you'll be able to decide how you want to invest your resources and who you want to invest them on. This opens up a lot of possibilities when it comes to character placement/formations. Even though there's little room for error when playing on hard, there's a ton of ways to overcome each challenge based on decisions you've made from prior experience.
Con:
- The camera controls are limited. I would have liked to see keys binded to auto-move to each of your characters. You have a max of 6 so f1-f6 or 1-6 would have been nice.
- No key binding. I know there's not a lot of use for the keyboard in this game.. but a skip function to automatically rest for willpower would have been very helpful.
All in all, it's a really good game. There's a lot of things to appreciate in this game and you can tell that a lot of effort was poured into polishing the experience. I hope that this game continues with further installments because I would gladly pay full price for more of this masterpiece!

Though I'm only 18 hours in as of this point, I must say it is the best cRpg I've played... It might not mean much seeing as I've only played baldur's gate 2 and drakensang before this, but this game should set an example to all future RPG games. The interactivity is amazing, if it's not the ground/a building you can interact with it, and in many ways. Even things that would be trivial in other games like crates and barrels, load up your inventory with them, go into combat, and make a maze while you're in combat, or sneaking around and dropping them off while you scurry back a safe distance to initiate.
Another thing that stands out is that EVERY stat/talent/ability matters, and you should have each member be varied in what they're expertised in so that you have someone for every situation. Perception lets you spot secrets/traps/switches, and is even needed for discovering things in the main story to continue so it's not just a trivial stat that you can reload every time you step on a trap, Having a character with leadership grants a boost to your whole parties initiative, damage, precision and so forth. Having a loremaster lets you identify items, enemies, and objects... and so on.
The crafting system is pretty nice too, generally if you think two items should combine they generally do. For example, a branch + nine inch nails would make a spiked club, though if things don't combine you may need a higher crafting level :P.
There's absolutely NO hand holding, past a few tutorial popups which just tell you the basics, When you're initiating a quest, you're expected to read through and actually find this location without any help markers, no ignoring the story you must read some of the finer details.
The things I've listed above are only what's on the surface, It's a very deep and detailed game, and compared to modern rpgs, a godsend. I wholly recommend this to anyone who is interested in classic rpgs, and even modern rpg fans (though the difficulty may be a bit much for a casual ;), there is an easy setting... I haven't tried it though, I hear it's much easier than default though.)

You start out as a random male character with no choice about it. The beard broke my immersion from the first ride. Finally, after completing the training exercises, I was allowed to choose my avatar. That is just insane. You should not have to level up to a female character. I grant it may seem like a small point to some people. After selecting one of the 3 female choices, & the costume, I realized I would have to reselect for every event. Not fun anymore. Most of us are here for the immersion.
The game has a heavy focus on competition. I wanted to explore the mountains and ride for the thrill. I enjoyed the wingsuit and would have liked to explore while gliding. Instead, it’s all marked out as competitions. I had in mind more of an open world sandbox with optional challenges. I was never able to find where to ride the balloons. And, probably because of the competition focus, even the single player requires you to always be online.

Some guy (voiceover) is setting the agenda for you. You don’t choose where, what, or when you play which sport. You often don’t know when he is switching you to a different sport until you are there and you have a different suit on. Sounds more like a job than a game. In many games you are self-defining. Like in American Truck Driver, you choose to take the jobs you want, & set your own routes. In The Hunter: Call of the Wild, you have an open world to travel around camping, hiking, & hunting. You can totally ignore the missions, or do them on your own timeframe & order.

In Steep, you are constantly seeing the missions in your face. And, you don’t travel from place to place. Instead, you teleport instantly from one competition to another. I have no idea how you would explore in those conditions. This creates a series of mini-games that you complete in a linear fashion. It seemed sort of like an amusement park with teleporting from ride to ride, but you had to follow the guide instead of choosing your own rides.
Some people may go for the mini-game eye-candy, because it did seem picturesque at each destination. The instant replay director mode allows good screenshots. But, getting there could have been part of the fun. After all, if I visit the Grand Canyon, I won’t teleport instantly. I’ll drive cross country or fly, and enjoy the view through the windows. Steep is not a whole map. It’s just spots on a map.

This whole game is trial and error guesswork that's clearly designed to screw you.

As soon as I played XCOM: Enemy Unknown for the first time, it quickly became my personal SOTY (surprise of the year). You play as the XCOM commander and an enormous weight sits in your shoulders since no decision is easy when you are at war.  Decisions will be made right from the very first time you play the game weather on choosing some locations above others, depending on what advantages each brings to the table as well what technologies you want to focus first. Strategy is key in both combat and the XCOM facility. It’s not about simply erasing any possible threat but also trying to capture some species for further analysis and study as well to bring more researches that can improve your armory and fleet giving you a better chance at surviving. It is also wise to build a squad in different ways, using different skills in the battle so you can be ready for the most scenarios the game will throw at you.
If you let immerse yourself during the brief introduction to the Story you will get a sense of constant panic and terror due to the global alien invasion showing no mercy killing everyone, civilians and soldiers. While the strength of XCOM is the pure strategy gameplay there will be plenty of time for you to get a raw sense of fear, as well for most of your untrained soldiers since panic will also be part of the battle and will influence their behavior during critical times.
Paying and attention and playing the Tutorial will be very useful in the game but later on you will learn from your own trial & error experiences. While some strategies can work based on some luck, other will require for you to grab every single chance and make every single bullet/turn counts. Difficulty can be a bit harsh if you are not used to genre but believe me, it’s worth learning the basic stuff. I would say that Easy difficulty felt like Normal and Normal sometimes felt like Hard (and so on). If you are a truly adventurer and fearless commander, higher difficulties will put your patience, skills and strategy to the test during every single turn.
The soundtrack is minimal since it’s not a big focus on this game but I felt quite excited each time I was in my paramilitary facility and I became aware of a new threat. The music right when you choose which member will fill your squad to fight in battle give you a decent sentiment of anxiety making you eager to find the next battle location, type of terrain, possibility of new threats and so on.
In the end, XCOM: Enemy Unknown proved to be a time sink, but a good one, there’s no doubt. There is plenty of options for you to make the game adjustable according to your difficulty preferences and there’s a decent amount of content while pushing for new technologies, new weapons, new armor and suits and new ways to fight the enemy. Make your choices wisely, time is short, resources are limited and remember, you can’t save everyone so expect losses in the battlefield without forgetting to extract wisdom from each battle, won or lost.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown is to the original XCom what Wasteland 2 is to the Fallout series. You recognise the game and what they were going for but something is missing. Somehow you don't get the feeling that you actually care for your little soldiers and that is the difference between them. I.. just.. don't.. care.. about.. them.
I remember in the original XCom that I had characters, maybe because a bug.. I don't remember now, that actually had so much XP that they started over. You cared about them like they were your own flesh and blood. They were your go-to guys that could save a battle and your noob soldiers could safely earn their wings in their shadows.
I remember the creeping feeling when you cut through the fog of war only to realise that you had overstreched your squad a bit and suddenly you had one guy alone with a Chrysalis. That actually sent chills down the spine. And also that feeling when you aced some tactical manouver and totally overwhelmed the aliens to the degree that they paniced.
You truly felt like Napoleon. The general of generals. Invinsible.
Now, whith that said Enemy unknown is a good game. No doubt about it. It's visually stunning and they also kept that randomness to the missions so you don't know exactly what to expect when you answer a call for help from some town somewhere in the middle of nowhere. You can't just relax and use the same tactics over and over. You have to assess the situation and place your squad carefully. Snipers to cover the assult guys that needs to have a medic close by just in case someone gets an unhealthy dose of plasma. Running like Rambo into a fight is a safe ticket back home in a body bag. Not watching your flanks, well.. you will realise quickly that the wall you thought would cover you isn't worth it's mortar when you suddenly have an enemy outflanking you and certainly didn't do the same mistake as you.
A tactical grenade and you have an opening into a house where you suddenly have the drop on the aliens. A bit of cover fire and you can move up into grenade distance and give the slimy little buggers a leadpoisoning they will regret for the rest of their short lives.
So.. is it living up to the great scores it got? Or is it just a little over hyped becase people were starving for a follow up? I think it's somewhere inbetween. It certainly has a ton of good stuff going for it but I really miss the feeling I had in the original game. Somehow it's a bit too cartoony. Somehow the challenge is that your guys suddenly can't hit a barn from the inside while the enemy is laserbeam accurate.
Is it difficult? Yes. Very much so. And that is what we want. But if you take your time and learn how to use your resources both in the base and on the battlefield, it is very rewarding. It also have that randomness, which I assume can happen in a real war, when you suddenly get hit by a stray bullet and it's game over. Of course you can choose how to play it, but I always like to do a little role playing and that means that if a guy is dead.. well.. then he's dead. Regardless of the impact. No reloads because of that.
So, should you buy it? Certainly. If you are into RTS and especially turn based battles then it's a no brainer. Like Derek says in Bad Taste:
"There's no glowing fingers on these ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, we've got a bunch of Extra-Terrestrial psychopaths on our hands, like a visit from a planet full of Charlie Mansons, they've started on something small, its my guess they'll go onto something bigger next time, Christchurch, Wellington..."
Or just "Stick all the bits of brain in a plastic bag, Barry. We'll need them for analysis."

Mirror's Edge. Painfully tedious at times, too heavily reliant on guns, unimpressive combat.
And yet, the best parkour game out there, probably. (Until ME: Catalyst comes out.)
Worth buying if you like these kinds of games.
Parkour was not a theme commonly used in games until recently. So when Mirror's Edge came out no doubt people would have been excited. And as a person that enjoys Titanfall, I think it's got the best first-person mobility on the market. (ME, not Titanfall, great game though it is.)
But the fluidity came at a cost. I can't help but feel DICE tried too hard to make it part-FPS. The combat breaks the smooth free feel of the game, unless you just run away. They're fixing this in Catalyst, making the combat more parkour-based, which is only good news. So, that's another box ticked for fans of the game.
One of ME's best qualities was that, in theory, most chapters could be beaten in one fluid run, without stopping. And it does a good job of replicating the adrenaline-filled leaps of faith that comes with rooftop running.
And you can't help but admire the art style of the city. It's a beautiful landscape of white and red that can hardly be put into words. It has to be experienced.
Except that you're kind of trapped in small areas in the levels. But, again, DICE is adressing this and giving Catalyst the open world that the original desperately needed.
To summmarise:
Good parkour
Bad mostly everything else, but that doesn't matter
Easy on the eyes - very easy
Needs open world and better fighting (both happening, thanks DICE)
Buy this if you can't be bothered to climb a building and jump off roofs yourself.

A great ARPG.
Sometimes a little to dark (however upping the gamma makes it look odd... just needs a few less shadows) but the art style is terrific & player characters are highly customizable.
While I think Diablo 3 looks better I think this has the better game play in every way except perhaps crafting.
This has a fairly in depth crafting system but there's no way to customize say a sword or helmet. The item you craft comes with set stats & then random stats on to which you can add a component (for diablo 2 players - a rune or gem basically). However unlike some other (A)RPGs you can't ensure your sword has a bonus to undead attacks or similar during.
Off to a slow early access start the game is very polished at this point & coming along nicely. Updates seem to be more regular than in the beginning & updates now seem to add something that's fairly exciting each time.
Monster variety is fairly standard for an ARPG but the reputation system adds a bit of flavour to the various factions you encounter. While it adds a bit of flavour it is mostly pointless & just makes it seem a bit more dynamic as in the end you'll kill enough of enemy factions to become the most hated etc.
Monsters scale roughly to your level making the challenge stay fairly steady if you back track however it also means that level 30 monsters in the area that used to be the starting level makes it seem like you have less character progression then you do. That said it in no way ruins the fun.
Over all one of the best ARPGs I've ever played being every bit on par with Diablo 2. More balanced then Titan Quest Immortal Throne & more in depth then The Incredible Adventures Of Van Helsing this game is well worth the North American price attached to it.

If you're a fan of Infinity era RPGs, the only reason you still haven't bought DOS is that you're afraid of yet another Larian child having come to life with three arms and one leg. After 12 hours, I have to conclude that, surprisingly, it seems to have the correct amount of parts in the right places. The graphics are pretty, UI is practical, gameplay is smooth and the story is coherent (at least so far). Despite that, nowadays even a good single player game where you have to spent hours just going around talking to NPCs and get excited over it is usually not enough to deter most people from playing their Counter Strikes, Dotas or what have you instead. Luckily, unless the developers consider split personality disorder fun, the game is intended to be played in co-op, which dramatically changes the experience for the better, although it takes time getting used to reading the dialogues in the chat log or having your friend retell them to you. There are a few other flaws like: long loading times, weird choice of music for some encounters, not enough ways to customize the look of your character, stealing and breaking in almost always goes unpunished unless you're doing it in plain sight etc. It's really not that big of a deal, especially  considering that the game supports modding and the developers are actively patching it as well. If you have a good friend willing to spend his precious time exploring the intricacies of Rivellon with you, I'd strongly recommend buying it. If you're a lonely nerd longing for a proper RPG game, pick it up and you won't be disappointed. Otherwise, keep playing Dota.

One of the best city builders I've ever played and also has the distinction of being the first I ever played, when I was an 8 year old kid obsessed with Ancient Egypt. I've also tried other city builders since then,  but I always come back to Pharaoh.
Pharaoh is a challenging experience with a fantastic premise, even though the game graphically has not aged well. It's still a very strong example of a city builder done well, and is the benchmark upon which I judge other games in the genre.
When it comes to the technical, the game runs a bit fast on launch, but those settings can be changed in options. Crashing seems to be an issue for others, but I did not have that happen after playing the game for 2 hours straight. I'm not sure if it's been patched or it's just my computer, but that common problem does not seem to be mine. Resolution for wide screen is not great, but I believe a patch has come out for that problem, so check for that if that's a deal breaker for you.
All in all, this is a great version of a classic game that I cannot recommend enough if you like the genre.
