I'm going to go ahead and give this a thumbs up, because it is a good game, but there are some issues with it. I'll label pros and cons.
Pros
Beautifully designed - Despite this game coming out in 2008, this game looks like it was created with today's graphics. It's really pretty and that alone almost makes the game worth playing.
Parkour game - I don't know about you but I've never heard of a parkour game before this came out, and it really shines a light on it. If you want to do parkour without risking injury, this is a good way to do it!
Characters - The characters are awesome (except Celes but that's my opinion lol). They are all really believable, and Faith.... Well, Faith is just awesome.
Cons
Lack of some tutorials - For instance, I went through most of the game, not knowing I could pick up dropped weapons. **SPOILER ALERT** I didn't find out until I went to save Faith's sister and found out you could pick up the sniper rifel. It's the same with the zoom option on weapons. If they did mention it in the tutorial, it must have been a text reference and I didn't see it.
Clunky controls - It took me most of the game to get used to them, and even after that, I couldn't always get Faith to do what I wanted her to. Like the backwards jump is really strange. I still couldn't do it half the time because the buttons are really weird. Also, slowing time does not garauntee you'll be able to disarm your opponent. I don't expect it to, but even when I did hit it at the right moment, I ended up getting hit. The opposite also happened.
Storyline - The story behind it is really wierd and convoluted. Some facets of it are believable, but it seems really rushed. I like stories in games to be very detailed and this one just isn't.
Very short - My game is showing 8 hours of game play. At least 2 of those were spent redoing areas where the controls went wonky or I had trouble getting past a certain part because I was unsure of where I was going, and one hour of that was spent on the pause screen, doing some chores and eating lunch. I expect that out of like God of War, but I expected this to be much longer than it actually was.
No Replay Value - Once you're finished with the story campaign, there's almost no replay value. Unless you want to go back and get the runner's bags, there's not really any point in going through it again. I suppose you can lump that in with no achievments, but I really don't care about achievments to begin with, but I know there are some out there that really go all out on that.
Conclusion
All in all, it has a lot of issues, and while it's not my type of game, I would still consider it a good game. It might just be that I'm not used to reactionary based games, so that might be my problem. I would still recomend it to someone, with a word of caution.

Simply a must for any ARPG fan.
Recently started a play of the game on hardcore mode, if you'd like to see it in action:
This little gem is pretty easily overlooked, yet I would say easily stands among the top ARPGs of all time.
Crate Entertainment has many of the vets from Titan Quest, and from what I've heard the game is running an enhanced version of the TQ engine, complete with the hilariously fun physics. (Which is not bad at all, if you look at how amazingly well TQ has aged.)
The pedigree shows here. The game is solid, and well polished. It includes many of the features you'd like to see in games of this sort as well.
Love ARPGs and multiplayer, but sick of other players grabbing all the good loot? Turn on instanced looting and it won't be a problem anymore. Everyone gets their own drops. Brilliant. You can even turn off all PVP and automatically put joining players in your party if you fancy the more coop style play; or keep it on if that's what you prefer.
Unlike certain other AAA titles, GD won't force you to go through the pathetically easy difficulty settings to unlock the next harder mode. You can start playing in veteran mode right off the bat, even with hardcore. (Though to get above that you will need to beat the campaign.)
The story is about as good as you'd expect for an ARPG. It has an interesting mix of things that if nothing else, give you a decent reason to go about slaughtering hordes of enemies.
The game does shake things up a bit to it's credit though. There are certain big bosses that may or may not spawn in your game (it's a chance thing, it seems), and their level scales, meaning you're going to be in for a fight no matter what level you try to take them on. There are secret areas, side quests, even secret people hiding out there that you can rescue and send back to your "base camp" which may lead to other quests or options in the future.
I stumbled across a man in the desert who asked me to avenge him, found the guy who he wanted me to kill, but instead of killing him and stealing his money, listened to his side of the story, and actually sided with him. He ended up showing up later in the game as a vendor for me because of it.
There are many little details and subtle things like that in the game, where seemingly little choices you make will have an impact on the game world. I love the way this makes the game world feel a touch more dynamic.
Customization is great as well. While you can't change your character's appearance much other than being a male or female, that's not a huge deal since you're gonna be suited up in all kinds of armor anyways. Skills and such are laid out in a very similar fashion to Titan Quest, if you've ever played that. (And if you haven't, you really should.) Meaning you can pick and choose how you upgrade your skills with a certain degree of freedom, and from level 10 on, you can even mix and match with skills from a second class.
On top of that, there's the huge devotion system to further kit out your character, and turn them into a horde slaying machine. (Something you'll be doing a lot of on higher difficulties, as swarms of enemies are plentiful.)
Aesthetically the game is quite dark and gritty. At first I was a bit put off by the whole Victorian styling and setting, it's quite unique and almost... weird. The more I played it though, the more I found myself enjoying it. It is different, and in this case, different is good.
TL/DR:
With a fairly lengthy campaign, and a substantial amount of polish, you've got yourself easily one of the best, yet least known Diablo rivals out there. (Personally I'd take GD over D3 any day of the week.) And coming in at only $25? What's not to love?

i miss story-centric adventure games a lot.  so, when i saw that this particular game had that in spades, i couldn't help but pick up a copy and started in on playing it.  if this is you, too, then you should absolutely get hold of this game.  perhaps not at full price, but you should certainly own it, if you loved the "choose your own adventure" books of the 80's, or just miss story-based gaming/adventure gaming at all.
there are mild implementation issues, which is why i wouldn't recommend it at full price, but we'll talk about those in a minute.
stories is an action rpg in the diablo vein.  enemies come at you and you use your sword-skills to kill those enemies off.  when you're not fending off a horde of ravens, you're making choices about how the story should flow.  so, each mission consists of:
until, at last, you come to a proper story conclusion.  if you've done certain "sections" of the game, you learn a truth and these truths help you uncover "how to find your way to the True Path so you can get the "actual ending"" [and not one that results in Something Terrible.]
this idea is great and the feeling of sort of stumbling blindly about, trying things until you figure out that "one true ending" is absolutely rewarding in the sense that the game keeps dropping little lore bombs all the time.  sure, you'll see one area several times, but each new run brings new information, related by the fantastic narrator.  in this way, the world and people of the world are wonderfully layered.
speaking of the people:  everyone here is a talking animal.  reynardo is a fox, his war buddy lapino is a rabbit.  the emperor, isengrim iii is a toad.  his adopted daughter is a cat.  they inhabit a wondreful, stylized world of floating isles that contain their cities and libraries and palaces.  each of these characters is a joy to meet and a joy to learn about, because - unlike most folks who have been written into a game, they are dense and have histories and one of the very best things about stories is discovering their backstories while you work your way through the levels.
this layered approach - revealing things slowly and peeling back the stories is fine, until...and the problem is that the "until" arrives pretty quickly.  unfortunately, while the narration is spot on and while the act of slaying bad guys is fulfilling, you end up seeing the same basic places over and over again and you end up hearing the same narration over and over again.  these twin things wouldn't be
bad if you could skip them, but you can't.  so, you will hear all about how the "clouds part over boreas" more times than you can count [especially if you're achievement hunting.]
there are related problems:  as a result of the way stories is set up, you will only fight a handful of enemy types - now, certainly, it's true, each raven does require a certain amount of finessing, but at some point, you'll get hero path rewards that suck
of the true challenge out of the game, leaving you desperately zipping across maps to see the new bits of story, rather than engaging with the enemies.
this title is all about excess, to some degree.  that excess is tied very heavily to the sheer, dumb number of stories on display, here.  there are so many, in fact, that i feel lots of folks will get fatigued by just what they're tasked with doing if they want to do a full run of the game.  i'm currently at 34 hours and i've "finished" the stories.  all i need to do is get my character to the maximum level to get all the skill points...and that's going to take a while, too.
and it is these little design flaws that ding it from a must have to a "must have with caveats."  watch a bit of a playthrough before buying, or if you're sure you're going to buy, but not sure you're in it for the long haul, buy it at a discount.

Reviewers sometimes would put Mirror's Edge as an underrated gem next to titles like Beyond Good and Evil, Enslaved or Spec Ops: The Line. Don't get me wrong, this isn't a bad game, it just doesn't live up to all the hype. Here's why:
Combat is a mess. Shotting feels forced an unncessary. The amount of time takes you to take bad guys' guns away from them is just enough for surrounding enemies to shoot you with pinpoint accuray. Of course, if you run out of ammo, you need to drop the gun you're holding and find some other lucky contestant currently unloading at you and involve in a painful timed takedown. For whatever reason, you cannot pick up guns from the floor.
Slowing down time is useless. Makes takedowns even harder since your button-smashing don't register even though you time them right. This feature also doesn't work outside combat though could make some stunts easier to produce.
The story is there to keep you running - won't spoilt it for you, it's as cliché as it gets making little to no sense whatsoever. Oh, and about the running: basically it's there to make the game a little less boring. Yes, you heard me right. What DICE did is they took Prince of Perisa (or any other parkour game), put it in a first person perspective, and made it lifeless, dull, and repetitive. Because animating all the streets and pedestrians was for some reason a no-no, you are running on the rooftops, which is as exciting as it sounds. You watch the skies, jump on top of cubic buildings, ventilation shafts and chimneys, fall down, and repeat. To break the monotony, you sometimes go into office buildings, construction sites and a boat, none of these interiors you haven't seen a million times in other games.
The graphics are polished enough, but the city is so cold and lifeless that even the running gets old quite quickly. The occasional rats and pigeons breathe some life into the surroundings, but apart from them you only get your snipers, cops, heavies and a few other enemies to keep you entertained. The animations are indie-like cartoons, and sometimes do no service to the story. My favorite cutscene is when your antagonist, Faith is running for about a minute in a 2D perspective. That's all to it, there's no added drama. I also 'love' when you are standing inside an elevator for two minutes, or in the back of a truck not being able to do anything - these events just make the 'adventure' a good few minutes longer, serving no other purpose.
The guy giving you directions through the earplant sounds like he's heart rate is at 220 all the time even though all he does is sit at a computer while you do all the dirty work for him. Chillax, man! One last thing that annoyed the hell out of me was that everytime you jump, climb or hit the ground, you sound like you're being gang♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ You remember how in old FPS games you made an 'UGH' sound everytime you jumped and landed? Here it is again, on a high pitch, for your audio pleasure.
Lastly the difficulty is unbalanced like sh*t, at times you just get from A to B, and at times a hundred cops are shooting at you (that you cannot return as described earlier) while you're trying to figure out where the heck you were supposed to go. Checkpoints are placed often enough, but you are forced to sit/skip through the scripts and cutscenes at some of the stages, which, needles to say is also a pain in the butt. So, is this a terrible game, you might ask? No, it's not, it's just passable and should not be on a piedestal. But at least it's cheap when on sale.

Let me start off by saying that I actually liked this game. However, there's A LOT of small problems with the game that make it not very fun or enjoyable. I was really excited to play this and was pretty disappointed halfway through and was completely over it by the end.
- The class and character system
This had the potential to be really cool and in-depth but classes are limited to 4 abilities and never change. There aren't any skill trees or advancing skills, you get the same 4 skills from the beginning to the end, the only thing changing are the numbers tied to each skill. This got boring really fast. The unique character system is kind of pointless, characters range from useful, to slightly useful, to pointless. Who would you rather have, the guy with +3 attack or the guy who only has +1 attack? The guy with +5 health who's more likely to live or the guy who costs -50% gold to revive after he dies because he sucks? Most of them are just pointless, especially after you unlock the game devs and restart your game.
-Lack of plot
I know that this is supposed to be more of a comedy/parody type thing, and I appreciated the humor, but the whole lack of an actual plot just made the game feel even more boring when you tie in the tedious and boring gameplay.
-Boring gameplay
Just keep clicking on the same skills over and over. Fight mobs without any sort of auto-battle or anything to streamline grinding (and trust me, there's a lot of grinding). On a PC this is the worst thing. Obviously if you have a touch screen computer (like I do) or play this game on a mobile platform (which obviously isn't the Steam version) then it's not so bad but still. Sitting there and clicking the same♥♥♥♥♥♥over and over gets boring really fast. The beginning of the game is fun because you're still new to everything and your skills and levels are rising fast, but everything plateaus equally as fast, especially the fun.
-Gold system
Everything in this game costs gold except for leveling up. Consumables cost gold, accessories cost an obscene amount of gold, TRAVELING costs gold (this is one of the stupidest things ever), reviving your dead characters cost gold and most quests cost gold as a result of traveling (despite them usually refunding the gold, if you don't have the initial gold you will have to grind). Now, this doesn't SOUND like that big a deal, but grinding gold is unbelievably slow. You can spend about half an hour to grind about 1000 or so gold through the early to mid game. To upgrade all of your characters' armor from lvl1 to lvl2 would cost roughly 1000+ and that's assuming you succeed because upgrading equips usually has a 50% and below chance to upgrade unless you invest either MORE GOLD or grind mines to upgrade your blacksmith. There's upgrades that increase your gold income rate but they don't do very much. The whole thing is just terrible.
There's not much the game does right, but what they actually DO right is pretty good.
+Balance
This is one of the few indie/joke/whatever RPGs that has actual balance. Most of them either don't try to have any semblance of balance and are too easy just so they can spout more ♥♥♥♥♥♥ memes. This actually feels like a really well done game and the battle mechanics were well thought out. It doesn't feel like there are any OP classes. Yeah, the rogue and hunter are really strong, but they're not overpowered. The game is decently challenging from beginning to end and never feels too easy or ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t hard. This is pretty hard to do so I have to commend the creators.
+Humor
This is a pretty funny game, lots of humor and lightheartedness, but it's an actual game. There are way too many ♥♥♥♥♥♥ indie games that just try to shove unfunny jokes everywhere and lack actual content. This game has both and once again, the creators did a good job.
Overall thoughts: I actually liked this game and had a good time playing it, it just has a lot of flaws. However, I also only paid about $4 for this and the DLC. If I had paid the full $15 for both I would have been extremely upset as this game does not provide for more than a couple of dollars worth of entertainment. As far as replay value goes, I don't want to ever play this again. It'll just remind me of how disappointed I was the first time playing it. If you can grab it for a couple of dollars (preferably the mobile version, avoid the steam version) go for it, but don't bother paying full price for this.

I've played this game many times, beaten it just as much too (only if Faith was acting up ;) ), not once got bored.
However it seemed the more that I played it, the less focussed I was in getting to the ending. Instead I just runned around, jumped on and off things, trying to find hidden, secret places and spots where you just weren't suppossed to be.
All in all this game was fun.
Pros:
-----
- Great graphics, the fact that there mainly are 3 prevailing colors (white, red and blue) just give it an unique feel
- Intense moments, when jumping from building to building not trying to fall face first onto the pavement 30stories    below always gets my heart going
- Not action oriented, I know some games that are the same yet are filled with action like you're suppossed to be some kind of surgeon yet you have to kill a bunch of aliens everytime you go to work. This game doesn't Faith isn't a fighter and even though you can partipate in the action, it usually is better if you don't because you will have to retry several times.
- Nice open feel. Again I know a lot of games that claim to have the same yet you are kept on a short leash the entire time. Here you can but not always, goof around, trying to find the obscure runner bags which I still haven't found all of. But I remember this one time when some freak glitch happened and I had managed to get on street level, some weird...things happen down there.
- Fluent control. Well at least most of the times, sometimes you'll run so fast and nail that perfect jump with the even more perfect landing. While other times, you'll get fried on some electric fences or take the one-way-express-elevator down. But working on your ingame parcour skills is what's most fun, doing all your moves in superspeed and getting from A to B in the quickest and most dangerous way possible
But no game is perfect
Cons:
------
- Confusing level design. Or maybe it's only me, but first time playing it I got stuck a lot. Didn't know where to go, sometimes I could spent up to an hour searching for where I was suppossed to go, other times there was an added pressure because I was being chased by a lot of guys with guns. I only had my feet...they are not faster than a hailstorm of bullets. When I haven't played it in a year I forget I run in the same problems, only they don't take as long anymore.
- Restrictions. Yes what I said earlier about open feel is still true, yet it isn't open world or sandbox. But it should've been, you can goof around as much as you like but you can't go further than the game lets you each level. You still have to go from A to B, how you do is up to you.
- Action. Must be a first for me where I actually think the action is kinda...forced, phoned in. Don't get me wrong, the action is fun, but this isn't an FPS. So therefor it shouldn't feel like one, there are some moments in the game when you are forced to pick up a gun and shoot someone. Like I said earlier, Faith isn't a fighter yet she can use 9mms, shotguns, sniper rifles and heavy machine guns all with deadly accuracy. But you will run slower with a gun and you can't mount objects either, you can I supposse avoid most if not all combat situations but for me it shouldn't even have been in there.
- Difficulty. This game can be pretty hard, but my point is actually at a more personal level. I don't expect that anyone agrees with me over this it's just me. I don't like the fact that in a higher difficulty setting 'Runner Vision' gets turned off. For those that don't know, any object you can use to get to your objective becomes red. This is the games way of saying, you need to use this. I understand without this vision the game becomes harder but for me not seeing splashes of red in a sea of whiteness destroys the entire game's feel. I really like the abscenes of most colors, everytime you see any other color it looks a bit odd because of it. But in the end this won't affect the scoring in anyway.
- Length. This game is too short! It's really short, you'll have fun, you'll get stuck, you'll be back on your way and then it's done.
Would I recommend this? Yes of course, if you actually had read any of it you wouldn't even be asking.
Overall score I'd give it an 8/10 for being a great game, in this world where they are but a few.

Reynardo the fox tumbles through a multitude of adventures to save the world (or destroy it) in Stories: The Path of Destinies. The best way I could describe the “story” of this game would be to liken it to one of those “choose your own adventure” novels where you are placed at several plot forks at different times, each leading to its own eventual “ending”. Like the books, a failed or undesired ending sends you right back to the beginning to start anew. By completing certain storylines you can unlock four “truths” and ultimately use them to find the final true ending.
This game features a great deal of combat, most of which is fairly simple and straightforward. Reynardo automatically homes in on the nearest enemy when you press the attack key and you can zip between multiple enemies by aiming towards your next target when you press it again. Occasionally there are different enemy types that will require you to dodge spells, disarm shields, or otherwise prioritize them over the regular raven enemies. At combat’s conclusion, you are rated by your style and flawlessness and given a score that becomes your experience point yield. Levelling up allows you to invest in a skill tree that has many options to lighten the overall difficulty of combat in the game. In addition, you can find various ores and components to craft new swords with new abilities including the option to unlock special element-based doors leading to slot-able gems that give their own unique abilities and boosts.
Stories TPoD is really fun for the first few hours, but after I managed to unlock most of the skill tree and find the gems I wanted, I realized some sad “truths” of my own. The special large chests you unlock seem to follow a set order of gem and component contents, meaning you can obtain all the gems simply by doing the same ones over and over again. Also speaking of repetition, the nature of this game demands that you go over previously encountered storylines and not all of it is skippable. This can be incredibly tedious at times and often I found myself wondering why I couldn’t just start my next “beginning” further up the plot tree. Combat gets repetitive too once you have abilities like ultimate sword-fu and the energy on kill gem, allowing you to slay loads of ravens with button mashing and elemental sword AoE damage.
Truth be told, I still enjoyed this game a lot but I wish the developers had considered implementing a sort of fast forward button or maybe a tree-chart that allowed you to choose different story nodes, skipping all the ones you had done already. Thankfully, reaching the true ending really only requires 4 play-throughs for the truths and I managed to figure them out by chance on my 6th playthrough. If it had taken much longer though, I’m not sure how eager I would have been to continue playing as the repetitiveness would have definitely gotten to me. Consider looking up a spoiler free truths guide, if there is one, for the best initial experience and leave all the alternate outcomes to the completionists.

Allow me to preface this review by saying that I do like it and that this is an increbily fun game. That being said, there are big flaws that are constantly nagging at me, slowly becoming worse as I continue to play. I DO recommend this game, and also kinda not. I'll try to explain below.
Let's start with the positives:
- Each job feels unique.
The jobs are varied significantly, each having their own abilities and "hat" that goes onto the player's. The players themselves each have a skill that they bring to the table and it's fun to min/max or switch out players with different jobs to see what they would work best as.
- The art direction is classic and very colourful.
The art direction reminds me a lot of the older FF games, and a few other sprite-based games that were brought out in the 90s and early 2000s. It's simple, colourful, and nice to look at. Nothing is too washed out and the colour choice isn't offensive to the eye.
- Cute references to Sci-Fi and Fantasy stories.
There are TONS of references to various shows, books, movies, ect littered throughout the game world. It's cute seeing the Tardis in the desert or fighting a Ninja Turtle in the sewers. I won't spoil any more for anyone reading this review, but I will say that if you don't mind referential humour then you will certainly enjoy many bits of this game.
- The music can be pretty enjoyable.
The music is simple, but not in a bad way. It feels a bit like the old Mario games in places. I'm afraid I can't really elaborate on exactly what I mean, sufficed to say that the music fits the areas that it's in.
So what about the negatives? Well, I'm afraid that this is where a majority of my review is going to be focused. There are quite a lot of issues littered throughout the game that bug me and I'll try to elaborate on why that is.
- The referential humor.
Okay, I know what you're all thinking, "Hey, didn't you just list that as a positive?" Well, yes, and it is... However, I also feel it's a bit of a negative. This game is a little too busy referencing so many things that it's a bit hard to tell where the references end and the original content begins. For instance, most of the player characters are references to either real life people or fictional people. Which this doesn't bother me too much, I do feel like it wasn't really needed. Is it really so hard to come up with original player characters? Well, apparently not, I mean, there are some. So why did we need a Paris Hilton or Ramona Flowers allusion? Also, the "Game Dev Gang" joke was cute at first but it got old way too fast. I may be the only one that's really bothered by this but this is a bias review so... Yeah.
- Job abilities.
Simply put? There aren't enough/ They're too easily unlocked. The jobs -are- still distinct from one another, I can't take that away. However, there's something to be said about being limited to four abilities. That, of course, being "why?" I'm not ignorant, I know you can only realistically fit in so many on a game that was originally a mobile game- but, this isn't a mobile platform I'm playing it on, this is the PC edition. Why are jobs so limited? Some jobs have 2 passive abilities and 2 abilities you need to activate. That doesn't seem right to me. For example: The Cleric job has a focus heal, a group heal, a divine attack that restores HP, and a Attack down debuff that spreads to 3 enemies. Those are all fine and dandy, but why doesn't it have a manner of Dispel? How about a passive ability to not be harmed by Divine attacks or something along those lines? This may be a nit-pick, but this is what was nagging me as I use certain characters. Now, that being said, I also feel that being able to unlock any of a job's abilities at any level is... Questionable. Again, might just be a nit-pick, maybe it only bothers me.
- Enemy Encounters.
I'll keep this one short: Add a 'random' option to the 'enemy choice' screen. I get what they're going for, allowing the player to pick the enemies your group encounters so as to best simulate both the DM and Player experience, but I don't feel like you should -always- have your cake and eat it like that. Dungeons are good for random encounters.
- Missing Dialogue/ Lack of Personality for the Players
There are moments in the various quests or on the world map when your players are either talking to an NPC or casually interacting with the "DM" of the group that, honestly, feel like they have dialogue missing from them. For instance, sometimes I'll have completed a quest and the NPC will say something along the lines of, "Oh, thank you! You're so helpful." I'll click to go to the next bit of dialogue, presumebly what the player would say to the NPC, but there's... Nothing. A blank screen that I click through to go to my quest rewards. What? It's even worse when there are times where an entire half of a conversation is missing- or the players don't react to what was said in any realistic manner. The grammar has mistakes on occasion, as well. So, the dialogue seems missing. That's a pretty big problem in-and-of itself, but then you couple that with none of the players, DMs, NPCs, even the enemies, having -any- kind of distinct personality? Well, that just rubs me the wrong way. In this age of having defined characters, enemies, and even monsters in our stories, this feels lazy. Hopelessly lazy.
- A lack of any kind of multiplayer support.
This game would be a MUCH better experience if I could get a group of five other friends to play with me, with someone to DM and actually create custom quests or something. Alas, that is not available here.
So, before I continue on for a few hours, what am I saying with all of this? This game, in all honesty, is just decent. It's a decent game and I enjoy it, but it is weighed down by some pretty substantial flaws. I enjoy it for what it is and would play it again, even if a grain of salt has to be taken with it. If they fix these problems, then fantastic. This would be an excellent game. As it stands right now, I recommend it- but only if you think you can handle the flaws.

If you've ever played an old game called Missile Command, you know the basic premise of this game. That said, Missile Cards takes Missile Command's formula and changes it from a "real-time arcade action game" into a "turn-based strategy game using cards."
PROS:
+ Very low system requirements.
+ Charming pixel-based graphics.
+ Easy-to-learn (but tough-to-master) turn-based strategy gameplay.
+ Inexpensive at $4.99 USD.
CONS:
- Gameplay can get repetitive after a while.
- The menu feels a little awkward.
- The "luck factor" can sometimes be annoying.
- The descriptions for some cards and upgrades could be more detailed.
- No Steam Cloud*
* If this changes, I'll amend my review.
VERDICT: If you enjoy card-based or turn-based games, aren't easily bored by somewhat repetitive gameplay, and don't mind (or even prefer) the pixel graphics, this is a great purchase. Add in the low price point and it'll be difficult to go wrong.

In a nutshell: "I'll just have one more round, I can do it this time - damn it!"
Then you realise it's 2am. :)
The developer, Nathan, has created a very addictive game here and I think I've only just scratched the surface after a few great hours of entertainment already - at a bargain price too.
While initially Missile Cards can appear to be fairly simple game (there is a tutorial) the depth soon becomes apparent:
- Do you go for higher scores by taking threats out later (see the x1, x2, 3x etc. grid numbers for score bonus) but then run the risk of being overwhelmed?
- There's a nice point based upgrade system for your base defences that's earned with experience gained, and you'll need those upgrades later!
- Each area introduces different mechanics and new dangers - which will have you cursing as you try to deal with them - but with that one-more-go feeling that good indie games always seem to have.
- You can discard your cards to power up your defences, but the choice to do so and when isn't always an easy one and adds a nice layer of depth to the game.
- There are some rounds where you wonder if you somehow insulted the random number generator's mother, which determines what order cards are dealt out.
It can sometimes be very difficult to claw a victory, but likewise, the RNG gods can smile upon you, and as you gain more experience and upgrades you're better able to deal with the odd curveball it throws your way, but it's all part of the fun and challenge.
All-in-all, Missile Cards is a great game that's well worth your time and money.
Developers like Nathan deserve a big pat on the back and our support to continue making good games like this - so go ahead and buy it, it's a steal for the amount of entertainment on offer here.

First off, let's get this out of the way: I'm not a fan of strategy games. My ADD-riddled ginger brain has never really taken to them; I just don't have the focus and patience necessary. That said, I really like the idea of a strategy game; in theory they're really appealing to me. The mental picture I have looks like this: Me (hey, that's me!) sitting on the couch, sipping delicious steaming coffee, nodding calmly like I know what I'm doing, contemplating my next move, placing my cup back on its coaster, then executing my move to resounding success. That's the picture I have of me playing a strategy game! Sounds fantastic, right? Try drinking coffee while you're playing (another favorite game of mine) Nuclear Throne and just SEE what happens! I'm not paying to have your couch cleaned.
In reality, the picture you'd see of me playing any other strategy game looks like this: Me sitting on the couch (hey, that's me again, but this time something's wrong. I look angry), profanity, frantic clicking, obtuse on-screen movements that I don't understand, me spilling coffee, more profanity, rage-quit.
Anyway, I've long entertained the thought of a strategy game that hit some magic balance of accessibility, action, entertainment, and presentation. Those are the ingredients it would take for me to obtain that ideal, nice, and relaxing time playing a strategy game.
Good news: That game is a finally reality and Missile Cards is its name.

Card games usually aren't my bag, but something about the retro aesthetic and Missile Command undertones triggered an urge to buy. The genre can so easily feel unfair--as if all the skill in the world won't compensate for a lack of luck--but that's not the case with Missile Cards. Unavoidable losses are rare, yet so are the instances in which you can get by without thinking ahead. Meanwhile, the game steadily lays on new concepts to consider, and keeps the dopamine flowing through unlockable cards and skills. The low-fi kathunks and kablams have an odd way of making matches more satisfying, too.
Now for some criticism: For me, the difficulty sweet spot occurred around the outset of stage 2. At first, the challenges seemed insurmountable, but I quickly learned and applied enough upgrades to score a victory. Since then, I've earned a lot more upgrades, and they've had the effect of skewing new challenges toward the easier side. I wonder if gating certain unlockables based on level progression--for instance, no 3-damage base laser until you've reached stage 4--might help maintain a balance.
But don't let that criticsm discourage you. This is an elegantly-designed card game that's satisfying to play, and it runs great on lightweight laptops (like my Surface Pro 3) so you can take it with you.
Without a doubt, one of the finest and most engaging games out there.

When I was young, I played a lot of tower defence games in Warcraft 3. But Orcs must die sets a new level in this genre.
Combining a 3rd person action game with tower defence, it created the ultimate action survival game.
Set in a fictional fantasy universe, you have to defend humanity against hordes of orcs from another dimension. For that, they built big fortress' around the portals, you have to defend.
For that, you not only have weapons and spells, but a big arsenal of traps and mechanical defend systems, from ordinary spike traps to big swinging clubs, burning pits and big brutal mechanical grinders.
Every level is made of one or several floors with one or several directions the enemys can spawn. You have to defend the rifts to the normal world, so the orcs dont conquer it.
Using the right collection of traps, wisly using your abilitys and being a tactical genius desides about victory and defeat. The game doesnt take you lightly. With the first levels being easily understandable and mostly fast to solve, some maps are difficult beyond everything encountered before. Some maps need tricks you have to find out all by yourself, some just need you to be fast like sonic, defending two rifts at once.

Divinity: Original Sin is one of the best games I've played in a long, long time. It strikes a very good balance between old school cRPG and modern design. It has plenty of text, quests, exploration, and discovery while including many of the usability improvements we've come to expect these days.
The combat system is probably the best I've ever played in a game like this. I've been on the fence of the Turn Based vs Real Time with Pause argument but this game makes a hell of a case for turn based gameplay. The elemental combinations and environmental interactions are exceptionally executed and allow for tactics I've never experienced in a game before.
As of this review I'm at 82 hours played on my second playthrough and still enjoy it tremendously. I absolutely cannot wait to see what mods we'll get for it.
It's not perfect (which game is?) but it's damn good. At the rate they've been updating the game (every few days) I expect Divinity: Original Sin to settle in nicely with the greats of the cRPG genre.
But, it's not for everyone. While the moment to moment writing is generally excellent the whimsical tone may turn people off and the overall plot rather bland. I've seen complaints from people accustomed to modern game handholding - it's true the game does not slap down objective markers and tell you where to go at all times. You need to talk to NPCs and pay attention to quest details. If you love exploring and the reward you get from discovery then you owe it to yourself to check out Divinity: Original Sin.

When I was a kid, I found it easy to get lost in a new game. I'd play for hours exploring a new world, despite the lousy graphics (compared to today at least), and not even notice time slipping by. As I've grown older, my responsibilities have grown as well and I've learned to keep a closer eye on the clock so I can get to bed at a decent hour. I've also gotten so used to new games that it's hard for a game to really invoke my sense of wonder and excitement.
Divinity: Original Sin is the first game in a long time to undo all of that. I'm nowhere near finishing it but the gameplay and story and graphics and everything are perfect. Every time I turn it on, I'm drawn into the game so deep that the outside world doesn't exist for a time. When I finally emerge from this finely crafted world and notice the time, I discover I've suddenly lost 6 or more hours of my life. I can no longer play this game on a week night because it guarantees I'll get 5 hours of sleep or less before I have to head to work the next day. Setting an alarm is useless because I'll unconsciously turn off the alarm without even being distracted from the game...
I could write more about this game and how amazing it is but it's hard to find the right words. Here's a few things of note though:
There are no quest markers on the map. If you don't pay close attention to the story and the world, you can easily leave quests unfinished. While some might complain that it makes it too hard, it's also part of what makes the game so immersive. Plus the challenge of deciphering clues to progress is a lot of fun in and of itself.
The music is fantastic. The easter eggs are hilarious. The graphics are gorgeous. The combat is both fun and challenging which is a hard combo to pull off. And despite the turn based nature, combat still somehow feels surprisingly fast paced.
I do have 1 negative comment. The conversation minigame for when 2 characters disagree is annoying to me. The first time or two I thought it was cool but after that... it got old fast. Especially in a single player game where I'm forced to either have both my characters always agree or I have to play a minigame where I may or may not get the actual outcome I want. In co-op it's even more annoying because I'd rather make a decision through actual conversation with my partner than through an a repetitive mini-game. When using the game to convince NPCs of something, it's perfect but when the two main characters are making a decision, it annoys me. I'd also like it if during conversations in co-op the second player could have more interaction that just reading chat bubbles over the other players head. Especially because if one player clicks too fast, the other doesn't even get a chance to read them. Other than that, I love this game. And even this little issue isn't enough to stop me from playing.

Gameplay-wise this is a simple action RPG. You have a basic attack, dash, hookshot, four spells and a combo meter. You must time your attacks right in order to get the combo meter high and unleash more powerful skills. There is a simple upgrade system which gives you one skill point on each level-up.
There are a few usability shortcomings:


Where the game shines, however, is its storytelling. It tells the story in a way that no other medium can, only computer games. Without wanting to spoil much, the game offers a combination of choose-your-own-adventure, where you make a few key choices, and an unreliable narrator, whose lies/mistakes you slowly uncover.
It's hard to tell more without spoiling it but once I understood what the game did, I smiled from ear to ear.
The writing seemed a bit too ironic and self-aware at first, but it quickly grew on me and later it even showed interesting nuance.
The gameplay is fun despite the above mentioned shortcomings and it was a pleasure to go through the story to the very end.

Stories isn't a bad game but it isn't too good either. The story choices bring some intrigue into how you want to patternize your path as you play the game. It freshens the overall story and that's a nice touch to bring instead of just one linear path. The characters are nicely personalized and portrayed, with your main character, Reynaldo being a whimsical foxy hero. As well as among other characters that speak for themselves and with the story to assist describing them nicely.
While this game looks asthetically pleasing and does hold up in it's story. I've found quite a few issues:
- Combat system. You'll notice that there is no specific buttons to block or roll about, is because that's built into time-based counters when you engage in combat. While I don't have a problem with this system, I do have a problem with how Stories has executed it. I feel that the timing is slightly spacy and requires specific timing in which to cancel out before attacking again or parrying off. This all works against you when you have a couple enemies coming at you at the same time though, so it works for a one-at-a-time method.
- Commentary during gameplay. I'm not a fan of a narrator describing every little thing I do. I'm okay with a narrator carrying the story to me as I'm playing. But I don't need it so that when I break boxes or go to another area, there has to be a witty quirk uttered. It just ends up annoying me. It works in games like Stanley Parable, because that's a game that would require narration, to help you understand what's going on and it succeeds in it's witty timing with an aftertaste of dry humor. Here in Stories, I was really underwhelmed with the wit it was trying to go by and I just found myself annoyed, especially from the times I've died. Do you really have to say something per death?
- Animation/Combo lock. This is another knock on the combat system. I love the mechanic of cancelling what you're doing mid-way and immediately interacting with a followup move onto oncoming threats. Stories, unfortunately, did not have this or it was executed poorly. You'll find this common in some hack and slash games or mechanics where you get too invested into chaining combos up where there isn't enough room to break away and resume in a timely fashion to accomplish good combos.
And I feel with these pegs against the game, despite it's charm, I cannot recommend.

The Walking Dead has always been one of my favorite video game series -- and Michonne one of my favorite characters. Despite loving the series and the games, I went in cautious after finishing season two of The Walking Dead, as I am sick of how little your choices seem to matter in the long run.
However, I was pleasantly surprised with The Walking Dead: Michonne, and I recommend it not only for those who like The Walking Dead franchise, but for those who enjoy story-based games themselves.
PROs
- The game, for some reason, runs much more smoothly than any of the other games. It isn't as clunky, the graphics are better, and the lip syncing and movements of the characters are more realistic.
- Choices appeared to matter more, as this is a miniseries, so choices could edit endings and gameplay better. As it also isn't going to have another installment, you don't have to worry about the different choices lining up in a continuing game -- so it feels more real, and you feel more in control.
- I could get worried about character deaths. In the regular seasons of The Walking Dead, if a character has the option of dying or surviving in episode two, you know they're going to die later on in the season, as it would be costly to animate them into every scene until the end. But in a miniseries with only three episodes, if someone is at risk of dying in episode two, they could very well survive until episode three. There are characters that do survive or die, and it's completely based on your decisions -- I appreciate that.
- I thought the length was perfect, though others may disagree. I was able to finish it in a single night, something I enjoy from a game. (It took me around 4 hours to complete it.)
- This is the first Walking Dead game I have played that has replayability -- again, because the choices seem to MATTER and affect things.
- WATER ZOMBIES.
- SUPERB voice acting from Michonne. She sounds just like she does in the show, and how I imagined from the comics.
- Michonne is a badass, unlike Clementine and even unlike Lee. Her fighting is unique and fun, and you feel excited and privileged to be part of the choreography. You also feel better about choosing "negative" choices, as it is more in character for her, the game isn't that long, and doesn't connect to anything.
- The nightmare and hallucination sequences are simply fantastic -- it adds just the correct hint of horror to this game. It takes it deeper, darker, and sadder.
- Characters that would have died off the bat in The Walking Dead seasons actually end up surprising me and surviving.
- On that note, I appreciated the characters in the story. This story, out of all of them, felt more character-driven than story, and that wasn't awful.
- It's a more casual gameplay experience -- more under the first point in CONs.
- The subtlety in the ending was phenomenal. Really. It was touching and it broke my heart.
- It feels like the perfect edition and story of what happened between Michonne's disappearance and reappearance into the group.

CONs
- Though your choices do affect the gameplay, unlike the other games, they never "web" back to you -- it's not BECAUSE of your reputation that things happen or don't. So there does feel like there's less weight to your decisions.
- Telltale is still Telltale. There are options that sometimes feel as if they don't matter, because something will always happen one way either way. (I, personally, appreciate that, because to me it feels as if it is saying, "There is sometimes no way to win." This game, unlike the other seasons, doesn't take it too far to the point where I get upset that it happens that way no matter what.)
- The story isn't that involved, to be frank. It involves one town and one family -- and you never add on to your crew. You're kind of caught in the middle, like usual, but it kind of feels... stupid... to be left in this situation.
- You never really find out if one of the motivations for most of your decisions actually happened or not.
- Personally, each scene took. For. EVER. to load. It was a little insufferable at times.
- There is a key character whose name you would never know unless the choices thing didn't tell you, and who never explains their reason for being there. It became a joke for my sibling and I to yell, "WHO ARE YOU?" every time they came on the screen.
- One of the characters gets badly hurt and then is able to use the hurt appendage with no issue? Another dies like a ♥♥♥♥♥ WAY too quickly? Like?? Are you kidding??
- I loved the characters, and wish I got to know them more. I felt like there was never a moment to learn more about their lives.
All in all, I think this game was excellent for what it is. Though it was a Christmas gift to me (and it was on sale for $5), I would pay the money to play it. If you enjoy games that touch on the subject of PTSD and/or psychological horror, this game may surprise you. I actually enjoyed many aspects of it MORE than the actual series -- and Clementine is my angel. If you have the opportunity, do delve into it. Go in knowing that it isn't a perfect game and some things may upset you, but follow the flow of the story and I don't think you'll be disappointed.

The Banner Saga is a gorgeous looking game, with fantastic universe. Looking at the majestic landscape while running for your life will create all kinds of weird feelings in you. When you combine it with truly beautiful soundtrack, interesting story full of hard choices and unforeseen events (which will break your heart more than your caravan) you'll get remarkable experience which you wont forget.
From the gameplay point of view it's not that great. The item progression is really weak, at the beginning you have nothing (duh) for a long time, and at some point you just have truckload of stuff, more often than not with high level requirements, so most of your characters can't wear them.
The learning curve is kinda weird, because it takes time to find out what it's all about. And by the time when you do understand the game, it's too late and most of your characters have bad stats.
Combat system tries to by original. You have strength, armor and willpower attributes and in most cases you have to bring armor down to inflict more strength damage. The most important thing is to group enemies together so you can inflict AoE damage. Although this system is original, I don't find it particularly enjoyable. It's extremely repetitive and to me, it doesn't make much sense. Difficulty levels are all over the place, which can get frustrating really fast. I finished the game and I still don't understand how could they inflict such a huge damage to my Varls.
Maybe it's just that I'm stupid and every other gamer out there understood it right away, but when I look at the forums it certainly doesn't look like it.
All things consider, I really thing that it's a game worth playing because of the story and atmosphere. But the game mechanics could be a lot better.

Dark, extremely gory, and full of despair, this is what Diablo III could (should ?) have been. The devs nailed the combat; movement is fluid and very responsive, weapon and spell effects are great, and characters feel quite powerful without being invulnerable. The overall art style is AAA-worthy -- amazing that the dev team consists of less than 10 people. The flesh explosions, in particular, should please even the most demanding gore hounds. I also liked the little snippets of text found in notes all over the game. Some are part of the main quest, but others are short stories of ordinary people caught in the Grim Dawn, and really flesh out the world. Speaking of the main quest, I found it a cut above most offerings in the genre. Instead of the Generic Big Evil that was awakened Greedy Mages, you have two warring factions and normal humans are squeezed between the two, just trying to survive and pull a miracle while the big guys aren't paying attention. Character customization is everything you'd hope for. It's deep, multi-layered, and detailed, with almost infinite variations of gear, including item sets (although the Legendaries are not in the game yet). Crafting is surprisingly deep -- wasn't expecting that at all -- and requires some planning in order to get the best upgrades. Finally, the music is first-rate, with some pieces good enough for stand-alone listening (if you're in a grim mood...)
As a final bonus, I play the game in NVidia 3D Vision and it is absolutely beautiful right out of the box. No tweaking needed at all, max out the graphics, and enjoy watching the action as if it were happening right outside your window.

So this game....is great! I have many kind words to say about this and being a huge Final Fantasy Tactics(SRPG's for that matter) fan this was a real treat to see on Steam's front page one day. I have some things about the game I love and I have some things about the game...well that I actually hate. Yes, it has left that much distaste in my mouth haha but thats not to discourage you. It is most likely something formed from my biased and practically purist views of SRPG's.
So first, the things I love ^_^
1-The Art
Cant say enough about this, its phenomenal and its like being in an interactive Disney game of brutality and brings me back to the SegaCD days and old PC of point and click adventure/exploring days. I could easily say; play this game to just be immensed inside this beautiful game.
2-The Music
It's very well composed and suited for everything thats going on in this story and era its cast in. I'm a musician/composer myself and cant help but appreciate it from that sense, but I would imagine most people who arent into music would only be pulled into the feelings of this game easier similar to a Hollywood movie.
3-SRPG Elements
Well..... I love this aspect of the game and its 90% of the reason I bought this game. I've played every SRPG I can get my hands on from Fire Emblem series and Final Fantasy Tactics to the overly diluted systems of Ogre Tactics and Disgaea. While I prefer a system that is well thought out with its boundaries and expansions within its systems, I do sometimes prefer a bit more of openness in the system such as Disgaea, but my mind tends to grow bored with endless options as everything becomes bland quicker than key roles that tend to shine within a system with some boundaries.
Back to this game though, its set up a bit differently. The classes are chosen ahead of time, if you can even call them classes, more like roles from the characters backgrounds. Archers,Bruisers,Tanks,Lancers,etc are some things you can expect to see early game. All with their own special moves and ranges on the map as well as movement across the map.
4-The Story Telling
Its great and very reminiscent of a great game that allows you to feel as if you have some control of the outlook of the characters,story,and ending. Games that come to mind are those of the Bethesda Series of Fallout and Elder Scrolls. Killing of key characters, ignoring causes for better or worse, choosing to help yourself or others, choosing sides/factions, and moving your "Army" around the map to different encounters...well its all here. While I love this open book approach and multiple answer dialogue options I can definitely feel the sting of any choice I make afterwards.
So onto ....the hated aspects.
1-SRPG Elements Constrainments
This game has control of your progression...very tightly. I'm only assuming the developers wanted control of how you progress and made this decision intentionally. Since I dont appreciate the restriction personally, I disagree with the direction almost entirely. I know building those mechanics would take a lot of hours to put in place and could have been a budget decision or they could have wanted this part to be light and not focused on heavily by the player. I just cant help but want to(ignoring the fact that i'm a veteran and have lots of things to compare this system to) considering you are fighting...well 75% of the time and you are always ALWAYS at a disadvantage. Not a single fight in this game are you evenly matched none the less above the enemy. So with no way inside their system to really cater to your playing style, I find myself getting irritated with the lack of in the system. Its presence is there, but its faint.
2-No Saving
Everytime I make a decision that affects something important, I prefer to be secure in my decision. I'm aware...Life doesnt have a pause button and once things are said and actions are done, the ripples around are permanent. But this isnt life, its a game. I prefer (personally) to have control over the game having control. So the lack of saving makes this...well a bit irritating. If you are similar to me then you too will be annoyed by the lack of this function. I dont play through Fallout 3 five times and make a different decision everytime I do something important. I would rather save and see what each option does. Personal way of playing and I wont claim its anything else. Its not right its not wrong, I just know I'm not the only person who does things this way with dialogue option heavy games such as this.
On top of that, its an autosave system. So lets say you make a decision and you think things were going well, you win the battle, you lose it, whatever. A character you've placed an item on,used your points on to level up,etc dies and you find out through dialogue. They are GONE. Caput. Reload your previous save to try and win the battle? Nope. Reload to make a different decision in dialogue? Nope. Outcome permanent.
Now that i've said that, I have to say there are some kind of ways around this. For one, it autosaves in multiple areas so if you can escape before the dialogue is done and reload there are more than one times I've used this to go back before the new autosave has saved the ripples in the ocean. Also it seems(if I recall right) when you quit abruptly(ouside of battle of course) it makes a save point at that direct point of leisure. So you can constantly quit the game and reload to beat this system. But this is....well redundant. There should simply be an intuitive save function in place to save yourself the annoyance.
On a final note, its my impression that the developers wanted you to push past these losses as they are constantly letting you know you are in an ocean that you have no control over and you will gain/lose characters often due to storyline but when you lose an invested in warrior to a minor choiceits nothing more than annoying.
Final Thoughts:
Its a great game and one many will love. I'm very happy to play what I have of this game and I plan on finishing it all the way through. Do I plan on playing it twice or more to see the other options? No. No. and No. But I feel compelled to see the rest of the story and love looking at this game. Not to mention it actually plays flawlessly and is very well developed in all aspects minus my disagreements with the character progression system and resource management. Play it if you like games similar to FFT and Fire Emblem and make your own opinion, I strongly urge this. Thank you Stoic for your modern SRPG and I look forward to your future works and to see you mature as a developer.

Shortly put, its an open world winter sports game that has a heavy emphasis on exploration, taking place in the Swiss Alps and Alaska. there's not one invisible wall in the entire maps and both are littered with interresting points of interrests.
the controls are okay. the game has an "trick safety" option turned on by default that won't let you do tricks that won't land and by concequence, it awkwardly cancels the animation, which annihaltes the immersion. On the other hand, having it turned off makes the game unforgiving towards newer players. this option applies to both snowboard and ski  (as they both work the same).
wingsuit skydiving is extremely intense. you can jump off any ledge and make any run an intense one (i love the fact that the closer you are to the ground, you can start hearing a heartbeat. theres also tons of air ballons that you can unlock and spawn from which makes for unlimited (or almost) runs.
paragliding is boring, however. its really only there for taking a breather and looking at the landscapes and it works at that at least, but i gave up on trying to do challenges for the paraglide.
did i mention challenges? there's plenty of them, all of which gives a generous reward for completing (the harder the challenge, the better). you can also create your own and share it with friends, which isnt a very used feature, but good to have either way.
my absolute favourite part about this game is how much freedom you are allowed to have. its not often we see a triple A game where you can change ambiance, time of day, character and costume on the go. you can even see a replay of your last run by pressing a single button, no loading times, and have access too a simple but effective diector mode. if you're grouped with people, you can spectate them and have access to the same settings.
the worst 2 things about this game is the online only drm (which is heavily enforced) and the lack of variety between challenges. you're gonna love the 4 sports (well, 3), but you will get bored of the repetitive challenges way before completing them all.
if you're worried about performance, be sure to have a good graphics card (cpu isnt as important) because this game is gonna need it. however, even with a rx470 4gb, i can get 30-45 fps on ultra.

Death rains down from above, you have a spread of powerups, weapons, and limited resources which you can use to deploy most (but not all) of them. What do you do? What to you prioritize? Every win and every loss brings you closer to the upgrades you need to succeed. Rounds are quick, but you'll always want to play more than one in each sitting. Give it a whirl.

I think this is a great game. I am a fan of Nathan Meunier's previous game, This Book is A Dungeon, so I was immediately intrigued. It's a turn based game where cards govern everything. Each card gets put onto a conveyor belt and you have so many turns to use cards, such as missiles, before they get dropped off and reshuffled back into the pack. Of course, this is also where the hazards come into play. Once you see a comet card heading towards the end of the conveyor it will drop into the left side of the screen, hurtling towards your base one step at a time.
It's quite surprisingly robust, with hidden depth and strategy needed in order to progress through the five missions. But don't be put off the mission count since each mission has three challenges to complete before unlocking the next mission. There's also upgrades and new cards to buy with gathered debris from missions. There's a great amount of content for such a small asking price!
I also really like the pixel artwork and 8-Bit style music.
All in all this is a great game for a low fee that I highly recommend. Oh and there's a button that allows you destroy all of humanity. What's not to like ^_^
Hope it does well.
P.S I hope there's future updates for it such as Endless Mode (if there isn't already a mode like that included, I haven't got that far into it lol) or hot seat multiplayer. That could be interesting, each player defending their own base, for example.

Being a huge fan of Diablo 1 & 2 (not so much D3), Grim Dawn offers many hours of the classic ARPG hack'n slash game-play I truly love. Having racked up 170 hours and completing the current content on three of my main characters so far, there is still much more the game has to offer. Re-playability is almost essential in truly grasping what the game has to offer and Grim Dawn really promotes this aspect in terms of its unique dual-class hybrid system.
Like Diablo 1 & 2, Grim Dawn promotes character uniqueness with the ability to invest main stat & skill points into where you want them - unlike the bland stream-line you get with Diablo 3. The ability to dual class really highlights what the game is all about - trying new things, giving players the platform to forge something that is different to the next persons. On top of this, all of the equipment you find can be enhanced to truly come up with some very bizarre and successful builds for your characters. For the most part, the character classes are your typical Warrior, Wizard, Rogue, and Warlock, but with a few funky name changes and unique abilities to go with it. These traits is what really seperates Grim Dawn from the rest of the games in its genre, which in my opinion makes Grim Dawn's future very necessary.
If you are looking to get addicted to something similar to those classic ARPG games but with an enhanced game platform with very good graphics, look no further than Grim Dawn.  Even in its Early Access state, the wilderness in Grim Dawn is very presentable and attractive to the eyes and is highly playable. Multiplayer is also available up to four players aswell as an in-game trade system to share your loot - no soul-bound items! (Except for pertinent quest items)
I HIGHLY recommend this game!

Even though it's still in early access, I am amazed by the detail in Grim Dawn; the landscapes are breathtaking; the maps are mazelike and complex, and the gameplay is fast-paced, energetic and intense.
I can't comment much on the story, as I'm still caught up in side-quests and exploring, but from what i've seen; there's a lot of attention to detail in every aspect of this game, and if you want an immersive experience; this is definitely worth a shot.
I can't wait to see what else Crate Entertainment has in store with future updates to this, because I have a feeling this could go big.

Picked it up on sale because I like the viking history stuff and strategy elements. Turns out that's all I really like about this game. The combat itself is challenging and very strategic, thankfully there is no permadeath from combat.
Outside of combat, however, is where the game fails. There is a lot of...waiting. The game is very intent on telling a story, and it will shove the huge scale of your passage in your face for what feels like hours whether you like it or not.
The game starts out with a pretty basic story. Escape your home because it's under attack, travel to find safety elsewhere. Unfortunately, the game asks you to make decisions between fights. You're trying to keep your people safe, so naturally you would want to pick the safest option, right? Haha, nope. If you're not trying to Rambo guns blazing 25/8 then a character is probably going to get killed. Because you hit "2" instead of "1". Not for tactical combat reasons, what the game bills itself as, but because trying to stop a cart from falling off a cliff. All in text, too, so it's very unfulfilling.
I can see why people like the game, because the combat IS fun, and the story IS cool, but the parts inbetween are severely lacking.

Everyone has their prefered genre for gaming, and inevitably we get a little too good at our prefered genre. Banner Saga was not only an exceptional game, but it also rekindled my love for Turned Based Strategy(TBS). A love that I was losing after finding recent TBS games a little too simple. Banner Saga's well thought out emphasis on both micro and macro management of resources put enough strain on me that I found myself actually engaged in the story line and concerened about the danger the characters and caravan where in. Banner Saga's blend of 'create your own destiny' story telling, carefully balanced TBS sections, and unique combining of macro resources with character leveling resources has forged a game that will keep you playing attentively straight to the end. The only down side to this game for anyone who is a fan of TBS games is that it leaves you wanting more content. Approximate play time is probably something like 8-11 hours on normal difficulty. Do not let that discourage you in ANY way this has been, by far, the best spent $20 this year or last year.

The concept and writing are great. The RPG aspects could use a lot of stuffing, considering I unlocked everything before I completed even 25% of the game's content. But honestly that's not too big a deal. The game is repetitive but fun. I'd say if you enjoyed Hand of Fate you'll love this too... but there are serious design flaws. The levels encourage exploration for treasure, yet you can get all the weapons and gems VERY quickly. When you do, there's literally no reason to explore these other areas.
The game is short, also. You can play levels over and over again to see each little way the "story" (AKA the 3-5 lines of narration between levels) changes, but if you just want to play through the levels and solve the story you're looking at maybe 2 hours of gameplay.
There's an even bigger issue.
This game is buggy as hell. Some of the bugs are game-breaking. It was released over a year ago and it still plays like it came out last week. There are levels you have to restart due to blockades. There are platforms/islands that don't render so things are floating on nothing. There are just FOUR weapons in the game, and two of them have bugs that are either extremely frustrating or kill you. One sword sometimes causes your movement to slow down until you can't move at all other than your dash. The other freezes enemies, but if one freezes right before it hits you, the game registers it as hitting you over and over again in the span of a second, and you take about 10 hits worth of damage and usually die.
These bugs have existed since the game's release. The Devs have seen and responded to them, but have done nothing to fix them. A month is understandable. A year is inexcusable. They just don't care, so you shouldn't either.

The game utilises a single-run system, every time you die, you reset back to a base version of a ship. Now I dont mind this system too much, but when you progress fairly far into the game, and are suddenly attacked by a massively overpowered enemy which eventually kills you, it makes you want to go back to change things, but alas, all is lost upon death. And with the upgrading system implemented into the game, this becomes an irritating factor.
Nontheless, this was a game that has been sitting in my steam library for quite some time now, neglected by my overwhelming masses of things i have yet to play (aka, the humble bundle effect), but I really enjoyed the few hours that i've spent on it so far, and I will definately advise other people to give this game a shot, fair warning to the difficulty though.

I really wanted to reccomend this game, and this is the first time I'm voting no. First - why I like the game:
The art work is beautiful and the world is truly a sight. The fighting mechanism is super fun and simple to understand (personally I don't like fight mechanisms that require me to have 4 hands to master) and I like to hack and slash things.
This game would have been perfect in those aspects. However, the game is so buggy that it just ruined my experience to the point where I don't want to play anymore. The first and most major bug is that you lose the mouse indicator. You can't play normally without it (since you can't aim comfortably), and you have to quit the game to fix it (try quitting the game without keyboard control and NO MOUSE POINTER..it can take minutes!). And then on top of it, since there's only auto save, you lose your progress because of this. There were other bugs, less critical, but still annoying.
Also, you cannot skip the narration. True, it's a story telling game, but for crack's sakes, some of the texts you have to hear over and over and over and over and over again - on second time, just let us skip!
Loading times are really long. It's been a while since I've encountered such a long loading time in a modern game that's not an MMO.
All in all, I can't reccommend the game. If you're super patient to bugs, then wait for a sale and buy it. But full price with the current bugs and annoyances? don't think it's worth it.

By taking the suspense, challenge and visceral charge of the original, and adding startling new realism and responsiveness, Half-Life 2 opens the door to a world where the player's presence affects everything around him, from the physical environment to the behaviors -- even the emotions -- of both friends and enemies. The player again picks up the crowbar of research scientist Gordon Freeman, who finds himself on an alien-infested Earth being picked to the bone, its resources depleted, its populace dwindling. Freeman is thrust into the unenviable role of rescuing the world from the wrong he unleashed back at Black Mesa. And a lot of people -- people he cares about -- are counting on him.

Stories: The Path of Destinies is essentially “trial-and-error” the video game and that's not an insult to the game, I actually love the idea of it! The game is meant to be played multiple times and each playthrough of the game can be drastically different depending on the choices you make and the lessons you learned through your past experiences. If I could compare this game's style of storytelling to anything it would be like those old “pick your own path” storybooks that some of you may have read when you were kids. You would read it a little bit then be told to make a choice and follow that path until the end and if you didn't like the ending that you got you simply just reread it and chose a different path to do to get a better ending and that's this game in a nutshell essentially.
The overall story here is short but quite good actually. In Stories you play as a fox named Reynardo that acquires a magical book from the ashes of a kid he promise to protect and from there on out you have to pick your own path on how you want to defeat the evil emperor who terrifies the land. Even though you may think you know what's going to happen on the path you chose this game always seems to throw a curveball at you making the outcome slightly or even drastically different than what you had originally expected. The story is full of twists and turns and filled with plenty of secrets to discover with the primary goal of discovering the true ending.
In the beginning the game's combat feels a little dull with it mostly feeling like an easy hack and slash game as you mow down hordes of enemies but as you start to progress in the campaign and the enemies become more difficult the game's RPG elements start to really shine as you level up and unlock new swords and special abilities to use during combat. The game also has a heavy emphasis on resource management. Things like health and energy for your weapons become very scarce in late game. Your health and energy do not recharge in between levels and pickups for them are very scarce making you have to plan carefully for your next engagement. Even though there's no real penalty for death in this game and even has an excellent checkpoint system it can still be quite brutal when you responded with only half of your original health. Even though I do quite like it I kinda wish they still include a difficulty selection for those of us who wish to play the game more casually just to get through all the stories easier.
The game's art and sound design is amazing and I commend the team behind it. You can really tell they've fully utilized the Unreal Engine here. It has this fun and cartoony yet serious look to it that I feel anyone could enjoy and even though it doesn't always run the best even on higher-end machines it is still quite a pleasure to look at it.
As you could probably tell the game is pretty short. I was able to beat the true ending of the game in a little over six hours and that's with me even exploring all the nooks and crannies of each level I played. However this is definitely one of those short-but-sweet type of scenarios. Yes the game may have been short but the story here was so well done and expertly narrated that you hardly mind it in the end. However there are a ton of different endings in this game to play through. I could see it taking a completionist quite a while to beat everything this game has to offer. So for the price I definitely feel you get more than what you pay for.
With most of the positive out of the way I do feel like I have to bring up some of the games negatives and oh yes there are quite a few of them. First off like I mentioned earlier even though most of the time the game ran at a buttery smooth 60fps for me at Max settings at 1080p I did have significant dips in frame rates at certain parts of the game even when there were no enemies around me (My PC specs in bio). Also I ran into numerous bugs and glitches during my experience that made me have to restart certain levels. Sometimes doors that were suppose to open just didn't open or sometimes parts of the map I was playing on didn't fully render and sometimes the game would just randomly freeze in the menus and I even had it fully crash on me once. However with that being said it was very few and far between and honestly can be easily forgiven for everything else this game does right but it's still worth noting.
All in all I did really enjoy this game. I acquired the indiebox collector's edition of this game from my local GameStop hoping that it would be a good game and I'm happy to say this game well surpassed my expectations. I will proudly display this game with the rest of my game collection. Well done Spearhead Games I look forward to seeing what else you come up with in the future.
