Now here's a good game.
I remember watching TechTV. I remember The Screen Savers sometimes talked about games, Doom 3 on one occasion, another being Half-Life 2, since it was a scandal. By the time I was watching TechTV HL2 became a game everyone already finished, but also a game that was fresh. I had a toaster that ran Quake 3 at best, and that was after extreme engine and Windows tweaking. I switched to console gaming until the end of the PS3 era, and then upgraded my computer. By then HL2 was nothing, and I think Valve had enhanced the graphics by this point.
The gameplay is basically the same as HL1, or any other shooter for that matter. You have a variety of guns, there are exploding barrels, blah blah blah. The enemy variety is quite low, really. You're mostly killing soldiers. There's the perhaps infamous watercraft section I hear a lot of people hate. I personally enjoyed it quite a bit, however I resented that they tacked on a puzzle in the middle of the action without any kind of smooth transition. That's really what I'd complain about with this game, albeit a minor to medium level complaint: pacing. Every time I encountered a puzzle on my initial playthrough I was irritated because I didn't feel like slowing things down a while and figuring♥♥♥♥♥♥out. I tend to enjoy my games no more complex than...I dunno, Super Mario Bros. 3. It's like when I listen to classical music. Yes, I understand that it's very complex. Yes, I understand that people find it beautiful. But since I can't see the overall picture in my head due to an insufficient IQ, I cannot grok classical music. Likewise, if you put someone like me in front of a physics puzzle, however innovative and interesting, Hulk smash. Honestly, if I'd looked up the solutions to the puzzles, I would've enjoyed myself more. That said, I was young when I played this, and I tended to be thick-skulled when it came to puzzles.
HL2 does something really cool with its interface: your ammo and health appear on the sides of your crosshair. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ Dead Space put health on the back of your dude's suit, which removed the interface requirement completely, but NO OTHER SHOOTER PUTS THE HEALTH AND AMMO AROUND THE CROSSHAIR. Why? Seriously, why? We're supposed to think CoD or CSGO or Gears of War or whatever else as being these big honking competitive games, but they're using an old fashioned interface? Not to mention aaaaaaall the shooters that came out between HL2 and now.
Headshots don't count in this game, so if you're using a pistol, just dump magazines into the bad guys. If you run out of ammo, there's always the physics gun you can use to pick things up and throw them, which is usually pretty fun. I'd say I probably enjoy and get the most mileage out of the gravity gun than the pistol for example. I wish, since this is a post CS game that it had similar dynamic crosshairs and headshots. This would open up a lot of opportunity for skillful players to show their♥♥♥♥♥♥ I appreciate the shotgun in this game: it has a primary fire that consumes one round and an alt fire that consumes 2 rounds, but does more damage. This is yet another thing I rarely see in shooters. Another word about the gravity gun: you could use the crowbar to break open ammo/health boxes, but the gravity gun is more fun. Oh, and this is a game where the assault rifle has a red dot sight, but you cannot use it. Woops.
Unfortunately, this game doesn't do any checkpointing, so it's up to you to save. This has 2 problems: 1) It causes players to savescum when the developer probably would prefer that you didn't. 2) I tend to forget to save because I get absorbed in the action. You might think the occasional puzzle would remind me to do it, but it's the combat that gets you killed, so what's when saving helps out. The levels certainly have good design overall, but sometimes I got confused about where I'm supposed to go. Not often, though. And that might be my fault. Ultimately, you can look at the environment, consider what a rational man would do in that situation, do that, and you'll figure it out. You can even use this to your advantage in Ravenholm and a part involving...a magnet, let's say. There are probably more, but I can't be bothered to remember them. But keep an eye out for exploding barrels and the like.
If you're into Quake or Serious Sam like me, you'll want to keybind your weapons to convenient keys so you can switch at the drop of a hat and adapt to the situation. Since there are a lot of weapons, this game lets you approach practically any battle in your own fashion. Interestingly, even the physics puzzles can be solved in multiple ways. You literally look at the environment, pick up a thing, put it in or on a thing, and you've solved the puzzle. You don't have any weird♥♥♥♥♥♥like empty buckets weighing more than big rocks either. That's pretty cool.
As far as story goes, it does a lot to endear important characters to you, so you care when they're threatened. The voice acting is damn near perfect. And by the way, a fellow named Dr. Howl does the voice for Dr. Kleiner. Look him up, he's great. The intro sequence is wonderful, does anything and everything it can to settle you into the setting. You have appropriate moments of panic and slowdown. And plenty of humor.
It's too bad I missed this game when it was at the peak of its relevance, but that's the way it goes. Lately I've been kicking around the idea of having an anniversary games list that I revisit once a year. This game, should I make such a list, would have to be on it because it does too many interesting things to ignore. That's good for people who've never played this game, actually, because even though it's old, it's quite good indeed. It lives up to its name.
Here's where I make a joke about HL3. Have a nice day.

I loved this game. I found this game through the super best friends playing it through a sponsored video and I was immediately interested when I found out the game's time gimmick.
- The story. This is the real thing that stands out. Every playthrough you can get different endings which gives the character knowledge on how he can succeed in his quest. I loved going through the book over and over again trying to find the right path and unlocking the different truths and endings. This got a little grindy at the end but the game puts shortcuts that you can use to let you skip battles and gain loot. The quest for the true ending was thoroughly fun for me but I can see it getting repetitive for others.
- The combat system is fun and fast paced. By the end, I really felt like I was using every skill I had to efficiently take out bad guys. There are a lot of skills you can specialize into such as grappling hook or dashing. Each has its uses and I thoroughly enjoyed going through the different trees. Things do get a bit messy when a lot of enemies get on screen and multiple enemies attack you at the same time but the chaos is all part of the fun.
-The crafting system in the game was a bit lackluster but it did have cool parts about it. You get ore and elemental essence to craft different swords. The swords themselves offer some interesting magic mechanics but the main thing you use them for is unlocking different doors. The different doors offer alternate paths through the game which can lead you to shortcuts or to better loot. I found the sword magic to not be all that useful so after I unlocked all the swords, I found myself skipping chests and going straight for the story.
- The graphics are lush and colorful. The graphics are a bit intensive for an indie game. I had to play the game on medium/low in order to get smooth framerates during big battles. However, there's a lot of nice touches such as the main character actually leaning in the direction that you move him.
Overall: 9.5/10

Half-Life 2, the game that like it's predecessor is seen as a classic. It's time for me to find out if the game still holds up.
The story takes place some years after the events of the original Half-Life. Gordon Freeman is woken up by G-Man to find out that the world had been taken by the alien Combine. Gordon is then joined by resistance fighters to find a way to free humanity.
The gameplay itself is a mixture of shooting, puzzle solving and exploration much like the first Half-Life game. However, all of this is differently executed in Half-Life 2. In Half-Life 2 everything is even more dynamic, because of objects being destructible and having physics, which can result in some memorable chain reactions.
The world felt to me like a real open world game, while it is still a pretty linear game. This has to do with the fact that you are mostly outside and you can explore the different areas and interact with npcs. The world you play in is around the same city area, which means that this time you aren't going to other alien dimensions.
When you think about it there aren't actually that many new things in Half-Life 2. But the things that are new still deliver new gameplay. For instance, the gravity gun that you get can grab and shoot objects which is great for murdering and puzzle solving. The gravity gun really adds a playfulness to the game. The other real new weapon is the bug bait which is a ball that you can throw on enemies or destinations, which will result in a group of your own aliens going to it and attacking the enemies. The only problem I had with this is that you can only use this weapon in a certain section.
The other new gameplay feature is that you can now drive a buggy at certain parts. I read people saying that it was the worst part of Half-Life 2. In my opinion even though the buggy feels clunky I loved that part the most. It really gives that open world explorer feeling, because of you have to get out of the vehicle to look around.
The sounddesign in this game was also done by the same team as the one that worked on the original Half-Life. I can say that I liked this soundtrack even more than the previous one, because of it having more of its’ own style. The epic music sometimes felt a little off though, but they are still fun to listen to. The sound effects add a quirky feeling, and the voice acting is also professionaly executed.
The storytelling of the game was mostly well executed, with also including storytelling through gameplay. Sadly, unlike in its’ predecessor, you are forced at certain parts to listen to conversations. This can be pretty annoying if you have to listen to it again, without the option to skip it.
I have to say that overall the world, story and gameplay doesn't feel as flawlesly connected as it was in the previous Half-Life. That probably has to do with the fact that the game also wanted to show everything impressive that the engine could do.
The game took me 12 hours to complete so it was shorter than the original Half-Life, but I guess that also has to do with the fact that at the beginning I unknowingly played on the easiest difficulty. Later I found out I could actually change it in the options menu.
Even with the complaints I have with Half-Life 2 compared to Half-Life 1, I can still recommend it. The game like its’ predecessor was greatly ahead of its’ time, and at some parts maybe still is. While playing I realized that every futuristic game that I played that came out after Half-Life 2 all had big 'inspiration' from the game.  Half-Life 2 is still adventurous enough that it still holds up.

An early access review for an early access game. This review is based on a playthrough of one character to level 25ish, partly played alone and partly played with a friend.
Kill, loot, rinse, repeat. You're a dude or lady that was nearly hung for being possessed, but was spared because of context. And now a gathering of NPCs look at you with hope/despair in wondering if you can save them from the end of the world. Which already happened, but they hope you won't make it worse. Given I've not personally completed the story, I cannot give a nay or yay regarding it.
I can state that it does set the post-apocolypse in semi-fantasy land well. Everyone looks unclean and filthy, and your equipment is no exception. None of your equipment shines or glows, or looks elegant. It is rough or practical looking, and portays the scavenger look as you are picking up fantasy pieces in fantasy land. Most of the land is in ruins, garbage strewn about is a constant land image.
The music is there, and serves its purpose but is lost under combat noise. I've not heard a track I would listen to outside of the game, but I've not had a reason to turn the music off.
Playing as the Soldier class, 1 of 5 classes available currently (six planned), I have not felt the need to dual class. Though I played on Veteran difficulty, and was underleveled for the first boss, I managed to defeat them by myself with the skills I invested in and resources I earned/purchased. Healing potions did not ensure my victory, and I definately needed them. From my perspective, devoting time to gaining levels to match the boss or finding more appropriate equipment to defend myself would have made the battle easier. But ultimately, like all ARPGs of this sort, it comes down to loot/equipment.
Loot in the game is not generous, but it is not lack luster. While my luck may just be poor, and I keep finding high qualities items that would better suit other classes, the pieces that I do find I have yet to replace. Add onto the componant items that can be collected and combined to impart even greater bonuses, which can be placed onto equipment to ensure their longevity, means there are always options to improve gear.
In multiplayer, loot can be set to personal or shared. With personal loot, all loot seen by you is yours.
There are tools within the game to help you determine what gear you need, though I personally find it hard to track incoming damage. It is hard to determine what enemies will attack what sort of defence immediately, and for me it was always trial by fire. And gear is not immediately available to immediately counter enemy attacks, it all has to be earned with time.
But that's the point of these kinds of games: repeatedly charge into dungeons to find better and better gear, for multiple situtaions. And, to the games great credit, their NPC crafters are not simple gamble-based machines. Despite the random statisics on the items, they will always make gear that is at least at your character's level.
One major complaint I have to make is the text box for NPC interaction is small, and that makes reading hard to do.
I have not seen all of the game yet, but what I've played I have enjoyed. It is a game that asks the player to micromanage their gear to fit their needs, but allows them headstrong acts of determination to push through challenges at the cost of resources. Character customization benefits from augment gear, to dual classing for combining skill sets, to a mostly passive bonus system gained from exploring and slaying monsters.
The game's look works. It does not strain the eyes, and sets the mood it intended to set. While more color would be appreciated, what I have seen I've not been distracted (beyond all the literal garbage. Loads of trash in places! Fantasy kingdom lacks littering laws.)
The story is there, and while not bad it can be overlooked. This may be a dangerous thing, however, as a choice made in the first portion of the game drastically changes the loot available to you. And the game does not give you the luxury of making that choice's importance to you apparant. Squint your eyes to read that text, because it may make your adventure all the easier.
This is a solid enty into the ARPG library. Not too easy, not unforgiving, but demands you pay attention.

I think Grim Dawn is the best loot treadmill ARPG of the current gen (not gonna fight about people who liked D2 best etc. etc.). I'll lay out briefly why.
Pros:
-There are so many levels of depth with making characters. Stats, dual classing, multiple paths per class, devotion trees on top of all that, equipment options (and the sheer number of modifiers for this gear! It's ridiculous)! Theorycrafting a character might take several hours or even days depending on how hard you want to push it.
-The enemy design is both quite challenging and yet manages to not be frustrating (at least to me). No cheesy or annoying effects, but the game definitely requires dodging and a variety of abilities to deal with various situations (boss kills v giant swarm kills of course need different skillsets).
-There is a lot of content. Like, dozens of hours of content+. At this price and given the quality of the content, this is very impressive to me.
-Progression is smooth. I never feel like it's taking too long to get new loot or some kind of new point to use on my character, and all the points make sense. Three major stats only, which also helps, but plenty of secondary stats with more specific effects.
-The art is very well-done, and the world, while preconstructed, has clearly been carefully thought out in my opinion. Very large variety of locales, lots of optional content and differing paths to run down. Story that is unobtrusive but still well-written if you care to pay attention to it. Very satisfied.
-Sound design is good, limited voice acting but honestly, I don't think that's a big need for this genre. Music and ambient sound is good, no complaints at all there.
-It's an early access game that has consistently for over a year delivered on their every promise. Nothing to sneeze at on Steam of late (unfortunately), and the game is very near completion. Content complete by EOY last I heard.
Neither Pro nor Con:
-Some people do not like the design decision to have partial level scaling for areas (seems to be a several level window for most zones, with optional zones having a larger window). I think this is good though, myself. It's a matter of taste more than good/bad though.
-Some do not like constitution, which is a bar that allows for limited out-of-combat quick healing (once it's out you need potions or abilities to heal, and there are drops to replenish constitution usually on bosses/champion mobs). I think it's a good way of seeing if your build is too squishy/not suited for what you're fighting. But that's also my taste.
No outright Cons (at least for me).
It comes with my highest recommendation if you like this genre at all. And at its price versus its content? It's a steal.

So, understand right off the bat that this is a mobile phone port -- nothing more, nothing less.  As such, it's overpriced (twice as much as the mobile app), but I would still recommend it.  I've played it on the phone and on the laptop, so I've played much more than the 13 hours it shows.
Imagine a D&D mod for a Final Fantasy game, and that's largely how Knights of Pen and Paper plays -- D&D feel, FF-type mechanics.
It has a great variety of traditional D&D classes (though simplified and somewhat reimagined for the FF-type mechanics), and each class really does play differently from the others.  Sure, you have your traditional D&D roles that each one fits, but they're not just strikers, glass cannons, rogues, etc with different skins.  For example, even though they are all traditionally tanks/strikers, a paladin is not a warrior is not a barbarian in this game.
You also have classes that excel verseus single targers, excel versus groups, and some that can do both fairly well.  The true variety between classes is probably the game's greatest selling point, in my opinion.  No two parties will feel the same, giving the game great replay value.
You also RP as the DM, as well as the players.  This lets you do things like decide exactly how hard most battles will be (with more xp for more/harder enemies).  It's a nice little touch.
Overall, buy it on sale without even thinking about it! Seriously! Pounce on any sale at all!
For full price, you probably need to have some D&D nostalgia to make it worth the $10.

Ever since the official launch of Grim Dawn, I have always meant to properly review the game after my 20+ hour impression in Early Access. With the release of the expansion, Ashes of Malmouth, I now have an excuse to return to Cairn from the very beginning. While it is perhaps not going to usurp the names of the free-to-play Path of Exile and the might of Blizzard’s Diablo, GD more than deserves to be recognized as one of the best ARPG within its genre even when its attempts to push the genre’s boundaries do not always end well.

If you have heard anything about Grim Dawn it is probably the comparison to Diablo 2 as well as the touted line, “This is the REAL Diablo 3.” There are many reasons why this tagline is more than deserving of Diablo’s legacy beyond similar graphical styles, though the colorful touches to Grim Dawn makes it anything but dull, because GD continues what D2 did so phenomenally well with variable classes as well as incorporate what made the developer’s previous series stand out, Titan Quest.
TQ introduced the idea of combining different classes where you level into each one through both masteries with passive stats as well as the skills they possess, thereby creating a unique class of your own. GD largely copies the same idea but further develops its execution by creating six (eight with the DLC) half-classes where their combination can result in your own tailored class. This is distributed evenly amongst elemental types as well as what roles each class occupies like Shaman’s two-handed, large pet and electricity specializations and the Occultists’ hex-based/vampirism attacks and small pets. Even if you were to choose the same specializations, you could make each character stand out in their own way with the addition of a third skill-system, Devotions.
Devotions are rewards for finding shrines throughout the land that unlock additional abilities for every class, which can be modifiers for existing abilities or new ones altogether. Rarely are any of these abilities, class-based or devotions, limited to weapon-sets, so the sense of experimentation with your build is the sublime feeling that makes replaying the game a greater reward than playing long-term for end-game content, which GD has in abundance with rogue-like dungeons, additional difficulties, unique gear and a new level cap of 100. The result is the game never feels repetitive because you are always doing something different and the grind never feels like a slog even past level 50 with how quickly you obtain XP.
However, as what often happens with experimenting with something new, not all attempts to reexamine previous methods will create something better, which highlights less of a problem with Grim Dawn but with ARPGs as a whole.

Action RPGs occupy a weird genre within its namesake. Role-playing is not within the traditional D&D sense of creating stories from player solutions, violent or nonviolent, but rather in the literal creation of the player’s build/role. This has largely stayed the same ever since the days of Diablo 1, and Grim Dawn attempts to add more traditional role-playing to the experience with little to no success.
Now it would be absurd to demand a persuasion skill that would deoptimize builds with story-related stats that would affect the PVE/PVP experience. However, Grim Dawn attempts to introduce more story-related choices within the limited scope of its reputation system.
Reputation occupies two roles in the game; it’s a progression system for enemies to become harder as well as offer greater rewards with the increased number of enemy hero spawns as well as to lower the cost of allied factions for the player to receive greater rewards.  Both of these features are great additions that do expand the traditional ARPG experience within its own genre, yet it feels threadbare with how it affects the story. There is only one decision between two factions that impacts future events between the Necromancer Order and the Zealots Order. Later on within Ashes of Malmouth, there is a slightly greater offering of choices within new factions that showcases how the previous acts after Homestead forgot to include these types of decisions towards the journey into the Necropolis.
While it is commendable for Grim Dawn to offer more than other games within its genre, the results are not good enough to make them anything other than a commendable attempt. The choices made within Ashes of Malmouth attempts to offer actual branching results of which towns/factions you can attack within the swamplands, then heads towards the conclusion much like before on one intended path. It’s this otherwise blemish on an amazing experience that makes progression mean something more than grinding as the progression systems reward the player’s time investment.
Now are all the new features for the better? I preferred when the game didn’t have the cinematics to restate the same plot as you had to learn about the world more naturally after waking up after being hanged on a noose through talking with NPCs and scattered notes that further delved into the Lovecraftian conspiracy with beings from another realm. Even with the addition of voice-acting, the game is heavily reliant on reading stats, etc. that it begins to feel like an Excel worksheet. As mentioned before about the late-game issues, there is also a strange difficulty scale between the final areas due to resistances like Aether and in the new expansion Poison that makes the constitution regeneration system worthless when you die in seconds.
In spite of all these minor gripes, Grim Dawn has slowly matured like wine into the sublime, polished experience it was always promised to be from the start, and if Crate Entertainment has proven anything by their Early Access system they can be trusted to create future projects with amazing results. The latest expansion has further cemented everything I enjoy about Grim Dawn as it is its Lord of Bhall equivalent to the Diablo 2 comparison. Of all the praise I could ever give, this game, along with Divinity Original Sin 2, is what Early Access games should strive to become, amazing games from the beginning that only become better with more time to blossom into beautiful eldritch abominations to lure the minds of men into the depths of its enticing chaos to drive men insane with its splendor.

Everyone has their prefered genre for gaming, and inevitably we get a little too good at our prefered genre. Banner Saga was not only an exceptional game, but it also rekindled my love for Turned Based Strategy(TBS). A love that I was losing after finding recent TBS games a little too simple. Banner Saga's well thought out emphasis on both micro and macro management of resources put enough strain on me that I found myself actually engaged in the story line and concerened about the danger the characters and caravan where in. Banner Saga's blend of 'create your own destiny' story telling, carefully balanced TBS sections, and unique combining of macro resources with character leveling resources has forged a game that will keep you playing attentively straight to the end. The only down side to this game for anyone who is a fan of TBS games is that it leaves you wanting more content. Approximate play time is probably something like 8-11 hours on normal difficulty. Do not let that discourage you in ANY way this has been, by far, the best spent $20 this year or last year.

I've been playin divinity sin for a while now, and well i'll give it much credence for being a game in the genre that is much needed.  It applies it in some of the worse possible ways.

I'm surprised by this game. It's recently out of beta and still has it's glitches and imbalances. I won't gloss over those - they are a problem, at times, but they are honestly insignificant. Sure pathfinding can get a bit weird at times, it can be difficult to know what you're getting into - either by misclicking and all of a sudden being accused of thievery, or missing a dialogue cue and ending up on a very different conversational tone than you expected - and these are problems that I do have hopes the devs will address in the coming months.
However, it's a remarkably enjoyable game to play. I feel like every dialogue I've had gives me meaningful choices, and I like how far they've gone, incorporating secondary conversations which are triggered off my actions and comments during in-game events.
I have to say, I was skeptical about this game. I did not enjoy several of the earlier editions in the series, though I admit I was a late-comer, only trying Divine Divinity a couple of years ago for the first time, so it is possible I was biased due the the game being dated when I picked it up.
My sumamry of this game when I speak with friends is that it feels a bit like Diablo, a bit like Baldurs Gate, and incorporates co-op which is actually well-executed, and is immensely enjoyable to play. This is high praise... I typically am hard on a games' flaws, so realizing that the ones this one possesses are minor enough to overlook in the face of the sheer enjoyment the gameplay offers is remarkable.
The crafting system feels robust, I haven't explored it terribly deeply but I do like how just about everything you can pick up is useful in one way or another, and it's not hard to ensure that you *can* make use of them if you so desire.
The levelling system... generally makes me feel like I'm gaining a respectable level of power at each level, as it should. My only complaint is minor, and that is that some levels feel significantly 'lighter' than others in terms of what you get. I suppose that is not unusual, and there's been enough levels where I do feel I get a lot, combined with generally feeling powerful throughout the game, to essentially negate the complaint. I just feel like levels should feel significant, and a couple of levels don't. I'd imagine this could be easily fixable by moving where the player recieves some bonuses to balance them across the spread.
Let's see... leveling, crafting, overall gameplay feel, and dialogue have been covered, what else?
The story is rich, and deep. There's a lot going on, but it's not difficult to track, and the journal does a very good job of sorting and keeping track of what you've been up to. It does follow some fairly common fantasy tropes, but it has enough of it's own brand and flavor that it isn't an issue.
Adventuring is fun, exploration is rewarded nicely in many ways, from hidden chests with nice loot, to robbing houses and finding legendary stashes hidden in trophies, or secret doors behind wall paintings. The challenge level of the game is variable, depending on when you go to certain areas, but a careful explorer can generally see and avoid fights that are beyond them ahead of time.
... There is a degree of permanency in this game. You can lock yourself out of quests and make permanent changes to your character by making the wrong decision in a dialogue or other event. This is true in many role playing games, but moreso here... exiting out of a dialogue early can prevent you from being able to ever complete that quest. Thankfully, there is a save feature which is always available, so follow the common RPG golden rule: save early, save often... and the issues related to 'missing out' more or less disappear.
All in all, a great game. I'll give it a 4/5 but emphasize that it is loads of fun, with only minor issues.

Recommend -- barely.
This game is fun, but it in no way lived up to the hype/my expectations, and it is quite pricey for what it is. I've played through twice, in about 15 hours altogether.
Basically, this game is "Viking Oregon Trail", with level ups. Very narrow level ups (stat selection for pre-made characters).
There's no character creation (though you do have access to several different character's POV during the game -- but you don't have control over switching between those). Events in the game (for example agreeing to let certain characters join or not join your caravan) don't really impact the game other than to provide a bit of flavor to your next play through.
The world is interesting enough, and some of the characters are intriguing, but by and large there's no pay off on that, because it's half a game. The game just stops, at about what I thought was the half way mark. So while there's hints at things that it might be interesting to learn about the characters, that's as far as it gets.
Furthermore, the characterisation is not that sophisticated, despite the praise heaped on the game. It's not terrible, but it's by no means outstanding. The characters are very trope-y: "Concerned Dad" "Teen Girl" "Lady Archer" "Rude Prince" "Pyscho Pyro" "Proud Warrior Race Guy" etc.
A final pet peeve: the dialogue in this game was very iffy in places. It's supposed to be reminiscent of a Viking Saga, but the characters are constantly going around using contemporary slang. I'm not expecting Shakespeare -- but it would be nice if the characters didn't use things like "ok". It's just -- not in keeping with the milieu.
So, I've told you my reservations for recommending. If you're reading this and thinking, "wow that's very picky", then maybe this game is for you! But if you're thinking "no, that would bother me too", maybe skip it or wait for a good sale.
As I said, I've played through twice. I doubt I will again -- fifteen hours and I feel like I've seen everything the game has to offer. I got the game on sale, which I'm really glad about. I feel like it was expensive at the price I paid. I think I'd be genuinely annoyed if I'd paid more.

This is the first of its kind for me. I've never really played a similar game. At first the fact that it's turn-based may seem like a turn-off (hehe) but that's not really the case. The turn based combat definitely does not feel slow most of the time. Sometimes the number of enemies getting turns in a row requires a little bit of wait. However, this ties in well with a mention of status effects. You quickly learn how to effectively freeze, stun, or knock-down enemies. I found I used these a LOT more than simply slowing, cursing, or lowering the attributes of an enemy force, those effects I'm sure are more necessary on hard (I played on normal) but the results are a little more subdued. The great benefit to me for the first list of statuses is that it means you don't have to wait for 5 enemy zombies to move in a row, hurray! One thing that was annoying at first but learned to avoid and appreciate later was avoiding stunning my own forces with various air/lightning spells. Sometimes I would think a unit was in the clear because she was near but not next to an enemy force but would still get stunned. I learned later on the usefulness of putting a fair number of points (and wearing appropriate gear) into the various Body Building and Willpower (or wearing armor with some form of immunity instead of just grabbing the highest armor value). Of course, this was a little easier to splurge on with the Secrets vendor exploit still in place.
Later on in the game it's very easy to just buff up armor/elemental resistance and go to town and watch enemies fail to do a lot of damage. Some late game enemies were actually somewhat interesting in this regard because they rely on brute strength of a few units rather then an ambush where you have to worry about engaging on multiple fronts for a larger number of enemies. I actually had to change my strategy a bit here since I really only had 1 person able to take many hits from them and my other units (2 mages and an archer) were simply too squishy for the heavy physical damage. Luckily I had two people capable of teleporting them to where they shouldn't be to help keep things in check. The game emphasizes strategy, but it's also incredibly unbalanced, which can be a benefit but is sometimes an annoyance.
The Act 1 boss fight was the first example of the game teaching me the great value of positioning (rather than just forgoing it since it was previously not something that I needed to worry about.) Early in the game, I could more or less simply turtle, buff/debuff, and then focus fire target by target until there were no more targets left. The four foes in that boss fight just do not go down that fast, so I needed to make smart use of summons, teleporting both the enemies and myself, and really paying attention to the turn order. Seems like basic stuff but up to that point I didn't need to be as focused, and instead would just analyze what should be done as unit turns rolled instead of any long-term planning.
Unfortunately, the level of that fight was never really met again until the penultimate boss fight. From the second map on, I had a pretty great rotation of summons, buffs, and engaging that I really didn't need to deviate from. Most of the mid game boss fights I didn't even need to worry about whatever the mechanic was for the fight. King SPOILER had an interesting elemental mechanic but was long dead before I even had to worry about it. Maybe I should have played the game on hard, but in act one Normal seemed like a great balance. I probably should have switched but in the middle of progressing through the game the ease of combat first feels empowering instead of boring. I guess that's what second playthroughs are for SOMEDAY
The last part of the game really dragged on for me and soured me a little bit. I was traversing the last area and would actually loathe seeing red dot enemy blobs since they were just wasting time. I suppose a consequence of the long run time of the game itself as well as the rote-ness that encounters had become by that point. The only interesting encounters in that area involved the a certain goblin enemy type since they were so tanky and I couldn't just take them out quickly. So instead I would wipe out all their friends and then just peg them down slowly or less slowly, far past to point of them being an actual threat. I really enjoyed the encounters around Cyseal and Hunter's Edge because the battles felt meaningful and paced between quest progression. The red dots in that final area and to a lesser extent, Hiberheim, it just felt like I was a cartographer scraping the edges of the map and clearing it out just for a sense of completion.
One of my gripes with the combat system, as as been mentioned by others, is that sometimes it's easy to "miss" a target if his idle animation moves him out from underneath your cursor and you end up walking up to give him a hug rather than attack. I wonder if a toggle for a snappy cursor would be a possible implementation. Sometimes you can click on the enemy portrait or zoom and wiggle the camera but a lot of times there are many enemies of the same time and you're unsure which portrait is his, and for me moving the camera can sometimes mess with my mental map.
The pet talking talent is super useful, and putting it on one of my source hunters was the only real piece of advice I went into the game with. I see a lot of talk about people restarting to try to perfect their characters while I just went with a long laundry list of imperfections that made the game somewhat interesting. It will be interesting enough to see people speed run (fewest turns possible) some of the bosses (assuming at the same level) to see what sort of truly overpowered builds people can create.
I only wish the game threw a couple more talents your way. Some of them seems crazy useful (Leech) while others seemed like a somewhat waste of points.
I didn't really like most of the indoor dungeons, I liked the encounters in the outside areas a lot more, generally (not in the phantom forest). The indoor areas mostly just felt like corridors filled with baddies or rooms filled with switches. The pixel hunt puzzles were so very grating. The area near where you fight a story boss in a library is especially memorable, as well as hidden buttons in the Dark Cove and the last dungeon. I didn't like the last set of puzzles much at all, until the very last part, which was nice but too easy. A hard thing to balance, surely. Either the solution seems a little obtuse or it's spelled out and feel like it's wasting your time. While I say I didn't really like them, it was still more interesting than finding a switch tucked away somewhere.
Not really a puzzle but something I'm reminded of are the reason/charm/intimidate skill checks. I really don't like the rock paper scissors implementation at all.
I never really found the need or desire to save scum for loot. I guess mainly because the crafting/upgrading of equipment is easy enough, and the importance skills and tactics is MUCH more important than whatever you are wearing. I recall not replacing Jahan's initial staff until he was level ~14 and I realized my Scarlett had a level 5 cap and boots until very near the end of the game. You could beat the game naked. If they fix the issues with the low level loot dropping from higher level areas, then I really don't have much of any problem with it. It doesn't bug me that I might have an old piece of equipment stick around since since I never happened to find a replacement. You make due with what you get.
The artstyle and whole tone of the game is definitely pleasant. The exuberant and over-acted mannerisms of some of the npcs definitely set the tone of the game early on. The environments are great, and the music is fitting, and areas like the Temple of SPOILER are haunting as they should be. Sometimes the character models don't look super when zoomed close, but that's minor.

I remember watching TechTV. I remember The Screen Savers sometimes talked about games, Doom 3 on one occasion, another being Half-Life 2, since it was a scandal. By the time I was watching TechTV HL2 became a game everyone already finished, but also a game that was fresh. I had a toaster that ran Quake 3 at best, and that was after extreme engine and Windows tweaking. I switched to console gaming until the end of the PS3 era, and then upgraded my computer. By then HL2 was nothing, and I think Valve had enhanced the graphics by this point.
The gameplay is basically the same as HL1, or any other shooter for that matter. You have a variety of guns, there are exploding barrels, blah blah blah. The enemy variety is quite low, really. You're mostly killing soldiers. There's the perhaps infamous watercraft section I hear a lot of people hate. I personally enjoyed it quite a bit, however I resented that they tacked on a puzzle in the middle of the action without any kind of smooth transition. That's really what I'd complain about with this game, albeit a minor to medium level complaint: pacing. Every time I encountered a puzzle on my initial playthrough I was irritated because I didn't feel like slowing things down a while and figuring♥♥♥♥♥♥out. I tend to enjoy my games no more complex than...I dunno, Super Mario Bros. 3. It's like when I listen to classical music. Yes, I understand that it's very complex. Yes, I understand that people find it beautiful. But since I can't see the overall picture in my head due to an insufficient IQ, I cannot grok classical music. Likewise, if you put someone like me in front of a physics puzzle, however innovative and interesting, Hulk smash. Honestly, if I'd looked up the solutions to the puzzles, I would've enjoyed myself more. That said, I was young when I played this, and I tended to be thick-skulled when it came to puzzles.
HL2 does something really cool with its interface: your ammo and health appear on the sides of your crosshair. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ Dead Space put health on the back of your dude's suit, which removed the interface requirement completely, but NO OTHER SHOOTER PUTS THE HEALTH AND AMMO AROUND THE CROSSHAIR. Why? Seriously, why? We're supposed to think CoD or CSGO or Gears of War or whatever else as being these big honking competitive games, but they're using an old fashioned interface? Not to mention aaaaaaall the shooters that came out between HL2 and now.
Headshots don't count in this game, so if you're using a pistol, just dump magazines into the bad guys. If you run out of ammo, there's always the physics gun you can use to pick things up and throw them, which is usually pretty fun. I'd say I probably enjoy and get the most mileage out of the gravity gun than the pistol for example. I wish, since this is a post CS game that it had similar dynamic crosshairs and headshots. This would open up a lot of opportunity for skillful players to show their♥♥♥♥♥♥ I appreciate the shotgun in this game: it has a primary fire that consumes one round and an alt fire that consumes 2 rounds, but does more damage. This is yet another thing I rarely see in shooters. Another word about the gravity gun: you could use the crowbar to break open ammo/health boxes, but the gravity gun is more fun. You might think the occasional puzzle would remind me to do it, but it's the combat that gets you killed, so what's when saving helps out. The levels certainly have good design overall, but sometimes I got confused about where I'm supposed to go. Not often, though. And that might be my fault. You can even use this to your advantage in Ravenholm and a part involving...a magnet, let's say. There are probably more, but I can't be bothered to remember them. If you're into Quake or Serious Sam like me, you'll want to keybind your weapons to convenient keys so you can switch at the drop of a hat and adapt to the situation. Since there are a lot of weapons, this game lets you approach practically any battle in your own fashion. Interestingly, even the physics puzzles can be solved in multiple ways. You literally look at the environment, pick up a thing, put it in or on a thing, and you've solved the puzzle. You don't have any weird♥♥♥♥♥♥like empty buckets weighing more than big rocks either. As far as story goes, it does a lot to endear important characters to you, so you care when they're threatened. The voice acting is damn near perfect. And by the way, a fellow named Dr. Howl does the voice for Dr. Kleiner. Look him up, he's great. The intro sequence is wonderful, does anything and everything it can to settle you into the setting. You have appropriate moments of panic and slowdown. And plenty of humor.
It's too bad I missed this game when it was at the peak of its relevance, but that's the way it goes. Lately I've been kicking around the idea of having an anniversary games list that I revisit once a year. Half-Life 2, the game that like it's predecessor is seen as a classic. It's time for me to find out if the game still holds up.
The story takes place some years after the events of the original Half-Life. Gordon Freeman is woken up by G-Man to find out that the world had been taken by the alien Combine. Gordon is then joined by resistance fighters to find a way to free humanity.
The gameplay itself is a mixture of shooting, puzzle solving and exploration much like the first Half-Life game. However, all of this is differently executed in Half-Life 2. In Half-Life 2 everything is even more dynamic, because of objects being destructible and having physics, which can result in some memorable chain reactions.
The world felt to me like a real open world game, while it is still a pretty linear game. This has to do with the fact that you are mostly outside and you can explore the different areas and interact with npcs. The world you play in is around the same city area, which means that this time you aren't going to other alien dimensions.
When you think about it there aren't actually that many new things in Half-Life 2. But the things that are new still deliver new gameplay. For instance, the gravity gun that you get can grab and shoot objects which is great for murdering and puzzle solving. The gravity gun really adds a playfulness to the game. The other real new weapon is the bug bait which is a ball that you can throw on enemies or destinations, which will result in a group of your own aliens going to it and attacking the enemies. The only problem I had with this is that you can only use this weapon in a certain section.
The other new gameplay feature is that you can now drive a buggy at certain parts. I read people saying that it was the worst part of Half-Life 2. In my opinion even though the buggy feels clunky I loved that part the most. It really gives that open world explorer feeling, because of you have to get out of the vehicle to look around.
The sounddesign in this game was also done by the same team as the one that worked on the original Half-Life. I can say that I liked this soundtrack even more than the previous one, because of it having more of its’ own style. The epic music sometimes felt a little off though, but they are still fun to listen to. The sound effects add a quirky feeling, and the voice acting is also professionaly executed.
The storytelling of the game was mostly well executed, with also including storytelling through gameplay. Sadly, unlike in its’ predecessor, you are forced at certain parts to listen to conversations. This can be pretty annoying if you have to listen to it again, without the option to skip it.
I have to say that overall the world, story and gameplay doesn't feel as flawlesly connected as it was in the previous Half-Life. That probably has to do with the fact that the game also wanted to show everything impressive that the engine could do.
The game took me 12 hours to complete so it was shorter than the original Half-Life, but I guess that also has to do with the fact that at the beginning I unknowingly played on the easiest difficulty. Later I found out I could actually change it in the options menu.
Even with the complaints I have with Half-Life 2 compared to Half-Life 1, I can still recommend it. The game like its’ predecessor was greatly ahead of its’ time, and at some parts maybe still is. While playing I realized that every futuristic game that I played that came out after Half-Life 2 all had big 'inspiration' from the game.  Half-Life 2 is still adventurous enough that it still holds up.

Одни пришельцы протягивают руку помощи в борьбе с могущественным Альянсом, захватившим Землю, а другие то и дело норовят попробовать человечину на вкус.

Затем мы бежим по коллекторам, спасаясь от полиции. Затем катимся по каналам на лодке, попутно отстреливая всё живое и механическое-летающее, что пытается встать на нашем пути. Затем игра превращается в Survival-Horror с отстрелом зомби в городе-призраке, когда твоими союзниками становиться лишь безумный священник и верный дробовик. А под конец всех похождений, нас ожидает революция и война против оккупантов.
Half-Life 2, это обилие врагов и представителей разных инопланетных рас. Насекомые переростки толпой прыгающие на игрока стоит ему наступить на песок. Гигантские синтеты, одним залпом рушащие здания. The Walking Dead Game series is one that is very close to my heart. Despite the poor reviews it's gotten from some people, TWD: Michonne is no exception for me.
This game, as far as I know (I haven't started New Frontier yet), is a complete standalone game. Choices from previous TWD games don't factor in, and even though I played this first just to be safe, it seems as if choices from Michonne won't matter in New Frontier, the next game in the TWD game series. If you're looking to be a completionist for the main series, this game probably won't help you there (though if I find out otherwise, I'll update my review).
Before this gets any longer, I'll start with the positives and negatives of this game, based off my experience.
+You don't have to be familiar with the comic/TV series to enjoy it, you don't even have to play the other games to enjoy it
+Story kept me hooked from the beginning
+Brand new cast of characters who you'll love and hate
+Michonne (character) feels well-written, has flaws and struggles like any good character should
-I had a lot of problems running this game. I had to alt+enter to make it fullscreen, as it wouldn't give me the option in the settings or in the window. At one point
, my screen turned white but the game audio still played. Pressing ESC didn't work, closing and reopening the window didn't work. I was lucky the game saved right before the screen turned white, because I could only fix it by exiting the game and waiting for a few minutes before restarting it. I also had some lag but that could have been my laptop, it doesn't run the greatest.
-Story didn't feel as good as the main series of TWDG.
-A little too expensive for all the bugs I had and for the amount of episodes, compared to a game from the main series.
-Characters are forgettable and now very fleshed-out/antagonists feel a little too much like ones from the main series
*-This one is just a personal thing but there were absolutely no settings to change screen resolution or mouse sensitivity, which really bugged me because I had problems with the window size when booting up the game and it was hard to do certain quicktime events or pick choices because I lost the USB to my controller and had to use a mouse and keyboard.
Quick summary:
TWD: Michonne was good, but not great. It seemed too much like a filler between seasons of the main series (though I did enjoy this more than 400 Days). The story kept me interested, but I was never on the edge of my seat. I'd also like to add that the character Michonne here is supposedly written to be more like her character in the comics rather than the TV series, though I haven't gotten into the comics yet and I'm not a big fan of the TV series. I really enjoyed her character here, but I cannot confirm if she's truly in character or not as I haven't explored much of the world of TWD outside the games. I honestly enjoyed the game, but I wouldn't recommend it to anyone who isn't a hardcore fan of the series or who is looking for something small to start the game series. I'd recommend watching a Let's Play of a small portion of this before buying it, or buy it on sale, if you aren't sure if this is for you. There is very little gameplay to it, but the quicktime events did catch me off guard quite often, though they still weren't difficult. I would also recommend trying this with a controller if you have the option available.

- run speed can go though the roof, to the point where it can be hard to maneuver. For me the bugged run speed started triggering every other level after around 3 hours, it could be a feature, but if it is I have no idea how to trigger it intentionally.
So why am I recommending it?
First the amount of voice dialogue, that is different voice dialogue. At one point I were playing the same area for the sixth time, and the game were still giving me different voice dialogue with the same general story/theme. While playing the game, I never I heard the same dialogue twice, and that's a first for me.
Second, the story, and the way it's presented (potential major spoiler
), no contradictions and a clear narrative also made really enjoyable.
Third, pathing. I found the levels designed in such a way that I did little to no backtracking, and even when replaying levels (medium spoiler
). Meaning there were small changes as well as options that kept the levels from being monotonous.
Fourth, solid combat. Event with a 21:9 ratio monitor and the camera zoom to close for comfort, I still found myself taking paths I knew/could-tell would lead to combat, trying to get a few flawless battles (if you don't have a re-bind-able controller combat might not be as fun).
How about the length then? I got the end credits rolling in a little more than 6 hours, NOTE there's at
two levels I haven't seen yet. A speedrun might be half (~3 hours), but if you decide to explore, my estimate is 20-25 hours, maybe more.

From a gripping story, to characters that feel real, The Banner Saga is an enormous feat of brilliance. Masterfully written, an art style filled with heart and soul, and gameplay that will leave you sweating, this game brings “saga” to it’s truest sense in both scale and experience. And what a saga it is.
With an opening that states “The Gods are Dead” you can tell that this is a harsh and unforgiving world, and you’ve been thrusted into the middle of it, with your clansmen at your side as you travel from settlement to settlement more often than not just trying to survive.
The gameplay is tactical and turn based, similar to XCOM and Shadowrun Returns, so before buying I’d suggest looking into it to be sure it is something you consider fun. If you are unsure I’d suggest letting this be your first! Though, even if the gameplay is not your cup of tea, if you like well told stories with great characters you might want to play it solely for that reason. Aside from a VERY abrupt ending the story and progression is golden. As you journey across the land the game feels very Organ Trail-ish as you watch your banner wave against the wind. Though, dying from dysentery is not a thing, so you can put that fear to rest if the mention of “Organ” gives you flashbacks.
Being funded by Kickstarter, the budget for this game did not allow for it to be fully voiced acted aside from a handful of moments where a few main characters will speak, but with the soundtrack by Austin Wintory (Journey) you will hardly mind. The soundtrack alone is worth the price of this game.
The experience refuses to leave my mind even days after completion. The Banner Saga has left me breathless and is one of those games that is both amazing and shows the power of what a well crafted game feels and looks like. I cannot suggest this game strongly enough!
P.S. This game could also be called, “The Banner Saga, or,♥♥♥♥♥♥Continues to Get Real even when you think the♥♥♥♥♥♥has Reached it’s Realest Levels.”

I bought this game and instantly played it for 4 hours without realizing the amount of time that passed. The only rason I even stopped playing was because of how late at night it is. This game is pretty good and rather enjoyable so far. There are two stories, and they alternate between chapters as you go along. I'm currently on the start of chapter 3 at the moment. I've no idea how many there is alltogether, but I like how the first two slide you into the game nicely. The first chapter shows you the a good deal of the game and the things you can do, and when chapter two comes along you get what's basically an post-match turn to place your units admist the blue highlighted areas along with maybe one or two more things. The game offers a good bit of choices, some of which I felt hard pressed to make my decisions on, and some that you can just either outright not delve into and remain silent, or just skip questioning alltogether. I also want to comment on the rather impressive combat style as well, with points your character(s) can use up for an extra move, extra damage, or for special abilities. And, not to mention how the enemy armor/health vs your armor/health is factored in. Certain enemies you need to demolish their armor down below your health before you can either do more than just one damage to, or just so you can  make an attack with no risks of it being deflected. It's an involved kind of combat where sometimes even where you start your units off at can dictate how the match goes for you. In all, there is likely some things that may need polishing here and there, but over all between the concept of the choices you make in and out of battle having effects on current situations, future situations, and how things seem to progress in general, and the concept behind the way battle is done, this game is really enjoyable to me so far.

300 hours in and I can honestly say that this is one of the most fun co-op shooter games available out there.
It's been a whirlwind of blood, bullets and bile drenching my screen with each satisfying headshot or swing of the sword.
The official maps, classes, avatars and weapons selection are plentiful and varied.
The Zed count increases after each wave depending on player count (up to 10 waves) and they get smarter and tougher the higher the difficulty.
The soundtrack is Metal af. Nuff said.
The playerbase is active at least in the U.S. population and the devs create ongoing weekly and seasonal events with unique cosmetic rewards.
You can solo the Zed horde mode and weekly & seasonal events, but it's more fun playing with a group of randoms or friends.
The cosmetic items are fairly-priced, are earnable in-game through random rewards, and they don't give any gameplay advantage.
The mod community is active and they continue to add tons of new maps, weapons and character skins.
There's no shortage of official and community-run servers, and matchmaking does a pretty good job of matching you with randoms.
One major gripe I have is that there's only 2 bosses that can 1-hit K.O. at higher difficulty (3 if you count the seasonal event boss), though I've been told more will be added in the future.
Another gripe I have is how unbalanced and unpredictable PVP/versus matches are, so I hope the devs continue to improve it.

Hello people searching for a review and hints for how to play.
First let me start by saying that this game is a board game. It plays exactly like the real board game and is made to be a board game. I share this as it is a fun game with friends. Playing alone is sort of lame. If you are looking for action and story this is not it. If you want to play against your friends, then you are in the right space. The board game space.
This being a board game is important as the rules are not clear unless you see the real thing. I had to read the actual physical game rules and play arround to find out how the game works. The arrows let you go in and out of the circles if you land exactly on them. Be sure to know how strong you should be to win. at first the outside of the board is best and then the insides get better. The inner circle has where you get missions. Get them. Win a mission get a Talasman. This lets you win and enter the final square. The center 9 boxes are the end game to win. You only move one here and chose right or left. Based on id you want to shoot or punch to the boss. Read these so you can gauge what level to be. You will be sent around the board for the mission but return to the mission sender once it is compleated. But in general focus on the out side early game.
The game works on D6 s you role to move and choose clock wise and counter clockwise. Since it is a game you can read what the space has to offer first. Pick the best option. In general you will want to get data slates. These have a chance of being; game breaking stuff, allies or enemies.
When data slates are drawn you can get stronger. If the data slates are friendlys you compare your leadership add a d6 vs the number they have and role to get a friend. if you win you get stronger. If you fail the unit sits on the planet for the next visitor. Enemies or units left behind are drawn and encountered or in place since they were not sucessfully roled for or not defeated by an ally. To win a fight you chose a skill of shooting or punching (basically). role a d6 add your score and they do the same. If you win the skill you used goes up one level. This is important. As every data slate can make you stronger. Stat boosts from winning fights are perminent till you die. So weak enemies are some of the best things to draw.
The other data sheet are items that break the game. Read their rules and look for when you can use them. They are the real prizes. But each is different and break the rules as their ability.
Now that the basics are covered I hope this helps in this board game.

While true to the world of snow sports in its mechanics, I can only describe the majority of this game as simply this: frustratingly simple.
A mile wide, but an inch deep: not quite enough to drown in. The controls absolutely require you to use a controller, but lack accuracy or consistancy. I often find myself sitting in my chair thinking "Now why the ♥♥♥♥ did my character do that?" As I go to simply pull a 360 while cruising down a flat section, I find that my character desides "THAT'S NOT X-TREME ENOUGH FOR ME" and procedes to attempt a front flip that drives his face into the snow. And that only scratches the surface.
The intense focus on X-treme big mountain helicopter skiing is this game's ultimate downfall, as it features the only terrain parks in the world to be lacking any sort of rails. While there are plenty of surfaces in the game that could be used to grind (guard rails, hand railings, picnic tables, etc.) not one has allowed me to grind after landing perfectly perpendicular to it with enough momentum to keep me going. Instead I find my character falling through the terrain and then magically reappearing moments later. With this focus on the X-treme, the game fails to even acknowledge the laid back freeing style of sport that skiing and snowboarding are.
What I did appreciate about this, however, is the announcer. You can flop your way through an entire "challenge," fail every jump and suck♥♥♥♥♥the whole way down the mountain; but at the end of it all, he will still utter such praise as "The sponsers really liked what they saw out there, you're really moving up in this world" or "This event is for the best of the best, and that's you!" It only reinforces how little exploration focus there is in this incredibly repetitive map. Most lines will even lead you to the same places, but how could you know? The tracks don't linger long enough for you to realise it.
These are my main problems with the game, there's not a lot too it: and without any real depth or diversity to the terrain for players to explore, it's understandable now how so many people get burnt out on this game. It's a true shame, as this really could have been something special: when it boils down to it it's only good, not great. A much more inclusive and FREE experience can be found from the game SNOW. If you're thinking about buying this game, give SNOW a go, then come back and try this if SNOW left you wanting more.
Not to mention, the sound and UI design in this game is ugly: the UI is incredibly intrussive (thankfully there's an option to turn it off; but even then, many of the components still linger on the screen) and the sounds the characters make while injured make me feel uncomfortable; the sounds remind me of two mannitees ♥♥♥♥ing. All other sounds are fine, it's just the character sounds that get on my nerves.
Don't even get me started on the always online bs. Ubisoft claims it's to make the game more competitive and improve interaction between players, so then WHY do tracks dissapear so quickly?! Other skiers' tracks improve the experience while actually skiing: you get to judge popular areas, follow others out of bounds and truly explore the mountain and trail-blaze for others... NOT IN THIS GAME! That would be TOO interactive.
The boundary lines in this game are ridiculous too, I'll find myself cruising through a forest when all of a sudden I get pulled back to mountain view because I dared to be too adventurous. That's another issue with big mountain skiing: without any trails or groomed and guided sections, "straying from the path" doesn't exist! Every section of the game feels like it's just part of the norm. There's nothing adventurous or extreme if every option you have is "adventurous" and "X-treme." SNOW is a perfect example of how a map should be designed, while nowhere near as large as the one offered in Steep, every square inch of SNOW is packed with something to discover: hotels that act as improvised terrain parks, actual terrain parks WITH RAILS, long flat groomed sections for just carving out a few turns, and even glaciers and rocky cliffs. My point being, the map is alive: there are places to go, things to see, player trails to follow, you can even spawn on other players to make cooperative matching easier.
What I did like:
The animation is nice and the customization is pretty great: you're very unlikely to encounter someone wearing the same outfit as you, even in the early player levels.
Verdict:
Overall, the game is good, there are just better options out there that offer a more complete experience. So I'd honestly recommend you go out and get yourself SNOW over this if you're new to the genre. Personally, I really enjoy what Steep brings to the table as I've been skiing my whole life: I just have my issues with it.
Definitely do NOT get the DLC or pay full price for this though.

Good enough game for a short game.
Upsides:
~  Humour holds it together. It manages to be mostly funny, sometimes even when it is sorta serious.
~  Anti-Hero done right. Closer to classic style, without that 90s brooding nonsense.
~  Female lead is good too, for that matter. Strong character. Not some do-nothing damsel type.
~  Good narration. Most of it is narration, in fact.
~  Vibrant, appealing art-style.
~  Gameplay is fun... if a bit spartan.
~  Most of the achievements (35 out of 37, if I remember) are really easy to get.
Downsides:
~  Very short if you're trying for the true end.
~  No boss fights. While the game does gradually introduce new minion types over the first few playthroughs, it is very limited, and that is all you fight for the entire game. No character battles. No bosses. The only thing that changes in the combat after that is the protagonist.
~  Two of the achievements are massively grindy... i.e. the one for getting ALL the story routes, and the one for maxing out the skill-tree.
~  Starts to get repetitive after the 2nd or 3rd story-route. Most of the routes have almost exactly the same gameplay through the same maps with only minor differences. If you're grinding for the two aforementioned achievements, expect to be driven to catatonic boredom by the repetition after a while. Unskippable choice page nonsense doesn't help.
~  The crafting system is also kinda threadbare. Given how long grinding out all the stories takes, the fact that you don't need to open any more chests past the 4th or 5th route kinda stands out.
~  While I can appreciate the massive amount of pop-culture references, a lot of them are REALLY shoehorned in and just make it look like the creators were trying too hard to be hip with the geek crowd. The game tends to be more fun when it isn't just regurgitating references to things.
~  Bugs. Glitches. To note a few...
~~~ Some cutscenes aren't skippable when they apparently should be, sometimes you get stuck in the landscape.
~~~ The Void Blade can mess up your speed (in either direction) depending on when you press / release the button. Use sparingly.
~~~ It is entirely possible to get stuck in the scenery if you're not careful.
~~~ The "True Ending" route is very buggy, including one section of one stage which completely fails to render... and the route being aborted to a different route if you quit to the main menu at the wrong time (or even if you pick the wrong option in one case).
In any case, I complain a lot, sure... but it was fun.  Kept me occupied for 2 days while I got all the cheevos.

WTF is it?   -   Orcs Must Die! is a third-person trap laying orc slaying monster delaying tower defense game. It is the second game made by Robot Entertainment whose studio is made up of people from the now defunct Ensemble Studios. Why is that significant? Well at one point in my life I was a console gamer, I won't go into specifics because those were dark times filled with low framerates, but I digress. The game that I played the most on xbox was Halo Wars which was developed by Ensemble. Being the amazing devs they are, they have yet again impressed me with Orcs Must Die! The objective of the game is to stop orcs from reaching the rift(s) on each level by placing traps and using weapons. Each level has multiple waves of orcs that increase in difficulty over the rounds and if enough orcs enter the rift(s) the rift score drops to zero and you lose. The plot of the game is surprisingly interesting aswell since you play as a War Mage who is the last member of an order dedicated to defending the rifts which are sources of magic for the two worlds. I think they could have gone more in depth with the story even though this is a somewhat silly game.
Verdict   -   Well worth the time and money.
BTW   -   This is better than that Rift mmo.

So, before I start, I'll say that you should not ignore this review because of the hours of game I got so far. I have played and beated the game 3 times already in Xbox360, one of them in Hard and Iron Man mode, so yeah, I know what I'm talking about. Let's now start with the review:
XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a Strategy game based on the unforgiving and old-school game named "X-COM; UFO Defense", and "UFO; Enemy Unknown", it depends on where you live and what version you got. Is it loyal to the source material? I can tell you that ANOTHER GAME of the series is NOT LOYAL AT ALL (I'M LOOKING AT YOU, BUREAU, YOU PIECE OF SH#T), but this one is quite amazing!
First and foremost, it's the best strategy game you can get for consoles, just as great as Defense Grid; The Awakening or the old but yet amazing Advance Wars 1 & 2 for GBA, but way longer, and with a lot of replayability. The game also has decent graphics and sound, but a bit lacking in music. As usual, I will get the bad parts of the game out of the way first:
The biggest problem I got, is the IA. It's not that they're brain-dead (they do play Kamikaze at times), or too smart, but rather in a gameplay element that's flawed and makes it feel wrong: Enemies will notice you right away, most of the times. Not only that, they will instantly move, even when it's not their turn, 99% of the times into cover. Why is it so bad? Let me give you an example:
You're moving your last guy, when suddenly you find 3 Sectoids (weakest aliens in the game, along with the drones). But guess what, they instantly move and flank you, your turn is over, AND THEY CAN SHOOT YOU DOWN RIGHT AWAY! Infact, that's so much bullsh#t that there are mods to disable it on pc, but I had to suffer that crap on Xbox360 for too long, and let me tell you, THAT MECHANIC CAN GO DIE IN A FIRE. It ruins any sort of Stealth aproach, and goes down into "Start shooting the closest alien you see".
The other thing I hate about this game, is the random factor. Now, hear me on this one, it's well done in most parts: Each playthrough is completely different, specially with the "Second Wave" options...But then, you have the fights. Hitting an enemy or not is a matter of odds. Of course, flanking them gives you higher chances of hitting, and extra chances for a critical hit, BUT THERE'S STILL CHANCES OF MISSING A POINT-BLANK SHOOT. Not only that, I got crit-hit from miles away with plasta-pistols of some lone-sole hacking Sectoids, and got instantly killed. The random factor of battles might♥♥♥♥♥♥you off, but you can always save often and reload if the game starts to screw you more than life itself.
There's also a minor issue: The fact that the things that where not added in release, and other things they could not finish in time, are added as a huge DLC. The "Enemy Within" is great, of course, BUT IT'S ALMOST AS EXPENSIVE AS THE GAME! It does make the game twice as good, but you should wait for sales on it.
Now, the good things the game has: The game is balanced, and it both randomizes and goes further into the Human's comeback to the Alien menace as you go on. If you want to clear the game fast, you can. If you want to take it slowly, you can. You feel as the one in charge, because you are (until the game gets lucky and no-scopes your♥♥♥♥♥. It has a similar way of playing as the Fire Emblem games, where you can lose characters permanently, but also recluit new ones, or even build robots, F#CKING ROBOTS. The game is challenging enough to♥♥♥♥♥♥you off enough to go back and kill their families, it can last really long, some special missions are quite cool, and even has a multiplayer mode packed in, even though they could have added a Coop mode, or something, rather than just "Choose your minions and go murder eachother".
Right now, I got the game for free because of a give-away, and I'm doing an "Impossible" Difficulty playthrough, and let me tell you, for smart assh#les like me, it's not even hard at all, but I do recommend you giving the special difficulties a try once you clear the game for the first one. Higher difficulties makes the game as hard as Dark Souls on steroids (AND THE STEROIDS ARE ON CRACK), while the "Iron Man" mode will only allow you to have one save file, that constantly saves. So yeah, permanent choices, no "That was stupid, let's reload and forget it happend". You f#ck up once, that brave soldier is gone, for good.
I recommend getting the game along with the "Enemy Within" DLC on a sale. Infact, if you like strategy games, and you don't have this, you're one stupid motherf#cker. I give this game "A critical headshot through the map / 10".
Oh and, in my "Impossible" run, I haven't yet lost a soldier, and I'm almost at the first Alien base raid. So yeah, beat that mofos.
