Let’s be honest, this game did not deliver. I so tried to like it, but this was just not it. The visuals are OK, price at the time I bought it was OK, too, but everything else is sub-par.
First of all, there’s no way to save manually, and I hate it. I really don’t see why you cannot implement manual saving when you release a game for PC, and I think you should not release a game for PC where you cannot, because, here it comes: You will die in this game, and you will die a lot, and all checkpoints have been placed in front of the difficult passages and not behind them, and then you will die even more, and have to endure the boring stuff again before you die in a millisecond because the required key sequences are weird und illogical and neither consistent with your learning curve nor  common sense,  and then you will leave the game and when you resume you will lose your voice over your enraged screaming, because you do in fact not resume where you left but you will have to play the entire level again because checkpoint does not mean checkpoint, it does mean “interim save that will be lost when you leave the game or when it crashes” and it crashed every single time I used alt +tab. And when I did not. And when I moved the mouse.
The combat elements are a farce. The only way to master combat is by pressing the slowmo button, and I do not want to press the pull-me-out-of-immersion-button, because the need for this element is proof of bad game design and nothing else. I get it, I’m supposed to avoid opponents, so, hey, wait, did you implement passages that cannot be finished without engaging combat? There is no consistent design in the entire game. Ah, and I do not want to run around like a headless chicken finding a solution to a logic puzzle because I am being followed by invincible headless chickens in ninja suits.  I either solve puzzles or kill everyone, but I do not do both at the same time, because when I’m supposed to, I have the insta-reflex to kill the chicken ninjas first and and then do one of the things at a time but, yeah, you guessed it, in this game you can’t.
See how Portal did it? If you die, you die because you did not find a solution or misinterpreted the surroundings, and not because you fail at using the lagging controls ME offers while fighting spawn-beaming ninjas. The chicken-ninjas do not spawn-beam through open doors, btw., those are impenetrable obstacles for immortal fast-forward-ninja-chickens.
OK, one last question – the root of the game’s setup is one single dead foreigner and that is the reason why you have to wipe out an entire army of ninjas, with no way to avoid combat at all, who shoot you because you… run on a roof? Deus Ex claims it is possible to play the entire game while being able to avoid almost any combat, as a genetically enhanced supers-merc. That’s a challenge to stay on the good side. And ME’s teenage alt chick needs to go all in and perforate ninjas in the dozens with machine guns? Ugh. If you play this game, you are not the good one, who you could have been, given the abilities to avoid combat by simply being able to retreat to areas where no one would be able to follow you. You are a mass murderer, in a suicide simulator.
I did not like this game, because the developers messed it up while the idea remains brilliant.

TL:DR: Good game, worth buying it at full price (lots of gameplay, high quality), needs a balance patch, overall only minor complaints.  Highly recommended.
Very good RPG, enjoying it immensely.  I have only minor complaints: A balance patch really needs to be deployed though - apparently certain "classes" are very OP by the end of the game, and others are eventually relegated to buff-bots.  It's possible to make your character impossible to kill and deal the best damage in the game, trivializing boss fights.  After they are done with their much-deserved vacation, I'm sure some things will be tweaked by the developers.
Hard difficulty makes it a bit tough to get a good start unless you run around town getting experience before moving outside the gates (and then in the right order, since some directions are lower level, some aren't).  Also, hybrid characters seem to have troubles by the last half of the game.  Again, balance patch or mods will eventually correct things like this, and it's a minor complaint.
The writing of NPC's is excellent and often hillarious.  For some reason the writing of the interaction between your two main protagonists is terrible, though.  You get choices in dialogue that seem to be either a little too sassy-pants ("It's getting annoying carrying the group by myself") or goody two-shoes ("You are amazing, and I want to be your groupie!").  This is confusing, as the writing for pretty much every NPC is phenomenal - the intelligent characters are wordy, the confident warrior lady is opinionated and in your face, etc.
Overall it's been a really fun time sink.  It's one of the very few games I wanted to pick up right away at full price.  90% of my other puchases are when they go on sale 6 months after release.  Not this one: I bought it right away and it's been completely worth it.  Getting a lot of hours out of it, and it's been fun the whole time.  Looking forward to a second playthough once the classes are more balanced late-game.

Though the looks may have updated, it still retains the classic feel of the game its based off of.  Which is great, because you can jump straight back to retro style immediately, and reuse your old save codes.  It also has secrets. Actual secrets. The kind you wouldn't be able to find without a walkthrough, trying everything, or by complete accident.  It can be slightly infuriating at times with the same stupid enemy knocking you off that one platform, but that's just the old-school charm.
My only real complaint is because its an old game, some sections and powers feel like you hardly get to use them at all before they are never needed again.  This is more a criticism of the base material, but it feels like powers were mostly about letting you access certain zones, and their individual special mechanics weren't needed much beyond that.  I don't see how the sunken ship is enhanced by being a piranha-man other than needing it to board.
But again, those complaints are mostly to do with the base game, and not with the remake.  Its a rather excellent remake, keeping the visuals and music close to their source material while still rendering them in HD if you want them, and even makes a point of deliberately leaving in typographical errors.  Its hard to get closer to the source than that.

Talisman: Horus Heresy is a board game in which you, a space marine warlord, must build your army by increasing your raw strength, recruiting soldiers, building naval armadas, and completing quests so that you can turn the tide at the legendary Battle for Terra.
The game is initially difficult to understand because the only ‘tutorial’ takes the form of infrequent and poorly described tool-tips. There should have been a comprehensive, narrated tutorial to help players understand every element of play. As it stands, the best way to learn the game is by playing it. After a few test-runs, you’ll quickly understand what you need to do: Increase your strength through equipment or raw combat, complete a quest, reach the final battle.
Without DLC, the base game has a TON of event cards, equipment cards, strategy cards, and other actions. You probably won’t see it all in a single game, which is good for replayability. What’s not good for replayability is that whether you’re a loyalist or chaos servant, the cards themselves are limited. Everything is +1 Resource, +2 Close Combat, +1 Stratagem, etc. There are a ton of cards and they all have some nice fluff written on them, but the actual effect of the cards is basically the same. Gameplay is symmetrical. Fighting The Emperor is the same as fighting Horus. Praying to Chaos Gods and rolling a 6 has a SLIGHTLY better effect than rolling a 6 in the Ultramar region. The result is that it really doesn’t matter what side you choose except that some warlords have more interesting bonuses than others.
It’s worth noting that enemy AI is TERRIBLE. It is some of the worst AI I’ve ever seen in a game and there’s no difficulty scale. AI Warlords will use strategy cards that hurt players on their own team. Playing as both Chaos and Loyalists, I was never once in danger of losing the game to AI. I’ve never seen enemy AI reach the final battle. Instead they endlessly patrol around the board, landing on avoidable game squares that only harm them. The game would certainly be interesting against a human player, but good luck finding someone to play with since Talisman: Horus Heresy somehow landed on the list of “worst Warhammer 40k games”
But despite these shortcomings, it’s not a bad game. Despite being a board game, it has elements of grand strategy. You have distinct immediate, short term, and long-term goals to keep you engaged throughout. Dice based movement keeps things fresh by never giving you exactly what you wanted. Tough enemies, warlord reinforcements, and equipment make battles exciting even when you’re just rolling the dice...but then you reach a point where you realize that none of the armies (except Daemons it seems) have special rules. Every single non-player enemy can be boiled down to a number between 1-14 and a d6 dice roll.
Because the AI is so irrevocably terrible, the end game gets really boring. The game is designed as a race to the final battle, but the enemy AI will never reach that point. As a result, you can spend as long as you want building your army until it’s impossible for you to lose. Once you start the final battle, it takes a whopping 10 turns of cakewalking to actually beat the game. 10 turns of doing nothing but mashing the spacebar. 10 turns of invincibility where you still have to give the other 3 players a chance to move. You must sit through 40 individual turns even when you are guaranteed to win the game. Worse, you continue to grow in strength throughout the final battle. Each success increases either your melee or ranged weapon skills, causing a snowball effect where powerful characters continue to become more powerful, while weak players and enemies are crushed over and over and over again.
And what do you get for your trouble? A book cover with the background removed. Not a cutscene, not a climax. You defeat the end boss after 2 hours of building your army and the game says “I remember when The Emperor killed Horus.” You don’t even get the credit.
After the end game, the specific character you used for that game gets experience points at an EXTREMELY slow pace. What do these level ups do? Presumably they unlock a special weapon a special piece of armor, and a special fleet for that character, but the game is terrible at telegraphing this. If you want to find out, you need to play the game with the same character 3 times to reach the first notch on the level up bar, BUT ONLY THE PLAYER WHO ACTUALLY DEFEATED THE BOSS GETS TO LEVEL UP. So much for teamwork. If your ally reaches the center square on the turn before last and then kills the boss on the next turn, you get 0XP for the entire game, even if you took 4/5 of the bosses' hit points. That alone is reason NOT to buy this game.
Did I mention there are over 50 characters per team and that changing your character’s color scheme counts as choosing an entirely different character? So, if I finish the game as Iron Hands Praetor, my Ultramarines Praetor doesn’t level up. It means that for reasons unknown (because the game doesn’t tell you) you’re encouraged to pick a favorite character from your very first game onward despite that each character has different playstyles and special abilities. However, when you finally reach this level up section, you realize that the game wants to reward you for playing as long as possible, gaining XP, fighting with your team, and recruiting your army. It's no wonder only 0.1% of players have gotten any of the level up achievements. The problem is that the game is already too easy. I have no incentive to pad out this game to make the next one easier when I’m already crushing my opponents.
If Talisman: Horus Heresy was asymmetrical and had a little more tactical or strategic depth, it would have been fantastic. As it stands, it’s merely OK. Not terrible. By no means bad. Worth a play just to see how it works, but not great. The gameplay gets repetative, the rewards are meaningless, there's a horrible undertone of unbalanced gameplay, and there's never a sense that you've actually gained or completed something because the game insists that you only helped win the game when in fact you did all the leg work.

In 1989 the Sega Master System released a real gem.
Wonder Boy Dragon's Trap. what a game it was, I spent endless hours
playing that game, it was hard, frustrating and it was the first game I
remember playing that required backtracking, which is a daunting thing
as a kid.  But I loved it anyway.
it was a rewarding game, after passing each section you could unlock a
new animal-man to turn into and the game would change completely based
on your new skills.  It was also the first game I remember playing where
you could upgrade your gear giving it a slight RPG element.
well kids, it's back! and in a big way!
The developers Lizardcube and publishers DotEmu have delivered a truly
amazing homage to a game that many people have loved for a long time.
This is by far the best remake I’ve ever come across.
the animation is completely hand drawn and it's absolutely beautiful.
the soundtrack has been re-orchestrated and composed by Michael Geyre,
using the original tracks and bringing them to life with orchestral
instruments.
the gameplay is exactly the same as the original, in face with the press
of a button you can even switch the graphics and sound to the original
that we all know and loved.
as a kid playing games with 8 bit graphics and sound I think my
imagination filled in the gaps and this remake of the game looks exactly
the way I imagined it when I was playing.  it's a true labour of love and
it is so finely polished that anyone who loved the original HAS to have
a play-through of this version.
I hope that this becomes the standard for re-booted games because this
really is as good as it gets.
it's an absolute pleasure to play, the animations, the backgrounds, the
music. It's all just so fantastic.
Wonder Boy: The Dragon's Trap is an absolute MUST HAVE for fans of the
original and anyone who loves games in general. I can't recommend it
enough.
Thank you Lizard Cube and DotEmu for delivering such a brilliant reboot.
I hope your work inspires other developers to put as much love and care
into their games as you have put into yours.

Honestly, Dead Island was fun for a while when it came out but I found myself burned out towards the end. Dead Island Riptide... more of the same. Dying Light is what i wish Riptide would have been! The devs literally destroyed their former work! I like the more serious tone here. So let's break things down.
Gameplay: Parkour... really that's all i need to say about it but i won't. It's very well done and jumping across rooftops,grappling up the side of a building and narrowly escaping death is a thrill! Especially at night when things get insane!
Controls: Tight and responsive, if you've played Dead Island it's pretty much the same thing here with the addition of parkour mechanics.
Graphics: The game looks beautiful. Great textures and really good lighting effects that shine through very well at night. It's a pretty game.
Audio: A high point without a doubt! Just the main theme alone reminds me of the 80's. ESPECIALLY films like George Romero's Day of The Dead (which i HIGHLY recommend you all watch on youtube for free!) So it goes without saying the music is great. The sounds of the infected, the sounds of guns and impact, everything is perfect here!
Story: Meh... the side quests have some interesting stuff but the main story is okay. Nothing amazing, nothing terrible, it's just kind of there.
Side Notes: The crafting is great, the leveling mechanics are great and all in all i love this game. The VS mode is fun especially with more than one human player. I definitely recommend this game if you love zombies, love open worlds and love classic 80's horror flicks.

I'm actually kind of sad I didn't back this kickstarter project, but I felt it wasn't worth it at the time.  How wrong I was.  I'm 21 hours in, what do I see?  A game with polish, good game play, tactical turn-based combat.  Good to excellent sound effects and music, with an interesting story line.  The game doesn't hand hold you, telling you to go from point A to point B.  You want to jump in against a group of level 7 bandits at level 4?  Go right a head.  Want to steal that quest item you just handed in?  Do it!
Tactical combat: Fun, it lets you setup your own traps, create your own pathways, and wreck enemies that would normally dominate you.  The environment, spells, and so on my boost enemies, or weaken them if they're elemental.
Questing: No hand holding.  This game won't tell you where to go, it will state when you have found something.  Many hints are found in the documents you find, recover or loot off corpses.  You may have quests above your level to complete, but you can always come back to them.
Complaints:  Invintory UI needs some more tweaking, the ability to sort isn't bad.  And different tabs to list items helps.  But still feels like some more work could be done.  Load times can be a bit annoying if you're a quicksave/reloader.  A SSD helps immensly on game load times as well, can you tell how spoiled we get these days by that?
Companion interaction is on the low side.  People who expect banter between your henchmen will be disapointed.  It's more akin to NWN in that regard.
A 'hold all' function would be nice, but dragging individual portraits away from the chain does the job well enough if you only want to explore with one person.
Story: 9/10
Music: 9/10
Sound Effects: 8/10
Gameplay: 8/10
Graphics: 8/10

TL;DR: The levels are too long, and the structure of the game was designed to compensate by ensuring you reach the true ending in 5 runs out of the 25 possible endings. the game would be much better if levels were shorter and you could earn multiple truths per run, but learning the truths didn't guide you right to the best ending, encouraging players to try what they want and see more of the endings instead of just railroading them.
I'll start by saying that this game probably just wasn't for me; all the plots of the stories I went through with the exception of the true ending (It's not a spoiler; literally after your first run you unlock a truth, are shown that it's 1/4. and that getting all 4 will "unlock" something.)  were cliche and predictable, but that might not bother some people.
However, my biggest issue with the game, and one that plagues it's design causing other issues, is that the individual levels are padded to be far too long. this might sound like a nitpick, but with the 25 or so endings available in game, and each set of 5 levels taking about an hour to get through, you're looking at spending about 25 hours to see everything. Most of this time will be spent walking over effectively empty terrain, and with only 10 levels, you are going to hear a lot of reapeated lines, and know the layouts by heart after about 5 runs.
By the way, likely as a result of level length, the progression in terms of upgrades will effectively be finished by the time you finish your fifth run (I had all the swords and gems fully upgraded, and a pretty complete build in terms of skill points). But that's ok, because since you're practically garuanteed a truth every run, and having all the truths will provide a path to the true ending, 5 runs is really all it should take to get there.
Speaking of truths, While you are guaranteed a truth every run (provided you aim vaguely in their direction), many endings seem to be capable of unlocking more than one truth, just not at once. meaning you can learn something but still need to make another ♥♥♥♥ing run just for Reynardo to catch up, forcing you back into 5 runs. Oh, and none of the truths are overly mind blowing, and an observant player can see all of them before they are unlocked properly.
There are about 25 endings, but each ending takes about an hour to get and since this is a branching story, just under half your time getting them is going to be spent hearing the same dialouge over and over again, while retreading the same 5 of the same 10 levels every time (with the last level always being the same no less).
I'm going to stop here because I've spent too much time typing this, but this is me ranting about the bad of the game, though there is plenty of good. I reccomend checking the other reviews if you want to hear about that.

As the title suggests, this is basically Talisman IN SPACE!!  Overall, it's not a bad game.  The interface is kinda weird and sometimes hard to follow when the AI players are taking their turns, but after I got the hang of what was going on, I will say that the one match that I played was mostly enjoyable.
The AI didn't put up much of a challenge, either - one of the traitors got himself killed without even getting into a fight, just by a combination of bad decisions and a few unlucky rolls.  I would chalk that up to Chaos making them stupid, but my Loyalist partner wasn't any better.  He picked up a quest to deliver 2 Resources to a particular location.  Not too tough, right? Except he kept spending his Resources on merc fleets and things like that rather than saving them for the quest.  And he kept going to a particular square that automatically lowered his Resolve, making him spend more Resources on getting it back up.  Seriously, Corvus, WTF?
By the endgame, when I finally managed to get a quest of my own (which took way longer than it should have IMO), I was so strong (15 melee, 20 Ranged) that I was able to power through the rest of the game and win it about 10 turns later, while the other players were still farting around in the outer regions.
One other thing that particularly struck me was that the center region didn't have fixed encounters like the original Talisman.  Instead, almost every square was just "draw 3 more random encounters".  I thought that took a bit away from the challenge and character of the original.
Overall I'd give it a solid Maybe.  If you're a fan of Talisman and 40k lore, and you can find some buddies to play with, I think this would be a decent purchase.  Otherwise you might want to give it a pass.

A modern take on the Balder's Gate genre of RPG. It's not just a modern graphical upgrade though. The new features and functionality they added to the genre are great:
-Interact with the environment
Don't have a key for a chest or door? Bash it! Oh but do that too much and the durability of your weapon will degrade.
Enemies standing in a pool of water? Cast a lightning spell on the water and watch them get stunned and electricuted. Or freeze them with some ice
-Character Interactions
Your PCs will banter with one another with amusing dialogue.
Every NPC is a shop. YOu can barter and trade with any NPC in the game.
Every NPC in the game has an attitude rating towards you. Win a lot of favor with a particular NPC and get more favorable trades from them and more dialogue options.
-Co-op
Play with a buddy, He'll take control of the 2nd main PC and you can configure who controls the up to 2 additional companions in your party. Split the PC 2/2 between you and your buddy or take control and split things 3/1
This game is very highly recommended!!

As a huge SEGA Master System fan I was wary of an attempt to modernise such a classic from the old library, but thankfully my fears were completely unfounded.
The love that has been poured into this remake is obvious. The graphics are gorgeous and unique (thank the heavens they didn't opt for the over-used anime style), and the music is beautiful and performed by real musicians. But they're not so arrogant as to force it on you; you can switch to retro graphics and audio at the touch of a button - wonderful!
There's personality oozing from every part of the presentation. An incredibly polished game for a small studio.
Oh, and the gameplay is pretty fun, too. It can be a bit frustrating at times but nothing you can't beat with a bit of practise.
I only hope this leads to more awareness of a wonderful library of games and a system that is often overlooked in favour of the NES.

Stories: The Path of Destinies can be very fun... If you get through the hardships.
I'll start by saying that the game was something completely new for me. I went into the game blind so maybe this made it only more fun for me. Path of Destinies has a certain gameplay mechanic that makes the game a lot of fun to play and adds a great amount of replayability. So, you basically play the game over and over again, making different kind of choices until you find the "True Ending". But after every playthrough you learn something new, making it easier to find this "True Ending". Though what dissappointed me near the end, was that
If I had known this beforehand, I would have finished the game a lot quicker.
Nonetheless, the story is amazing and very fun to go through. The narrator only adds to it and the concept of the game made the storytelling all the better.
So the gameplay mechanic is, though innovative and refreshing, good but not great. The story is impressive. What more is there to the game? Not a lot. Mostly a bunch of issues:
Combat is interesting but can be a hassle sometimes, because of unresponsive controls. Sometimes, when you get charged by two enemies and you can't counter them because you can only counter one of the two and not one after another (because you're too slow) you HAVE to dodge it. But even that button prompt doesn't always react in time, which leads to lots of unnecessary deaths. Annoying. Or when you get hit, you flinch. But during this animation, you can easily get hit by another enemy. Getting hit like this in quick succesion can bring you to low health very quickly.
Solution? Get an attack speed gem and spam left mouse button. On top of that, it doesn't properly save how much health you had at a checkpoint: you just spawn with 50% of anything. Not sure if thats a good idea. Sometimes good, sometimes bad.
There also is a gamebreaking bug which forces me to redo a whole stage. I ragequitted after it happened, only to encounter it again. Pretty annoying, because the level it self is quite a hassle.
But when you figure out how to properly get through the stages, nailing the combat and evading the bugs, it's pretty cool. Though after replaying the different kinds of "Paths of Destinies" combat start to become boring because you will inevitably to the same thing over and over again, just to get through the stages as quickly as possible.
The game is also compatibly with a controller, though I only used mouse and keyboard. Movement can be very clunky, as you move with the mouse. For example, the player can sometimes be stuck walking in a certain direction. Not gamebreaking, but simply annoying.
One last thing: terrible optimization. Some levels run fine, most don't. The graphics aren't that good but still I manage to only get 20-40 fps, when I'm used to higher in better looking games.
(tl;dr)
But I still recommend this game (at a discount). Why? Because, if you figure out the combat and can handle the perfomance stuff, it's really worth a try for the story and the interesting game mechanic. I still felt like finishing the game and I still had a bunch of fun.

300 hours in and I can honestly say that this is one of the most fun co-op shooter games available out there.
It's been a whirlwind of blood, bullets and bile drenching my screen with each satisfying headshot or swing of the sword.
The official maps, classes, avatars and weapons selection are plentiful and varied.
The Zed count increases after each wave depending on player count (up to 10 waves) and they get smarter and tougher the higher the difficulty.
The soundtrack is Metal af. Nuff said.
The playerbase is active at least in the U.S. population and the devs create ongoing weekly and seasonal events with unique cosmetic rewards.
You can solo the Zed horde mode and weekly & seasonal events, but it's more fun playing with a group of randoms or friends.
The cosmetic items are fairly-priced, are earnable in-game through random rewards, and they don't give any gameplay advantage.
The mod community is active and they continue to add tons of new maps, weapons and character skins.
There's no shortage of official and community-run servers, and matchmaking does a pretty good job of matching you with randoms.
One major gripe I have is that there's only 2 bosses that can 1-hit K.O. at higher difficulty (3 if you count the seasonal event boss), though I've been told more will be added in the future.
Another gripe I have is how unbalanced and unpredictable PVP/versus matches are, so I hope the devs continue to improve it.
I've never played the original Killing Floor, but I do own it. I can't really compare how much KF2 improved on KF1, but it's safe to say that the visuals and textures have improved.
Overall, it really is a fun time when you get past the repetitive format of matches. What drove me to continue playing was setting the goal of maxing out each class/perk which I've accomplished.

Stories was advertised as a game where every playthrough is different.
Least, thats what I was told. Really its repetitive, same map every time, different ending, with each one being a bit predictable until you get the true ending.
I'm getting ahead of myself I think so I'm just gonna run a list of things I have issue with such as the fact treasure chests are nigh useless within a few playthroughs, as swords get upgraded fairly fast and chances are you'll find all the gems even faster. So at that point its remembering which door will let you cut through half the map because theres nothing more unfun than the repetition.
And speaking of unfun! The Narrator! He needs to shut up, I think that would be absolutely lovely if he only gave me new info and not pop culture references every 10 seconds, or if he talked faster for that record, I mean you can turn off the narrator but then that leaves the subtitles, so I think just turn both off would be pleasent.
I gotta say though, I didn't complete every single ending because the game doesn't feature that much variation or interest in each individual ending that I don't feel its worth getting each one, I get thats the appeal but the repetition of the game itself makes it feel like a chore.
Even battling is a chore, where it got to the point I just worked it to insta-kill the enemy every time, the combat style is like Batman: Arkham style but less fun.
The story itself is ok I guess. Only really worth it with the true ending.
I got a kick though when the narrator said "Reynardo had an idea, what if he changed the puzzle every time he saw it! That would be really interesting." Why yes narrator, it would be, wonder why it's not a thing.
Final score: Too repetitive. Feels like the definition of insanity.

This is a nice short little game which takes you on a CYOA type story/path which is actually worked into the lore for you to ♥♥♥♥ up and learn from your mistakes while a charismatic narrator reacts to your play. The gameplay is alright, the combat isn't extremely in-depth but uses a system similar to the arkham games, while countering is like in metal gear revengeance (stick and button press minus the intricate timing). It's good enough.
The real selling point is the story which lets you make decisions and leads to a bunch of different endings. Eventually you can unlock the "real" ending after discovering 4 major plot points and using them to your advantage. I thought I'd have it in me to unlock all the endings but the game is all-or-nothing with skipping cutscenes (no skipping individual lines of dialogue) and it's unskippable when giving you your choices. Given that you do play through the game, and maybe some levels multiple times, it has different layouts and the enemies get tougher over the whole game, so you won't face little trash mobs on the first level again, but what you expect to face on the next level after the end. It's a nice touch for a game which expects you to replay through it multiple times.
Overall, the game is alright at a cheap price. At full price I don't think I'd take it. You can beat the whole thing in maybe 3-4 hours, but some of the extra storylines are entertaining enough, and there are plenty of them where unlocking all of them would probably stretch it out to 10-15 hours? The music is great though, and the game has good charm. It's a nice little "appetizer" or a side dish game.

A massive amount of information, and history packed into a pretty cool game. This game's strengths also tend to be its flaws. For example the games are insanely lengthy. This is cool because it really allows you to see how even small changes can impact the stance of your society in the longrun, but at the same time it causes games to drag on forever. Similarly the skill cap on the game is so high, that it takes an enormous amount of time to become great at the game. Again very cool because theres so much room for improvement, but you might be a huge noob for a very long time. I also didn't really find it too fun to play the game alone. For these reasons I kind of find it to be a pretty niche game that you'd basically spend a quarter of a day with a small group of relatively intelligent friends playing. All that said I'd still definitely recommend checking the game out. Under the right conditions it's pretty fun.

Rating: 8.1/10
Overview:
Mirror's Edge was developed by DICE in 2009. It is an action/adventure first-person shooter parkour game.
The game is based around the  female protagonist “Faith” who is part of a group of couriers called “runners” who carry packages around the city. Using their parkour skills, they avoid police by running along rooftops, sliding down rails and ziplines, bashing through doors, and jumping off walls.
Gameplay:
I played this game using an Xbox 360 controller which synced all controls instantly. The controls and game feel like they were made for a controller. The movements are very fluid, the button setup is flawless, and it all feels natural in your hands.  Graphically, it is a masterpiece of its own.  It has a beautiful art style with graphics matching the time of the game’s release. The soundtrack matched the game very well; exciting and fast paced when it needed and slow melodies to soak in the beautiful cityscape.  The game itself was fun. It had its fair share of puzzles and fights that required the use of its multi-button parkour system. There were almost always multiple routes the any destination. The only downside to the style of gameplay was that at times it felt repetitive. It doesn’t give the desire to keep playing until the end, but still exciting enough to beat the game.
Price:
$4.99 during Winter sale. $19.99 regularly. Absolutely worth the price on sale. But I would still say the game is worth $15.
Conclusion:
A must play. This game is fun and exciting with a one of a kind style.  A controller is recommended. This is recommended for anyone who enjoys FPS, puzzles, or the idea of doing parkour and become a street ninja without actually risking their life.

This game has grown on me from a 1 to a 9.
Part of this is certainly the work the devs put into it.  They are expanding and adjusting every aspect of the game monthly to a degree not normally seen in paid DLCs.  They could have stopped where every other team would have, and released mediocrity.
Part of this is adjusting to the game's initially glaring weaknesses.  The graphics are fine - for models and textures - but the direction is so muddy that it's next-to-impossible to make out one enemy from another - or from your character - or from a bush - or from, I don't know what else there is, because it's all the same color... and texture.  But over time, I've adjusted.  I can now nearly make out my helmet.
Most of this, though, is in how the game opens up over time.  Through rebuilds and restarts, levels and faction and legendary gear...  It took until my fourth character before I even liked my build - and that's from someone who normally feels on his first build in every ARPG that I just instinctively "nailed it."  This game made me WORK for that feeling.  And read, and discuss.  And level.  And go through all of Normal, on Veteran.  Loot finally opened up, skills finally synergized, and devotions finally leveled up enough to make the procs character-defining.
The character-building in this game is, eventually, the most rewarding I've ever seen in a game.  And, yes, I've played to max in PoE.  That's right, I think this is more rewarding.  The difference is that while PoE is more rewarding to tinker on paper, the playstyle and game-feel don't mirror the work put into materia, passives, and gear.  It still somehow feels... "sparse."  This game really nailed a missing layer to other games with its devotions, which do take until late game to really shine..
If you like ARPGs, don't judge this game early.  I know that seems a little obvious, but it is frighteningly cliche and dull for about 30-40 levels.  It's a poor game design decision that's hard to avoid for this kind of character-builder, but it's worth it if you're looking for the next clicker fix.
We'll see how I feel a year from now, but I think I've found my ARPG for the long term, for those nights where I really don't care to read or get immersed or risk adrenaline.  For when I just want to mash buttons and lay waste.  Good times

After a lot of thought, this still remains my favourite game. The feeling of running through buildings and jumping over rooftops is almost magical and has not been matched by any other game for me. The lighting, appearance of the levels and music is fantastic and increadably atmospheric, giving the feeling of true freedom of leaping across the dystopian City of Glass. Despite, its relative age now, the game still looks great and, partly due to its age, it runs incredably well and smoothly, even on older hardware.
However, the game is by no means perfect. The story and characters are lackluster at best and I didn't really feel any interest or excitment in finding out more - I only wanted to continue for the gameplay, not because of a drive to progress the story or save the characters in danger. The gameplay is also flawed to an extent. For a game about running freely over rooftops, it would make sense to make the game open world but instead the game is made of linear levels. Fortunately, in most cases, there are many ways to progress through the levels, allowing for better replayability as you try to find the optimum routes. The game could be better if these factors were improved, but they did not greatly negatively affect my experience.
The main problem with this game which does cause an issue, however, is its combat system. Firstly, in my opinion, I don't think the game needed offensive combat mechanics since the protagonist, Faith, is a Runner. It would make much more thematic sense for her to just dodge and run past attackers rather than stop and try to fight them. This is a strategy that can be employed most of the time but there are three times in the game where it forces you to fight. The first two sections can be somewhat avoided or minimised by following better routes but there is no way to get past the third section. These completely break up the enjoyment and faced paced action of the rest of the game as you are forced to stop and deal with enemies. The combat system itself is very poor so these sections are by far the worst part of the game. Disarming enemies for a not-lethal takedown (the combat method that seems to fit Faith's character best) is very hard, especially at first, as the trigger is slightly after when you'd expect. After my 8 or so playthroughs of the game, I am still not consistant at disarming enemies who kill you very quickly if you mess up, making me often have to try 10 or more times to get past the combat sections. The gunplay is mediocre and very simple, leading to combat sections feeling like they were added later to the game and didn't have enough development time.
Despite all of these flaws however, the increadble unique feeling that this game offers is unmatched by anything else and it makes me feel excited and in awe every time that I play this game even though I already know the best routes to follow and every level inside out. No other game has or continues to make me feel as thrilled every time I play it. I can't fully describe why I love it; it's just a very special and magical game to me.
Mirror's Edge goes on sale a lot and I've seen the price of this game go very low so if you have a spare few dollars, try it and see for yourself what an amazing experience running freely through the rooftops is.

So, before I start, I'll say that you should not ignore this review because of the hours of game I got so far. I have played and beated the game 3 times already in Xbox360, one of them in Hard and Iron Man mode, so yeah, I know what I'm talking about. Let's now start with the review:
XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a Strategy game based on the unforgiving and old-school game named "X-COM; UFO Defense", and "UFO; Enemy Unknown", it depends on where you live and what version you got. Is it loyal to the source material? I can tell you that ANOTHER GAME of the series is NOT LOYAL AT ALL (I'M LOOKING AT YOU, BUREAU, YOU PIECE OF SH#T), but this one is quite amazing!
First and foremost, it's the best strategy game you can get for consoles, just as great as Defense Grid; The Awakening or the old but yet amazing Advance Wars 1 & 2 for GBA, but way longer, and with a lot of replayability. The game also has decent graphics and sound, but a bit lacking in music. As usual, I will get the bad parts of the game out of the way first:
The biggest problem I got, is the IA. It's not that they're brain-dead (they do play Kamikaze at times), or too smart, but rather in a gameplay element that's flawed and makes it feel wrong: Enemies will notice you right away, most of the times. Not only that, they will instantly move, even when it's not their turn, 99% of the times into cover. Why is it so bad? Let me give you an example:
You're moving your last guy, when suddenly you find 3 Sectoids (weakest aliens in the game, along with the drones). But guess what, they instantly move and flank you, your turn is over, AND THEY CAN SHOOT YOU DOWN RIGHT AWAY! Infact, that's so much bullsh#t that there are mods to disable it on pc, but I had to suffer that crap on Xbox360 for too long, and let me tell you, THAT MECHANIC CAN GO DIE IN A FIRE. It ruins any sort of Stealth aproach, and goes down into "Start shooting the closest alien you see".
The other thing I hate about this game, is the random factor. Now, hear me on this one, it's well done in most parts: Each playthrough is completely different, specially with the "Second Wave" options...But then, you have the fights. Hitting an enemy or not is a matter of odds. Of course, flanking them gives you higher chances of hitting, and extra chances for a critical hit, BUT THERE'S STILL CHANCES OF MISSING A POINT-BLANK SHOOT. Not only that, I got crit-hit from miles away with plasta-pistols of some lone-sole hacking Sectoids, and got instantly killed. The random factor of battles might♥♥♥♥♥♥you off, but you can always save often and reload if the game starts to screw you more than life itself.
There's also a minor issue: The fact that the things that where not added in release, and other things they could not finish in time, are added as a huge DLC. The "Enemy Within" is great, of course, BUT IT'S ALMOST AS EXPENSIVE AS THE GAME! It does make the game twice as good, but you should wait for sales on it.
Now, the good things the game has: The game is balanced, and it both randomizes and goes further into the Human's comeback to the Alien menace as you go on. If you want to clear the game fast, you can. If you want to take it slowly, you can. You feel as the one in charge, because you are (until the game gets lucky and no-scopes your♥♥♥♥♥. It has a similar way of playing as the Fire Emblem games, where you can lose characters permanently, but also recluit new ones, or even build robots, F#CKING ROBOTS. The game is challenging enough to♥♥♥♥♥♥you off enough to go back and kill their families, it can last really long, some special missions are quite cool, and even has a multiplayer mode packed in, even though they could have added a Coop mode, or something, rather than just "Choose your minions and go murder eachother".
Right now, I got the game for free because of a give-away, and I'm doing an "Impossible" Difficulty playthrough, and let me tell you, for smart assh#les like me, it's not even hard at all, but I do recommend you giving the special difficulties a try once you clear the game for the first one. Higher difficulties makes the game as hard as Dark Souls on steroids (AND THE STEROIDS ARE ON CRACK), while the "Iron Man" mode will only allow you to have one save file, that constantly saves. So yeah, permanent choices, no "That was stupid, let's reload and forget it happend". You f#ck up once, that brave soldier is gone, for good.
I recommend getting the game along with the "Enemy Within" DLC on a sale. Infact, if you like strategy games, and you don't have this, you're one stupid motherf#cker. I give this game "A critical headshot through the map / 10".
Oh and, in my "Impossible" run, I haven't yet lost a soldier, and I'm almost at the first Alien base raid. So yeah, beat that mofos.

It is an interesting choice but certainly makes the game convenient to play. The rest is the usual stuff: the orc waves are getting more and more difficult and the player unlocks more types of traps. Oh, and of course, on later levels we have to look out for more areas as the enemies can approach our base from several directions.
If you are bothered by the fact that one single orc reached your base and because of that you lost a couple of points you are free to replay all previous levels for better results. This replayability and the dozens of available levels make sure OMD is a long-lasting experience. At the time of writing this review the game has a 75% discount and its GOTY edition certainly is a catch for just 2 euros.

Well, after 3.6 total hours of gameplay, I finally managed to beat the first stage -- as in, surviving it for 60 seconds. Maybe, if I'm really diligent, I'll beat the second one some day! The third... I'm really not seeing that.
.
is twitch gaming at its most distilled. The screenshots tell you everything really: your job is to rotate a triangle around a center point in such a way that it won't hit the oncoming bands of color heading towards it, going either left or right. That's it, those are all the rules. It's just you, the game, and your reflexes.
Calling
unforgiving is beside the point: it lives in its own universe of abstraction where concepts like "forgiveness" are utterly meaningless. It is definitely fair, though, in that you and you alone are responsible for success and failure, with failure just being a lot more likely. But oh, does every extra second you manage to survive feel like a wonderful victory.
Not recommended for people with photosensitive epilepsy or people who are easily frustrated -- for both categories, this game is a health hazard. Recommended for people who like twitch games, and at a sale, even for people who don't, just so they can remind themselves why they don't like twitch games.

The Banner Saga's biggest missed opportunity, in my opinion, is with the combat system. It's a very bare-bones system that adds nothing significant to the genre, and begins to feel quite repititive as you progress through the game and often repeat battles due to the game's high difficulty.
It's functional and all, but overall just feels competent at best, and ultimately disappoints, as a stronger combat system could really have propelled The Banner Saga into the realms of the greats. But overall, it's a solid debut effort from Stoic, and if you're a fan of this genre, is worth checking out once the price drops a bit.
The Nitty Gritty

You've seen my videos, right? If not, I invite you to scroll to the bottom and lavish in all that hand-drawn magnificence. The Banner Saga is, hands down, one of the prettiest I've seen in recent history. You'd think that Stoic would take every opportunity to showcase precisely how masterful their art team might be but they don't. The jaw-dropping graphics, which are evocative of 60s' Disney animations, are deployed with the precision of a brain surgeon. There's an attention to detail that makes me want to sit and drink in every frame. Embroideries are never just squiggles on the cloth, they're meticulously written into the fabric. Rings are obviously but understatedly ornate, horns embossed with the passage of a varl's years. (Bonus points: Stoic Studios didn't go for the low-hanging fruit by adding buxom Viking barmaids. The women? Happily realistic-looking. Kudos, fellas.)

A fun fact: I ordinarily play with games muted. I don't know why. I just do. Call it habit. I used to own a laptop with a busted sound card for the longest time. Yet, The Banner Saga's soundtrack had me so smitten I kept the game on for background music even when I wasn't actively playing it. What's most fascinating about it is the simple fact that there is so little of it to speak of. Long periods of silence, broken only by the clang of metal or the howl of the blizzard, alternate with the swell of wind instruments. Like the graphics, the fully orchestral score, heavy with intent, is gorgeous but not overwrought.
There's not really much to be said here outside of the fact that The Banner Saga plays out pretty much exactly you'd think something like this would: with the mouse functioning as your bridge to the world. Almost all of the sparse interface will be instantly familiar to anyone who has spent any amount of time with a video game. The only exception is the sometimes infuriating inability to change camera angles during battle.
> Rich and alluring lore
> Mechanisms battle though simplistic, operate
> Charming design and wonderful music
> Those who lament the books-games will be delighted with the game
> Poor content and cuts to interpretation and interactivity with the game
> Minimal character development
> Imbalance in battle but also the evolution of the game
> Preface Although reminiscent tutorial «normal» game.
Worth the buy ? Yes, in my opinion it is for what you get.

Start with this, I enjoy board games, yet never played Talisman, so not too clued in, but following the motions. so far it goes a little like this, you are limited to the outer track at first, and have to earn your way to the middle & inner track, encounters get a bit more difficult towards the middle. at some point along the way, you find the Talisman, which is the rights to beat the boss.
Roll a die, check the spaces for what you will encounter, move to the most favourable, might be 3 things on that space, some times you can choose what you encounter on that spot. this could be a item, or a chance roll or a battle. you might get loot, either way your turn ends once you resolve it.
One of these chance squares, you can get a gift from the Dark Gods, there are 6 results; 1-turn into a (useless) chaos spawn for 3 turns, 2-5 relate to each of the 4, you get a +1 to something, and a 6 - Power of a Daemon Prince (2 different stat points).
This is what I dislike about most digital board games., you would think it's one in 6; you have a d6 and 6 results., but no, it's about 1in3 chances you roll a 1. you will see more 1-3 that 4-6 on chance rolls, seems to me that chance rolls are 2x d6, keep the lowest.
In battles too, you and the AI enemy roll a d6, you might have skill 3 or 4 at the beginning, so skill+d6 is you combat score., enemies do the same, typically it's combat score result is one more than yours. your skill 4 will still lose against a skill 2 half the time (this could be the AI gets 2x d6, declares the lowest d6 if that would defeat you, or the higher)
Early game you lose the majority of battles, eventually the outer track should become easy as you gain modifiers my current game is at turn 44 and couple characters get to walk over some outer enemies for their modifiers/skill boosts..
It's a board game, it shouldn't need dice trickery to get an edge, the only dice rolls that feel fair are movement and against other players

One thing I'd like to point out, is that Telltale has been on point when it comes to soundtrack. Michonne is no different, and I believe their music choices are fantastic and suit the game very well, as shown in this, and their previous game, Tales from Borderlands.

Knights of Pen and Paper has its charm, albeit it is not well-maintained throughout the game. The dialogues are funny, the characters and classes available for selection are varied, and its simple UI design makes it easy to get into. There are many features you can play around with, like the ability to decorate your room with items that grant bonuses to stats, and trying out different party setups after you've unlocked new classes and players. You also get to pick and choose which quests to do. The experience you receive from completing quests is also scaled according to your levels, so doing the lower level ones that you missed won't be a complete waste of your time when you're level grinding.
On the minus side, the quests are fairly uninspired and they get repetitive. The battles eventually suffer from the same flaw as well. I only did the storyline quests and the ones that unlocked new classes. The story itself is also quite weak. There's nothing compelling or awe-inspiring to it. Having a great story is certainly not one of this game's selling points. Despite all the shortfalls, Knights of Pen and Paper can still keep you entertained for hours until the repetitiveness catches up and playing the game becomes more like a chore, where you're still playing because you haven't unlocked the other achievements yet.

I finally finished this game. Nearly 200 hours spent playing, and I have to admit one or two points along the way requiring a google for finding a little locking mechanism on the wall. Here's what I love: The Plot, the bosses, the loot, and the ability to craft inside the game. Here's what could be better: Blacksmithing, Becoming a merchant inside the game, the idea that not only are you on a quest but possibly engaging with these characters in the game world like some other RPGS.
Here's what sucked: Little mechanisms and figuring out the tricks of having to use that teleport device to get past certain points in the game. Having to use google to figure out the steps to do these things.
Here's what I think could have made this game better: Crafting didn't offer me a better way to have better equipment, you couldn't own buildings. You could only hire 2 companions, it would have been nice to hire folks. And albeit there was some great story line interactions it would have been nicer towards the end of the game for more interactions rather than just hack-n-slashin.

It doesn't matter what you do if the dice rolls against you, and the progression mechanic means that in the late game it is quite possible for one or more of the players to be completely unstoppable.
That being said, if you like Talisman and 30k, or like 30k and want a simple game to play to waste some time, I would recommend this game. It is also available on mobile platforms, where I think it is a better choice, as there is no advantage to playing it on the PC.

then, I started the campaign.
This game... Has SO MUCH POTENTIAL and it is already amazing.
The action in this game is more than just running around spamming skills at hordes of enemies or dull bosses like in Torchlight II, here the enemies are varies and have special abilities, you have to know your enemies, and you have to kite them (or build yourself a tanky character which is also possible, but still will require kiting and moving around in combat).

1. When your weapon has elemental damage on it (like fire or lightning) it is not visible on the weapon itself, only on attacks. I like wielding weapons with effects like they're burning or have lightning around them, just something I personnaly like and think is missing.
2. Some enemies feel unbalanced, for example: the "Fury" enemy is a tanky zombie with powerful attacks that has a chance of draining life on hit and shows up rather early in the game. With the help of HP potions they are not a big deal but at a certain point in the game they show up more often and in bunches which I find pretty hard to deal with. Grim dawn is a deep loot driven rpg, with a unique setting, and good atmospheric graphics running on a heavily updated and improved version of the titan quest engine. If you thought that developers won't invest in this style of game again, think again. Love has gone into this.
You start with a classes character, if you are a titan quest fan - you know the drill. If you do not, you start out without a class, think elder scrolls. Then you pick up an item, do some damage, and eventually you get some gear. By this point you will have leveled up and you can choose your class. Usually the player chooses something depending on what they have picked up, however you can choose something completely different and scour for items to match what you are going for.
Once you level up some more, you can choose a second class. Allowing for two to coexist concurrently - also like it's father titans quest. There are large number of class combinations. I don't find that every combination is satisfying, however most are at least interesting and fun to experiment with. One issue I have with the second class choice is that they are usually targeted at a specific item combination. For example, the soldier tree has many two handed skills, whereas the rogue tree has many duel wielding. That means you won't be able to pick the major skills in either tree. Since it's wasteful to be good at a two handed weapon and duel wielding skills. Unless you hotkey weapon switching. It's far better to just invest fully in whatever items you choose. Which means you are scouring the second tree for non-weapon based skills. It's not ideal.  However almost any combination you choose will be viable. And thats good enough. At least it represents freedom. If you want you can just stick to the one class.
The loot system is solid, although it lacks the "pop you got a legendary" sensation that diablo managed. The melee combat, while being weaker than magic, feels better due to the hitting animations being beefy feeling good on contact. This may make you want to play as a melee character even though magic is technically more damaging. A little more balance in this area would go a long way. That said, you need to take into consideration that this game still feels better to play at it's worst - than many action rpg's do at their best. It's just not quite as crunchy as diablo 3. This game's freedom of choice and depth of systems makes up for that. But clearly it would be great to have the best of all worlds. I find that visually the game can sometimes be a little bit over dark. And on certain monitors it may be an issue for players. VA panels in particular.
Overall, I think this game is great. I've spent 150+ hours in the game, and have only scratched the surface. Restarting and playing new builds before I even got to the second act. That's right, that's 150 hours of build experimenting and grinding. And I loved every second of it.
It's content rich. It's systems are deep. It's carefully crafted in many ways, without being as limited as diablo 3 yet not as free as sacred 2. Combat feels better than van hellsing and sacred 2, yet not as good as diablo 3. Although not that far off. And the world is more original than all of the mentioned games.

My friend and I have had the game crash multiple times throughout the game (Once on the LAST MISSION forcing us to quit the game for the Free Weekend), it's possible to make some missions unbeatable unless we'd do a Mission Restart due to the Super Powers being able to mess up vital parts of some missions, the friendly NPCs are abysmal when they're driving veichles as they crash into walls and buildings making us have to (Once again) restart the mission, there are some serious clipping issues as we've found ourselves stuck under the floor or in a building we're not supposed to get into, the whole thing is just a mess.

Horrendously good fun. My main grievance is that the Warmage (the protagonist) is a complete idiot and the game takes every opportunity to beat you over the head with that fact. The score system gives you an incentive to go back to earlier levels with your new toys and make orcs die in new and interesting ways. You can approach each level in a variety of ways, so if you prefer setting up a death alley and watching the carnage from afar you can do so. But if you prefer getting up close and personal with a blade whilst a tar pit slows your enemies down, that's a valid option. Later in the game you unlock 'Weavers', giving you mid-game temporary upgrades for your traps and skills which add to the number of strategies you can use.
I didn't have any technical issues with the game although on an older machine the game did slow down a little when a lot of enemies were around, but otherwise it runs well.
Overall I'd recommend it to tower defense fanatics as well as action or strategy game fans.

The original Wonder Boy: The Dragon's Trap was the first game I had ever played back in 1989, so naturally I bought the remaster the first day it was available. Had I looked into it more I would have bought it on the Nintendo Switch instead, since it's actually a pretty quick and easy game if you're familiar with the system and where to go. As one could tell from my currently short play time, it doesn't take too long to beat, but it takes longer when you experience the game for the first time, and don't conveniently remember all the secrets.
For fans of the original, the game was remastered quite well, charm stones were revised and now have hidden challenge dungeons, including one for Hu-man, they can be solved without much difficulty if you think about what weapons you have access to, and how to get around certain obstacles.
For anyone new to the game, if it feels like a 90's game, it's because it's actually an 80's game. It's a classic from the time, and if you like platformers it's a good way to spend an a few afternoons.
The controls are exactly like the original, which may not feel precise by todays standards, but they are as the game was originally designed, and once you get used to them they are not an issue.
The music and sound effects are quite nice in their modern versions, yet as a player of the original I preferred the older sounds with the new graphics. Luckily, the developers allow us to change between classic and modern sound or graphics any time, including mashing the switching graphics button to get it stuck with old graphics on one side of the screen, and new on the other.

Remastered versions of classic videogames are some of the trickiest things to get right nowadays. If a developer changes things too much, it may end up driving away the fans of the original game. On the other hand , if the developer plays it "too safe" and offer changes that are minimal to the overall experience, it will most likely be ignored by new audiences as well as most of the fans of the original game who may have wanted to see something new. Wonder Boy: The Dragon's Trap is a remastered version of the third title in the Wonder Boy series that appeared on the Sega Master System 8-bit console almost 30 years ago. And it is impressive to see a remastered game that looks so different yet so close to the original classic title.
The story is unchanged from the original title. After being cursed by Meka Dragon and turned into a "Lizard Man", Wonder Boy must travel through Monster Land in order to find the Salamander Cross and lift the curse. However most of the areas are guarded by a Dragon Boss who will curse you into a different creature after their defeat (a mouse, a piranha, a lion and a hawk. Each with their own strenghts and weaknesses!). This gives the game a certain "metroidvania" feel since some areas are only available if you have the correct transformation.
The most obvious changes are the game's looks and sounds. The game now features gorgeous cartoon-like graphics and backgrounds (not quite on the same level as titles such as the impressive looking "Cuphead", but still a joy to behold!) that still manage to stick closely to the cute looks of the original game. (every character on the game would make a great plush toy, even the bosses!)
The music and sound effects are worthy of praise as well. The music tracks are now performed with real instruments and some of the music tracks have been expanded or modified to fit better with the current background stage, yet they manage to stick closely to the original musical score. (in the original game, there was a single specific track that plays everytime you enter an enemy stronghold, in this version every stronghold plays a different remix of this very track that is close to the stronghold current motif such as the sunken ship or the japanese castle!)
For better or worse, the controls are mostly identical to those of the original game. Playing on a xbox 360 controller gives you more buttons for a more precise control than the original title had back in the day (the SMS control pads were a two-button only affair so this is apreciated!) Some of the newer gamers may find the characters somewhat heavy to control (small jumps and you can't stop on a dime) but this is close to the original design were timing and positions were key to beating the game!
Other gameplay related changes to take notice would be the inclusion of difficulty levels, an overhaul of the charm system (which is quite appreciated since this was nothing more than annoying padding back in the original game!). But the highlight would be the fact that it is possible to change between the original version and the remastered version of the game's graphics and sounds with the touch of a button at any moment! This feature alone goes to great lenghts in showing just how nicely the game's fundamentals hold up in gaming nowadays. Even, as a nice bonus, the old passwords from the original game still work!
It is important to notice that this game was never a long quest in the first place, and with the charm system modifications, it is even faster to complete. Also there are times where newcomers may have troubles to figure out were to go next, but this was a small issue in the original and is a small issue here as well.
Overall, I can't show enough praises for what the developers at Lizardcube have done for Wonder Boy: The Dragon's Trap to adapt the game to more recent times while keeping what made the game a SMS classic. Here's hoping that more remasters of such quality can make their arrival someday! (Alex Kidd in Shinobi World, pretty please?) ;)

Stories: The Path Of Destinies was a game that I enjoyed enough to get all of the endings on twice - once on the PS4 and once on Steam.  I'm glad that I played it and I give the game my recommendation, but it's extremely clear that the game suffers from some serious pacing problems and the multiple endings are mostly rendered pointless as a result.  You see, there are 25 endings in this game - 24 bad endings and 1 good ending - but you only
to see one bad ending in each of four categories to unlock the good ending.  If you play the game that way, the pacing is fine.  You'll unlock the few abilities you'll actually want to use, upgrade your swords and find some nifty gems.  Then, you'll beat the game and feel like you didn't waste your time.
The problems manifest for those who go for all of the endings.  When you beat the game 25 times, you have no reason to explore by your sixth playthrough.  You'll already have all of the gems and all of your swords upgraded.  You'll still level up, but most of the abilities aren't really useful once you reach a certain point in the game.  So you're basically just mindlessly running through the story.  The paths can be entertaining - the writing is often sharp and I really liked the characters - but they all lead to bad endings so it becomes an exercise in futility.  You can learn truths early on that should change the narrative flow of the game, but in most paths, you're forced to ignore those truths and just watch helplessly as Reynardo makes stupid mistakes and dies.
The gameplay is fine.  Having played it with both a controller and mouse/keyboard, I didn't have many complaints with the controlls.  It would have been nice to be able to move my character with the WASD keys, but I got the hang of the mouse-based movement fairly quickly.  Zipping around the map, slashing enemies and using elemental sword magic was enjoyable early on, but again, playing through the game 25 times is bound to make everything monotonous.  There aren't a great variety when it comes to enemy types and there are no bosses to speak of, which may disappoint some people.
But at the end of the day, I'm asked if I recommend this game or not.  I do recommend it, as I've said.  It's not a perfect game, but there is a great foundation here for a future sequel, should it actually come to fruition.  But even if this is the only Stories game ever made, it's worth playing even if you only do the bare minimum to get to the good ending.  The other paths are worth checking out as well, but you should explore them at your own pace and not hammer through them one after the other.  It's a fun game, but it grows stale over time.

What put me off at first was the combat system which is a poor attempt at an Arkham combat. It is spammy with no timings and with addition of certain power gem's that bypass some combat mechanics, you don't need to do anything other than left click. But the combat in and of itself wasn't the bigest issue.
True the combat system is not very good, but what made it extremely frustrating is the controll scheme. Everything (with exception of dash and hook) including your movement, yes you don't move with WASD as you would expect, is bound to left and right click and you can not change it. In fact you can not rebind anyt controlls at all.
Left click is your attack (hold for a grab). Hold right click is movement while right click + left click towards an opponent is counter. (Left click alone seems to work too though.) This immediately creates an issue with movement in combat. Since there is a 1 second or so delay before you actually start moving. So dodgeing before you unlock the dash is nearly impossible. To top it of your character often gets stuck on terrain or refuses to attack for seemingly no reason or in rare occasions enemy attacks take priority over your counters and you get hit. Which also seems to sometimes happen when you try to use enemies impaled on your sword as meat shields. All of this results in an unnecesarilly frustrating combat that gets a while to get used to.
At least as far as mouse and keyboard controlls go. It might work better on a gamepad, but since I absolutely despise gamepads I have no idea.
Once you unlock some of your skills, especially the double combo counter which in turn unlocks the ability to attack your enemies form afar and most notably the one-hit kill. The combat becomes a lot more managable.
There are a total of five enemy types that I encountered. Grunt, shield bearer, warlock, buffer and a suicide bomber. And while the shieldbearers require to throw enemies at them first, changing the combat a bit. You will soon get a gem that makes your sword break through shields and back we go to spamming left click against everything.
On the topic of enemies another issue is that there are no bosses. At least I have not encountered any in the several playthroughs I completed. Which is very disappointing. Every time you get to the point that you think you'd fight a boss the Narrator takes over and just describes to you what happened.
This is no fun, you might say. My thoughts exactly, but what made me come back to this game to replay it over and over was not the mediocore combat system. It was the story the game is telling, you make choices that affect the story leading you on branching paths and eventually to multiple endings that the game have to offer. Each time you complete a story it also affects the new stories that you will play. Giving you new insight, new comments from the narrator and unlocking more branching paths. The game was designed to replay it many times and while it does a good job at providing new content. It is not without issues.
You end up going through the same locations over and over again and eventually you will be hearing the same narrator commentary. They really tried to go for that Bastion feel here, but neither the narrator nor the writing is as good as the Bastions was. Biggest issue here is that you can not skip vast majority of cutscenes and dialog. And while I noticed that some maps allows you to skip certain parts of it once you replay it for the nth time. You are still going to have to run through and watch the cutscenes over and over.
While at first its not really an issue, since you are unlocking new swords that open various gates and new areas of the maps that contain treasure chests and intel. Once you unlock all the swords and gems. Which happened on my fourth playthrough for me, the only thing you will be looking for is intel for some backstory. Otherwise its all about rushing to the end of the map as fast as possible. Making this game best played in short sessions of one or two playthroughs at a time.
That beeing said picking different branching paths and trying to figure out what to do to get a good ending is satysfaying. After some of the playthroughs you learn "truths" which will help you make educated guesses on the decisions that you make (as well as unlock higher tiers of skills) hopefully making you into the hero that you want to be.
Graphically the game is pleasing to the eye with it cartoonish aesthetic, nothing to write home about though. Voice acting is good, there is only one voice actor. The narrator who does all the different voices for all the characters. But he does a pretty good job making unique voices for each character.
Overall it is an enjoyable game if you play it in short sessions to avoid the repetitiveness. Have a high replay value and as long as you look for a more story driven game rather than a hack and slash you should be fine.
